## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library, complete, uniform, convenient, economical, of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers, whether Latin or Greek, who flourished from the apostolic age to the age of Innocent III (A.D. 1216) for the Latins, and to the time of the Council of Florence (A.D. 1439) for the Greeks: a chronological reprint of all the surviving monuments of Catholic tradition through the first fifteen centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, compared with one another and with certain manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest care; continuously elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and various readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the completion of the most extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with ordinary or even analytical indexes following the individual volumes or authors of some importance; arranged with chapters properly set within the text itself, and with headings distinguishing the upper margins of the individual pages and indicating their contents; amplified with works both doubtful and apocryphal, yet possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched by two hundred and forty indexes, in every respect—that is, alphabetical, chronological, analytical, analogical, statistical, synthetic, etc.—presenting works, subjects, and authors, so that all the Holy Fathers may be accessible not only to the student but also to the man occupied with business, and even, if such there be, to the indolent and unlearned; but above all by two immense and general indexes: one, namely, of subjects, by consulting which one may see at a glance whatever not merely this or that Father, but every single Father without any exception, has written on any topic whatsoever; the other, of Holy Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers, and in what places in their works, have commented upon the individual verses of the individual books of Scripture, from the first of Genesis to the last of the Apocalypse: a most accurate edition, easily to be preferred to all others if one weighs the clearness of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently alike throughout the whole course of Patrology, the low price, and especially this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and little works hitherto scattered here and there, or even unpublished, but now for the first time brought together in our library from works and manuscripts belonging to every age, place, language, and form, and marvellously producing a unique work out of innumerable writings constituting Catholic tradition.**

**Latin Series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Tertullian to Innocent III. Prepared by J.-P. Migne, editor of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of the Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical science. Patrology, after the pattern of the Church itself, is divided into two parts, namely the Latin and the Greco-Latin. Both parts have now been completely produced. The Latin, comprising 222 volumes, is sold for 1,110 francs. The Greek has been issued in a double edition. The former includes the Greek text together with a parallel Latin translation, and, for the first series, does not exceed 104 volumes in 109 tomes. The latter provides the Latin translation only, and is therefore contained within 55 volumes. The second Greco-Latin series reaches only 58 volumes; while its purely Latin translation is completed in 29 volumes. Each Greco-Latin volume is sold for only 8 francs, and each purely Latin volume for 5 francs. In either case, however, in order that the buyer may enjoy the benefit of this price, he must purchase the entire collection, whether Latin or Greek; otherwise the size and the differing difficulties of each volume will entail differing prices. Therefore, if anyone buys, even complete but separately, only the Greco-Latin collection, or the same collection translated from Greek into Latin, he will then obtain each volume for only 9 or 6 francs respectively. These conditions will be applied to the later Latin Patrology series, presenting the Fathers from Innocent III to the Council of Trent. The Patrology consisting of manuscripts resting in libraries throughout the world, and likewise the Oriental Patrology, will be subject to special conditions and will be announced in due time, if time does not fail us for committing them to print.

# [Indexes of the *Patrologia Latina*]

[Col. I]

# Important Notice

According to one of the providential laws governing the world, works above the ordinary are rarely produced without contradictions more or less forceful and numerous. The Catholic Workshops could scarcely escape this divine mark of their usefulness. At one time their existence or importance has been denied; at another it has been said that they were closed or were about to close. Yet they have pursued their course for twenty-four years, and the productions issuing from them become ever more substantial and careful. Thus it seems certain that, unless events occur which no human prudence could foresee or prevent, these Workshops will close only when the Library of the Clergy has been completed in its 2,000 quarto volumes. The past seems a sure guarantee of the future, both as to what may be hoped and what may be feared.

Among the calumnies to which they have been exposed, however, two have been continually repeated, because, being the most fundamental, their effect entailed the greatest consequences. Petty and ignorant competitors have therefore persistently repeated everywhere, through their correspondence or travelling agents, that our editions were badly corrected and badly printed. Unable to attack the substance of the works—which for the most part are merely the masterpieces of Catholicism, recognized as such in every age and country—they had to turn upon the form in its most serious aspect: correction and printing. Even masterpieces, indeed, would possess only half their value if their text were inaccurate or illegible.

It is quite true that, at the beginning, an unprecedented success in the annals of typography forced the Publisher to resort to machinery, in order to proceed more quickly and furnish the works at a lower price; four volumes of the double Course of Holy Scripture and Theology were printed with the inadequate correction ordinarily given in printing houses to almost everything published. It is also true that a certain number of other volumes, belonging to different publications, were printed either too dark or too pale. But since those remote times machinery has yielded the work to hand presses; and the printing which issues from them, though not luxurious—for luxury would be out of place in works of this nature—is perfectly suitable in every respect.

As for correction, it is a fact that it has never been carried so far in any ancient or contemporary edition. And how could it be otherwise, after all the efforts and expenses we undergo in order to purge our proofs of every fault? The custom in typography, even in the best establishments, is to correct only two proofs and collate a third with the second, without having made any preparation at all of the author’s manuscript.

At the Catholic Workshops the difference is almost beyond measure. By means of proofreaders grown grey in the harness, whose typographical eye shows no mercy to errors, the copy is first prepared from beginning to end without excepting a single word. The first proof is then read against the copy thus prepared. The second is read in the same manner, while being collated with the first. The same is done with the third, collating it with the second; likewise with the fourth, collating it with the third; and again with the fifth, collating it with the fourth. These collations aim to determine whether any of the errors marked in the proof margins by the proofreaders in the office has escaped the correctors at the stone and metal. After these five full readings, checked one against another and in addition to the preparation already mentioned, comes a revision, often two or three; then the plates are made. Once the stereotyping has been completed, and hence the purity of the text has been fixed, a further reading is made from one end of the proof to the other against the copy; a further revision is undertaken; and printing begins only after these innumerable precautions.

Thus at Montrouge there are proofreaders of every nation, and in greater number than in twenty-five Paris printing houses combined. Correction there costs as much as composition, whereas elsewhere it costs only a tenth as much. Finally, although the assertion may appear rash, the accuracy secured by so much expenditure and care causes most editions of the Catholic Workshops to leave far behind even those of the celebrated Benedictines Mabillon and Montfaucon and the celebrated Jesuits Petau and Sirmond. Let anyone compare any sheets whatever from their editions with the corresponding sheets from ours, in Greek as well as Latin, and he will be convinced that the incredible is a reality.

Besides, these eminent scholars, more concerned with the meaning of texts than with their typographical aspect, and not professional proofreaders, read not what the proofs actually contained but what ought to have been there, their lofty intelligence supplying the faults of the edition. Moreover, the Benedictines as well as the Jesuits almost always worked from manuscripts, a perpetual cause of numerous errors, whereas the Catholic Workshops, whose particular role is above all to revive Tradition, most often work only from printed books.

The Reverend Father De Buch, a Bollandist Jesuit of Brussels, wrote to us some time ago that in eighteen months of study he had been unable to find a single error in our Latin Patrology. M. Denzinger, professor of theology at the University of Würzburg, and M. Reissmann, Vicar-General of the same city, informed us on 19 July that they likewise had been unable to detect a single error either in the Latin or in the Greek of our double Patrology. Finally, the learned Father Pitra, Benedictine of Solesmes, and M. Bonnetty, director of the *Annales de philosophie chrétienne*, challenged to convict us of one typographical error, were compelled to acknowledge that we had not estimated our perfect correction too highly. Among the clergy there are good Latinists and good Hellenists, and, what is rarer, very positive and practical men; well then, we promise them a premium of twenty-five centimes for every error they discover in any one of our volumes, especially in the Greek ones.

Despite the foregoing, the Publisher of the Complete Courses, increasingly conscious of the importance, indeed the necessity, of perfect correction if a work is to be truly useful and estimable, has for more than a year devoted himself, and is resolved to devote himself to the end, to a long, laborious, and costly undertaking: namely, the complete and universal revision of his innumerable stereotype plates. Thus each of his volumes, as it is put back under the press, is corrected word for word from beginning to end. Forty men are or will be occupied with this for ten years, and a sum no less than half a million francs is devoted to this important verification. In this way the publications of the Catholic Workshops, which already distinguished themselves from all others by the superiority of their correction, will have no rivals in this respect in any age or country. For what publisher could or would undertake, after the fact, labours so gigantic and so exorbitantly expensive? One must surely be deeply imbued with a divine vocation for this purpose, not to recoil from either effort or expense—especially when learned Europe declares that no volumes have ever been published with as much accuracy as those of the Universal Library of the Clergy.

The present volume is among those revised, and all those revised in future will bear this notice. Consequently, in judging the productions of the Catholic Workshops with respect to correction, one must take only those which bear at their head the notice printed here. We recognize only this edition and those that follow it upon our metal plates thus corrected. It was formerly believed that stereotyping fixed errors permanently, since a metal plate is not elastic. Not at all: it introduces perfection, for a means has been found to correct it until errors are extinguished. Hebrew has been revised by M. Drach, Greek by Greeks, and Latin and French by the foremost proofreaders in the capital for those languages.

We have the consolation of being able to end this notice with the following reflections. At last our example has shaken up major publications in Italy, Germany, Belgium, and France: the Greek Canons of Rome, the Gerdil of Naples, the Saint Thomas of Parma, the *Religious Encyclopedia* of Munich, the collection of declarations concerning rites at Brussels, the Bollandists, the Suarez, and the *Spicilège* of Paris. Until now, people had known how to reprint only works of short compass. Quartos, in which folios are swallowed up, inspired fear; no one dared touch them, for fear of drowning in these bottomless and shoreless abysses. But at last they have ventured to imitate us. More than this: under our impulse, other publishers are preparing a Universal Bullarium, the Decisions of all the Congregations, a general Biography and History, etc., etc. Unfortunately, most editions already made or now being made lack authority because they lack accuracy; their correction seems to have been done by blind men, whether because its seriousness was not appreciated or because expense was feared. But patience: a correct reproduction will soon arise, if only through the light of the schools that have been founded or will yet be founded.

[Col. I]

# Preface

> **Note:** [Col. I] The Latin and French versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.

[Col. II] At last we publish the Indexes of our *Course of Latin Patrology*, so solemnly promised and so eagerly sought by all. If the Reader has experienced any delay, let him not lay it to the charge of the Publishers, who themselves underwent it unwillingly. We hope, therefore, for ready pardon, particularly from those willing to weigh the magnitude of the undertaking, consider the strenuous efforts, the six hundred obstacles, the time required for so great a work, and the immense necessary expense.

For, since we offer two hundred and thirty Indexes drawn from the 217 volumes of the *Patrology*, it was necessary, in creating every single Index, to have each volume at hand, to turn over millions upon millions of pages, and, so to speak, to fix eyes and mind upon every word, so that everything might be set apart with the utmost accuracy for whatever special purpose was intended. This enormous labour, repeated two hundred and thirty times, amounts to an analysis of fifty thousand volumes of our edition. Bring forward, if you can find him, a man so learned and industrious, endowed with intelligence so acute and steadfast and a mind so discerning, that he can subject one of our volumes to analytical examination within fifteen days; even in eighteen hundred years he would not accomplish what we have completed in only a few. But that we might reach the goal more quickly, no fewer than fifty men devoted themselves to elaborating the work for more than ten years, and the desired results soon became available.

Yet because the beginnings of things very often falter in some respect, other men were summoned to review and correct the writings of the former workers; to complete what was unfinished; to erase what was superfluous and useless and clarify what was ambiguous. At last one man set his hand to this second collection, perhaps still carrying the defect of its birth—the defect, namely, of lack of unity—in order to unite what fitted together poorly and bring the work happily to its best conclusion.

Since this is so, may we not cry out: What are the twelve labours of Hercules? What are modern literary undertakings compared with ours? What are other typographical labours? Beside ours, childish trifles. Never has any work been so completely turned to the Reader’s use and brought forth in every respect. Among works hitherto published and enriched with very many indexes, two especially stand out: the *Great Library of the Fathers*, collected by Margarin de La Bigne, and the theological *Summa* of Saint Thomas, edited by Nicolai; and yet they possess only ten [Col. III] indexes. Our Patrology, however, has been pressed and crushed in every way like a grape in the winepress, lest even the smallest drop, so to speak, of precious liquid should escape.

What, then, should be said of the immense expenses with which we have been burdened? Since fifty men have laboured on the Indexes for ten years, even if each received only a thousand francs in annual wages, and this was repeated fifty times over the decade, we have spent five hundred thousand francs on this work, not even mentioning the printing expenses. From it we shall scarcely receive twenty thousand francs; but what is that to us? The financial wound is slight. It will be a great and sweet consolation to us that we have made the Patrology purchasable and accessible to all.

Indeed, beholding the immense mass of volumes, readers will no longer be frightened or discouraged; no one will complain any longer: “Who could ever explore such an abyss? Who can read through so many and such great writings of the Fathers?” Behold, we provide Indexes which furnish and show the method and path; now every mountain is made low, the valley is raised, crooked things become straight, and rough places become smooth roads. Nothing remains but to open the book and inquire. Access to the Fathers has been made easy and plain, no less than access to any alphabetical lexicon; and just as every word may be found in the latter, so likewise everything is found in the former without effort.

Thus our immense Course diminishes; distances become smaller; the first volume joins with the last. Certainly, each person may read those writers whom he most loves, and will not therefore be deprived of the others; for the Indexes will teach him what should be read attentively or cursorily, and what should be passed over altogether. How much time will thereby be saved! Rail and air travel yield place; we rival that force to which amber has given its name—electricity!

With what delight will the theologian or controversialist, preacher or professor, see at a single glance whatever the Fathers have written on this or that subject! With what joy will he immediately have at hand all the texts which contend for and favour his cause! How great will his authority thereby become! He no longer moves alone, like sounding brass or a clanging cymbal. He no longer invokes merely human dissertations, literary, philosophical, or theological opinions. He has as witnesses and supporters not one Father alone, but all the Fathers, or indeed every passage of every Father on the same subject; and thus, relying upon the tradition of the universal Church, he descends prepared for the contest.

He who lacks time need not read everything in order to find what he desires and collect what he has found; we have turned over and searched out everything before him and for his sake, and therefore indicate it by a sure sign. Yet if one Index does not provide what is sought, [Col. VI] let the Reader consult others treating of the same subject, and he will find it; for all things are presented by one Index or another.

For example, if you wish to address priests, an Index at once opens before you, reporting everything the Fathers have said about clergy both regular and secular; about priestly dignity and holiness; ecclesiastical offices and virtues; clerical learning; the vices and even the smallest faults to be avoided by a priest; etc. If the task of speaking to the faithful during the month of Mary falls upon you, then the sayings of the Fathers concerning the Blessed Virgin, from the Immaculate Conception to the Assumption, are presented to you in the Index concerning Mary. If you should wish to compose a thesis on the sciences or arts, twenty Indexes will immediately assist you, through which their origin and development over the course of years will become known to you. In a word, on whatever dogmatic, moral, canonical, or liturgical subject you may wish to write or speak, a reliable and lucid Index will immediately be at hand concerning every theological matter and its branches, near and remote, without exception.

But lest we dwell too long upon these advantages, which the reader readily understands, let us now briefly review the two General Indexes, one of **Subjects**, the other of **Holy Scripture**. They are of such great importance and possess such authority for accomplishing good, for nourishing the priest with the substance of Scripture and the Fathers, that, when inspired by the divine Spirit to conceive them in our minds, we might well have fallen upon our knees to praise God and return thanks to him.

Indeed, if these Indexes are considered, they will appear like the two Tables of the Law: the former resolves more intricate theological questions; the latter illuminates the more obscure intricacies of Scripture. The former provides perfect and complete theology; the latter the fullest and clearest interpretation of Scripture. The former recalls, in alphabetical, logical, analogical, and chronological order, whatever not merely this or that Father, but every Father, has written in his works on any subject; the latter, following the canonical order of the sacred Books, sets forth the various explanations of all the Fathers, from Tertullian to Innocent III, for every verse of Scripture, from the first of Genesis to the last of the Apocalypse.

If, for example, you wish to discover how many Fathers, how often, and in what places in their works, have expounded, commented on, or interpreted some particular text, even though you had devoted six hundred years to study, searched through everything, and consulted all learned men, this would nevertheless remain unknown to you; yet our Index will promptly inform you of it. Here Scripture, than which nothing excels in holiness, is explained by the Holy Fathers, who constitute the highest and most venerable authority among Catholics. Here every individual sense is set forth; and if you interpret otherwise, you incur the danger of error, for you depart and wander outside tradition. Hence we unquestionably provide the Reader with the best possible Commentary.

No one has ever been able to conceive such an Index, for the material from which it could be made did not exist: there was no complete and uniform collection to which it could be adapted. By our Course of Patrology we have filled this gap; the Catholic Church at last rejoices in having been endowed by us with her tradition; and this our universal Patrology, enriched here with these two Indexes, surpasses every collection. Let us therefore no longer wonder that a very distinguished man, professor of theology in one of the Paris seminaries, has said more than once that these two Indexes are worth as much as the entire Work.

Now let us explain the arrangement which we have followed in this gigantic labour, which we hand over to students of patristic learning. We have established two parts; and because a cause always precedes its effect and a principle its consequence, the first part presents general Indexes concerning Authors and Works, while the latter presents special Indexes on every subject: dogmatic and moral, liturgical, canonical, disciplinary, philosophical, historical, literary, etc., etc., etc.

But that the Work might prove at once more fitting and more useful to the Reader, we arrange twenty-four series, and in each series gather all Indexes of the same kind, though differing in species. Thus the first Series of the first part contains thirteen Indexes, through which all writers individually become known under every aspect, and each author’s volume and columns are specified. Since no collection has ever produced so many Indexes, we have placed first in this series an Index of Indexes. This Index, hitherto unheard of, may perhaps seem to some foreign to the purpose; yet we judged it wholly necessary. For it alone provides, in a single synoptic view, all the Indexes of the *Patrologia Latina*; and thus, with its assistance, easy access opens into the edifice which we are constructing of patristic learning.

Since this is so, let every Reader run through this Index attentively and completely; for whatever material he seeks, he will find other Indexes dealing with similar matters, although from another viewpoint. If he neglects this, he will lack very many aids available from the Patrology.

[Col. X] There follows a French Index of Authors, Works, and minor writings, arranged in the chronological order of our edition. We offer it in French because it acknowledges as its author the very learned D. Bonnetty, a man distinguished among Catholics and deserving well of our religion, who published it in his collection entitled *Annals of Christian Philosophy*. Next appear the alphabetical and chronological Indexes of all Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers—2,614 in number—whose works and minor writings, even the smallest, are printed in our Course of Patrology; the Statistical and Hierarchical Indexes, through which each author’s native country, diocese, order, rank of honour, and dignity become known; the Indexes of both Regular and Secular Clergy; of laypersons, both men and women; the Biographical and Analytical Indexes, through which both the lives and writings of the various authors become known; and an Index of modern writers who have illustrated the works of the Fathers by commentaries, notes, or dissertations, presenting a brief analysis of their studies.

With these Indexes serving him, every Reader will be able to learn who a particular writer is whose works he has desired to read; at what time he lived; whence he came; what dignity he held; how many, how extensive, and what kind of writings he produced; whether he departed from the orthodox faith; etc., etc.—and all this without even touching the volumes of the Patrology. Such is the content of the first Series of the first part.

In the second Series all Works are set forth in alphabetical, chronological, synoptic, and analogical order. Thereafter we place before the eyes all writings of both Regular and Secular Clergy, as well as of laypersons, and likewise anonymous, doubtful, apocryphal, or falsely attributed writings. In addition, we provide two Bibliographical Indexes. The former lists all editions of the Fathers and ecclesiastical writers published since the invention of printing and used in forming the Course of Latin Patrology; the latter specifically comprises writers who have treated the lives and works of the Holy Fathers and Doctors.

Finally, like a giant, rises the general analytical Index of **Subjects**, arranged alphabetically by matters and chronologically by writers. Moreover, like the crown of this series, there is added an Index of concordance between the two Courses of Theology and Patrology. In it we present in logical order the various arguments treated by theology, supported by the writings or more illustrious passages of the Fathers, indicating the volume and page of both Courses, so that a teacher or student, in constructing any thesis whatever, may have the assistance not only of theological [Col. XI] but also of patristic authors—that is, of nearly the universal tradition of the Catholic Church—without labour of his own, while benefiting from that of another.

The third Series contains only three Indexes, namely a complement to those preceding, in which are listed both pagan and Christian poets whose writings the Fathers have introduced into their works, as well as writers alien to the faith from whom the Fathers borrowed arguments in order to strengthen their own teaching, and whose virtues they sought to praise, and whose vices and errors they sought to criticize and combat. Such is this first part, comprising the general Indexes, of which the first volume consists. Yet it is, so to speak, only a preface to the Work which we commit to the press. Let us now proceed to the latter part, or special Indexes.

In this part we undertake, indeed, special Indexes on every subject. But among matters so numerous and so extensive, with regard to the reader’s benefit, we shall strive, so far as can be done, to attain a logical order consonant with reason. We here set this order before the Reader in summary.

Thus, in the fourth Series, which is the first of the second part, we set forth in succession everything which the Holy Fathers and ecclesiastical Doctors have written concerning God and his divine attributes; the unity of his essence and the Trinity of persons; Providence and its benefits toward humankind, both temporal and spiritual; Creation and the beings created in the beginning; good and evil Angels and their properties; the physical World, its duration and end; Man, his origin and double substance; the human Soul, its immateriality and immortality; human Reason, its excellence, power, and weakness; the earthly Paradise and the fall of the first parents, whose effects are transmitted to all human beings.

After this, in the fifth Series, we bring together everything concerning Sacred Scripture, insofar as it is the word of God and the foundation of all religion. First, we set forth whatever the Fathers have said concerning the inspiration, authenticity, and truthfulness of the Scriptures; then we add all the general commentaries; all explanations of the various chapters of each book and of the more noteworthy passages. Thereupon appears an exegetical index of all the verses, from the first of Genesis, as we have already said, to the last of the Apocalypse, according to the canonical order of the books, so that the reader may at a single glance observe all the writers, in chronological sequence, from Tertullian to Innocent III, [Col. XIV] more than two or three hundred, or even more, who have elucidated or commented upon this or that verse of Scripture. Moreover, indexes are appended on the Allegories, Figures, and Parables of both the Old and the New Testament; finally, the more distinguished men and women of both Testaments whom the Holy Fathers have mentioned in their writings are arranged alphabetically. Thus not even a single word, or iota, of the Scriptures cited in the *Patrologiae Cursus* will escape us; and if elsewhere we have promised labours more than Herculean, this series alone would discharge that promise.

Having thus far discussed the first principles of things, from which all things flow, as it were, from a most abundant fountain—namely God, Creation, and the Scriptures—we now, in the sixth Series, treat Religion in the broader sense: that is, insofar as it is a society between God and human beings, embracing their mutual relations, and consequently the rights of God and the duties of humanity. We treat divine Revelation to creatures, and its possibility, usefulness, and necessity; Prophecies and Miracles, together with their nature, marks or characteristics, and evidentiary force. Next we set forth the various errors which both pagans and philosophers have raised against religion, as well as objections both popular and scientific. And since the Holy Fathers, especially those who flourished in the earliest centuries, attacked these errors in polemical and apologetic writings, we append several indexes concerning them.

Christ is the foundation of the whole Christian religion; the Holy Spirit sustains and illumines it; the Blessed Virgin Mary protects and favours it. Therefore, before approaching this religion itself, in the seventh Series we provide indexes concerning the Incarnation of the Word and the Redemption of humankind: that is, we show Christ as promised and awaited, born, living, and suffering for the salvation of the world. Moreover, we add in alphabetical order the various names by which the Fathers designated the Saviour, and an index on the Name of Jesus—that is, on its excellence, power, and the miracles wrought by its invocation. Thereafter follow indexes on the Holy Spirit and on the Virgin Mother of God. The former recalls all the varied opinions of the Holy Fathers concerning the divinity of the Holy Spirit and his procession from the Father and the Son; concerning his gifts and operations toward humankind; and concerning his various attributes, names, and figures. The latter treats Blessed Mary and her life from her Nativity to her Dormition; her virtues and privileges; and the many feasts and titles by which Christians throughout the centuries have honoured the Lady of Angels.

[Col. XV] In the eighth Series we speak of Christianity properly so called. Beginning at its cradle, that is, at the time when the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, dispersed to evangelize the world, we follow it as it gradually advances through the various regions which it irradiates with its light; harassed on every side, yet, despite its enemies, wonderfully extending its benefits even toward its persecutors. Hence come historical, geographical, and bibliographical indexes on the Preaching of the Gospel and the Conversion of the Nations—that is, indexes alphabetically arranged by preachers, regions, and writers; indexes on the Persecutions raised against Christ’s religion by pagans, emperors, and the impious; on the Benefits of Christianity toward peoples constituted in society, toward the family and the private individual; and on the customs, practices, and so forth of Christians, which we present to the reader in this Series.

When Christ had established his religion and was about to return to heaven, he neither could nor wished to leave his disciples orphaned and tossed about by every wind of doctrine. Therefore, by his own authoritative power, he established the Church, upon which lay the burden of issuing commands and acting in his stead upon earth. Accordingly, in the ninth Series we diligently gather everything relating to the true Church of Christ. Thus, we first treat its origin, antiquity, and the four chief marks by which it is especially distinguished from others: unity, holiness, catholicity, and apostolicity. We contemplate its admirable hierarchy of both order and jurisdiction, and also the Supreme Pontiff, Christ’s vicar, Peter’s successor, the head and centre of Catholic unity, setting forth the constant tradition of the Fathers concerning his primacy and authority, both spiritual and temporal; concerning indefectibility, and so forth. Next we provide indexes on Cardinals, Patriarchs, Metropolitans, Bishops, Priests, and other inferior ministers, together with their different offices and duties. Thereafter we show the Church of God attacked by Heresies, rent by Schismatics, yet always unmoved, like a rock amid storms. We further enumerate innumerable saints and martyrs, and the sacred communion of intercessions, good works, and merits by which all members of the Church, united through one Spirit by the bond of charity, are gathered together. Finally, since ecclesiastical doctors and authors have always asserted Catholic doctrines in writing and defended them against heretics, we supply special indexes of these dogmatic writings.

The Church is the Mother and Teacher of all the faithful whom she brings forth for Christ; hence Sacraments and Graces are bestowed and received in her alone. Accordingly, in the tenth Series we include everything concerning these matters. [Col. XVIII] First we report the various opinions of the Holy Fathers concerning Grace itself and its connection with human free will: how it was attacked by heretics and most vigorously defended by the orthodox. We treat the Sacraments in general, both under the Mosaic and the Gospel law, and their number, power, and efficacy. Then we examine each separately: Baptism and its necessity, matter, and form; Confirmation and its excellence and effects; the Eucharist, insofar as it is both sacrifice and sacrament; the Sacrifice of the Mass, which is the distinctive and supreme act of the Catholic religion; Penance as a virtue and as a sacrament, with the parts required for it—contrition, confession, and satisfaction; canonical penance formerly practised in the Church; Extreme Unction and its effects upon body and soul; Orders, by which spiritual power is conferred, and the conditions necessary for them; Matrimony, with the duties and obligations arising from it; second marriages; polygamy. In short, we recall in this Series all matters pertaining to sacraments and grace.

Since the Church is the pillar, foundation, and guardian of truth, and that fountain to which Christ entrusted supreme teaching authority, and since her authority is the sole means capable of producing in Christian minds a firm and secure faith, she had to teach all the faithful what they must believe, do, and avoid lest they stray from salvation. Accordingly, she took care to collect briefly into one body the primary and principal articles of faith, and thus fashioned various creeds, which are a summary of the articles proposed for belief to all. Therefore our eleventh Series presents these creeds and the various professions of the Catholic faith to the reader.

Religion, as we have already said, is nothing other, in the broader sense, than a society between God and human beings, embracing their mutual relations, and consequently the rights of God and the duties of humanity. Moreover, humanity consists of body and soul together and, in this twofold substance, is bound to render itself wholly subject and devoted to God. Therefore, in order that religion might provide humanity with a manner of rendering to God the duties owed through the body, it established external signs, which are called worship. Accordingly, in the twelfth Series we treat external worship and its various kinds; the worship of saints, relics, and images; and the fruits flowing from this veneration. Thereafter, since the liturgy is the norm of worship and the Calendar orders the times and days of festivals, we set forth in two indexes everything treated by the *Patrologia* concerning these matters.

Finally, the Church, the society of those who truly worship God, was established and ordered by Christ the lawgiver, [Col. XIX] who granted it legislative power. Hence the Church’s twofold authority, human and divine; hence ecclesiastical laws require due submission and inward assent, and bind in conscience. Accordingly, in the thirteenth Series we present indexes on the legislation and laws of the Church; decrees of the Supreme Pontiffs; Councils; Canon Law; discipline, censures, excommunications, irregularities, and so forth; civil legislation insofar as it concerns religion; and the immunities and privileges of the Church of God granted by secular authority.

So much thus far concerning dogmas. But before proceeding to morals, we have resolved to place here indexes on the Last Things of human beings, which pertain equally to dogmatic and moral knowledge. Thus, in the fourteenth Series, there are successively completed indexes on death; on the particular and private judgment after death; on Heaven and heavenly blessedness; on Hell and the eternal punishments of the damned; on Purgatory and the suffrages by which the souls of the righteous detained there may be aided; on the worship of the dead; on Antichrist and the signs which ought to precede, accompany, and follow him; on the final end of this world; on the future resurrection of the dead; and on the general Judgment, at which all humankind together will stand before the tribunal of the supreme Judge.

Such is the plan and method we have attempted; and in fact our indexes thus produce a treatise on religion, presenting the constant tradition of the centuries to anyone wishing either to study or to defend it. Up to now, compendia of every sort and indexes of every kind, whether analytical or analogical, have been brought to light; but no one has ever attempted to compose from indexes a theological treatise such as we provide. Nor do we therefore suppose that we have achieved the best arrangement, although it is logical and easy to understand. Yet, with its aid, each person will be able to devise one more suitable to himself and, guided as if by a thread through the various numbers and series we have set forth, will not find it difficult to disentangle the complications. Let us now proceed to morals.

In the fifteenth Series we present all the works, or even shorter works, of the Holy Fathers concerning moral virtues and evangelical perfection. Hence there are eight indexes—alphabetical, chronological, and analogical—of authors and works, providing a concise analysis of each; to these is appended an index on Conscience, which is the dictate of reason and the inward rule of moral actions.

Since law is the principle and measure of acts, by which we are induced to do good and restrained from evil, we bring together in the sixteenth Series everything concerning Law, [Col. XXII] the Decalogue, and the precepts of the Church. Yet, lest our indexes grow too numerous, in the same place we discuss the Decalogue in general and each commandment of the Decalogue separately, carefully distinguishing one from another in order to avoid confusion and to assist the reader more usefully. The same method is observed concerning the precepts of the Church. Certain matters, however, of greater importance are treated separately; hence indexes on Love of Enemies and Forgiveness of Injuries; Almsgiving; Fraternal Correction; Festivals; Fasting and Abstinence; Mortification of the senses, mind, and heart; and so forth.

From observance or transgression of God’s commandments arise virtues or sins. Accordingly, in the seventeenth Series there are successively arranged indexes on the theological virtues—Faith, Hope, and Charity; on moral virtues; on the duties or offices of the regular and secular clergy; on continence and celibacy; on virginity and virgins; on nuns consecrated to God; on widows, kings, and so forth; an anecdotal index recalling the most outstanding deeds; another containing more memorable sayings extracted from the Holy Fathers; and the virtues which the Fathers have extolled among the heathen. The eighteenth Series sets forth indexes on sins in general, Original Sin, and capital sins; on vices alphabetically arranged; on homicide, duelling, and suicide; on simony and usury among clerics; on profane and unlawful pleasures, games, dances, and spectacles; and on the errors and vices of pagans which the Fathers attacked in writing.

Since no one can do good and turn aside from evil unless he relies upon divine mercy, it is necessary to have recourse to God in prayer. Therefore the nineteenth Series proposes indexes on prayer in general—namely, on its necessity, excellence, effects, various conditions, and so forth—and on prayers commonly used among the faithful in the Catholic Church: the Lord’s Prayer, the Angelic Salutation, and so on. So much concerning moral theology. Yet we have not reached our goal; a great road still remains before the work can become perfect and complete, so that no benefit to be drawn from the Holy Fathers may escape the reader.

Historical annals and sermons constitute a great part of the *Patrologia*; therefore, in two series, we gather everything pertaining to these. In the twentieth Series we place before the eyes indexes concerning historical authors and their various works; concerning sacred, Jewish, ecclesiastical, and secular history, whether universal or [Col. XXIII] particular; chronicles, and so forth; and indexes of abbeys and monasteries, making known their foundations, laws, rules, privileges, and monks more illustrious for holiness and learning. Furthermore, we arrange alphabetically dioceses, cities, and monasteries, now destroyed and surviving only in memory, with their names translated from Latin into French. Thereafter we add two biographical indexes, alphabetically listing the Lives inserted in the *Patrologiae Cursus* and their authors.

The twenty-first Series unfolds everything concerning the art of oratory, sermons, and homilies. First, the various opinions of the Holy Fathers concerning the ministry of preaching and its necessity, rules, and effects are recalled. Thereafter, a fourfold synopsis enumerates all sermons on Scripture according to the canonical order; sermons for the Temporal Cycle, according to the course of the year, from the first Sunday of Advent to the final Sunday after Pentecost; sermons on Saints, alphabetically by name; and sermons on Various Subjects, according to a logical and analogical sequence of themes. Homilies are arranged in the same manner. In addition, we provide a preaching index to the Epistles and Gospels read during the solemnities of Mass throughout the year, recording the various explanations, sermons, and homilies appropriate for elucidating each Epistle or Gospel. With the assistance of these indexes, therefore, anyone will immediately be able to ascertain at a single glance whether the Fathers treated a given subject, which Fathers did so, how often, and in what volume they discussed one matter or another. From these collections, then, as from a most abundant and perennial spring, one may confidently draw an abundance of material for sermons, whether less or more highly polished.

The twenty-second Series consists of only two indexes. The first comprises alphabetically all authors who wrote in strict prose; the second presents all their works, or even shorter works, arranged according to an analogical order of subjects and genres.

The *Patrologia* contains almost innumerable and highly important letters. But lest the reader, undertaking a burdensome and fruitless labour, should depart empty-handed amid such great and numerous riches scattered through two hundred volumes, we resolved to assist him. To achieve this, we distributed all letters into various classes: the first contains dogmatic letters, the second moral letters, the third canonical letters, and the fourth disciplinary letters; the fifth contains all letters treating any subject whatever, arranged according to analogy of subjects and the chronology [Col. XXVI] of authors. Moreover, alphabetical indexes follow of authors and of those to whom the letters are addressed, and another index of the same persons arranged according to the nation and rank of each. Thus not even the smallest letter will escape the reader in this twenty-third Series.

Finally, the Fathers and Catholic doctors have constantly and in every way laboured for whatever might shape the morals of peoples and cultivate a more civilized human life. For this reason they have always fostered the sciences, letters, and arts, in which most of them themselves became distinguished. Accordingly, in this twenty-fourth and final Series, we gather every individual index concerning sciences, letters, and arts; we are reluctant to enumerate them here, for they are already found at the end of the *INDEX OF INDEXES*, which we append with the titles of each explained, so that the reader may perceive what benefit is to be drawn from each.

After such solemn promises, we at last deliver to the public, which awaits them impatiently, the TABLES of our COMPLETE COURSE OF LATIN PATROLOGY. The delay that we seem to have caused will find a legitimate excuse in the eyes of the reader who can appreciate the immensity of such a work, the incredible difficulties we had to overcome, the almost incalculable time required by such an undertaking, and the immense funds that we had to advance.

Indeed, we provide TWO HUNDRED AND THIRTY-ONE TABLES for our Course of Latin Patrology, comprising 217 volumes. Now, in order to prepare EACH of these Tables, it was necessary to turn over and turn over again, to analyse from beginning to end, EACH of these 217 volumes; and this operation necessarily had to be repeated 231 times. This amounts to the analysis of more than 50,000 volumes of our format. Suppose that a person possessed judgment sufficiently rapid, vision sufficiently certain, and intelligence sufficiently broad to analyse one of our volumes within fifteen days: he would require more than 1,800 years to accomplish what we have accomplished in a few years. To achieve it, we applied more than fifty men to this work for more than ten years, and the result was obtained.

Nor is that all. After this first draft, which doubtless left something to be desired, other men came and took in hand the work already completed, in order to revise it, abbreviate what was too extensive, complete what was merely sketched, correct what was false or erroneous, and remove what was weak or superfluous. Finally, one man alone was charged with carefully and attentively examining all these disparate Tables, the product of different minds, coordinating and unifying them with one another in order to form from them a rational and logical whole, as we shall shortly demonstrate.

After all this, have we not the right to exclaim: What are the twelve Labours of Hercules beside our 231 Tables? What are all other literary labours? What are the Encyclopaedias of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries? What are all other typographical works? Children’s play, the greatest of which is nothing beside ours. We may say, without fear of contradiction, that no great publication has ever been so thoroughly worked over for the convenience of the subscriber. Indeed, among works which, up to this [Col. IV] day, have offered the greatest number of Tables, we know only Marguerin de la Bigne’s *Bibliotheca Maxima Patrum* and Nicolaï’s edition of Saint Thomas’s *Summa Theologica*, [Col. III] each of which nevertheless contains only ten. Our *Patrologia*, by contrast, has in some sense been pressed and tortured like grapes beneath the winepress, so that not the smallest drop of the precious liquor might escape.

[Col. IV] What shall we say of the enormous expenses we have had to bear? More than fifty men working on the Tables for more than ten years, even at the modest compensation of 1,000 francs per year for each man, amount to more than 500,000 francs, without counting all printing expenses. Yet these Tables may not bring us even 20,000 francs. But no matter: a wound to one’s purse is not fatal, and we shall have the consolation of having made Patrology ACCESSIBLE and INTELLIGIBLE to all.

Indeed, no one henceforth will be frightened by the sight of these masses of volumes. No one will be able to say: “Who will sound this abyss? Who could ever find time to study all these Fathers and read writings of every kind?” Our Tables have opened the way; they level the mountains and make straight the most tortuous paths. Nothing remains except to consult them. The study of the Holy Fathers has suddenly become as easy, as brief, and as certain as that of a dictionary; and everything may be found as readily as any word in an ordinary vocabulary. With the help of our Tables, this great Course becomes small; distances are brought together; the first and last volumes touch. Certainly, each person will be able to read his preferred Fathers, or a part of them; but he will not thereby lose those whom he has not read. Our Tables will indicate everything, and one will know beforehand what must be studied, what need only be skimmed, and what must be omitted altogether. What a saving of time! It is more than the railway, and even than the balloon: it is electricity!

How pleasant it will be for a theologian, controversialist, preacher, professor, and so forth, to see at a single glance everything the Holy Fathers have written upon a given subject. With what ease, with what delight, he will instantly find at hand the various texts that bear upon the matter he treats and strengthen it. What authority his words will then possess! It will no longer be individualism, or sounding brass; no longer human dissertations, private opinions—literary, philosophical, or theological. It will not be one Father, but all the Fathers. What do we say? Not only all the Fathers, but all the passages in each Father where the same matter is discussed! Thus one will proceed in every subject supported by the entire Tradition, applied not only to general doctrine [Col. V] but to every particular subject, and sanctioning it. One who is pressed for time will not be obliged to read everything to find what he wants; we shall have read before him and for him, and shall provide him with the precise indication of every passage he needs. If, nevertheless, a particular Table should leave something to be desired by the inquirer, since several Tables relate to the same object, let him consult them, and he will find everything; for everything is reflected in one or another of our Tables.

Thus, for example, are you a preacher of ecclesiastical retreats? You will find a Table that tells you everything the Holy Fathers wrote concerning the regular and secular clergy; the holiness and greatness of the priestly character; the virtues and duties of ecclesiastics; the learning required of priests of Jesus Christ; the vices and faults they must avoid; and so forth. Do you preach a Month of Mary? Consult the Table concerning the Blessed Virgin: there you will see what the Holy Fathers said of her, from her Immaculate Conception to her glorious Assumption. Do you wish to discourse on the Sciences and the Arts? At once twenty-five different Tables will come to your aid, showing their origin, progress, and successive development through the centuries. In short, whatever dogmatic, moral, canonical, or liturgical subject you may wish to write or speak about, you will have a Table on every object of theological science in all its branches, without any exception.

But, without delaying longer over the immense benefits our particular Tables may offer the reader, who readily understands them, let us say a word concerning our two great GENERAL TABLES: one OF SUBJECTS, the other OF HOLY SCRIPTURE. The idea of these two universal Tables seemed to us so felicitous, so powerful in accomplishing good and nourishing the priest’s word with the substance of the Fathers and Scripture, that, as soon as God favoured us with the grace of this illumination, we fell on our knees to thank and bless him for it. If one considers the nature of these two Tables, one will recognize that they are, as it were, the two Tables of the Law. For by the first one has the immediate solution to all theological difficulties, and that from the most competent judges; by the second the most embarrassing questions Scripture can present are resolved. That is to say: by the first you hold in your hands the most imposing and complete of theologies; by the second, the broadest and most incontestable explanation of the word of God.

The first offers you, in an order at once alphabetical, logical, analogical, and chronological, not merely what this or that Father, but what every Father without exception has written in all his works on a particular matter. The second gives you, according to the canonical order of the Holy Books, the various interpretations of all the Fathers, from Tertullian [Col. VIII] to Innocent III, upon each verse, beginning with the first of Genesis and ending with the last of the Apocalypse. If, for example, you wished to know by how many Fathers a particular passage or verse of the Bible had been commented upon or explained; how many times it had been treated by the same Father; and in what place in his writings this explanation is found: fifty years of study and consultation of all scholars could not inform you of it. Well, our Table will tell you surely and in the twinkling of an eye.

In short, this Table is the explanation of what we possess that is most sacred, Holy Scripture, by what we possess that is gravest and most worthy of respect in the matter of authority, Patristic Tradition. All meanings will be seen there; and if one interprets it otherwise, one risks interpreting it incorrectly because one would stand outside Tradition. This will therefore necessarily be the best [Col. VII] of commentaries. The idea of such a Table had never until now been able to arise in a single mind, because the foundation for making it was lacking: there was no complete, uniform collection capable of supplying its materials and to which it could have been adapted. By our Course of Patrology, we have filled this gap; we have endowed the Church with her Tradition, which she did not yet possess, although it was so necessary. And our two General Tables alone make it the most precious publication that can be conceived upon the two capital branches of ecclesiastical science. We are therefore no longer surprised that a celebrated professor of one of the seminaries of Paris repeatedly said that these Tables alone would be worth the price of the entire Collection.

[Col. VIII] Let us now be permitted to enter into some details concerning the course we have followed and the order and plan we have adopted in this gigantic undertaking, the result of which we deliver to the friends of patristic learning. First, we divide our work into two great parts. Because the cause comes before the effect and the principle before the consequence, in the first Part we provide all the general Tables concerning Authors and [Col. VII] Works; in the second, we bring together all the special Tables on the various dogmatic, moral, liturgical, canonical, disciplinary, philosophical, historical, literary, scientific, artistic, and other subjects.

[Col. VIII] But in order to arrive at a whole more satisfactory, more rational, and at the same time more convenient, we establish twenty-four Series, in each of which we group all Tables of the same genus, though concerning different species. Thus, the first Series of our first Part contains thirteen Tables, all treating authors in general and considering them from every standpoint best suited to make them known, with an indication of the volume and column where each author is found in our Course of Patrology—an indication common to each of the 231 Tables. Since no Collection has ever offered such a great number, at the head of this first Series we have placed the Table of Tables, or *Index Indicum*. It is without doubt the first of its kind since books have been made. Yet, although without precedent, it seemed no less necessary to us, for it alone has the advantage of showing the reader, within a very limited compass and at a single glance, all the Tables existing for Patrology. It is, as it were, the Key [Col. IX] to the Edifice we are now constructing.

We therefore urge anyone who needs a Table to read this one attentively from beginning to end, because, whatever subject he seeks, he will unfailingly find other Tables treating analogous subjects and completing his own. Without this precaution, he risks failing to know a considerable portion of the assistance that the Fathers can provide for his work.

Following this first Table, we give the French indicative Table of Authors and Works, according to the chronological order followed in our edition. We give it in French out of regard for its author, the learned M. Bonnetty, who inserted it in his *Annales de Philosophie chrétienne*. Then come the Alphabetical and Chronological Tables of all Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical Writers—in a word, all those whose writings, however slight, appear in our Course of Patrology—to the number of 2,614; then the Statistical and Hierarchical Tables, indicating the country, Diocese, rank, and dignity of each; the Tables of authors from both the Regular and the Secular Clergy; that of lay writers, men and women; the Biographical Table, providing a brief notice on each; the Analytical Table, supplying under each author’s name, in alphabetical order, an outline of his writings; and finally the Table of modern authors who have made patristic writers known through dissertations, commentaries, prefaces, or notes, with an analysis of their works.

In this way, and with the assistance of these first General Tables, every reader will be able, before even opening the *Patrologia*, to know what the author is whom he wishes to study; when he lived; to what country and rank in the ecclesiastical hierarchy he belonged; what are the extent and nature of his writings; whether he departed from the Catholic faith; and so forth. Such are the Tables presented by the first Series of our first Part.

In the second Series, we offer successively the titles of all Works in alphabetical, chronological, synoptic, and analogical order; those of writings by the Regular and Secular Clergy; those by laypersons; and anonymous, doubtful, apocryphal, or spurious works. We then give two Bibliographical Tables making known modern authors and works concerning the Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers; and the various editions of these same Fathers, from the origin of printing to our own day—editions which have contributed more or less to the formation of our Complete Course of Latin Patrology. Then comes the General Analytical Table of subjects, arranged alphabetically for matters and chronologically for authors. Finally, as the crowning feature of this second Series, we add a Concordance Table between our Course of Theology and our Course of Patrology. That is, we offer, in a logical order, the principal subjects treated in the Course of Theology, strengthened and elucidated by the writings or passages of the Fathers on the same subject, taking care to indicate equally the [Col. XII] volume and page of each of the two Courses where the matter is treated. In this way, with our Table, the teacher or student of Theology preparing a thesis will have [Col. XI] at hand not only the theologians of the great Course, but also all patristic writers—that is, the almost universal Tradition of the Catholic Church—and this without any labour except that of adapting to their own work a labour undertaken before them, but for them.

[Col. XII] In the third Series, we provide three Tables which are, as it were, the complement of those preceding them, and which acquaint the Reader with the Christian Poets and the Pagan Poets whom the Fathers cited in their writings, as well as with the various secular authors from whom they borrowed certain arguments to strengthen their own doctrine, whose virtues they praised, and whose vices or errors they censured and opposed. Such is the plan that we have followed in the three Series of our first Part, comprising the General Tables which form our first volume. Yet this is, so to speak, only the Introduction to the work that we publish and that constitutes the subject of our second Part, or the 203 special Tables.

[Col. XII] In this second Part, indeed, we take up the Tables particular to each subject. But amid such a great abundance of materials, in order to obtain a truly useful result, we have had to adopt, as far at least as possible, a natural and logical order in the arrangement [Col. XI] of all these Tables. It is this order followed by us that we wish to make known to the Reader, by giving a brief outline of it in a short analysis.

[Col. XII] Thus, in our fourth Series, which is the first of this second Part, we present successively to the Reader’s mind all that the Holy Fathers and ecclesiastical authors have written concerning God and His various attributes; concerning the unity of His essence and the Trinity of His Persons; concerning His Providence in the temporal as in the spiritual order; concerning the work of Creation and its admirable effects; concerning good and evil Angels, their fall or perseverance, their beneficial or harmful influences upon other creatures; concerning the visible World, its governance, its duration, its end; concerning Man, his origin, his twofold substance; concerning the spiritual and immortal Soul, its greatness and lofty destinies; concerning human Reason, its excellence and weakness. Then, [Col. XI] transporting ourselves into the earthly Paradise where our first parents were placed after their creation, we witness their temptation, their disobedience, and the punishment which followed it and which still reverberates even to us.

[Col. XII] Following these first truths, we pass to Holy Scripture, which, being the word of God and the foundation of our Religion, here finds its natural place. Thus, in our fifth Series, we set forth all that the Holy Fathers have written concerning the Inspiration, Authenticity, and Truthfulness of the Holy Scriptures. We provide all the Commentaries on each Book, each Chapter, and even each Verse, beginning, as has been said, with the first of Genesis and ending with the last of the Apocalypse, taking care to observe the canonical order of the Bible. Thus, with the aid [Col. XIII] of this final Table, the Reader will see at a single glance, and in chronological order, from Tertullian to Innocent III, all the writers—sometimes numbering several hundred—who have explained, commented upon, or paraphrased this or that verse of the Holy Books. Next come the Tables of Allegories, Figures, and Parables, both of the Old and the New Testament; then two further Tables, which present in alphabetical order the chief persons of these same Testaments of whom the Fathers have spoken in their writings. In view of this, we do not hesitate to say that there will not be a single word in the 217 volumes of the Latin Patrology relating to Holy Scripture which has not found a place in this Series; and if elsewhere we have ventured to announce a Herculean task, this Series alone would furnish the clearest proof of it.

After these principal points, from which all else flows—God, Creation, the Scriptures—we treat, in our sixth Series, matters concerning Religion in general: that is, the relations of God to humankind and of humankind to God; Revelation, its necessity and its certainty; Prophecies, their possibility, nature, and importance; Miracles, both under the Old Law and under the New Law, and their evidentiary force in support of the Religion for which they were wrought. We then attack the various Errors raised against Religion by Pagans, Philosophers, and the Impious; we gather together the different Objections, both learned and popular, forged against its Dogmas and beliefs, indicating the refutations of the writers who fought them. Finally, since the Fathers, and especially those of the first centuries, constantly rose up against all these errors in both their Polemical and Apologetic works, we conclude this sixth Series with the Tables relating to these two kinds of writings.

Jesus Christ is the cornerstone of the Christian Religion; the Holy Spirit is its support and its Light; the Blessed Virgin is its sure Protectress. Therefore, before speaking of Christianity, we present in our seventh Series the Tables relating to the Incarnation of the Word and to the Redemption of humankind; that is, we show Jesus Christ promised and awaited, born, living, suffering, and dying for the salvation of the world. To this first Table we add, as its necessary complement, an alphabetical list of all the Names given by the Fathers to the Saviour of humankind; then the Table on the holy Name of Jesus, in which we demonstrate the efficacy and power of this divine Name on behalf of those who invoke it, and the miracles wrought by that invocation alone. In the Table on the Holy Spirit, we treat of His divinity, His Procession from the Father and the Son, His Gifts, and His various Operations on behalf of humankind. In that on the Blessed Virgin, we gather all that the Holy Fathers have written concerning the Mother of God: from her birth on earth to her assumption into Heaven; concerning her life, her Virtues, her sufferings, her Glory, her Prerogatives, her Feasts; and the particular names which [Col. XV] Christians of all centuries have delighted to give her—in a word, all that the Patrology contains concerning the Queen of Heaven.

[Col. XVI] With our eighth Series, we enter Christianity properly so called. We take it at its cradle: that is, at the point when the Apostles, after receiving the Holy Spirit, disperse to proclaim the Good News; we follow it in its successive developments and through the different lands in which it bears its brilliant light. Hence come an alphabetical Table of Preachers from the Apostles onward; an alphabetical Table of the Countries evangelized, and of the Fathers who recorded their history in their writings. We next depict this Religion of Christ as assailed by Pagans, Emperors, and Unbelievers, yet made fruitful by the very blood of its Martyrs; as overrunning the world and, despite all the fury exerted against it, spreading its innumerable benefits among societies, families, and individuals through its institutions, through [Col. XV] its precepts, and especially through the pure morals that it knows how to inspire in its disciples, or through the evangelical counsels whose practice it teaches.

[Col. XVI] Jesus Christ, after laying the first foundations of His Religion and being about to leave the world, could not and would not leave His Disciples orphaned, exposed to be tossed about by every wind of doctrine. He therefore established an Authority which was to represent Him on earth and continue there His divine Mission. This Authority, entrusted with His powers, is the Church. In our ninth Series, therefore, we treat of the true Church of Jesus Christ: of its origin, its antiquity, and the striking marks which distinguish it from all those that are not it—namely, its Unity, its Holiness, its Catholicity, and its Apostolicity. We then contemplate its admirable Hierarchy: first in the Pope, whom we regard as the Vicar of Christ, the successor of Saint Peter, the Head and Centre of Catholic Unity, the source of all jurisdiction, etc., recalling the views of the Fathers concerning his indefectibility and his spiritual and temporal authority; then in Cardinals, Patriarchs, Primates, Metropolitans, Bishops, Priests, and other inferior ministers. We show it constantly attacked by Heresies, torn by Schisms, yet ever standing, unmoved like a rock amid storms. We see it triumphant in its Saints and Martyrs, and full of solicitude in the Relations which it establishes between all the members composing it in this land of exile. Finally, since the Church owes its victories over Heresies to the various writings of the Doctors and Fathers who defended its teaching, we conclude this Series with the Tables relating to the Dogmatic Works contained in the Patrology.

In instituting His Church, Jesus Christ willed that it should be the common Mother of all the Faithful, the true and sole dispenser of the Sacraments and of Graces. Accordingly, in [Col. XVII] our tenth Series, we bring together all that is connected with these two points. We first show, according to the Holy Fathers, what Grace is in itself; how it is reconciled with human free will; in what manner it has been attacked by Heretics; and who have been its most zealous and intrepid defenders. We treat of the Sacraments in general, under the Old as under the New Law, of their number and their efficacy. We then take up each Sacrament in particular: Baptism—its necessity, matter, and form; Confirmation—its excellence and effects; the Eucharist, considered under the twofold aspect of sacrament and sacrifice; Sacrifice in general, and in particular the Sacrifice of the Mass, which is the greatest and most solemn act of the Catholic Religion; the sacrament of Penance, with its three essential parts, Contrition, Confession, and Satisfaction. In passing, we cast a rapid glance at public penance, once practiced in the Church; we then present Extreme Unction and its bodily and spiritual benefits; Orders, their effects and the dispositions necessary to receive them; Marriage and the obligations it imposes; second marriages and Polygamy. In a word, in this Series we group together all that relates to Grace and the Sacraments.

The Church is not only the dispenser of the Sacraments and Graces; it is also the Guardian of truth. It alone is charged with teaching and spreading it. By this title and in this capacity, it must preserve the Faithful from every error and provide them with an easy means of learning and retaining its principal Dogmas, knowledge and faith in which are indispensable to salvation. In order to fulfill this twofold mission, the Church formulated its beliefs and reduced them to different articles which it set down in its Creeds. These Symbols proposed or accepted by the Church, together with the various Professions of faith, form the subject matter of this eleventh Series.

As we have already said, Religion consists especially in the relations of God to humankind and of humankind to God. Man is composed of body and soul, and in this twofold substance he owes himself wholly to God. To answer these two obligations of the creature toward the Creator, Religion has necessarily had to express itself through outward signs, and these signs constitute what is called Worship. In our twelfth Series we concern ourselves with everything relating to outward Worship, considered in its various forms; we treat of the Worship of Saints, Relics, and Images, and of the innumerable and miraculous favours obtained through their intercession. Then, since the Liturgy is the rule of Worship and the Calendar determines the dates of its principal solemnities, we gather in two special Tables all that the Holy Fathers have written concerning the Liturgy, the Calendar, the ecclesiastical Year, Computation, etc.

Finally, the Church is a true Society instituted by God, and in that capacity [Col. XX] it has received from Him all the authority necessary to establish the laws by which it is governed and to enact Decrees to which its subjects must submit and obey. In our thirteenth Series, therefore, we gather together all that concerns ecclesiastical Legislation: Papal Bulls, Councils, Canon Law, Discipline, Censures, Excommunications, Irregularities, etc.—in a word, all that pertains to ecclesiastical Legislation. We also discuss civil Legislation in everything touching the Christian Religion, as well as the Immunities and Franchises granted to the Church of God by secular and political authority.

Such is our work on Dogma. But before leaving it to pass to Morals, we have thought it proper to place here, as in the most suitable place, everything concerning the Last Ends of humankind, which pertain alike to Dogma and to Morals, of which they are the foundation and sanction. Thus, in our fourteenth Series, we provide all the Tables on Death and its certainty; on the particular Judgment and its consequences; on Heaven and its joys; on Hell and its torments; on Purgatory and its expiations; on relief to be provided for suffering souls; on the Worship of the dead, ever practiced in the Church; on Antichrist and what must precede, accompany, and follow his coming; on the End of the present world; on the Resurrection of bodies and the general Judgment at the end of time.

In this way, and thanks to the course we have followed, our Tables form a genuine Treatise on Religion, and we thereby supply the sanction of the Christian centuries to anyone wishing to study and defend it. Until now, Tables of every kind and analyses of every sort have been made, but no one had ever conceived the idea of forming, out of Tables, a Treatise on Theology; and that is what results from our work. Undoubtedly, we do not have the vain pretension of believing that the order we have adopted is the best; but at least we believe it simple and logical, and with its assistance the Reader may arrange another that he judges more in harmony with his own ideas and more convenient [Col. XIX] for his use. With the aid of our Series and ordinal numbers, he will always readily find his way amid all our Tables. Let us now see what we have done for Morals.

[Col. XX] First, in our fifteenth Series, we begin by making known all the Treatises and writings of the Holy Fathers that relate especially to Morals in general; we then provide all those concerning Asceticism, which is its most sublime and touching part. Hence eight different Tables, presenting in alphabetical, analogous, and chronological order all the [Col. XIX] Authors and all the Works relating to these two points. We add to them the Table of Conscience, which is, as it were, the basis of all that follows.

[Col. XX] The Commandments are the principle and rule of Christian Morals: through them we know the Evil that we must avoid and the [Col. XXI] Good that we must practice. In our sixteenth Series, therefore, we establish all that concerns the Decalogue and the Commandments of the Church. But in order to avoid an excessive multiplicity of titles, we treat in a single Table of the Decalogue in general and of each Commandment in particular, taking care nevertheless to arrange them successively in their proper order, in order to spare the Reader searches. We act in the same way with the Commandments of the Church, so that these two Tables contain a good many others. Yet, because certain points seemed to us too important to be included in these two general Tables, we treat separately of Love of enemies and Forgiveness of injuries, Almsgiving, and Fraternal correction; then of Feasts, Fasting, and Mortification of the senses, mind, and heart.

From the observance or violation of the Commandments flow Virtues and Duties, Sins and Vices. In our seventeenth Series, therefore, we present all the Tables on the theological Virtues—Faith, Hope, and Charity; on the moral Virtues; on the Virtues and Duties proper to ecclesiastics, regular as well as secular; on Celibacy; on Virginity and Christian Virgins; on the obligations of Widows, the Rich, Kings, etc. We then provide a Table recounting the fine Examples and noble instances of virtue supplied by Ecclesiastical History in the Patrology; another presenting the finest Sentences drawn from the Fathers; and one concerning the virtues which they praised in secular authors. In our eighteenth Series, we treat of Sins in general; Original Sin; Capital Sins; Duelling and Suicide; Simony and Usury; unlawful Diversions—games, spectacles, dances, songs, etc. We also provide a general alphabetical Table of Vices and Passions, and another on the vices peculiar to Pagans censured by the Fathers.

Finally, since by ourselves we are incapable of doing good and avoiding evil, we must have recourse to God through Prayer. Accordingly, in our nineteenth Series we provide a Table on Prayer in general, in which we demonstrate its necessity, importance, efficacy, and the dispositions it requires, etc.; then those on the particular prayers most commonly used in Christianity: the Lord’s Prayer, the Angelic Salutation, etc. Such is the equally rational and logical order which we have followed for Morals. But our task is not yet completed.
