Let us now show what we have thought necessary to add to all that precedes, in order to make our work complete and to leave nothing out of all the resources of every kind that the Patrology presents.

History and Sermons occupy a broad place in Latin Patrology; we have therefore devoted a particular Series to each of these two subjects. Thus, in our twentieth Series, the Reader will see unfolded before his eyes the Tables of historical Works: those of the general [Col. XXIV] history of peoples; of Sacred history in particular; of the history of the Jews, with their laws and misfortunes; of general Ecclesiastical history; and of histories particular to each country—that is, of all the chronicles left to us by tradition. Next come the Tables of Religious Orders, with the account of their foundation and the names of the monks who became most famous; and that of Monasteries, with the legacies and donations made in their favour. Then, for the Reader’s greater convenience, we provide [Col. XXIII] in Latin and French an alphabetical Table of episcopal Cities, Abbeys, and Monasteries which, now destroyed, exist for the most part only in historical memory. We conclude this Series with two Biographical Tables making known the particular Lives included in the Patrology, as well as the writers who transmitted them to posterity.

Our twenty-first Series contains everything relating to sacred Eloquence, Sermons, and Homilies. We first provide a Table recording all that the Fathers wrote concerning Preaching—its necessity, rules, and effects. We then divide all Sermons into four great parts: on the Scriptures, following the canonical order of the Holy Books; on the Time of the year, from the first Sunday of Advent to the last after Pentecost; on the Saints, in alphabetical order; and on various subjects arranged analogically according to the logical order of matters. We proceed in the same way for Homilies. Finally, we add two Tables in which we adapt Sermons and Homilies to the Epistles and Gospels of each Sunday of the year, so that, with the aid of the Tables contained in this Series, the Reader will be able to know in an instant whether a subject he desires and may need is treated in the Patrology; by which Fathers or writers it has been treated; how many times it has been treated; and in what volume and at what column it may be found. This will bring an immense advantage and great saving of time to every Preacher who consults us. It will be, [Col. XXIII] we do not doubt it in the least, a genuine Dictionary of the Pulpit, a fertile and inexhaustible Repository in which every Christian orator will gladly and without fear of error seek ready-made materials for his most solemn as well as his simplest discourses.

[Col. XXIV] In our twenty-second Series, we gather together everything relating to works in verse, and provide a general alphabetical Table of all Poets and a general analogous Table of Works arranged according to the logical order of subjects.

Letters or Epistles are very numerous in the Patrology, and often treat very important matters; but scattered as they are through the 217 volumes of our Course, how will the Reader, amid such an overabundance, direct his researches and make use of the precious resources that they can furnish in many circumstances? Here again, we have wished to spare him work that is at once long and tedious. To achieve [Col. XXV] our aim more surely, we divide all these Letters into four distinct classes: Dogmatic Letters; Moral Letters; Canonical Letters; Disciplinary Letters. In a fifth class, we gather all those relating to various other subjects, taking care to establish an analogous order for subjects and a chronological order for writers. We go further still: not only do we provide an alphabetical Table of the authors of all these Letters, but we also add an alphabetical Table of the persons to whom they were addressed; and in a third Table we distribute them according to the various countries to which these same addressees belonged. Thus, no Letter of any importance whatever can escape the Reader.

Finally, the Fathers and ecclesiastical writers have always shown themselves favourable to Sciences, Letters, and the Arts; several have even cultivated them successfully. In our twenty-fourth and final Series, therefore, we provide all that relates to these three branches of human knowledge, thereby showing also that everything touching Civilization, Education, and Letters was treated by the doctors of Catholicism. This Series contains twenty-four Tables on the Sciences and Arts, and concludes the work we have undertaken. We refrain from enumerating them here: the Reader will see their detailed titles at the end of the TABLE OF TABLES following this Dissertation. We shall now place before the Reader the list of all our Tables, in the order in which we have published them. With the aid of this list and of the explanatory title of each Table, he will know and assess in advance the assistance they can furnish for his particular studies, whatever their nature may be.

[Col. XXV]

TABLES OF THE COMPLETE COURSE OF PATROLOGY. FIRST PART.—GENERAL TABLES. *INDICES PATROLOGIAE CURSUS COMPLETI* [Indexes of the Complete Course of Patrology].

[Note: [Col. XXV] The Latin and French versions of the following document are printed in parallel in Migne.]

FIRST PART.—GENERAL INDEXES.

FIRST SERIES. INDEX OF INDEXES AND GENERAL INDEXES OF AUTHORS.

[Col. XXVI]

1. Index of Indexes, that is, setting forth in logical order every individual Index of the Latin Patrology according to the sequence in which they are published, together with an expanded title of each Index, as follows:

2. An Index written in the French language, enumerating, according to the chronological order of our Edition, all writers and their works, and showing how many volumes each author occupies, at what price he is sold, in what year he was published, etc.

3. A general Alphabetical Index of all the Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical Writers, numbering 2,614, whose Works and Opuscula, even the smallest, are printed in our Course of Patrology, giving the volume and column for each one (a practice, moreover, observed in all the Indexes).

4. A general Chronological Index of the same, displaying before the eyes the chain of Catholic tradition continuously connected through the individual centuries and almost through individual years, from Tertullian to Innocent III.

5. A general Statistical Index, in which all Patristic writers are properly arranged according to their importance and rank, their status and condition, their nation and homeland, etc.

6. A Statistical Index of the same, arranged in a new order: namely, one in which every writer is assigned to his own Diocese, and in which the various nations and the Dioceses of each nation are arranged alphabetically.

7. A Hierarchical Index of the same, assigning the rank of each, from the Supreme Pontiff to the lowest cleric, arranged in analogous order, but preserving within that analogy both alphabetical and chronological order.

8. An alphabetical Index of all Authors who flourished in learning within the regular Order and state.

9. An alphabetical Index of all Authors who, established in the secular Clergy, became distinguished through works and various writings.

10. An alphabetical Index of all lay Writers, men as well as women, whose Works or least Opuscula are listed in our Course of Patrology.

11. An Index of modern Writers who have elucidated the Works of the Holy Fathers by Prolegomena, Dissertations, Annotations, or Commentaries, and whose writings are found in this Course of Patrology; arranged alphabetically and providing a brief analysis of their studies.

12. A Biographical Index of all Authors of Latin Patrology, arranged alphabetically and presenting concise chronological information concerning each one.

13. An Analytical Index of Authors, arranged alphabetically by name and furnishing the Reader with a concise summary of each author’s Works.

SECOND SERIES. GENERAL INDEXES OF WORKS.

14. A general Alphabetical Index of all Works and Opuscula collected in our Course of Latin Patrology, arranged according to the title assigned to each.

15. A general Chronological Index of the same Works, with the name, age, and standing of each author appended, from the first to the last of the volumes, according to the order adopted in our Edition.

16. A general Synoptic Index of Works, or universal survey of the subjects which the Holy Fathers have expounded according to the sequence and order of the various sciences and which are recorded in the Course of Patrology.

17. A general Analogous Index of the same, setting forth in logical order all Works and Opuscula of the same kind, collected under one and the same title.

[Col. XXX]

18. An Index of all Works and Opuscula written by the regular Clergy, arranged alphabetically by Authors.

19. An Index of all Works and Opuscula published by the secular Clergy, compiled in the same order.

20. An Index of all Works and Opuscula published by laypersons, both men and women, prepared in the same order.

21. An Index of anonymous, doubtful, apocryphal, etc. Works and Opuscula found in the Patrology, according to the chronological order of the volumes.

22. A Bibliographical Index displaying the various editions of the Fathers and ecclesiastical Writers which have appeared since the invention of printing and have been used in compiling the Course of Latin Patrology.

23. A second Bibliographical Index, specifically including the Authors who have treated the Life and Works of the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical Writers, arranged alphabetically.

24. A general Analytical Index of the chief subjects, arranged alphabetically and at the same time logically, analogically, and chronologically, in which at a single glance may be seen whatever not merely this or that Father, but every single Father without any exception, has written on any subject whatever.

25. A Patristic-Theological Index, or Concordance between the two complete Courses of Theology and Patrology, in which the various subjects discussed by Theology, strengthened by the more illustrious writings or passages of the Fathers, are presented in logical order, and the volume and columns of each Course are indicated at the same time.

THIRD SERIES. INDEXES OF AUTHORS MENTIONED BY THE FATHERS.

26. An Alphabetical Index of pagan Poets, both Latin and Greek, whose writings are cited by the Holy Fathers.

27. An Alphabetical Index of Christian Poets whose sayings are mentioned in the course of this Patrology.

28. An Alphabetical Index of pagan Writers from whom the Holy Fathers borrowed various arguments and whose virtues they endeavoured to praise, and whose vices and errors to combat.

FIRST SERIES. TABLE OF TABLES AND GENERAL TABLES OF AUTHORS.

[Col. XXV]

1. Table of Tables, arranged according to the logical order in which they are published and giving the explanatory title of each, as follows:

2. French indicative Table of Authors and Works according to the order followed in the Patrology, setting forth in detail the writers contained in [Col. XXVIII] each volume, the extent of their writings, the price of each volume, the year of printing, etc.

3. General Alphabetical Table of all Fathers, all Doctors, and all ecclesiastical Writers, numbering 2,614, whose Works, Opuscula, and least writings have found a place in our Course of Latin Patrology, with an indication—common, moreover, to each of the 231 Tables—of the volume and column; this we point out here once for all.

4. General Chronological Table of these same Authors, from Tertullian to Innocent III, by means of which the Reader sees unfold before him, century by century and almost year by year, the uninterrupted Tradition of the Western Church.

5. A combined and curious Statistical Table of all Patristic Writers, giving the surname and given names of each, his nation, country, profession, etc.

6. A general statistical Table of the same Writers, in which each is assigned to the particular Diocese of which he was a member, arranged according to the alphabetical order of the various nations and, within each nation, according to the alphabetical order of Dioceses.

7. A general Hierarchical Table of the same, making known the offices and dignities that each held in the Church, from the Supreme Pontiffs down to the last degree of the clerical scale.

8. A general alphabetical Table of all ecclesiastical Writers who, during their lifetime, belonged to the regular Clergy.

9. A general alphabetical Table of all those belonging to the secular Clergy.

10. An alphabetical Table of all lay Writers, men or women, whose least Works are contained in our Patrology.

11. An alphabetical Table of all modern Writers—editors, commentators, etc.—whose Notes, Dissertations, Prefaces, or literary labours have been inserted in our Course.

12. A general Biographical Table of all the Writers forming our Patrology, arranged alphabetically and supplying sufficient notice concerning each, with chronological dates.

13. A general Analytical Table of all Patristic Writers, providing under the alphabetically arranged names of each a brief outline, a rapid summary of their various Works.

SECOND SERIES. GENERAL TABLES OF WORKS.

14. General alphabetical index of all Works and Shorter Works contained in the *Course of Latin Patrology*, drawn up according to the exact title of each.

15. General chronological index of the same Works, arranged in the order followed in our Course, from the first to the last of our 217 volumes.

16. Synoptic index of all Works or Shorter Works reproduced in our Course, presenting at a single glance the entire body of writings relating to the same point of doctrine, morals, learning, history, and so forth.

17. General analogous index of the same, bringing together in a rational order all writings of the same kind and tending toward the same end.

[Col. XXIX] 18. Index of the various Works produced by the regular clergy.

19. Index of the various Works produced by the secular clergy.

20. Index of the Works and Shorter Works of all lay authors, men or women.

21. Index of anonymous, doubtful, apocryphal, uncertain Works, and so forth.

22. Bibliographical index informing the reader of the various editions of the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers which have contributed, more or less, to the formation of our *Course of Latin Patrology*.

23. Bibliographical index offering, in alphabetical order, the various authors and different works which have dealt more especially with the life and works of the writers reproduced in our Course.

24. General analytical index of subjects, presenting at once in alphabetical, logical, analogous, and chronological order not only what one Father or another, but what each of the Fathers without exception, has written in all his works upon any given subject.

25. Patristic-Theological Index, or Concordance between our *Course of Theology* and our *Course of Patrology*, presenting in logical order the principal subjects of the *Course of Theology*, supported by the writings and passages of the Fathers upon the same subject, with an indication of the volume and column in each of the two Courses where these subjects are found.

## THIRD SERIES. INDEXES OF AUTHORS CITED BY THE FATHERS

26. Index of pagan poets, Greek or Latin, whom the Fathers cited in their writings.

27. Alphabetical index of Christian poets likewise cited by the Fathers.

28. Index of pagan authors from whom the Fathers borrowed certain arguments to support their own doctrine, whose virtues they praised, and whose vices and errors they censured or opposed.

## SECOND PART.—SPECIAL INDEXES. *PARS SECUNDA.—INDICES SPECIALES.*

[Col. XXIX] [Note: [Col. XXIX] The Latin and French versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

## FOURTH SERIES

[Col. XXX]

29. Index concerning God and His various Attributes, setting forth in logical order all that the Fathers wrote concerning the Godhead and its existence, essence, unity, foreknowledge, and the perfections by which it is a necessary being, etc.

30. Index concerning the Trinity, logically presenting the opinions of the Holy Fathers on the harmony of that incomprehensible mystery with reason, on the faith to be held concerning it, and on the errors by which it has been assailed.

31. Index concerning Providence, by which God continually preserves the things created by Him and always governs them most wisely [Col. XXXI]; it sets forth, in order, the opinions of the Fathers on its existence and its benefits toward humankind in the natural and supernatural orders, etc.

32. Index concerning Creation, in which, from the Holy Fathers, there is in turn a treatment of beings created in the beginning; of the various opinions of philosophers concerning Creation; of the Work of the Six Days, etc.

33. Index concerning Angels: their creation, fidelity, confirmation in grace; their hierarchy, nature, and various properties; their missions to human beings, etc.

34. Index concerning guardian Angels, reminding the reader of all that the Fathers said concerning their care and solicitude for the human race, nations, kingdoms, and private persons, in temporal as well as spiritual matters, etc.

35. Index concerning evil Angels or Demons, setting forth logically all that the Fathers handed down concerning their fall and the names then given them; the prerogatives inherent in their nature; the punishments and the power by which they attack human beings, etc.

36. Index concerning the physical world, expounding the various opinions of ecclesiastical writers on its governance, duration, and end; the signs that will precede that end; and the final conflagration.

37. Index concerning Man, made in the image and likeness of God, including also his origin, his twofold substance, his freedom, and his ultimate end.

38. Index concerning the human soul, and consequently its existence and origin, immateriality and immortality, its union with the body and its seat; its present and future state, etc.; and, as in an appendix, it treats of the soul of brute animals.

39. Index concerning human Reason, setting forth in logical order all that patristic writers said concerning its nature and end; the gifts, excellence, and power of human reason; and likewise its weakness.

40. Index concerning the earthly Paradise, which, setting aside the question of original sin, notes all that the Fathers wrote concerning the history of Eden, from Adam’s translation there to his expulsion; or, in other words, expounds what was done before, during, and after the fall of the first parents.

41. Index concerning original Sin, in which there is a logical summary of what the Fathers wrote concerning its existence, nature, and causes; its transmission and propagation to all human beings; and its principal effects, etc.

## FIFTH SERIES

42. Scriptural Index, expounding all that the Fathers wrote concerning the inspiration, authority, truthfulness, and integrity of the sacred books; their canon, authors, versions, interpretation, and various senses, etc.

43. General Index of Commentaries, arranged according to the order of the sacred books, from Genesis to the Apocalypse, chronologically providing all their explanations printed in the *Course of Patrology*.

44. Index of chapters and notable passages of Holy Scripture elucidated by the Holy Fathers in commentaries and explanations, drawn up according to both the canonical order of the books and the chronological order of the interpreters.

45. Exegetical Index of every verse of Holy Scripture, from the first verse of Genesis to the last of the Apocalypse, recalling in chronological order of writers the various commentaries and explanations of the Fathers upon every verse.

[Col. XXXIV] 46. Index of the allegories of the Old Testament concerning God, Jesus Christ, the Blessed Virgin Mary, Angels, etc., etc., arranged analogically and preserving alphabetical order within each analogy.

47. Index of the allegories of the New Testament concerning the same subjects and arranged in the same order.

48. Exegetical Index of Old Testament figures, gathering into five chapters the figures relating to Christ; to the Church; to the Apostles and the righteous; to Jews and Gentiles; and to heretics and the ungodly; recording the various interpretations of the Fathers in analogous order, while preserving within each analogy the alphabetical order of subjects and the chronological order of writers.

49. Exegetical Index of New Testament figures, composed concerning the same subjects and in the same order.

50. Exegetical Index of the principal parables of the New Testament, arranged according to both the alphabetical order of subjects and the chronological order of the Fathers, thus presenting the various explanations of them found in the *Latin Patrology*.

51. Index of the most distinguished men and women of the Old Testament, concerning whom the Fathers treated in any manner in their writings, arranged alphabetically by names; within the alphabet, however, the chronological order of writers is retained.

52. Index of the most distinguished men and women of the New Testament, concerning whom the Holy Fathers spoke, arranged in the same manner as the preceding.

## SIXTH SERIES

53. Index concerning Religion in general, or taken in its broader sense—namely, insofar as it is a society between God and human beings—recalling the various opinions of the Holy Fathers concerning it.

54. Index concerning divine Revelation, logically presenting all that the Fathers wrote concerning its possibility, usefulness, and necessity; the means by which God disclosed to creatures truths previously unknown, etc.

55. Index concerning Prophecies, arranged logically and recording the various opinions of the Fathers concerning the definition of prophecy and its possibility, usefulness, inspiration, characteristics, and principal objects—Christ, the Blessed Virgin Mary, the Church, etc.

56. Index concerning Miracles, treating in turn of miracles understood generally; of the miracles of the Old and New Testaments, etc.; and of the various prodigies wrought by demonic art, especially before Christ’s advent.

57. Mythological Index, listing in alphabetical order of names all gods and goddesses to whom pagans formerly offered public worship, and recording the statements of the Fathers by which these superstitions are attacked and ridiculed.

58. Index concerning the doctrines or errors of ancient philosophers mentioned in the *Patrology*, arranged alphabetically by subjects and displaying the various arguments by which the Fathers refuted them.

59. Name Index of those same ancient philosophers, briefly and concisely recalling both their errors and the Fathers’ refutations.

60. Index of both common and learned objections by which Gentiles, philosophers, and heretics attacked the Christian Religion, composed according to the syllogistic form of arguments and the alphabetical order of subjects.

61. Alphabetical index of authors whose apologetic works or shorter works are found in the *Course of Latin Patrology*.

[Col. XXXV] 62. Apologetic Index, or Synopsis of Works and Shorter Works for the Christian Religion, arranged in logical order of subjects.

63. Polemical Index, or alphabetical synopsis of authors who fought vigorously for the defense and glory of the Catholic religion.

64. Polemical Index, or synopsis of Works and Shorter Works concerning the defense of the Christian Religion, arranged alphabetically according to the errors which they attack and overthrow.

## SEVENTH SERIES

65. Index concerning Christ’s Incarnation, drawn up in logical order and successively setting forth all that the Fathers wrote concerning the possibility, excellence, fittingness, necessity, causes, and effects of this mystery; it also records books treating specifically of it.

66. Index concerning Christ, treating successively and logically of His divinity and humanity; His earthly life from the Nativity to the Ascension; His doctrine, miracles, and the various offices of the Word, etc.; the errors concerning the person of the Son; and the duties of human beings toward the Savior of the world.

67. Index concerning the Mystery of Redemption, recording all that the Fathers said concerning the salvation of the world through Christ.

68. Alphabetical Index of all Names by which the Holy Fathers and ecclesiastical writers designated Christ in their works.

69. Index concerning the Name of Jesus, logically arranging all that the Fathers wrote concerning the origin and meaning of that Name; its excellence and power; the miracles wrought in this Name; and the necessity of invoking it, etc.

70. Index concerning the Holy Spirit, recalling in analogous order the various opinions of the Holy Fathers concerning His divinity, attributes, gifts, and operations, etc.; it also records the various errors concerning the Holy Spirit and the books treating of Him.

71. Marian Index, or Index concerning the Blessed Virgin, placing before the reader all that the Fathers wrote concerning the Virgin Mother of God and her life from the Immaculate Conception to the Assumption; her virtues and privileges; the feasts and titles by which Christians honored Mary through the centuries; and, moreover, appending an alphabetical series of sermons, homilies, and various works and shorter works concerning the Blessed Virgin collected in our Course.

## EIGHTH SERIES

72. Historical Index of the Preaching of the Gospel and the Conversion of the Nations, arranged alphabetically by preachers, from the Apostles to the year 1216, showing Christianity’s gradual advance through the various regions which it illuminates with its light and brings under Christ.

73. Geographical Index of the Conversion of the Nations, setting forth alphabetically all parts of the world, provinces, and cities first endowed with the light of the Gospel, and recording the preachers who brought them the Words of Life.

74. Bibliographical Index of the Preaching of the Gospel, in which the various authors who transmitted to us in writing the history of the Conversion of the Nations are arranged alphabetically.

75. Index concerning Persecutions raised against Christ’s Church by pagans, emperors, and all ungodly persons [Col. XXXVIII], presenting in chronological order the various trials by which the Christian Religion was attacked from its beginnings.

76. Index concerning the benefits of Christianity for the individual, logically setting forth the various opinions of the Holy Fathers concerning the effects of Christ’s Religion upon the human intellect, which it enlightened; upon the heart, which it purified; upon the body, which it protected; etc.

77. Index concerning the benefits of Christianity for society, or for persons established in society, logically presenting all that the Fathers said concerning the duties of Christ’s Religion toward the family which it established, and toward peoples whom it made at once gentler and more equitable by its laws, etc.

78. Praxeological Index, or Index of Practical Life, expounding in alphabetical order of subjects the various works, practices, and customs of religion, piety, and devotion which prevailed among Christians in the Western Church at different times.

## NINTH SERIES

79. Index concerning the Catholic Church, arranged in logical order of subjects and recording in twenty-three chapters all that the Fathers wrote concerning its institution, origin, and antiquity; its spiritual goods; the four chief marks by which it is distinguished from others; its authority and power, etc., etc.

80. Index concerning the ecclesiastical Hierarchy, establishing wherein consists the twofold power of clerics—namely, that of Order and that of Jurisdiction or Government—and those who share in it.

81. Index concerning the Supreme Pontiff, especially insofar as he is Christ’s Vicar, Head of the Church, and Center of Unity, chronologically presenting the constant tradition of the Fathers concerning his election and primacy; his authority, both spiritual and temporal; his indefectibility, etc., etc.

82. Index concerning Metropolitans, by which, according to the Fathers, we learn why they were so called and what jurisdiction they possess over their suffragans.

83. Index concerning the Episcopate and Bishops, logically expounding the various opinions of the Holy Fathers concerning the institution of the episcopate; the qualifications, election, duties, virtues, and authority of bishops; episcopal administration and jurisdiction over priests; the reverence owed to bishops, etc.

84. Index concerning the Priesthood, treating logically, according to the Fathers, of priestly dignity, power, and holiness; the virtues befitting a priest; the vices he must avoid; priests’ duties and learning; pastoral care or burden and reward, etc.

85. Index concerning Clerics, presenting both the rights and the various obligations of the Church’s inferior ministers, what is prescribed or forbidden to them, and the obedience due from them to their superiors.

86. Index of all Heresies that arose in the Church from the earliest beginnings of the Christian Religion to the thirteenth century, arranged alphabetically by terms and recalling the various authors who attacked them in writing or crushed them by censures; to which is appended a chronological and analytical survey of these sects.

87. Index concerning Schisms, making known the origin, causes, and history of the various schisms from the beginnings of Christianity to the thirteenth century; the crime and evils of schismatics, etc.

[Col. XXXIX] 88. Hagiographical Index, or Index of all Saints whose life, account, eulogy, or mere mention is narrated in our *Course of Patrology*, drawn up alphabetically by names.

89. Index concerning the mutual relations of all members of the Church Militant, or concerning the Communion of Saints in the stricter sense, presenting the spiritual goods of the Church held in common by the faithful and Christians’ mutual participation in labor and rest.

90. Dogmatic Index, or alphabetical Synopsis of all authors who asserted dogmatic truths and whose writings are printed in the *Course of Patrology*.

91. Index, or Dogmatic Library of the Fathers, recording all Works and Shorter Works concerning Christian dogmas and supplying a concise analysis of each.

92. Index of the same dogmatic Works, distributed analogically into various chapters.

93. Alphabetical Index of the same Works treated in the two preceding libraries, according to the original title of each.

## TENTH SERIES

94. Index concerning Grace, logically recording all that the Fathers said concerning its name, essence, nature, necessity, and effects, as well as its harmony with the human free will; it also records the various errors concerning Grace and the writers who defended it most vigorously.

95. Index concerning the Sacraments in general, treating successively of the nature of the sacraments of both the Old and New Law; their institution and number; matter and form; power, minister, and recipient, etc. Books treating of the Sacraments are also enumerated.

96. Index concerning Baptism, logically presenting the various opinions of the Fathers concerning the nature and figures of that sacrament; its institution, matter, and form; its necessity and unity; the various kinds, effects, and ceremonies of Baptism; the conduct to be maintained after Baptism, etc.

97. Index concerning Confirmation, expounding the excellence and necessity of that sacrament; the dispositions for receiving it and its effects; whether it can be repeated, etc.

98. Index concerning the Eucharist, treating logically according to the Fathers of the nature and institution of that sacrament; the Real Presence and Transubstantiation; its excellence and necessity; its effects and use among ancient Christians, etc.

99. Index concerning Sacrifice understood in the broader sense; spiritual sacrifice; ancient sacrifices; various offerings, first-fruits, and tithes, etc.

100. Index concerning the Sacrifice of the Mass, expounding according to the Fathers the various figures and prophecies of this sacrifice; its institution, nature, and excellence; its form, matter, and power; to whom and for whom it may be offered; who is the minister and what is the manner of offering, etc.

101. Index concerning Penance understood in the broader sense, or concerning the virtue of penance, presenting the nature, necessity, conditions, and fruits of true penance, as well as outstanding examples of penitents.

102. Index concerning the Sacrament of Penance and its constituent parts, namely Contrition, Confession, and Satisfaction; the principal qualities and duties of the confessor, etc.

103. Index concerning public Penance, recording all that was formerly in use concerning it in the Catholic Church [Col. XLII], and the various collections of penitential canons provided by the *Course of Patrology*.

104. Index concerning Extreme Unction, offering little, but everything that is found in the *Patrology* concerning the excellence and effects of that Sacrament.

105. Index concerning Order, treating logically of the institution, effects, minister, and recipient of this Sacrament, as well as of the conditions for lawfully receiving orders and the various ranks from clerical tonsure to the Supreme Pontificate.

106. Index concerning Marriage, presenting the matter and form of this Sacrament; its honorableness, dignity, and effects; its unity and indissolubility; also treating of second marriages and polygamy, the impediments and obligations of Marriage, etc.

## ELEVENTH SERIES

107. Index concerning Creeds in general and each Creed in particular—the Apostles’, Nicene, and Athanasian Creeds—as well as the various professions of the Catholic faith admitted or proposed by the Church which are mentioned in the *Course of Patrology*.

## TWELFTH SERIES

108. Index concerning external Worship in general, recording the various opinions of the Holy Fathers concerning its necessity and advantages, especially for human society, whose savage and depraved morals it softened and corrected.

109. Index concerning the Worship of Saints and the Veneration of holy Relics and Images, setting before the eyes the constant tradition of the Holy Fathers of the Western Church concerning their invocation, against heretics and ungodly persons.

110. Index concerning benefits granted by God to human beings through the merits and intercession of Saints, arranged in the chronological order of the Fathers.

111. Liturgical Index, recording in alphabetical order of subjects all that pertains to the rites, prayers, and ceremonies of Catholic worship, and of which the *Patrology* treats.

112. Index concerning ecclesiastical Computation: the various calendars, the Paschal Cycle, and the different calculations of the ecclesiastical year, arranged alphabetically by subjects.

## THIRTEENTH SERIES

113. Index concerning Canon Law, establishing from the Fathers the power of the Catholic Church to enact laws which Christians must obey, and recording all the various collections of decrees and canons reviewed in the *Course of Patrology*.

114. Index concerning ecclesiastical and monastic Legislation, recording in alphabetical order of subjects all laws, decrees, and decisions relating to religion and ecclesiastical and monastic life.

115. Index concerning Councils mentioned in the *Patrology*, alphabetically recounting their history and various proceedings, together with a chronological series of them.

116. Index of all Canons cited in the *Course of Patrology* [Col. XLIII], arranged alphabetically according to the initial letter of each canon.

117. Index of Bulls and other writings relating to the government of the Church, issued by Supreme Pontiffs and arranged alphabetically by authors.

118. Index of Decrees, Decisions, etc., issued by Supreme Pontiffs, emperors, or kings and having the force of law among Christians, arranged alphabetically according to their initial letter and briefly expounding the purpose of each.

119. Disciplinary Index, presenting analogically, or under various headings, all that pertains to ecclesiastical and monastic discipline, while retaining alphabetical order within each analogy.

120. Alphabetical Index of all Works and Shorter Works concerning both ecclesiastical and monastic discipline listed in the *Course of Patrology*.

121. Alphabetical Index of authors who treated ecclesiastical or monastic discipline in their writings.

122. Index concerning ecclesiastical Censures, logically discussing from the Fathers excommunication and the excommunicated; irregularity, suspension, deposition, and interdict.

123. Index concerning civil Legislation, arranged alphabetically by subjects and recording the various laws and decrees insofar as they relate to religion.

124. Index of Immunities, Exemptions, and Privileges granted by ecclesiastical and civil authority to churches, monasteries, etc., arranged alphabetically by grantors and briefly expounding the nature of privileges and immunities.

## FOURTEENTH SERIES

125. Index concerning Death, providing the reader in logical order with all that the Fathers wrote concerning its nature, causes, and effects; its day, certain yet uncertain; and ways of dying well derived from consideration of the death of the righteous and the wicked. Outstanding examples are also recorded.

126. Index concerning the particular and private judgment of each person after death, examining the various opinions of the Holy Fathers concerning its circumstances.

127. Index concerning Heaven, logically treating the definition of its name and reality; the notion of beatitude in general and heavenly beatitude; how highly it should be esteemed; to whom it is given or denied; the location of the Kingdom of Heaven, etc.

128. Index concerning Hell, logically expounding all that the Fathers wrote concerning its existence, the punishments of the damned, and their eternity. The various errors concerning Hell are also refuted here.

129. Index concerning Purgatory, showing its existence and punishments; which sins must be expiated in Purgatory; whether and how souls detained there may be relieved; the perpetual agreement of the Catholic Church concerning this dogma, etc.

130. Index concerning Worship and Veneration toward the departed, demonstrating from history, liturgy, and monuments the constant tradition of the Latin Church concerning this matter.

131. Index concerning Antichrist, placing before the reader, according to the opinions of the Holy Fathers, the various signs that foretell, accompany, and follow his coming, as well as his final end.

132. Index concerning the Resurrection of bodies, in which errors concerning it are attacked; the doctrine of faith concerning it is asserted; when and how the Resurrection will occur; what changes will take place in bodies, and how these will be unto glory for the righteous but unto shame for the reprobate.

[Col. XLVI] 133. Index concerning the general and final Judgment, logically recording the opinions of the Holy Fathers concerning its certainty; its time, place, and circumstances; the Judge and His sentence, etc.

## FIFTEENTH SERIES

134. Moral Index, or alphabetical Synopsis of authors who explained moral truths and whose writings are listed in the *Course of Patrology*.

135. Moral Library, comprising all Works and Shorter Works of the ancient Fathers of the Latin Church concerning Christian ethics, in alphabetical order of authors, and supplying a concise analysis of each.

136. Library of the same Latin Fathers, arranged analogically and preserving within each analogy both alphabetical and chronological order.

137. Alphabetical Index of Works and Shorter Works mentioned in the two preceding Libraries, according to the original title of each.

138. Ascetical Index, or alphabetical synopsis of all authors who treated Christian and religious Perfection and whose Works or Shorter Works are found in the *Course of Patrology*.

139. Ascetical Library, comprising all Works and Shorter Works of the ancient Fathers of the Latin Church concerning religious Perfection, in alphabetical order of authors, and supplying a concise analysis of each.

140. Library of the same Latin Fathers, arranged analogically, while retaining within each analogy both alphabetical and chronological order.

141. Alphabetical Index of Works and Shorter Works mentioned in the two preceding Libraries, according to the original title of each.

142. Index concerning Conscience, logically setting forth the various opinions of the Holy Fathers concerning this dictate of reason, by which the internal rule of moral actions is commonly established; right or erroneous conscience, etc.

## SIXTEENTH SERIES

143. Index concerning the Decalogue, logically gathering all that the Fathers wrote concerning the ten Commandments of God and the fulfillment of their observance; then setting forth in order the various obligations of each commandment.

144. Index concerning Love of Enemies and the Forgiveness of Injuries, showing from the Fathers the effects of this obligation for us.

145. Index concerning Almsgiving, logically recording the various statements of the Holy Fathers concerning its nature and necessity; its conditions, subject, and fruits, etc.; also recording the more outstanding examples concerning it and books treating of it.

146. Index concerning fraternal Correction, expounding the circumstances and conditions required for each person to be bound by this precept toward a neighbor, and the fruits to be received from it.

147. Index concerning the Precepts of the Church, logically recording the opinions of the Fathers concerning the necessity of fulfilling these commands and setting out in order the duties of Christians concerning each one.

148. Index concerning Feasts, treating successively and logically of feasts in general and their origin, number, and antiquity; vigils and octaves; the feasts of the Lord, of the Blessed Virgin Mary, and of the Saints; Sunday; and gathering all that pertains to each feast [Col. XLVII], namely offices, liturgical prayers, sermons, hymns, etc.

149. Index concerning Fasting and Abstinence, logically presenting the various statements of the Holy Fathers concerning their nature and necessity; their conditions and virtue; their time, etc.; recording remarkable examples of fasting and books treating of it.

150. Index concerning Mortification of the senses, mind, and heart, gathering in logical order the various opinions of the Holy Fathers concerning it.

## SEVENTEENTH SERIES

151. Index concerning Faith, considered insofar as it is a theological virtue, providing the teaching of the Fathers on its nature and excellence; necessity and effects; qualities, object, and reward, etc.

152. Index concerning Hope as the theological virtue by which the mind is raised to hope for eternal blessedness to be obtained from God by His help, treating its nature and certainty; its necessity, excellence, object, and effects; and presumption and despair, which are opposed to it.

153. Index concerning Charity insofar as it is a theological virtue, asserting its excellence, necessity, effects, and object—namely, toward God, neighbor, and oneself; books treating of Charity are also enumerated.

154. Index concerning the moral Virtues, arranged alphabetically by names and recording in numbered entries the various opinions of the Fathers concerning each virtue.

155. Index concerning priestly Virtues, logically recording all the obligations, duties, or offices of God’s ministers which the Holy Fathers treated.

156. Index concerning the continence of clerics and monks and priestly celibacy, logically gathering all that Tradition presents concerning this universal law in the Catholic Church; its nature and prerogatives; the penalties to be inflicted on violators, etc.

157. Index concerning the Duties or Offices of Monks, comprising all that the Fathers said concerning monastic life; its origin; what monks must fulfill and avoid; also supplying the various Rules, Constitutions, and all writings relating to the religious state.

158. Index concerning Virginity and Virgins, treating successively and logically of the nature and excellence of virginity; its preservation and loss; the various duties of virgins; what they must fulfill and avoid; their consecration, etc.

159. Index concerning Nuns consecrated to God, treating their profession and consecration; their duties, offices, and virtues; government and enclosure; various superiors, etc., etc.

160. Index concerning Widows, expounding the opinions of the Holy Fathers concerning the praise of widowhood, the care and honor of widows; their duties and virtues; life and profession, etc.

161. Index concerning Kings, treating royal power, especially in ecclesiastical affairs; the duties of kings; their anointing and titles; the duties of subjects toward them, etc.

162. Index concerning Poverty and the Poor, presenting the statements of the Fathers concerning true poverty and the fruits received from it; the duties of the poor, etc.

[Col. L] 163. Anecdotal Index, arranged alphabetically by subjects and presenting to the reader the most illustrious deeds recorded in the *Course of Patrology*.

164. Index of memorable Sayings excerpted from the Holy Fathers, especially pertaining to virtues and the shaping of Christian life, arranged alphabetically by subjects.

165. Index concerning the distinctive Virtues of pagans which the Fathers extolled in praise, arranged alphabetically by subjects.

## EIGHTEENTH SERIES

166. Index concerning Sins, logically treating the nature, gravity, effects, and punishments of sin; original sin and its consequences; the capital sins—namely pride, avarice, lust, envy, gluttony, anger, and sloth—and each individually.

167. Index concerning Vices and Desires, arranged alphabetically by subjects or names and recording all that the Fathers wrote concerning their disgrace and remedies.

168. Index concerning Homicide, logically presenting the statements of the Fathers on homicide, suicide, dueling, infanticide, abortion, etc.; also presenting the legislation and jurisprudence current in the Middle Ages concerning these matters, and the penalties inflicted for these crimes, etc.

169. Index concerning Simony, Usury, and Avarice among clerics, placing before the reader the various opinions of the Holy Fathers on these matters; laws and decrees enacted by both civil and ecclesiastical authority against transgressors, and the penalties inflicted upon them.

170. Index concerning profane and unlawful Pleasures, comprising all that the Fathers wrote concerning profane love, songs, drunkenness, games, dances, spectacles, banquets, etc., and certain recreations forbidden to clerics, such as noisy hunting, etc., etc.

171. Index concerning the distinctive Vices and Errors of the pagans which the Holy Fathers reproved and attacked, drawn up alphabetically by subjects.

## NINETEENTH SERIES

172. Index concerning Prayer in general, logically treating the necessity and conditions of prayer; its effects, time, and place; mental and vocal prayer, and its objects, etc.

173. Index concerning prayers in use among the faithful in the Catholic Church—namely, the Lord’s Prayer, the Angelic Salutation, and others—providing their various explanations.

## TWENTIETH SERIES
174. Alphabetical index of historians and chroniclers whose works are printed in our *Patrology Course*.

175. Historical index, or four-part synopsis, successively presenting everything in the *Patrology Course* relating to sacred history; ecclesiastical history; universal secular history; and the particular history of individual peoples—the last arranged alphabetically by nation.

176. Index concerning the Jews, briefly comprising from the Fathers their history and laws, heresies and crimes, likewise their punishments and dispersion among the nations, and their conversion at the end of the age.

177. Alphabetical index of all historical and chronological works found in the *Patrology Course* [Col. LI], drawn up according to the original title of each.

178. Index of all monasteries, both of men and of women, mentioned in the *Patrology*, setting forth the place and time of each foundation or restoration, together with the privileges of the Supreme Pontiffs and the diplomas and charters of kings and noblemen; from which the more distinguished monks become known.

179. Index of dioceses mentioned in the *Patrology Course*, in which dioceses are arranged by provinces and, within each province, alphabetically. To each diocese individually are attached the letters, privileges, and bulls relating to it; likewise the monasteries and councils contained or held therein; men distinguished for sanctity or learning belonging to them; etc.

180. Index, written in French and arranged alphabetically according to Latin names, of episcopal cities, abbeys, and monasteries mentioned in the *Patrology*.

181. Alphabetical index of all biographical authors printed in our *Patrology Course*.

182. Biographical index, or synopsis of the Lives reported in the *Patrology*, arranged in a hierarchical sequence of persons and, within each sequence, alphabetically by name.

**TWENTY-FIRST SERIES.**

183. Alphabetical index of all writers whose sermons and homilies are found in the *Patrology Course*.

184. Index concerning the ministry of preaching, presenting various judgments of the Holy Fathers concerning the necessity, subject matter, rules, and effects of preaching; the qualities of its minister; the manner of hearing the word of God; etc., etc.

185. Index of all sermons on the Scriptures extant in the *Patrology*, arranged according to the canonical order of the sacred books.

186. Index of all sermons for the Proper of Time, arranged according to the course of the ecclesiastical year—that is, from the First Sunday of Advent to the last Sunday after Pentecost.

187. Index of all sermons on the Saints extant in the *Patrology*, arranged alphabetically by saints.

188. Index of sermons on various subjects, arranged analogically according to the logical order of topics, and thus readily furnishing the reader with what is desired.

189. Index of homilies on the Scriptures.

190. Index of homilies for the Proper of Time.

191. Index of homilies on the Saints.

192. Index of homilies on various subjects. These homilies are presented to the reader in the same order as the sermons.

193. Preachers’ index to the Epistles read during the solemnities of Mass throughout the year according to the Roman rite, setting forth various explanations, sermons, homilies, and commentaries suitable for elucidating each Epistle, whence the reader may be pleased to draw both useful and agreeable material as from a richer source.

194. Preachers’ index to the Gospels read during the solemnities of Mass throughout the year according to the Roman rite, compiled in the same manner.

**TWENTY-SECOND SERIES.**

[Col. LIV]

195. Alphabetical index of all authors who wrote in strict verse, and whose works or even shorter works are found in our *Patrology Course*.

196. Index of all poetic works and shorter poems, arranged analogically by subject and genre, in which are successively unfolded exegetical, dogmatic, moral, and liturgical poetry; didactic, dramatic, elegiac, and satirical poetry; etc., etc., printed in the *Patrology Course*.

**TWENTY-THIRD SERIES.**

197. General alphabetical index of writers whose letters, of whatever kind or number, are listed in the *Patrology Course*.

198. Index of dogmatic letters, preserving an order at once analogical by subject and chronological by author.

199. Index of letters concerning morals, arranged in the same order.

200. Index of letters dealing with canon law, presented in the same order.

201. Index of letters treating liturgical matters, ceremonies, or rites, arranged in the same manner.

202. Index of letters concerning ecclesiastical discipline which, proceeding from lawful authority, possess some authority, arranged in the same manner.

203. Index of letters on various subjects, compiled according to an analogical order of topics and chronological order of writers.

204. Alphabetical index of all persons to whom letters were addressed.

205. Index of the same persons arranged alphabetically by regions.

206. Index of the same persons arranged according to their hierarchical rank or dignity: emperors, kings, princes, etc.

**TWENTY-FOURTH AND LAST SERIES.**

207. General index of sciences and arts, drawn up alphabetically by subject, setting forth their origin and their progress over the course of time.

208. Index of inventions mentioned in the *Patrology*, making known their authors, the time, and the writers who recorded them.

209. Index of occult sciences, relating alphabetically by subject everything the Fathers wrote concerning sciences forbidden by the Catholic religion—namely astrology, magic, necromancy, etc., etc.

210. Index of astronomy and meteorology, setting forth alphabetically by subject the various judgments of the Holy Fathers concerning sciences dealing especially with knowledge of the stars.

211. Index of cosmogony, in a four-part series, setting forth everything the Fathers wrote concerning eternity, time, the physical world, and the elements; and preserving within each part an alphabetical order of topics.

212. Index of geology and palaeontology, relating alphabetically by subject everything the Fathers wrote concerning the terrestrial globe and its various changes; the universal Flood and its consequences; earthquakes; etc.

213. Index of mineralogy, presenting alphabetically by subject everything concerning minerals contained in the *Patrology Course*.

[Col. LV] 214. Index of geography, alphabetically listing each and every nation, region, city, and various place mentioned in the *Patrology*.

215. Index of ethnography, arranged alphabetically by subject, presenting everything the Fathers said concerning the origin and kinds of nations or peoples; their various migrations, dress, customs, practices, etc.

216. Index of anthropology, in which, drawing alphabetically on the Holy Fathers, there is discussion of man as a rational animal composed of soul and body, or of physical and moral man.

217. Index of physiology, relating alphabetically by subject everything the Fathers said concerning the structure of the human body and all its individual members and parts; concerning life and the senses; and concerning their relations to moral matters.

218. Index of anatomy, setting forth alphabetically everything concerning that science contained in the *Patrology Course*.

219. Index of medicine, presenting the various opinions of the Fathers concerning the art of healing, arranged alphabetically by subject.

220. Index of botany, mentioning alphabetically by subject everything the Fathers wrote concerning various plants and their properties; prefaced by a division and historical synopsis of this science.

221. Index of agriculture, gathering alphabetically everything the Fathers said concerning cultivation and production of the soil; agricultural implements; the more suitable seasons; etc., etc.

222. Index of zoology, relating alphabetically by subject everything the Fathers wrote concerning beasts or living creatures; prefaced by a synopsis, written in French, of the various divisions of natural history according to modern science.

223. Index of arithmetic, setting forth the various treatises on the science of numbers contained in the *Patrology*, and providing a brief analysis of each.

224. Index of geometry, arranged in the same manner as the preceding.

225. Index concerning measures, weights, and coins mentioned in the *Patrology Course*, arranged in logical order.

226. Index of archaeology, presenting alphabetically everything the Fathers wrote concerning architecture, sculpture, painting, etc.

227. Index concerning priestly, monastic, and lay garments mentioned in the *Patrology*, setting forth their mystical meaning.

228. Epigraphic index, recording every inscription, whether lapidary or numismatic, mentioned in the *Patrology Course*.

229. Index of music, setting forth the various treatises on this science supplied by the *Patrology*, and providing a brief analysis of each.

230. Index of linguistics, noting everything the Fathers handed down concerning the origin, character, use, etc., of various languages and dialects. At the same time are given the innovations or corruptions of words that have crept in over the course of time, etc.

231. Philological index, gathering alphabetically various words translated and elucidated by the Holy Fathers from Arabic, Chaldean, Hebrew, and Syriac into Latin.

**FOURTH SERIES.**

29. Table concerning God and His various attributes, presenting, in logical order, everything the Holy Fathers wrote concerning the Godhead, its essence, and the qualities inseparable from its nature and without which it could not exist; etc.

30. Table concerning the Trinity, offering in logical order what the Holy Fathers said concerning this mystery, impenetrable to human reason without being contrary to it; which we must believe without seeking to sound its depth; etc.

31. Table concerning divine providence, relating everything the Holy Fathers wrote concerning [Col. XXXII] its existence, its benefits toward humankind in both the temporal and spiritual orders, and the various errors raised against it; etc.

32. Table of creation, presenting in logical order what patristic writers said concerning beings created in the beginning; the various opinions of philosophers on this subject; the successive work of the six days and the things created on each of them; etc.

33. Table of the angels: their creation, fidelity, confirmation in grace and glory; their hierarchy; their spiritual and immortal nature; their qualities; and their various functions in heaven and on earth in relation to creatures; etc.

34. Table of guardian angels: their care for nations, peoples, empires, and individuals entrusted to their charge; their beneficial influence in both the material and spiritual orders; etc.

35. Table of evil angels or demons, treating successively of their disobedience and fall; their prerogatives lost or retained; their punishments; their power, limited in relation to human beings and earthly things; etc.

36. Table of the physical world, relating the various opinions of the Fathers and ecclesiastical authors concerning its formation, governance, duration, and end.

37. Table of man, presenting in logical order everything the Holy Fathers wrote concerning his origin, his twofold substance, his freedom, and his future destiny.

38. Table of the human soul, speaking successively of its origin, nature, spirituality, and immortality; its union with the body; its present and future state; etc.; and concluding with an appendix on the souls of animals.

39. Table of human reason, offering the various opinions of the Fathers and patristic writers concerning its excellence, qualities, power, weakness, etc.

40. Table of the earthly paradise, placing before the reader the various scenes occurring there before, during, and after the trial of our first parents.

41. Table of original sin, presenting in logical order everything patristic authors wrote concerning its causes and its sad effects in our first parents, and concerning its transmission to their descendants; etc.

**FIFTH SERIES.**

42. Table of Holy Scripture, making known in logical order everything written concerning the inspiration, authenticity, and truthfulness of the sacred books; their different versions; the various senses according to which they may be interpreted; the canon of Scriptures received by the Church; etc.

43. Table of all commentaries on each book of the Old and New Testaments, drawn up according to the canonical order of Scripture, from Genesis to Revelation, and according to the chronological order of commentators.

44. Table of commentaries on each chapter and on the most remarkable passages of Holy Scripture, drawn up in the same order as the preceding.

45. Exegetical table of every verse of Scripture, from the first verse of Genesis to the last of Revelation, showing in chronological order all writers in the *Patrology* who explained, commented upon, or paraphrased each verse.

[Col. XXXIII] 46. Table of the allegories of the Old Testament, presenting in analogical order all those relating to God, Jesus Christ, the Blessed Virgin, angels, etc.; and, within that analogy, preserving the alphabetical order of subjects.

47. Table of the allegories of the New Testament, drawn up in the same order as the preceding.

48. Exegetical table of the figures of the Old Testament, arranged analogically, but preserving within the analogy the alphabetical order of subjects and the chronological order of authors; by means of which the reader will see every figure concerning Jesus Christ, the Church, the Apostles and the righteous, the Jews and the Gentiles, etc.

49. Exegetical table of the figures of the New Testament, presented in the same manner as the preceding.

50. Exegetical table of the principal parables of the New Testament, compiled according to the alphabetical order of topics and the chronological order of authors, offering the various explanations found in the *Patrology*.

51. Table of the principal persons, both men and women, of the Old Testament whom the Fathers discussed in their writings, presented according to the alphabetical order of names and chronological order of authors.

52. Table of the principal persons of the New Testament, drawn up in the same manner as the preceding.

**SIXTH SERIES.**

53. Table of religion in general, or of the relations of God to human beings and of human beings to God, giving in logical order what the Holy Fathers said on this subject.

54. Table of revelation, offering in logical order the views of the Holy Fathers concerning its possibility, fittingness, necessity, and the means God used to manifest Himself to creatures.

55. Table of prophecies, presenting in logical order what the Holy Fathers wrote concerning prophecies: their usefulness, divine inspiration, characteristics, and principal objects—Jesus Christ, the Blessed Virgin, the Church, etc.

56. Table of miracles, treating of miracles in general; miracles of the Old and New Testaments; those performed in the time of the Apostles and in subsequent ages; false miracles produced by the intervention of the Devil; etc.

57. Mythological table, placing before the reader, in alphabetical order, the many deities to whom the pagans rendered public worship, and indicating the various passages in which the Fathers rose up against these shameful or ridiculous superstitions.

58. Table of the various errors professed by ancient philosophers and opposed by the Fathers, arranged according to the alphabetical order of subjects.

59. Alphabetical nominal table of philosophers of antiquity, offering a brief analysis of the principal errors of each and likewise indicating the patristic writers who opposed them.

60. Table of both learned and popular objections devised against the Christian religion by pagans, philosophers, and heretics, presented in syllogistic form and according to the alphabetical order of subjects.

61. Special alphabetical table of apologists, or authors who wrote in defense of the Christian religion.

[Col. XXXVI] 62. Special table of apologetic works in defense of the Christian religion, presented in a logical order of subjects.

63. Special alphabetical table of polemical authors who, in their writings, contended for the defense and glory of the Christian religion.

64. Table of the various polemical works written in defense of the Christian religion, arranged according to the alphabetical order of the errors they oppose.

**SEVENTH SERIES.**

65. Table of the Incarnation of the Word, making known in logical order everything the Fathers wrote concerning this mystery—its importance, necessity, causes, effects, etc.—and providing a list of works specifically on this subject.

66. Table of Jesus Christ, treating successively and in logical order of His divinity, humanity, life from His birth to His Ascension, doctrine, miracles, functions, etc.; of errors raised against His person; and of the duties owed to Him.

67. Table of the redemption of the human race, offering what the Holy Fathers said concerning this mystery.

68. Alphabetical table, or nomenclature, of all the names by which the Fathers and ecclesiastical writers comprising the *Patrology* designated the Savior of humankind.

69. Table of the Name of Jesus, showing in logical order everything the Fathers wrote concerning the origin, meaning, and excellence of this divine Name; miracles performed through its invocation; the necessity laid upon us to have recourse to it; etc.

70. Table of the Holy Spirit, summarizing in logical order the opinions of the Fathers on His divinity, attributes, gifts, and various operations; and relating the different errors raised against the Holy Spirit, together with the works specifically on this subject.

71. Table of the Blessed Virgin, bringing together at a single glance everything patristic authors wrote concerning the Mother of God, from her Immaculate Conception to her glorious Assumption; her life, virtues, sufferings, glory, prerogatives, feasts, etc.; likewise offering an alphabetical nomenclature of the principal titles Christians have delighted to give her in every age, followed by that of the sermons, homilies, works, and shorter works contained in our *Course* in honor of the Queen of Heaven.

**EIGHTH SERIES.**

72. Historical table of the preaching of the Gospel and the conversion of peoples, arranged alphabetically by preachers, from the Apostles to 1216, showing Christianity gradually spreading among the nations which it enlightens with its divine light and subjects to faith in Jesus Christ.

77. Table of the benefits of Christianity to society, relating in logical order what the Fathers said concerning the beneficial influence of the religion of Christ upon peoples: it restrained their excesses, softened their manners, and improved their condition through its institutions; etc., etc.

Table of the episcopate, bringing together in logical order everything the Fathers wrote concerning its institution; the qualities and virtues proper to bishops; the duties and obligations they must fulfill; their authority and jurisdiction over ordinary priests; the use they must make of it; etc., etc.

Table of the priesthood, showing in logical order everything the Holy Fathers said concerning the greatness, dignity, and holiness of the priestly office; the virtues proper to priests; the vices they must avoid; the duties they must fulfill; the learning necessary to them; pastoral responsibility; etc.

Table of all heresies which arose in the Church from the birth of Christianity to the thirteenth century, presented alphabetically, with an indication of the writers who opposed them; followed by a chronological table of the principal sects, offering an analysis of the errors which they endeavored to spread.

# INDEXES OF LATIN PATROLOGY

## PART ONE. GENERAL INDEXES

### FIRST SERIES. GENERAL INDEXES OF AUTHORS

[Col. 0001]

[PREFACE.]

This first series comprises thirteen indexes through which all and each of the authors whose writings, even the smallest, are found in our *Course of Latin Patrology* may readily become known to readers in every respect. We offer, in turn, alphabetical and chronological, statistical and hierarchical, biographical and analytical indexes, etc., etc., etc., as will be evident to anyone consulting them. With the aid of these indexes, every reader will be able to learn who any given writer is whose works he may wish to read; in what time he lived; from where he came; with what dignity he was distinguished; how numerous and of what character each author’s works are; whether he ever departed from orthodox faith; etc., etc., etc.

Thus this first series affords the reader the greatest benefit, and these indexes are suitably placed before this gigantic work which we at last offer to men devoted to study and friends of learning, and to the completion of which, with God’s help, we shall endeavor promptly and successfully to set our hand.

[Col. 0005]

## I. INDEX OF INDEXES, LOGICALLY SETTING FORTH IN ORDER ALL AND EACH OF THE PATROLOGY INDEXES

**NOTE.** Since the index which occupies the first place in this series has already been set forth above, it need not be repeated here. The reader should therefore consult page XIII of our Preface, where it will be found written in two languages, namely French and Latin.

[Col. 0005]

## NOTICE TO THE CATHOLIC WORLD AND TO LEARNED MEN OF EVERY COUNTRY

If we are asked why, before all else, we present the first Table in French, here is our candid answer. We have done so:

1. Because the complete *Course of Patrology* appeared in France; because we ourselves are French; and, finally, because the greater number of subscribers is found in France. Hence there is a remarkable facility for investigating matters, available to anyone who scarcely has even the briefest moments of time, and especially to the many who, as commonly happens, grasp the vernacular language more quickly and better than an obsolete idiom;

2. Because almost all learned men, in whatever region under heaven, already understand French or will soon understand it. Hence it provides an almost universal means, as well as a more expeditious way of examining every kind of subject;

3. Because the French language, clearer and less ambiguous than Latin, expresses more successfully all the subjects embraced by the *Course of Patrology*. Hence investigations will have an easier outcome;

4. Because, finally, this table written in French acknowledges as its author a man eminent among Catholics and deserving well of our religion, most learned alike in the number, extent, and excellence of his works: namely M. Bonnetty, author and editor of the two collections entitled: 1. *Annals of Christian Philosophy*; 2. *The Catholic University*. To his singular diligence we owe this notable service, which we present to the Catholic world as a kind of gateway to the revived monument of Christian tradition.

Paris, 18 March 1862.

L. MIGNE.

## SECOND CENTURY

### VOLUMES I–II. Price: 20 francs

**I. TERTULLIAN**, Quintus Septimius Florens, born at Carthage about A.D. 150, converted in 185, made a priest in 192, and died about A.D. 220.

### VOLUME ONE, comprising 1,336 columns—1844

1. Preface by the editors, the Benedictine Fathers of Solesmes, under the direction of Dom Pitra. They treat of the author’s authority; the use that may be made of him; the various manuscripts, editions, and translations of his Works; and the care taken in preparing this edition, for which they largely followed that of Priorius of 1664. [Note: [Col. 0009] The new editors nevertheless added a considerable number of new pieces and collected the various notes, thus forming a variorum edition. [Col. 0010] They also supplied a new division of the author’s treatises. (A. BONNETTY, *Annals of Christian Philosophy*).]

The following are the continuation of these studies:—2. *Life of Tertullian*, containing the history of twenty-four years of his life, by Jac. Pamelius.—3. Responses of Tertyllien, a Roman jurist, found in the books of the *Digest*.—4. Dissertation on the age and doctrine of Tertullian’s writings, by Fr. Gottfried Lumper, Benedictine.—5. Tertullian’s paradoxes with their antidote, by Fr. Pamelius, Jesuit.—6. Tertullian’s proverbial sayings, with a brief explanation, by Beatus Rhenanus and And. Hoyus of Bruges.—7. Preface to the book of the *Apology*, by Sigeb. Havercamp. The author’s shorter works now follow.—I. *Apology against the Gentiles on Behalf of Christians*, with variants and variorum notes.—8. Investigations concerning the date of the *Apology* and the beginning of Severus’s persecution, by John Lucian Mosheim.—II. *To the Nations*, in two books, with variants and notes.—III. *On the Testimony of the Soul against the Gentiles*, likewise.—IV. *Exhortation to Martyrdom*, likewise.—V. *The Book of the Shows*, with preface and notes by Lumper.—VI. *The Book on Idolatry*, with preface and commentary by Lumper.—VII. A book addressed to Scapula, proconsul of the province of Carthage, in order to dissuade him from persecuting [Col. 0010] Christians.—9. Dissertation on the *Apology*, the two books addressed to the Gentiles, and the one addressed to Scapula, by Fr. le Nourry, Benedictine, comprising 438 columns and providing a complete explanation not only of these books but of all Christian antiquity.—10. Prolegomena to the book *On Prayer*, by Ludovico Antonio Muratori.—11. Preface to that same book, by Pancirolus.—VIII. *The Book on Prayer*, with variants and variorum notes.—IX. *The Book on Baptism against Quintilla*, who taught that water was unnecessary for it and propagated the error of the Cainites, likewise.—12. Preface to the book *On Repentance*, by Lumper.—X. *The Book on Repentance*, with variants and notes.—XI. *The Book on Patience*, likewise.—XII. *To His Wife*, in two books, likewise. He advises her, should she become a widow, not to remarry, or at least to marry only a Christian.—XIII. *On Women’s Dress*, in two books, likewise.

### VOLUME II, comprising 1,392 columns—1844

**TERTULLIAN (continued).**—XIV. *The Book of Prescriptions against Heretics*, with preface by the editors, variants, and notes.—The following books were composed by Tertullian when already a Montanist.—XV. *On the Soldier’s Crown*, composed in 201, in which he proscribes the use of crowns of every kind, with preface by the editors, variants, and notes.—XVI. *On Flight in Times of Persecution*, written in 202; against the saying of Jesus Christ, he maintains that flight is not permitted.—XVII. *The Scorpiace*, or *The Scorpion*, against the Gnostics, who maintained that martyrdom was useless.—XVIII. Book against Praxeas, a heretic who denied the Trinity of persons and maintained that it was the Father who suffered.—XIX. Book against Hermogenes, a heretic who professed Stoic doctrines and maintained that matter is eternal.—XX. *Against Marcion*, in five books, written in 207. Marcion, having been expelled from the Church because of incest, had embraced Cerdon’s errors and maintained that the God who gave Moses’ law was not the same as the one who gave the [Col. 0011] Gospel; that the latter was good and the former evil; with prefaces by Dupin and Lumper.—13. Preface to the book *Against the Valentinians*, by the editors and Pamelius.—14. Tables, after Pamelius, of the names of Valentinus’s Aeons and gods, in Greek, with their Latin explanation.—15. Gnostic table after the fables of Valentinus and his disciples.—XXI. Book *Against the Valentinians*, with variants and notes.—XXII. Book *Against the Jews*, likewise.—XXIII. *The Book on the Soul*, likewise.—XXIV. *The Book on the Flesh of Jesus Christ*, against those who denied that he had taken human flesh, likewise.—XXV. *The Book on the Resurrection of the Flesh*, likewise.—XXVI. On the obligation of virgins to enter church only with their heads covered by a veil, likewise, with introductory remarks by Lumper and the editors.—XXVII. *Exhortation to Chastity*; at times it permits, and at times condemns, second marriages.—XXVIII. *On Monogamy*, which he believes alone to be permitted.—XXIX. *On Fasts*; therein he defends Montanus’s fasts against Catholics, whom he calls “psychics,” or carnal persons.—XXX. *On Modesty*; he maintains that those who transgress it cannot be admitted to penance, with summaries by Pamelius.—XXXI. *On the Cloak*: an apology to his fellow citizens for having exchanged the toga for the cloak—that is, paganism for Christianity.

**Works attributed to Tertullian.**—First appendix.—[I.] Poem in verse against Marcion, in five books, with preface by the editors and by the Venice edition, and notes by Pamelius.—[II.] *On the Judgment of the Lord*, in verse.—[III.] *Genesis*, likewise.—[IV.] *The Destruction of Sodom*, likewise.—[V.] To a senator who, having been a Christian and consul, allowed himself to be named priest of Isis or of the Mother of the Gods, likewise.—[VI.] *On Jonah and Nineveh*, likewise, with notes by Fr. Juret.—[VII.] *On the Tree of Life*, likewise.—Second appendix.—[VIII.] Fragments from the book *On the Horror Which One Ought to Have for the Gods of the Gentiles*, published by J.-M. Suarès.—Third appendix.—[IX.] Fragments and notes on Tertullian’s works, extracted from Greek works, with notes by Pamelius.—[X.] Extracts from the *Apology*, drawn from Eusebius and Nicephorus, with the threefold Latin version of Rufinus, Christophorson, and Langius.—[XI.] Tertullian himself mentions a Greek translation of his books *On the Shows*, *On the Veiling of Virgins*, and *On Baptism*.—Fourth appendix.—[XII.] Fragments, mentions, and notes extracted from Tertullian’s lost books: 1. *On the Tribulations of Marriage*. 2. *On Fate*. 3. *On Clean and Unclean Animals*. 4. *On Circumcision*. 5. *On Aaron’s Garments*. 6. *On the Trinity*. 7. *On the Origin of the Soul*. 8. *Against the Disciples of Apelles*. 9. *On Paradise*. 10. *On the Hope of the Faithful*. 11. *On Ecstasy*, in six books. 12. *Against Apollonius*.—Fifth appendix.—16. Notes by Dom Corbinian Thomas, German Benedictine, on the books *On Baptism* and *On Repentance*, in which the ceremonies of the ancient Church are compared with those of the present day, with a preface by the editors.—17. Index to Tertullian’s Latin usage by Schulzius, explaining words often very difficult to understand.—18. Index of ancient writers cited in Tertullian’s writings, by Pamelius.—Analytical table.

LIV. CONSTANTINE, the first Christian emperor, who reigned from 306 to 337.

1. His life, in Latin only, by Eusebius, in four books. — I. The surviving decrees and constitutions of Constantine, according to the Theodosian Code, with notes and variants by Godefroy and Hoenel. — II. Constantine’s law on piety toward God and the Christian religion (Greek and Latin), with notes by Valois. — III. Discourses extracted from Eusebius. — IV. Discourse to the Assembly of the Saints, or to the Church, with notes by Valois. — V. Letters taken from Coleti’s collection of councils or from Eusebius. These letters number thirty-nine.

Appendix to the works of Constantine, containing apocryphal writings, with notes by Binius. — [I.] Letter attributed to Pope Melchiades, and probably by Isidore, who may have completed it from various authors. — [II.] Edict of Constantine addressed to Pope St. Sylvester. — [III.] Autograph document concerning love and concord between Emperor Constantine, Pope St. Sylvester, Tiridates, king of Armenia, and the divine Gregory, illuminator of the Armenians. [Note: [Col. 0016] It is a genuine service rendered to ecclesiastical scholarship to have thus brought together in a single body all these documents concerning the great event of the accession to power of the Christian religion. (A. BONNETTY, *Annals of Christian Philosophy*.)]
