CI. SAINT EUSEBIUS, bishop of Vercelli; died about 370, known for his zeal in defending the faith against Arius and for the persecutions inflicted upon him by the Emperor Constantius. Complete Works. The edition of Blanchini, dedicated to John V, King of Portugal, was used as the basis.

The works of Eusebius consist of several letters, a profession of faith concerning the Trinity, and a copy of the celebrated Old Latin version of Scripture used in the Church before that of Saint Jerome called the Vulgate. This ancient version is given here from four manuscripts, set beside one another on the same page, with notes by Blanchini and variant readings. [Note: [Col. 0020] It is a most precious monument and one very difficult to obtain. We must therefore thank the editor for this important publication, made accessible to everyone. (A. BONNETTY, *Annals of Christian Philosophy*.)] The contents of this volume now follow in order.---1. Preface to John V, King of Portugal, by Blanchini.---2. Notice concerning the manuscript of Eusebius preserved at Brescia, by Ph. Garbellus.---3. Dissertation by Dom Martianay on the Old Latin version of the text of Saint Matthew and on the manuscripts of Corbie and Saint-Germain-des-Prés.---4. Dissertation on the manuscript of the Gospels preserved at Vercelli, by Ruggerius.---5. Blanchini’s judgment concerning the same manuscript.---I. The Gospels of Saint Matthew, Saint John, Saint Luke, and Saint Mark, preserved by Eusebius according to the four manuscripts of Vercelli, Verona, Corbie, and Brescia, accompanied at the foot of every page by Blanchini’s variants and philological and critical notes.---6. Appendices to these Gospels: letter by Blanchini on comparing certain variants.---7. Another by the same, elucidating certain readings of the Brescia codex.---8. Another letter by the same, describing the Greek-Latin codex of the Gospels and Acts preserved in the Cambridge library.---9. Concordance of the readings of the four Gospels, with the Greek text in passages departing from the Vulgate.---10. Passages of the Old Testament quoted by Jesus Christ and the apostles, compared with this Greek text and with the Old Latin and Vulgate versions, to determine whether Jesus Christ and his apostles used the Hebrew text or the Septuagint version.---II. Four letters, taken from Gallandus.---III. Confession or creed concerning the Trinity, with an introduction and dissertation on the author of this creed, taken from Eug. de Levis’s *Sacred Anecdotes*, with notes.---11. On the life and writings of Eusebius, by Gallandus.---12. On his writings and editions, by Schoeneman.

CLIX. ULFILAS, died about 388. Ulfilas, who became bishop of the Goths in 348, is known to have translated the Scriptures into their language. [Note: [Col. 0025] This translation is all the more precious because it is the only monument remaining to us of the original Germanic language of the northern peoples. Various editions of this work have been published. The edition which Abbé Migne gives here is the most recent and complete; [Col. 0026] it provides not only the text of the Gospels in that language, for which he had an entire typeface of Gothic characters cast, but also adds the grammar and dictionaries necessary for learning that language.] The various components of this work, occupying two thirds of this volume, are as follows.---1. Epistle to Maximilian, King of Bavaria, by the editors.---2. Preliminaries containing everything known concerning the life of Ulfilas, his labors, and the manuscripts in which they are preserved.---I. Grammar of the Gothic language, translated from German into Latin by Tempestini.---4. Gothic-Latin glossary.---5. Greek-Gothic glossary.

Chronicle of various histories. [Note: [Col. 0031] This Chronicle, edited by Fr Bivar, provoked a major controversy upon its publication in 1624. It was alleged to have been composed by Fr Higuera, a Spanish Jesuit who died in 1611 and who, distressed by historians’ silence concerning the establishment of Christianity in Spain, had himself composed this Chronicle under the name of Dexter, incorporating traditions current in Spain and fragments from the Chronicles of Dexter, Maximus, Luitprand, and others. Fr Bivar, a Cistercian, upheld its authenticity when publishing it, adding commentaries twice as extensive as the text. It is this edition which M. Abbé Migne reproduces, so as to omit nothing.] With Bivarius’s commentaries, comprising all events from the birth of Jesus Christ down to 430. Among the numerous commentaries are curious pieces taken from ancient Spanish breviaries: those of St Isidore, of Toledo, the Gothic, and the Mozarabic.---Appendix.---[I.] On Daniel’s prophecy concerning the four animals.---5. VOLUMES XXXII–XLVII. Price: 80 francs.---1845.

CCXXXIV. ST AUGUSTINE, Aurelius, the foremost of the Fathers of the Latin Church, bishop of Hippo, born in 354 and died in 430. His complete Works are reproduced here according to the Benedictine edition, whose text has been collated with the old editions. [Note: [Col. 0031] It is known that, despite the care bestowed by the Benedictine Fathers upon their edition, many errors nevertheless escaped them. Critics reproached them sometimes for neglecting to collate their text with the old editions, sometimes for failing to arrange their variants uniformly, placing them now at the foot of the pages, now in the margins. Moreover, the numerous additions and corrections placed at the end of each volume showed that they themselves had recognized the imperfection of their work.

The new editor has taken advantage of every criticism, restored uniformity to the text by putting all notes at the foot of the pages, and in several places given a new arrangement to the matter contained in the former volumes.]

CCXXXV. MARIUS MERCATOR, friend of St. Augustine, writing from 408 to 450; according to the edition of Fr. Garnier, Jesuit, but with the notes and variants of the editions of Baluze and Gallandus.—1. Fr. Garnier’s general preface to all Mercator’s works.—2. Baluze’s preface.—3. Literary notice by Schoeneman. Works of Mercator.—First part, containing writings relating to the heresy of Pelagius, or rather of Caelestius.—I. Commentary against Caelestius, offered to the emperor, Theodosius the Younger, with numerous commentaries.—II. The book of annotations on Julian’s words.—Translation of various Greek writings.—III. Translation of the three letters of Nestorius.—IV. Translation of the same author’s treatise against the heresy of Pelagius or Caelestius.—V. Translation and refutation of the creed of Theodore of Mopsuestia.—First appendix.—[I.] Letter of Pope Anastasius to John of Jerusalem concerning Rufinus.—[II.] Profession of faith, containing twelve anathemas, made by a certain Rufinus.—Second appendix.—[III.] The following seven dissertations on the heresy of Pelagius: On the authors and defenders of the heresy of Pelagius; On the synods held on this matter during St. Augustine’s lifetime; On the constitutions of the emperors concerning this heresy, from the year 418 to the year 430; On subscriptions required from heretics; On professions of faith composed by the heretics Theodore of Mopsuestia, Rufinus, Pelagius, Caelestius, and Julian of Eclanum; On writings composed against Pelagius before St. Augustine’s death; On the origin and growth of Pelagianism.—[IV.] Final part, containing works relating to the Nestorian heresy.—4. Historical preface containing what occurred during the years 427–433.—VI. Translation of fifteen discourses of the impious Nestorius, with Mercator’s preface and notes by Fr. Garnier.—VII. Translation of three letters from Nestorius to St. Cyril, and four letters of the latter.—VIII. Mercator’s letter on the Nestorian heresy.—5. Extracts from Nestorius’s works; translation of the extract from these works submitted to the Council of Ephesus by Peter.—6. Translation of other extracts made by St. Cyril of Alexandria.—7. The twelve chapters of Nestorius’s blasphemies, with Mercator’s refutation.—IX. Translation of the apology written by St. Cyril for the twelve chapters against the bishops whose objections Andrew of Samosata had drafted.—X. Translation of [Col. 0038] the same author’s apology against Theodoret.—XI. Translation of the same author’s scholia on the incarnation of the Only-Begotten, the Son of God.—XII. Extracts made by Mercator from the books of Theodore of Mopsuestia, Theodoret of Cyrus, and Eutherius of Tyana, Nestorians.—8. Dissertation of Fr. Garnier on the heresy and works of Nestorius.—9. Another dissertation on the synods convened against Nestorianism.—10. Various indexes.

This volume contains the ancient collection of canons, and, as it were, the body of ancient canon law, placed after Saint Leo because Quesnel had falsely claimed that most of these canons had been made by that pope, whereas the editors prove that they were much earlier than him. BOETHIUS (continued).---VI. Dialogues on Porphyry, translated by Victorinus, in five books [Note: [Col. 0047] We ask our readers to note here the first return to pagan rhetoricians and philosophers; it was from this commentary that scholasticism and all its language, so confused and so little Christian, later arose. For these dialogues concern the following matters: genus, species, difference, property, accident, and so forth—other abstractions which possess, one knows not, more or less reality, but which are to become the foundation of science. It is the philosophical world put in the place [Col. 0048] of the real world. Jesus Christ had delivered us from this language; here it returns, never again to leave us.].---VII. Commentary on Porphyry, translated by Boethius himself, in five books.---VIII. On Aristotle’s Categories, in four books. This is again a new language introduced into Christian minds. Here are the titles of these nullities: On equivocals; On univocals; On demonstratives; On substance; On quantity; On relatives; On quality; On acting and being acted upon; On situation and position; On where and when; On having; On opposites; On the modes of the first; On the modes of the whole; On species; On movement; On the modes of having [Note: [Col. 0048] We have transcribed these theses here because all the wisdom and all the activity of the human mind will soon revolve around them. This is the foundation of science, etc. It is a complete revolution in the human mind. This is still only the isolated study of a prisoner, but it will soon become the language of every school throughout the whole world.].---IX. On Aristotle’s books *On Interpretation*, in two books and in two editions.---X. Translation of the two books of Aristotle’s *Prior Analytics*.---XI. Translation of the two books of the *Posterior Analytics*.---XII. Introduction to categorical syllogisms.---XIII. On the categorical syllogism, in two books.---XIV. On the hypothetical syllogism, in two books.---XV. Treatise on division.---XVI. Treatise on definition.---XVII. Translation of the eight books of Aristotle’s *Topics*.---XVIII. Translation of the two books of sophistical arguments.---XIX. Commentary on Cicero’s *Topics*, in six books.---XX. On topical differences, in four books.---XXI. Speculation on the kinship or bond of rhetoric.---XXII. Distinction of rhetorical topics.---Appendix.---[I.] On the discipline of students.---[II.] Commentary on the third book of the *Consolation of Philosophy*, omitted in the preceding volume.---Second part. Theological works.---XXIII. How the Trinity is one God and not three gods, with the commentaries of Gilbert of Poitiers.---XXIV. Whether the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit may be predicated substantially, idem.---XXV. How substances, in that they are, are good, although there are no substantial goods, idem.---XXVI. Short exposition of the Christian faith.---XXVII. Treatise on person and the two natures against Eutyches and Nestorius, idem.---11. Here is the order of the materials contained in it.---1. Prolegomena, Greek and Latin, extracted from the *Dialogues* of Saint Gregory the Great.---2. Prefaces on the Rule.---3. Testimonies of the ancients.---I. The Rule, with numerous notes and commentaries.---II. Discourses.---III. Letters.---Appendix.---[I.] Two spurious letters.---[II.] Monastic Order, a short work more probably by Saint Benedict of Aniane.---[III.] Documents relating to the Works of Saint Benedict.

CCCXLIV. ALBERIC the deacon.---I. Discourse on Saint Scholastica.

CCCXLV. SAINT PAUL and SAINT STEPHEN, abbots.---I. Rule for monks.

CCCXLVI. SAINT FERREOLUS, bishop of Ucetum (Uzès), about the year 558.---I. Rule for monks.

CCCXLVII. TARRATA or TARNADA, a town in the Alps or the Viennois.---I. Rule for the monks of this town, about the year 513.

[Col. 0049] CCCXLVIII. SAINT COLUMBANUS, patriarch of the Scots, in 540.---I. Rule called the Rule of a Certain Father, in all probability his.---II. Another Rule.

CCCXLIX. ANONYMOUS.---I. Ancient Roman *ordo*, for the use of monasteries.---1. Very extensive index.

VOLUME LXVII, comprising 1,296 columns. Price: 7 francs.---1848.

CCCL. DIONYSIUS THE LITTLE, Scythian monk and Roman abbot, died about the year 536. His works, collected for the first time in one volume and printed separately. The following is the order of his works.—I. Translation of the synodal letter of St Cyril and of the Council of Alexandria against Nestorius.—II. Two letters on the calculation, or date, of Easter.—1. Justellus’s preface to the following work.—III. Code of the canons of the universal Church: the Council of Nicaea, in Greek and Latin; Ancyra, 314; Neocaesarea, 314; Gangra, 325; Antioch, 341; Laodicea, 364; Constantinople (Second Ecumenical), 381; Ephesus (Third Ecumenical), 434; Chalcedon (Fourth Ecumenical), 450.—2. Justellus’s notes on the councils.—IV. Ancient code of the canons of the Roman Church, presented to Charlemagne by Adrian, including the canons of the apostles, etc.—V. Collection of decrees of eight Roman pontiffs, from Siricius, 385, to Anastasius, 498.—Ascetical works.—VI. Translation of Gregory of Nyssa’s book on the formation of man.—VII. Translation of the Life of St Pachomius.—VIII. Translation of the discourse of Proclus of Constantinople on the Virgin, Mother of God.—IX. Preface to this translation.—X. Translation of the letter of the same Proclus on the faith, addressed to the Armenians.—XI. Translation of the account of the discovery of the head of John the Baptist, Greek and Latin, with a prologue.—Appendix.—[I.] Discourse delivered at the discovery of the head of the Forerunner, Greek-Latin, translated by Combefis.—[II.] Encomium of the holy father and confessor Theodore the Studite, for the third discovery of this head, Greek-Latin, by the same.—[III.] History of Dionysius’s Paschal cycle, by Benjamin Hoffman.—[IV.] The Paschal cycle.—[V.] Paschal arguments examined according to Egyptian learning, with numerous notes.—[VI.] Translation of the letter of Proterius, bishop of Alexandria, to Pope Leo, on the celebration of Easter.—[VII.] Dionysius’s letter on the calculation of Easter, written in 526.

CCCLI. FACUNDUS, bishop of Hermiane in Africa, in 547.—1. Notice by Gallandus.—I. Defence of the Three Chapters of the Council of Chalcedon, in twelve books, addressed to Justinian.—II. Chronological table concerning the defence of the Three Chapters.—III. Book against Morianus the scholastic.—IV. Letters on the Catholic faith in defence of the Three Chapters.

CCCLII. FULGENTIUS FERRANDUS, deacon of the Church of Carthage, in 547.—1. Notice by Gallandus.—I. Seven letters.—II. Abridgment of the canons.—2. Life of St Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, placed in vol. LXV.

CCCLIII. ST JUSTUS, bishop of Urgel in Spain, in 540.—1. Notice after Fabricius.—I. Letter to Pope Sergius.—II. Mystical exposition of the Song of Songs.

CCCLIV. VIVENTIOLUS, bishop of Lyons, in 540.—1. Notice by Fabricius.—I. Two letters.

CCCLV. TROJANUS, bishop of Saintes, in 540.—I. One letter.

CCCLVI. PONTIAN, bishop in Africa, in 540.—I. One letter to the Emperor Justinian.

CCCLVII. ST CAESARIUS, bishop of Arles, in 542.—1. Notice by Gallandus.—2. His Life, by Cyprian, Firminus, and Viventius, bishops, in two books.—I. One hundred and five sermons, inserted in vol. XXXIX (the works of St Augustine).—II. Twenty homilies.—III. Rebukes addressed to those who, though having wives, are not ashamed to commit adultery.—IV. Homilies inserted in vol. L, among the works of St Eucherius.—V. Constitution of the holy bishops who assembled in the city of Arles for the observance of the canons.—VI. Discourse on widowhood, preceded by a letter of the editor Amadutius.—VII. Rule for monks, preserved by his nephew St Tetradius.—VIII. Rules for virgins.—IX. Discourse to religious women.—X. Three letters.—XI. His testament.—Appendix: doubtful works.—[I.] Two letters and three discourses.—3. Commentary on St Caesarius, taken from the Bollandists and placed at the end of the volume.—4. Letter of Pope Hormisdas confirming various statutes of St Caesarius.

[Col. 0050] CCCLVIII. ORANGE.—I. Second council, held in 529, on grace and free will.

CCCLIX. RUSTICUS, deacon of the Roman Church in 549.—1. Notice by Gallandus.—I. Disputation against the Acephali.

CCCLX. CARPENTRAS.—I. Council held in 527 and presided over by Caesarius.

VOLUME LXVIII, containing 1124 columns. Price: 6 francs.—1847.

CCCLXV. VICTOR, bishop of Capua, in 550.—I. Translation of Ammonius of Alexandria’s Gospel harmonies, with preface.—II. Translation of the responses of St Polycarp concerning certain sayings of the Saviour.—III. Fragment on the Paschal cycle, at the end of the volume.

CCCLXVI. ST NICETIUS, bishop of Trier, in 551.—1. Notice by Gallandus.—I. On the vigils of the servants of God.—II. On the benefit of psalmody.—III. Two letters.

Dissertation on the Third Synod, occasioned by this abridgment, concerning whether Origen was truly condemned there.—2. Index to the works of Arator.

VOLUME LXIX, containing 1366 columns. Price: 8 francs.—1848.

CCCLXXIII. JUSTINIAN, emperor, from 527 to 565.—I. Book against Origen, Greek and Latin.—II. Confession of the true faith against the Three Chapters.—III. Letter to the holy synod against Theodore of Mopsuestia.—IV. Letter against the defenders of the latter.

CCCLXXIV. GILDAS THE WISE, Saxon monk, in 556.—1. Notice by Gallandus.—I. Book of lamentation on the desolation of Britain, divided into three parts: one entitled *History*, another *Letter*, and the third *Rebukes to the Clergy*.

Dissertation on the monastic life of Cassiodorus.—5. Certain reasons of Baronius for proving that Cassiodorus was not a Benedictine monk.—6. Testimonies of the ancients.—I. Various letters, in twelve books.—II. Ecclesiastical history, called the *Tripartite History*, drawn from the three Greek authors Sozomen, Socrates, and Theodoret, translated by Epiphanius Scholasticus and abridged by Cassiodorus, in twelve books.—III. Chronicle, beginning with the kings of [Col. 0051] Assyria and continuing to the consulship of Eutharic and Justin, in 510.—IV. Paschal computation.

7. Tables of contents.

CASSIODORUS (continued).—V. Exposition of the Psalms.—[I.] Exposition of the Song of Songs.—VII. On the institution of divine letters.—VII. On the arts and disciplines of liberal learning.—[II.] Commentaries on rhetoric and the eight parts of rhetoric.—VIII. On orthography.—IX. On certain figures and tropes found in the commentary on the Psalms, in dictionary form.—X. On the soul.—XI. Compilations on the Epistles of the Apostles, on Acts, and on the Apocalypse, with Maffei’s preface and commentaries.—XII. Supplement taken from Cardinal Mai.—8. Table of contents.

CCCLXXVIII. ST GREGORY OF TOURS, Georgius Florentius, born in 544, died in 593. His works, after the edition of Dom Ruinart. Paris, 1699.—1. Dedication to President Achille de Harlay by Dom Ruinart.—2. Preface, by the same.—3. His Life, by Abbot Odo.—4. Testimonies of writers concerning St Gregory.—5. Preliminary material on France, the Frankish peoples, and the annals of France, from 255 to Charlemagne, in 778.—I. Ecclesiastical history of the Franks, in twelve books, with notes by Dom Ruinart.

Chronicle by the same, with its continuators, serving as an appendix to Gregory of Tours’s history of the Franks.—Continuation of Fredegar’s Chronicle: first part, by an anonymous author; second part, by another anonymous Austrasian; third part, written at the command of Count Childebrand; fourth part, written at the command of Nibelungus.—III. Certain other extracts from Fredegar relating to history: the books of miracles by Gregory of Tours; *On the Glory of the Blessed Martyrs*; *On the Passion, Miracles, and Glory of St Julian, Martyr*; *On the Glory of the Blessed Confessors*.—IV. On the miracles of St Martin, bishop of Tours, in four books.—V. Prose on St Martin.—VI. The Lives of the Fathers, or on the lives of certain blessed persons.—VII. Fragment of a commentary on the Psalms.—Doubtful works.—[I.] On the miracles of the blessed Andrew, apostle.—[II.] Another fragment: recension of the Passion of St Julian.—[III.] History of the Seven Sleepers.—[IV.] Fragment on the life of St Mauritius.—[V.] Antiphon on Saints Medard and Gildard, bishops.—[VI.] Life of St Aridius, abbot.—Appendix to his works.—[VII.] Certain ancient documents which he cites, or which explain his works.—[VIII.] Inscriptions, letters, decrees, testaments, liturgies, diplomas.—5. General index of contents.

VOLUME LXXII, containing 1140 columns. Price: 6 francs.—1849.

Exhortation to humility.—VI. Against anger.—VII. On Easter.—VIII. Verses on a basilica, on the refectory, and his epitaph.

Investigations concerning the Gallican cursus, that is, the origin and progress of the divine office in the churches of Gaul.—Appendix.—[I.] Certain proofs in support of the preceding books [Col. 0052].—3. Variants of Holy Scripture found in Gallican offices.—II. The Gallican sacramentary, or book of sacraments of the Gallican Church, published by Muratori.—4. Muratori’s preface, divided as follows: the daily Roman Mass; Advent lessons; daily lessons; Sunday lessons; blessings and exorcisms; penitential judgment, or regulation of penances to be imposed; rationale of ecclesiastical offices; Apostles’ Creed; canon of Scripture.

CDXLI. ST EUTROPIUS, abbot and bishop of Valence.—1. Historical notice taken from Antonio’s *Spanish Library*.—I. Letter to Pope Peter on the eight vices.—II. On the correction of monks and the ruin of monasteries.

CDXLII. TARRA, the monk, in 600.—I. One letter to King Reccared.

CDXLIII. DINOTHUS, abbot in 600.—I. Reply to the monk Augustine, who demanded submission to the Roman Church.

CDXLIV. DYNAMIUS, patrician of Gaul, about 601.—I. Two letters, with a notice by Fabricius.—II. Life of St Marius.—III. Life of St Maximus.

CDXLV. ST AUGUSTINE, apostle of the English, in 604.—1. Note on his life by Bollandus.—2. His Life by the monk Goscelin.—I. Letter among those of St Gregory, in vol. LXXVII.—II. Foundation of the abbey of St Augustine of Canterbury.—III. Privilege of the same abbey.

CDXLVI. ST BONIFACE IV, sixty-eighth pope, from August 608 to May 615.—1. Notice by Anastasius.—I. Roman council.—II. Decree of the Roman synod held in 610.—III. Letter of this council to Æthelberht, king of the Angles.

CDXLVII. BULGARANUS, the count, in 610.—1. Notice by Antonio.—I. Three letters.

CDXLVIII. PAUL OF MÉRIDA, deacon in 610.—I. Life of the Fathers of Mérida, followed by a dissertation on the history of that city, by T. de Vargas.

CDXLIX. GONDEMAR, king of the Goths, in 610.—I. Decree concerning the Church of Toledo, with a notice by Mariana.

CDL. MARK OF MONTE CASSINO, disciple of St Benedict, in 612.—I. Verses on St Benedict, with a notice by Fabricius.

CDLI. ST WARNAHARIUS, priest of Langres, in 615.—I. Acts of the martyrs Speusippus, Eleusippus, and Meleusippus, with a notice by Fabricius.—II. Life of St Desiderius.

CDLII. ST COLUMBANUS, abbot and confessor, in 615.—1. [Col. 0056] Notice by Fabricius.—2. Preliminary material by Gallandus.—I. Monastic rule.—II. On the measure of penances to be imposed.—III. Various instructions, or seventeen sermons.—IV. Six letters.—V. Letters and verse treatises.—3. Goldast’s notes on the writings of St Columbanus.—VI. Certain diplomas relating to the saint.

CDLIII. ST ALPHANUS, bishop of Benevento, in 615.—I. Charter renouncing the rights of the church of St Martin, with a notice by Ughelli.

CDLIV. ST AILERANUS, Irish abbot, in 615.—I. Mystical interpretation of the ancestors of our Lord Jesus Christ, with a notice by Fabricius.—II. Moral explanation of their names.

CDLV. ÆTHELBERT, king of the Angles, in 616.—I. Donations to various churches, with a notice by Fabricius.—II. Decree against plunderers of the possessions of God and of the Church.

CDLVI. ST DEUSDEDIT, sixty-ninth pope, from October 615 to November 618.—1. Notice by Anastasius.—I. Letter to Gordian, bishop of Seville.—II. Decree on the election of the Supreme Pontiff.

CDLVII. SISEBUT, king of the Goths, in 621.—1. Notice by Antonio.—I. Eight letters to various persons.—II. The life and passion of St Desiderius.

CDLVIII. ST BERTRAMNUS, bishop of Le Mans, in 623.—1. Notice by Mabillon.—2. Verses by Fortunatus on this bishop.—I. His testament.

CDLIX. ST PROTADIUS, archbishop of Besançon, in 624.—1. Notice by Dunod.—I. His liturgy composed of praises or litanies.—II. Martyrology.—III. Charter restoring the chapter of St Stephen.—IV. Two catalogues of the bishops of the Church of Besançon.

CDLX. ST BONIFACE V, seventieth pope, from December 619 to October 625.—1. Notice after Anastasius.—I. Four letters.

CDLXI. ST SONNATIUS, archbishop of Rheims, in 625.—I. Statutes, with a notice after the *Gallia Christiana*.

CDLXII. VERUS, bishop of Rodez, in 625.—I. Two letters.

CDLXIII. CLOTHAR II, king of the Franks, from 584 to 611.—1. Notice after the *Literary History of France*.—I. His edicts or ecclesiastical decrees.—II. A decree on serfs and places of refuge.—III. Edict concerning the Synod of Paris.—IV. Edict for the church of St Denis.—V. Letter to Arnulf.—Appendix.—[I.] Four charters or diplomas.

CDLXIV. HONORIUS I, seventy-first pope, from October 625 to October 638.—1. Notice after Anastasius.—I. Sixteen letters.—II. Two decrees.—III. Verses on the Ascension.—IV. Privileges granted to a monastery.—2. Extract from two letters of St Maximus in defence of Honorius.—3. Letters of Anastasius the Librarian in the same defence of Honorius.—4. His epitaph.

CDLXV. DAGOBERT, king of the Franks, from 628 to 638.—1. Notice after the *Literary History of France*.—I. Forty diplomas or edicts concerning ecclesiastical affairs.

CDLXVI. ST HADOINDUS, bishop of Le Mans, in 638.—1. Notice by Mabillon.—I. His testament and one charter.

CDLXVII. ST SULPICIUS, surnamed the Pious, bishop of Béziers, in 640.—1. His Life by an almost contemporary anonymous author.—I. Three letters.

CDLXVIII. ST AUTBERTUS, bishop of Cambrai, in 640.—1. Notice from the *Gallia Christiana*.—I. One charter for a monastery.

CDLXIX. JOHN IV, seventy-third pope, from December 640 to October 642.—1. Notice by Anastasius.—I. Four letters.

CDLXX. ST MAXIMUS, bishop of Saragossa, in 644.—1. Notice by Antonio.—I. One letter.—II. Chronicle, from 430 to 595.

CDLXXI. EUTRANDUS, subdeacon of Toledo.—I. Chronicle, from 608 to 630.

CDLXXII. VICTOR, bishop of Carthage, in 646.—1. Notice by Baronius.—I. One letter.

CDLXXIII. ST BRAULIO, bishop of Saragossa, in 646.—1. Notice by Antonio.—I. Forty-four letters.—II. Life of St Emilianus the Confessor.—III. Hymn for the same.—IV. Acts of the martyrs of Saragossa under Diocletian.

CDLXXIV. TAIUS, bishop of Saragossa, in 646.—1. Notice, by Antonio.—I. Letter.—II. Sentences, or Treatise [Col. 0057] on Religion, in five books.—Appendix.—[I.] A vision of Bishop Taio.

Addenda.—1. Critical dissertation by Fr. Marcellinus Molkenbuhr on the question whether Honorius was condemned in 680 by the Sixth General Council.

VOLUMES LXXXI–LXXXIV. Price: 28 francs.

CDLXXV. ST. ISIDORE, bishop of Seville. His Works, according to the edition of Fr. Arevalo, 1796.

VOLUME LXXXI, containing 976 columns.—1850.

1. The editor’s preliminaries, under the title *Isidoriana*, on the author’s life, deeds, and doctrine, with the prefaces of all earlier editions.—2. On apocryphal works, in four parts.—3. Comments by the Bollandists on the author.—4. History of the translation of his body.—5. Preface to a collection of his canons.—6. The author’s preface, taken from Cardinal Mai.—7. Tables.

VOLUME LXXXII, containing 1660 columns.—1850.

ST. ISIDORE (continued).—8. Prefaces to Grial’s edition.—9. Life of St. Isidore, probably by Lucas, bishop of Tuy.—10. Historical notice, by Fabricius.—11. Testimonies concerning St. Isidore.—12. Dom Grial’s notice.—I. *Etymologies*, in twenty books, with numerous notes.—II. Various fragments.—13. Variant readings drawn from different editions and manuscripts.—14. Notes by Semler.—15. Annotations by Zacharia.—16. Notes by Arevalo.

VOLUME LXXXIII, containing 1380 columns.—1850.

ST. ISIDORE (continued).—III. On Differences and the Proper Meaning of Words, in two books.—IV. Certain Allegories of Holy Scripture.—V. On the Birth and Death of the Patriarchs Praised in Scripture.—VI. On the Books of the Old and New Testament.—VII. On the Numbers Mentioned in Scripture.—VIII. Questions on the Old and New Testament, with Answers.—IX. On the Catholic Faith, against the Jews.—X. Sentences, or Treatise on Religion, in three books.—XI. On Ecclesiastical Offices.—XII. Synonyms, or Lamentations of the Sinful Soul, in two books.—XIII. Rule for Monks.—XIV. Thirteen Letters.—XV. On the Order or Arrangement of Created Things.—XVI. On the Nature of Things, a kind of treatise on physics.—XVII. Chronicle, from Adam to 654.—XVIII. History of the Kings of the Goths, Vandals, and Sueves.—XIX. The Book of Illustrious Men.—Appendix.—[I.] The Ancient Bishops of Toledo.—[II.] Certain verses attributed to St. Isidore.—[III.] Chronicle of the Visigothic Kings, from 369 to 701.—[IV.] Chronology, or Series of Gothic Kings.—[V.] Exposition of the Song of Songs.—[VI.] On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues.—[VII.] Exposition of the Mass.—[VIII.] Fourth Book of the *Sentences*.—[IX.] Exhortation to Humility.—[X.] Sentences from Scripture and the Fathers.—[XI.] Four Discourses.—[XII.] On Ecclesiastical Dogmas.—[XIII.] On the Active and Contemplative Life.—[XIV.] Rule of Life.—[XV.] and [XVI.] Two poetic pieces on penitence.—[XVII.] and [XVIII.] Two discourses.—[XIX.] and [XX.] On the Birth and Death of the Patriarchs, and on the Numbers of Scripture.—[XXI.] Glosses on Holy Scripture.—[XXII.] On the Differences and Proper Meanings of Words.—[XXIII.] Glossary, or Explanation of Barbarous or Little-Used Words.

VOLUME LXXXIV, containing 1086 columns.—1850.

ST. ISIDORE (continued).—[XXIV.] Collections of Canons attributed to St. Isidore, in ten books.—17. Preface by Ant. Gonzalès, librarian of Madrid, for the edition of 1821.—18. Councils of the Greeks down to the Council of Chalcedon; of Africa, Gaul, and Spain down to 704; decretal letters of twenty popes.—19. Historical-critical dissertation on the true and authentic collection of St. Isidore’s canons, by C. de la Serna Santander, published at Brussels in 1800.—20. Table of the canons.—21. Index of the principal passages of Scripture cited in St. Isidore’s works.—22. Index of subjects and words contained in all his Works.

VOLUMES LXXXV–LXXXVI. Price: 14 francs.

[Col. 0058]

CDLXXVI. MOZARABIC LITURGIES, long in use in Spain.

VOLUME LXXXV, containing 1064 columns.—1850.

This volume contains the Mixed Missal, according to the edition of Fr. Leslée, Jesuit, who added lengthy notes to it. The work is divided as follows.—1. Preface in the form of a dissertation, by Fr. Leslée.—I. Mozarabic Calendar.—II. The Missal, divided into two parts: the Dominical and the Sanctoral, or the feasts of the saints; its principal chants are notated.—Appendix.—[I.] Mass of St. Pelagius, composed about 930.—[II.] Ancient Calendar.—[III.] Gothic-Spanish Calendar.—2. Table of contents.

VOLUME LXXXVI, containing 1352 columns.—1850.

MOZARABIC LITURGY (continued). This volume contains the Gothic Breviary, according to the edition of Ant. Lorenzana, archbishop of Toledo. Its principal divisions are as follows.—3. Lorenzana’s preface.—III. Gothic Calendar and Breviary.—IV. The Psalter.—V. The Canticles.—VI. The Hymns.—VII. The Canonical Hours.—VIII. Commons of Saints.—IX. The Sanctoral, or Office of Saints.

VOLUME LXXXVII, containing 1472 columns. Price: 7 francs.—1851.

This volume contains writers who flourished in the second half of the seventh century, as follows:

CDLXXVII. ST. GALL, abbot and confessor, died 646.—Notices by Fabricius and Gallandus.—I. Discourse delivered at Constance at the consecration of a bishop.

CDLXXVIII–CDLXXXVII. BERNARD, COLUMBAN, ECKERARD, HARTMAN, NOTKER BALBULUS, NOTKER MEDICUS, RATPERT, STRAB, GALLUS OF FULDA, TUTELON, WALDRAM, and anonymous authors.—I. Epigrams, or sacred hymns, by these ancient Fathers of the monastery of St. Gall, with notes by Canisius.

CDLXXXVIII. ST. THEODORE, 74th pope, from November 642 to May 649.—1. Notice by Mansi, with notes by Binius.—I. Six letters, among which are one from the Churches of Africa, one from Paul, patriarch of Constantinople, to this pontiff who had rebuked him, and one from Victor, bishop of Carthage; the final three Greek-Latin.

CDLXXXIX. MAURUS, archbishop of Ravenna in 648.—I. Letter to the Roman pontiff against the Monothelites, Greek-Latin.

CDXC. ST. MARTIN I, 75th pope, from July 649 to September 655.—1. Historical notice after Mansi.—2. His Passion, after an ancient author.—I. Seventeen letters, mostly Greek-Latin, all relating to the condemnation of Monothelitism and to the persecutions which he suffered on that account.—II. Three privileges for various monasteries.

CDXCI. ST. GALLUS, bishop of Clermont, in 650.—I. One letter, printed later among those of St. Desiderius.

CDXCII. ST. PAUL, bishop of Verdun, in 650.—1. Historical notice from the *Gallia Christiana*.—I. Two letters printed there.

CDXCIII. RAURACUS, or RAURACIUS, bishop of Nevers, in 650.—I. One letter, there.

CDXCIV. FELIX, bishop of Limoges, in 650.—I. One letter, there.

CDXCV. ST. PALLADIUS, bishop of Autun, in 651.—I. One letter, there.

CDXCVI. CONSTANTIUS, bishop of Albi, in 651.—I. One letter, there.

CDXCVII. ST. ABBO, bishop of Metz, in 651.—I. One letter, there.

CDXCVIII. ST. DESIDERIUS, bishop of Cahors, in 651.—1. Notice from the *Gallia Christiana*.—2. His Life, by an anonymous author.—3. Basnage’s observations on his Life and letters.—I. Thirty-seven Letters.—II. Fragment of his testament.

CDXCIX. ST. DONATUS, bishop of Besançon, in 651.—1. His Life, after the *Histoire littéraire de la France*.—I. Rule for Virgins.

D. ST. LANDERIC, or LANDRY, bishop of Paris, in 651.—1. Notice from the *Gallia Christiana*.—I. [Col. 0059] Charter by which he grants certain immunities to the abbey of Saint-Denis.

DI. ST. SIGEBERT II, king of Austrasia, from 638 to 651.—1. Notice from the Bollandists.—2. Another Life, by Sigebert, monk of Gembloux.—3. Further details drawn from various authors.—4. Preliminaries to his diplomas.—I. Two letters and four diplomas.—Appendix.—[I.] A charter of Grimoald.

DII. ST. LIVINUS, bishop and martyr, in 654.—His Life by Boniface, a contemporary author.—I. Poetic letter to Florbert, abbot of Ghent, on the epitaph of St. Avon.

DIII. ST. EUGENIUS III, bishop of Toledo, in 657.—1. Notices by Gallandus and Antonio.—2. Another Life.—I. Thirty-one short works in verse on various subjects.—II. Dracontius’s *Hexaemeron*, corrected by St. Eugenius at the command of King Chindaswinth.—III. Eighty-nine miscellaneous poems.—[IV.] Certain apocryphal verses.—IV. Four prose letters.

DIV. VALERIUS, abbot, in 656.—1. Notices after Fr. Antonio.—I. Ten letters, or pieces, on various subjects.—II. Life of St. Fructuosus, bishop of Bracara (Braga in Spain).

DV. ST. ANNEMUNDUS, bishop of Lyons, in 656.—1. Notice from the *Gallia Christiana*.—I. One charter, printed in Volume LXXXVIII.

DVI. VERUS, bishop of Rodez, in 656.—1. Notice from the *Gallia Christiana*.—I. Letter to St. Desiderius.

DVII–DVIII. STS. ELOI and AUDOIN, bishops of Noyon and Rouen, in 659.—1. Notice from the *Gallia Christiana*.—2. Life of St. Eloi, written by St. Audoin, in two books.—I. Sixteen homilies of St. Eloi.—II. One discourse published by Cardinal Mai.—III. Letters and charters of the two saints.

DIX. CLOVIS II, king of Neustria and Burgundy, from 638 to 656.—I. Diplomas of King Clovis.—[I.] Three apocryphal diplomas.

DX. ST. BATHILDE, wife of Clovis.—1. Notice on Bathilde, after Mabillon.—2. Life of the saint after a contemporary author.

DXI. MARCULF, the monk, about 660.—Formulas concerning private and public affairs, in two books, with Bignon’s preface and notes, and a notice by Fabricius.—Appendix.—[I.] Ancient formulas, by an anonymous author.—[II.] Ancient formulas according to Roman law, edited by Sirmond.—[III.] Other formulas by an unknown author, edited by Bignon.—[IV.] Another edition of Marculf’s formulas, edited by Lindenbrog, with significant variants.—[V.] Formulas called those of Angers.—[VI.] Other ancient formulas, collected and edited by Baluze.—[VII.] Other formulas, edited by Lepelletier, called *Alsaticae*, relating to the time of Louis the Pious and to the kingdom of Austrasia, whereas those of Marculf relate to the kingdom of Burgundy.—[VIII.] Fifteen unpublished formulas, published by M. Pardessus.—[IX.] Ancient formulas concerning the promotion of bishops after the restoration of freedom of elections.—[X.] Ancient formulas of exorcism and excommunications.—[XI.] Formulas used to regulate, among combatants, trials by the judgment of God, with a preliminary and very curious dissertation by Muratori.

DXII. ST. CUMMIANUS, bishop or abbot, in 661.—I. Letter on the Easter controversy.—II. On the Measure of Penances to Be Imposed, with a preface by Labbe.

DXIII. VITALIAN, 77th pope, from July 657 to January 672.—I. Ten letters, taken from Mansi.

DXIV. JONAS, abbot of Elnonai, in the diocese of Tournai, in 670.—I. Life of St. Columban.—II. Life of St. Eustasius, second abbot of Luxeuil.—III. Life of St. Attala, of St. Bertulf, and of St. Burgundofara, with her testament.—IV. Book of the Miracles of St. John, abbot of Reomus, diocese of Langres.

DXV. ST. FRUCTUOSUS, bishop of Braga, in 670.—1. Notice taken from Antonio’s *Spanish Library*.—I. Rule for Monks.—II. Common Monastic Rule.—III. One letter.—IV. Three poetic pieces.

DXVI. CHRODOBERT, bishop of Tours, in 670.—I. Judgment concerning the adulterous woman, printed in Volume LIV.

DXVII. ST. FARO, bishop of Meaux, in 670.—1. Notice from the *Gallia Christiana*.—I. Two charters of privilege.

DXVIII. ST. ADEODATUS, 78th pope, from April 672 to June 676.—1. Notice from the *Liber Pontificalis*.—I. One letter and one privilege.

DXIX. ST. DONUS, or DOMNUS I, 79th pope, from November 676 to April 678.—1. Notice after Mansi.—I. Poetic epitaph of Pope Honorius.—II. Greek-Latin letter addressed to him by Emperor Constantine concerning the reconciliation of the Eastern and Western Church.

[Col. 0060] DXX. ST. AGATHO, 80th pope, from June 678 to January 682.—1. Notice after Mansi.—I. Four Greek-Latin letters concerning Church affairs.

DXXI. DAMIANUS, bishop of Ticinum (or Pavia), in 679.—1. Notices by Fabricius and Ughelli.—I. Letter to Emperor Constantine.

DXXII. ST. AMAND, bishop of Utrecht, in 679.—1. His Life, by an anonymous author.—I. One charter and his testament.—2. Two hymns in his honor.

DXXIII. ST. MANSUETUS, bishop of Milan, in 680.—I. The letter written in his name by Damianus.

Diplomas and pious donations of the four Frankish kings of the first dynasty, from 660 to 700.

DXXIV. CLOTAIRE III, king of Neustria, from 656 to 670.—I. Five ecclesiastical precepts.

DXXV. CHILDERIC II, from 656 to 673.—I. Eleven diplomas, with preliminaries.

DXXVI. ST. DAGOBERT II, from 672 to 679.—I. Four diplomas, followed by four documents of Abbess Irmina and the testament of Adela, daughter of Dagobert.

DXXVII. THEODORIC III, king of Neustria, from 673 to 691.—I. Seventeen diplomas.—II. Two charters.

DXXVIII. LOMBARD KINGS.—I. Forty-six ecclesiastical diplomas given by them or during their reigns, taken from Muratori.—II. Eight donations.

VOLUME LXXXVIII, containing 1552 columns. Price: 8 francs.—1850.

DXXIX. VENANTIUS FORTUNATUS, bishop of Poitiers, in 600, after the edition of Michelangelo Luchi, 1786.—1. Editor’s preface.—2. Life of Fortunatus according to his works.—3. Testimonies of the ancients.—First part, in verse.—I. Miscellanies, in eleven books, with numerous notes.—II. Life of St. Martin, in four books.—III. On the Misfortunes, or Ruin, of Thuringia.—Second part, in prose.—IV. Lives [lacuna] of St. Hilary, bishop of Poitiers.—V. Of St. Germanus, bishop of Paris.—VI. Of St. Albinus, bishop of Angers.—VII. Of St. Paternus, bishop of Avranches.—VIII. Of St. Radegund, queen.—IX. Of St. Amantius, bishop of Rodez.—X. Of St. Remigius, bishop of Reims.—XI. Of St. Medard, bishop of Noyon.—XII. Of St. Mark, bishop of Paris.—XIII. Of St. Leobinus, bishop of Chartres.—XIV. Of St. Maurilius, bishop of Angers.—XV. Passion of Saints Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius.—XVI. The creed called that of St. Athanasius, found in the Breviary and probably by Fortunatus.—XVII. Exposition of this creed, certainly by Fortunatus.—Appendix.—[I.] Various newly edited poetic pieces.

DXXX. DEFENSOR, monk of Ligugé near Poitiers, in the eighth century.—1. Notices after the *France littéraire* and Fabricius.—I. Collection of Sparks, or Sentences Drawn from the Orthodox Fathers.

DXXXI. EVANTIUS, abbot of Troclar in the diocese of Albi, about the eighth century.—I. Letter against those who say that animal blood may not be eaten, with a notice from the *France littéraire* and Fabricius.

DXXXII. ST. ARCULF, bishop, and ST. ADAMNAN, abbot, about 690.—1. Notices by Cave and Fabricius.—2. Basnage’s observations on St. Adamnan.—3. Other testimonies extracted from the Martyrology.—I. Life of St. Columba, in three books.—4. Mabillon’s observations on the following book.—II. On the Holy Places, according to the account of Arculf, bishop of Gaul, in three books.—5. Curious description of the condition of Palestine at that time, with several woodcuts.—III. Eight canons.

DXXXIII. CRISCONIUS, bishop of Africa, in the eighth century.—1. Notice by Fabricius.—2. Justellus’s notice.—I. Abridgment of the Canons of Fulgentius Ferrandus, deacon of Carthage.—II. Canonical abridgment and concordance of the decrees of councils and popes down to Gelasius, with a table of contents at the end of the volume.

DXXXIV. MAGISTER, unknown author of the seventh century.—I. Rule for Monks.

DXXXV. ANONYMOUS.—I. Rule for Virgins, under the name *Cujusdam Patris* (“Of a Certain Father”).—II. Discourse on the Ten Virgins.

Pious donations of the last Frankish kings of the first dynasty.

DXXXVI. DAGOBERT III.—I. Twenty-six diplomas.

DXXXVII. CHILPERIC II.—I. Ten, the same.

DXXXVIII. THEODORIC IV.—I. Ten, the same.

DXXXIX. CHILPERIC III.—I. Four, the same.

DXL. Donations, pious testaments, etc., of bishops, abbots, mayors of the palace, dukes of France, and illustrious [Col. 0061] Franks, down to the end of the second dynasty: eighty-one in number.

EIGHTH CENTURY.

VOLUME LXXXIX, containing 1344 columns. Price: 7 francs.—1850.

DXLI. SERGIUS I, 85th pope, from December 687 to September 701.—1. Notice from the *Liber Pontificalis*.—I. One letter and one privilege.

DXLII. JOHN VI, 86th pope, from October 701 to January 705.—1. Notice from the *Liber Pontificalis*.—I. Letters or councils, with Pagi’s observations on Wilfrid, bishop of York.

DXLIII. JOHN VII, 87th pope, from March 705 to October 707.—1. Notice, same source.—I. Two letters.

DXLIV. ST. ALDHELM, bishop of Shrewsbury, in 709, after the edition recently published in London by Dr. Giles.—1. His Life, by Fabricius.—2. Another Life.—3. Extracts concerning St. Aldhelm.—I. Fourteen letters.—II. In Praise of Virginity.—III. Letter to Acircius, or the Book of the Number Seven and of Metres.—IV. Riddles and rules concerning metrical feet.—V. His poems: Praises of Virgins.—VI. On the Eight Principal Vices.—VII. On the basilica built by Bugge, daughter of the king of the Angles.—VIII. On the altars dedicated to Mary and the twelve apostles.—IX. Verses in honor of the apostles.—X. Fragment on the Day of Judgment.—XI. Letter of an anonymous writer to his anonymous sisters.—XII. Eight diplomas.

DXLV. CONSTANTINE, 89th pope, from March 708 to April 715.—1. Notice from the *Liber Pontificalis*.—I. Four letters.

DXLVI. CEOLFRID, Anglo-Saxon priest, in 709.—1. Notice after Fabricius.—I. Letter to Nectan, king of the Picts, concerning Catholic Easter and the Roman tonsure.

DXLVII. FELIX, bishop of Ravenna, in 717.—1. Historical notice taken from Ughelli.—I. Prologue to the sermons of St. Peter Chrysologus.

DXLVIII. ST. BENEDICT CRISPUS, bishop of Milan, in 725.—1. Notice taken from Ughelli.—I. Complaint in the synod against Pope Constantine, who had deprived him, contrary to ancient custom, of the consecration of the bishop of Pavia.—2. Muratori’s response to the preceding piece.—3. Cardinal Mai’s observation on the following poems.—II. The Poetic Physician.—III. Epitaph of King Céadual.

DXLIX. ST. EGBERT, archbishop of York, in 729.—1. Notice after Fabricius.—2. Mansi’s notice.—I. Extracts from the sayings and canons of the holy Fathers for the establishment of ecclesiastical discipline.—II. The Penitential.—III. Dialogue on Catholic Instruction.—IV. Canons on the Remedies for Sins.

DL. ST. GREGORY II, 90th pope, from May 715 to February 731.—1. Notices after the *Liber Pontificalis* and Fabricius.—I. Nineteen letters.—II. Four penitential canons.—III. One capitulary.

DLI. ST. WILLIBRORD, bishop of Utrecht, in 739.—I. Eighteen charters or diplomas.

DLII. ST. GREGORY III, 91st pope, from March 731 to November 741.—1. Notice from the *Liber Pontificalis*.—I. Nine letters.—II. Extracts from the Fathers on various crimes and their remedies.

DLIII. ST. BONIFACE, bishop of Mainz and martyr, in 747.—1. Notice by Fabricius.—2. Mabillon’s preface on the two following Lives.—3. Life by Willibald, his disciple.—4. Another Life, by Othlo, an eleventh-century Benedictine monk.—5. Appendix to this double Life.—6. Editor’s notice.—7. Serrarius’s preface to the letters of St. Boniface.—8. Two prefaces by Wurdtwein.—9. Preface by Dr. Giles.—I. One hundred and twelve letters.—II. Oath by which he binds himself to Pope Gregory II.—III. Eleven councils held in his time.—10. Mansi’s dissertation on these councils and on the letters of Boniface and Zachary.—IV. Fifteen discourses.—V. Short works: Life and Martyrdom of St. Livin.—VI. On Penitence.—VII. Riddles on the virtues, sent in verse to his sister.

DLIV. ST. ZACHARY, 92nd pope, from November 741 to March 752.—1. Notice from the *Liber Pontificalis*.—I. Twenty letters.—II. Three decrees.

DLV. STEPHEN II, 93rd pope, in March 752, and dead after four days’ reign.—1. Notice from the *Liber Pontificalis*.—I. Thirteen letters.—II. On a revelation which he received.—III. Nineteen canons.

DLXV. BEDE THE VENERABLE, English Benedictine, born in 735.

His Works, according to the recent edition of Messrs. Smith and Giles. Bede was the encyclopedic man of his age; his Works represent the universal learning of his time. We shall describe them precisely.

VOLUME XC, containing 1200 columns.—1850.

Preliminaries.—1. Historical eulogy, taken from Mabillon’s Benedictine Acts.—2. Another Life, written partly by Cuthbert, his disciple, and partly by an anonymous eleventh-century author.—3. Another Life, written by a very ancient anonymous author.—4. Another, very short Life.—5. Preliminary comments on his Life, composed by Turgot and taken from the Bollandists.—6. Research on the commentaries of the Venerable Bede and Florus, deacon of Lyons, on St. Paul, according to the words of St. Augustine, taken from Mabillon’s *Analecta*.—7. Dissertation on his writings, by Oudin.—8. Notice taken from Fabricius.—9. Testimonies of ancient authors concerning Bede.

First part of the Works: didactic works.—I. Book of Orthography, in dictionary form.—II. Book of Metrical Art, or the Measurement of Words.—III. On Figures, or Tropes, of Holy Scripture.—IV. On Nature, in one book, with the *variorum* notes. This book contains all the physical science known at that time; the notes provide figures of all divisions, spheres, computations, and the geography of heaven and earth.—V. On the Division of Time.—VI. On the Reckoning of Time, or explanation of days, weeks, months, years, centuries, etc., among all nations, with numerous figures.—VII. An abridgment of history under the title of the Six Ages of the World.—VIII. On the Method of Computation, in which several of the foregoing questions are taught by questions and answers.—IX. On the Celebration of Easter, or the Spring Equinox.—X. On the Order of Easter Weekdays.—XI. Book on Thunder.—Doubtful or apocryphal books.—[I.] The elements of Donatus’s grammatical art, revised by Bede.—[II.] On the Eight Parts of Speech.—[III.] On Arithmetical Numbers.—[IV.] Dialogues on Computation.—[V.] On the Division of Time.—[VI.] Arithmetical Problems with Their Solutions.—[VII.] On the Method of Calculating.—[VIII.] On the Division of Numbers.—[IX.] On the Method of Speaking and Counting on the Fingers.—[X.] On Ounces and Pounds.—[XI.] On Lunar Arguments, or problems for finding weekdays, epacts, dates, etc.—[XII.] Popular Computation, or Ephemeris, on the same problems as the preceding works, with a list of months bearing the saints, together with a poetic martyrology for every month.—[XIII.] Computation of Embolisms.—[XIV.] On the Calculation [Col. 0063] of the Year Established by Julius Caesar, and on its use for ecclesiastical feasts.—[XV.] Theory of Embolisms, by Manfred.—[XVI.] Nineteen-Year Cycles, according to the calculations of Dionysius Exiguus, the Blessed Cyril, and Bede, computed to the year 1633.—[XVII.] On the Easter Cycle, to the year 1595.—[XVIII.] Canons of the Nineteen Lunar Revolutions.—[XIX.] On the Constitution of the Celestial and Terrestrial World.—[XX.] Theoretical Music and Square, or Notated, Music.—[XXI.] On the Circles of the Sphere and the Pole.—[XXII.] On the Planets and Their Signs, with ancient plates.—[XXIII.] Order of the Planets according to Their Nature and Number, according to the Hebrews.—[XXIV.] On the Signs, or Constellations, of Heaven and the Stars Composing Them.—[XXV.] Notes, or Labors of the Months, with figures.—[XXVI.] Weather Prognostication according to the day on which the year begins.—[XXVII.] Method of making a dial or clock from the shadow of the human body.—[XXVIII.] On the Astrolabe.—[XXIX.] On the Birth of Children.—[XXX.] On the days on which one should be bled or purged, and the veins that must be opened.—[XXXI.] On the Seven Wonders of the World, different from those ordinarily related.—[XXXII.] Letter of Petosiris to Necepsus, king of Egypt, on divination concerning life and death, with a figure for divining.—[XXXIII.] Philosophical sentences or axioms, collected from Aristotle, Cicero, Averroes called the Commentator, the author of the *Six Principles*, Porphyry, the Alchemists, Boethius, Aristotle cited under the name “the Philosopher,” Seneca, Plato, Avicenna—who says, “God does not understand simple things” (col. 990, line 69)—Themistius, Aegidius, Marcilius Priscian, Apuleius, Petrus Hispanus, and Simplicius, with certain explanations and qualifications in alphabetical form. It is scholasticism beginning to develop.—[XXXIV.] Proverbs drawn from Scripture and arranged alphabetically.—[XXXV.] Book of Substances.—[XXXVI.] Elements of Philosophy, in four books.—[XXXVII.] Form of Noah’s Ark.—[XXXVIII.] On the Languages of Nations.—[XXXIX.] Explanation of the Sayings of the Sibyls.—[XL.] *Famina Hisperica*, a work in an unusual Latin, published by Cardinal Mai and placed here as an appendix.—10. Table.

VOLUME XCI, containing 1260 columns.—1850.

On the Acts of the Apostles.—XXX. Lindenbrog’s dedication and preface.—8. Notice by John Trithemius.—I. *On the Deeds of the Lombards*, in six books, with numerous notes. The following engravings are found therein: the golden crown of King Agilulf; a coin of Liutprand; the golden crown called the Iron Crown; the golden crown of Queen Theodelinda; a bas-relief representing these crowns and the baptism of Our Lord Jesus Christ; a specimen of the writing of the *Miscellaneous History*; two bas-reliefs from Monza Cathedral, representing the coronation of the Lombard kings.—II. DCVI. DAGULFUS, in 809.—I. Certain verses placed upon the Psalter written in golden letters which he was sending to Charlemagne, who presented it to Hadrian I.

DCVII. SAINT ANGILBERT, abbot of Centulum (Saint-Riquier near Amiens), in 814.—1. Notice by Mabillon.—I. On the restoration of the monastery of Centulum.—II. Certain rubrics.—III. Six poems.

DCVIII. LEIDRAD, bishop of Lyons, in 816.—1. Notice by Gallandus.—I. Book on the sacrament of baptism, sent to Emperor Charles.—II. Three letters.

DCIX. AMALARIUS, archbishop of Trier, in 815.—1. [Col. 0069] Notice by Fabricius.—I. Letter to Charles the Great concerning the baptismal ceremony.

Extract from the Penitential of John of God.—IV. Observations and notes on Theodore’s work.—V. Defence of Theodore against every charge of novelty.

DCXI. ASCARIUS and TUSAREDUS, of the eighth century.—I. Two letters.

9. Index to Saint Paulinus.

VOLUMES C–CI. Price: 15 francs.

DCXII. BLESSED FLACCUS ALBINUS, or ALCUIN, abbot, an Englishman who came to France about 790, where, together with Charlemagne, he restored letters, and where he died about 864.

VOLUME C, containing 1,176 columns.—1851.

1. General preface.—2. Commentary on Alcuin’s Life by the editor Frobenius.—3. Another Life of Alcuin.—4. Preface to this Life by André Duchesne.—5. Testimonies of authors concerning Alcuin.—Works. First Part.—I. Two hundred and thirty-two letters, followed by an index of persons.—Second Part. Exegetical Treatises.—II. Questions and answers on Genesis.—III. *Enchiridion*, or a devout and brief exposition of the penitential psalms, Psalm 118, and the gradual psalms.—IV. Epitome on the Song of Songs.—V. Commentary on Ecclesiastes.—VI. Explanation of the Hebrew names of the ancestors of Our Lord Jesus Christ.—VII. Commentary on the Gospel of Saint John, in seven books.—VIII. Treatise on the three Epistles of Saint Paul to Titus, Philemon, and the Hebrews.—IX. Short commentary on certain sayings of Saint Paul.—X. Commentary on the Apocalypse, in five books.—6. Index to the commentaries on the Apocalypse.

VOLUME CI, containing 1,520 columns.—1851.

BLESSED FLACCUS ALBINUS, or ALCUIN, abbot (continued).—Third Part. Dogmatic Works.—XI. *On Faith in the Holy and Indivisible Trinity*, in five books, addressed to Charlemagne.—XII. Twenty-eight questions on the Trinity addressed to Fredegisus.—XIII. Book on the procession of the Holy Spirit.—XIV. Book against the heresy of Felix.—XV. Against Felix, bishop of Urgel, in seven books.—XVI. Against the letter addressed to him by Elipand, in four books, in which he refutes its perverse assertions, with four preliminary letters.—XVII. Alcuin’s letter to his daughter in Christ, to guard her against the doctrines of the Adoptionists.—7. Historical dissertation on the heresy of Elipand of Toledo and Felix of Urgel, by Frobenius.—8. Dogmatic-historical dissertation showing, against the Christian Walch, that Alcuin rightly accused Felix and Elipand of Nestorianism, since they maintained that Jesus Christ is Son of God by adoption, by Dom Enhueber.—Fourth Part. Liturgical and Moral Works.—XVIII. Book of Sacraments.—XIX. On the use of psalms, with various formulae adapted for daily use.—XX. Offices for weekdays, with psalms, hymns, confessions, and litanies.—XXI. Letter on the ceremonies of baptism.—XXII. Book of Virtues and Vices.—XXIII. *On the Reason of the Soul*, a book addressed to the virgin Eulalia.—XXIV. On confession of sins.—Fifth Part. Hagiographical Works.—XXV. Life of Saint Martin of Tours.—XXVI. Life of Saint Vedast, bishop of Arras.—XXVII. Lives of Saint Richarius, priest, and Willibrord, bishop of Utrecht, in two books, prose and verse.—Sixth Part. Poetic Works.—XXVIII. Prayers, histories, songs, inscriptions, epistles, epigrams, enigmas.—XXIX. Poem on the pontiffs and saints of the Church of York.—Seventh Part. Didactic Works.—XXX. Grammar, in dialogue form.—XXXI. On orthography.—XXXII. Dialogue on rhetoric and the virtues.—XXXIII. On dialectic.—XXXIV. Dialogue between Pippin, a royal and noble young man, and Albinus the teacher (Alcuin).—XXXV. On the course and leap of the moon and leap-years.—Eighth Part. Doubtful Works.—9. Dissertation on the antiquity and author of the following confession of faith, by Mabillon, with a refutation of Basnage’s critical remarks [Col. 0070] against the Dissertation.—[I.] Confession of faith, in four parts.—[II.] Disputations of children, by questions and answers.—[III.] Fifty-three propositions of Alcuin, teacher of Charles the Great, emperor, to stimulate young people.—[IV.] Nine prose and verse treatises also attributed to him.—Ninth Part. Spurious Works.—[V.] Book of Divine Offices.—[VI.] Marian verses, by Amalarius, archbishop of Trier.—[VII.] Book of Antichrist, by Adso, abbot of Dervum (Montier-en-Der), near Châlons-sur-Marne.—[VIII.] Four homilies.—[IX.] Various poems.—Appendices.—[X.] Three letters of Angilbert.—[XI.] Letter of a Spanish bishop to the bishops of Gaul on Adoptionism.—[XII.] Synodal letter of the Council of Frankfurt.—10. Nine letters of Dom Gregory Majancius on the acts and writings of Elipand.—[XIII.] Candidus, *On the Image of God*.—History.—[XIV.] Notice on the churches of the city of Rome.—[XV.] Very fine correspondence between Alexander, king of Macedonia, and Dindimus, king of the Brahmans.—11. Critical remarks on the preceding letters, by Henri Martin.—Liturgy and History.—[XVI.] Book of Sacred Prayers.—12. Historical notes.—13. Historical eulogy of Alcuin, taken from Mabillon’s *Acts of the Benedictine Saints*.

VOLUME CII, containing 1,140 columns. Price: 6 francs.—1851.

Learned and devout explanation, from the holy Fathers, of the Gospels and Epistles read in churches during the course of the year, accompanied by a summary by the editor George Ulrich.—II. *The Diadem of Monks*, in one hundred chapters.—III. Commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict, with a preface in verse.—IV. *The Royal Way*: exhortations on the various virtues.—V. Account of the acts of the Roman conference concerning the creed of faith, between Pope Leo and two envoys of King Charles.—2. Some notes on the conferences of Smaragdus, by Dom Pitra.

DCXIV. LOUIS THE PIOUS and his son LOTHAIR.—I. Five charters.

DCXV. MAGNUS, archbishop of Sens, died in 818.—I. Book on the mystery of baptism, published by Charlemagne’s command.—II. Notes or abbreviations used in legal books, sent to Charlemagne.

DCXVI. SAINT LEO III, ninety-eighth pope, from December 795 to June 816.—1. Historical notice taken from Mansi.—I. Eighteen letters, and in addition one Greek-Latin letter from Nicephorus, patriarch of Constantinople.—II. Three privileges or bulls.

DCXVII. STEPHEN IV, ninety-sixth pope, from August 768 to February 772.—1. Historical notice taken from Mansi, containing certain extracts from his bulls.

DCXVIII. PASCHAL I, one-hundredth pope, from January 817 to February 824.—1. Notice after Mansi.—I. Five letters.

DCXIX. REMIGIUS, bishop of Chur in Raetia, in the year 820.—I. Notice after Hartzheim.—I. Forty-nine canons for the use of his Church.

VOLUME CIII, containing 1,476 columns. Price: 8 francs.—1851.

Explanation of the difference between summaries, chapters, and canons of the Gospels, with arguments for each evangelist and an explanation of those arguments.—III. Book of Christian Rulers or Governors, addressed to Charlemagne or Louis the Pious, with a preface by Cardinal Mai.—IV. Explanation of Saint Jerome’s prefaces to the Gospels.

Code of monastic and canonical rules prescribed by the holy Fathers for monks, canons, and nuns, with observations by Father Marianus Brochius; it is the collection of all the rules of Eastern and Western Fathers.—II. Concordance of all these rules.—III. Two letters.—IV. Five treatises.—V. Sixteen charters relating to the monastery of Aniane.—2. Table of contents for the concordance of rules.

VOLUME CIV, containing 1,352 columns. Price: 7 francs.—1851.

DCXXII. SAINT AGOBARD, bishop of Lyons, born in 779, died in 840.—1. Notice after Gallandus.—2. Preface by Baluze.—3. Eulogies written of him by authors.—4. Preface of Papirius Masson for his edition of 16[…..]5.—5. Epitome of his Life, by the same author.—I. Book against the doctrine of Felix of Urgel, addressed to Louis the Pious, with Baluze’s notes.—II. On the insolence of the Jews.—III. Letter of Agobard, Bernard of Vienne, and Ebo of Cavaillon to Emperor Louis the Pious on Jewish superstitions.—IV. Consultation and supplication to the great men of the palace concerning the baptism of Jewish slaves or serfs.—V. Letter to the bishop of Narbonne on the need to avoid familiarity and association with Jews.—VI. Against the law of Gundobad and the impious combats it authorized.—VII. On priestly privilege and right.—VIII. Against the absurd popular beliefs concerning hail and thunder.—IX. Against the objections of Abbot Fredegisus.—X. Against the impious precept concerning the baptism of Jewish serfs.—XI. On the illusion of certain signs or marks, [diabolical].—XII. Tearful letter of complaint concerning injustices, addressed to Manfredus, a great man of the palace.—XIII. On the form of ecclesiastical government.—XIV. Against the superstition of those who believe that paintings and images of saints ought to receive a duty of adoration.—XV. On the dispensation of ecclesiastical affairs.—XVI. Book of Divine Sentences, with certain short notes against the condemnable opinion of those who think that God’s judgment is manifested by fire, water, or arms.—XVII. Exhortation to the people on the truth of faith and the establishment of every good.—XVIII. Letter full of tears on the division of the empire of the Franks among the sons of Emperor Louis.—XIX. Comparison between ecclesiastical and political government, proving that the dignity of the Church is far above the majesty of empire; it includes a letter of Pope Gregory IV to the bishops of the Franks.—XX. Apologetic book for the sons of Emperor Louis against their father.—XXI. Small charter offered to King Lothair at the Synod of Compiègne.—XXII. Letter on hope and fear.—XXIII. Book on divine psalmody.—XXIV. On the correction of the Antiphonary.—XXV. Against the four books of Abbot Amalarius.—XXVI. Two poems.

Continuation of this chronology, from St. Gregory the Great to Stephen III in 768, by Cajetan Cenni, with a preface by the same.—36. Appendix containing fragments of a Julian calendar, with festivals and the principal events of the Julian family, and several other inscribed monuments relating to chronology.—37. Analytical treatise on the pre-eminence and authority of the Holy See, or Dogmatic History of the Holy See down to St. Leo, written in French by Sommier, archbishop of Caesarea, and translated into Latin by Cenni.—38. Charter of donation made by a certain Theudovius to a church, with various engraved monuments of that period, and a preface by Bianchini. The work of Anastasius now follows:

I. History of the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs, from St. Peter to St. Sylvester in 335. In each life are found: first, Anastasius’s text; second, the catalogue of pontiffs called that of Liberius, the fullest extant; then the variants or marginal notes of Fabrotti, Lucas Holstenius, and Francesco Peña; followed by the *variorum* notes of Bencini, Binius, Labbe, Bianchini, Ciaconius, Pagi, Sommier, d’Altaserra, and Schelestrate; finally Bianchini’s notes, divided into chronological and historical notes.—Second, engraved monuments serving as proofs. These monuments are: first, a glass patera bearing the image of St. Xystus and St. Timothy; second, Pope Pius I consecrating St. Praxedes and St. Pudentiana to God; third, six medals, and the condition of Britain under the first emperors; fourth, the celebrated statue of St. Hippolytus, bishop of Porto, with its inscriptions; fifth, various urns and certain instruments used for Mass; sixth, Constantine and the judges administering justice; seventh, another patera containing the figures and names of St. Peter, St. Paul, and Mary.—Moreover, there are the Annals of the pontificate of St. Peter, from the Ascension to the foundation of the three sees of Rome, Alexandria, and Antioch.

VOLUME CXXVIII, containing 1468 columns.

ANASTASIUS, called the Librarian (continued).—Continuation of the lives of the popes, from St. Mark in 336 to Stephen V in 885, including the popes from Adrian II to Stephen VI, believed to be the work of William the Librarian, successor of Anastasius; with the same notes as in the preceding volume, supplemented by those of Maffei, Baldinus, Cenni, and Thomas Acetus.—The engraved monuments in this volume are: first, a medal of Crispus Caesar, son of Constantine; second, figures of the holy martyrs Maximus and Scandinus; fourth, representation of the crib of Jesus Christ preserved in the Liberian basilica; fifth, Abraham extending hospitality to the three angels; sixth, the appearance of the body of St. Leo the Great at the opening of his tomb in 1714; seventh, mosaic constructed by Pelagius II; eighth, a medal of Emperor Honorius; ninth, an interior view of the Pantheon; tenth, a medal of Pope Honorius; eleventh, a ring bearing the title “Maximus the Levite”; twelfth, a medal of Chilperic.—39. Seventh catalogue: the lives of the Roman pontiffs, from St. Peter to Paul I in 767, from a manuscript of Verona.—40. Eighth catalogue of popes, ending with Vigilius in 555.—41. Alphabetical index of subjects.

By Sigebert.—II. Book of Ecclesiastical Writers, with a notice from *La France littéraire*, the scholia of Aubertus Miraeus, and a table of the writers whom he discussed.—III. Three letters: one against Pope Paschal; two against the slanders of laypeople concerning married priests; the third letter to Hildebrand, who was slandering royal power. The editors did not publish these three letters because of certain slanders against the popes. We do not believe that this suppression was necessary; the authority of the sovereign pontiffs is firmly enough established not to require concealing a few false accusations.—XI. Rhythmical poem on Saint Lucy.—XII. Fragment on Saint Lullus.

[Col. 0133]

III. ALPHABETICAL INDEX OF ALL DOCTORS, FATHERS, OR ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS WHOSE WORKS AND WRITINGS, EVEN THE SMALLEST, ARE FOUND IN THE LATIN PATROLOGY.

[Note: [Col. 0133] NOTE. The first number indicates the date or year; the second, the volume; the third, the column.]

NOTICE.

In this Index, as its title indicates, are found not only authors and the innumerable writers scattered throughout the volumes of the entire *Patrology*, but also all those whose writings remain deposited here and there among the works of all these authors—whether friendly, foreign, or even hostile to the Catholic faith. Therefore, friendly Reader, do not be surprised if here you encounter the names of pagans and even of heretics; we have printed these in italics, so that no one may mistake the latter for the former. Moreover, all the authors of ancient documents occur here; here is the beautiful and pious host of donors, benefactors, and founders, whose names shine like stars amid the darkness of the ages; there are the framers of laws, canons, and holy Rules. And, insofar as possible, we have recorded the year, age, and profession of each.

# IV. CHRONOLOGICAL INDEX OF ALL DOCTORS, FATHERS, AND ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS OF THE WESTERN CHURCH WHOSE WORKS AND WRITINGS, EVEN THE SMALLEST, ARE FOUND IN THE COURSE OF LATIN PATROLOGY

## Notice

In compiling this index, we initially hesitated over whether a true and properly so-called chronology ought not to be preferred to the chronological order adopted by the editors of the *Patrologia*. For the writings of authors are not everywhere published strictly year by year; rather, they are arranged only approximately, either for a better form of the volume or because of the connection and affinity of the same subject matter, with the result that chronology is sometimes slightly disturbed. But, after more mature consideration, we judged it much more useful and in every respect more convenient for each reader to alter nothing in the order already followed for the authors, and to proceed through the volumes, as through the columns, without any interruption. Thus mind and eye may become more readily accustomed to the individual volumes and retain their locations—something that could scarcely have been achieved otherwise. Moreover, the periods in our *Course* are not so transposed that they cannot easily be restored, as is apparent to the reader. As for authors whose writings are found scattered here and there in different places or even volumes, we have restored to each what properly belongs to him, and the various columns in which his writings are read are assigned. We took the greatest care to avoid confusion both of years and of names, and that nothing should be attributed to anyone except what properly belongs to him. As in the preceding index, we have marked in italics pagan authors, those alien to the Catholic faith, and anonymous writers.

The Roman numeral indicates the volume; the Arabic numeral before the dash gives the year, while that after the dash gives the column or columns.

V. STATISTICAL INDEX OF ALL AUTHORS WHOSE PRINCIPAL WRITINGS ARE PRINTED IN THE COURSE OF LATIN PATROLOGY.

PRELIMINARY NOTICE.

The preceding indexes contain authors of various kinds, among whom it is important to establish certain distinctions. Accordingly, there follows a statistical list in which the succession of these authors is presented, no longer indiscriminately interwoven, but arranged in orders according to their importance and rank, their status and condition, and their country and nation. Hence come the series of holy Doctors, Fathers, Supreme Pontiffs, and writers of greater and lesser importance from every nation. At the same time, the individual ranks of the ecclesiastical hierarchy are collected, as are also those who, although belonging to the civil order, nevertheless treated matters of the Church.

We divide all the authors of Patrology into two series. The first comprises holy Doctors, Fathers, and Supreme Pontiffs; the second lists writers both of greater and of lesser importance.

In this index we follow chronological order, indicating neither volume nor column. If the reader wishes to know these, let him consult Index III, namely the alphabetical index of authors.

FIRST SERIES: DOCTORS, FATHERS, AND SUPREME PONTIFFS. This series includes the holy Fathers of the Church, of whom a threefold order is distinguished: 1. holy Doctors of the Church; 2. those customarily called Fathers; 3. Supreme Pontiffs, by reason of their rank.

FIRST ORDER.

Eight holy Doctors are commonly reckoned among the Latins—or ten, if Saints Bonaventure and Thomas Aquinas are added, who are not yet included in our Course:

Cyprian (Saint), bishop and martyr, African, 259. Hilary (Saint), Bishop of Poitiers, Gaul, 369. Ambrose (Saint), Bishop of Milan, Roman, 397. Jerome (Saint), priest of Stridon, Ligurinian, 420. [Col. 0226] Augustine (Saint), Bishop of Hippo, African, 430. Leo the Great (Saint), Pope, Italian, 461. Gregory the Great (Saint), Pope, Roman, 604. Bernard (Saint), Abbot of Clairvaux, Gaul, 1153.

[Col. 0225] Among these are two popes, four bishops, one priest, and one abbot; three Romans or Italians, two Africans, two Gauls, and one Ligurian. All are numbered among the saints, and one received the palm of martyrdom.

SECOND ORDER.

[Col. 0227]

Saint Avitus, Bishop of Vienne, 494. Vigilius, Bishop of Thapsus, 493. Saint Eleutherius, Bishop of Tournai, 525. Saint Fulgentius, Bishop of Ruspe, 533. Saint Laurence, Bishop of Novara, 540. Saint Paulinus, Bishop of Aquileia, 804. Saint Benedict, Abbot of Aniane, 822. Saint Abbo, Abbot of Fleury, 1004. Saint Peter Damian, Bishop of Ostia, 1072. Saint Lanfranc, Archbishop of Canterbury, 1089. Saint Bruno, founder of the Carthusians and abbot, 1101. Saint Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, 1109. Blessed Ivo, Bishop of Chartres, 1115. Saint Bruno, Bishop of Asti, 1125. Blessed Hugh of Saint-Victor, canon, 1142. Blessed Guerric, Cistercian monk, 1157. Peter the Venerable, Abbot of Cluny, 1158. [Col. 0227] Of these holy Fathers, thirty-eight are bishops; eight priests; one a deacon; and nine abbots or religious. Twenty-one are Gaulish-Franks; eight Italians; seven Spaniards; seven Africans; four English; three Ligurians and Lombards; two Irish; two Belgians; one German; one Illyrian; one Thracian; and two of uncertain origin: fifty-eight in all. Among them, thirty-eight are reckoned saints.

THIRD ORDER.

The Roman Pontiffs are deservedly counted among the Fathers. Although their writings do not always occur under the designation of literary works, they nevertheless deserve to be considered true authors and called Fathers. Since the course of this Patrology begins only with the time of Tertullian, or Pope Saint Stephen, we have supplied his predecessors with the aid of Anastasius the Librarian and Isidore Mercator, so that an unbroken succession of holy pontiffs may be presented; nevertheless, we distinguish them by italic type. Note that we begin with Anacletus, not with Linus and Cletus, to whom no one attributes anything.

[Col. 0229] Of the preceding Supreme Pontiffs, sixty-two are regarded as saints in the Church. By origin, 123 are Romans or Italians; 11 Greeks; 4 Syrians; 4 Germans; 6 Gauls; 3 Sicilians; 3 Africans; 1 Briton; and 1 Sardinian: 156 in all.

SECOND SERIES: ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS.

The writers customarily so called are divided by us into two orders: the first comprises those considered major on account of their works; the latter consists of those considered of lesser importance because of the limited extent of their writings.

FIRST ORDER.

# ORDER II. Ecclesiastical Writers of Lesser Importance

The writers of this order are divided into two categories: the first consists of those whose writings are distinguished by a title in the *Patrology*; the second, of those whose writings are read among the works of others or are contained in collections.
