## XI. INDEX OF MORE RECENT WRITERS WHO HAVE ELUCIDATED THE WORKS OF THE HOLY FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND ALL WRITERS OF THE CHURCH BY PREFACES, DISSERTATIONS, NOTES, OR COMMENTARIES, AND WHO ARE FOUND IN THIS COURSE OF PATROLOGY; ARRANGED ALPHABETICALLY AND INCLUDING A BRIEF ANALYSIS OF THEIR STUDIES

(In this index, a Roman numeral indicates the volume and an Arabic numeral the column; where the Roman numeral is absent, the reader is referred back to the preceding volume.)

**ACHERIUS (Dom Jean Luc),** industrious and most learned Benedictine of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, born at Saint-Quentin in 1609 and died in 1685. Author of the *Spicilegium of Ancient Writers*, etc.

—Writings.—Notice on the Rule of St Chrodegang, LXXXIX, 1055.—Notice on the Capitularies of Ahtyton, bishop of Basel, CXV, 9.—Notes on Haymo’s book *On the Body and Blood of Christ*, CXVIII, 815 ff.—Acherius published certain chapters collected by Flero, deacon of Lyons, CXIX, 419.—Notice on St Paschasius Radbertus’s treatise *On the Virgin’s Childbirth*, CXX, 1366.—Notice on Ratramnus’s book *On the Incarnation*, CXXI, 82.—Notes and observations on Ratramnus’s book *On the Body and Blood of Christ*, 126.—Notice on Ratramnus’s book *Against the Objections of the Greeks*, 223.—Notice on the Martyrology of Wandelbert, monk of Prüm, 575.—Notes on the same Martyrology, 577 ff.—Notice on the book of Aeneas, bishop of Paris, *Against the Greeks*, 683.—Notice on Abbo’s sermons, CXXXII, 761.—Preface to the works of Atto, bishop of Vercelli, CXXXIV, 25.—Notice on Ulrich, monk of Cluny, and on his collection, CXLIX, 633.—Prolegomena to the works of Blessed Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury.—Dedicatory epistle, CL, 9. Preface to the reader: the occasion of the new edition, 11; what has been accomplished, 13; on citations of Scripture, 14; sources of the letters, 16; Lanfranc’s doctrine and talent, 18; other achievements in the new edition, 25.—Notes and observations on the Life of Blessed Lanfranc, bishop of Canterbury, 58 ff. Form of a petition for permission to make profession, 60. Blessing of monks, ibid. On Berengar’s letter to Ascelin, 66. On the charter of foundation of the Abbey of St Stephen at Caen, 69. Privileges, 71 ff. Succession of abbots of St Stephen of Caen, 77. Table of the foundation of Holy Trinity at Caen, 79. List of the abbesses of the same monastery, 83.—Notes and observations on Blessed Lanfranc’s letters, 551 ff.—Remarks on Lanfranc’s book *On Concealing Confession*, 631.—New edition of the works of Venerable Guibert, abbot of St Mary of Nogent. Dedicatory epistle, CLVI, 9.—Preface to the reader, 14.—Synopsis of the Life of Venerable Guibert, 17.—Notes and observations on certain works of Venerable Guibert of Nogent, 1018 ff. Notice on the Chronicle of John, monk of Bèze, CLXII, 753.—Account of Theobald of Étampes, CLXIII, 760.—Notice on the Chronicle of Hariulf, abbot of Centula, CLXXIV, 1211.—Notice on Hermann of Tournai’s history of the restoration of the abbey of St Martin of Tournai, CLXXX, 38.—Notice [Col. 0308] on his edition of the history of the monastery of Vézelay, by Hugh of Poitiers, CXCIV, 1562.

**AGOBARD,** archbishop of Lyons, died 840. He assigned a proper name to a manuscript of Tertullian’s works; this manuscript is preserved to the present day in the Imperial Library, where it now stands under no. 1622. I, Preface, 33.

**AGRICOLA (Rudolph),** one of the restorers of learning and letters in the West, born at Raffelnae in 1442 and died in 1485.—He published commentaries on Boethius’s books *On the Consolation of Philosophy*, LXIII, 885 ff.

**AGUIRRE (José Sáenz),** Spanish cardinal and theologian, born at Logroño in 1630 and died at Rome in 1699.—Notes and observations on the works of Montanus, bishop of Toledo, XV, 51.—Annotations on St Valerius, abbot, LXXXVII, 417 ff.

**ALEXANDER (Natalis),** theologian and historian of the Dominican Order, born at Rouen in 1639 and died in 1724, author of an *Ecclesiastical History*.—Dissertation on images, XCVIII, 971.—Dallaeus’s objection, drawn from the Carolingian Books, is set forth, ibid. The answer of those who held that the Carolingian Books were the work of some heretic and not of Charlemagne is refuted, 975. The objections drawn from the Carolingian Books are answered, 979.—Account of Pope Sylvester II, CXXXIX, 57.

**ALTASERRA (Antoine-Antoine Dadin de Hauteserre),** jurist and historian, died 1682.—Notes on St Boniface IV, pope, LXXX, 99.—Likewise on St Deusdedit, pope, 358.—Likewise on Boniface V, pope, 432.—On Honorius I, pope, 465.—Likewise on Sergius I, pope, LXXXIX, 11.—On John VII, 39.—On John VII, 53.—On Constantine, pope, 321.—On St Gregory II, pope, 460.—On Gregory III, 564 ff.—On Zacharias, pope, 898, and throughout.—On Stephen II, pope, 970 ff.—On St Paul I, pope, 1129, and throughout.—Notes on the life of each Roman pontiff written by Anastasius, CXXVII, 1047 ff.

**ALBASPINA (Gabriel de l’Aubespine),** bishop of Orléans, born at Beaune in 1579 and died at Grenoble; a distinguished archaeologist. Among other works, he wrote notes on Tertullian, I, 1154, 1159, 1160, and throughout.—Critical notes on St Optatus’s book *On the Donatist Schism*, XI, 885, and throughout.—Observations on St Optatus, bishop of Milevis: 1. On the errors of the Donatists, XI, 1159; 2. Wherein the Novatians and [Col. 0309] Donatists agreed or differed, 1165; 3. Certain obscurities in this history, ibid.; 4. Whether Melchiades was a judge in this case, 1166. On the laying on of hands, 1167. The same explanation is confirmed, 1170. Objections are resolved, 1172. Whether the Donatists reordained certain persons, 1174. On the Council of Arles, 1176.

**ALEAUME (Jean),** Parisian professor of theology, published at Antwerp, in 1757, the works of Peter Lombard; in accordance with this edition his *Sentences* are reprinted, CXCII, 519.

**ALVAREZIUS (Didacus).**—Note on the teaching of John Cassian: his error concerning the necessity of God’s grace and the natural powers of free will, L, 367.

**AMADESIUS (Joseph A.).**—Dissertation on the ecclesiastical metropolis of Ravenna. Preface, LII, 91. Whether the Church of Ravenna was subject to the Church of Milan during the first four centuries, 92. On the letter of Pope Clement II asserting the pre-eminence of the bishop of Ravenna over that of Milan in councils, III. What may be thought concerning the origin of metropolitan dignity in the Church of Ravenna, 145.

**AMBOOESIUS (François),** man of letters and royal councillor, born in Paris in 1550 and died in 1620.—He published the works of Peter Abelard in 1616.—Apologetic preface for Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 71. On the carelessness of copyists, ibid. On Heloise and her learning, 74. The editor’s purpose, 75. On Abelard’s dispute with St Bernard, adjudicated at the Council of Sens, 78. On the articles for which he was censured, 79. Diverse testimonies of various persons concerning Peter Abelard, 82. Encomia of Abelard, 86. What is said concerning St Bernard, 89. On the letters of Abelard and Heloise, 90 ff. What Robert of Auxerre relates concerning Abelard in his Chronicle, 93; and Bertrand d’Argentré, president of Rennes, 95. On the relationship of Heloise and Abelard, 96. On his condemnation by the Council of Sens, 98. He is defended by Berengar, 99. On studies in Abelard’s time, 103. In what year he died, 104.

**ANNALES CAMALDULENSES,** Venice, 1756. Historical account of Theuson, hermit and monk of St Mary of Florence, CXLIII, 884.—Notice on an ancient Sacramentary, CLI, 823.—Introduction to certain extracts from ancient liturgical codices of Fonte Avellana, 878.

**ANONYMOUS I, on Lactantius.**—Outline of Lactantius’s doctrine, VI, 81. His defects and errors, whether theological, 85; chronological, 88; or philosophical, ibid.—Censorious annotations, 87 ff. Ninety-four propositions excerpted from the edition of Isaeus and to be read cautiously by Catholics, 91. Catalogue of manuscripts of Lactantius, 93.—Various editions of Lactantius’s works, 103. Translations, 108. Dissertations on Lactantius, 109.

**ANONYMOUS II.**—Dogmatic investigations into Lactantius. Chapter 1: On religion considered generally, VII, 1011. Chapter 2: Arguments by which Lactantius demonstrates that the Christian religion alone is true, 1022. Chapter 3: Other arguments by which Lactantius establishes the truth of the Christian religion are examined, 1055. On the books of the Old and New Testaments from which Lactantius drew the institutions and teachings of the Christian religion, 1070.

**NOTES OF VARIOUS ANONYMOUS WRITERS** on Nazarius’s Panegyric of Constantine the Great, VIII, 581.—Likewise on the Panegyric of Maximian and Constantine by an uncertain author, 609.—For Eumenius’s Panegyric of Constantine Augustus, the Preface, Notice, and Synopsis are supplied, 619 ff.—On Eumenius’s Oration to Constantine Augustus on behalf of the Flavienses, 641.—On the Panegyric of Constantine Augustus by an uncertain author, 653.—Likewise on Victorinus’s book *On the Generation of the Divine Word*, 1019.—On the letter of Candidus the Arian, 1035.

**ANONYMOUS, on St Zeno.**—History of the translation of St Zeno, XI, 207. At what time and on what occasion this translation took place, ibid. The piety of King Pepin, ibid. At his command, a devout solitary named Benignus was summoned, ibid. The king scarcely obtained some relics by his prayers, 208. The marvellous ceremonial of the translation, ibid. How richly endowed the new church became, 209. The relics of St Zeno work miracles, 210.

**A VERY RECENT ANONYMOUS WRITER, on St Optatus.**—He supplied an introduction to St Optatus’s geographical map, CXI, 871. Who supplied a similar map after Optatus, ibid. Variations in the spelling of names, ibid. On adjectival and substantive names, 872. Other difficulties, ibid. Who laboured in explaining these matters, 873. The labours of M. Dupin, ibid. Matters noted for the reader, 874.

**ANONYMOUS.** On the author of the Panegyric for Emperor Julian, and the time and place at which it was delivered, XVIII, 407. Synopsis of the Panegyric, ibid. Annals of Claudius Julian, 429.—Notice on Publius Victor’s description of the city of Rome, 435.

[Col. 0310]

**ANONYMOUS,** author of the Prolegomena to the writings of Faltonia Proba, poetess of centos, in the Pesaro edition of 1766. The name, character, and period of Valeria Faltonia Proba, XIX, 801. Her writings, ibid., and editions, 802.—The same person published the works of Ausonius, XIX, 817. Prolegomena: Ausonius’s age and religion, ibid. Ausonius’s writings, 819.

**ANONYMOUS, on Montanus.**—Notice on the Life of Montanus, LXV, 47. The Life of Montanus; when he flourished, 47. His eloquence, 48. His fame throughout all Italy, 49. In what year he died, 50.

**ANONYMOUS, on Fulgentius of Ruspe.**—He prefixed a preface to the works of St Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, LXV, 105. The distinctive excellence of the writings of the Holy Fathers, 105. The place Fulgentius occupies among them, ibid. His first work, ibid. His banishment to Sardinia, 106. Books on prayer and fasting, 107. His letters, 108–109. His profession of faith, 110. When Thrasamund died, he returned from exile to his see, 111. He composed new writings, ibid. On the occasion upon which he wrote his book *On the Trinity and the Incarnation*, 112. How Fulgentius’s writings are to be divided, 114.—Introduction to two unpublished sermons sent by Cardinal Francesco Barberini, 833.—Introduction to the book *On Predestination and Grace*, 844.—Introduction to the sermons in the Appendix, 855.

**ANONYMOUS, on John Scotus.** Treatise on the life and doctrines of John Scotus Eriugena, CXXII, 1. Where and when Scotus was born, ibid. His learning and literary attainments, 8. His position under Charles the Bald, 15. What Erigena did in theological controversies, 21. His other activities, especially his final ones, 42. On Eriugena’s writings not yet catalogued, 47.

**ANONYMOUS.** Account of Godfrey of St Victor, with certain fragments of his writings, CXCVI, 1418.—Account of Adam of St Victor, 1422.

**ANTONIO (Nicolás),** Spanish bibliographer, born at Seville in 1617 and died in 1684, author of the *Bibliotheca Hispana*.—Account of St Maximus, bishop of Saragossa, LXXX, 609.—Historical account of St Braulio, 639. Elucidatory notes, 641 ff.—Historical account of Tajo, bishop of Saragossa, 719. Annotation, 721 ff.—Historical account of St Eugenius, bishop of Toledo, LXXXVII, 347. Likewise of St Valerius, abbot, 417.—Account of St Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, 1087. Notes on the same, ibid. ff.—Historical account of St Ildefonsus and his writings, XCVI, 9 ff. Notes on St Ildefonsus, ibid.—Account of St Julian, bishop of Toledo, with notes, 427.—Historical and literary account of St Elipandus and Felix, etc., 847 ff.—Account of Isidore of Pacensis, 1245.—Account of St Prudentius, bishop of Troyes, CXV, 965.—Historical account of Paul Alvarus of Cordoba, CXXI, 387. Survey of his writings, 393.—Account of Cyprian, archpriest of Cordoba, CXXXII, 787.—Investigation of the author of the chronicles attributed to Liutprand: who Liutprand was, CXXXVI, 937. Two preliminary letters to the pseudo-Liutprand chronicle are attacked in two ways, 943. On certain additions and interpolations, 951. In certain passages the character and purpose of pseudo-Liutprand are demonstrated, 954.—Account of Oliva, bishop of Vic, CXLII, 589. Historical and literary account of Peter Alfonso, a Jew converted to Christianity, CLVII, 527.—Account of Munio of Mondoñedo, Hugh, bishop of Portugal, and Gerard, priest, authors of the *History of the Church of Compostela*, CLXX, 875.—Account of St Olegarius, archbishop of Tarragona, CLXXII, 1358.—Account of Robert of Ketton, CLXXXIX, 1073.

**ANTONIUS (Paul-Gabriel),** of the Society of Jesus, learned theologian, born at Lunéville in 1679 and died in 1743.—Historical account of St Eutropius, LXXX, 9. Note on the same, ibid.—Account of the monk Taram, with a note, 19.—Historical account of Count Bulgaranus, LXXX, 107.—Likewise of Paul of Mérida, III. Observations for the student of Spanish affairs, 113, and on the writings of Paul of Mérida, 115 ff.—Historical account of Sisebut, 363.—Likewise of Claudius of Turin, CIV, 610.

**AREVALUS (Faustinus).** At Rome in 1792 he published the works of Juvencus of Aquileia. Dedicatory letter to Don Gregorio Alfonso Villagómez Laurenzana, archdeacon of Calatrava and canon of Toledo, XIX, 9.—Prolegomena. The opinion that Juvencus was formerly accorded religious cult is rejected, 11. The manuscripts of Juvencus are catalogued, 25. Editions of Juvencus’s poems, 31. Praises of Juvencus from the ancient Fathers and certain modern writers, 41. A passage of Matthew read otherwise by Juvencus than in the Vulgate, 48. The usefulness of collating Juvencus manuscripts; method of this edition, 51.—Variant readings and critical notes placed beneath each page of text, 53 ff.—Likewise he published the writings of Caelius Sedulius in 1794. Dedicatory letter, XIX, 433. Prolegomena: Sedulius’s life and deeds, [Col. 0311] 435. The works of Sedulius are catalogued, 447. Manuscripts of Sedulius, 463. Editions of those writings, 477. On Asterius, who collected the works of Sedulius, 486. Praises of Sedulius, 504. On correctors and corrupters of manuscripts, 513. What has been accomplished in this new edition, 530. Notes appended to the text, 533 ff.—At Rome in 1793 he published the works of Aurelius Prudentius, illustrated with notes and observations.—Dedicatory letter to Pius VI, Supreme Pontiff.—Prolegomena. Plan and division of the whole work, LIX, 571. Life of Prudentius, 578. Works of Prudentius, 607. Manuscript codices of Prudentius’s works, 619. Editions and translations of his works, 640. Judgment of the Magdeburg writers and others concerning Prudentius’s doctrine, 664. On the cult and veneration of saints according to Prudentius’s poems, 664. He is wrongly criticized concerning the doctrine of free will, 670. Ecclesiastical rites now current in the Church and customary in Prudentius’s time, 674. An answer is given to [lacuna] Prudentius, who asks with Persius: “Pontiffs, tell me: what is gold doing in a holy place?” 684. On the custom of burying the dead, 687. In what sense he called the soul “fluid and gentle,” 693. Did he favour the Pythagoreans? 698. Prudentius’s opinion concerning the punishments of the damned, 706. The ignorance of those who thought that *aenigma* means an interpretation of Scripture, 712. Two notable passages of Prudentius are examined. Faults of metre attributed to Prudentius, 724. Metrical rules observed by Prudentius, 727. Prudentius corrupted by others, 735. Prudentian metres, 744. Prudentius’s Latin style, 748. On the selection of variants, 761.—Critical notes and observations, 767 ff. Preface to vol. II, LX, 9.

He published the works of St Isidore of Seville with notes and observations at Rome in 1796. Dedication, LXXXI, 9. Prolegomena, Part I: On the life, deeds, and doctrine of St Isidore, and on editions containing all his works, ibid. Such an edition is not easy, ibid. Death of Blessed Isidore, 30. His praises, 53. On his lives, 68. Sequence of the life and deeds of Blessed Isidore, 81. His country, parents, and birth, 95. Whether he professed the monastic life, 111. He is appointed bishop of Seville after Leander, 116. Councils over which he presided, 119. Whether he held the primacy of Spain, 125. Whether he ever went to Rome, 128. In what year he died, 138. His miracles, 145. Isidore as Doctor of the Church, 147. He is praised by Roman pontiffs, 162. Certain modern judgments concerning Isidore are examined, 203. Editions of his works.

Part II: The works of St Isidore are catalogued, 305. Judgments of learned men concerning Isidore’s *Etymologies*, 320. Editions of the *Etymologies*, 344. On glossaries attributed to him, 366. What is to be thought of the author of the Isidorian Glossary, 378. Editions of the book *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers*, 382. Isidore’s prefaces to the books of the Old and New Testaments, 401. Whether Isidore published literal commentaries on sacred Scripture, 414. The three books of *Sentences*: editions and manuscripts, 433. The *Synonyma*, or soliloquies, of St Isidore: editions, 461. Rule of monks, 471. Sermons attributed to Isidore: whether genuine, 482. Letters to Claudius and Eugenius: whether genuine, 500. Editions of the book *On the Nature of Things*, 516. Isidore is the true author of the Chronicle, 523. The history of the kings of the Goths is vindicated for Isidore, 543.

Part III: On doubtful and spurious works. Poems attributed to Isidore, 573. Other doubtful works, 589. Scriptural testimonies and the book *On the Order of Created Things*: doubtful, 595. Whether the exposition of the Mass and the book *On the Canon of the Mystical Offering* are by Isidore, 608. Other short works attributed to him, 624. Whether he took part in the Gothic Bible, 651. Whether in the Gothic Offices, 668. Whether the Spanish collection of canons is Isidore’s, 707.

Part IV: Description of manuscripts. On the Vatican manuscripts, 763. Catalogue of eleven Vatican manuscripts, 774. Manuscripts of the library of the queen of Sweden transferred to the Vatican, 819. Manuscripts of the Vatican Palatine Library, 854. Copies in the Vatican-Urbino Library are described, 883. Other Roman manuscripts, 915. On copyists of ancient codices, 924. Appendices to the Isidorian works, 935.

Preface to the works of St Isidore, LXXXII. On the method and purpose of this edition, 9–10.—Appendices to the first ten books of the *Etymologies*, 727.—Likewise to the latter ten, 755.—Variant readings of the *Etymologies*, 759 ff.—Arevalus’s notes on the same books, 855 ff.—Notes on various writings of St Isidore, LXXXIII, 9, and throughout the volume.

**ARNOLDUS (Christopher),** at Nuremberg in 1692 published the works of Optatianus Porphyrius.—Dedicatory epistle to Henry Rantzau, a nobleman of the king of Denmark, XIX, 387. Notes, 391 ff.

**ARNTZENIUS (Johann-Henric),** born at Nijmegen in 1734 and died in 1797, a learned man. He prefixed a preface to the works of Arator, subdeacon of the Roman Church, LXVIII, 46. On his own studies on Arator’s works, ibid. On Arator, 48. His family and native country, 49. The period in which he flourished, [Col. 0312] 53. Synopsis of Arator’s books on the Acts of the Apostles, 58. Commentary on Arator, 63 ff.

**AUGUSTINUS (Antonio),** archbishop of Tarragona, learned philologist, born at Saragossa in 1516 and died in 1586.—Notes on the decrees of Pope Adrian, XCVI, 1068 ff.—Observation on the Venetian edition of the same canons, 1096.

**BACCHINIUS (Benedict),** learned Italian Benedictine, born at San Donnino in 1651 and died in 1721.—Observations on the life of St Peter Chrysologus: his age and election, LIII, 19. Agnellus acknowledges that the Church of Ravenna was subject to that of Rome, 23. Peter Chrysologus’s letter to Eutyches, 24. Whether he wrote another, 25. Whether he wrote its final periods, 26. Whether the church of Tricoli was built by Peter, ibid. Chapel of St Andrew, ibid. Gifts made to the church at Corneliana, 27.—Notes on Felix, bishop of Ravenna, LXXXIX, 358.—Dedicatory epistle to Agnellus’s *Pontifical*, CVI, 435.—Bacchini’s preface to Agnellus’s *Pontifical*, 435. It had not previously been published, ibid. On Agnellus’s view regarding the Apostolic See, 437. From what sources it ought to be published and illustrated by notes, ibid. On monuments of history, 438. How Jerome Rubeus interpreted history, ibid.; and Agnellus, though barbarous, 440. Therefore it was fitting to publish it, 441. What the editor needed to accomplish, 441. On the granting of the pallium, 442. Agnellus refutes Agnellus, 443. How important the question of the pallium is, 445. In what respect the Church opposes it, 446. What abuse had crept in, 448. It belongs to the Church, not to the emperor, to alter the rights of metropolitans, 449. Succession of the bishops of the Church of Ravenna, 450.—Observations on certain verses prefixed to Agnellus’s *Pontifical Book*, 451 ff. Observation on verses added to the preceding ones in the same manuscript, 458.—Dissertation I: On the age of the first twelve bishops. The disagreement of Jerome Rubeus and Baronius concerning the questions; the view of Bolland and his companions, 461. On Roman councils, and on the occasion and date of the controversy, 469. What was Severus’s period? 474.—Notice, 475.—Observations on the life of St Apollinaris, 477; likewise observations on the life of St Aderitus, 482; likewise on the life of St Eleucadius, 483; St Martian, 485; St Calocerus, ibid.; Proculus, 488; Probus, ibid.; Datus, 490; and Severus, 496. Dissertation II: The opinions of Rubeus and Faber concerning Liberius II, Probus, Florentius, etc., 499. Observations on the life of St Ursus, 507. Dissertation III: On the age of the bishops of Ravenna. First part: difficulties arising from Agnellus and other documents which impede history and chronology are explained, 597. Second part: a probable method for arranging the succession of bishops, 510. Observations on the lives of Saints Peter, 516; Neon, 523; Exuperantius, 526; John Angeloptes, 541; Peter Chrysologus, 559; Aurelian, 570.—Dissertation: On the dates of Ecclesius, Ursicinus, etc., 571. Observations on the lives of Saints Ecclesius, 589; Ursicinus, 599; Victor, 602; Maximian, 612; Agnellus, 622.—Dissertation on the age of Peter the Elder, John, Marinianus, and each John, 624.—Observations on the life of St John the Elder, 641; John Romanus, 643; Marinianus, 648.—Dissertation on the age of the following bishops of Ravenna—Bonus, Maurus, Reparatus, etc.—Observations on the life of Bonus, 670; Maurus the schismatic, 674; Reparatus, 681; Theodore, 689; Damian, 698; St Felix, 711.—Chronological excursus on the dates of the remaining bishops of Ravenna treated by Agnellus, 715. Observations on the life of John, 723; Sergius, 729; Leo, 733; John, 736; Gratiosus, 740; Martin, 744; Petronacius, 745; George, 750.

**BAGATA (Raphael) and PERETTI (Baptist),** in 1586 jointly prefixed a preface to the Veronese edition of the works of St Zeno, XI, 239. Some matters concerning the life of St Zeno, ibid. The plan of that edition, ibid. The tradition of the Church of Verona is invoked, 241. What works are not by St Zeno, ibid. Certain points concerning his teaching, 212. On those who laboured to amend these works, 213. What is to be thought of this edition, 247.

**BAILLETUS (Adrien),** priest and learned critic, born at Beauvais in 1649 and died in 1704, wrote the Life of Victor, bishop of Vita in Africa, LVIII, 177.—He is entered in the Roman Martyrology on 23 August, ibid. He is believed to have been bishop of Utica, ibid. The place of his exile is unknown, 178. He wrote the history of the Vandal persecution in 487, 179. When Huneric died, Gondebald succeeded him, ibid. Victor was made primate of the Province of Byzacena, ibid. He incurred the anger of King Thrasamund and was banished to Sardinia, 180. There he died about the year 510.

**BALDINIUS (Giovanni Francesco),** learned Italian of the Somascan Congregation, born at Brescia in 1677 and died in 1765. Annotations on St Boniface, pope, LXXX, 101.—Likewise on St Deusdedit, pope, 358.—Likewise on Boniface V, 432.—On John VII, pope, 55. On Constantine, pope, 330.—On St Gregory, pope, 481.—On St Zacharias, pope, 915.—On St Stephen II, pope, 975 ff.

BALDUINUS (Francis), an eminent jurist, born at Arras in 1520 and died in 1573; he taught law in many places. He is responsible for the dissertation on Minucius Felix’s *Octavius*, III, 179. He shows that the little work or dialogue entitled *Octavius* is truly by Minucius Felix, not by Arnobius, as he had at first thought; that Minucius Felix was a distinguished advocate of the Roman bar, ibid., and a serious Christian, 201. At what time Minucius appears to have pleaded cases at Rome, 202. His zeal for knowledge of divine matters, ibid. The condition of the Roman bar in the time of Minucius Felix, 203. Why Minucius chose the form of a dialogue, 204. That Arnobius and Lactantius argued the same case as Minucius, 205. He relates Caecilius’s arguments in the case concerning the gods, which Octavius vigorously refutes. How calumnies against Christians are easily refuted, 210. Prefaces to the first edition of the Works of St. Optatus.—Baudouin’s letter to J. Lentellerius, bishop of Aix, XI, 1103. The reason for publishing these works with greater fidelity. The distinction to be made concerning African authors, 1105. The character of St. Optatus, 1106. His letter to Calvin, 1108. He rebukes him because, having been led by him into error, he abused his good faith to confirm impious doctrines; and he vehemently declares that he in no way agrees with such a manner of acting, 1109. Certain points are discussed by which he clears himself of every stain arising from this connivance, 1110. He recalls Calvin to the sound judgment of Saints Basil, Chrysostom, Optatus, etc., 1118.—Preface to the reader, XI, 1130. Reason for the new and second edition of St. Optatus, 1130. Whence St. Optatus came, 1131. The meaning of “of Milevis,” ibid. Critical annotations on the seven books of St. Optatus, 1135 ff. Letter to John Tilius, bishop of Meaux, on the history of the Conference of Carthage, 1439.—Notice to the reader, 1441.

BALLERINI (Peter and Jerome), highly learned philologists and critics. The elder flourished at Verona from 1698 to 1764; the younger from 1702 to 1780. They edited many ancient works, including the works of St. Zeno and St. Optatus, XI.—Dedication to Cardinal Passionei, 9. Preface: some matters concerning Zeno, bishop of Verona, and his writings, 11. Editions of these works, 13. The new and more accurate edition, 14. The manuscript in the Benedictine library at Reims, 15. The Venetian codex, 17. Vatican codices, 18. Urbino manuscripts, 19. Veronese manuscripts, 20. The Pompeian manuscript, 21. The usefulness of collating manuscripts, 23. Why the heading *Tractatus* is retained rather than *sermo*, 24.

First Dissertation: On the genuine treatises of St. Zeno and his date, XI. Preface, in which, after reviewing various critical opinions, it proposes what is to be determined concerning the remaining genuine works, ibid. ff. Chapter 1: it is established that the treatises have one author, 33. Chapter 2: the author is shown to have written in the fourth century, 40. Chapter 3: the author is Zeno, bishop of Verona, 65.

Second Dissertation. Preface on the excellence of Zeno’s treatises, 81. Chapter 1: What Zeno thought concerning the eternal generation of the Word of God, 84. Chapter 2: Why he wrote on the generation of the Word, and which formulas he condemned, 114. Chapter 3: Various formulas of Zeno concerning Christ’s incarnation defended, 118. Chapter 4: What the author taught concerning the sin of the first parents, 121. Chapter 5: How rightly he understood divine grace, 123. Chapter 6: Whether St. Zeno, when speaking of faith or charity, went too far, 126. Chapter 7: On second marriages, 129. Chapter 8: An examination of St. Zeno’s distinctive testimony concerning certain demoniacs, 138. Chapter 9: What the author thought about the Last Judgment, 140. Chapter 10: St. Zeno’s view of the state of righteous souls after death, 142.

Third Dissertation: On the Acts of St. Zeno and his cult, XI, 145. Preface. Chapter 1: On Zeno’s deeds up to his death, ibid. Chapter 2: The controversy concerning St. Zeno’s martyrdom, 157. Chapter 3: On the more notable things related after St. Zeno’s death, 169. Chapter 4: On the ancient cult of St. Zeno, 174.—Introduction to the documents concerning St. Zeno, XI, 189. Investigations into his life, ibid. Life of Zeno by Coronatus, 199. Account of his translation, 207. His miracles written in verse by the priest Jacob, 204. Masses and offices of St. Zeno, 213.—Testimonies of the ancients concerning St. Zeno, 223.—Critical notes appended to the text, 253 and throughout. Schoenemann’s opinion of this edition of Zeno’s works, XI, 247–248.

The Ballerini issued an edition of the Works of St. Hilary of Arles. Notes on his life, written by his disciple, L, 1219.—They also edited the works of St. Leo the Great. Dedicatory letter to Benedict XIV, LIV, 9. General preface, 13. Another edition to be set against Quesnel’s edition, ibid. Benedict XIV’s counsel, 15. Libraries in which investigations were pursued, 17. What needed correction, 19. On Quesnel’s labors, 21. The difficulty of attacking an adversary who is present, ibid. The reason for this prolixity, 25. Simon Richard’s opinion of the Quesnellian edition, ibid. Quesnel’s two principal prejudices, 27. Synopsis of the entire work, 29.—Preface on the manuscript sources from which, and especially by which, St. Leo’s sermons are to be corrected, [Col. 0314] 118. Chapter 1: On manuscript lectionaries, 119. Chapter 2: On manuscript collections of St. Leo’s sermons, their classification and use, 125. Introduction to the first two sermons, 137 ff. Critical notes appended to the text, 141 ff.—Preface to the Appendix to St. Leo’s Sermons, LIV, 467. On the Quesnellian edition, ibid. ff. On sermons published among the works of other Fathers, 469. The two chief sources of spurious works, 475. Introduction to the sermon or treatise against the heresies of Eutyches, 477. Introduction to Sermon 8 on the Lord’s Resurrection, 495. Likewise to Sermon 14, on the Chair of St. Peter, 503. To Sermon 19, on the feast of the seven Maccabean brothers, 515. Observations on certain sermons of St. Leo the Great, 521.

Preface on the manuscript codices used in correcting the letters, 551. Classification of the collections containing Leo’s letters, ibid. On Collections 1 and 2, 553; 3–9, 555 ff.; 10–12, 559; 13–16, 563; 17–18, 565 ff.; 19, which is the most excellent, through 24, 571 ff. On certain codices, 575. On Greek manuscripts, ibid. Features distinctive to this edition, 579. Introduction to the first two letters, 581. On the codices containing those letters, 582. Argument for their authenticity, 583. Objections to the letter to Januarius answered, 585. Who was the bishop of Aquileia to whom Leo wrote, 589.—Introduction to the fragment of Cyril’s letter to Leo concerning Easter of 444, 397. Likewise to Leo’s letter to the bishops of Mauretania, 639; to the bishops of Sicily, 703; to Flavian of Constantinople, 719; to Peter Chrysologus’s letter to Eutyches the presbyter, 737; to Leo’s letter to Flavian, 751; to Pulcheria Augusta, 783; to Julian, bishop, 801; to Theodosius Augustus, 817; to Anatolius of Constantinople, 833; to Valentinian’s letters to Theodosius Augustus, 855; to Leo’s letter to Faustus the presbyter, 895; to letters concerning Easter of 455; to the letter of the Council of Chalcedon to Leo, 949; to three letters, 1073; to letters to Basil of Antioch and Euxitheus of Thessalonica, 1117; to Leo Augustus, 1127; to the same, 1151; to Neon of Ravenna, 1189; to Rusticus of Narbonne, 1197.—Dissertation on lost letters, 1217. Individual years indicated from 431 to 460.—Preface to the Appendix of Letters, 1233. Introduction to Letter 1 to the bishops of Gaul, 1235; to Letter 3 of certain bishops, 1237; to Leo’s judgment on apocryphal writings, 1239; to Letter 5, 1241; to Letter 6, from Bishop Julian to Leo, 1241; to Letter 7 on Eutyches, 1243; to Letter 9, or Act 16 of Chalcedon, 1249. Introduction to the Appendix of fragments of St. Leo, 1255.—Notes on Paschasius Quesnel’s observations on the works of St. Leo, 1263 ff.

Preface to the Book of Sacraments of St. Leo the Great, LV, 9. Blanchini attributed it to Leo in 1735. Others adopted differing opinions, ibid. What is certain, ibid. Pope Gelasius is not the author of that book, 11. What appears more probable, 13. Observations on the Masses, 15. On its authority, 17. He shows the very ancient origin of most prayers, 19. Certain features of the manuscript itself, ibid.—Notes and observations on the Book of Sacraments of the Roman Church, 21 ff.—Introduction to the Breviary against the Arians (see vol. XIII), 179.—Introduction to the life and works of St. Hilary of Arles, 181 (vol. L). Introduction to Quesnel’s first dissertation, 183. Annotations on the sixth dissertation, 627 ff. Observations on the seventh dissertation, 663 ff.; likewise on the eighth, 685; ninth, 725; tenth, 753.

The collection of Sabinus, bishop of Heraclea, ibid. An ancient Greek codex of canons, 19. Various catalogues, 24. Chronological annotations, 32. Sardican canons, 41. Preface to the codex of ecclesiastical canons and constitutions of the Apostolic See, LVI, 354. Critical notes on the text, 367 ff.—Introduction to chapter 2, 411. The Ballerini’s observations on Paschasius Quesnel’s twelfth dissertation concerning the codex of canons of the Roman Church, LV, 947. It is proved that the codex of the Roman Church was not published by Quesnel, 942. Quesnel’s arguments refuted, 955.—Likewise observations on Quesnel’s thirteenth dissertation, on African councils against the Pelagians, 1005. The error in the heading of chapter 14 of the codex of canons must be attributed to the author of that codex, 1007. The first African council, which Quesnel places at the beginning of Zosimus’s pontificate, is rejected, 1010. Zosimus’s first letter was written only about 21 September 417, 1012. Quesnel’s view of the date of the autumn council under Zosimus refuted, 1016. Three passages of Augustine explained, etc., 1022. Zosimus’s judgment near the end of March 418, against Quesnel, 1025. Honorius’s law against the Pelagians was sought from Zosimus immediately after the Roman judgment, not by the Africans, 1027. The plenary synod of 1 May 418 is the same as that which replied to Zosimus, 1034. Father Constantius’s system concerning affairs under Zosimus examined, 1039.—Observations on Quesnel’s fourteenth dissertation, on professions of faith inserted in the codex, LVI, 1067. The profession attributed by Quesnel to Gregory of Baetica more probably belongs to Gregory Nazianzen, ibid. The one attributed to Augustine is affirmed to belong to the First Council of Toledo, 1070. On the author of the Creed of St. Athanasius, 1071.—The Ballerini’s observations on Dissertation XV. The great authority by which the Council of Telepte is shown genuine, 1091. Ferrandus’s abridgment of canons defended against the charge of interpolation, 1096. A fragment of the Council of Zella rescued from the charge of forgery, 1089. Likewise a fragment of Pope Siricius’s letter attached to it, 1102. Observations on Quesnel’s sixteenth dissertation, concerning the first use in Gaul of the Dionysian Collection, 1125. The use of this collection before Charlemagne’s time is shown, 1125. Which translations the Gallicans used, 1129.—Introduction to unpublished sermons of St. Leo the Great, 1131.

Dedicatory letter for the works of Ratherius, edited at Verona in 1765, CXXXVI, 9.—Preface: On the author’s renown, and the usefulness and excellence of his works, 11. Previously published works of Ratherius, 14. What has been accomplished in this collection and edition, 25.—Life of Ratherius. His homeland and nobility, 28. He embraces monastic life, 30. He follows Hilduin’s party, 34. The calamitous beginnings of his episcopate, 39. He is sent to prison, 45. From there he is banished to Como, 48. He returns to Italy, is captured by Berengar, 51. He goes to Germany, 59. He is received by Bruno, brother of King Otto, 64. He is placed over a monastery, 75. He returns to Italy with King Otto, 88. He issues two decrees against Milo the usurper, 97. He writes a book on contempt for the canons, 102. New tribulations, 108. Events of 967, 120. Events of 968, 129. He is received by the bishop of Liège and Fulcuin, abbot of Lobbes, 138.—Introduction to Ratherius’s books of *Preloquia*, CXXXVI, 143.—Notes, 145 ff. Introduction to *Phrenesis*, 363. Notes on the same work, 363 ff. Introduction to the confessional dialogue, 391. Introduction to the invective on the translation of St. Maternus, 449. Introduction to Ratherius’s synodical letter, 551.—Notice on Burchard and his Collection of Canons, CXL, 497.—The Ballerini’s investigations concerning Ivo’s twofold collection, CLXI, 41 ff.—Historical and literary notice on Gregory, Roman presbyter, CLXIII, 747.

BALUZIUS (Étienne), born at Tulle in Limousin in 1630 and died at Paris in 1718. First librarian to Monsieur Colbert, and shortly afterwards holder of the chair of canon law in the college founded by the king.

[Col. 0316] Critical notes on the Letters of St. Cornelius and on those written to him as pope, III, 700 and throughout. Likewise notes on St. Cyprian’s letter to Antonianus, 763, and to Cornelius, 795; likewise, 856 ff. On St. Cyprian’s letter to Quintus, 1103 ff.

He likewise annotated the collection of St. Cyprian’s letters, IV, 191 ff.; also that doctor’s shorter works: *On the Dress of Virgins*, 439; *On the Lapsed*, 463; *On the Unity of the Church*, 493; *On the Lord’s Prayer*, 519; *To Demetrianus*, 543; *On the Vanity of Idols*, 563; *On Mortality*, 581; *On Works and Almsgiving*, 601; *On the Good of Patience*, 621; *On Zeal and Envy*, 637; *Exhortation to Martyrdom, to Fortunatus*, 651; the three books of *Testimonies*, 679; *On Public Shows*, 779; *On the Praise of Martyrdom*, 787.

Notes on Lactantius’s book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, VII, 297. Baluze’s two critical letters on the same book, 379, 381. Notes on the Acts of St. Felix, bishop, VIII, 679; likewise on the proceedings concerning the vindication of Felix, bishop of Aptunga, 715; on the proceedings concerning Caecilian, 726. Preface to the Acts of the Conference of Carthage, XI, 1224.—Baluze’s preface to the Works of Marius Mercator, XLVIII, 43. Those who had already undertaken the care of Marius Mercator’s works, ibid. The occasion on which Baluze himself was induced to complete an edition of Marius Mercator’s works, 45. The Vatican codex not consulted by Jean Garnier, 46. Notice concerning the author, ibid. Corrections and notes on Mercator, 98 and throughout.—Annotations on Vincent of Lérins, L, 638 ff.

Baluze corrected and annotated the works of St. Salvian the presbyter, LIII, 20. Critical notes on the text, 25 ff.—Notes on the Life and Writings of Pope Gelasius, LIX, 9.—Introduction to the books *On Genealogies* and *On the Computation of Easter*, by an anonymous author, LIX, 519. Critical observation on the *Book of Monastic Order*, by an uncertain author, 561.—Annotations on the edicts of Chlothar, king of the Franks, LXXX, 451 ff.

Baluze’s preface to Charlemagne’s Capitularies, XCVII, 63. The author’s purpose, ibid. What a capitulary is, 64. The distinction between laws and capitularies, 66. How capitularies were enacted, 67. Where they were read to the people after enactment, 68. Jacob Gretser’s judgment, injurious to princes, 69. Baronius himself deceived, 70. Blondel wandered astray by another path, ibid. To whom kings formerly entrusted enforcement of capitularies, 73. The obedience even of Roman pontiffs commends the dignity of our capitularies, 76. What Monsieur Thiers thought concerning enforcement of capitularies in the diocese of Tours, 83. On the canons of the Council of Bourges, 86. Rhenanus first published the capitularies in 1531; then Joachim Vadianus in 1536, 87. The collection made by Ansegisus, 89. Its arrangement, 91. The collection of Benedict the Levite of Mainz, about 845, ibid. Tilius’s edition of 1548, 95. Peter Pithou subsequently worked over the same collection, 97. A second edition by François Pithou, 1603. On very many codices, 103 ff. What has been done in this edition, 106 ff.

Annotation on Charlemagne’s Capitularies, XCVII, 121 ff.—Preface prefixed to his edition of the works of St. Agobard, CIV, 10.—Eulogies of Agobard, 13.—Baluze’s notes, 29 ff. BARLANDUS (Hadrian), professor of eloquence at Louvain, born in Holland in 1488 and died in 1522.—Notice on St. Willibrord, bishop of Utrecht, XXXIX, 536.

BARONIUS (Caesar), learned ecclesiastical historian of the Oratory congregation and cardinal, born at Sora in 1538 and died in 1607.—Notice concerning certain letters attributed to St. Chromatius, XX, 371.—Historical notice on Victor, bishop of Carthage, LXXX, 635.—Observation on St. Adaman or Adamnan, LXXXVIII, 725.—Dissertation on the Council of Frankfurt, XCVIII, 941. BARREUS (Renatus-Laurentius), at Paris in 1580 published the Works of Rufinus, dedicated to John of St. Andrew, XXI, 70. Now that the art of printing has been discovered, the offspring of genius will not perish as they did when it was unknown, 71. Many of Rufinus’s own works have been lost, ibid. The authority of Rufinus and his disagreement with Jerome, 74. Whence this discord arose, ibid. The usefulness of reading these books, 75.

BARTHIUS (Caspar), German philologist, born at Küstrin in 1587 and dead in 1658. He illustrated the writings of Felix Ennodius with notes, LXIII, 14 and throughout.—Annotations on the minor works of St. Eugenius of Toledo, LXXXVI, 359.

BASNAGIUS (Jacques), distinguished Protestant minister, born at Rouen in 1653 and died in 1723. Observation on Ruricius, LVIII, 67. Observation on the books *On the Deeds of Charlemagne*, 1370. Notes on those books, 1374 ff.—Observation on the Penitential of Halitgar, bishop of Cambrai, CV, 647.—Notice on the book *On Monastic Formation* by Jonas, bishop of Orléans, CVI, 121.—Notice on the book *On Royal Formation* by the same author, 278.—Notes on the Martyrology of Hrabanus Maurus, CX, 1122 ff.—Observation on Notker’s Martyrology, CXXXI, 1027.—Observation on Wipo, CXLII, 1250.—Notice to the reader on the account by the monk Udalcalch of the disputes between Hermann and Egino, CLXX, 837. BAUDRY (Paul), at Utrecht in 1692 supplied very extensive notes on Lactantius’s book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*. They are published with a preface, VII, 587 ff.

BAYERUS (Francisco Pérez), learned priest, born at Valencia in 1711 and died in 1794.—Historical dissertation on Damasus and Laurentius, insofar as they are claimed and vindicated for Spain. The weak foundations of the opponents, 554. Second part: On the homeland of Laurentius; the former and present state of the controversy, 583. Old Spanish arguments confirmed, 591. New endeavors in favor of the Spanish position, 602. Prudentius supports the common opinion, 613. Arguments of the opponents examined in order, 620. Further arguments considered from Prudentius’s hymn on Laurentius, 627. Blanchini’s argument resolved, 637. The opponents’ final efforts checked, 662. Conclusion, 665. Additions and explanations, 667.

BEAUGENDRE (Antoine), Benedictine of the Congregation of St. Maur, learned preacher, born at Paris in 1628 and died in 1708. The beginnings of his life, ibid. Whether he was a monk, 65. Hildebert becomes bishop, 66. His various acts; he is imprisoned by Henry I, king of England, 71. Who Count Elias was, 74. He tends his flock, 77. In 1127 he consecrates the church of Redon, 78. On Oliver’s charter, 80. Notice on Hildebert’s letters, 135. Explanatory notes, 141 ff.—Notice on his minor works, 963.—Notice on the book *On Moral Philosophy*, 1005. Notes, 1007 ff.—Notice on the theological treatise, 1067.—Preface to the writings of Marbod, bishop of Rennes, 1457. Connection between the writings of Marbod and Hildebert, ibid. Encyclical letter of the monks of St. Albinus at Angers, 1463. Verses in praise of Marbod, 1464.

BELLARMINE (Robert), Jesuit and later cardinal, [Col. 0318] learned theologian and canonist, born at Montepulciano in 1542 and died in 1621.

Notice on St. Faustus, bishop of Riez, LVIII, 775.—Notice on Gennadius, LVIII, 1054.—Refutation of the booklet falsely entitled *The Synod of Paris*, XCVIII, 1293. No decrees are found in it, ibid. The letter of Michael is shown to be that of a most impious and wicked man, 1294. On certain testimonies, 1295. On Pope Eugenius’s letter to Michael and Theophilus, 1298. On Louis’s letter to Pope Eugenius, 1300.

BENCINUS. Date unknown.—Notes on the Lives of Roman Pontiffs by Anastasius, CXXVII, 1013 ff.

BENEDICTINE MONKS.

Their work on St. Hilary.

Dedicatory letter for the edition of the Works of St. Hilary, IX, 9. General preface, 11. Various editions of St. Hilary’s works, 14. Manuscript codices, 17. Hilary’s lost works, 19. Why Hilary’s style is obscure, 26. St. Hilary’s orthodox faith demonstrated, 30. What he thought concerning the sacrament of the Eucharist, 43. Concerning Christ’s humanity, 52. Whether Hilary thought that, at Christ’s death, the Word withdrew from the human flesh, 78. Certain expressions concerning Christ’s glory and that of human beings after the resurrection explained, 87. His view of Christ’s kingdom as distinct from the kingdom of God the Father, 95. The Last Judgment, 106. His opinion concerning the fire of judgment, 111. Whether knowledge of spiritual things escaped Hilary, 115.

Life of St. Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, compiled from his own writings and ancient records, IX, 125. Hilary’s birth, ibid. His learning, faith, and manner of life until his admission to the clergy, 128. His acts from the Synod of Milan to that of Béziers, 136. His acts from the Synod of Béziers and his exile, 140. His pursuits and acts in exile down to 358, 143. What Hilary did from the end of 358 to the Council of Seleucia, 148. What he did at Constantinople, 155. His remaining labors for the Church there, 158. Hilary’s return from exile and his labors to purge Gaul of heresy, 162. The rest of Hilary’s deeds and his death, 175. His miracles, relics, and disciples, 178. What Jerome says about his life, 184.—Notice on the Life of Blessed Hilary written by Fortunatus, his servant and later bishop, 183. Notes on this Life, 185 ff.—Testimonies of the ancients concerning St. Hilary, 203.—List of manuscripts and printed editions by which Hilary’s works were corrected, 219.

Introduction to Hilary’s treatise on the Psalms, IX, 221 ff. Notes of the Benedictine Fathers, 231 and throughout the treatise.—Introduction to the Commentary on the Gospel of St. Matthew, 909. Hilary’s primacy among Latin writers in interpreting Scripture. What he thought of Tertullian’s writings, ibid. Whether he borrowed anything from Origen in this work, ibid. The style of this Commentary, 910. Hilary’s method of interpretation, ibid. Material drawn from Scripture’s innermost meanings, 911. How he investigates what the Holy Spirit secretly signified, ibid. His excellence while preserving the truth of history, ibid. The title of this work, 912. The preface supplied by Hilary himself is lacking, ibid. On the list of headings, ibid. Hilary is truly its author, 913. Lists placed at the beginning of books by the ancients, ibid. This work was wrongly divided into canons; the origin of this practice, 914. Date of the work, ibid. What Hilary professed concerning the Trinity, 916. Notes and commentaries appended to the text, 919 ff.

Preface to the books *On the Trinity*, X, 9.—How much praise the attribution of these books to Athanasius brought Hilary, ibid. Their varying title, ibid. How they are against all heresies, 11. The Arians are refuted, as are the Sabellians, 12. Hilary’s moderation, ibid. The title that should be retained, 13. Erasmus’s calumny, 14. He constantly proclaims God’s nature in the Holy Spirit, 15. Book X is against Apollinaris’s errors, 17. When Hilary wrote this work, 18. Whether Hilary sent these books to Constantius, 19. His reasons for writing them, 20. The spirit in which he undertakes the work, 21. He demonstrates the faith from the same Scriptural passages by which it is attacked, 22. His style accords with Quintilian, ibid. Notes added to the text, 25 and throughout the work.

Preface to the book *On the Synods*, X, 471. Where and when it was written, ibid. Its occasion and purpose, 472. Summary of the book, ibid. It is not translated from Greek, 473. Its title, ibid. Its authority, 474. The apologetic character and usefulness of this book, 475. The grounds on which Hilary clears himself, 476. The many places in the book showing that he did not approve the faith of the Easterners, 477. He did not accept the false Council of Sardica as genuine, 478. Notes on the text inserted throughout, 479 ff.

Introduction to the two books addressed to Constantius Augustus. Order of these books, X, 553. Something is missing in the first, 555. When it was written, ibid. Its occasion, 556. Why it is called the first, [Col. 0319] ibid. His opinion on freedom of faith, ibid.—Critical notes, 557 ff. Introduction to the second book addressed to Constantius, 563.—Critical notes, 563 ff.—Preliminary dissertation on the book *Against Constantius*. This book seems to conflict with the others, 571. It is reconciled with the book *On the Synods*, ibid. Hilary’s gentleness demonstrated, 572. Constantius’s impiety, 573. The flattery of pseudo-bishops, ibid. Reason for its vehement language, 574. Many examples of Hilary’s moderation drawn from the same book, 575. That book was written while Constantius was alive, 576. It is not incomplete, but was enlarged by another hand, 577.—Notes and observations follow, 577 ff.—Introduction to the book *Against Auxentius*: the purpose of this book, 605. When it was written, 607. Eusebius of Vercelli and Hilary are maligned before the emperor by Auxentius, 607. Auxentius’s confession of faith is lacking, 608. Notes, ibid. ff.

On the works of St. Ambrose.

Dedicatory letter to François de Harlay, archbishop of Paris, XIV, 9. Preface on the merits of this edition, 13. Earlier editions, 15. The Montealto edition also incomplete, 18. Benedictine corrections, 20. Ambrose’s style, 22. His imitation of Philo the Jew, 24. Why Ambrose cites Greek Fathers while almost always suppressing their names, 25. He feeds the people with the word of God, ibid. Arian intrigues, 76. He writes *On Widows*, *On Virginity*, etc., 77; then *On Faith*, ibid. He loses his brother Satyrus, 78. He produces the book *On the Duties of the Clergy*, 81. The cases of Syagrius and Anemius, 81–82. He receives Augustine as a friend, 87, and baptizes him, 95. Many of his letters are cited, 98. His freedom toward the emperor, on behalf of a certain bishop, 99. The book *On Elijah and Fasting*, 101. He denies Emperor Theodosius entry to the church, 102. Theodosius’s death, 104. How he acted toward the tyrant Eugenius, 106. Theodosius defeats Eugenius, 109. Ambrose therefore gives thanks to God, ibid. Ambrose’s most pious death, III ff.—Introduction to Ambrose’s *Hexaemeron*, XIV, 119. Textual notes throughout.—Introduction to the book *On Paradise*, 273; likewise to *On Cain and Abel*, 314; *On Noah and the Ark*, 359; *On Abraham*, 417; *On Isaac and the Soul*, 499; *On the Good of Death*, 533; *On Flight from the World*, 567; *On Jacob and the Blessed Life*, 595; *On Joseph*, 637; *On the Blessings of the Patriarchs*, 671; *On Elijah and Fasting*, 693; *On Naboth the Israelite*, 727; *On Tobit*, 755; *On David’s Intercession*, 798; *Apology of the Prophet David*, 849; the second Apology, 883; the Expositions of Psalm XII, 917; likewise the Exposition of Psalm CXVIII, XV, 1193; the Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke, 1525; the Collection of Commentary on the Song of Songs, 1851.

Preface to Volume II, XVI, 9. On the genuine, doubtful, and spurious treatises published, ibid. On the prefatory notice placed before each treatise, ibid. Matters requiring correction, 10. Books to be rejected, 11. On two manuscripts preserved in the library of St Gall, 12; and on certain manuscripts in the Ambrosian Library, 13. Prefatory notice on *On the Duties [of Clerics]*, 17; likewise on *On Virgins*, 183; *On Widows*, 233; *On Virginity*, 263; *On the Education of a Virgin*, 305; *On Exhortation to Virginity*, 333; *On the Mysteries*, 583. Preface to *On the Sacraments*, 409. Prefatory notice on *On Penance*, 461; likewise on *On the Faith*, 523; *On the Holy Spirit*, 697; and *On the Sacrament of the Lord’s Incarnation*, 815. Likewise, prefatory notice on the Letters of Ambrose, newly arranged: rationale of the new arrangement, 849; first class, 851; second class, 867.
