Prefatory notice on the book *On the Forty-Two Encampments of the Children of Israel*, XVII, 9. Prefatory notice on the commentaries upon the Epistles of St Paul, 39; likewise on sermons circulated under the name of St Ambrose, 585. Notice on two prayers attributed to St Ambrose, 751. Prefatory notice on the exposition of the Apocalypse, 763. Notice on *On Penance*, 969; on *On the Holy Spirit*, 1005; likewise on *On the Dignity of the Human Condition*, 1014; on an Exorcism, 1017; on the Acts of St Sebastian, 1019; on *The Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, 1057; on *The Customs of the Brahmans*, 1131; on two letters concerning a possessed monk, 1153; and on certain hymns attributed to St Ambrose.

## Benedictines on the Works of St Jerome

Dedicated to Innocent XIII, Supreme Pontiff, an edition of St Jerome’s translation of the Holy Books, XXVIII, 29. — Prolegomenon I, Preface to Jerome’s Divine Library, 31. On the name “Divine Library,” ibid. Jerome’s purpose, 34. His study of the Hebrew language, 36. Those who encouraged him, [Col. 0320] 39. He avoided excessive novelty, 45. — Prolegomenon II: On the date of Jerome’s translations and their use in the Church, XXVIII, 47. Jerome did not preserve the order of the books, 49. Books translated by Jerome at once began to be read among Greeks and Latins alike, 55. Contemporary writers themselves used them, 58. They were especially preferred in Gaul, 66. By public decree the Church declared St Jerome’s Latin translation authentic, 60. — Prolegomenon III: On the canon of Hebrew truth and the scholia, XXVIII, 69. What the canon of Hebrew truth is, ibid. Jerome frequently mentions this canon, 73. The Greek and Latin Fathers acknowledge it, 75. On the individual parts of that canon, 85. Additions to Daniel and Esther, 87. Who authored the scholia, 90.

— Prolegomenon IV: On titles and chapters, verses and metres of the sacred Bible, XXVIII, 101. Ancient sacred writers divided texts in different ways, ibid. These sections were called titles, short sections, and chapters, 106. What distinctions of verses were made by the ancients, 109. Whether there is metre in Scripture, 126. Jerome’s opinion defended, 127. — Eulogy of distinguished men, with an index of manuscripts and editions on whose authority Jerome’s Divine Library has been restored, 135. Synopsis of the Divine Library, 141. Critical notes appended to the text, 147 ff.

## Benedictines on the Works of St Augustine

Dedication to Louis the Great of the new edition of the works of St Aurelius Augustine, published at Paris from the monastery of St-Germain-des-Prés in 1679, XXXII. — General Preface. On the magnitude of the work, 13. On assistance and privileges granted by the king, ibid. On comparison of manuscripts, 15. On the four requirements for carrying out the task, ibid. Observation concerning grace, ibid. Prefatory notice concerning *On Rebuke and Grace*, 21. Defence of free will, 23. Julian’s definition of sin to be rejected, ibid. “Free” is sometimes used by Augustine in the sense of “voluntary,” ibid. Augustine’s saying concerning free will, 25. The editors devoutly invoke both indulgence and the aid of the holy bishops of Gaul, 26. — Short Preface to Augustine’s Works, XXXII, 27. Works regarded as spurious or falsely attributed are relegated to the Appendices, ibid. Rationale of this division, ibid. The true authors of these works are assigned insofar as possible, 29. On the Life of Augustine arranged by the editors, ibid. An index of spurious opuscula is provided, ibid. On the various editions of the works of St Augustine, 31. The editors are encouraged to courage of spirit by the kindness of the Lords de Noailles, Archbishop of Paris, and Le Tellier, Archbishop of Rheims, ibid. — A few remarks on the Life by Possidius, ibid.

Life of St Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, compiled chiefly from his own writings, XXXII, 65. Book I: On the first twenty-nine years of Augustine, from his birth to his departure for Italy, ibid. Book II: On his departure for Italy until his return to Africa, 96. Book III: On his return to Africa until his episcopate, 157. Book IV: How Augustine lived in the episcopate, 209. Book V: On Augustine’s actions from the year 400 to 405. Book VI: On his deeds from 405 to the Conference of Carthage, 347. Book VII: From 411 to 419, he combats the enemies of God’s grace, 439. Book VIII: From 420 to 430, 511. — The manuscripts by which the books *Retractations* were corrected, 583. Prefatory notice on the *Confessions*, 657. Purpose and synopsis of that work, ibid. The year in which he wrote it, 659. Prefatory notice on *Against the Academics*, 902. Why it is placed here, ibid. Synopsis and year in which it was written, 903. Prefatory notice on *The Happy Life*, written by Augustine at nearly the same time as *Against the Academics*, 957. Prefatory notice on the two books *On Order*, 977; likewise on *On the Greatness of the Soul*, 1033; on the six books *On Music*, 1079. The year in which Augustine wrote these books, ibid. The subject of each book, 1081. Augustine’s own account of this work, ibid. Prefatory notice on *On the Teacher*: what Augustine testifies concerning this book, 1193. Prefatory notice on the three books *On Free Will*, 1219: against whom and at what time he wrote them, ibid. Augustine’s letter to Marcellinus, 1221. Prefatory notice on *The Morals of the Catholic Church and the Morals of the Manichaeans*, 1309. The year in which he wrote them, ibid. Likewise, prefatory notice on the spurious books *On Grammar*, *On the Principles of Dialectic*, and *On the Categories*, 1385.

Preface to Volume II. Augustine is chiefly to be learned from his letters, XXXIII, 9. The authority of Augustine’s letters, ibid. Disorder among them, ibid. They are restored to chronological sequence, ibid. They are divided into four classes, ibid. Certain short treatises are retained among the letters, 11. Some new unpublished letters are supplied, ibid. Four indexes appended, 13. — The chronological order of the letters demonstrated by arguments, 13. Letters of the first class, ibid.; second class, 19; third class, 36; fourth class, 48. — List of manuscripts against which St Augustine’s Letters were collated, 59. — Prefatory notice on letters relegated to the Appendix and those whose authority is insufficiently established, 1093.

[Col. 0321] Preface to Volume III, on Augustine’s commentaries on Sacred Scripture, XXXIV, 9. The book *On Christian Doctrine* as a key to the Scriptures, ibid. Augustine’s twofold aim in his scriptural commentaries, ibid. Augustine became a heavenly oracle even for his contemporaries, ibid. His modesty was as great as his understanding, 11. How he employed allegories, ibid. On those who reproach Augustine for ignorance of languages, 11. He followed the Septuagint version, ibid. — Prefatory notice on *On Christian Doctrine*: the time at which Augustine wrote it, 14. Synopsis of these books, ibid. Angilbert, abbot of Corbie, copied this work for the use of King Louis, 15. Notice concerning the collation of manuscripts, 15. Likewise, prefatory notice on *On True Religion*, which the holy Doctor published before becoming a priest, 121. What Paulinus says concerning it, ibid. Notice on the book *Locutions*, XXXIV, 485; likewise on the book *Questions*, 545; likewise on the *Mirror from Sacred Scripture*, 887; on *The Harmony of the Evangelists*, 1039. The reason for writing it, ibid. Synopsis, 1041. On *The Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, 1229. The year in which he wrote this book, ibid. — Prefatory notice on the seventeen questions on Matthew, XXXV, 1363. The time when Augustine completed it, ibid. On the inopportune silence of Eugyppius, ibid. Prefatory notice on the Tractates on John, XXXV, 1375. To what year they seem assignable, ibid. Augustine acknowledges that he delivered these sermons, ibid. How many passages were excerpted from them by Bede, Alcuin, Florus, and others, 1377. — Prefatory notice on the spurious work *On the Wonders of Sacred Scripture*, XXXV, 2149. Why it is falsely attributed to St Augustine, ibid. St Thomas’s view, ibid. Who appears to be the author of this book, ibid. Likewise, prefatory notice on *The Blessings of Jacob the Patriarch*: it appears to be Alcuin’s, 2199. Prefatory notice on *Questions on the Old and New Testament*. Why it is not to be attributed to Augustine, 2205. Errors with which it abounds, ibid. Prefatory notice on the *Exposition of the Apocalypse*, compiled from the words of Victorinus the martyr, Primasius, and Bede as well, 2415.

Preface to Volume IV. The reasons that led Augustine to expound the Psalms, XXXVI, 9. He did not plan to expound the whole Psalter in sequence, ibid. Rather, upon occasion, he expounded one Psalm or another to the people, 11. While expounding them, the holy Doctor rebuked the errors and vices of his age, ibid. On division into decades, 13. On the rules Augustine observed in expounding the Psalms, ibid. On the various senses of Scripture, ibid. He very frequently placed David’s words in Christ’s mouth, 15. He wonderfully perceived Christ prefigured in the Psalms, ibid. On the authority and veneration of the version of the Seventy interpreters, 17. On the Vulgate and Lucian’s edition, 18. — Variant readings excerpted from diverse manuscripts, XXXVI, 21. List of manuscripts against which this work was collated, 66.

Preface to Volume V. Augustine was an outstanding preacher of the divine word, XXXVIII, 9. Not only at Hippo, but at Carthage and elsewhere, ibid. In *On Christian Doctrine* he provides rules for effective speech, ibid. Hardly had he begun to preach when everyone was already flocking to him, ibid. A new order among his sermons is established, 11. Defects of the old order, ibid. Possidius in no way mentions the various classes of sermons, ibid. On the origin of those classes, 12 and 13. On the distribution of St Augustine’s sermons by Robert de Bardis, Chancellor of Paris, ibid. On the far more reasonable division into four orders—on Scripture, on seasons, on saints, and on miscellaneous subjects—15. On the careful distinction between genuine and falsely attributed works, ibid. The Vulgate is the ancient version called the Old Latin, corrected by Blessed Jerome against Greek manuscripts, 17. The editors strictly examined the doctrine of the sermons, ibid. Among Augustine’s sermons were found works intermixed from Ambrose, Origen, Cyprian, Maximus, Leo, Gregory the Great, Alcuin, etc., ibid. What the theologians of Louvain thought of doubtful or falsely attributed sermons ascribed to Augustine, 21. — List of manuscripts against which Augustine’s sermons were collated, ibid.

Preface to Volume VI. Augustine’s opuscula concerning the formation of morals, XL, 9. No slight care was also expended on works relegated to the Appendix, ibid. Prefatory notice on *On Faith*, rejected by the theologians of Louvain: among the Augustinian works, XL. The reason for restoring it to him, ibid. Prefatory notice on the *Enchiridion*, written by St Augustine in 421, 230. The occasion on which he completed this opusculum, ibid. Prefatory notice on *On the Christian Struggle*, XL, 289. The year to which that book should be assigned, ibid. Why he called it thus, ibid. Its subject matter, 289. Notice on *On Continence*, acknowledged by Augustine as his own in Letter 262 to Count Darius, 347. On *The Good of Marriage*, XL, 371. Likewise on *The Good of Widowhood*. Erasmus endeavours to take this book from Augustine and give it to his adversary Julian, 429. He is refuted. Possidius lists this book among the letters, ibid. Prefatory notice on *On Patience*, 609. Erasmus judges it not to be Augustine’s, ibid. It contains nothing contrary to Augustine’s genuine teaching, ibid. On the carelessness of certain persons, [Col. 0322] ibid. Prefatory notice on *The Creed for Catechumens*, 625. — Prefatory notices on the falsely attributed books of the Appendix, XL: on the book of Twenty-One Questions, 725; likewise on the Dialogue of Sixty-Five Questions, 733; *On Spirit and Soul*, 779; *On Friendship*, 831; *On Loving God*, 847; *Soliloquies of the Soul to God*: the Soliloquies written by St Augustine are very different from those attributed to him, 863; likewise on *Meditations*, which, although the theologians of Louvain retained it among genuine works, they nevertheless doubted, along with Erasmus, 897. What is disputed concerning Anselm, ibid. On *Contrition of Heart*, 941; the *Manual*, 950; *Mirror of the Sinner*, 983; *The Ladder of Paradise*, 997; *On the Knowledge of True Life*, 1003; *The Christian Life*, 1031; *Wholesome Precepts*, 1045; *On the Twelve Abuses*, 1077; the treatise *On the Seven Vices* and *On the Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit*, 1087; likewise *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, 1091; *On True and False Penance*, 1111; *On Antichrist*, 1130; *On the Consolation of the Dead*, 1157; the treatise *On the Uprightness of Catholic Conduct*, 1167; and sermons *To the Brothers in the Desert*, 1235.

Preface to Volume VII. On the polemical writings of St Augustine, XLI, 9. In his illustrious work *The City of God*, he first combats pagans, ibid. The great importance of this work, ibid. The exclamation of Macedonius, who had nevertheless seen only its first three books, ibid. Augustine wrote it at Marcellinus’s request, ibid. This work, begun in 411, was completed only in 427, 11. — List of manuscripts against which *The City of God* was collated, 11. — Prefatory notices on books of the Appendix: the Letter of Lucian to the Whole Church, 807; the Letter of Anastasius to Landuleus, concerning the account of the translation of St Stephen, 817; the Letter of Severus to the Whole Church, 821; and *On Miracles*, 833.

Preface to Volume VIII. We present the labours and struggles of the holy Doctor against heretics, XLII. How he attained his end, ibid. Jerome’s words to Augustine: “Well done for your courage; you are celebrated throughout the world.” Praises of the holy Doctor, ibid. The adversaries he had to combat, 11. He first draws the sword against the errors of the Manichaeans, ibid. He then turns against the Priscillianists and Origenists, 13. Soon he rises against the Arians in brilliant writings, ibid. — Several works whose authenticity is insufficiently established are transferred to the Appendix. — Prefatory notice on *On Heresies*: the occasion and date of its composition, 15. Prefatory notice on *On the Usefulness of Believing*, 63. *Against Fortunatus*: the identity of Fortunatus and the date on which Augustine refuted him, 111. Prefatory notice on *Against Felix*, 517. Prefatory notice on the conference and two books *Against Maximinus the Arian*, around 427 or 428, XLII, 707. Prefatory notice on the books *On the Trinity*. Augustine kept this work in hand for many years, 815. Synopsis of each book. He drafted them around the year 400. — Prefatory notices on each Appendix book: the treatise *Against Five Heresies*, 1099; sermon *Against the Jews*, 1115; *On Faith, against the Manichaeans*, 1139; *On the Unity of the Trinity*, 1155; *On the Trinity and Unity of God*, 1193; *On the Essence of Divinity*, 1199; and *On the Doctrines of the Church*, 1313.

Preface to Volume IX. On Augustine’s books *Against the Donatists*, XLIII; their schism arose forty-three years before Augustine’s birth, ibid. A brief history of that schism, ibid. The identity of Donatus and Caecilian, ibid. On Caecilian’s ordination, ibid. All Africa divided into two parties, 11. At the Council of Rome in 313, Caecilian was acquitted and Donatus condemned, 11. The obstinacy of the Donatists, ibid. A new conference in Africa before the proconsul Aelian, ibid. Soon the Council of Arles was convened, in which Caecilian’s cause again prevailed, 13. The Donatist schism turned into heresy, 13. Donatus’s pride, ibid. For quite a long time they even secretly maintained bishops in Rome itself, ibid. They boasted that Catholics had stirred up three persecutions against them; under Constans’s care peace was restored to nearly all Africa, 14. Donatist bishops return from exile by flattering Emperor Julian, 15. Soon countless massacres and dreadful crimes follow, 15–16. The Donatists divided among themselves, 17. Primian, Donatist bishop of Carthage, when Augustine was ordained priest, ibid. Augustine routs the Donatists by his writings, ibid. Having become bishop of Hippo, he combats them, 19. Honorius orders the Conference at Carthage in 411, 21. Augustine publishes the book titled *After the Conference, to the Donatists*, 22. Council of Carthage in 418, to extinguish the remnants of the Donatists, 23. The book concerning the subdeacon Rusticianus, a doubtful work, is relegated to the end, ibid. — Prefatory notice on *Against the Letter of Parmenian*: the identity of Parmenian, XLIII, 31. Written about 400, 33. Likewise on *Against the Letters of Petilianus the Donatist*, 243. The identity of Petilianus, ibid. Baronius on the year in which those books were written, 245. Likewise on *The Unity of the Church*, 389. Its various titles, ibid. It seems to belong to 402, ibid. Certain unusual features in Augustine are noted here, ibid. [Col. 0323] Prefatory notice on the Abridgment of the Conference, 613. Note: the Conference was held and the book written in 411, ibid. Likewise on *After the Conference, to the Donatists*, 651. Prefatory notice on *Against Fulgentius the Donatist*, by an uncertain author, 759. Judgment of the Louvain theologians, ibid. It is demonstrated not to be Augustine’s, ibid., 761.

Preface to Volume X. Scarcely had the Donatist faction been defeated when the Church had a new and no less dangerous enemy in Pelagius, XLIV, 9. Pelagius’s native country, manner of life, and character, ibid. Pelagius’s earliest writings already imbued with the poison of heresy, 12. Origin of the Pelagian heresy, 15. Caelestius, Pelagius’s disciple, is accused by Paulinus and condemned at the Council of Carthage in 412, 17. Augustine attacks the Pelagians first in sacred sermons, then in written books, 19. In 412 he replies to Pelagius and confirms the doctrine of God’s grace, 23. Pelagius offers the poison of heresy to the virgin Demetrias and slanders Jerome, 25. Augustine recalls Timasius and Jacob from Pelagius’s error, 29. Orosius disputes with Pelagius at Jerusalem, 33. Pelagius accused by Heros and Lazarus, 39. He conceals his heresy; Theodore of Mopsuestia defends him, 45. Certain writings of Jerome are brought to Africa by Orosius, 49. Innocent anathematizes Pelagius’s errors, 53. Caelestius comes to Rome; Zosimus considers him innocent, 57. Pelagius’s letter and profession of faith, 61. Council of Carthage: 214 bishops, 63. Zosimus replies to the Fathers of the Council of Carthage, 65. Honorius penalizes the Pelagians by law, 67. All bishops subscribe to Pelagius’s condemnation, 71. Augustine exposes all Pelagius’s deceits in *On Christ’s Grace and Original Sin*, 75. Augustine’s book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, 79. Alypius carries these books to Italy around the beginning of 421, 85. Pelagius is condemned in Syria, Julian in Cilicia, 87. Augustine writes once and again to the monks of Hadrumetum, 91. He brings Leporius back to the truth, 97. In Augustine’s old age the Semi-Pelagians arise, 101. — Prefatory notice on *The Perfection of Righteousness*; likewise on *The Proceedings of Pelagius*, 317; likewise on *Marriage and Concupiscence*, 409; on *The Soul and Its Origin*, 473; *Against the Letter of the Pelagians*, 547; and *Against Julian*, of which a synopsis is supplied, 637. Augustine himself gives notice of *On Grace and Free Will* in a letter to Valentinus, 875; likewise Valentinus’s letter to Augustine at the head of *On Rebuke and Grace*, 911. Prefatory notice on *The Gift of Perseverance*, XLV, 993. Augustine refutes the errors of the Semi-Pelagians, ibid. Those by whom the book is cited as Augustine’s work, ibid. Bellarmine’s view concerning it, ibid. Prefatory notice on the *Unfinished Work against Julian’s Second Reply*, 1033. On Julian and his writings, ibid. On Augustine’s *Unfinished Work*, 1043. From Augustine’s letter to Quodvultdeus, 1047. Prefatory notices on books of the Appendix, whether doubtful or spurious: the book titled *Hypomnesticon*, 1609. Those who have attributed these books to Augustine, ibid. Likewise on *Predestination and Grace*. The arguments showing that this book is not Augustine’s, 1665. — Variant readings of the genuine sermons of St Augustine, 1157.

## Benedictines on St Gregory the Great

Dedication to Pope Clement XI of the works of St Gregory the Great, illustrated with corrections, additions, and notes, LXXV, 9 ff. — General preface placed at the beginning of this edition, 15. Various editions of St Gregory’s works, ibid. Which appears more accurate, 17. Gussanville and the Roman editors defended, 19. Plan of the new edition, 21. Its collaborators, ibid.; and benefactors, ibid. Arrangement of the entire work, 23. Whether the holy Doctor expounded the four Gospels, 25. St Gregory’s doctrine concerning the various heretics, ibid. What he thought concerning the blessedness of the saints, 27. What he taught concerning the Eucharist, 29. He opposes the error of the Quietists, 31. The scriptural versions he used, 35. On his style and method of writing, ibid. — Preface on the three Lives of St Gregory the Great, LXXV, 37. On the Life written by Paul the Deacon of Monte Cassino and first in order, ibid. Another by John the Deacon, likewise of Monte Cassino, ibid. Certain additions concerning Paul the Deacon, 39. On the Life written by the Benedictines themselves, 41. — Corrective and explanatory notes on the Life of St Gregory written by Paul the Deacon and John, 41 ff.

Life of St Gregory the Great, newly composed chiefly from his own writings. Book I: his history from birth to the supreme pontificate, LXXIV, 242. Book II: the first four years of St Gregory’s pontificate, 283. Book III: St Gregory’s deeds from 594 to 599, 343. Book IV: the remainder of St Gregory’s life, 413. — Preface to the books *Morals*. The time when Blessed Gregory wrote these books, 469. How eagerly they were received, ibid. How assiduous the ancients were in reading and collecting these books, 501. The manuscripts used by the editors, ibid. Corrections made, 504. They preserved the division established by the holy Doctor, [Col. 0324] 505. Notes on the books *Morals*, 509 ff., and LXXVI, 9 ff. — Prefatory notice on the books of Homilies, 781. Annotation, 785 ff. — Prefatory notice on the book of Homilies on the Gospels, 1071. — Preface to the book *Pastoral Rule*, LXXVII. On other writings of St Gregory, 9. How eagerly his *Pastoral Rule* was received, ibid. The holy Doctor worked on it for a long time, ibid. When he completed it, 10. On corrections, 11. On the various manuscripts, ibid. Notes on the *Pastoral Rule*, 13 ff. — Preface to St Gregory’s *Dialogues*, 137. Those who have challenged the attribution of these books to St Gregory the Great, 138. The indications by which they are known to belong to Gregory, 139. On belief in miracles, ibid. What St Gregory achieved among the Lombards through his *Dialogues*, ibid. St Gregory is the true author of these books, 442. Gregory himself relates the occasion and method of their composition, ibid. The date at which they were written, 145. What has been accomplished in this edition, ibid. As most acknowledge, Zacharias translated them into Greek, 146. — Notes on the books *Dialogues*, 149 ff. — Preface to St Gregory’s Letters, on the excellence and dignity of the work, LXXVII, 431. On errors neglected by Gussanville, ibid. On the order of the letters, 434. Materials to be relegated to the end, 435. On interwoven notes, ibid., 437. Brevity had to be considered, 438. Replies to certain objections, ibid. On manuscripts, 439. Extract from Gussanville’s preface, 441. — Notes and observations on the text, 441 ff.

Preface to the Book of Sacraments. — Various opinions concerning this book, LXXVIII, 9. Selection among editions and manuscripts, ibid. Why the editors used the manuscript of Jumièges, 11. The great care with which that book was preserved in churches, 12. Sources from which the editors drew their notes, 13. Certain remarks on Hugh Menard, ibid. — Interwoven notes, 25 ff. — Notice on additions *On Blessings*, 601. — Preface to St Gregory’s Antiphonary. Gregory was a collector and corrector rather than an author, 636. On the antiphon at the Introit and the Gradual, ibid. Who restored it after its corruption among the English and Gauls, ibid. Later published by Pamelius, ibid. — Notes on the Antiphonary, 641 ff. — Preliminary observations on the Collection of Responsories, Antiphons, and Verses, 720. — Interwoven notes, 725 ff. — Preliminary commentary on the Roman Order, LXXVIII, 851. Knowledge of Roman rites is necessary, ibid. On the Roman Order, 855. On the ancient basilicas and titles of the city, 857. On the ancient rite of the offices, 864. On collects, stations, and litanies, 866. Rite of the Mass, 869. How and when communion under both kinds ceased, 884. On sacred ordinations, 909. On the consecration of a pontiff, 917. Whether ancient rites are always to be preferred to new ones, 932. Annotation on the sixteen Roman Orders, 937 to the end. Prefatory notice on the first Order, 935; the second, 967; the third, 975; the fifth, 984; the seventh, 993; the eighth, 999; the tenth, 1007; the author of the twelfth Order, Cencius, 1061; the fourteenth, by Cardinal Jacobus Caietanus, 1121; the fifteenth, by Peter Amelius, bishop of Senigallia, 1274.

Preface to St Gregory the Great’s Commentary on the Books of Kings. On three opinions concerning the author of these books, LXXIX, 9. Against Gussanville, similarity of style with that of St Gregory is demonstrated; in doctrine it is nearly identical with Gregorian writings, 11. Features not characteristic of Gregory, 13. Indication that the work was interpolated by Claudius, his disciple, 13. Replies to other objections, 15. — Notes and explanations appended, 17 ff. — Prefatory notice on the Expositions of the Song of Songs. How the Venerable Bede fashioned this book from Gregory’s writings, 467 ff. — Assessment of the books *Exposition of the Seven Penitential Psalms*, 547. — Notice on the Harmony of Certain Scriptural Passages, 857. — Preface to St Paterius’s book *Exposition of the Old and New Testament*, and the similar work of Alulf, LXXIX. The identity of Paterius, 677. How he undertook this work at Gregory’s counsel, 679. On manuscripts, ibid. — See *Literary History of France*.

## Benedictines of the Restored Monastery of Solesmes, Authors of *Origins of the Roman Church*

Preface to the Catalogue of Roman Pontiffs set down under Liberius, XIII, 441. When it became possible to commit the individual traditions of the Church to writing, 441. Systematic investigation of the *Origins*, 442. Documents published by the most learned Bucherius in 1634. Why these especially concern us, 443. What Henschenius maintains, 444; Pagius, ibid. New edition of Liberius’s Catalogue at Antwerp in 1675. The Vienna manuscript, 446. Schelstrate published it in *Antiquities Illustrated*, ibid. — Inquiry into the date, author, and authority of the same Catalogue, XIII, 454. Dodwell’s view, 455. Tillemont’s view, ibid. The author of this Catalogue: the opinion of Tillemont and Pagius, 456. What Dom Cellarius objects, 457. Its authority, 458. The method once observed by Christians in reckoning consuls, 459. Certain conjectures are quite rightly made, I, 461. Examples drawn from Dom Ruinart, 462. Facts are brought forward to prove the conjectures, 463. Mabillon published a similar Catalogue, [Col. 0325] almost of the same age and for use by the Church of Carthage, 466. Dodwell’s objection, 467. Refuted, 468. Refutation of Pearson’s objections, 469. On his errors, 470.

**Beslius (Jean)**, historian of Poitiers, died in 1641. — Preface to the history *On the Journey to Jerusalem*, by Peter Tudebode, priest of Siurac, CLV, 758.

**Bertinellius (Joseph)**, year unknown. He edited the works of Victor of Vita and dedicated them to Cardinal J. M. Ottobono, bishop of Padua, LVIII, 125.

**Besselius (Godefredus)**, abbot of Göttweig Abbey of the Order of St Benedict, born at Berchem in 1672 and died in 1749. He prefixed a preface to the Viennese edition of the Works of St Augustine. On the letters of the most holy Doctor whose date is less certainly known, XXXIII, 49. The question of the origin of souls, ibid. Augustine’s book on the same subject, ibid. The letters of St Optatus on the same question, 50. Optatus receives from Augustine letters concerning it, 50. What Augustine asks of him, 51. Which writings of Augustine on this matter have or have not been published, ibid.

**Bethmann (Ludwig Conrad).**

Notice on Robert of Torigni, CCII, 1306. — In the Appendix to Baldwin, Emperor of Constantinople, he published genealogies of the counts of Flanders, by the priest Witger and various others, with notes and variant readings, CCIX, 927.

**Betulaeus (Sixtus).** Native of Memmingen; born in 1500 and died in 1554. Lactantius’s works, with his commentary, were published at Basel and Paris in 1563, VI, 106; VII, 98 ff.

**Beza (Theodore)**, an eminent controversialist among Protestants, born at Vézelay in Nivernais in 1519; died at Geneva in 1580.

Letter by which he dedicates to the University of Cambridge a Greek-Latin copy of the four Gospels and Acts, drawn from the monastery of St Irenaeus at Lyons—mutilated indeed, but of great value because of its antiquity—XII, 874. Note written in Beza’s hand and inscribed in the manuscript, 876.

**Bignonius (Jérôme)**, learned Chancellor of the realm, born at Paris in 1589 and died in 1656.

He annotated and published the two books of Marculf’s formularies. — Preface, LXXXVII, 693. Notes appended to the text, 697 ff. — He also added notes to the Roman formularies published by Sirmond, 780 and passim. — He likewise illustrated with notes certain formularies by an uncertain author, 197 ff.

**Binius (Severinus)**, canon of Cologne, died in 1641.

Certain notes by him on the letters ascribed to Saint Cornelius, III, 843; and on the Appendix, VII, 1091. — His notes likewise on the Appendix to the works of Constantine the Great, VIII, 565; also notes on Sylvester, 795 ff., 825; on Saint Mark, p. 849; on Saint Julius, p. 857; on Liberius, p. 1331; textual notes on Pope Saint Felix, XIII, 9; likewise on Siricius, XIII, 1115. — Notes on Saint Anastasius, XX, 52 ff. Notice on Saint Anastasius’s letter to John of Jerusalem, 65. Cited by Jerome, ibid. Inserted among Jerome’s letters, ibid.; and in Marius Mercator, ibid. Rufinus suspects that it was fabricated by Jerome, 66. The year in which it was written, ibid. Origen condemned by Anastasius, ibid. Anastasius condemns Rufinus without passing sentence, 67. Textual notes, 75. Critical notes on Pope Saint Innocent I, XX, 459. Notice on Letter 2, to Victricius, XX, 465. Its authenticity is not rendered doubtful by what is stated therein about Siricius, ibid. It is not to be assigned to the year 405, ibid. It is called the Book of Rules, 466. Laws forbidding members of municipal councils to leave the curia, 466. The conditions under which curiales were permitted to enter the clergy, 467. Notes on the text, 469 ff. — Notice on Letter 3, XX, 481. This letter is shorter in some manuscripts and longer in others: the reason why, ibid. It is addressed to the bishops of the Synod of Toledo or Toulouse, 482. How it came to be addressed to the Synod of Toledo, ibid. It was written to the fathers of the First Council of Toledo, 483. These fathers are three in number, ibid. They place the council in the year 447; the council was held in the year 400, 484. This establishes that the letter was written to this council, ibid. — Notice on Letter 17, to Rufus, Eusebius, etc. The time when it was written, XX, 521; its occasion, ibid. Certain laws of ecclesiastical discipline, 522. Quesnel’s opinion, ibid. The distinction established by the holy pope, 524. His view confirmed from the Greek source of the Council of Nicaea, 525. Notes appended to the text, ibid. ff. — Notes on Pope Zosimus, 639. — Notes on the life and writings of Pope Saint Hilary, LVIII, 9 ff.; likewise on the life and writings of Pope Simplicius, 31 ff. Observations on the life and writings of Pope Saint Felix III, LVIII, 891 ff. — Notes on the writings of Pope Symmachus, LXII, 51. — Observations on the notice concerning Pope Hormisdas, LXIII, 363; likewise on his writings, 370 ff. — Notes on the life of Pope Felix IV, XV, 9; likewise on the life of Pope Boniface II. — Likewise on the life and writings of Pope John II, LXVI, 9 ff.; likewise on the life and writings of Pope Agapetus I, 33. — On the life and writings of Pope Silverius, [Col. 0326] 79. — Notes on the canon of the Second Council of Orange concerning grace and free will, 1142. Notes and observations on the life and writings of Pope Vigilius, LXIX, 9 ff. — Likewise on Pope John III, LXXII, 9 ff. — Likewise on the life of Pope Benedict I, 681; on the life and writings of Pope Pelagius II, 701. — Notes on the Council of Auxerre, 761 ff. — Notes on Pope Boniface IV, LXXX, 97; notes on Pope Saint Deusdedit, 355. — Likewise on Boniface V, 430. — On Pope Honorius I, 464 ff. — On Pope John IV, 599. — Notes on Pope Saint Theodore, LXXXVII, 71. — Likewise on Pope Saint Martin, 105; likewise on Pope Saint Deodatus, 1159 ff. — Pope Saint Donus, 1145; and Pope Saint Agatho, 1153. — On Pope Sergius, LXXXIX, 10. — On John VI, 35 ff. — On John VII, 53; on Pope Constantine, 315. — On Pope Zachary, 894. — Notes on Pope Stephen II, 959 and passim. — On Pope Saint Paul I, 1125 and passim. — On Pope Leo II, XCVI, 383 and passim, and on his writings, 411 ff. — On Benedict II and his letters, 421 ff. — On Pope John V and his writings, 424. — Notes on the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs by Anastasius, CXXVII, 1019. — Notes on the writings of Pope Stephen V, CXXIX, 785 ff. — Severinus Binius’s admonition on the synodal sermon of Udalric, CXXV, 1069.

**BIVARIUS (Fr. Franciscus)**, procurator of the Cistercian Order of Saint Bernard, in 1624 published the Works of Flavius Lucius Dexter and dedicated them to Cardinal Gabriel de Trejo, XXXI, 9. The cardinal’s reply to him, 11. Likewise a second letter of Luke Wadding to the editor, 13. — Life of Flavius Dexter, collected from his own writings and those of others, 13. Barcelona in Spain, especially made illustrious by its martyrs, ibid. Dexter derived his origin from there and had Saint Pacian as his father, 15. Related by blood to Orosius, ibid.; he made great progress in letters, 16. At his request Jerome composed his Catalogue, 17. Saint Jerome’s letter to Dexter, ibid. Arcadius raised him to the prefecture of the praetorium, 18. Two years later he returned to his native country and brought his universal history to its conclusion in the year 430. His death, 20. — Apology for Dexter’s Chronicle. Its author is truly Dexter, 25. On its authority, 34. Bivarius’s Commentary on the Chronicle of the Universal History of Flavius Dexter, 49 ff. — Apologetic reply to the objections of a certain Pennotius against Dexter’s Chronicle, 591. The reason for the apology set forth, ibid. The measures Pennotius devised to destroy the Chronicle’s authority, 595. Pennotius’s tripartite argument is entangled in the same knots with which he tries to bind Dexter’s history, 600. Pennotius’s inconsistencies exposed, 604. Cistercian rights defended, 609. Abbot Joachim defended against Pennotius’s calumnies, 614. Reply to Pennotius’s objections against the Chronicles of Dexter and Maximus, 627.

**BLANCHINIUS (Josephus)**, born at Verona in 1704, died in 1770; priest, theologian, and archaeologist. He composed an illuminating dissertation on the Paschal Canon of Saint Hippolytus, from which the Prolegomena to the Chronicles of an anonymous author were extracted. — Synopsis. Various opinions of learned men concerning the author of this Chronicle, III, 651. Some thought it should be ascribed to Saint Hippolytus, bishop and martyr, 633. But its author appears to be either Heron, a Christian convert from philosophy and a martyr, or, more probably, an anonymous writer who lived under Alexander Severus, ibid. Du Cange’s opinion that Hippolytus was the author of the Chronicle is presented, 654. Yet the writer of the Chronicle differs from Hippolytus in chronological calculations, ibid. This is demonstrated by examples adduced, 656. Conclusion of Blanchini’s demonstration, 657. Various editions of the said Chronicle, 658. — His dedicatory letter to John V, King of Portugal, on the occasion of the edition of the Gospel-book of Eusebius of Vercelli, XII, 9. — Blanchini’s judgment on the Eusebian codex, XII, 73. What the Acts of Eusebius of Vercelli published by Ughelli teach, ibid. Written in Eusebius’s own hand, ibid. Its cover, of silver and gold, restored by Berengar in 888. How Saint Ambrose, 75, and Tertullian, 76, are cited; Mabillon, 77, and Montfaucon, 77. Examples of variant readings in Irenaeus, Cyprian, Ambrose, Augustine, etc., 81 ff. On the Ethiopic and Armenian versions of the Bible, 107; likewise the Punic, 109. Another, purer and more useful source of variant readings, 111. Testimonies of the Vienna codex, 113, 114 ff. — Letter to Musellius, XII, 123. How the Vercelli Codex preserves the old Latin translation received in use from apostolic times, ibid. How the codex is attacked by some, 124. It is defended with Tertullian, 125; John Chrysostom, 126; Augustine, ibid.; Vigilius of Thapsus, 127; and John of Damascus, ibid. Collation of the Verona and Vercelli codices, together with those of Corbie, Brescia, Vienna, and Saint-Germain, 127 ff. — Blanchini’s critical notes appended to the text, 141 ff. — Letter in which certain variant readings of the Evangelists are criticized, 837 ff. — Letter describing the Greek-Latin codex of the Gospels and Acts preserved in Cambridge Library, [Col. 0327] 866. — Readings of the fourfold Gospel agreeing with the Greek text where they differ from the Vulgate edition, XII, 875: Saint Matthew, ibid.; Saint John, 879; Saint Luke, 885; Saint Mark, 894. Readings of the fourfold Gospel agreeing with ten Greek manuscript codices preserved at Rome, 895: Saint Matthew, ibid.; Saint John, 897; Saint Luke, 898; Saint Mark, 900. — Readings of the Gospel-book of Verona agreeing with the Syriac, Arabic, Persian, and Ethiopic versions where they differ from the Vulgate: Saint Matthew, 901; Saint John, 904; Saint Luke, 909; Saint Mark, 914. — Old Testament testimonies cited in the Gospels according to the Hebrew, Greek, Vulgate, and Old Latin editions, 917 ff. — Notes on Pope Saint Boniface IV, LXXX, 29; likewise on Pope Saint Deusdedit, 355 and passim; likewise on Boniface V. Preface to the writings of Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVII, 27. On the title, date, authors, origin, and growth of his book, ibid. ff. — Preface to volume II of the Roman-Vatican edition, 103. Addition of Mabillon’s notes, 104. On the description of the regions of the City, 105. Notes of various authors to be recorded, 107. — Preface to volume III of the same edition, CXXVII, 109. — Brief notes on the chronology of the Catalogue of Roman Pontiffs, 124. — Catalogue covering 865 years, from an ancient codex, 133. — Catalogue of pontiffs and decrees, 141. Notes on the preceding catalogues, 147. — Appendix to Schelstrate’s dissertation, 219. Dissertation on the ancient catalogues of Roman pontiffs and on their comparison and selection, 235. Rules for the examination of chronology, ibid.; the rules are given, 237. Chronology to be established from the surviving monument in the Basilica of Saint Paul on the Ostian Way, 248. On the series of Roman pontiffs depicted in the mosaic of Saint Leo the Great in the central nave of that church, 261. This series is presented, 273. Notice, 281. On continuing the chronology of the Roman pontiffs, 312. — Observations on three chronological treatises, 315. — Likewise a preliminary notice to two others, 343. — On the description of the city of Rome, 348. — On papal, imperial, and consular chronology, 383. — Appendix to the Chronology, 924. — Preliminary observations on the Cornutian Charter, 971. — Chronological notes on the Life of each Roman pontiff written by Anastasius, CXXVII, 1020 ff.

**BLANCHIUS (Horatius)** published at Rome the Works of Paul the Deacon of Cividale.

Notice on Paul the Deacon’s *History of the Lombards*, XCV, 411 ff. — Notes on the same history (which are not marked), interspersed among the Lindenbrogian and Modenese notes, 433 and passim.

**BOILEAU (Jacques)**, Doctor of the Sorbonne, learned theologian, born at Paris in 1655 and died in 1716.

Dissertation on Ratramnus’s book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, defending it from every suspicion of novelty or heresy against Father Hardouin of the Society of Jesus, CXXI, 171. Occasion of this dissertation, ibid. The argument by which the book is restored to its author, ibid. How de Marca was deceived regarding the author of this book, 172. The book was in everyone’s hands at that time, 173. How slight the critical basis of the dissertation writer’s opponents is, 174. Words wrongly interpreted in this book, 175. The author of the dissertation excuses John Scotus in order to reproach Ratramnus, 176. On the prayer of Saint Gregory’s Sacramentary, 177. Reply to many objections, 178 ff.

**BOLLANDUS (John)**, a learned member of the Society of Jesus, born at Antwerp in 1596 and died in 1665.

He prepared the *Acts of the Saints*. — Notice on Saint Domnolus, bishop of Le Mans: his life, writings, cult, and relics, LXXII, 629; the time of his episcopate and death, 632. — Prologue to the itinerary to the Holy Land ascribed to Antoninus of Piacenza, 897. He appears to have read “Antoninus” in place of “anonymous writer,” ibid. — Life of Saint Marius, LXXX, 25. — Admonition on the Life of Saint Augustine, apostle of the English, 41. Historical notice on Saint Sigebert, king of the Franks, LXXXVII, 301. Birth of the elder Saint Sigebert, 303; baptism and education, 305; kingdom of Austrasia and death of Dagobert, 308; death of Pepin, Grimoald, and the Thuringian War, 309; almsgiving, death, and burial of Sigebert, 312. Notes on the Life of Sigebert, 303 ff. — Extracts from various authors pertaining to Saint Sigebert, 313. — Preliminary commentary on Saint Henry, emperor, CXL, 9. The saint’s family, name, and surnames, ibid.; his age, day and year of death, cult, and eulogies, 14; canonization and translations, 19; relics and offices, 24; writers of his life, 39; chastity preserved with his wife Cunegunda, 49; chief deeds of Saint Henry arranged chronologically, 60; the bishopric of Bamberg founded by him, 65; Saint Henry’s coronation at Rome, 76; the remainder of Henry’s life until his happy end, 82. — Commentary on Pope Saint Leo IX: various acts, writings, veneration, and relics, CXLIII, 510. Chronology and controversies decided, [Col. 0328] 513. Events of the years 1050 and 1051; of 1052 and 1053; his blessed death in 1054. — Notes on the Acts of Saints Arialdus and Erlembald, CXLIII, 1439 ff. Bollandus’s notes on the Life of Saint Maurus of the Order of Saint Benedict, CXLIV, 945 ff. — Commentary on Saint John Gualbert, abbot of Vallombrosa: his country, name, and lineage, CXLVI, 765; mercy toward an enemy, 710; writers of his life, 714; foundation of the Vallombrosan Order, 724; writings and prayers of John Gualbert, 730; chronology of his life, 739; whether the saint could have associated with Saint Romuald in the Camaldolese wilderness, 745; canonization of Saint John Gualbert, 750. — Preliminary commentary on the Life of Saint John of Beverley, archbishop of York, by Folcard, CXLVII, 1161. — Preliminary commentary on Pope Saint Gregory VII: Gregory’s eulogists and defenders, CXLVIII, 11; translation of the body and cult of Saint Gregory, 16; Saint Gregory’s monastic life and priorship at Cluny, 23; how this saint was lately enrolled in the Vallombrosan Order, 29; his lineage, 34. Preliminary observation on the Life of Saint Stephen, king of the Hungarians, CLI, 1203; likewise observation on Saint Stephen’s laws, 1243.

Preliminary commentary on the Acts of Saint Bruno, founder of the Carthusians, CLII, 9. Which Lives or Acts should be published, ibid. Saint Bruno’s noble lineage, homeland, and time of birth, 23. His studies, 34. Where he went after Berengar of Tours had departed, 48. The kind of pupils he had, 60. He opposed the shameful enterprises of Manasses, his archbishop, 65. Manasses defended his case at Rome, 77. When the saint was restored at Reims to a better condition, 88. The cause of Bruno’s withdrawal into the wilderness, 108. Testimonies earlier than the sixteenth century produced, 126. When the saint fled to the wilderness, 269. Whether he wrote a new rule, 296. Whether Pope Victor III approved the Carthusian Order. Bruno summoned by the supreme pontiff, 309. He comes to Rome, 320. The concession granted him by Count Roger, 338. He procures the consecration of a church built in the wilderness of Calabria, 357. Whether he attended the Council of Piacenza, 365. The saint rescues Count Roger from danger, 389. He comments on the Psalms and Saint Paul’s Epistles, 425. In which church he was buried, 449. Leo permits the saint’s cult, 461. Whether that same Leo X canonized Saint Bruno, 470.

Notice on the Life of Saint Hugh, CLIII, 759. — Preliminary commentary on the Life of Saint Swithun by Goscelin, CLV, 47. Swithun’s cult, miracles, and relics, ibid. On the writers of his life, 50. Some questions concerning Saint Swithun’s life and death resolved, 54. — Preliminary commentary on the Life and the biographers of Saint Ivo, bishop of the Persians, buried in England, 79. Likewise preliminary commentary on the Life of Saint Werburga, virgin, 93. Her royal descent, life, writings, and time as monastic superior, 93. Her relics transferred to Chester and publicly venerated, 95. Preliminary commentary on the Life of Blessed Ida, countess of Boulogne, 43. Preliminary commentary on the Life of Saint Robert, first abbot of Molesme, CLVII, 1255. The beginnings of Robert’s reform of the Benedictine Order, ibid. The rightfulness of the monastery of Cîteaux, 1260. Recall and return of Saint Robert to Molesme, 1266. — Process of the canonization of Saint Robert, 1288. — Notice on the miracles of Saint Benedict related in sequence by Rudolph of Tortario, CLX, 1238. — Preliminary commentary on the twofold Life of Saint Robert of Arbrissel, founder of the Order of Saint Ebrald, CLXII, 1017. His name and the holiness of that order, ibid. Robert’s homeland and life, 1022; his holiness, death, and tomb, 1027; Blessed Robert’s first companions, 1030; Robert’s miracles, 1034. — Notice on the Life of Pope Paschal II by Peter of Pisa, CLXIII, 14. — Notice on the Life of Pope Gelasius II by Pandulf of Alatri, 473. Notice on the Life of Saint James, bishop of Tarentaise, 1410. — Preliminary commentary on the Life of Blessed Charles the Good, count of Flanders: the writers of his life and his relics, CLXVI, 874. A tale concerning the murder of Blessed Charles, 879. This tale examined, 883. Murder of Blessed Charles perpetrated by the Erembald family, 889. Line of the castellans of the city of Bruges, 897. Murder of Blessed Charles from the acts of Louis the Fat, king of the Franks.

Historical notice on Saint Stephen, abbot of Cîteaux: birth, monastic life, pilgrimage, arrival at Molesme and Cîteaux, and his priorship, CLXVI, 1361. He is made abbot; his first statutes; a house miraculously removed; his prayers and humility, 1363. He has visions. Arrival of Saint Bernard, 1367. He builds various monasteries in accordance with the Charter of Charity, 1370. He lays down the burden of the abbacy; illness, death, and cult, 1372. — Notice on Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, 1563. — Commentary on the Life of Saint Walter, abbot and canon of Limoges, CLXXI, 1563. — Preliminary observations on the Life of Blessed Bernard, founder of the Congregation of Tiron in France, CLXXII, 1363. Life and writings of Blessed Bernard, [Col. 0329] ibid. The time of Blessed Bernard’s life and death, his entry in the calendar, and his title, 1366. — Historical notice on Anacletus, antipope, CLXXIX, 687. — Preliminary commentary on the Life of Blessed Aelred, abbot of Rievaulx in England, by an anonymous author, CXCV, 195. — Life of Saint Hildegard, abbess, CXCVII, 9. Acts of Saint Hildegard and their authors, ibid. Birth, childhood, and monastic life of Saint Hildegard, 12. She founds a monastery on Mount Saint Rupert, 20. Her fame becomes illustrious, 28. Letters of Anastasius IV and Adrian IV to her, 31. She is consulted concerning hidden matters, 35; concerning reforms, 43; likewise concerning theological questions, 48. Her letters to Philip, abbot of Park; she frees her monastery from every burden, 61. Her writings celebrated with praises, 73. Death of the saint about the year 1179. — Commentary on the Life of Saint Rupert written by Saint Hildegard the abbess, CXVII, 1081. Likewise notice on the Life of Saint Disibod by the same saint, 1094.

**BOLSUINGIUS (Gerardus)**, at Cologne in 1526. He published the Works of Paulus Orosius and dedicated them to Lord Hermann, archbishop of Cologne, XXXI, 667.

**BONACHIUS (Franciscus)**, year uncertain. Book I, on the sermons and martyrdom of Saint Zeno, XI, 599. Whether Saint Zeno is the author of the sermons ascribed to him, ibid. These sermons known from antiquity, 600. Judgment of Sixtus of Siena, 601. On the sermon *On Continence*, 603. Tillemont’s errors, 604. On the diversity of style noted by Sixtus, 607. On chronological congruity, 608. On Bellarmine’s judgment, 610; Philip Labbe’s judgment, 611; Dupin and Combefis, 613. There is but one Zeno, bishop of Verona, ibid. Which sermons should be ascribed to Saint Zeno, 617. — Book II, on the martyrdom of Saint Zeno, 617. That he was a martyr is proved from monuments of the Church of Verona, ibid.; of the Church of Pistoia, 619; and from external authorities, 621; from the authority of the Roman Martyrology, 622. How much credence is due to Zeno’s Life by a certain Coronatus, 625. Panvinio is explained when he says that Zeno was not venerated as a martyr, 624. On Usuard’s Martyrology, 625. Objections of Dupin and Tillemont, 627. What Papebroch reports is examined, 630. Epilogue, 632.

First dissertation on the era of Saint Zeno, bishop of Verona, XI, 631. Zeno must be placed before the Arian period, 633. The age of the errors enumerated extends as far as Gallienus, 642. Texts of Zeno adduced which are thought to oppose Arius’s errors, 643. Zeno’s opinions directed against Arians, 647. Knowledge of the heresies mentioned by Zeno was common about the time of Gallienus, 653. Saint Zeno nowhere mentions formulas proper to the Arians, 662. Fathers later than Arius express characteristic Arian formulas in their works, 664. The treatises on faith mentioned by Saint Zeno must not be understood as concerning Arian formulas, 668. Saint Zeno does not address other heresies arising in the fourth century, 685. On Treatise 14, 689. Baronius rightly judges that Saint Zeno lived long before the age of Christian emperors, 698. Nothing can be inferred from Saint Ambrose’s letter to Syagrius of Verona, 709, nor from the order of the bishops of Verona, 713. What should be thought of Coronatus’s narrative, 722; of the office of Saint Zeno, 726. Arguments confirming that Saint Zeno’s era belongs in the third century, 733. — Second dissertation: examination and judgment of the arguments brought by the Ballerini brothers for and against Saint Zeno’s martyrdom, XI, 739. Whether Saint Ambrose may be invoked, ibid. On Saint Gregory the Great, who calls Zeno a martyr, 740; on others who followed Saint Gregory, 745; on the tradition of the Church of Verona, 746; on other monuments, 752. Manuscript authors and monuments asserting Saint Zeno’s martyrdom, 756. Conclusion, 760.

**BONGARSIUS (Jacobus)**, Calvinist and learned critic, born at Orléans in 1546 and died in 1612.

Notice on Raymond of Aguilers, canon of Le Puy, CLV, 592; likewise notice on Robert, monk of Saint-Remi in the diocese of Reims, 697. — Notice on Walter, *On the Antiochene War*, 994. — Notice on William of Tyre, archbishop, CCI, 202.

**BORDERIUS (Jean-François)**, abbot of Saint-Victor at Paris, in 1525 published the works of Hugh of Saint-Victor. Dedicatory letter, CLXXV, 151. He published poems in praise of Hugh, 153 ff.

**BOSSUETIUS (Jacques-Bénigne)**, bishop of Meaux, most celebrated theologian, historian, and controversialist. Born at Dijon in 1627 and died in 1704. — Historical note on Bernard, abbot of Fontcaude, and on the Waldensians against whom he wrote a book, CCIV, 793.

**BOUILLARTIUS (Jacobus)**, of the Benedictine Congregation of Saint-Maur, born at Meulan in 1669 and died in 1726.

He published Usuard’s Martyrology at Paris in 1718, according to Sollier’s edition. — Preface. — Letter of J. B. Sollier of the Society of Jesus, CXXIII, 587.

**BOUQUET (Dom Martin)**, among the most learned Benedictines of Saint-Maur, [Col. 0330] born at Amiens in 1685 and died in 1754; author of the collection of historians of France.

Notice on the diplomas of Pepin and Charlemagne, XCVII, 119. Inscriptions, ibid. Monogram, subscription of the chancellor, 120. Subscriptions of the great men, 121. Year of the Incarnation; indiction, 122. — Notice on Ermoldus’s poem, CX, 551. — Variant readings and notes on the Annals of Saint Prudentius of Troyes at Bertin, CXV, 1377 ff.

**BOURASSE (J.-J.)**, canon of the metropolitan church of Tours. He recently published the works of Hildebert according to the edition of Dom Antoine Beaugendre of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, with a preface.

Preface. He defends Hildebert from certain accusations brought against him while he was archdeacon of Le Mans, CLXXI, 17. On Hildebert’s beginnings, 18 ff. That he was never a monk of Cluny, 21. Baronius, deceived, accuses Hildebert, 23. Hildebert obtains the episcopate in the fortieth year of his life, 27. Some matters relating to the history of the Church of Tours in Hildebert’s time, ibid. On additions in the new edition, 29; on appended notes, 31; on the ancient use of pictures and inscriptions, 35; on other works falsely ascribed to Hildebert, 38–39. He becomes archbishop of Tours, 82. His grief at the death of Ralph, 83. He refutes his accusers, 84. On the charter of Guigo, 86. He dies about the year 1134. — Short preface to the writings of Marbod, bishop of Rennes, 1457.

**BRAIDA (Petrus)** published at Udine in 1816 an edition of the works of Saint Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia.

Preface, XX, 247. Notices on the various editions, ibid.; on Galland’s edition, 249; on the praise of Saint Chromatius, 250; on the writings or minor works of Saint Chromatius, 251; celebrated text of Saint Chromatius on the Holy Trinity, 253; what he put forward at the Council of Aquileia in 381, under Bishop Valerian, against Palladius, 255; those who have treated his life and deeds, 255–256; diversity of opinions concerning Chromatius’s era, 259; whether the works ascribed to him are genuinely his, 261; Ceillier’s opinion, 262, and the reply to it, ibid.; why, in what order, and on what occasion the minor works were composed, 264; he seems to have expounded the whole Gospel according to Matthew, 267; doxologies used by him, 268; elucidation of certain passages of Saint Chromatius, 270 ff.; argument developed by Ceillier, 275; Chromatius’s eulogy by the presbyter Rufinus, 288; why and how the Roman pontiff was called *maximus* by some, 291; time of his death, 294; coins of Chromatius, 295; monumental stone at Aquileia, 301; another stone likewise, 303; to whom these stones were dedicated, 306; Hadrian’s licence and vanity, ibid.; some matters concerning the Annian Way toward Aquileia, 307. Notice on the lost writings of Saint Chromatius, 369. — Examination of certain sermons ascribed to Saint Peter Chrysologus, LII, 179 ff. — Petrus Braida’s preface to his recension of the minor works of Saint Nicetas, LII, 837. On the true author called Nicetas, ibid. Plan of his labours in publishing these minor works, 838. Testimonies of the ancients concerning Saint Nicetas, 843. Readings proper to use in the diocese of Udine for the office of Saint Nicetas, 845. Marginal notes, 847 ff. — Dissertation on Saint Nicetas. Prologue; purpose and order of the dissertation, 875. The two disputed minor works are by one author, whoever he may be, 877. Niceas or Nicetas, friend of Paulinus of Nola, held the episcopate not at Romatiana on this side of the Danube, but in a city beyond the Danube, 882. Nicetas, bishop of Romatiana, is not the same Nicetas who was Saint Paulinus’s friend, 895. Nicetas, bishop of the city of Romatiana, mentioned by Gennadius, is that Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, who flourished in the time of Leo the Great and to whom a letter survives, 924. The city of Romatiana is not to be sought in Dacia, but in the former diocese of Aquileia, and is probably the port of Romatiana, 947. Probably Nicetas of Aquileia was called by some “of the Church of Romatiana” on the same principle, 959. The weighty arguments of the distinguished Zabeo against the episcopate of Nicetas at Aquileia answered, 995. On Saint Nicetas of Aquileia, to whom the writings are ascribed, 1033. Matters noteworthy both in doctrine and discipline, 1080. Examination of passages in which Saint Nicetas might seem to have spoken less exactly or somewhat harshly, 1110.

**BREQUINIUS (L.-G. Oudard)**, learned historian, member of the French Academy and of the Academy of Inscriptions, born at Grandvilliers in 1716 and died in 1795. Notes on the ecclesiastical ordinances of Dagobert I, king, LXXX, 499 ff. — Likewise notes on the writings of Saint Hadoind, 367, and of Saint Autbert, 595. Notice on the charter of Saint Annemund to the monastery of Saint Peter at Lyons, LXXXVII, 473. — Prolegomena to the diplomas of Clovis II: which are genuine, 677; which spurious, 679. Notes on the diplomas of Clovis, 681 ff. — Notes on the charters of Saint Faro, 1133 ff.; and on the appendix, 1137. Notes on the diplomas of Saint Amand, bishop of Maastricht, 1271 ff. — Likewise [Col. 0331] on the diplomas of Kings Chlothar III, Childeric II, Dagobert II, and Theuderic III, 1277 ff. — Notes on the diplomas of the last kings of the first Frankish dynasty, LXXXVIII, 1079 ff. Notes on the diplomas of Saint Willibrord, XXXIX, 535 ff. — Observations on Alcuin’s letters, C, 137. — Notice on his edition of the Registers of Innocent III, CCXIV, VII (see Mansi). — Notice concerning a manuscript codex copied by Ernest Andrentius in 1603. — Notes on the deeds of Innocent III, XVII ff.

**ROMAN BREVIARY.** Lesson concerning Saint Gregory VII, Roman pontiff, CXLVIII, 9.

**BRIAL (Dom M.-J.-Joseph)**, Benedictine of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, member of the Academy of Inscriptions, born at Perpignan in 1743 and died in 1828.

Notice on Latin manuscripts of the Royal Library, treating the letters of Stephen, abbot of Saint-Euverte at Orléans, subsequently of Sainte-Geneviève at Paris, and finally bishop of Tournai, CCXI, 306. — Notes on the letters of the same Stephen, 309 ff.

**BRIDFERT OF RAMSEY** (year uncertain). He wrote a gloss on Bede’s book *On the Nature of Things*, XC, 188 and passim; likewise on the book *On the Reckoning of Time*, 297 ff. Gloss on the book *On Speech*, 685 and passim.

**BROCKIE**, author of the codex of Rules. — Critical observation on the Rule of the Order of the Holy Spirit in Saxony, believed to have been founded by Pope Innocent III, CCXVII, 1129.

**BROWERIUS (Christophorus)**, of the Society of Jesus, historian, born at Arnhem in 1560 and died in 1617.

He published Rabanus’s poems, illustrated with notes and observations, CXII, 1583 ff.

**BRUNUS (Bruno).** Through his care Pope Pius VI, in Rome in 1784, caused a new edition of the works of Saint Maximus of Turin to be printed by the press of the Sacred Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith, dedicated to Victor Amadeus, King of Sardinia, LVII, 194. — Preface. Introduction, on the excellence of Saint Maximus’s works. Part I: the textual and manuscript aids used, and the method by which we completed this edition, 15. Part II: on Maximus’s doctrine and the other matters treated in the Prolegomena, 41. — Life of Saint Maximus of Turin: his homeland and lineage, LVII, 127. Whether there were one or two bishops of Turin named Maximus, 129. When Maximus entered upon the episcopate, 137. His diligence in teaching the people, 139. His concern that heresies should not invade, 141. Neither excessively severe nor indulgent, 149. His virtues, 159. What he did in the presence of Genseric, 160. In 465 he came to Rome to attend the synod convened by Hilary, ibid. Death of Saint Maximus, 162. — An admonition at the head of every homily or treatise provides philological or critical observations; besides this, annotations occur throughout to elucidate matters and words.

He supervised the Roman edition of 1789 of the works of Saint Bruno of Asti. — Dedication to Charles Emmanuel, King of Piedmont, CLXIV, 9. — Prolegomena. Introduction, 11. On the edition of Maurus Marchesi, 12. On discrepancies among annotators, 15. On manuscript codices and lost writings, 18. On the version of Scripture used by Saint Bruno, 19. On his interpretation of the Psalms, 23. On the Exposition of the Pentateuch, 27. On theological doctrines, 31. Several Lives of Saint Bruno, bishop of Asti, exist, 90, 98. Testimonies of ecclesiastical writers concerning Saint Bruno, 138. — Notes on various expositions of Scripture, 147 ff. — Admonition on the Life of Saint Peter of Anagni, CLXV, 1135.

**BUCHERIUS (Aegidius)**, of the Society of Jesus, learned, born at Arras in 1576 and died in 1665. — Catalogue of Roman pontiffs, CXXVII, 119. — Register of the burials of bishops, 122. — Register of the burials of martyrs, 123.

**BULLARIUM.** Notice on Pope Paschal II, CLXIII, 9.

**BURONTIUS DEL SIGNORE (Carolus)**, at Vercelli in 1768, through whose labour and study the works of Atto, bishop of Vercelli, were published, CXXXIV, 9. Dedicatory letter, ibid. Notice to the reader, ibid. On the author, 9. He flourished about the year 924, 11. Muratori’s words concerning Andrew of Milan, 18. On Atto’s outstanding merit, 16. His generosity toward canons despoiled by barbarians, 18. His testament, 20. He is said to have lived until the year 960, 22. — On Atto’s writings, 23. Notes: see passim.

**BUNEMANNUS (J.-Ludolphus)**, learned bookseller, born at Calbe in Prussia in 1687 and died in 1759. He published the works of Lactantius, illustrated with notes placed beneath the text, VI, 111 and passim.

**CACCIARIUS (Petrus-Thomas)**, of the Carmelite Order.

*Exercises on the entire works of St. Leo the Great*, LV, 768.---Dedication to Pope Benedict XIV, 769.---Preface, 771. The plan and purpose of the whole work, ibid. What accusations are brought against Quesnel’s edition, 773. On the necessity of restoring the text, 774. What Quesnel’s aim was, 775. On his dissertations, 777. In these exercises [Col. 0332] account is taken of the four principal heresies which agitated the Church of God in the time of St. Leo, 778.---Book I, *On the Manichaean Heresy and Its History*, LV, 783. On the principal Manichaean authors, 784. At what time Mani flourished, 788. His artifices, 832. He is seized by Persian officials, 861. On the year of Mani’s death, 876. Book II. The author’s purpose, 889. How this heresy spread after Mani’s death, 891. On Manichaean books, 896. The severity of the imperial laws against Manichaeans in Africa, 913. In what year the Manichaeans came to Rome, 933. Leo the Great’s Roman inquest against the Manichaeans, 936. Likewise in the time of Gelasius, 954; and of Hormisdas, 970.---On the Priscillianist heresy and its history, 991. Who Priscillian was, ibid. At what time, and especially where, this heresy began to rage, 993. Instantius and Salvianus follow Priscillian, 996. On the councils of Toledo concerning the Priscillianists, 1007. On the schism, 1026. Paschasius Quesnel’s false judgment concerning the ancient codex of the canons of the Roman Church, 1044. Paschasius Quesnel wrongly invents two Turribiuses in Leo’s time, 1062.---On the Pelagian heresy and its history, LV, 1065. How that heresy survived in St. Leo’s age, ibid. St. Leo’s zeal against the Pelagians, 1067. St. Prosper writes treatises against the Pelagians, 1071. St. Leo’s letter to Januarius of Aquileia, 1079. On writers’ opinions concerning those letters, 1086.---On the Eutychian heresy and its history, LV, 1095. Eutyches is accused by Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum, 1098. Flavian requests from Leo the Great confirmation of the acts of the council, whatever Quesnel may say, 1101. Quesnel is refuted by arguments, 1109. On Eutyches’ appeal to the Apostolic See, 1115. On Eutyches’ letter, 1136. On the Council of Ephesus, 1144. On St. Flavian’s appeal to the Apostolic See, 1173. On the three Sardican canons, 1196. St. Flavian is beaten, 1211. Theodosius dies while doing penance, 1219. Affairs in the East changed for the better, 1223. Book II, 1229. The first Council of Ephesus, once convoked, is transferred to Chalcedon, 1235. On the date, number of Fathers, and sessions of the council, 1241. Dissertation on the fourth session of the council, 1246. Theodoret, deposed by the Robber Council of Ephesus, appealed to the Apostolic See, 1255. On the remaining proceedings of the council, 1286. St. Leo restrained Anatolius’s ambition in many ways, 1299. St. Leo devoted every effort to extinguishing the remnants of the Eutychians, 1310, and applied the greatest zeal to confirming the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon, 1318.

CAESARIUS (John), born at Julier in 1450, died in 1551; he published an edition of the works of Paulus Orosius.---His dedication, XXXI, 645.

CAJETANUS (Constantine), monk of the Cassinese Congregation, born at Syracuse in 1560 and died in 1650. Dedicatory letter to Pope Paul V, CXLIV, 15.---Dedicatory letter to volume II, CXLIV, 502. Preface, 503.---Preface to volume III.---Observation on the Life of St. Anselm of Lucca, CXLVIII, 905.---Preface to Peter de Honestis’s *Rule of Clerics*, CLXIII, 691.

CALLYUS (Peter) published the works of Severinus Boethius at Caen in 1679.

Dedicatory letter to the Dauphin, LXIII, 547.---Preface. On the scantiness of almost all commentaries on Boethius, 549. The Duke of Montausier’s opinion of these commentaries, 553. What was accomplished in that edition, ibid. and following.---Life of Boethius.---His birth and names, 555. He loses his father, 556. He cultivates virtue, 557. From youth he is adorned with offices of dignity, 558. He incurs the enmity of wicked men, 559. He is sent into exile, 560. He is killed, 561.---Various testimonies concerning Boethius, 562. Preface to Boethius’s book *On Arithmetic*, LXIII, 1079.---Commentary on Book III of *The Consolation of Philosophy*, 1245.---Preface to Boethius’s theological works, 1247.

CANISIUS (Henry), born at Nijmegen about the middle of the sixteenth century, taught canon law at Ingolstadt for twenty-one years.

Jacques Basnage published his *Ancient Readings* in 1725. Among them are readings, with notes by various scholars, from an anonymous author’s chronicle, III, 659 and throughout. CARUSIUS (Giovanni Battista), Sicilian historian, born at Polizzi in 1673, died in 1724.---Notice on Geoffrey of Malaterra and his Sicilian History, CXLIX, 1088.

CAVEUS (William), English theologian, born at Pickwell in 1637, died in 1713.

Historical notice on Aurelius Symmachus, XVIII, 141.---Life of Symmachus excerpted from a very ancient edition, ibid.---Notice on Arnobius the Younger and his writings, LIII, 240.---Some matters concerning the life of Uranus the presbyter, LIII, 887. CELLARIUS (Christoph), philologist and scholar, born at Schmalkalden in 1638, died in 1707. He published an edition of Lactantius with notes, VI, 107. Although corrected, it was nevertheless not wholly free from fault, ibid., VII, 101 and throughout.

CELLOTIUS (Louis), Jesuit, controversialist, and historian, born at Paris in 1588 and died in 1658. He illustrated with notes and observations the *Capitula* of Walter, bishop of Orléans, CXIX, 725 and following.---Historical notice on Hincmar, bishop of Laon, CXXIV, 967. He harasses the clerics and laity of his church, 975. The king sends him into custody at Silvanectum, 970. The council of Douzy against him, 977. Pope Adrian’s judgment concerning that council, ibid.

CELTES (Conrad, called Meissel), Latin poet, born at Wipfeld in 1459 and died in 1508.---Preface to the works of Hrotsvitha, CXXXVII, 967.

CENNIUS (Gaetano), scholar and beneficiary-priest of the Vatican Church in the eighteenth century.

CHAPPEAUVILLE (J.), theologian and historian, born at Liège in 1551 and died in 1617.---Historical notice on Godfrey, monk of Stavelot, CXLIX, 287.

CHELONIUS (Benedict), abbot of the Scots at Vienna, published in 1518 the books of Sentences of Master Bandinus, theologian.---Dedication, CXCII, 965.---His letter to Abbot Sigismund, 967. What Dr. John Eck relates concerning Bandinus’s Sentences, and what is to be observed in the appended note, 969.

CHENEVET, priest of Dijon, in 1782. He supplied a notice on the priory called des Feuillants, near Fontaine-Dijon, built above the castle of Father Bernard, CLXXXV, 1634.

CHIFFLETIUS (Pierre-François), very celebrated Jesuit scholar, born at Besançon in 1592 and died in 1682.---Elucidations on Victor of Vita, LVIII, 127. *Defense of Vigilius of Thapsus.*---Preface, LXII, 471. The five books against Eutyches, 473. The disputation under Athanasius’s name, 474. Vigilius’s book *Against Palladius*, 475. Likewise on the *Dialogue against Arians and Sabellians*, 551. Decretal of Pope Hormisdas, 537. Notes on the book *Against Felicianus*, 541. Likewise on the book *Against Palladius*, ibid.

Notice on Bernold’s tract concerning Berengar’s condemnation, CXLVIII, 1450. Preface to the same tracts, ibid. Notes, 1450 and following.

CIACONIUS (P.), canon of Seville, critic and philologist, born at Toledo in 1525, died at Rome in 1581. CLERICUS (Jean), celebrated theologian and Protestant critic, born at Geneva in 1657 and died at Amsterdam in 1736. Critical notes on the letters of Sulpicius Severus, XX, 223.

CLICHTOVIUS (Josse), learned theologian who did not fear to refute Luther, died at Neufport in 1543.---He elucidated the sequences composed by Adam of St. Victor, CXCVI, 1423 and following.

COCQUELINUS, collector of bulls and privileges of the Supreme Pontiffs, Rome, 1739.---Notice on Innocent II, Roman pontiff, CLXXIX, 21.

COLETTI SEBASTIANI (Giovanni Domenico and Giacomo), distinguished Venetian printers of the seventeenth century, published the works of Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari.---Dedicatory letter, XIII, 691.---Preface to this edition, 695. Who the first editors were, ibid. The rationale of this new edition, 697. On Lucifer’s use of Holy Scripture, 669. Theological observation on certain expressions of Lucifer, 710. Critical inquiry into several passages of Lucifer, 719. On the time when Lucifer wrote, 735. On his life: what Methodius and Juvenal report, 737; why it is uncertain, ibid. Two Lucifers, the Sardinian and the Sardican, 738. He sets out for Vercelli and is received by Eusebius, 739. Controversy concerning the Council of Milan, ibid. Which council Lucifer presided over in the name of Pope Liberius, 742. He vigorously defends the cause of St. Athanasius, 742. He escapes every ambush, 743. CONEN (V.-P.), licentiate in Sacred Theology, prior of the Premonstratensian monastery of St. Mary at Tongeren (date lacking).---Preface to the book entitled *Inevitabile*, etc. There the author, subject matter, and purpose of the book are treated, CLXXII, 1191 and following.

CONTIUS (Antoine), learned jurist and professor at Orléans, died about 1586.---He provided notes on the Chronology of St. Nicephorus, CXXIX, 513 and following.

CONSTANTINUS (R.), see CONSTANTIUS.

CORBINIANUS (Dom Thomas), born at Augsburg in 1694; he became a monk about 1715 at the imperial monastery of Elchingen and taught mathematics at the University of Salzburg, II, 1135. Notes on each chapter, ibid. and following.

CRESCIUS (Nicolaus), Florentine Cistercian monk, [Col. 0336] gives Lanfredinus Antonius his judgment on the books *On the Consolation of Philosophy*, LXIII, 870 (Glareanus edition).

COUSTANTIUS (Pierre), Benedictine of the Congregation of St. Maur, born at Compiègne in 1672 and died at Paris in 1721; he laboured long on the works of the Holy Fathers of the Church.

Cyprian’s to Cornelius; 3. the African bishops’ to Cornelius; 4. where the penance of higher clergy in the first three centuries is discussed, III, 689. What Morin’s opinion is, 691. Urbanus, Castorius, and their companions condemned, 14. The condemnation of Castorius is ratified at Rome, 15. Marcellinus is proved to have burned incense, 16. On the decree attributed to him, concerning children offered by their parents to monasteries, 22. Third, notice on St. Eusebius, pope: when and for how long he sat, VI, 25. What chiefly moved Zosimus’s mind in the affair of Pelagius and Caelestius, 648.---Notes beneath the text, ibid. Notice of lost writings concerning Pope Zosimus, XX, 685.---Prolegomena to Pope St. Boniface, XX, 745. On the election of St. Boniface in 418, ibid. The party of Eulalius, 747. Both elections are referred to Emperor Honorius, ibid. What the Roman cleric did, ibid. How Honorius approved Boniface, 748.---Notice on the first three letters, 749. Attached critical notes, ibid. and following. Notice of lost writings of Pope St. Boniface, 783.---Annotations on the writings of Pope Celestine I, L, 417 and following.---Notice of the remaining writings concerning Celestine, 557. Decrees attributed to Celestine, 364.---Likewise, notice on the remaining writings of Pope Sixtus III, L, 617.---Notice on Robert Granjon, printer and type-founder, [Col. 0337] who himself first published the works of Gualterus of Châtillon, namely the *Alexandreis*, CCIX, 462.

CUPERUS (Gisbert), celebrated Dutch critic, born at Hemmen in 1644 and died in 1716. He supplied notes on Lactantius’s book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, VI, 108. They are published in VII, 471, and prefaced in VII, 463.

CUYCHIUS (N. D.), theologian of Louvain and subsequently bishop of Roermond, in 1616 published the works of John Cassian, illustrated with censorial notes. His preface, XLIX, 25. On the fact that the charges made against John Cassian should be imputed not to him but rather to those whom he cites, 25. Arguments for this assertion, 26. Which books are attributed to Cassian, 27. Whether he wrote in Greek or Latin, 28.---Cuychius’s annotations on John Cassian’s works, L, 311 and following.

DANIEL (Gabriel), Jesuit, historiographer and philosopher, born at Taunton in 1562, died in 1617. He published the poems of Gottschalk, illustrated with notes and observations.---Notes, CXLI, 1325 and following.---Notes on various sequences, CLI, 807.

DAVISIUS (J.), celebrated London scholar, born in 1679 and died in 1732. He supplied a supplement of notes to Commodian’s poem *Against the Pagans*, V, 202 and throughout.

DENZINGERUS (Heinrich), professor of theology at the University of Würzburg.---Selection and critical assessment of what recent critics have established concerning the Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals, CXXX, I. Opinions of modern scholars divided into three classes, ibid. What materials may have been available for fabricating the Pseudo-Isidorian wares, VIII. Otgar of Mainz: the moral occasion of the decretals, X. Supreme pontiffs used the decretals, XI. Nicholas did not pronounce upon the authenticity of these decretals, XII.---Critical investigation of the eleven Gallican Masses discovered by D. Mone, CXXXVIII, 856. Examples of autographs, 861.---Notes on these Masses, 865 and following.---Notice on Bishop Heribert, CXLI, 1369.---Edition of the works of St. Bruno, bishop of Würzburg.---Prolegomena on the life and deeds of St. Bruno, CXLII, 9. On Bruno’s sanctity and cult, 20. On Bruno’s writings, 24. What has been accomplished in this edition, 28. Appendix of documents, 31 and following.---Notes on St. Bruno’s writings, 31 and following.

DIONYSIUS (Michael). At Vienna in 1792 he published the works of St. Aurelius Augustine. His preface to the new unpublished sermons, with certain doubtful ones intermixed, excerpted from an old twelfth-century manuscript preserved at Vienna, XLVI, 813. In it he gives a synopsis of these sermons, twenty-five in number, 814 and following.

DOCTORS OF PARIS. Censure of the works of Abelard and Heloise, CLXXVIII, 109 and following.

DODWELLUS (Henry), English professor of theology, born at Dublin, Ireland, in 1641; though a layman, he excelled in ecclesiastical learning and wrote learned dissertations on various Fathers, especially St. Cyprian. His opinion on the date at which Minucius Felix flourished, III, 198. His view concerning the author of the Chronicle, 652. He wrote three dissertations on St. Cyprian.---The first, on Letter 8 of St. Cyprian, concerning visions, V, 9. It is shown that visions and prophetic gifts continued until Cyprian, 10. In the Apocalypse, Hermas, Clement, Ignatius, Quadratus, Polycarp, Justin, Melito, Irenaeus, Attalus, Perpetua, and Saturus, II and following. The Church did not leave the Montanists even the pretext of prophecies, 13. Visions of Natalis and Potamiana, 16. Origen acknowledges prophecies, 17. Vision of Dionysius of Alexandria, 17; of Cyprian himself, ibid. Visions were customarily proclaimed publicly, 20. Arguments, 23. Various gifts, 23–24. Whence comes the criterion of truth, 25. Not all utterances of prophets were prophetic, 26. At times errors coexist with genuine prophecy, 27. The visions of young men were distinctive, 30. What should be thought of those who ridicule the prophecies of the ancients, 31.

Dissertation 2, on Letter 24 of St. Cyprian, *On Presbyters Who Were Teachers*, etc., V, 33. Presbyters who were teachers existed in the Church before Cyprian, 33; they were contemporaries of the apostles, 35. Whence their office derived, ibid. This was not the office of all presbyters, 36. Hearers were the same as catechumens, 38. The instruction of catechumens corresponded to the mysteries, ibid. Lower ministers, 39. Cyprian’s embassies, 40. Embassies earlier than Cyprian, 42. Embassies in the apostolic age, 43. They were then especially honourable, 47.

Dissertation 3, *On the Second Baptism of Martyrdom*, V, 47. Why this dissertation was written, 49. Our most ancient opinion, ibid. External union with the Church required beforehand, 51. The ancients preferred baptism of blood to baptism of water, 52. In what manner, ibid. Observations, 55 and following. Heretics contemporary with the apostles denied martyrdom, 59. Observation, 62. This baptism took its place not only in initiations but also in covenants, ibid. Further observations, 63 and following. How it stands in fact, 68, and why, 69. Final observations, 71 and following. The ancients defended, 77. We also pledge martyrdom in the Eucharist, [Col. 0338] 78. What right we acquire through martyrdom, ibid.

The same Dodwell wrote a dissertation on the *Ripa Striga* (on Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, §12), VII, 175. This bank was of a river, not of the sea, ibid.
