Whence the word *striga*, 176. Among the Romans, the boundaries of fields, camps, and provinces were especially rivers, 177. The same is proved from Attila’s province wrested from the Romans, 180. This mention of the riverbank-strip agrees with Diocletian’s plan and route, ibid.---There follows his chronology of the persecutions together with Stephen Baluze’s Diocletianic chronology, 181 and following.

DUCAEUS (Fronto), Jesuit, celebrated scholar, born at Bordeaux in 1558 and died in 1624. Notes and observations on the letters of St. Paulinus, LXI, 843 and throughout.

DUELLIUS (Raimund), canon, learned German historian, died in 1740.---Preliminary observation on the *Shield of the Canons*, by Brother Arno, CXCIV, 1490.

DUMGE (Carl Georg), professor of history at Heidelberg, after much labour by others and himself, published at Heidelberg in 1812 Gunther’s *Ligurinus*, or book on the deeds of Emperor Frederick, CCXII, 255.---Dedicatory letter, 255.---Editor’s preface, 257.---Preface to the first edition, by Marcard of Stein, 260.---Dissertation I: on the author, date, fortunes, and editions of the work, 262. The author’s identity and country, 265. On the date of composition, 275. Character and authority of the work, 277. Testimonies of scholars, 280. Defects of manuscripts, 283. Editions, 286. On the labours of various writers upon the *Ligurinus*, 296. Dissertation II on the *Ligurinus*: on the birth, lineage, and deeds of Frederick I Augustus, 299.

DUNODUS (Fr. Ignatius), jurist and historian, born in the French city of Saint-Claude in 1679 and died in 1752, author of a history of Besançon.---Historical notice on St. Protadius, written in French, LXXX, 409. Note on the same, 121.

DUPINIUS (Louis Ellies), distinguished Doctor of the Sorbonne, historian and critic, born in Normandy in 1657 and died in 1719. His is the preface to St. Optatus, XI, 460. On the Life of Optatus, 761. On the books, 762. On editions of these books, 766. Documents appended by Optatus himself to his books, 768.---Ancient testimonies concerning St. Optatus and his books, 769. Critical notes on St. Optatus’s book *On the Schism of the Donatists*, 885 and throughout.

DUVALLIUS (André), Doctor of the Sorbonne, 1564–1646.---Notes on the book *On Three Letters* by Remigius, bishop of Lyons, CXXI, 987 and following.

EDITORS AT COLOGNE of the works of the Venerable Bede, 1616.---Notes on the preface and on the book *Hexaemeron*, XCI, 9.

---THEOLOGIANS OF DOUAI. Preface to the *Ordinary Gloss*, CXIII, 11.---Observations on the canonical and non-canonical books of the Bible, 19. On translators of the Bible, 23.

---OXFORD EDITORS, 1682. Their selected notes and observations on the individual books of St. Cyprian, IV, 1032–1150. See the entries Fell and Pearson.

---Vatican editors. Annotations on the works of Magnus Felix Ennodius, LXIII, 13 and following.---Preface to the Prolegomena to the writings of Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVII, 33. The *Liber Pontificalis* must be corrected, 34. What is to be thought of the labours of Holstenius and Schelestratus, 35. How that book may be divided, 38. What indications should be supplied, 45. On the indication of years and consulships in the first Catalogue, 49. On ordinations, 52. Marble tablets to be consulted, 54 and following. What Baronius maintained concerning the various authors of this book, 101.

---Venetian editor, 1843. He published the works of St Peter Damian in accordance with the studies and labours of D. Cajetan.---Editorial notice, CXLIV, 9. On the work of Constantine Cajetan in collecting and arranging the writings of St Damian, ibid. A new edition prepared from the Roman and Paris editions, 10. On the order of the writings, 11 and following.

EDITORS OF THE PATROLOGY published at Mont-Rouge, among whom the principal was the Reverend Father Pitra of the Order of St Benedict.

Preface to the works of Tertullian, I, 9. On Tertullian’s authority and use, 11, 18. On Tertullian’s literary annals, 32. On manuscripts, ibid. On the individual editions, 35. On the new Paris edition, 68 and following. Preface to Volumes III and IV; List of Authors, III, I.---On the authority of St Cyprian, VI.---On the use of St Cyprian in disciplinary matters, XVII. Literary annals, XLIV. On this new edition, LXXXVII.---Prolegomena to the letters relating to St Cornelius, pope and martyr, III, 677. History of the life of St Cornelius, III, 677. Writings of St Cornelius, pope and martyr, 682. Synopsis of Cornelius’s letter to Fabius of Antioch, 687.

Notice on the three sermons of St Ambrose, explaining why they have hitherto been deferred, XVIII, 89. Notice concerning the edition of the writings of Ulfilas, XVIII, 456.---Notice at the beginning of the Works of St Augustine concerning the new recension of the Benedictine edition, XXXII, 5. On certain changes affecting typography, ibid. On the faithful reproduction of this most distinguished edition, ibid. As regards the chronology of Augustine’s works, there is a slight departure from the order of the Maurist Fathers, 7. On transferring the dedicatory letter of Father Mabillon and both lives of St Augustine from the end to the beginning of the works, ibid.---Notes on Schoenemann, who is excessively favourable to his own sect, in the notice on St Augustine, XLVII, 19. Likewise a note on the not equally commendable orthodoxy of various persons who expounded the works of the Fathers, XLVII, 197.---Notice introducing a new edition of the writings of Marius Mercator, XLVIII, 9. According to Garner’s recension, but enlarged with the annotations both of Baluze and Gallandi, ibid. On certain Greek fragments from St Cyril quoted by Marius, which are referred to the soon-to-be-published Greek Patrology, ibid., note.---Notice introducing a new edition of the works of St Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, LII, 837.---Notice introducing a new edition of the works of St Paulinus, LXI, 153.---Notice introducing the volumes of the works of St Gregory the Great, LXXV, 37. Likewise on the same, LXXVIII.---Notice on the works of St Isidore of Seville concerning Arévalo’s edition, LXXXII, 8.---Notice explaining why the collection of canons is placed here among the Isidorian works, LXXXIV.---Notice on Bede’s Martyrology, XCIV, 798.---Notice on the *Historia Miscella*, XCV, 743. By what marks the source of the notes is made known, ibid.---Notice on the new recension of Alcuin’s letters, C, 138.---Notice on the Gloss of Walafrid Strabo, CXIII, 11.---Notice on the manner of citing Scripture among certain medieval writers, CXIX, 7.---Notice on the Hirsau Constitutions of St William, CL, 923.---Notice on the hymns and sequences for the use of the monastery of the Paraclete attributed to Abelard, CLXXVIII, 1766.---Preface to the ecclesiastical history of Orderic Vitalis, an Englishman, CLXXXVIII, 9.---Notice on the edition of Peter Lombard’s *Sentences*, CXCI, 519.---Epilogue to the reader and conclusion of the whole Latin Patrology, CCXVII.

EGGSIUS (G.-J.), a learned canon, born at Rheinfelden in 1670, died in 1750.---Notice on Pope Benedict VII, CXXXVII, 313.---Notice on Pope Gregory V, 899.---Notice on Humbert, cardinal-bishop of Silva Candida, CXLIII, 911.---Notice on Cardinal Stephen, 1407.

ELMENHORSTIUS (Gerhard), a learned philologist, born at Hamburg in 1560, died in 1621. He published Arnobius’s writings with notes in 1603, V, 360; and again in 1610, V, 362.---Elmenhorst’s critical notes on Gennadius’s book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, LVIII, 999 and following.

ENHUEBERUS (John Baptist), prior of St Emmeram.

A historical-dogmatic dissertation against Christian Walch, demonstrating that Felix and Elipand were rightly accused of Nestorianism by Alcuin, CI, 337. On the origin of Nestorianism and Adoptionism, 338. The latter heresy for the most part arose from the former, 339. What was the occasion of Nestorianism, 340. What the Arians asserted, 341. What the Nestorians asserted, 342. On Diodorus of Tarsus, 346. The Apollinarians wrongly attacked, 348. On Nestorius, 350. The doctrine of the Most Holy Trinity long disputed in Spain, 352. Arian errors strengthened through the invasion of the barbarians, 353. The struggle against Migetius, 355. He appears to deny the divinity of the Word, 358.---On the principles and assertions of Nestorianism and Adoptionism, 361. Principles of the Nestorians, 362. How the Adoptionists argue, 380. Examination of the historical testimonies on which Walch relies, 390. Reply to his evasions, 391.---On the manner in which St Cyril contended against the Nestorians and Alexius against the Adoptionists, 393. The dissertation concludes, and certain further subtleties of Walch are answered, 436.

ERASMUS (Desiderius), highly learned in letters and sciences, philologist, critic, and controversialist; born at Rotterdam in 1467, died in 1536; intimate of Froben, to whom he was of the greatest assistance. He collected, corrected, and annotated the works of St Cyprian in 1520, III, LXX, preface. His annotations are very few, ibid. He published other editions of the same Father, ibid.---Erasmus inserted notes in certain books of Lactantius, VII, 9.---Censure of the books of the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*, XLVII, 197. Critical observations on the book of *Retractations*, 201. Critical observations on the book of *Confessions*, 204. Likewise on the books *Against the Academics*, 218; on *The Happy Life*, 219; on *Order*, 220. Censure of the books of *Soliloquies*, 222; of *The Immortality of the Soul*, 224; and so on through the individual minor works of Augustine in this volume.---Letter to the reader in Volume II of the Works of St Augustine, XLVII, 239. Critical observations on *Christian Doctrine*, 335; on *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, 341. Critical observations on the same book, 342; likewise on the books of *Expressions*, 349; on the *Questions on the Heptateuch*, 350; on the *Mirror*, 351; on *The Harmony of the Evangelists*, 355; on *The Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, 359; on the tractates on John, [Col. 0340] 362; on the exposition of the Epistle to the Romans, 365; on the exposition of Galatians, 366.---Critical observations on the *Expositions of the Psalms*, 367.---Erasmus to the reader in Volume VII, 409.---Critical observations on the book of Seventy-Three Questions, 410; on various questions, 412; on the book *Questions of Dulcitius*, 415; on the censure of the book *On Faith*, 413; likewise on the book *On Faith and the Creed*, 416; on *Faith and Works*, 417; on the *Enchiridion*, 418; and so on through the various minor works of this volume, see 425, 426 and following.---Erasmus to the reader in Volume VIII. Critical observations at the beginning of each minor work, 505, 508, 509 and following.---In Volume IX: critical observations, 525, 532, 534 and following.---Edition of the Works of Haymo, bishop of Halberstadt: Dedication, CXVI, 191.

ERNESTIUS (J. August), doctor of letters and theology, born in Thuringia in 1707 and died in 1781. He added a preface to Lindner’s first edition of the works of Minucius Felix, published by us, III, 219.

ERNESTIUS (Cyprian), of the family of the preceding, born at Jena in 1703; he added notes and observations to Gennadius’s book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, LVIII, 1060.

ESPINOSA (D. Antonio), a skilled Spanish printer, at Segovia in 1782 first brought to light the Works of St Martin, priest of León and regular canon of the Order of St Augustine.---Notice to the reader, CCVIII, 9.

FABER (Nicholas), a most learned philologist, born in Paris in 1544 and died in 1612. He wrote the preface to the fragments of St Hilary, X, 887. What kind of work this is, ibid. That it is Hilary’s, 889. Who Ursacius and Valens were, ibid. The following letter, now Fragment XII, written in 363, 892. The imprudent outcome of the Council of Rimini, ibid. Germinius’s defection from Valens and Ursacius, 893. What was the formula dictated by Marcus of Arethusa, 894. Of which bishops that Synod of Sirmium was composed, 895. At what time it was held, ibid. On what occasion, 897. Epilogue, 898. The Paris Synod, now Fragment XI, 900. When Hosius died, 901. To what bishops the letter of the Synod of Philippopolis was addressed, 903. The Sardican decrees unknown to Augustine, 904. History of the Council of Rimini, 905. The devices of the Arians. On the Nicene formula, 906. On the Council of Carthage under Genethlius, 907. On Musonius and Restitutus, 908. History does not conceal the lapses of eminent men, 909. The falls of Hosius and Lucifer, 910. What the general defection of the Fathers at Rimini teaches, 911. For what purpose councils are necessary, ibid. These fragments discovered by the guiding will of divine Providence, 913. Eulogy of Pithou, 916. Proverb, 916.---Notice on the exhortation of St Caesarius of Arles to preserve charity, LXVII, 1151.

FABRICIUS (Johann Albert), learned bibliographer, born at Leipzig in 1668, died in 1738. He published St Philastrius’s book *On Heresies* in 1721. Preface, XII, 1097.---Notice on Sedatus, bishop of Béziers, LXXII, 769.---Historical notice on Emperor Constantine, LXXIV, 522. Critical notes on the life of Constantine, 522.---Historical notice on St Severinus, 843.---Notice on Armenicus and Honorius, commonly called monks, 1243.---Notice on Dinotheus, abbot, LXXX, 21.---Likewise on Dynamius, 23.---Notice on St Warnar, 185. Notes on his writings, 195 and following.---Notice on St Columbanus, 201.---Likewise on Ailerán, the Scot-Irish abbot, 327.---Note on the same, ibid.---Notice on Ethelbert, 341.---Notice on Verus, bishop of Rodez, 445.---Historical notice on St Isidore of Seville and his writings, LXXXII, 57 and following.---Historical notice on St Gall, abbot, LXXXVII, 9.---Likewise on Marculf, monk, 691.---Likewise on St Cummian, 969.---Likewise on Jonas, abbot, 1009.---Notes on the life of St Columbanus written by Jonas, 1011 and following.---Notice on Damian, bishop of Pavia, 1259.---Notice on Defensor, monk of Locojeux, LXXXVIII, 595.---Likewise on St Adamasus, 723.---Likewise on Cresconius, African bishop, 815.---Likewise on Ceolfrith, Anglo-Saxon priest, LXXXIX, 347.---Likewise on Egbert, bishop of York, 377.---Notice on Pope St Gregory II, 493.---Likewise on St Boniface, bishop of Mainz, 597.---On St Chrodegang, bishop of Metz, 1054.---On St Sturmi, abbot of Fulda, 1257.---Notice on St Ambrose Autpert, 1265.

Fabricius’s notice on the Venerable Bede, with a survey of his writings, XC, 102. What is lacking among his volumes, 112.---Observation on Bede’s little book *On Thunder*, 609.---Historical notice on Paul Winfrid and his works, XCV, 413.---On Cyricius, bishop of Barcelona, XCVI, 9.---On St Lull, bishop of Mainz, 819.---On Wicbod, 1101.---Likewise on the abbots Abedoc and Ethelwolf, 1279. Notice on the collected chapters, ibid.---Notice on St Simpert, abbot of Murbach, XCIX, 737.---On Amalarius, archbishop of Trier, 886.---On Smaragdus, abbot, CII, 9.---On Sedulius Scotus, CIII, 9.---On Einhard, abbot, CIV, 351. Notes, ibid.---Historical notice on Theodulf, CV, 187.---Testimonies concerning Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, 189.---Historical notice on Fredegisus, [Col. 0341] abbot of St Martin of Tours, 751.---Likewise on Hilderic, abbot, 759. On Haito, bishop of Basel, 761.---Notice on Symphosius Amalarius, 815.---Likewise on Dhuoda, author of the little book *Manual*, CVI, 109.---Literary notice on Jonas, bishop of Orléans, 119.---On Hildemar and Lambert, 394.---On Thegan, chorepiscopus of Trier, 402.---On Agnellus, abbot, 430.---On Frotharius, bishop of Toul, CVI, 863. Notes, ibid.---On Joseph, priest, 890.---On Christian Druthmar, monk of Corbie, 1259. Likewise on Aurelian, monk of Reims, 1521.---Bibliographical notice on the Works of Rabanus, CVII, 127.---Historical notice on Walafrid Strabo, monk of Fulda, CXIII, 9. Survey of his writings, ibid.---Historical notice on Angelomus, monk of Luxeuil, CXV, 106.---On Hartmann, monk of St Gall, CXVI, 23.---On Ermanric, monk of Reichenau, 23.---Likewise on Erchambert, bishop of Freising, 31.---On Nithard, abbot of St Riquier, 35.---Historical and bibliographical notice on Haymo, bishop of Halberstadt, CXVI, 185 and following.---On Florus, deacon of Lyons, CXIX, 9.---On Ratramnus, monk of Corbie, CXXI, 9.---On Gottschalk, monk of Orbais, 345.---Notice on Wandalbert, 573.---On Iso, monk of St Gall, 779.---On Milo, monk of St Amand, 925.---On Adrevald, monk of Fleury, CXXIV, 899.---Notice on Heriveus, monk of Auxerre, 1129.---On Aimoin, monk of Saint-Germain, CXXVI, 1009.---On Anastasius the Librarian, CXXVII, 14.---On Angilbert, abbot of Corbie, CXXIX, 783.---On Remigius, monk of St Germanus of Auxerre, CXXXI, 47.---On Odilo, monk of St Medard of Soissons, CXXXII, 375.---On Hucbald, 823.---On Cappidus of Stavelot, CXXXIII, 858.---On Cosmas the Iapygian, 879.---On Fredegod, Benedictine monk, 977.---Bibliographical notice on Flodoard, CXXXV, 19.---Notice on Helperic, monk of St Gall, CXXXVII, 16.---Likewise on Berner, abbot of Homblières, 49.---Historical notice on Widukind, monk of Corbie, 113.---On John, abbot of St Arnulf at Metz, 211.---On Folcuin, abbot of Lobbes, 530.---On Lethaldus, bishop of Micy, 781.

Historical notice on Pope Sylvester II and his writings, CXXXIX, 61.---On Rorico, monk of Moissac, 587.---On Aimoin, monk of Fleury, 617.---On Heriger, abbot of Lobbes, 955.---On Rotger, bishop of Liège, 1139.---On Byrhtferth, monk of Ramsey, 1423.---On St Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, CXLI, 183.---Notice on Guido, abbot of Arezzo, 375.---On Aribo, archbishop of Mainz, 1109.---On Wazo, bishop of Liège, CXLII, 725.---On Hermann the Lame, CXLIII, 19.---Likewise on Odo, monk of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés, 846.---On Humbert, cardinal-bishop of Silva Candida, 914.---On Bovo, abbot of St Bertin, 1367.---Likewise on Roger, CXLVI, 1485.---On Guarferius, monk of Monte Cassino, CXLVII, 1282.---Notice on William Calculus, monk of Jumièges, CXIX, 778.---Likewise on Guitmund, archbishop of Aversa, 1426.---On St William, abbot of Hirsau, CL, 889.---Likewise on Guido, abbot of Farfa, 1191. Notice on the monastery of Farfa, 1191.---Notice on Deusdedit, Roman priest, 1566.---Likewise on William of Poitiers, archdeacon of Luxeuil, 1573.---On Bernard of Toledo, CLV, 146.---Likewise on Manegold, 147.---Notice on Fulcher of Chartres, 821.---On Richard of Dammartin, 1627.---On Lietbert, CLVII, 711.---On Walram, bishop of Naumburg, CLIX, 985.---Likewise on Gilbert, bishop of Luni in Ireland, 995.---Likewise on Gilbert Crispin, abbot of Westminster, 1003.---On Berengosus, abbot of St Maximin of Trier, CLX, 935.---Notice on Reimbald, provost of St John at Liège, CLXII, 750.---Likewise on Peter Chrysolanus.---On Laurence, deacon of Verona, CLXIII, 513.---On Albert of Aachen, author of a history of the Jerusalem expedition, CLXVI, 387.---Likewise on Franco, who wrote the treatise *On the Grace of God*, 715.---On Donizo and Abbo, CLXVI, 1339.

Historical-literary notice on Drogo, cardinal and bishop of Asti, 1514.---On Hermann, a Christian converted from Judaism, LXX, 803.---Likewise on Udascalc, monk of St Ulrich at Augsburg, 835.---On Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 35.---Historical and literary notice on Rudolph, abbot of St Trudo, CLXXIII, 9.---On Hariulf, abbot of Aldenburg, CLXXIV, 1211.---Notice on Linard, cleric of Tours, CLXXIV, 1589.---On Hugh of St Victor, CLXXV, CXXXVIII. Survey of his works, CXL.---On Abelard, abbot of Rhuys, CLXXVIII, 54.---On William of Malmesbury, monk, CLXXIX, 42.---Notice on Hermann, abbot of St Martin at Tournai, CLXXX, 9.---On William, abbot of Saint-Thierry [Col. 0342] near Reims, CLXXX, 186.---On Henry of Saltrey, 971.---Notice on Hildebrand the Younger, CLXXXI, 1691.---On Zachary, bishop of Chrysopolis, CLXXXVI, 9.---On Gratian, Benedictine monk, CLXXXVII, 7.---Notice on Guerric, abbot of Igny, CLXXXVIII, 983. Likewise on Atto, bishop of Pistoia, 985.---On Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, 1087.---On Odo, abbot of Morimond, 1643.---On Robert of Retz [Robertus Rethenensis], CLXXXIX, 1073.---Notice on Wibald, abbot of Stavelot and Corvey, 1075.---On Peter Lombard, Master of the Sentences, CXCI, 30.---On Lord Gerhoh, provost of Reichersberg, CXCIII, 479.---On Arno, provost of Reichersberg, CXCIV, 1490.---Likewise on Hugh of Poitiers, 1559.---On Eckbert, abbot of Schönau, and St Elisabeth, his blood-sister, CXCV, 9.---On Aelred, abbot of Rievaulx, 203.---On Henry, archdeacon of Huntingdon, 798.---On Hugh of Fouilloy, CXCVI, 1558.---On Godfrey of Viterbo, CXCVIII, 871.---On Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1047.---Literary notice on John of Salisbury, CXCIX, XIV.---On John of Cornwall, CXCIX, 1041.---On Walter of St Victor, prior at Paris, 1128.---On William of Tyre, archbishop, CCI, 201.---On John Beleth, Parisian theologian, CCII, 9.---Likewise on Hugh Eterianus, 166.---On Gilbert Foliot, bishop of London, 1146.---Historical-literary notice on Philip of Harveng, abbot of the monastery of Bonne-Espérance, CCIII, VIII.---Literary notice on Henry of Marsiac, abbot and cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, CCIV, 215.---On St Stephen of Muret, founder of the Premonstratensian Order, CCIV, 999.---Notice on Ermengaud, CCIV, 1235.---On Peter of Vaux-de-Cernay, CCXIII, 541.

FABRICIUS (Francis), born at Düren in 1524, died in 1573. He annotated and published the histories of Paulus Orosius.---Dedicatory letter, XXXI, 649. Letter of his pupil Ruremond, 651.

FABROTTUS published Anastasius’s *History of the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*.---Notes with variant readings, CXXVII, 1003 and following.

FELLUS (John), born at Longworth in 1625 and made bishop of Oxford; he published the life and works of St Cyprian with notes, III, 856, 860.

FEUARDENTIUS (Brother Francis), a Minorite, born at Coutances in Normandy in 1530, died in 1610. He published Prolegomena to Arnobius the Younger, LIII, 237. He collated the text with an Arnobius manuscript, discovered but not previously published, which he commits to print with only a few corrections, ibid. Critical notes appended to the text, 239 and following.

FLODOARD, canon of Reims and historian, died in 966.---Historical notice on Ebbo, bishop of Reims, CXVI, 9.---Notice on Seulf, bishop of Reims, CXXXII, 1063.

FLOREZ (Fr. Henry), of the Order of St Augustine, theologian, historian, and archaeologist, born at Valladolid in 1701, died in 1773; author of *España sagrada* (*Sacred Spain*).---Notice in Spanish on the Compostellan history and its authors, CLXX, 879. The usefulness and occasion of this history, ibid. The age of its author, 881. Manuscripts, 885. On this new edition, 886.---Notes on the Compostellan history, 891 and following.

FLOSS (Heinrich Joseph) revised and published the works of John Scotus.---Preface. Plan of the edition, CXXII. Manuscripts, II. A brief and very necessary explanation of the whole work, VI. On the expositions of the mystical Trinity, VII. On his exegetical works, VIII.---Observations on the life and writings of John Scotus, IX.---Preface to John Scotus’s translation of the works of St Dionysius the Areopagite, 1023. Notes and variant readings, 1029 and following.

FONTANINUS (Justus), bishop of Ancyra, controversialist and theologian, born at San Daniele del Friuli in 1666, died in 1736; literary notice on St Chromatius, XX, 375. Chromatius, an Aquileian by birthplace, ibid. He succeeded Valerian, 377. Praised by great men, 380. At his request St Jerome translated the sacred books into Latin, 381. He endeavours to reconcile Rufinus and Jerome, 382. He supports the cause of John Chrysostom, 385. Chrysostom’s letter to Chromatius, 386. Chromatius dies and is enrolled in the calendar of saints, 388. On the writings of St Chromatius: homilies, 389. Why and by whom he was called Roman bishop, 391. He is the author of the homilies, 395. He is defended against calumniators, 400. Chromatius’s style and purpose, 402.---Life of Tyrannius Rufinus, priest of Aquileia, XXI, 75. Rufinus’s birth and name, ibid. His native country, 77. He becomes a monk, 80. A friend of Jerome from youth, 81. Their separation, 82. He comes to Rome, 85. He sets out for Jerusalem with Melania, 86. He suffers for the faith, 89. He spends six years at Alexandria, [Col. 0343] 93. He comes to Jerusalem, 94. Rufinus’s account, 95. The origin of the hostility between Jerome and Rufinus, 97. He communicates with Epiphanius, 99. A new occasion of dissension, 100. Melania defends Rufinus’s cause, 101; likewise Theophilus, 102. The friendship of Jerome and Theophilus grows cold, 104. He extinguishes the schism, 104.---Rufinus found guilty of no error, 108.---Rufinus returns to Rome with Melania, 109. He arrives at Nola, 110. At what time these events occurred, 110 and 111. Baronius’s opinion on Rufinus, 114. He stayed at the monastery of Pinetum, where he translated certain works of Origen into Latin, 115, 116. Rufinus dedicates to Macarius the first book of Pamphilus’s *Apology for Origen*, 121. Rufinus’s dissertation in defence of Origen, 122. Again he translates Origen’s four books *On First Principles*, 124, 131. On the death of his mother, Rufinus writes to Jerome, 134. He returns to Concordia and passes through Milan, 133. Another Rufinus receives Jerome’s letter and carries it to Rome to be delivered to Rufinus, 137. Rufinus’s apology against Jerome’s letter, 141. Rufinus shows himself wholly Catholic, 147. Another apology of Rufinus addressed to Anastasius, 150. A synopsis of both apologies is sent to Jerome, 153. Jerome’s reply, 154. What Pamphilus wrote, 157. Jerome’s replies to Rufinus’s accusations, 162 and following. Rufinus sends his books to Jerome and attacks him vehemently, 170. St Chromatius strives to establish concord between them, 172. Homilies of Origen translated from Greek by Rufinus, 177; likewise eight homilies of St Basil the Great and ten minor works of St Gregory Nazianzen, 188, 189; likewise minor works of Evagrius, 200; the *Recognitions* of Clement, 208; and he renders Eusebius’s history into Latin, 222. The eremitic history of another Rufinus, 235. On the holiness of Jerome and Rufinus, 243. On the commentary on the Apostles’ Creed, 251. Anatolius of Alexandria, 257. Whether Rufinus was the translator of the works of Flavius Josephus, 258. On books falsely attributed to him, 267 and following. Rufinus was by no means condemned by Anastasius, 279. He departs from the city for Palestine, 285. Rome besieged and plundered by Alaric, 290. Rufinus’s death and praises, 291 and 292.

FRANGIPANUS (Octavius Fraga), of the Benedictine Order of Monte Cassino, 1820. He published ten new sermons extracted from manuscript codices and attributed to St Augustine. Letter to Pope Pius VII, XLVI, 939. Editor’s preliminary address, ibid. Privilege, 945.

FRITZSCHE (O.-F.), the learned man who issued in 1844 the notice which he supplied in the preface to the Leipzig edition, VI, 1017. He added some notes, VII, 9 and throughout.

FROBENIUS, prince and abbot of St Emmeram at Regensburg.---Preliminary notice to Amalarius’s letter to Charlemagne, XCIX, 887.---He published the Works of Blessed Alcuin, enlarged with various documents and illustrated with notes. General preface: who Canisius was, C, 9; who Martène, Mabillon, Baluze, Pez, and others were, ibid. Hence the reason for a new edition, 10. On continuing the work of D. Oliver Legipont, 11. Sources of assistance, 12. On D. Temler, 14. On the investigations of Philip Louis Lieble, librarian at the Abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, 16; and of Jacques Claude Vincent, librarian of the Abbey of St Remigius at Reims, ibid. On the manuscripts discovered, 17.---Treatise on the life of Blessed Albinus, or Alcuin, 18. Preface. On the various names, native country, and parents of Blessed Alcuin, ibid. Blessed Alcuin’s education and teachers, 22. His monastic profession, 27. His school and pupils, 32. His summons and arrival in France, 38. On restoring literary studies, 42. Alcuin’s school at the palace, 49. Alcuin returns to England, 55. Alcuin’s appointment to the monastery at Tours, 59. Celebrated pupils of this school, 64. Alcuin’s bodily infirmity, 72. His death, tomb, and epitaph, 76. Alcuin’s learning and doctrine, 80. On grace and free will, 84. On confession, 85. On the Eucharist, 86. On the Church, 87.---Testimonies concerning Blessed Alcuin, 121 and following.---Notice on Alcuin’s letters, C, 135.---Notes, 139 and following.---Preliminary notice on the *Questions and Answers on Genesis*, 515.---Notice on these words of Genesis, “Let us make man according to, etc.”; likewise on the *Enchiridion*, 570.---Notice on the compendium on the Song of Songs, 639; likewise on the letter to Daphnis, 663. Preliminary notice on the commentaries on Ecclesiastes, C, 666. Preliminary notice on the interpretations of Hebrew names, 723; likewise on the commentary on the Gospel of St John, 733; likewise on the treatise on the Epistles of St Paul to Titus, Philemon, and the Hebrews, 1007.

Preliminary notice on the book *On Faith in the Most Holy Trinity*, CI, 9.---Likewise on the book *Against Felix*, 83.---Historical dissertation on the heresy of Elipand and Felix of Urgell, 303. State of the controversy, ibid. Who first initiated the controversy, 304. In what year the dissension broke out, 305. Who first opposed the new doctrine, 306. The zeal of Beatus and Etherius, ibid. Elipand’s efforts, 307. Whether a council was ever held is doubtful, 308. Objections answered, ibid. The error opposed at Regensburg in 792; [Col. 0344] at Rome by Hadrian, 310. Felix’s confession of faith, 311. Felix revives his error in Spain, 313. Alcuin obeys the king’s summons, 314. The Council of Frankfurt summoned by Charlemagne in 794. Alcuin and other British bishops attend the council, 316. Felix does not appear, 318. Alcuin disputes with Felix at the Council of Aachen, 321. Felix composes and publishes a confession of faith, 323. Alcuin rejoices in his conversion, ibid. Many doubts clarified, 324 and following.---Preliminary notice on Alcuin’s liturgical works, 439.---Likewise on his hagiographical works, 655.---Preface to his didactic works, 847. Preliminary notice on grammar, 849.---Likewise on orthography, 901. On the book *On Rhetoric*, 919.---On the book *On Dialectic*, 949. On the treatise on the course of the moon and the leap year, 979.---Preliminary notice on Alcuin’s doubtful works, 1001. Critical observation on Basnage’s censures of Mabillon, 1023.---Preliminary notice on the debates of boys, 1097. Notice on propositions for sharpening young minds, 1143; likewise on the book *On the Divine Office*, 1173, and on the little book *On Antichrist*, 1290.

FRONTONUS (John), regular canon of St Geneviève at Paris, born at Angers in 1614, philosopher and theologian, died in 1662. He published the Works of Ivo of Chartres in Paris in 1647.---Dedicatory letter, CLXI, 9.---Life of Lord Ivo, 12.

GABELENTZ (H.-C.) and LOEBE (J.). Dedicatory letter of the Gothic translation of the Bible by Ulfilas, addressed to Maximilian of Bavaria, XVIII, 457.---Prolegomena: Ulfilas’s family, origin, and age, 461. He succeeded Bishop Theophilus in 355 and preached the Gospel faith to the Goths; then he journeyed to Constantinople in 388 to defend his own faith and that of his people, where, overtaken by illness, he died, ibid. The character of the Bible translation attributed to him, 462. Philostorgius’s implausible opinion concerning why Ulfilas did not translate the books of Kings, ibid. The Goths possessed a translation of the entire body of Scripture, but much has perished, 468. The Goths who occupied Italy used Bibles in the Gothic language in their churches, 464. How this language ceased to be used after the passage of six centuries, 465. Yet one codex was found in the sixteenth century at Ruremonde in the Low Countries, in the monastery of Werden, ibid. Franciscus Junius published it in 1655, together with fragments of the Epistle to the Romans found in the library at Wolfenbüttel, 465. Whether this version of Ulfilas is truly Gothic, 466. This is demonstrated, 467. What should be thought concerning the integrity of Ulfilas’s version, 468. How it is truly a work of Ulfilas, 469. From what source the Gothic translator drew, 470. In many places very many words are extant in Latin versions, 471. Yet this version more probably derives from Greek sources, 472. The light of the Gospel shone forth from the Greek world, 473. On the four Gospels, 475. Whether the fragments of the Epistles agree with the Gospels, 478. Very few fragments of the Old Testament, 479. Ulfilas rendered the authority of the Greek text word for word, a point on which all now agree, 482. There are places where he seems to have translated less accurately, 484. On passages where Ulfilas appears to have erred against the laws of his own language, 485. It would be the task of a careful critic to avoid all discrepancies, 488. On the various manuscripts, 491 and following. Observations on the orthography of the letters, 496.---Critical notes on the Prolegomena and the text, 463 and following.

GALEARDUS (P.), canon of Brescia, in 1738 wrote a dedicatory letter to Angelo, cardinal and bishop of Brescia, concerning the edition of St Philastrius’s book, XII, 1051. His preface, 1053. St Philastrius’s name is known, ibid. It is written in two ways, 1055. Augustine mentions him, ibid. His origin is unknown, 1056. He held the episcopal see of Brescia from 365 to 374, probably, 1059. Gaudentius reports remarkable things concerning Philastrius’s preaching, 1063. Two of his pupils in the Church of Brescia, 1066. In what year Augustine saw Philastrius at Milan is uncertain, 1068. Besides the book *On Heresies*, certain other works are attributed to him, 1073. On the usefulness and employment of the book *On Heresies*, 1075. Heterodox judgments concerning Philastrius examined, 1080. On the Corbie manuscript and its corrections, 1083. On the six chapters of Philastrius recently discovered in the Corbie manuscript, 1086. On this new edition, 1094. Various editions of the Works of St Philastrius, 1096. Galeardus’s textual notes, 1120.---Preface to the Works of St Gaudentius, XX, 795. On his age and election, ibid. What we learn from his sermon on his own ordination, 797. On his deeds in the East, ibid. In what year he assumed the episcopate, 798. His doctrine and eloquence, ibid. His birthplace uncertain, 799. Several men named Gaudentius, 800. How great was the piety of our Gaudentius, 802. With other bishops he was sent by Pope Innocent to Constantinople, but was expelled from the city with his companions, detained in chains, and suffered many things; at last they all returned to Rome, 803. When he died, 805.---Gaudentius’s genuine and spurious works identified, 807. Judgment of a recent writer concerning Gaudentius, 811. On the plan and arrangement of the Paduan edition, 816. On this new edition, 820.---Critical notes, 827 and throughout.

[Col. 0345] GALEUS (Thomas), learned antiquary, born at Scruton in 1636 and died in 1702. He published John Scotus’s work *On the Division of Nature* at Oxford in 1681. Preface, CXXII, 87.

GALLANDIUS (Andreas), born at Venice in 1707 and died in 1779. A celebrated Oratorian who, after exceedingly great labours, edited the *Library of the Holy Fathers*. He published a commentary on Novatian’s book *On the Trinity*, III, 885.—He elucidated the writings of Commodianus with notes, V, 202.—Notice on Victorinus the African, VIII, 993: his status and conversion, ibid.; how long he lived after his conversion, 994; the nature of his authority, 995; editors of his short works, 996; observations on his treatises, ibid.; the time when these books were written, 998.—Historical notice on Hosius, bishop of Corduba, 1310. History of the Council of Sardica, XIII, 13. Prolegomena to Faustinus and Marcellinus, XIII, 29: what Gennadius says about them, ibid.; when Faustinus’s work appeared at Rome, 30; on the memorial addressed to the emperors, 31; on its preface, 32; observations on this book, 33.—Historical notice on Saint Vigilius, bishop and martyr of Trent, XIII, 543: what his Acts relate, 545; by whom he was ordained, ibid.; how long he governed the Church of Trent, 546; what Gennadius says about Vigilius’s writings, 547; when he wrote the letters attributed to him, 549. Brief introduction to the writings of Saint Pacian, bishop of Barcelona, XIII, 1051. Prolegomena to the writings of Julius Hilarianus, 1093.—Prolegomena on the sanctity and doctrine of Saint Martin, bishop of Tours, XVIII, 9: on the work attributed to him, the *Confession, or Sermon on the Holy Trinity*, ibid.; Thomas Beauxanus, its first editor, 10.—Prolegomena on Tyconius the African, XVIII, 13: Tyconius’s origin and talent, ibid.; only his book *On the Seven Rules* survives, ibid.; notice concerning two short works by an anonymous author, 71; likewise concerning two sermons ascribed to Ambrose, 89; critical notes, 94 ff.—Prolegomena to the writings of Saint Phoebadius, bishop of Agen, XX, 9: life and deeds of Saint Phoebadius, ibid.; his doctrine, 10; his writings, 11.—Prolegomena on Saint Anastasius, pope, XX, 53. Prolegomena on Sulpicius Severus, XX, 79: his life, deeds, and writings, 79–80. Prolegomena to the works of Saint Chromatius, XX, 319: life and deeds of Saint Chromatius, ibid.; his doctrine, 322.—Prolegomena on Saint Victricius, bishop of Rouen: his origin and age, XX, 437; summoned to the see of Rouen, ibid.; goes to England in 394, ibid.; then to Rome in 403; returning to Rouen, he dies in 409, 438.—Prolegomena on Saint Innocent I, pope, XX, 461.—Prolegomena on Paulinus of Milan, 703: not the same person as Paulinus of Nola, ibid.; survey of Paulinus’s writings, 705; the writer’s reliability is not to be called into doubt by anyone, 706; Celestius’s artifices, 707; what Quesnel and Noris devised, 708; some matters concerning the treatise *On the Blessings of the Patriarchs*.—Prolegomena on Saint Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, XX, 1007: his origin, life, and election, ibid.; the time when he occupied the see, ibid.; which writings are his, 1009; critical notes, 1009 and throughout.—Prolegomena on Bacchiarius the monk: when he flourished, XX, 1015; that he was a monk, 1017; that he cultivated letters, ibid.; certain matters concerning the Floriana edition, Rome, 1748, 1018; critical notes, ibid. ff.—Prolegomena on Zacchaeus the Christian and Evagrius the monk, concerning their deeds and writings, XX, 1061 ff.

Gallandius’s notice on Paulus Orosius, XXXI, 653: his family and homeland, ibid.; he goes to Africa to Saint Augustine, ibid.; in what year, 655; he stays with Jerome, 656; controversy among critics over Orosius’s *Apologeticus*, 657; what Augustine reports, ibid.; the opinion of Schott and Vossius, 658; how the text of the *Apologeticus* appears corrupted in Havercamp’s edition, 658; Orosius was still living in Palestine in 415, 659; having returned to Africa, at Augustine’s urging he writes the books of *Histories*, ibid.; in what year, ibid.; the ancients held this history in high esteem, 660; notice on the method of reckoning customarily used by Orosius, 662; notes on Orosius’s tract *On Freedom of Choice*, XXXI, 1187 ff.—Prolegomena on Leporius’s tract *On Amendment*, XXXI, 1215: Leporius’s family, homeland, and age, ibid.; he goes to Africa and, through Saint Augustine’s care, recognizes and abandons his error, 1217; some think that the tract attributed to him is Saint Augustine’s, ibid.; answers to the objections, 1218.—Corrections and notes on Marius Mercator, XLVIII, 66.—Prolegomena to the monastic rule of Vigilius the deacon, L, 373: where and when he lived, ibid.—Prolegomena to the writings of Faustidius, bishop of the Britons, L, 379: in what year he lived, 381; on what occasion he wrote, ibid.; how he adhered to Pelagius’s errors, 382. Notice on Celestine I, pope, L, 409.—On Sixtus III, pope, L, 574.—On Vincent of Lérins, L, 625.—Prolegomena on Hydatius, bishop of Aquae Flaviae, LI, 869: his family and year, ibid.; on his *Chronicle*, 870 ff.; Sirmond’s observation, 872. Notice on the life of Saint Valerian, bishop of Cimiez, LII, 683.

[Col. 0346] Prolegomena on Salvian, priest of Marseilles: his life, LIII, 9; his writings, ibid., and editions, 10; Salvian was only a priest, not a bishop, 11; if he was born at Cologne Agrippina, how he could be a Gaul, 12.—Prolegomena on the anonymous author of the book *Predestined*, LIII, 579: who that author was, ibid.; Holstenius’s opinion, 581; synopsis of the books, 581; editors of this book, 582.—Prolegomena on Claudianus Mamertus, LIII, 693: where and in what year he lived, ibid.; what kind of man and how great he was, 694; his books, ibid.; his error concerning the nature of angels, 695; editions of his books, 696; two letters not yet published, and a hymn, 696–697.—Prolegomena on Saint Patrick, LIII, 789: those who described his deeds, ibid.; on the recension of his short works, 791 ff.—Prolegomena on Capreolus, bishop of Carthage, LIII, 841: whom he succeeded, ibid.; which writings are his, ibid. ff.; certain deeds of his, 843.—Notice on Salonius, bishop of Vienne, and on his writings, LIII, 967.—Notice on Saint Lupus, bishop of Troyes, LVIII, 61.—Notice on Sidonius Apollinaris, LVIII, 437: his family, homeland, and year, ibid.; elevation to the episcopate, ibid.; difficulty concerning the date of his death, 438; Sidonius flourished in poetry and rhetoric, 439; how highly he should be esteemed, 440.—Prolegomena on Saint Avitus, bishop of Vienne, LIX, 191.—Prolegomena on John the deacon, 398.—Notice on Merobaudes the scholar: what is uncertain concerning him, LXI, 971; Boethius twice praises him as an orator, 972; the *Poem on Christ* (*Carmen de Christo*) is attributed to him, ibid.—Notice on Saint Orientius, bishop of Auch: disagreement concerning his homeland and the age in which he flourished, 973; he himself reveals his name, 974; his acts, 975; on his writings.—Prolegomena on Peter the deacon: his homeland and qualities, LXII, 79; on the occasion upon which he wrote the tract *On the Incarnation and Grace*, 81.—Prolegomena on Felix Ennodius, whose family, homeland, age, and deeds are described, LXIII, 9; his writings and short works, 10; their editions, 12.—Notice on Facundus, bishop of Hermiane, LXVII, 521: his homeland and the time when he flourished, ibid.; his works, 522.—Notice on Fulgentius Ferrandus, 878: his family and age, ibid.; letters, 879 ff.; abridgement of the canons, 885; matters to be observed in that abridgement, ibid.—Notice on the life and writings of Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles, 998.—Notice taken from Gallandius on the life and writings of Rusticus, deacon of the Holy Roman Church, 1165.—Notice on Saint Leontius, bishop of Sens, LXVIII, 9. Likewise on Junilius, African bishop, 11: his family and homeland, 11; what Sixtus of Siena and Cassiodorus say concerning him, 13.

Notice on Saint Nicetius, bishop of Trier: by whom he was commended, LXVIII, 361; what writings are his, 362; those who have treated his writings, 383.—Notice on Agnellus, bishop of Ravenna, 379. Notice on Victor, bishop of Tunnuna, 937.—Likewise on Gildas the Wise, LXIX, 327: his name, surname, homeland, and age, ibid.; his writings, 328 ff.—Notice on Saint Martin, bishop of Braga, LXXII, 17. Notice on Marius, bishop of Avenches, LXXII, 791.—On John, abbot of Biclar, 859: he wrote a *Chronicle* from 568 to 590, 861. Notice on Saint Columbanus, and notes on his writings, LXXX, 293.—Notice on Saint Gall, LXXXVII, 9. On Saint Eugenius, bishop of Toledo, 347.—On Evantius, abbot, 719.—On Saint Pirminius, abbot, LXXXIX, 1029.—On Leidrad, bishop of Lyons, XCIX, 853.—Historical notice on Saint Agobard, bishop of Lyons, CIV, 9.—On Andradus, chorepiscopus of Sens, CXV, 15.—On Amulo, bishop of Lyons, CXVI, 77.—On Florus, deacon of Lyons, CXIX, 9.—Notice on Gozechin the scholar, CXLIII, 886.—Notice on Humbert, cardinal-bishop of Silva Candida, 927.—On Durand, abbot of Troarn, author of the *Treatise on the Body and Blood of the Lord*, CXLIX, 1374.—Notice on the treatise of Abbot Hermann *On the Incarnation of Jesus Christ*, CLXXX, 9.

GALLIAE CHRISTIANAE AUCTORES [AUTHORS OF *CHRISTIAN GAUL*]. Notice on Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, LXXII, 53.—On Saint Aunarius, bishop of Auxerre, 759.—On Saint Autbert, bishop of Cambrai, LXXX, 593.—On Saint Palladius, bishop of Auxerre, LXXXVII, 215. On Constantius, bishop of Albi, 217.—On Saint Abbo, bishop of Metz, ibid. On Saint Desiderius, bishop of Cahors, ibid.—Historical notice on Saint Annemundus, bishop of Lyons, 470.—On Verus, bishop of Rodez, 473.—On Saint Eligius, bishop of Noyon, and Audoenus, bishop of Rouen, ibid.—On Saint Faro, bishop of Meaux, 1131.—Historical notice on Saint Leodegarius, bishop of Autun, XCVI, 330.—On Angelramnus, bishop of Metz, 1031.—On Fardulf, abbot of Saint-Denis, XCIX, 823.—On Magnus, bishop of Sens, CII, 979.—On Jeremiah, bishop of Sens, CV, 729. On Jesse, bishop of Amiens, 779. On Saint Aldric, archbishop of Sens, 795. On Hilduin, abbot of Saint-Denis, [Col. 0347] CVI, 9. On Jonas, bishop of Orléans, 117.—Historical notice on Rodulf, bishop of Bourges, CXIX, 699.—On Rothad, bishop of Soissons, 745.—Notice on Aeneas, bishop of Paris, CXXI, 681.

On Herard, archbishop of Tours, 761.—On Saint Remigius, bishop of Lyons, CXXI, 985. On Vulfad, bishop of Bourges, 1335.—On Isaac, bishop of Langres, CXXIV, 1073. On Odo, bishop of Beauvais, 1109.—Notice on Fulk, archbishop of Reims, CXXXI, 9. On Riculf, bishop of Soissons, 13. On Robert, bishop of Metz, CXXXII, 527.—On Waldram, bishop of Strasbourg, 573. On Stephen, bishop of Liège, 641.—On Hervaeus, archbishop of Reims, 659. On Walter, bishop of Sens, 717.—On Dado, bishop of Verdun, 777.—On Aeginon, archbishop of Narbonne, 779.—Historical notice on Rorico, bishop of Laon, CXXXIII, 951.—On Arthald, archbishop of Reims, 953. On Odalric, archbishop of Reims, 963.—On Richard, abbot of Fleury, CXXXVI, 1301.—On Adalbert, scholar of Metz, 1309.—On Odo, deacon of Auch, CXXXVII, 311.—On Theodoric, bishop of Metz, 359.—On Adalbero, archbishop of Reims, 503.—On Erkembald, bishop of Strasbourg, 582.—On Guy II, bishop of Le Puy, 851.—Notice on Notger, bishop of Liège, CXXXIX, 1135.—On Ebles, archbishop of Reims, CXLI, 1109.—On Leduin, abbot of Saint-Vaast at Arras, 1333.—On Othelbold, abbot of Saint Bavo at Ghent, 1337.—On Poppo, bishop of Trier, 1398.—On Angelramnus, abbot of Saint-Riquier at Centula, 1401.—Notice on Hugh, bishop of Langres, CXLII, 1321.—On Halinard, bishop of Lyons, 1333.—Historical notice on Guy of Châtillon, 1402.—On Saint Leo IX, pope, CXLIII, 548.—On Drogo, bishop of Beauvais, CXLIII, 862.—On Hugh II, bishop of Nevers, 1365.—On Raimbald, archbishop of Arles, 1390.—On Gervasius, archbishop of Reims, 1398.—On Leodegarius, archbishop of the Church of Vienne, 1403.—Notice on Hugh, bishop of Troyes, CXLVI, 1435. On Deoduin, bishop of Liège, 1437.—On Guy, bishop of Amiens, 1503.—On John, bishop of Avranches, CXLVII, 9.—On John, abbot of Fécamp, 413.—Historical notice on Bruno, bishop of Angers, 1199. On Gebuin, bishop of Lyons, 1205. On Galterius, bishop of Meaux, 1211.—On Hermann, CL, 1177.—On Gerard II, bishop of Cambrai, 1379.—On Raynald I, archbishop of Reims, 1385.—On Radbod II, bishop of Noyon, 1493.—On Aganon, bishop of Autun, 1539.—On Poppo, bishop of Metz, CLV, 1650.—Historical notice on Godfrey, abbot of Vendôme and cardinal of Saint Prisca, CLVII, 9.—On Pibo, bishop of Toul, 413.—On Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, 487: noble by birth and first bishop of Die, ibid.; various testimonies concerning him, 488 ff.; how he became archbishop of Lyons, 489; what less worthy things are reported about him, ibid. and 490; whether all these are authentic, ibid.; what occurred in 1092, 491, and in 1095, 492; in 1097 and the following years, 496. Notice on Galter, CLVII, 708.—Notice on Walter, bishop of Chalon-sur-Saône, CXL, 1159: form of Walter’s election, 1163.—Historical notice on the bishops of Chartres, CLXI, IX: life of Saint Ivo, XVIII; his writings, XXVII.—On Lambert, bishop of Arras, CLXII, 615.—On Galo, bishop of Paris, 722.—On Godfrey, bishop of Amiens, 731.—On Richard, cardinal and archbishop of Narbonne, 1593.—On Theoger, bishop of Metz, CLXIII, 769.—Notice on William of Champeaux, bishop of Châlons, 1037.—On Radulf, archbishop of Reims, 1415.—On Arnald, abbot of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif at Sens, 1474.—On Pons, abbot of Cluny, CLXVI, 835.—On Saint Baldric, archbishop of Dol, 1049.—On Bruno, bishop of Strasbourg, 1347.

Notice on Stephen of Baugé, bishop of Autun, CLXXII, 1271.—On Gerard, bishop of Angoulême, 1311.—On Raynald, archbishop of Reims, 1339.—On Geoffrey, bishop of Châlons, CLXXIII, 1394.—On Stephen, bishop of Paris, 1399.—List of the abbesses of the convent of the Holy Spirit at the Paraclete, CLXXVIII, 1849.—Notice on Bartholomew, bishop of Châlons, CLXXXI, 1722.—On Rainard, abbot of Cîteaux, 1723.—On Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, CLXXXVI, 1151.—On Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, CLXXXIX, 9.—On Peter Lombard, Master of the Sentences, CXCI, 9.—On Hugh, archbishop of Amiens and Rouen, CXCII, 1112.—Notice on Gilduin, abbot of Saint-Victor, CXCVI, 1366. See CLXXVII, 193.—On Ervisius, abbot of Saint-Victor, CXCVI, 1374.—On Guarinus, abbot of the same monastery, 1375.—On Joscelin, archbishop of Tours, 1534.—On Henry I, brother of King Louis VII and archbishop of Reims, 1559.—On Hugh of Champfleury, 1583.—Notice on John of Salisbury, CXCIX, IX.—On [Col. 0348] Guichard, archbishop of Lyons, 1086.—On Peter, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, 1119.—On Roger, abbot of Saint-Euverte at Orléans, 1125.—On Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, CCI, 9.—On Alan, bishop of Auxerre, 1380.—Notice on Saint Stephen of Muret, founder of the Premonstratensian Order, CCIV, 997.—On Stephen of Liciac, prior of Grandmont, 1163.—On Bernard, fifth prior of Grandmont, ibid. On William and then Gerard Iterius, 1177.—On Peter the Chanter, CCV, 9.—Notice on Garnier, bishop of Langres, 555.—On Maurice de Sully, bishop of Paris, CCV, 887.—On Odo, bishop of Toul, 913.—On William of Champagne, archbishop of Reims, CCIX, 818.—On John de Bellesmains, archbishop of Lyons, 873.—On Odo de Sully, bishop of Paris, CCXII, 47.

GALOPINUS (George), Benedictine of the monastery of Saint Ghislain in Hainaut; Mons, 1639. He edited the works of the Venerable Peter the Chanter, of the Church of Blessed Mary at Paris and professor of theology.—Preface to the reader, CCV, 22.—Notes and observations by G. Galopinus on Peter the Chanter’s *The Abbreviated Word*, published separately from the text, CCV, 369 ff.

GARBELLUS (Philip), in 1744 wrote to Blanchini concerning the Brescia codex of the Gospels of Eusebius of Vercelli, XII, 11. He reports that he selected from Eusebius’s Gospel readings diverging from the Vulgate, 12; the great care he bestowed, 13; on the silver codex of this Gospel, 15; frequent interchange of letters in it, 16; that these exemplars were in use before Jerome’s time, according to Capitolinus, 17; the Eusebian Canons were prefixed to the Gospels, ibid.; a preface drawn from it, 18; the character of the copyist, 19; Valesius’s observation, ibid.; it was wrongly corrected in certain places by unskilled critics, 20; on the ancient use of such codices, 21; fragment of an ancient bull, ibid.; Mill’s opinion on the authenticity of these manuscripts, 24; observations on the four Evangelists, 29, 30 ff.; what suggests that it was so read in antiquity, 38; in times of persecution codices were burned, became scarce and corrupt, but were soon restored to their ancient truth by piety and integrity of faith, 41 ff.; discussion of the earliest times, 43; Clericus’s opinion concerning the Word, 48; source of the diversity of the first editions, 52; on the lost autographs of the apostles, 55; on the most ancient versions, 58.

GARETUS (Dom J.), a most learned Benedictine, born at Port-Grâce in 1627 and died in 1694. He edited the works of Cassiodorus, elucidated by notes and observations, LXIX, 421. Dedicatory letter, ibid.—Preface, 425: why this new edition, ibid.; account taken of earlier editions, ibid.; appended observations, 426; on the codex of Sainte-Marie de Liré, 427; the difficulty solved by Quesnel, 428; annotations on proper names, 429; on the *Chronicle*, 429; on the history of the Goths, 430; that some assert without grounds that these books are merely abridgements of Augustine, 431; what commentaries should not be ascribed to Cassiodorus, 435; views concerning certain other books or treatises, and what had necessarily to be done in editing them, 433 ff.—Life of Cassiodorus, LXIX, 437. Part I, on Cassiodorus’s names, ibid.; his grandfather and father, 438; his relations and kinsmen, 439; his homeland, ibid.; year of his birth, 440; Cassiodorus’s education, 441; his deeds, 442 ff.; he becomes quaestor, 444; deeds, 445 ff.; he writes a history of the Goths, 449; why and how, after becoming a senator, he wrote to the supreme pontiff, 452; his concern as a senator that taxes should not burden the people, 455; he brings relief to Rome in famine, 456; he attempts to establish sacred schools at Rome, 458; his piety toward certain nuns, 459; he assists provinces during famine, 460; he punishes plunderers of the Church’s property, 461; how he provides for the tranquillity of the kingdom, 462; he grants freedom to prisoners, 463; he writes the books of the *Variae*, 464; how his piety shines forth, 465. Part II, Cassiodorus’s condition after renouncing the world, ibid.; the opinion of the Centuriators is rejected, 466; likewise Trithemius’s view, 466; reason for his withdrawal, ibid.; how Rome is said to have flourished, 467; what Cassiodorus’s monastery was like, 464; whether he made profession, 469; that he was an abbot, ibid.; Cassiodorus teaches philosophy to monks, 471; commends the study of Scripture, 472; trains monks in copying sacred codices, 475; what books he published as a monk, 478; what he thought of the Fifth Ecumenical Council, 480; he rests in a holy end, 482.

Dissertation on the monastic life of Aurelius Cassiodorus, LXIX, 483: it is demonstrated that Cassiodorus knew the Rule of Saint Benedict, 483–484; Cassiodorus followed it, 485; this conclusion follows not only from his deeds but also from his writings, 486; authors who did not hesitate to acknowledge that Cassiodorus professed the Rule of Saint Benedict, 488; Baronius’s argument and certain contrary considerations examined, [Col. 0349] 490; conclusion, 496. Notes and various observations on Cassiodorus’s books, 501 ff.

GARNERIUS (J.), theologian and learned bibliographer of the Society of Jesus, born at Paris in 1612 and died at Bologna in 1681. In 1673 he edited the works of Marius Mercator, illustrated with notes.

General preface, XLVIII, 11. Introduction, ibid. Chapter 1: On the birth, age, and authority of Marius Mercator, ibid. Chapter 2: On the works of Marius Mercator, 17. Chapter 3: What is contributed by this edition, 22; survey of both parts, 23. Chapter 4: A specimen of Marius Mercator’s works, 27: those relating to the Pelagian heresy, ibid.; those relating to the Nestorian heresy, 51; how these works came into our hands, 33; on Saint Augustine’s letter to Mercator, 37.—Historical preface to the *Commonitorium concerning Celestius*, 61: who Celestius was and his artifices, ibid.; Mercator writes against him, 63; corrections and Gallandius, 63 and throughout; defence of Pope Zosimus in the affair of Celestius, 79, among the notes.—Notice on the book of *Subnotations*, 107. Notice on the three letters of Nestorius, 171.

Preface to the Appendix of Marius Mercator’s Works, containing seven dissertations, XLVIII, 255. Dissertation I: On the first authors and principal defenders of the Pelagian heresy, 257; on Paul of Samosata, ibid.; Theodore of Mopsuestia, 258; Rufinus, Celestius’s teacher, 261; Pelagius, 266; Celestius, Pelagius’s disciple, 277; Julian, bishop of Eclanum, 286; Anianus the deacon, 298; the author of the book *Questions of the New and Old Testament*, or Augustine, 305; the author of the commentaries on the Epistles of Blessed Paul once attributed to Ambrose, 316.

Dissertation II: On the synods held against the Pelagians during Augustine’s lifetime, 319: Council of Carthage in 412, 321; Jerusalem, 415; Diospolis, 415, 327; Carthage, 416, 331; Milevis, 416, 333; Rome, 417, 336; Rome in the same year, 338; Antioch, 417, 344; Carthage, 418, 347; another Carthage council, 418, 350; another African council of the same year, 353; Rome, 355; Carthage in the same year, 418, 358; Carthage, 419, 350; Anazarbus in Cilicia, 423, ibid.; Constantinople, 424, 361; Rome, 424; an African general council in the same year, 363; Arles, 427, 367; Verulam in England, 429, 371; Ephesus, 431, 373; eight synods held in the fifth century in this same affair of the Pelagians, 375.

Dissertation III: On imperial constitutions concerning the Pelagian heresy from 418 to 430. Constitution I of Honorius, 389; Constitution II of the same, 392; Constitution III of Honorius, 394; Constitution IV, 400; Constitution V, 404; Constitution VI, 408; Constitution VII, 409; constitutions of Theodosius, 413.

Dissertation IV: On subscriptions required in the Pelagian controversy, XLVIII, 415: cause and purpose of the dissertation, ibid.; what a subscription is, and its cause and usefulness, 417; necessity of demanding subscriptions in the Pelagian controversy, 418; teachings concerning which subscription was demanded in this case, 429; whether the Pelagians acknowledged as theirs what the Fathers of the councils charged against them, 431; by what authority the law requiring subscription was established, 435; the pleas of those refusing to subscribe, 438; artifices they used to evade the issue, 441; manner in which those refusing were dealt with, 444.

Dissertation V: On written professions of faith and the principal defenders of the Pelagian heresy, XLVIII, 445: creed of Theodore of Mopsuestia, 446; profession of faith by Rufinus, 449; confession of faith by Pelagius, 488; profession of faith offered to Pope Zosimus by Celestius, 497; summary of Celestius’s letter to the Roman clergy of his party, 505; profession of faith by Julian of Eclanum, 508.

Dissertation VI, Part 1: On the writings of the orthodox against the Pelagians before Saint Augustine’s death, 535; writings of Saint Jerome against the Pelagians, 537; Augustine’s writings in the same controversy, 546; Orosius’s writings against the Pelagians, 566.—Part 2: On the writings of the Pelagians against the orthodox during Augustine’s lifetime, 585; writings of Julian of Eclanum, 622; likewise those of Theodore of Mopsuestia, ibid.; writings of Pelagius, Rufinus, and Celestius, 587; what Celestius wrote in particular, 615; writings of Arminius the deacon, 626.

Dissertation VII: On the origin and development of the Pelagian heresy, XLVIII, 629: what must be accomplished in this dissertation, 629; how three principal errors arise from one error, 635; Adam’s mortality, 638; original sin, 645; necessity of God’s grace, 670; Jerome’s opinion of the Pelagians, 681; certain verses attributed to Saint Prosper examined, 694.

Historical preface to the latter part of Mercator’s Works, XLVIII, 699: writings against the Nestorian heresy, ibid.; reason for providing a synopsis of the Council of Ephesus, ibid. After Sisinnius’s death Nestorius became archbishop of Constantinople, though not without turmoil, XLVIII, 700; his homeland, formation, and character, 701; summoned by Theodosius himself, ibid.; he demolishes the church of the Arians, ibid., [Col. 0350] and zealously persecutes all heretics of that time, thereby winning over courtiers and populace, ibid.; he then thought that he could safely introduce his heresy, 703; he began through the mouth of Dorotheus, who cried out that Mary was not *Theotokos* (“God-bearer”), ibid.; but Anastasius the priest protested against this, ibid., and the people followed him, so that they abstained from the liturgical assembly, ibid.; Nestorius, raging, persisted in many sermons, 703; Eusebius was the first of all publicly to set forth an admonition against Nestorius, 705; Marius Mercator writes a letter on the matter, ibid.; anger of the people, ibid.; Proclus, bishop of Cyzicus, delivered an address to the people on behalf of the Virgin *Theotokos* against Nestorius in 429; Nestorius replied in vain, 706; he sends a book through the provinces to disseminate his error and throws the whole East into turmoil, 707; Cyril of Alexandria writes against him: the beginning of open conflict, 709; Nestorius attempts every artifice, ibid.; Mercator offers Theodosius a memorial, ibid.; Nestorius contrives calumnies, 711.

Pope Celestine, having received letters and treatises from Nestorius, orders that he be refuted through Cassian the deacon, ibid., in 430. A synod is held at Rome, where Nestorius is condemned, 713. Warned of the apostolic sentence, Nestorius tries to turn the storm upon Cyril’s head, accusing him before Theodosius of impiety and requesting the calling of a general council, 715. Cyril formulates the doctrine of the faith in twelve anathemas; Nestorius answers them with an equal number of opposing propositions, 717. Marius Mercator performs an outstanding work of refutations against Nestorius’s blasphemies, ibid. Nestorius comes to Ephesus with a large retinue, where the council was being convened, 719; Cyril and many bishops also arrive there, ibid. When all the Fathers had come and were seated in the church called that of Mary, Nestorius arrived there with his followers and ordered it opened. But Nemeron, bishop of the Ephesians [reading uncertain], refused, and the people devoted to the Virgin opposed him. Thus the first session proceeded. Sixteen days later, when summoned, Nestorius refused to appear; consequently, a sentence of deposition and excommunication was pronounced against him as contumacious, 721.

Count Candidianus reported all these proceedings to Theodosius, ibid. All the Fathers of the council jointly warned the churches of Constantinople to keep everything under guard until a new bishop was elected; but Irenaeus, an imperial count with whom Nestorius had come, forcibly convened a synod in his lodging and procured the pronouncement of excommunication against those who had condemned Nestorius himself; he then dismissed each person except Cyril and Memnon, 723. Bishops subscribed to this sentence, 724. Why John of Antioch acted thus, ibid. The emperor ordered everything annulled as proceedings conducted irregularly, ibid. The Fathers of the council, summoned again at Saint Mary’s and having read Theodosius’s letters, judge that everything has been duly carried out and request permission to depart, 725. Yet Cyril and Memnon demand justice for the wrong inflicted on them by John. When John was summoned a third time, in contempt of the synod he ordered a document to be produced by which not only Cyril and Memnon but all the Fathers were accused, ibid. John and the bishops with him were excommunicated together, and everything done against Cyril and Memnon was declared void, 725. What occurred at Constantinople, 727. A tumult is provoked by John at Ephesus, 729. The synod chooses several persons to watch over the security of Cyril and Memnon, 731. New calumnies before the emperor from Nestorius’s supporters at Chalcedon, 735. The individual Fathers, having gained the victory, returned to their churches; Cyril himself was received triumphantly by his people, 737. What occurred in 432, 739, and in the following year, 433, 745.—Corrections and notes on Mercator’s remaining works, 753 ff.

Notice on the first collection of excerpts from Nestorius, XLVIII, 865. Notice on Saint Cyril’s *Apologeticus*, 931. Notice on Saint Cyril’s *Scholia on the Incarnation of the Only-Begotten*, examining by whom and when it was written, 1001. Likewise, notice on excerpts from Theodore of Mopsuestia, Theodoret of Cyrrhus, and Euthenius of Tyana, 1039. Observations on the creed and its refutation, 1049.—On excerpts from Theodoret of Cyrrhus, 1063.

Dissertation I: On Nestorius’s heresy and books, XLVIII, 1090: state of the question, 1090; the character of Nestorius’s heresy concerning the kind of union by which the two natures in Christ are joined, 1095; on Arius, Apollinaris, and Eunomius, association with whom Nestorius falsely charged against the Catholics; Nestorius compared with earlier heretics, association with whom was charged against him, 1124; on Nestorius’s works, 1154.

Dissertation II: On the synods held in the Nestorian controversy, 1167: Roman synod under Pope Celestine, 429, ibid.; Alexandrian synod of the same year, 1170; Alexandrian synod under Cyril, 430, 1172; Roman synod, 430; Constantinopolitan synod in the same year, 1177; Athicensian synod in Egypt, the same year, ibid.; Roman synod in the same year, 1184; [Col. 0351] Ecumenical Council of Ephesus, 430, 1188; schismatic conventicle at Ephesus under John of Antioch, 1202; Constantinopolitan synod at the ordination of Maximian, 1207; schismatic synod of the Easterners, 1209; synod, or rather consultation, of the bishops of Constantinople in the palace before the emperor, ibid.; schismatic synod of Beroea under Acacius, 1211; Egyptian synod concerning the making of peace between the Churches, 1214; Roman synod under Pope Sixtus in 433, 1215.—Notice to the reader.

Dissertation on Liberatus concerning the Fifth Synod and the events preceding it, LXVIII, 1051: when Justinian issued an enactment against Origen, 1052; on the Council of Constantinople convened by Mennas, 1058; when Justinian composed the edict against the Three Chapters, 1062; on the Council of Constantinople held in the affair of Mennas, 1067; whether Origen was condemned at the Fifth Synod, 1073; several observations on the acts of the synod, 1090; on confirmation of the synod, 1093.

Garnerius edited, with notes and observations, the *Liber Diurnus of the Roman Pontiffs*.—Dedication, CV, 9. Critical notes, 23 ff.—Dissertation I, on the notes to chapter 1, concerning the schedule for writing a letter, 119. Dissertation II: On the ordination of the supreme pontiff, 130; letters concerning the ordination of the supreme pontiff, 129; rite by which the supreme pontiff was ordained, 131; professions of faith issued by supreme pontiffs at their ordination, in general, 132; first profession of faith, 143; second profession of faith, 145.—Dissertation III: On the use of the pallium, 166.

GARZONIUS (T.), theologian, hagiographer, and archivist of the Republic of Venice, edited the works of Hugh of Saint Victor at Venice in 1688.—Preface, CLXXV, CLX. How he attempted to make Hugh a Lateran canon, CLXIV.—Notes on the books of *Allegorical Excerpts*, CLXXVII, 193 ff.

GARZONIUS (Juan Mateo), a Spaniard of the Society of Jesus, chancellor of the Academy of Gandia, about 1763 elucidated the *Chronicle* of Hydatius the bishop with corrections, scholia, and dissertations, LXXIV, 675.

Notice to the reader, 677.—Preliminary dissertation on the life and writings of Hydatius, 681: Hydatius’s homeland, ibid.; his birth, pilgrimage to Palestine, and return to Spain, 682; he dedicates himself to God, 683; Hydatius’s writings, 685; epochs inscribed in the *Chronicle*, 685; Abrahamic era, 687; Olympiad years, 691; on the *Fasti* and their being Hydatius’s work, 698.—Annotations, 701 ff.—Notes on Hydatius, 750 ff.—Dissertation I: On the seventh Jubilee from the Lord’s Ascension, 822; that the words “Seventh Jubilee,” etc., were appended to the *Chronicle* is established by the silence of ancient writers concerning such a Jubilee, 823; it is shown from Hydatius’s own *Fasti* that the same words were appended to the *Chronicle*, 824.—Dissertation II: On the beginning of the Spanish era, 825; the liberty copyists have taken in publishing chronicles, ibid.; when and on what occasion the public use of the era began in Spain, 828; on the beginning of the era, 851; examination of Saint Julian of Toledo’s passage comparing era 724 with the second year of King Ervig, 835; the Spanish era appears to begin with the triumvirate of Lepidus, Antony, and Octavian, 836; how long the beginning of the era remained doubtful, 838.

GAZAEUS (Alardus), a learned Benedictine, born at Arras in 1566 and died in 1626, edited the works of John Cassian with annotations at Douai in 1616.

Preface. Survey of the various editions of his works, XLIX, 29. Notice concerning Gazaeus himself in the notes, ibid. Cassian’s lineage, 31. Educated in Palestine and Egypt among monks, 32. On what occasion he wrote the Conferences, 33. He was a deacon, 34. How there are two Cassians, 35. Baronius’s opinion, ibid. At Marseilles he founded two monasteries, one for men and the other for women, 38. On the title *Domnus*, already in use in those times, ibid. Whether Cassian is honored with the title of saint, ibid. and following. The words of Pope Gelasius did not utterly condemn Cassian’s works, 40. Cassian merely wrote down the words of others, 41. Testimonies of Prosper and Gennadius, 42. What has been done in this edition, 43.—Testimonies of eminent men concerning John Cassian, 46.—The commentary of the same Alardus Gazaeus, attached throughout to the text, passim.—A few propositions requiring a pious interpretation, L, 361.—Extract from Gazaeus’s defense of Cassian, concerning the doctrine and faith of Gennadius, LVIII, 1057.

GENTIANUS (Benedict), monk of the abbey of Saint-Denis and Doctor of Theology, in the fifteenth century supplied observations on the inscription of Charlemagne’s codex, XCVIII, 51.

GERBERONIUS (Dom Gabriel), learned Benedictine of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, born at Saint-Calais in 1628 and died in 1711, edited the corrected and annotated works of Saint Anselm.

Prefatory Discourse, CVIII, 13. Manuscripts to be consulted, ibid. What arrangement was adopted in the books, 14. Appendix added, 15.—Critical assessment of Saint Anselm’s works, ibid. and following.—Critical assessment [Col. 0352] of the works in the Appendix, 39.—Variant readings and notes on Saint Anselm’s *Monologion on the Essence of Divinity*, 141 and following.—Likewise on the *Proslogion*, *Apologeticus*, etc., 224 and following.—Preface to the works of Eadmer, Benedictine monk of Canterbury, CLIX, 345. Variant readings and notes, passim.—Notes on the *Life of Hugh, Abbot of Cluny*, 858.—Apology for Dom Rupert, Abbot of Deutz. Prologue, CLXVIII, 23. Synopsis, 30. Part I contains a critical examination of Dom Rupert’s works, 43. Part II vindicates him from the errors imputed to him, 99.

GERBERTUS (Martin), learned theologian, born at Horb in Austria in 1720 and died in 1793. He published *Monuments of the Ancient Liturgy of Alemannia*.

Notes on the order of sacraments, CXXXVIII, 949 and following.—Observations on the monks’ midday meal according to the custom of the Roman Church, 1346.—Literary notice on Guido of Arezzo, CXLI, 377. Reader’s notice on Berno’s little work on music, CXLII, 1098.—Reader’s notice on the musical little works of Hermann the Lame, CXLIII, 414.—Reader’s notice on the music of Saint William, Abbot of Hirsau, CL, 1147.—Reader’s notice on the music of Aribo the scholastic, 1307.—Likewise on the treatise *On Music* by John Cottanus, 1391.—Likewise a notice on musical treatises, CLI, 651.—Notice on Berner, Abbot of Saint Blasien in the Black Forest, CLVII, 719.—Reader’s notice on Theoger’s music, 777.

BONA (John), learned theologian and cardinal, born at Mondovì in 1609 and deceased in 1674.—Introduction to the ancient Mass, CXXXVIII, 1301.

GERVASIUS (N.), first a missionary among the Indians; after returning from there, he became provost of the Church of Tours around 1718, where he composed in French a work entitled *History of Boethius, with an Analysis of All His Works, Notes, and Theological Dissertations*, LXIV, 1411.

Preface, 1413. History of Boethius, Book I, 1415; Book II, 1447. Analysis of Boethius’s works: the book *On the Two Natures of Christ*, 1511. Likewise, the book considering whether Father and Son can be affirmed substantially of divinity, 1517. Likewise, the treatise on the Trinity, ibid. Analysis of the books *On the Consolation of Philosophy*, 1521. Glareanus’s opinion concerning the author of this work is examined, 1541. Analysis of the book *On Arithmetic*, 1543. Dissertation on the year in which Boethius died, 1555. Dissertation on these words of Gundobad to Saint Avitus, Bishop of Vienne: “Grant me in particular the anointing of chrism,” 1559. First part: by these words King Gundobad was requesting neither baptism nor confirmation, ibid. Those are refuted who maintain that Arians were at times reconciled to the Church through the sacrament of confirmation, 1566. Third part: Gundobad asked for nothing other than the imposition of penance, which was also administered by anointing, 1571.—Elucidations concerning Faustus, Bishop of Riez, and his doctrine, 1573. Letter of Faustus to Lucidus the priest, 1575. Letter of Lucidus to Faustus, 1579.—Elucidation, 1587.

GHISELBERTUS (Godfrey), at Antwerp in 1659 published the works of Adam the Scot, a Canon Regular of the Premonstratensian Order.

Preface to the reader, CXCVIII, 11. Eulogy of the author and his principal deeds, 11 and following. On the editorial undertaking, 15 and 16.—Prolegomena: On the life of Adam the Scot, 19. When he lived, 23. His name, surname, and homeland, 25. He embraced the religious life, 28. The order and discipline of the Premonstratensians, 34. On the studies in which he excelled, 38. His devotion and holiness, 41. Catalogue of Adam’s works, 46. By whom he was celebrated, 49. His death, 61.

GIBBONUS (Richard), theologian of the Society of Jesus, at Antwerp in 1613 published the works of Blessed Amadeus, Bishop of Lausanne.—Preface, CLXXXVIII, 1303.

GILBERT OF POITIERS. Distinguished theologian and philosopher, Bishop of Poitiers, born at Poitiers in 1070 and died in 1154. He composed commentaries on Boethius.

His commentaries on Boethius’s book *On the Trinity*, LXIV, 1255 and following. Commentary on Boethius’s book on the predication of the three persons in the Trinity, 1302. Likewise on the book *How Substances Are Good*, 1313.—His commentaries on the book *On the Two Natures and One Person of Christ*, 1353 and following.

GILLESIUS (J. A.), Doctor of Oxford, in 1844 edited the letters of Saint Boniface of Mainz.

Preface, LXXXIX, 681. Alphabetical arrangement of the letters, 683. New arrangement compared with the old, 686. Notes, 689 and passim.—With Dr. Smith he edited at Oxford the works of the Venerable Bede.—Reader’s notice on the book *On the Reckoning of Time*, XC, 291. Notes on Homily 22, XCIV, 249.—He published in 1845 the life and various documents relating to Saint Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, together with his letters.—Double dedicatory letter, CXC, L.—Preface: surveys of various studies concerning the life and deeds of Blessed Thomas, ibid. On his letters, XVIII. Historical documents [Col. 0353] concerning Saint Thomas of Canterbury. The dispute between the bishops of Canterbury and London, CXC, 371. Chapters of the Council of Tours, 390.—Conference between the cardinals and the archbishop, 394. The dispute between the King and Thomas, 395. On oaths publicly made in England against the Roman Church, 402. Revocation of the articles of the English Church, 406. On the translation of Saint Thomas, 407. On the promise of Blessed Thomas the martyr, 426.—Giles’s Preface to the writings of Gilbert Foliot, Abbot of Gloucester, CXC, 739.—Catalogue of kings and popes named in Gilbert’s letters, 743.—His Preface to the surviving works of Herbert of Bosham, confidential clerk to Saint Thomas of Canterbury, 1070.—Preface to the works of John of Salisbury, CXCIX, XIX.—Edition of the works of Arnulf of Lisieux, Oxford, 1844. Dedicatory letter, CCI, 15.—Preface, ibid.—Notes and variant readings, 21 and following.—Observations on editions of the works of the Venerable Peter of Blois, CCVII, XXIII.

GLAREANUS (Henricus Loritus), learned philologist, born at Glarus in Switzerland in 1488 and died in 1563.

Dedicatory preface to the works of Severinus Boethius, LXIII, 537. Boethius wrongly judged by some, 539. On his various writings, ibid. Why no mention of Christ occurs anywhere in his treatise *On the Consolation of Philosophy*, ibid. Whether that work is truly Boethius’s, 541. On the various editions already examined, ibid.

GLOSSA, by an uncertain author.—What is meant by the name “Gloss,” XC, 187. Its glosses and scholia on Bede, 187 passim.—Recapitulation of the Gloss on the book *On the Reckoning of Time*, 304 and following. Gloss on the book *On Speech*, 686 and passim.

GOLDASTUS OF HEIMINSFELD (Melchior), Swiss historian, born at St. Gall in 1576 and deceased in 1635.—Notes, with a preface, on the poems of Saint Columbanus, LXXX, 295.

GONZALEZIUS (Francisco Antonio), prefect of the public library of Madrid, 1821. He published a new edition of the Spanish collection of canons.

Preface to the reader: who labored on this undertaking, LXXXIV, 9. Whence the collections arose, ibid. That this is the earlier collection in Spain, 11. On the collection of Isidore Mercator, ibid. That Isidore is fictitious, 13. Spain’s most scrupulous observance of canons, ibid. The study of antiquities in preceding centuries, 15. Arrangement of the articles, ibid. Review of the book, 18 and 19. On the manuscripts, 22.

GOTHOFREDUS, Jacobus (Godefroy), Genevan jurist and philologist, 1587–1652.

His critical notes elucidating the ancient monuments pertaining to Donatist history, XI, 1179. His commentary on the law of Emperor Honorius imposing monetary fines on Donatists, 1419.

GRANDIDIER (Philippe André), archaeologist and historiographer, born at Strasbourg in 1732 and deceased in 1787. He edited, with notes, the municipal laws of Erkembald through the favor of the city of Strasbourg, CXXXVII, 583 and following.

GRANDIUS (Guido), Camaldolese monk, born at Cremona in 1671 and deceased in 1742.

Dissertation *On the Camaldolese Character of the Institution of Saint Peter Damian and the Avellanites*, CXLIV, 17. Aim, subject, and occasion of writing, ibid. Origin of the Avellanite hermitage, 21. Comparison of the Avellanite and Camaldolese institutions, 27. Other points of agreement, 34. Likewise, a new affinity between them, 44. Damian among the disciples of Saint Romuald, 50. The principal arguments of Laderchi are refuted, 62. Some of Laderchi’s criticisms of Peter Damian, 79.

GRANJON (Robert), skilled printer and punch-cutter of type, who himself published at Lyons around 1558 the works of Walter of Châtillon, as is established by the royal privilege, an official instrument, CCIX, 460. Testimony concerning him by Father Dom Coustant, 462.

GRAVIUS (Father Henry), learned bibliophile, deceased at Nijmegen in 1552.

Notice on Wolbero, Abbot of Saint Pantaleon at Cologne, CXCV, 1001.—Dedicatory letter concerning the edition of Wolbero’s *Commentary on the Song of Songs*, ibid.—Reader’s notice, 1006.

GREMAUD (J.), in the publication entitled *Mémorial de Fribourg*, in 1854 supplied a notice on Blessed Amadeus, Bishop of Lausanne, CLXXXVIII, 1277. Notes on the same notice, ibid.

GRETSERUS (Jacob), learned German controversialist, born at Markdorf in 1561 and died in 1625. He edited the Carolingian Codex.

Preface: On the letters of the holy pontiffs belonging to this codex, XCVIII, 45. A charge by Baronius refuted, ibid. Letters previously lacking and sought by Baronius are supplied, 47. Devices of the Centuriators, 47, 48.—Reader’s notice on the fragment by Adelbold, Bishop of Utrecht, [Col. 0354] *On the Deeds of Emperor Saint Henry*, CXL, 87.—Apology for Saint Gregory against the sectarians, CXLVIII, 190.
