The hatred of modern innovators toward Roman pontiffs, ibid. Whom they imitate, 192. Traces and specimens of their calumnies, 198. They attacked some holy pontiffs with special severity, 198; among them Gregory VII, ibid. Bellarmine vigorously vindicated him, 199. Other testimonies by various persons concerning Saint Gregory, 201 and following.—Preface to Paul of Bernried’s book on the deeds of Saint Gregory VII, pope, 219.—Fragment of a dissertation on the Council of Worms against Gregory VII, 229.—Another fragment of a dissertation on the oath that Henry IV rendered to Gregory VII, 231.—Reader’s notice concerning the author of certain little works, CXLVIII, 1057.—Reader’s notice on the brief commentary of Hesso the scholastic, CLXIII, 1082.

GRIALIUS (J.), Spaniard, most distinguished man, at Madrid in 1599. He edited the works of Saint Isidore of Seville, furnished with notes, scholia, and observations, LXXXI, 214.

Dedication to Philip III, LXXXII, 11. Preface to the reader, 13. What was accomplished in this edition for each of Saint Isidore’s books, 14 and following. Notes on the *Life of Saint Isidore* written by a Canon Regular, 19 and following. Introduction to the books of the *Etymologies*.—Notes on those same books, 73 and following.—Notes on various books of Saint Isidore, LXXXIII, 9 and passim among Arevalo’s notes.

GUÉRANGER (Dom), Superior General of the Benedictines of Solesmes, author of *Liturgical Institutions*.

Dissertation on the Office of Saint Gregory VII: a Benedictine defended by a Benedictine, 234. Gregory was great in life, greater after death, 235. Opinion of contemporary historians, 236. Certain Catholics led astray, 238. The veneration of the people of Salerno for Gregory, 240. Pontiffs who proceeded toward his canonization, 242. Disputes between the Roman Curia and the Gallicans, 245 and following. What should be thought of the legend of Saint Gregory VII, pope, 248. How it was received in France, 250. What the Bishop of Auxerre did, 251 and following. The order of this bishop is condemned at Rome, 258. Likewise condemned were the orders of other bishops that rejected the reading concerning Saint Gregory, 259, 260. The Bishop of Auxerre is censured by a Gallican cleric, 265. Some subscribe to a letter favorable to the king, 267. What the Bishop of Nîmes publicly declared before the king, 268. How the cult of Saint Gregory was attacked in other regions, 270. But at last the memory of this saint is vigorously vindicated by the illustrious de Bonald, now cardinal and Archbishop of Lyons, in his pastoral letter of 4 March 1838; see its words at 277.

GUERARDUS (Dom R.), Benedictine of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, born at Rouen in 1641 and deceased in 1715.

Historical notice on Folquin, monk of Saint-Bertin, CXXXVI, 1181.—Notice on Pope Gregory VI, CXLII, 570.—Reader’s notice on the ancient Agano, CLV, 179.

GUIBERTUS, a native of Tournai and of the Order of Friars Minor, composed the life of Saint Eleutherius, Bishop of Tournai.

Prologue, XV, 59. Legendary origin of the city of Tournai, 61. Birth, education, exile, and episcopate of Saint Eleutherius, 63. A dead woman raised by Saint Eleutherius, 66. Saint Eleutherius’s journeys to Rome, 69. His final illness, death, and miracles, 72. Elevation of his body, 76. Through his aid the imprisoned Fereolus is released, 78. Translation of Saint Eleutherius’s body to the city of Tournai, 82.

GUIGNARD (Philippe), archivist and librarian of the city of Dijon, 1855. Letter to M. de Montalembert, nobleman and member of the Paris Academy, concerning the relics of Saints Bernard and Malachy, abbots of Clairvaux monastery, and concerning the true location of the former monastery, CLXXXV, 1662. Heads of Saint Bernard and Saint Malachy preserved in the church at Troyes, 1663. Their bodies formerly lay in the church at Clairvaux, 1667. What became of them in 1793, 1684. Investigations into the former site of the Abbey, 1698.—Appendix, 1714. On the image of Saint Bernard, 1743. His seal, 1746.

GUSSANVILLAEUS (Peter), most learned priest of Chartres, edited at Paris in 1675 the corrected and annotated works of Saint Gregory the Great.

Defense of Saint Gregory’s *Dialogues*, LXXVII, 120. How and on what grounds these books were denied to Saint Gregory by some, 129. What should be noted, ibid. On Tajo, Bishop of Zaragoza, ibid. What Hildefonsus, Julian, Bede, Paul the Deacon, Anastasius, Paschasius Radbertus, Lanfranc, Anselm, etc. thought, 131. On a style and method of writing consonant with Saint Gregory, 133. Agreement of doctrine, 155. The four books of the *Dialogues* must be attributed to no one other than Saint Gregory, 137.—Preface to the Antiphonary [Col. 0355] ascribed to Saint Gregory, LXXVIII, 639. John the Deacon attributes it to him, but the true author remains shrouded in some obscurity, ibid. Method of chanting, 639. On the difficulty of defining most words that signify ancient practices of the Church with respect to chant, ibid.—Prolegomena to the works of Peter of Blois in the new Paris edition of 1667.—Dedicatory letter, CCVII, 9.—Life of Peter of Blois drawn from his own writings and those of contemporaries, XI.—Preface to the reader, XV.—Catalogues of his works, XVII. (See the article GILLESIUS.)—Notes on the letters of Peter of Blois, CCVII, 1 and following.—Likewise, notes on poems ascribed to him, 1135.

HARDUINUS (Father Jean), most celebrated Jesuit, born at Quimper in 1646 and died in 1729.—Notes on the letters of Pope Saint Hilary, LVIII, 13 and following. Notes on the writings of Pope Gelasius, LIX, 14.

HARDY (Charles Duffus). London, 1840. He edited the *Deeds of the Kings of the English* and the *Modern History* by William of Malmesbury. Preface, CLXXIX, 945.

HARTZHEIMUS (J.), Jesuit bibliographer, born at Cologne in 1694 and died in 1763. Historical notice on Remigius, Bishop of Chur, CII, 1093.

HAVERCAMPUS (Sigebert), most learned philologist, born at Utrecht in 1683 and died at Leiden in 1742 while exercising evangelical ministry at the village of Haringvliet on the island of Overflakkee. He commented with the greatest care and success on Tertullian’s *Apologeticum*, I, 256. The authors on whom he relied and whom he added, 232 and Preface, 61. The praises by which he extols Tertullian, 251. He deserved first place among commentators on the *Apologeticum*. Havercamp’s notes occur passim under the signature HAVER. or HAV.

He edited the works of Paulus Orosius and illustrated them with outstanding notes at Leiden in 1737.—Dedicatory letter to Nicolaus de Griis, ambassador of the King of Denmark, etc.—Preface. What Orosius’s homeland was, XXXI, 637. Investigations concerning this, 638. On the first editors of Paulus Orosius, 639. On his manuscript codices, 640, 641. What should be thought of his little book *On the Freedom of the Will*, 642.—Notes and critical observations placed beneath the text, 663 and following.

HENKIUS (Ludwig Theodor), Doctor of Theology, and LINDENKOHL (Georg Stephan), senior theologian of the Philippian seminary, edited at Marburg in 1851 Peter Abelard’s book *Sic et Non* (“Yes and No”). Preface, CLXXVIII, 1329.

HENRIQUEZIUS (Juan Chrysostom), of the Cistercian Order, born at Madrid in 1595 and died at Louvain in 1632.

*The Great Beginning of the Cistercian Order*. Distinction 1: On the beginnings of the Order, CLXXXV, 995. Distinction 2: On the virtues and miracles of Saint Bernard, 1023. Distinction 3: On certain disciples and brothers of Saint Bernard, 1049. Distinction 4: On certain other monks of this Order, 1095. Distinction 5: Salutary admonitions proved by examples, concerning the danger and punishment of certain vices, 1125. Distinction 6: On the sacrament of the altar and confession, on the souls of the departed, etc., 1177.—Monuments of the holy Abbey of Clairvaux, CLXXXV, 1550.

HENSCHENIUS (Godfrey), hagiographer of the Society of Jesus, born at Venray in 1600 and died in 1681.—Preliminary commentary on Blessed Peter Damian, founder of Holy Cross at Fonte Avellana, CXLIV, 87.

Peter Damian’s writings; edition of his lives; his feast day, 93. His devotion toward Saint Benedict, 96. Earlier acts of Blessed Damian, 100. Schism of Cadalous, the pseudo-pope, 105. Peter as legate to the Florentines and the people of Ravenna, 110.—Notes on the *Life of Blessed Peter Damian* written by John, his disciple, 115 and following.—Notes on the *Life of Saint Anselm of Canterbury*, CLVIII, 49 and following.—Notes on the *Modern History* by Eadmer, monk of Canterbury, CLIX, 359.—Notes on the *Life of Saint Anselm* by Eadmer the monk, CLVIII, 49.

HERALDUS (Desiderius), advocate and philologist, died at Paris in 1579. He was an opponent of Salmasius.

He added notes and annotations to Tertullian, Minucius, and Arnobius, V, 717 and passim. See moreover the edition of 1651, Leiden, V, 363.

HERBORN (Nicholas), of the Order of Friars Minor, Cologne, 1531.—Reader’s notice on Haymo of Halberstadt’s exposition of Isaiah, CXVI, 715.

HERINGIUS (Johann), jurist and syndic of the cathedral church, published the works of Matthew of Vendôme at Bremen in 1642.

Dedicatory letter, CCV, 927.—Variant readings and notes, 933 and following.

HEROLDUS (John), historian and critical scholar, known as Acropolita, born at Hochstadt in 1511 and died in 1581.

Dedication of Eugyppius’s works to Dom Stoer, Abbot of Murbach, LXII, 549.—Life of Eugyppius, 555. His lineage, homeland, and age, ibid. His most devout education, 557. He discusses Augustine’s [Col. 0356] deeds and writings, ibid. He compiles Augustine’s works, 558. On the order of succession, 42.

HEUMANNUS (John), professor at Göttingen, born in the Duchy of Saxe-Weimar in 1681 and died in 1764.

Around 1758 he supplied an appendix to various annotations on the works of Tertullian, I, 63. Then an analysis of the book *On Prescriptions*, ibid. His opinion concerning the status of Minucius Felix, III, 195.—He published an edition of Lactantius’s works, far more complete and corrected than its predecessors, VI, 107.

HEYNIUS (Christian Gottlob), Reader’s notice on the letters of Assaricus and Tusaredus in the *Bibliotheca Anecdotorum*, published at Berlin after his death in 1849, XCIX, 1231.

HIGUERA (Jerónimo Román), of the Society of Jesus, man of letters and scholar, born at Toledo in 1538 and died in 1611.

Prologue to the *Chronicle* of Liutprand, CXXXVI, 965.—Notes on the same *Chronicle*, 967.

LITERARY HISTORY OF FRANCE, a work written in French by the Benedictines of the Congregation of Saint-Maur.—Historical notice on Chlothar II, King of the Franks, LXXX, 447.—Notice on Dagobert I, King of the Franks: his life and deeds, LXXX, 495. His laws and decrees, 497.—Historical notice on Saint Donatus, Bishop of Besançon, LXXXVII, 267.—On Defender, Bishop of Lodeve, LXXXVIII, 595. On Evantius, abbot, 717.—On Hincmar, Archbishop of Rheims, CXXV, 11.—Bibliographical notice on Hincmar: surviving writings, 17. Lost writings, 34. On Hincmar’s talent, learning, and doctrine, and on his manner of writing, 39. On editions of Hincmar’s works, 42.—Historical and bibliographical notice on Hucbald, monk of Saint-Amand, CXXXII, 815. Life of Hucbald, ibid. His writings, 818.—Historical notice on Gunzo, grammarian and deacon of Novara, CXXXVI, 1279.—Investigation into the writings of Gerbert, or Pope Sylvester II, CXXXIX, 63.—Reader’s notice on Saint Abbo’s nineteen-year cycles, 571.—Notice on Rorico, monk of Moissac, 587.—Notice on Aimoin, monk of Fleury, 618.—Notice concerning Saint Bernard Scholasticus of Angers, CXLI, 123.—Notice on Saint Fulbert, Bishop of Chartres, 167. His life, ibid. Writings, 172.—Notice on William V, Duke of Aquitaine, CXLI, 823.—Literary notice on Robert, King of the Franks, 902. Preliminary introduction to Emma, Queen of the English, CXLI, 1374.—Reader’s notice on the book by Garcia, monk of Saint Michael of Cuxa, on the origin of his monastery, 1442.—Introduction to Berno’s poem, CXLII, 1206.—Reader’s notice on Wipo the priest, 1214.—Historical notice on Helgaud, 1263.—On Saint Anselm, monk of Saint-Remi at Rheims, 1410.—Preliminary introduction to the book *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, by Pope Saint Leo IX, CXLIII, 559.—Historical notice on Humbert, cardinal bishop of Silva Candida, 915.—On Adelmann, Bishop of Brescia, 1279.—On Frellandus, Bishop of Senlis, 1370.—On Avergotus, Abbot of Le Mans, 1431. Literary notice on Guy, Bishop of Amiens, CXLVI, 1566.—Reader’s notice on the *Sentences* of Blessed Lanfranc, CL, 637.—Historical notice on William, Abbot of Saint-Arnulf at Metz, CL, 871.—On Theodoric, monk of Saint-Ouen, 1182.—On Gilbert, monk of Elnone, 1433.—On William, monk of Cluny, 1447.—On Radbod, Bishop of Noyon, 1495.—On Fulcoius, subdeacon of Meaux, 1551.—On Valcand, monk in Lorraine, CLI, 583.—Reader’s notice on Raymond Arnald, 659.—Notice on Guigo, General Prior of the Grande Chartreuse: his life, CLIII, 581. Genuine writings, 584. Spurious writings, 590.—On Paul, monk of Saint-Peter at Chartres, CLV, 175.—Notice on Godfrey of Bouillon, CLV, 369. His life, ibid. His writings, 381. Reader’s notice on the letter of Anselm of Ribemont to Manasses, Archbishop of Rheims, concerning the expedition to Jerusalem, 470. Notice on Walter the chancellor, author of the history of the war of Antioch, CLV, 994.—Notice on Radulfus Ardens, 1293. On his writings, 1295.—On Sulcard, monk of Westminster, 1634.—Literary notice on Geoffrey, Abbot of Vendôme: on his letters, CLVII, 11 and following. On his shorter works, 19. On Geoffrey’s sermons, 23. On his other works, ibid. He is vindicated from accusation, 25.—Literary notice on Hugh, Archbishop of Lyons, 409. On his letters, ibid.—On Lietbert, 711.—Literary notice on Blessed Odo, Bishop of Cambrai, CLX, 1043.—On Radulfus Tortarius, monk of Fleury, 1171.—On Lambert, Bishop of Arras, CLXII, 618.—On John the deacon, monk of Saint-Ouen, 1151.—Notice on Anselm, canon of Laon: his life, 1173. Writings, 1180.—Historical and literary notice on Hugh of Saint Mary, CLXIII, 791.—Reader’s notice on works [Col. 0357] falsely attributed to Callixtus II, 1366.—Notice on Hugh of Ribemont, CLXVI, 831.—On John of Mont-Saint-Michel, 853.—On Baldwin, Archbishop of Dol, CLXVI, 1051.—Historical-chronological dissertation *On the Life and Writings of Dom Rupert, Abbot of Deutz*: history of his life, CLXX, 703. His genuine writings, 707. Rupert’s doctrine is examined in each of his books, 708 and following. Writings falsely attributed to Rupert, 800. Editions of his works, 801.—Notice on Honorius of Autun: history of Honorius’s life, CLXXII, 13. His published works, ibid. Unpublished or lost works, 24. His talent, learning, doctrine, and manner of writing, 26.—Historical notice on Gaufredus Grossus, monk of Tiron, 1361.—On Giles, Bishop of Tusculum, CLXXIII, 1385.—On Stephen, Bishop of Paris, 1407.—On Hugh of Saint Victor and his writings, CLXXV, CXXV. His life, ibid. Unpublished works of Hugh, CXXXI. His talent, knowledge, and manner of writing, CXXVI.—Historical-literary notice on Abelard, Abbot of Rhuys, CLXXVIII. History of his life, 9. Abelard’s works already published, 19. His manuscript works, 38. His lost, doubtful, or spurious writings, 42. His doctrine, 43. His talent, learning, and manner of writing, 50. Editions and translations of his works, 51.—Historical-literary notice on Hilary and Berengar, disciples of Abelard, CLXXVIII, 1851.—On Hugh Farsitus, CLXXIX, 1774.—On Arnulf, CLXXIX, 1811.—Historical-literary notice on William, Abbot of Saint-Thierry, CLXXX, 187. History of his life, ibid. His writings, 190.—On Ulger, Bishop of Angers, CLXXX, 1642.—On the Venerable Hervaeus, monk of Bourg-Dieu, CLXXXI, 14. On Aymo, Abbot of Saint Peter at Divion, 1703.—On Herbert the monk, 1719.—On Hugh of Mâcon, first Abbot of Pontigny, 1739.—Notice on Suger, Abbot of Saint-Denis, CLXXXVI, 1163. His life, ibid. Writings, 1173.—Notice on William, monk of Saint-Denis and disciple of Suger, 1467.—Notice on Fastred, third Abbot of Clairvaux, CLXXXVIII, 1658.—On Peter the Venerable, Abbot of Cluny, CLXXXIX, 11. On Wibald, Abbot of Stavelot and Corvey, 1077.—On Peter Lombard, Master of the Sentences, CXCI, 11. His life, ibid. Writings, 13. Manuscript or lost works, 23. His doctrine, learning, talent, and manner of writing, 24. Editions of his works, 26.—Notice on Hugh, Archbishop of Rouen, CXCII, 1118.—On Isaac of Stella, Alcher, and Peter of Roya, monks, CXCIV, 1683 and following.—On Odo of Deuil, Abbot of Saint-Denis, CXCV, 991.—Notice on Joscelin, Archbishop of Tours, CXCVI, 1536.—On Saint Stephen of Muret, CCIV, 998.

HOENELLIUS (Theodore Edward Gustav)—Edited and annotated the writings of Constantine the Great, VIII, 93 and following.

HOFFMANNUS (Benjamin)—Illustrated the history of Dionysius’s cycle with notes and observations, and dedicated it to the magistrates of the Republic of Wrocław, LXVII, 455 and following. Frederick Struntzius also congratulates him, 519.

HOLSTENIUS (Lucas), a Protestant who became Catholic and a canon at Rome, most eager for learning at the beginning of the seventeenth century. He flourished at Leiden.—He illustrated with notes the book *On the Acts of Saints Perpetua and Felicitas*, ascribed to Tertullian, III, 13. What Ruinart thought concerning them, 11.—Critical letter on the spits of Ephesian Diana mentioned by Minucius in chapter 21, III, 365. Documents concerning Pope Symmachus, LXII, 41.

HORSTIUS (Jacob Merlo), learned parish priest of Cologne, born at Horst in 1597 and deceased in 1644.—Exhortation to sectarians, urging that they read Saint Bernard profitably, CLXXXV, 639.

HOYO (Andreas), theologian of Bruges, in 1583 provided corrections and additions to proverbial expressions excerpted from Tertullian by Beatus Rhenanus, I, 209 and following. Pamelius himself had entrusted this task to Hoyo for the Parisian Pamelian edition, Preface, 42.

HUGONINUS (Flavian), licensed priest of the Faculty of Paris and alumnus of the ecclesiastical school of the Carmelites, in 1854 dedicated to the Most Reverend Dom A. Sibour, Archbishop of Paris, his *Investigations concerning Hugh and the Foundation of the Parisian School of Saint Victor*, a work written in French, CLXXV, 1. Introduction, ibid.—Chapter 1. Beginnings of this school under William and Gilduin, ibid. and following.—Chapter 2. Rule of the Canons of Saint Victor, XXIV. Chapter 3. History of Hugh, XL.—Chapter 4. Hugh’s philosophical doctrine; the relations between philosophy and theology, L. Hugh’s method and his mysticism, LXVI.—Studies in the twelfth century. Hugh introduced no innovation; the aim and organization of learning, LXXIII. Hugh’s writings, LXXXII.—Critical observations on the works of Hugh of Saint Victor, XCIX. Critical work already performed on those works, ibid. Each book is considered, C and following. On the author of the book entitled [Col. 0358] *On the Cloister of the Soul*, CXII.—Two ancient catalogues edited by Dom Haureau and illustrated with French notes are presented, CXLII.—Notice on Richard of Saint Victor of Paris, CXCVI, XIV. History of his life, ibid. Richard’s writings, XVIII. Theological works, XXII. Miscellanies, XXVII; manuscript works, XXIX.

ISAEUS (Caesenas) edited in 1616 Lactantius’s works, corrected from the Bologna and twelve Vatican manuscript codices; the notes by which he illustrated them are given separately, VI, 883 and following. See also VII, 14 and passim.

JACKSONIUS (John), English priest and prebendary of Wherwell in Hampshire; through his efforts Novatian’s writings were published and illustrated with notes, as may be seen at III, 886.

JACOBUS OF BOLOGNA: lecture on Severinus Boethius, LXIII, 871.

JANVIER (Dom Ambrose), Benedictine of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, edited at Paris in 1671 the works of Blessed Peter of Celle, afterward Abbot of Saint-Remi at Rheims and finally Bishop of Chartres.—Dedicatory letter, CCII, 397.—Preface on Peter and his writings, 399.

JOHN OF NOYON.—He composed scholia on Venerable Bede’s book *On the Nature of Things*, XC, 188 and passim.—Likewise scholia on the book *On the Reckoning of Time*, 301 and following.—Scholia on the book *On Speech*, 668 and passim.—Scholium on Bede’s book *On the Nineteen-Year Cycles*, 826.

JUNIUS (Francis), born at Bourges in 1589, migrated to Holland, became a minister, and taught theology at Leiden; this skilled philologist labored especially on correcting Tertullian and successfully made highly useful corrections; [the dates as printed are uncertain: “in 1596, died in 1602”]. He is praised in I, 10 and Preface, 43.—He edited at London in 1638 the works of Gilbert Foliot, Bishop of London.—Dedicatory letter, CCII, 1147.

JURETUS (Francis), student of letters and canon of Langres, born at Dijon in 1553 and died in 1626.—Among other works, he supplied notes and observations on Ivo of Chartres, CLXII, 298 and following.

JUSTELLUS (Christopher), scholar, born at Paris in 1580 and died in 1649.—Notes and observations on the codex of canons of the universal Church, LXVII, 93 and following.—Reader’s notice on Cresconius’s abridgment of the canons of Fulgentius Ferrandus, LXXXVIII, 817.

KOLLARIUS KERESTENIUS (Adam Francis de), learned orientalist, born at Tarchoura in Hungary in 1723 and died in 1783, edited *Analecta of Viennese Monuments*.—A Benedictional vindicated for Saint Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 627.

LA BAUME (Jacob). Introduction to Pacatus’s panegyric for Theodosius the Great, XIII, 471. Chronological index of Theodosius’s deeds, ibid. On the author and date of this panegyric, 476. Synopsis of the panegyric, 477. Critical notes on the text, 477 and following.

LABBEUS (Philippe), of the Society of Jesus, born at Bourges in 1607 and died at Paris in 1667. Possessing outstanding learning, he was a most expert chronologist.

The chronicle of an anonymous author attributed to Saint Hippolytus he corrected, and he collected its innumerable variant readings, III, 659 and throughout.---His critical notes, 841.---Prolegomena to the writings of Pope Siricius, XIII, 1115.---In the prolegomena on Pope Saint Anastasius, his life, XX, 51.---In the prolegomena on Pope Innocent I, biographical notice, XX, 457.---Biographical notice on Pope Zosimus, 638.---Notes on the account of the councils held under Gelasius, LIX, 158 and following.---Annotation on the writings of Pope Boniface IV, LXXX, 104.---Reader’s notice on the book *On the Measure of Penances*, attributed to Saint Cumian, LXXXVII, 977. Notes on the same book, 981 and following.---Observation on the Rule of Saint Chrodegang, LXXXIX, 1095. Notes on the confirmation of the privilege, 1121.---Note on the acts of the Roman conference, CII, 971.---Historical notice on Pope Adrian II, with notes, CXXII, 1245 and following.---Notes on the Lives of the Roman pontiffs, CXXVII, 1019 and following.

LA BIGNE (Margarin de), theologian, dean of the Church of Le Mans, born at Bernières in Normandy in 1546, died in 1590. Author of the *Library of the Fathers*.---Notice on Saint Lawrence of Novara, LXVI, 87.---Annotation, 124.---He published the works of Saint Isidore of Seville, illustrated with notes, at Paris in 1680, LXXXI, 209. What he added to that edition, ibid.

LA BOUDERIE (D.), vicar general of the Church of Avignon. At Paris in 1824 he published the book *On Clerical Discipline* by Alphonsus Peter, CLVII, 531. Its author’s life and deeds, 531. Analysis of his dialogues, 532. A rabbi converted through Peter’s book, 533. Old French translations, 534.

LACERDA (J. Lud.), of Toledo, of the Society of Jesus, critic, commentator, and accomplished grammarian. In 1624–1630 he published Tertullian’s works, illustrated with summaries, explanations, and notes [Col. 0359], I, 48. Preface. What judgment should be made of this edition, ibid. That both volumes are rarely found together, even in the fullest libraries, 49. That a rather meagre summary is prefixed to each book, whereas each chapter has a fuller title, and each section is followed by an explanation in which the text is unfolded by paraphrase, 48. We published his notes in our commentary with the author’s signature.

LATINIUS (Latino), born at Viterbo in 1513; died at Rome in 1593. He composed notes and observations on Tertullian’s works; he is cited, I, 10, 40. He assisted Pamelius, ibid., in 1579.

LAURIMANNUS (Cornelius), of Utrecht, published at Lyons in 1672 the works of John Beleth, Parisian theologian.---Preface to the reader, CCII, 9.---A few particulars on the life of John Beleth, from John Trithemius, 14.

LEANDER (D.), author of the Preface to Saint Ambrose and to three of his sermons extracted from the Sessorian manuscript, XVIII, 89. Synopsis: the writings of Saint Ambrose were held in the highest honor, but many had formerly been corrupted by the Maurists, ibid. The Maurist edition is enriched with three sermons taken from the Sessorian codex, 91. Antiquity of that codex, 91. Why these sermons are considered unpublished, 92. Titles and analysis of these sermons, 92. Evidence by which the three sermons are assigned to Saint Ambrose, 94. Authors who used the Sessorian codex, 100. Its contents, 102. Conjectures concerning the age of the Ambrosian sermons and the time at which they were delivered, 107. Their doctrine, 108. The editor’s division and notes, 109. Critical notes appended, 89 and following.

LEBEUF (Jean), canon of Auxerre, celebrated scholar, member of the Academy of Inscriptions, born at Auxerre in 1687, died in 1760. He prefixed a preface to the book *In Praise of the Saints* by Saint Victricius, bishop of Rouen, XX, 437. Similarity of style between Saint Paulinus and Saint Victricius, 439. On the time when the relics of the holy Apostles were brought to Rouen, ibid. On the letters of Theodulus and Eustachius, ibid. On the antiquity of that little book, 440. Who wrote the Life of Saint Victricius, 441. What relics of Saint Victricius exist and where they are, 442.---Notice on the death of Hugh, son of Charlemagne, CXXX, 1205.

LE BRUN-DESMARETTES (Jean), Jansenist liturgical writer, born at Rouen in 1650 and died in 1731. He published the works of Saint Prosper at Paris in 1711, to which he appended a Life compiled from Prosper’s own writings, LI, 17 and 58. Synopsis. Ancient and modern encomia upon Prosper, and the character of his style, 17. Prosper’s youth and conversion, 19. How the calamities of his age stirred him to piety, 21. He attacks the Semipelagians, 23. He defends Augustine’s reputation and his own, 25. He answers Vincent, 28. He goes to Rome with Hilary, 30. He writes against Cassian, 34. On his writings, 36. He writes against the Eutychians, 38. On certain other writings attributed to Prosper, 40.

Dissertation I: On the letters of Saint Paulinus of Nola, LXI. In what year Paulinus’s conversion is to be placed, 744; in the same year he goes to Italy, ibid. Augustine’s Letter 27 to Paulinus, at the beginning of 395. He wrote to Amandus and Delphinus of Bordeaux in 396, 745. Paulina, wife of Pammachius, dies in 397. Cardamas approaches Paulinus in 398, 748. In 404 Victricius, bishop of Rouen, wrote to Paulinus, 751. In 405 he writes to Aper and Amandus, 753; in 406, already a bishop, he writes to Macarius, then to Augustine, 754.

Dissertation II: On Paulinus’s poems.---To Gestidius, about 390, 755. About the same year, the poem on Saint John, ibid. Which works are to be assigned to 393, 756. Poem V on Saint Felix, about 398, and Poem VI on the same saint, about 400, 757. The tenth birthday-poem on Saint Felix, in 403, 758.

Dissertation III: On Saint Sulpicius Severus, disciple of Blessed Martin, 758. Sulpicius is designated bishop of Bourges, LXI, 757. Writers dispute about the name of this Severus, 759. With what reverence the Gallican Church always honored him, ibid. On Alethius, whom Jerome cites when writing to Algasia, 760.

Dissertation IV: On Saint Victricius. History of Saint Victricius, bishop of Rouen, 759. Victricius is made bishop of Rouen, 762. Paulinus writes to Victricius, 763. Likewise Pope Innocent I writes to Victricius, 765.

Dissertation V: On Saint Aper. Life of Saint Aper, bishop of Toul, 767. Aper’s conversion, 758. He is advanced to the priesthood, 760.

Dissertation VI: On the lost, doubtful, and spurious works of Saint Paulinus, 771. On the letter to Marcella, 772.

Dissertation VII: On the captivity of Saint Paulinus. Paulinus gives himself up as a captive for a captive, 775. At what time this captivity occurred, ibid.

[Col. 0360] LEGLAY, highly learned librarian of Cambrai, was compiling a *Christian Cambrai* in 1849.

Notice on Halitgar, bishop of Cambrai, CV, 649.---Historical notice on Gerard, bishop of Cambrai, CXLII, 1267.---Notice on Saint Lietbert, bishop of Cambrai, CXLVI, 1447.---Historical notice on Blessed Odo, bishop of Cambrai, CLX, 1039.

LEIBNITZ (Gottfried Wilhelm), philosopher, mathematician, historian, etc., born at Leipzig in 1646 and died in 1716.

Notice on the Life of Saint Matilda, princess of Italy, by the priest Donizo, CXLVIII, 947.---Notes on the same Life, 949 and following.---Preface to the Introduction to the Collection of Writers Useful for Brunswick History; it treats there of the deeds of the Normans in Calabria and Apulia, CXLIX, 1023.

LENGLET DUFRESNOY (N.), learned priest and philologist, born at Beauvais in 1674 and died in 1755. Author of the Preface to Lactantius, VI, 57. Plan of his new edition of Lactantius, ibid. The nature of Lactantius’s authority, 58. Plan of the *Divine Institutions*, ibid.; why he treated the same matters as Tertullian and Minucius Felix, 59. Where he taught literature, 60. How scholars may investigate these addresses of Lactantius to Constantine, 62. Lactantius in good faith fell into certain errors, ibid. He spoke insufficiently theologically concerning the generation of the divine Word, 64. Jerome’s judgment, ibid. The most learned have always held his books in the highest esteem, 65. Observations for understanding Lactantius’s works, 66. On their editions, 68. On Lactantius’s other minor works, 69. Notice on Lactantius’s life, 75.---Lenglet’s notice on Lactantius’s book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, VII, 157.

LE NOURRY (Nicolas), priest and monk of the Benedictine Congregation of Saint-Maur, born at Dieppe in Normandy in 1647 and died in 1725. He published a dissertation on Tertullian’s *Apology*, notes on its books, and notes on *To Scapula*, in his apparatus for the *Library of the Holy Fathers* in 1715.

Analysis of the *Apology*, I, 705. On the age, title, Greek translation, and style of the *Apology*, 755. On its manuscript codices, editions, scholia, and observations, 756. On the two books *To the Nations*, 765. On the book *To Scapula*, 774. New observations on these books, 781.

Dissertation on Cyprian’s books *To Demetrianus* and *On the Vanity of Idols*.---Chapter 1: On the book *To Demetrianus*. Chapter 2: On its subject, date, manuscript codices, editions, and certain persons’ notes, IV, 983. Chapter 3: New observations on this book, 991. Chapter 4: Cyprian’s arguments by which he refutes Demetrianus are examined, 1000. Chapter 5: On Cyprian’s book *On the Vanity of Idols*, 1011. Chapter 6: New observations on this book.

Dissertation on Arnobius’s seven books *Against the Nations*. Analysis of the whole work, V, 365. On the author and date of these books, 390. Observations on the same books, 405. The character of Arnobius’s arguments, 416. Arguments of the pagans, 420; the Gentiles’ argument from public calamities, 434. The arguments for the Christian religion advanced by Arnobius are examined, 451. On the distinguished men cited by Arnobius, 667.---He added certain annotations on Arnobius, 668 and throughout.

Dissertation on Lactantius’s book *On the Wrath of God*, VII, 147. Analysis of this book, ibid. On its subject, title, author, and date, 153. On the occasion upon which Lactantius wrote this book, 155.---Dissertation on the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, attributed to Lactantius, VII, 839. Preliminary notice, ibid. Analysis of this book, 840. On the manuscript codex, 848. On the title and subject of this book, 850. Why Lactantius wrote it, 851. On the book’s author, 853. Various arguments, 855. Other arguments, 859 and 865. On Donatus, to whom the book is dedicated, 868. On the various editions, 871. On the notes and observations of various scholars, 872. New observations on the same book, 875. What Caecilius related concerning Christian morals and certain doctrines is examined, 882. On the first persecutors of the Church and their deaths, 893. On other persecutors of the Church, 904. On the last, especially Diocletian, 908. On Diocletian’s wife Prisca and his daughter Valeria, 935. On Emperor Maximian Herculius, 942. On Maxentius, 948.

Dissertation on Minucius Felix’s *Octavius*, III, 371.---Analysis of this book; who its author was, and who Caecilius and Octavius were, introduced in it as disputants, ibid. On the age, style, title, subject, divisions, manuscript codices, and editions of this book; on various scholars’ observations on it; on corrupt passages; and on what Minucius drew from others and others from him, III, 386. New annotations on Minucius Felix’s book; first, the arguments by which Caecilius denies God’s existence and Octavius proves it are examined, 409. On a certain book which Minucius seems to have promised to write, and on [Col. 0361] certain obscure passages, several writers, and atheists mentioned by him, 645.

Dissertation on the seven books of the *Divine Institutions*. Chapter 1: Analysis of the seven books, VI, 825. Chapter 2: On their author and title, 858. Chapter 3: At what time Lactantius wrote them, 868.

LEONTORIUS (F. Conrad), of Maulbronn, published at Basel in 1507 the works of Gunther, Cistercian monk.---Preface to the reader, CCXII, 97.

LEPAIGE. Author of a library of the Premonstratensian Order, at Paris in 1633.---Life of Philip, abbot of the monastery of Good Hope, CCIII, VI.

LESLEUS (Alexander), of the Society of Jesus, antiquarian, born in the county of Aberdeen in 1694 and died in 1758; he published the Mozarabic Liturgy according to the Rule of Saint Isidore, adorned with notes and elucidations.

Preface on the Mozarabic Missal published by Cardinal Ximenes, LXXXV, 9. Plan of the new edition, ibid. On the first part of the Mozarabic Missal, 11. How Ximenes entrusted Alfonso Ortiz with the care of his edition, 12. On the Missal’s title, 13. Its constituent parts, 14. The second part of the Missal, concerning the Proper of Saints, the Common, and votive and funeral Masses, 17 and following. Whether the ancient Mozarabic Missal is a sacramentary, 20. Whether the liturgy of the Mozarabic Missal is Gothic-Hispanic, 20. Whether it is the same as the Gallican liturgy, 24. Certain difficulties are answered, 26. Reply to those who say that the liturgy of Ximenes’s Missal is corrupt, 29. Whether the Mozarabic Missal is free from the errors of Felix and Elipandus, 41. Whether the liturgy of Ximenes’s Missal is apostolic, 46. Whether the earliest Spanish liturgy was the same as the Roman, 48. Whether Saint Leander is to be regarded as the author of this liturgy, 49. Whether Saint Isidore is, 61. Whether it has been in use in Spain since the age of the Apostles, 63. Whether the Roman liturgy was adopted in the Church of Braga from the time of the First Council of Braga, 73. On the origin of the earliest Gallican liturgy, 78. Inquiry into the author of the Mozarabic Missal, 82. Comparison of that Missal with Gallican books, 86.---Critical notes, 103 and following.

LESTOCQ (Nicolas de), doctor and fellow of the Sorbonne, dean and vicar general of Amiens Cathedral, abbot of Saint-Acheul. Author of an investigation into the author of the book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, VII, 157. Opinion of Baluze and Dom Le Nourry, 159. Opinion of Saint Jerome, 160. Lactantius is shown to be the author of *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, 162. This is demonstrated by the style, ibid., and by the similarity of its text to that of Lactantius’s other books, ibid. Another argument in support of this assertion, 169. What is to be thought of Dom Le Nourry’s argument, ibid.---Also his, as we believe, is the Appendix on two passages in which the edition of Father Le Nourry has a changed reading, VII, 171.

LETTENHOVE KERVYN, in 1853 presented to the Royal Academy of Brussels *Studies and Investigations into the Deeds of the Cistercians and the Count of Flanders, on the Occasion of the Conflict between Boniface VIII and Philip the Fair*, CLXXXXV, 1854. Proposals made to the king of England by the count of Flanders, 1853.

LEVISIUS Eugenius (Eugène de Lévis).

Notice on the *Confession of the Trinity* of Saint Eusebius of Vercelli, first published by him, XII, 953.---Preliminary investigation concerning Eusebius of Vercelli’s exposition of faith, or the author of this Creed, 955.---Textual notes, 959 and following.

LEYSERUS (Polycarp), theologian of the Augsburg Confession, born at Winnenden in 1552 and died in 1601, author of the *History of Medieval Poets and Poems*.---Notice on Henry of Settimello, CCIV, 841.---Notice on Peter of Riga, CCXII, 13.

LINDENBROGIUS (Friedrich), learned philologist, born at Hamburg in 1573 and died in 1616. He published the works of Paul the Deacon with explanatory material.---Preface, XCV, 431.---Marked notes on the *History of the Lombards*, 433 and throughout.

LINDNERIUS (Johann Gottlieb).

He published Minucius Felix’s *Octavius*, illustrated with notes and observations, in 1760, III, LXXXV. Preface with logical analysis, III, 225 and following. Textual notes, 234, 235, and throughout.

LIRONIUS (Jean), Benedictine of Saint-Maur, exceptionally learned, born at Chartres in 1665 and died in 1748. He wrote a dissertation in French on Victor of Vita and composed his life. Why that author’s life has hitherto been unknown, LVIII, 151. The state of the question is set out, 153. He was not a bishop before 487. Victor the historian is not identical with the person of whom the African notice is given, 162. He was never exiled by Huneric, 162. Agreement between the notice and the manuscripts with Vandal history presupposes two bishops of Vita, 165. On certain fictitious *Acts* attributed to him, 167.---Life of Victor, bishop of Vita in Africa, LVIII, 169. His origin, ibid. Priest of Carthage, 170. Edict of King Huneric demanded by the Arian bishops, 171. Victor’s council, ibid. First signs of persecution, 172. Huneric seeks an occasion for persecution, 173; he sends 4,963 bishops, priests, or deacons into exile, ibid., and puts them to death by various tortures, 174. Victor’s piety, ibid. A new edict of Huneric, 175. The African bishops are summoned to Carthage, 176. They suffer diverse wrongs, ibid. Huneric dies miserably and the persecution is calmed, ibid. Victor, witness of all these events, wrote the history, 177.

LORENZANA (Francisco Antonio), cardinal and archbishop of Toledo, born at León in 1722 and died in 1804. He published the Mozarabic Liturgy.---Preface to the reader, LXXXVI, 9. On Ximenes’s labors in restoring the monuments of the Mozarabic Liturgy, ibid.; on the various titles of this liturgy, 10. Ximenes did not thereby detract from the Roman liturgy, 11. Those who later imitated him, 12. What is to be said concerning Psalm 151. This liturgy in many places adheres to the ancient Italian version of Scripture, 15. On the relations of Saints Leander and Isidore with Saint Gregory the Great, ibid. On the antiquity of the Gothic-Hispanic liturgy, 16. On Gothic manuscript codices, 17. On the ancient condition of the Spanish Church, 18. On the doctrine of the celebrated Hosius of Córdoba, 19. All the essential parts of the liturgy are found in the Mozarabic text, 23. On the conformity of the Mozarabic Breviary with the Roman, 24. On the spelling of certain words, 25. On the distribution of the Hours, 26. On chant, 28. The Roman Church itself borrowed many things from the Greeks, 30. Other testimonies of Saint Isidore, 31. Rabanus Maurus borrowed very much from the Gothic office, 32. The manner of chanting, 33. Objections raised, ibid. Four rules are established, 34. Gothic calendar, 73. Rule of the office, 44.---Life of Saint Eugenius III, bishop of Toledo, LXXXVII, 353. Lorenzana published the works of Saint Ildefonsus of Toledo. Notice on the Life of Saint Ildefonsus, bishop of Toledo, XVI, 41. Notice on Saint Ildefonsus’s book *On the Perpetual Virginity of the Mother of God*, 51. Notes and variant readings on the same book, 53 and following.---Notice on the minor works *On the Knowledge of Baptism*, 109. Notes, 117 and throughout.---Notice on certain letters of Saint Ildefonsus, 191.---Notice on doubtful works, 205.---Notes by various scholars on the book *On the Virgin’s Childbirth*, 207 and following.---Doubtful sermons of Saint Ildefonsus: notice, 235. Notes by various scholars, throughout. Short preface to the Continuation of Saint Isidore’s Chronicles, 317. Notice on the Life of Saint Julian written by Felix, 443. Commendatory notes on the same Life, 415 and following.---Notice on the treatise *On the Future Age*, 451.---Notice on Saint Julian’s book *On the Three Chapters*, 525. Likewise on the book *On the Demonstration of the Sixth Age*, 535. Notice on the alphabetical index of apparently conflicting passages, 585.---Notice on the commentary on the prophet Nahum, 703. Notice on the *History of Paul’s Rebellion against Wamba, King of the Goths*, 759.---Notice on works spuriously attributed to Saint Julian, 809.---Notice on the new edition of the works of Saint Eulogius, archbishop of Toledo, CXV, 703; notes, 705 and following.---Notice on the translation of the holy martyrs George, Aurelius, and Natalia, 939.

THE THEOLOGIANS OF LOUVAIN. They censured two letters falsely attributed to Saint Augustine, XXXIII, 1120.---Notice on Saint Augustine’s book *On Predestination*, XLIV, 946. Several letters are supplied, 947, 953.

LOYAUTE (D.), of the supreme court of the Parliament of Paris.---He supplied notes on the deeds of the bishops of Le Mans, CLXXI, 102 and following.

LUCHIUS (Michael Angelo), first a Benedictine monk and later cardinal, most learned philologist, born at Brescia in 1744 and died in 1802.---He produced a new edition of Fortunatus’s works.

Preface: occasion of this edition, LXXXVIII, 9. Plan of the work and editorial labor, 13. Order of the writings, ibid. Why he did not insert Broverius’s notes, 15. What works of Fortunatus have been lost, ibid. On his learning and talent, 18.---Life of Venantius Fortunatus, bishop of Poitiers, 19. Discussion of his name, 21. On his father and birthplace, 22. On the location of the castle of Duplavil, 23. He is admitted into the monastery of Aquileia, 24. He goes to Ravenna for study, 26. He suffers from his eyes, 27. In what year he came into Gaul, 28. Why the journey is to be dated to 567, 30. Sigebert receives him, 32. On the conflicts stirred up by Fredegund, 33, 34. Fortunatus becomes bishop of Poitiers, 34. Queen Radegund’s regard for Fortunatus, 36. On Fortunatus’s poems, 42. Whether Radegund embraced monastic life, 15. On Fortunatus’s fame, holiness, and learning, 48. What others thought of him, 51.---Annotation on Fortunatus’s text, LXXXVIII, 59.---Preliminary notice on the Life of Saint Medard, bishop of Noyon and Tournai, 534. Likewise on the Life of Saint Maurilius, bishop of Angers, 561. On the Acts of the Passion of Saints Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, 573. On Fortunatus’s exposition of the Creed, 583.

LUMPER (P. Gottfried), Benedictine monk of the Imperial [Col. 0363] monastery of Saint George in the Hercynian Forest, formerly prior at Villingen. In 1799 he composed a Life of Tertullian and annotated his writings, I, 66, Preface; 619, Notes. Subject of the book *To Scapula*, I, 697. Preface to the book *On Penance*, 1223. Preface to the book *On Flight in Persecution*, II, 101. Likewise to the book *Against Praxeas*, II, 153, and the book *Against Hermogenes*, 195. Likewise to *Against Marcion*, 248.

The same author wrote prolegomena on the works of Marcus Minucius Felix, III, 193.---Who Minucius Felix was, ibid. What his profession was, 194. Controversy concerning his rank; Heumann is refuted, 195. Arguments advanced to the contrary, and why they prove nothing, 196. That Minucius was brought up in paganism, abandoned it in advanced age, and embraced the Christian faith, 197. Following Plato’s example, he fashioned a dialogue under the title *Octavius*, ibid. Other details of Minucius’s life are uncertain, 198. What is to be said about the book *On Fate*, ibid.

His dissertation on the life and writings of Novatian, Roman priest, III, 861. Chapter 1: History of his life, 861. Chapter 2: Novatian’s writings, 869. Chapter 3: His doctrine, 878.

The same author supplied prolegomena on the anonymous author of the book *On Rebaptism*.---First examined is who the author of this book was, III, 1177. Analysis of the same book, 1179. Certain observations, 1182.---Likewise prolegomena on the anonymous author of the treatise *Against Novatian*, 1203.---Remarks by Dom Lumper on the two dissertations of R. Molkenbuhr concerning Firmilian, 1414.

Prolegomena to Pontius, deacon of Carthage, on the Life of Saint Cyprian.---On Saint Pontius, author of the Life of Saint Cyprian, 1477. Writings of the deacon Pontius, 1479. On the acts appended to Pontius’s history.

His historico-dogmatic dissertation on papal authority, attacked by certain modern writers because of the well-known action of Cyprian and soundly defended by the most learned theologians of France, dated at Avenay, 1740, III, 1273.---Preface, ibid. Brief Life of Saint Stephen, pope and martyr, extracted from ancient monuments, 1283. Appendix defending Saint Stephen’s course of action, 1293. Part I of the dissertation, 1313. According to the universal theology of the French, the question debated between Stephen and Cyprian concerns discipline alone, 1314. That Cyprian well knew this custom alleged by Stephen, 1320. Part II, 1325. Proofs showing that Cyprian knew it as a question of discipline, 1325. Objections answered, 1337. Cyprian knew that the custom defended by Stephen was universal and had been observed from antiquity by all bishops, 1346. Prolegomena on the doubtful, lost, and falsely attributed writings of Saint Cyprian, IV, 803. Article 1: Doubtful works of Saint Cyprian, ibid. Article 2: Works attributed to him, 811. Lost works of Saint Cyprian, 817. Notice on Sixtus II, Roman pontiff, XXIII, V, 79.---On the years of Sixtus II’s pontificate, ibid. When he was crowned with martyrdom, 80. On the sentences of Xystus: whether they are truly his, 82.---Prolegomena on Dionysius, Roman pontiff.---Article 1: History of his life, V, 99. Article 2: On his writings, genuine and spurious, 104. Article 3: His doctrine, 108.---Historical notice on Saint Felix, Roman pontiff.---Felix becomes Roman pontiff in 269, V, 135. When and how long he held office, 137. Whether Saint Felix was a martyr, 138. He receives the encyclical letter written to his predecessor, 139. The judgment of Emperor Aurelian honorable to the Roman See, ibid. Authenticity of the same fragment, 140. Lequien’s contrary opinion, 141. Words of Hypatius, ibid. What the Catholic position is, 142. The Apollinarians are defeated, 143.---Notice on Pope Saint Eutychian, V, 155. Eutychian is made pope in 275; he dies in 283. On Manes and the Manichaean heresy, 157. Whether he was a martyr, ibid. His letters, 158.---Historical notice on Saint Caius, Roman pontiff, V, 179. Caius’s pontificate and death, ibid. Caius’s decretal letter, 180.---Prolegomena on Commodianus of Gaza, V, 189. History of his life, ibid. He is considered African, 191. When he flourished, 192. Gennadius’s opinion, ibid. The opinions of Rigault and Dodwell, 193. On his little book, 195. Value and assessment of the work, 196. On editions of Commodianus, 198. On Antonius, author of the poem *Against the Nations*, 200.---Prolegomena on the life and writings of Saint Victorinus. Synopsis of his life, V, 281. On his genuine writings, 284. On doubtful or spurious works, 289. Observations on his genuine writings and their editions, 295.---Notice on Magnes, priest, V, 343. His life, ibid. His writings, 348. Likewise, notice on Arnobius the African, V, 349. Arnobius, famous rhetorician at Sicca in Africa, 351. Jerome’s testimony, ibid. At what time he composed the work *Against the Nations*, 352. Value of the work, 353. On the principal contents of that work.

LUSCINIUS (Ottomar), doctor of pontifical law, learned philologist, born at Strasbourg in 1497 and died in 1535.

[Col. 0364] Preface on the expositions of the Epistles of Blessed Paul by Haymo, bishop of Halberstadt, CXIX, 359.

LYRAEUS (Nicholas), of the Order of Saint Francis, theologian of the diocese of York, died in 1340.

He wrote a prologue on the interpretation of Holy Scripture in general, CXIII, 25, and another on the author’s intention and method of procedure, 29. A third prologue, however, concerns the moral sense of the Bible, 33. To these are appended the additions of Paul of Santa Maria, CXIII, 35 and following, and the reply of the Franciscan P. Thoring, 59.

MABILLONIUS (Jean), Benedictine of Saint-Maur, one of the truly most learned men of France, born at Saint-Pierremont in 1632 and died in 1707. He came to Paris in 1664. He published the works of Saint Caesarius of Arles and illustrated them with notes.

Preface, LXVII, 1001. Introduction, ibid. Saint Caesarius’s birthplace, parents, clerical life, 1002. His virtue and merit, 1004. He is reluctantly elevated to the episcopate, 1006. Caesarius’s various deeds, 1010. He visited the holy pontiff, 1016. Fervor of his preaching, 1020. Various miracles, 1025. Other miracles, 1035.---Dedicatory letter in the edition of the book *On the Gallican Liturgy*, LXXII, 99, 101.---Preface: the Gallican liturgy gave place to the Roman from Charlemagne’s time, 102. The oblivion into which the Gallican liturgy fell under Charles the Bald, ibid. On the conjecture of Matthias Flacius Illyricus, ibid. Synopsis of the three books, 105 and following. Note from the Gothic Missal, 107. What ancient missals represent to us, 109.---Notices on the missals of the Gallican order, 217. On the Luxeuil lectionary, ibid. What Cardinal Bona writes concerning the Gothic Missal, ibid. On the Frankish Missal cited by Jean Morin, ibid. On the third missal which Thomasius calls Gallican, 219. Notes, ibid.—On Pope Valentine, 645.—On Gregory IV, CVI, 841. Notes, ibid.—On Pope Sergius II, 905. Notes, ibid. Historical notice on Freculf, bishop of Lisieux, 916.—Life of Pope Nicholas I, CXIX, 753. Notes on the same, ibid.—Notice on John VIII, CXXVI, 649.—On Pope Marinus I, CXXVI, 965.—On Pope Formosus, CXXIX, 821 ff.—On Pope Stephen VI, 853.—On Pope Romanus, 859.—On Pope John IX, CXXXI, 27.—On Pope Benedict IV, 39.—On Christopher, usurper of the Apostolic See, 45.—On Pope John X, 797.—Historical notice on Pope Stephen VIII, 1050.—On Pope Leo VII, 1065.—On Agapetus, CXXXIII, 890.—On Pope John XII, 1011.—On Pope John XIII, CXXXV, 949.—On Pope Benedict VI, 1079.—On Pope John XV, CXXXVII, 825.—On Pope Benedict VIII, CXXXIX, 1577.—On Pope Clement II, CXLII, [Col. 0370] 577.—On Pope Leo IX, CXLIII, 551.—On Pope Victor II, 802.—On Pope Stephen X, 867.—Note and conjectures on the subscriptions of the diplomas and letters of Pope Nicholas VI, 1321. Notice on Pope Alexander II, 1275.—Prefatory notice on Pope Victor III, CXLIX, 918.—Prefatory notice on the book *On Holy Places*, by Fretellus, archdeacon, CLV, 1038. Notice on Pope St Gregory VII from the councils, CXLVIII, 183.—On Paschal II, Roman pontiff, CLXIII, 9.—On Pope Calixtus II, 1073.—On Pope Honorius II, CLXVI, 1213.—On Pope Innocent II, CLXXIX, 23. On Pope Celestine II, 761.—On Pope Lucius II, 819.—On Pope Eugenius III, CLXXX, 1004.—On Pope Anastasius IV, CLXXXVII.

Historical notice on Pope Adrian IV, CLXXXVIII, 1349.—Prefatory notice on the book *On the Divine Works of a Simple Person*, by St Hildegard, CXCVII, 741.—Historical notice on Pope Alexander III, 9.—On Pope Urban III, CCII, 1329.—On Pope Gregory VIII, 1335.—On Pope Clement III, CCIV, 1273.—On Pope Celestine III, CCVI, 833.—On Pope Innocent III, CCXIV, XI.

MARACCIUS (Hippolytus), of the Congregation of Regular Clerics of the Mother of God at Lucca; at Rome in 1652 he edited and annotated the Marian work of V. Adam, abbot of Perseigne.

Dedicatory letter, CCXI, 697.—Preface to the reader, 699.—Notes, 754 ff.—Notes on the fragments, 771.

MARANUS (Dom Prudentius), distinguished theologian of the Benedictine Congregation of St Maur, born at Sézanne in 1683 and died in 1762.

He composed the preface and Life of St Cyprian, IV, 15.—Cyprian’s opinion on the unity and infallibility of the Church, 15. The primacy of the Roman Church always acknowledged by St Cyprian, 23. On his disagreement with St Stephen, 27. He insufficiently understood the position of his opponents, 31. The grounds on which Cyprian defended himself, 35. The sacrament of penance demonstrated from the testimonies of St Cyprian, 39. Whether, in Africa before St Cyprian, communion after penance was denied for the gravest crimes, 47. Whether a new discipline was introduced under St Cyprian, 51. Whether Cyprian denied penance to the lapsed at the point of death, 55. What the Council of Carthage did concerning relapsed persons, 59. On Christ’s presence in the Eucharist, 62. On communion under both kinds, 66. Cyprian’s opinion on sacrifice and purgatory, 67. On Christ’s divinity and grace, 71.

On Cyprian’s conversion, IV, 77. On his studies and writings up to ordination, 81. He becomes priest and then bishop, 82. On the persecution of Decius, 86. On those who obtained certificates of sacrifice, 89. Cyprian’s withdrawal, 93. The Roman clergy write to Cyprian, 95. His first reply and the thirteen letters preceding the second, 96. Five letters of Cyprian concerning the lapsed, 101. His letter to the clergy on the ordination of Saturus and Optatus, 110. The persecution grows more severe; peace is revealed to Cyprian, 113. The schism of Felicissimus, in 251, 117. Cyprian returns to Carthage; the book *On the Lapsed*, 119. His prudence in the Novatian schism, 123. At what time Novatian was ordained, 128. Order of events in the case of Cornelius, 131. On Cyprian’s deeds and writings before the persecution, 136. The persecution is renewed, 141. Cyprian’s remarkable charity during the calamity of plague, 146. On his writings after the persecution, 149. Disputes concerning baptism, 152. On the Third Council of Carthage, 160. Observations on the controversy over baptism, 164. Confession and martyrdom of St Cyprian, 167. On the books attributed to him, 171.

MARCA (Pierre de), theologian and historian, archbishop of Paris, born in Aquitaine in 1594 and died in 1662.—Dissertation on Vigilius’s decretal letter confirming the Fifth Synod, LXIX, 127. Occasion of this dissertation, ibid. Importance of Vigilius’s letter, 128. Clarification concerning the Three Chapters, 129. Justinian condemns these, ibid. Vigilius criticizes this, 130. How Vigilius was compelled to condemn the Three Chapters, ibid. Justinian’s threats, 131. Vigilius offers an explanation, 132. Baronius’s opinion, 133. What troubled Vigilius, 134. Words of Peter of Antioch, 135. In what year the Fifth Synod ended, ibid. Decree of Vigilius, 137. Nature of this decree, 138. What truth Vigilius attained, 139. The Latin acts, though genuine, are nevertheless truncated, 140–141. The consideration that moved Vigilius in his decree regarding the Three Chapters, 142.—Testimony on the Chronicle attributed to Isidore of Pax Julia, XCVI, 1251.—Prefatory notice on the Truce of God, CLI, 738.

MARIANA (Juan), of the Society of Jesus, theologian and historian, born at Talavera in Spain in 1537; died in 1624.—Historical notice on Gundemar, king of the Goths, XXXI, 179.—Prefatory notice on the Chronicle attributed to Isidore of Pax Julia, XCVI, 1251.

MARLOT (Dom Guillaume), learned Benedictine, prior of St Nicaise at Rheims, born at Rheims in 1596 and died in 1667.—Notice on Arnulf, archbishop of Rheims, CXXXIX, 1539.

MARRERIUS (Dom Martin), of the Order of St Martin of the Fields, Paris, edited the works of St Odo, abbot of Cluny.

Preface, CXXXIII, 105.—Notes on Odo’s Rules concerning the abacus, 807.—On the book *On the Translation of the Relics of St Martin from Burgundy*, 815; and on the testament of William the Pious, 843, and of Dom Berno, abbot, 853.

MARUS (J.-Bapt.), [place and year absent], edited the writings of Peter the Deacon, illustrated with notes.—Dedicatory letter, CLXXIII, 1003.—Preface to the same works, 1005.—Critical notes, 1009 ff.

MARTENIUS (Dom Edmond), of the Benedictine Congregation of St Maur, a most learned man, born at Saint-Jean-de-Losne in Burgundy in 1654 and died in 1739.

Preliminary observation on the poem addressed to Felix, attributed to St Cyprian, IV, 1025. What should be thought of it, 1027.—Notes on the Life of St Benedict, LXVI, 125. Preface to the Rule of St Benedict, LXVI, 205. The esteem in which this Rule has hitherto been held by all, ibid. Method of treating it, ibid. On those who have commented upon this Rule, 206. On Smaragdus, ibid. On Hildemar, 207. Hucbald expounds the same Rule, 207. Edmund Stoughton on St Hildegard; the Cassinese writers Bernard and Nicholas of Fautura, 208. Richard of St Angelo; Peter Bonerius, 209. Anthony of Perugia, Alfonso de Sanvittorez, and others, 211. Assessment of the exposition by Benedict Haeften, 212.—Testimonies of the ancients concerning the Rule of St Benedict, 213.—Notes and variant readings on the Rule, 215 ff.—Commentary on the Rule of St Benedict, 219 ff.—Critical observation on the treatise *On the Monastic Order*, 937.—Critical observation on the Rule of Saints Paul and Stephen, 949.—Likewise on the Rule of St Ferreolus, 959.—On the Rule of the monastery of Tournai, 977.—On the Rule of a certain Father, 987. On the consensual Rule of monks, 993.—Critical observation on the Rule of St Aurelian, bishop of Arles, LXVIII, 385. Likewise on his Rule for virgins, 398.

Introduction to the exposition of the ancient Gallican liturgy by St Germanus, bishop of Paris, LXXII, 83. Who sought to rescue the ancient Gallican liturgy from oblivion, ibid. What usages were distinguished among the Franks before the Roman liturgy was adopted, 85. What doctrines have been confirmed by such an inquiry, 87.—Prefatory notice on the appendix to the works of St Germanus of Paris.—Notes on the Life of St Radegund by Venantius Fortunatus, bishop of Poitiers, LXXII, 651 ff.—Critical observation on the Rule of St Leander, 874. Critical observation on the Rule of St Columbanus, LXXX, 207.—Likewise on the Rule of St Donatus, bishop of Besançon, LXXXVII, 271. Notes on the diplomas of King St Sigebert, 319 ff.—Prefatory notice on the Rule of St Fructuosus, 1098. Critical observation on the Rule called that of the Master, for monks, LXXXVIII, 943. Likewise on the Rule of a certain Father for virgins, 1054.—Preliminary observations on the works of St Boniface of Mainz, 843.—Preliminary introduction to the prayer-book, XCIV, 515.—Preliminary observation on questions concerning the Octateuch written by Wigbod, XCVI, 1102.—Preliminary observation on questions on Daniel by Peter, archdeacon, 1347.—Note on the bishop’s commonitory to priests, 1375.—Preliminary observations on the exposition of the Roman Mass, 1481.

Preface to the edition of the works of Claudius, bishop of Turin, CIV, 619. Notes appended to the preface, ibid.; annotation on the writings, 623 ff.—Preliminary observation on the Commentaries of Rabanus Maurus on the Book of Joshua, CVIII, 999.—Preliminary observation on St Paschasius Radbertus’s book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, CXX, 1255.—Notes on the same book, 1263 ff.—Preliminary observation on St Paschasius’s book *On Faith, Hope, and Charity*, 1387.—Introduction to the Life of St Romanus, bishop, CXXXVIII, 174.—Preliminary introduction to a fragment of Cardinal Humbert, CXLIII, 1211.—Preliminary introduction to the history of the monastery of Hasnon, by Tomellus, monk, CXLVII, 585.

Preliminary introduction to the *Deeds of Tancred*, by Ralph of Caen, his associate, CLV, 490.—Observation on the *History of the Deeds at Jerusalem*, written in verse by Gilo of Paris, 942.—Preliminary introduction to the book *On the Steward of Iniquity* by Blessed Odo, CLX, 1127.—Preliminary introduction to the books of Seher, abbot of Chaumousey, CLXII, 1119.—Preliminary observation on the treatise *On Free Will and Grace*, CLXVI, 1319.—Notes on the letters of Frederick, bishop of Cologne, 1350.—Notice on Adalbert, archbishop of Mainz, CLXXII, 1335.

Observation on the doctrine of Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 67.—Preliminary [Col. 0372] observation on an exposition of the Hexaemeron, 729.—Preliminary observations on Peter Abelard’s *Christian Theology*, 1114.—Preliminary observation on the book of Pope Eugenius III *On Miracles*, CLXXX, 1010.—In the work entitled *Literary Journey of Two Benedictines*, 1717, he supplied a description of the tombs of the monastery of Clairvaux, CLXXXV, 1622.—Preliminary observation on the writings of Joscelin, bishop of Soissons, CLXXXVI, 1479.—Preliminary observation on the Life of Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, CLXXXIX, 15.—Preliminary observations on the letters of Wibald, abbot of Stavelot, 1087.—Preliminary introduction to the Dialogues on theological questions of Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, CXCII, 1138.—Preliminary observation on his treatise *On Memory*, 1299.—Preliminary introduction to the *Eulogy* of John of Cornwall, CXCIX, 1042.—Prefatory notice on the continuation of William of Tyre’s history of the Holy War, composed in French five hundred years ago, CCI, 893.—Historical notice on Pope Lucius III, 1067.—Preliminary observation on the Life of St Stephen, by Gerard, prior of Grandmont, 1005.—Prefatory notice on an anonymous treatise against a Jew, CCXIII, 747.

MARTIANAY (Dom Jean), a most learned Benedictine, born at Saint-Sever in Aquitaine in 1647; died in 1717. Author of a dissertation on the Italian translation of the Gospel according to Matthew, copied from the Corbie and Saint-Germain manuscripts. Preface, XII, 59. This translation bore many names among the ancients, 60. The Vulgate did not have a single author, 61. Its copies were intermingled with many additions, 62. On the chapter-headings prefixed before the text, 63. On the usefulness of this translation, 66.---Life of Saint Jerome, composed principally from his writings, XXII. Saint Jerome’s native country, year, name, and parents, ibid. His learning, 14. He is baptized, 16. He comes to Aquileia and then proceeds to Gaul, 18. He returns to Stridon, 20. He sails for the East, 22. Description of the journey, 24. He writes the Life of Saint Paul the Hermit, 32. Some disturbance concerning him at Antioch, 34. He writes the Dialogue against the Luciferians and is ordained priest by Paulinus, 39. He is consulted at Rome concerning a synod, 46. He instructs several noblewomen by letters, 49. Damasus dies; yielding to calumnies, he leaves Rome, 53. He returns to the East and withdraws to Bethlehem with Paula, 58. Jerome’s manner of life, 63. He composes a commentary on Ecclesiastes, 70. He publishes the Vulgate edition, correcting it from the Septuagint translation, 71. He translates the Old Testament from Hebrew, 77. He writes various letters, 83. He combats Jovinian, 87. On account of Origen he breaks with Rufinus, 92. Their reconciliation is difficult, 101. Rufinus returns to Jerome’s favor, 111. A new quarrel between them, 122. The affair of Theophilus, 133. Jerome answers Rufinus’s books, 141. A dispute arises between Jerome and Augustine, 149. He comments on the Minor Prophets, 157. The capture of Rome and the death of Marcella overwhelm him, 164. He attacks Pelagius while writing on Jeremiah, 169.

Critical and textual notes, 1222.---Critical notes on the Dialogue against the Luciferians, XXIII, 155. Notes on the book On Hebrew Names, XXIII, 771 and throughout.---Preface on Origen’s Lexicon of Hebrew Names, XXIII, 1199. What is to be said especially concerning this offspring of Origen, ibid. Huet’s unproven statement concerning Origen’s skill in the Hebrew language, ibid. It is conjectured that Origen did not observe the order in which these names are now presented, 1202.---Preliminary explanation of the ten names of God, 1270. A second explanation, with notes, 1273.---Critical and textual notes separately collected, on various minor works of Saint Jerome, 1479 ff. Likewise on the commentaries on Isaiah and Jeremiah, XXIV, throughout.

Defense of Jerome’s learning against J. Clericus, XXV, 1577. Notice, ibid. Chapter 1. On the learning of Blessed Jerome and the ignorance of J. Clericus, 1578. On Jerome’s Greek learning, ibid. On his Hebrew learning, 1585. On the integrity and usefulness of the new edition of Saint Jerome’s works, 1590. On J. Clericus’s singular incompetence in the first question, 1592. Annotation, 1598. Index of the remarkable falsehoods and petty conclusions of J. Clericus, 1605.---Notes on Saint Jerome’s Divine Library, XXVIII, 147 and throughout.---Notice on the Appendix to Part I of Saint Jerome’s Library.---Notes on other books translated from Greek, 23 ff. Notice on Jerome’s prefaces to the books of Paralipomenon and to the books of Solomon, XXIX, 399. Likewise, Notice on the collection of variants in Saint Jerome, 875. Variant readings of the manuscripts of the Divine Library, 879 ff.

MARTINIUS DEL CASTILLO (Fr. R. P.), a Franciscan of the Observance from Burgos in Spain, published the works of Saint Peter Chrysologus furnished with notes, Lyons, 1676.---Life of Saint Peter Chrysologus, LII, 27. His native country and the name “Chrysologus,” ibid. His education and election to the bishopric of Ravenna, 30. Various deeds and virtues of Saint Chrysologus, 34. On Chrysologus’s pious death, 37. On the writings of Saint Peter Chrysologus, 40.

MARTIN (Dom Jacques), of the Order of Saint Benedict, born at Fanjeaux in Aquitaine in 1684; died in 1751. He prefixed a preface to the letters of Blessed Augustine, XXXIII, 53. On the Bessel edition, ibid., and on the most accurate and at the same time most ample edition possible, ibid. Wherein the Bessel, or Göttweig, manuscript errs, 54.---Notice on Saint Augustine’s Letter 184 bis, 55. Likewise on Letter 202 bis, ibid. In what year it was written, 57. Who that Optatus was to whom Augustine wrote, 58. The opinion of Dom Dubois, ibid.

MASSON (Jean Papire), historian and geographer, born at Saint-Germain in Liguria in 1544; died in 1611. He published at Paris in 1588 the Proceedings of the Council of Carthage, collated and corrected, XI, 880. His preface is rather brief, 1223.---Preface prefixed to his edition of the works of Saint Agobard, CIV, 15.---On the Life of Agobard, bishop of Lyons, and on his doctrine, 17.---Preface to the book of the recluse Dungal against Claudius of Turin, CV, 457.

MATHOUD (Hugh), a Benedictine monk, published at Paris in 1655 the works of Robert Pullen, cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church.---Dedication, CLXXXVI, 626. Scholiast to the Reader, 529. Testimonies of certain writers concerning Robert Pullen, 633.---Observations on Robert Pullen’s books of Sentences, 1010.---Preface to the reader for the edition of the works of Peter of Poitiers, CCXI, 783. Arguments of the five books of Sentences, 785.

MESLINGER (F.-Joseph), priest of the monastery of Blessed Mary of Stella Maris. He wrote a description of a Cistercian journey, Lucerne, 1667. Notice to the reader, CLXXXV, 1566. Familiar letter on the journey to the general chapter of the holy Cistercian Order, 1569 ff.

MEIBOM (J.-H.), called the Elder, a man of letters and publicist, born at Lüneburg in 1555 and died in 1625.---Historical notice on Hrotsvitha, virgin and nun in Germany, CXXXVII, 939.

MENARD (Claude), historian, born at Angers in 1580; died in 1652. He supplied a preface to the first two books of Saint Augustine’s unfinished work, XLVII, 564.---Remarks on the same work, 566.

MENARD (Nicolas-Hugues), Benedictine of Saint-Maur, born at Paris in 1585; died in 1644. He published, at Paris in 1642, Saint Gregory the Great’s Book of Sacramentaries, illustrated and corrected with notes and various observations.---Preface to the Book of Sacramentaries, on the occasion which led him to annotate and purge this book, LXXVIII, 15. On the very ancient missal of Saint Eligius, ibid. On another manuscript of Rodradus, 17. Division of the book, 18. On the Corbie manuscript, 19. On the Roman Order, 20.---Notes and elucidations, 263 ff.---Prolegomena to the concordance of the Rules of Saint Benedict, CIII, 702. Preface to the reader for this concordance, 703. Notes, 713 ff.---Notes on Halitgar’s penitential, 709 ff.

MERENDA (Anthony), dedicatory letter to Cardinal Lambergh, bishop of Passau, concerning the writings of Pope Saint Damasus.

Notice to the reader, XXII, 109, 111.---On the minor works of Saint Damasus, ibid. Damasus’s family and native country, 112. As deacon, he follows Liberius into exile, 114. By whom he was ordained priest: Baronius’s opinion, 115. Jerome’s testimony concerning Damasus, 118, and Rufinus’s, ibid. An anonymous author, with ignorance and bad faith, slandered the election of Damasus, 120, 121. Observations on the election of Ursinus, 122. Ursinus is condemned to exile by the Emperor Valentinian, 126. How Ursinus’s supporters attempt to stir up the people against Damasus, 127. The letters of Aginatius on Damasus’s cause, 128. Peace having been restored, Damasus administers the Church, 129. The malicious accusation of the aforesaid schismatic author against Pope Damasus, 131. It is refuted, ibid. On the condemnation of Auxentius, 132. On Damasus’s synodal letter, 134. The bishops of Illyricum agree with Damasus, 136. What Baronius’s error is, 138. On Valentinian’s law against wicked clerics and false monks, 140. The Ursinians are recalled from exile, 141. The Amsterdam anonymous writer is refuted, 144. The dispute between Meletius and Paulinus, 146. Marcellus is defended from heresy, ibid. Dorotheus the deacon comes to Rome, 150. Sozomen is examined, 153. Sabinus returns to the West, 154. Damasus sends back letters to Basil, 157. Why these letters displeased Basil, 158. On Athanasius’s death, 161. Basil and others send Dorotheus to Damasus, 162. A synod convened by Damasus, 163. Law 20 of the Theodosian Code, 164. On Vitalis the Apollinarian, 167. Dorotheus considers a third journey to Rome, 171. Simplicianus, ibid. Dorotheus goes to Rome, 172. Damasus and the synod delay in meeting the wishes of the Easterners, 174. On the affair of Meletius, 177. The bad faith of the anonymous writer, 179.

Jerome’s letter on the three hypostases, 180. Whether Jerome regarded Vitalis as Catholic, 185. Gracchus destroys the cave-shrine of Mithras, 187. A certain Roman council, 188. End of the Antiochene schism, 190. Synod of Antioch under Meletius, ibid. On the date of this synod, 192. Acacius comes to Rome, [Col. 0374] 195. Synod under Damasus, 196. On the letter of the Roman council to Gratian, 202. Damasus was nowhere accused of adultery, 208. Damasus declares Maximus’s ordination invalid, 211. Whether he afterwards changed his judgment, 216. On the First Council of Constantinople, 216. On Flavian’s ordination, 221. On the Council of Aquileia, 224. The letter of this council is examined, 227. Damasus prevents the restoration of the Altar of Victory, 233. The celebrated council at Rome, 235. Causes of this council, 236. What was decided, 242. Baronius’s conjectures, 246. The book of Faustinus: on matters relating to Damasus, 249. Whether Faustinus and Marcellinus were Luciferians, 250. Damasus’s letter to the Easterners, 254. On the creed of the Synod of Ephesus attributed to Nicaea, 257. The final year of Damasus’s pontificate, 259. What writings of Damasus exist, 262. Life and acts of Pope Saint Damasus, 266. On the holy martyrs Vitalis and his companions, 267. On the Eusebian sepulchral inscription, 271. On the author of the poem On Uncertain Martyrs, 274.

Disquisition on the acts of Liberius in exile, 281. Contemporary writers, ibid. Testimonies of Hilary, 284.

MERIC CASAUBON. He appended critical notes to the books of Saint Optatus, XI, 386 and throughout.

MERLIN (Charles), of the Society of Jesus in the diocese of Amiens, died at Paris in the College of Louis-le-Grand in 1747. He published in French: *The True Key to the Works of Saint Augustine against the Pelagians*.

Dedicatory letter, XLVII, 883. Part I, 889. Jansenius interpreted Saint Augustine in bad faith, 889. The foundations of Jansenius’s heresy wrongly attributed to Augustine, 901. The key to Augustine supplied by Jansenius is altogether false, 912. Part II. The perfection of righteousness: this is the true key to Saint Augustine’s doctrine, 923. On Pelagian impeccability, 924. What commandments are impossible in Augustine’s sense, 933. On sins arising from invincible ignorance, 942. What freedom we lost through Adam’s sin, 947. What grace we cannot resist and do not possess universally, 958. What kind of grace is commonly denied to us, 965. Part III. Examination of the book entitled *Key to the Works of Saint Augustine against the Pelagians, Recently Discovered at Padua*, XLVII, 967.---Critiques of various writings of Saint Augustine, scattered here and there in Bayle’s *Dictionary*, XLVII, 989. Part I. On the accusation of moral laxity, ibid. Part II. On Bayle’s mad saying, “I have hunted Saint Augustine down again,” that is, “I pursue Augustine anew,” 993. Part III. On Saint Augustine’s judgment concerning Lucretia’s suicide, 1041. Part IV. On the passage because of which Bayle asserted that Saint Augustine was happier than prudent, 1045.

Dissertation On the Nature of the Mosaic Law, 1053. Part I. The state of the question between the apostles and the Jews, 1055. Part II. Between the Fathers and the Manicheans, 1061. Part III. Between Saint Augustine and the Pelagians, 1073. Part IV. Between the defenders of the Council of Trent and modern heretics, 1081. On the end God set before himself in establishing the Old Law, 1083. On the end of the ancient Law with respect to the Israelites, 1088. On the aid of God’s grace under the Old Law, 1093. On the Synagogue precisely as Synagogue, 1104. A parallel between the Manicheans and the Jansenists regarding the Mosaic Law, 1111.---Dedicatory letter to the works of Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 1. Origin of general councils, 3.

MESSINGHAM (Thomas), author of the *Florilegium of the Island of Saints*, Paris, 1624.---Preface to the Treatise on the Purgatory of Saint Patrick, Apostle of the Irish, CLXXX, 974.

METZLER (Jodocus). Observations on Saint Gall, abbot, and his poems, LXXXVII, 35.

MEURSIUS (Johannes), skilled philologist, born at Leiden in 1579; died at Sorø in Denmark in 1639. What he published on Arnobius, V, 360, in the year 1598.

MINGARELLI (Giovanni Luigi), bibliographer, born at Bologna in 1722; died in 1793. Preface to Paulinus’s birthday poems, LXI, 503. Variant readings from various manuscripts, ibid. and following.

MIRAEUS (Aubertus), in 1639 at Antwerp published the works of Gennadius with notes and scholia, LVIII, 1060 ff.---Notes on the form of institution for canons and nuns.

MITA (Dominic), parish priest of Ugutionello, formerly devoted to the study of law and legal practice, long labored to prepare, adorn, and correct an edition of the works of Saint Peter Chrysologus, and finally committed it to print at Bologna in 1643. Preface to the works of Saint Peter Chrysologus, LII, 51. Sequence of editions, ibid. On errors everywhere proliferating, 42. Collation of manuscripts, 43. Furnished with an alphabetical index, ibid.---Life of Saint Peter Chrysologus, whose lineage he wishes to derive from Troy, founded by Greeks, LII, 45. Peter’s birth and baptism, 47. His education, ibid. He is made a levite and deacon, 48. He is raised to the episcopal see of Ravenna by Blessed Sixtus, 49. [Col. 0375] He is soon consecrated, 50. His deeds and character, 51 ff. How great was his eloquence, 53. He attacks the enemies of the faith, 54. His virtues, 56 ff. How he obtained the relics of Saint John the Evangelist, 38. He ordains Saint Projectus bishop in 449. Every Sunday he preaches the word of God, 50. He foreknows his death and dies, 60. Miracles performed by him, 62. His writings consigned to oblivion by the calamity of the times, 63. Reply to objections, 65. Testimonies in favor of Saint Peter Chrysologus, 71.

MOLINA (Juan Ignacio), of the Society of Jesus, man of letters and philologist, born at Talca in Chile in 1740; died at Bologna in 1829. He taught canon law at Louvain.---Observations on the collection of canons of Ivo of Chartres, CLXI, 29 ff.

MOLINET (Claude), regular canon of the Congregation of France, at Paris, 1679, published the works of Stephen, abbot of Sainte-Geneviève at Paris and subsequently bishop of Tournai. Historical notice on the same Stephen, CCXI, 205.---Preface, 303.

MOLKENBUHR (Fr. Marcellus), of the Order of Saint Francis of the Strict Observance, emeritus lecturer in sacred theology and minister of the Province of the Holy Cross in Saxony, wrote two dissertations on Firmilian in 1788, III, 357. Preface, ibid. Synopsis of both dissertations, 1361.

Dissertation 1. On Firmilian’s letter to Saint Cyprian and his other works, ibid. Proposition 1. This letter appears to have been composed by a Latin, ibid. Proposition 2. Saint Firmilian does not appear to have been its author, 1365. Proposition 3. This letter appears to have been written by some African Donatist, 1401. Contrary arguments are offered, 1405. Proposition 4. It is not probable that Saint Firmilian published any books in a public writing, 1408.

Dissertation 2. On the year in which Firmilian died and in which Paul of Samosata was deposed, 1410. Proposition: the Synod of Antioch at which Paul of Samosata was deposed was not held before 277, ibid. Corollary, 1413.

Critical dissertation on the question whether Pope Honorius I was condemned as a heretic by the Sixth General Council in 680. Preface, LXXX, 991. Arguments that Pope Honorius was condemned as a heretic, 997. Authorities in favor of Honorius, 999. The heresy of the Monothelites, ibid. Who and what Honorius was, 1000. During his lifetime he was not accused of heresy, 1001. Honorius’s letter to Sergius, 1002. Cyrus of Alexandria promotes heresy, ibid. Sophronius opposes the Monothelites, 1003. He is sent to Rome by Stephen, ibid. Heraclius’s *Ecthesis* is published, 1005. It is condemned by John IV, ibid. The letter of Honorius objected by the Monothelites is explained by John, ibid. Pyrrhus and Paul are excommunicated, 1009. A sufficiently Catholic confirmation, 1010. A suspect epilogue favors the *Type* of Constans, 1011. Honorius’s second letter, ibid. The emperor’s letter convening the council, 1013. First session of the council, 1016. Pope Honorius is accused of heresy, ibid. Whether the accusation was interpolated, 1017. Third session of the council, 1018. The letters of Pope Vigilius are forged, 1019. The letter of the Latin bishops contains nothing against Honorius, 1022. To which letters the Greeks answered nothing, 1023. Bishop Theodore is openly said to have lied, 1025. Macarius and Stephen are condemned as falsifiers, 1027. The number of letters is increased, 1032. Whether Sophronius’s letter is genuine, 1033. Papers and manuscripts sent by the emperor, 1035. The original letters of Sergius and Honorius, 1040.
