Thirteenth session of the council. Honorius’s first letter is condemned as heretical, 1041. Pope Honorius is condemned as a heretic, ibid. The second letter is found and burned, 1044. Honorius is condemned anew, 1046. The clause concerning Honorius appears interpolated, 1048. Honorius is condemned anew, 1049. From the acts alone it is not proved that Honorius was condemned, 1051. The letter of the Sixth Synod condemning Honorius, ibid. Several letters sent on both sides, 1053 ff. Papebroch’s exception is rejected, 1064. The acts of the Sixth Synod are burned, 1066. Honorius’s condemnation is proved from the Council in Trullo, which is rejected, 1069. When the fable of Honorius was fabricated, 1071. Bede’s testimony, 1076. Corollaries, 1078.

MONTFAUCON (Bernard), the very celebrated Benedictine of Saint-Maur, Hellenist and archaeologist, member of the Academy of Inscriptions, born at Soulatgé in Aquitaine in 1653; died in 1741. Notice in the Appendix to the writings of Lucifer of Cagliari, On His Profession of Faith, XIII, 1041.---Notice on the letter of Henri Clerc to Stephen, CL, 1346.

MORALES (Ambrosio), historiographer of Philip II, born at Córdoba in 1513; died in 1590.---Scholia on the Life of Saint Eulogius, CXV, 725 ff.---Likewise scholia on all the works of Saint Eulogius, 870.---Letter prefixed to the edition of Ambrosio Morales, 911.---Method of chronology from the works of Saint Eulogius, 922.---On the origin, location, and antiquity of the city of Córdoba, 926.

MORCELLI (Stefano Antonio), of the Society of Jesus, archaeologist, born in 1737 at Chiari in Lombardy. He published *African Annals in the Cyprianic Period*.---From the year 243 to 247: Donatus, bishop of Carthage, III, 1417. From 248 to 250: Cyprian, bishop, 1421. In 250, under Bishop Cyprian, the persecution of Decius breaks out, 1424. In 251 Cyprian complains that even the confessors themselves are shamefully corrupted and cannot be governed by the presbyters. In 251 Cyprian restores the lapsed to the faith and issues the book On the Lord’s Prayer, 1440. In 235 persecution of Christians again rages, 1450. In 254, under new consuls, peace is at length granted, 1455. In 255 the dispute of Stephen and Cyprian concerning the baptism of heretics is raised, 1460. In 256 Sixtus occupies the place of Saint Stephen, slain for Christ; Cyprian’s disposition; he publishes the book On Jealousy and Envy, 1464. In 257 persecution revives both at Rome and Carthage, 1468. In 258, under the proconsul Galerius Maximus, Cyprian is recalled; Sixtus is slain at Rome. Three hundred are said to have been sent in chains at Utica; Cyprian pays the debt of faith by glorious martyrdom.

MOREL (Frédéric), called the Elder, distinguished man of letters and most learned printer, published the works of Saint Cyprian at Paris in 1564, with notes and observations, III, preface LXXV.

MOSHEIM (Johann Lorenz von), learned theologian of the Reformed Church, writer and philologist, one of the founders of German literary culture, born at Lübeck in 1694 and died in 1755. Author of the *Inquiry into the Date of Tertullian’s Apologeticus and the Beginning of the Persecution of Severus*, I, 535 and preface 62, in 1724.---The great usefulness of such disputations is shown, I, 537. Two classes of diverse opinions on this subject are established, 539. It is shown by many arguments that the afflictions of Christians began under Severus before he enacted special decrees for that purpose, 540 ff. Dodwell’s subtleties in particular are examined, 546. Those who say that the *Apologeticus* appeared after Severus’s death are refuted, 548. He assigns to the second class those who, though they hold that it was certainly composed before the year 200, nevertheless disagree concerning its precise year, 549. Mosheim’s opinion begins to be set forth: first he shows that it was written under Severus, and then after the disturbances of Albinus, 550. Those disturbances began in 196 and were suppressed in 197, 551. Thus Mosheim decides in favor of 197, confirming this by a notable passage of Tertullian himself, 556. Conclusion, 558.

MÜNTER (Friedrich), bishop of Zealand in Denmark, antiquarian, born at Gotha in 1760; died at Copenhagen in 1830. On the death of Michael Hertz, he took up again Hertz’s labors on the works of Firmicus Maternus.

Prolegomena, XII, 971. Almost no traces of this author survive, 973. The author of the earlier book is a pagan, but that of the later book a Christian, 875. The source from which he drew, 976. Firmicus entirely unknown until the sixteenth century, 978. Title and subject of the book, 980. Its editions, 982. Critical notes placed beneath the text, 983 ff.

MURATORI (Lodovico Antonio), a very learned man, archaeologist, historian, man of letters, and librarian to the Duke of Modena, born at Vignola in that duchy in 1672; died in 1750.

He published prolegomena to Tertullian’s books On Prayer in 1715, to which he added a preface composed by Dom Panciroli of Reggio, I, 1143 and 1145. Both illustrated the same book with notes, 1150, 1152, 1153 and throughout. Muratori is praised, III, 169. His opinion concerning the fragment on the Canon of Scripture by an uncertain author, ibid.---He published and enriched with notes the writings of Commodianus, V, 200, 263 note.---Disquisition on the letter to Dionysius of Alexandria published under the name of Pope Julius. Its synopsis, VIII, 938. Gennadius and the Centuriators wrongly ascribe this letter to Pope Julius I, ibid. Facundus of Hermiane more correctly assigns it to him. It contains nothing worthy of Julius, 841. Leontius of Byzantium does the same with Evagrius, 942. The author of this letter removes the soul from Christ’s body, as does Apollinaris, ibid. Many things condemned by Saint Gregory of Nyssa are likewise taught there, 945. Hypatius, Anastasius, Eulogius, Ephraem, and others vindicate Saint Julius from that calumny, 949. Who Dionysius was, to whom this letter is feigned to have been given, 951. Notice on the same letter, 952.

Likewise, he published the works of Saint Paulinus of Nola with notes and variant readings, adorned with a life of the holy Doctor, again published at Paris in 1685. Printer’s preface to the reader, LXI, 11. Preface to the Paris edition, recounting the various editions, 13.---Life of Saint Paulinus, bishop of Nola, 15. Saint Paulinus’s birth, family, and wealth, ibid. His studies and learning under his teacher Ausonius, 18. He marries Therasia, 21. How he lived in the world, 23. He withdraws to Spain, 25. He dedicates himself to God and sells all his possessions, 29. His humility, 33. Ausonius reproaches Paulinus for being changed, 42. He is ordained priest, 46. He comes to Italy, 49. He settles at Nola, 51. He is tempted, 55. Paulinus’s piety toward the saints, [Col. 0377] 60. Paulinus’s friendship with Sanctus and Amandus, 66. He falls ill, 68. Saint Augustine writes to Paulinus, 69. Paulinus writes to Jerome through Vigilantius, who handles the matter badly, 73. He consoles Pammachius on the death of his wife, 78. He writes an excellent letter to Jovius, 82. The Goths spread terror in Italy, 93. He builds a basilica at the tomb of Saint Felix, 97. He writes letters to many persons, 103, 105, 107, etc. Paulinus is made bishop of Nola, 112. He is invited to the Synod of Ravenna, 118. Paulinus’s illness and death, 120. Eulogies of Saint Paulinus, 125.---Notes and observations on the works of Saint Paulinus, 153 ff. Variant readings, 419.---Notice on the three *Natalicia* of Saint Paulinus, 301.---Preface to Paulinus’s thirteenth *Natalicium*, 567.---Preface to Paulinus’s final poem, 689.---Variant readings, 709.

Dissertations on Saint Paulinus’s poems. Dissertation I, On Turcius Apronianus, LXI, 779. Dissertation II, On Asterius, son of Turcius Apronianus, ibid. Dissertation III, On Avita and Eunomia, 781. Dissertation IV, On Albina. Dissertation V, On Therasia, 783. Dissertation VI, On Pinianus, 785. Dissertation VII, On Melania, 787. Dissertation VIII, On Amilius, 787. Dissertation IX, On Saint Paulinus’s offices and dignities, 791. Dissertation X, Saint Paulinus, consular of Campania, 793. Dissertation XI, On Paulinus’s remaining deeds, 795.

Dissertation XII, On the time when Paulinus assumed the episcopate, 797. Dissertation XIII, On the buildings founded by Paulinus at Nola, ibid. Dissertation XIV, On Saint Felix of Nola, 799. Dissertation XV, On the year in which the bodies of Saints Gervasius and Protasius were found by Saint Ambrose, 801. Dissertation XVI, On Saint Paulinus’s line, 402: “For many things, indeed,” etc. Dissertation XVII, On Paulinus’s line: “A little cell from many,” etc. On the tombs of ancient Christians, 811. Dissertation XVIII, On Saint Paulinus’s twelfth *Natalicium*, concerning vows and votive offerings made by Christians in veneration of the saints, 815. Dissertation XIX, On Saint Paulinus’s thirteenth *Natalicium*. On the birthdays of holy martyrs, 819. Dissertation XX, On Saint Paulinus’s final poem: Saint Paulinus’s view of the elements is considered, 825. Dissertation XXI, On the cross of Nola, 830. Dissertation XXII, A gleaning from the lost works of Saint Paulinus, 831.

Preface to a new edition of the Gallican Sacramentary, LXXII. It is demonstrated that it belongs to the Gallican liturgy, 447. This order is neither Roman nor Mozarabic, 449. In all respects it agrees with the Gothic-Gallican Missal, ibid. It is not easy to determine to what province it belonged, 450.---Explanatory notes, 451 ff.---Preface to the Antiphonary of the monastery of Bangor.---It was once famous in Ireland, LXXII, 579. At what period it was in use, 581.---Origin of ecclesiastical chants and offices, 605.---Preface to the book of Peter the Deacon, On the Illustrious Men of Monte Cassino, CLXXIII, 1003.---Preface to the history of Landulf the Younger of Milan, CLXXIII, 1430.---Preface to the triple life of Pope Innocent II.---Preface to the *Pantheon* of Godfrey of Viterbo, CXCVIII, 872. Notice on Godfrey, ibid. His learning, 873. His writings, 874.---Notice on Sicard, bishop of Cremona, CCXIII, 9.---Preface to Sicard’s chronicle, 437.

Muratori furnished the Gelasian Sacramentary with annotations, 1057 ff.---Dissertation on the Judgments of God, LXXXVII, 953. What these judgments were, ibid. What purgation by the Eucharist was, 955. It was at times approved by certain councils, 956. On the ordeal by cold water, ibid. Blessing of cold water for the detection of theft, 958. Adjuration of the person; adjuration of the water, 958. Adjuration of blessed bread and cheese, 961. Blessing over boiling water, 962. Ordeal of the cross, 965. All these things are to be ascribed to the wretched ignorance of that age, and were condemned by religious and learned men, though far too few. Aventinus wrote against these judgments, 967; so did Agobard of Lyons, ibid.; Pope Stephen V, Ivo of Chartres, John, Ferrandus, etc., ibid.

Annotations on ecclesiastical diplomas of the Lombard kings, 1347 ff.---Censure of the oration of Benedict Crispus, LXXXIX, 366.---Preface to the Lombard history of Paul the Deacon, XCV, 419.---Preface to the miscellaneous histories, XCV, 739. Notes, 743 ff.---Notes on the letters of Paul the Deacon, 1383 ff.---Preface to Ernold’s poem *On the Deeds of Louis the Pious*, CV, 553. Notes, 569 ff.---Preface to the *Pontifical Book of Ravenna* by Agnellus, CVI, 431.---Notice on Pope John VIII, CXXI, 647. Notice on the Computus of a certain anonymous writer, CXXIX, 1273.---Notice on the book of Gezo, abbot of Tortona, *On the Body and Blood of Christ*, CXXXVII, 369. Prolegomena to the history of Landulf, CXLVII, 819. Dissertation on John Peter Puricelli. Whether Saint Ambrose permitted his clergy to marry a virgin once, 970. What Datius and Landulf thought, 970. What those who maintain the affirmative position object, 971. What Bernardino Corio says, 973. His false assertion concerning Saint Ambrose, 974. It is shown that Ambrose thought otherwise, ibid. What he teaches in his letter to the Church of Vercelli, 976. In the commentaries on the letters of Saint Paul, 977. Ambrose did not attend the Council of Constantinople, as Datius invents, 982. How Ambrose is to be understood when he says that perfection lies not in chastity but in charity, 984. What is to be thought of the Councils of Ancyra and Neocaesarea, 986. And what was decided by the Council of Nicaea, 989. Ambrose’s words, 992. What Landulf says concerning married Greeks, 994. The answer made to him, ibid. What Jerome pronounces to Pammachius, 998. What Augustine says, 1000. What Saint John Chrysostom says, 1001.---Preface to Donizo’s poem on the life of Countess Matilda, CXLVIII, 942.

Preface to the Norman poem of William of Apulia on the deeds of the Normans in Sicily, Apulia, etc., CXLIX, 1019.---Preface to the history of Geoffrey Malaterra, Benedictine monk, CXLIX, 1087.

Dissertation on the rhythmic poetry of the ancients, CLI, 755. The Italian language and Italian poetry have the same origin, ibid. Two kinds of poetry, rhythmic and metrical, 757. The character of rhythmic cadence, 760. Orderic Vitalis praises rhythmic verses, 760. Trochaic verses frequently in use, 762. What rules German critics establish, 765. On the periods of barbarian invasions, 769. Fragment of Gaidhald, who appears to have been a parish priest in the city of Vercelli, 776. Various examples, 774 ff., of rhyme derived from rhythm, 777, and of homoeoteleutic, or similarly ending, verse, 779. Verses of Saint Columbanus, 780. Verses of Bede, 781. On alphabetical poetry, 782. Lantfrid’s epitaph, 784. Various examples, 785 ff. On the origin of Italian vernacular poetry, 794. Notice on Lupus Protospatharius, CLV, 119.---Notice on the book of Manegold against Wolfelm of Cologne, 137.

NOESSELT (Johann August), flourished about 1757.---Author of the Dissertation on the True Date and Doctrine of the Surviving Writings of Quintus Septimius Tertullianus, Halle, 1799, I, 63, preface, and 85, note.---On Tertullian’s genius, style, and reputation, I, 89. On his books whose date and orthodoxy are certain, 96. On his books whose date and Montanism are manifest, 122. On Tertullian’s books whose date, doctrine, or both are unknown, 144. Fourth class: books in which only Montanism is evident, 157. For what reason this dissertation was published here, 69, preface.

*NOMASTICON*, or *CISTERCIAN CUSTOMS*, Paris, 1664. Notice on the Charter of Charity, CLXVI, 1378.---Likewise, notice on the more ancient usages of the Cistercian Order, 1383.

NORISIUS (Henricus de), a learned theologian and textual critic, cardinal; born at Verona in 1631, died in 1704.—Observations on St. Augustine’s Letter XLVII, 175, 270. Further observations by the same on Augustine’s letters, 176, 291. Observations on the same letter, 319.—*Augustinian Vindications.* Preface, XLVII, 571. It is shown that St. Augustine’s teaching on predestination and grace is neither difficult nor obscure, 575. Those who charge St. Augustine’s teaching with contradiction are refuted, 588. Modern heretics accuse St. Augustine’s teaching against the Pelagians of excess, 593. The same persons wrongly impute several errors to St. Augustine, 685. They produce the testimonies of thirty-five doctors—popes, cardinals, bishops, and others—against St. Augustine; their reliability is examined, 745. Commendations of Augustinian teaching against the Pelagians, issued by holy popes, are defended against the hostile interpretations of modern writers, 788. Augustine’s teaching, approved by the Apostolic See, is defended against the perverse interpretations of innovators, 806. Those who limit St. Augustine’s authority on the basis of a letter of Pope St. Celestine are refuted, 878. One hundred and thirty-five insults, taunts, and censures of modern writers against St. Augustine are repelled by that holy doctor himself, 831.

ODO (St.), canon of St. Martin’s at Tours; born in 879, died in 942. He wrote the Life of St. Gregory of Tours, LXX, 115. It was annotated by Ruinart; see throughout.

OEFELIUS (Andreas-Felix d’), a learned German, born at Munich in 1706, died in 1780.—Notice concerning the life, deeds, and writings of Bonizo, bishop of Piacenza, CL, 782.

ORELLIUS (Johann Conrad), published the works of Arnobius at Leipzig in 1816, and elucidated them with most learned annotations; see these appended to the text, V, 748 and throughout. He passes over much in the commentaries of Heraldus and Helmenhorst on the same books.

ORSIUS (Joseph Augustine), of the Order of Preachers and cardinal; born at Florence in 1692, died in 1761. He wrote an apologetic dissertation for the orthodoxy of Saints Perpetua, Felicity, and their companions, III, 61.—The orthodoxy of the holy women is defended by external arguments, ibid. Basnage’s external arguments against the holy martyrs are answered, 74. A general response is given to Basnage’s internal arguments against the martyrs, 97. The abundance and richness of visions and other heavenly gifts during the earlier ages of the Church are discussed, 104. Nothing is contained in Perpetua’s revelations that does not suit a Catholic martyr in the highest degree, 122. The virtues of our martyrs and the fruits of their visions show that they were inspired by the divine Spirit and that their revelations must be ascribed to God, 137. It is demonstrated that Perpetua and her fellow martyrs were inspired by the prophetic Spirit, 152.

OUDINUS (Casimir), a most learned bibliographer, formerly of the Premonstratensian Order; born at Mézières in 1638, died in 1717.

Dissertation on the Venerable Bede, priest and monk, XC, 71. On volume I of his works, containing various shorter writings, 73. On volume II: *On the Nature of Things*, *On the Reckoning of Time*, the Chronicle on the Six Ages of the World, etc., 77. On volume III: the *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, etc., 81. On volume IV: the *Hexaemeron* and various explanations of Holy Scripture, 84. Volumes V and VI: expositions on the Gospels, 85. Volume VII: on his homilies, 88. Volume VIII: on doubtful and spurious works, 95. How Bede’s works ought henceforth to be arranged, 98.

Historical and bibliographical notice on Anastasius, Roman abbot, CXXVII, 9.—On John the Italian, Cluniac monk, CXXXIII, 883.—On Æthelwold, bishop of Winchester, CXXXVII, 77.—On Adso, monk of Derve, 597.—Literary notice on St. Abbo, abbot of Fleury, CXXXIX, 415.—On St. Anselm, bishop of Lucca, CXLIX, 435.—On St. Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, CXLI, 163.—On Robert of Tombelaine, abbot of St. Victor, CL, 1360.—On Constantine the African, monk of Monte Cassino, 1559.—On Goscelin, monk of Canterbury, CLV, 9.—On Bruno, 145.—Historical notice on Anselm, scholastic and canon of Laon, CLXII, 1170.—On Peter de Honestis, cleric of Ravenna, CLXIII, 690.

Dissertation on the life and writings of Peter Abelard: on the life of Peter Abelard, CLXXVIII, 57; on the works of Peter Abelard, both printed and still extant in manuscript, 63; the remainder of Peter Abelard’s life until his death, 66.—Notice on Guy of Cariloc, abbot, CLXXXI, 1719.—On Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, CLXXXVIII, 1090.—On Ernald, abbot of Bonneval in the diocese of Chartres, CXXXIX, 1507.—On Achard, abbot of St. Victor, CXCVI, 1371.—On Ado, prior of St. Victor and later abbot of St. Geneviève at Paris, 1398.—On Peter Comestor, CXCVIII, 1045.—Historical-literary notice on Peter, abbot of Clairvaux, CCI, 1391.—On Laborans, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, CCIV, 867.—On Peter the Chanter, CCV, 9.—On Matthew of Vendôme, 925.—On Thomas the Cistercian and John Algrin, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, CCVI, 9 and 11. Judgment of the Master of the Sacred Palace concerning the author of Thomas the Cistercian’s book, 14.

Historical-literary notice on Alan of Lille, bishop of Auxerre, CCX, 9.—Dissertation on Alan, sole abbot of Riveaux, bishop of Auxerre, and finally a Cistercian monk at Cîteaux, who died in 1203, CCX, 9. On Alan’s epitaph, ibid. Which claims rest upon no foundation of truth, 14. Statements concerning Alan’s life and death are examined, 16. The less worthy features of the Life of Alan of Lille are set forth, 20. Alan’s works are examined, 22.

Notice on Absalon, abbot of Springiersbach, CCXI, 9.—Notice on Adam, abbot of Perseigne, 579. Notice on Peter of Poitiers, chancellor of the University of Paris, CCXI, 779.—Notice on Guibert, abbot of Gembloux, CCXI, 1281.—Likewise on Peter of Riga and Giles of Paris, CCXII, 9 and 15.—Notice on Gunther, Cistercian monk, CCXII, 95.—Historical-literary notice on Helinand, monk of Froidmont, 477.

PAGIUS (Antoine), Franciscan, learned chronologist; born in Provence in 1624, died in 1690.

Observation on the decree of Pope Gelasius concerning the divine Scriptures, LIX, 179.—Observation on the letter of the priest Trifolius, LXIII, 536.—Observation on the letter of Pope Vigilius to the Frankish legates, LXIX, 113 ff.—Observation on the letter of Pope Pelagius to Sapaudus, bishop of Arles, 403. Note on Pope St. Boniface IV, LXXX, 102.—Likewise on Pope St. Deusdedit, 360.—On Pope Honorius I, 465.—On Pope John IV, 599.—On Pope Sergius I, LXXXIX, 14.—On Pope John VI, 35.—Observations on the Wilfridian case, 42 ff.—On Constantine, 319.—On Gregory III, 560 and throughout.—On Pope Zachary, 893 and throughout.—On Stephen II, 964.—Notes on Pope St. Paul I, 1129.—Observation on Charlemagne’s letter to Leo III, XCVIII, 923.—Notes on the Life of each Roman pontiff written by Anastasius, CXXVII, 1042.—Observation on the letter of Pope Formosus, CXXIX, 950.

PAMELIUS (Jacobus), doctor of theology of Bruges, 1579. He wrote Tertullian’s life over a period of twenty-four years.

After some preliminary remarks on Tertullian’s identity, education, and talent, I, 73–41 [as printed]. He places Tertullian’s conversion in A.D. 194, 49. On the occasion upon which he became a Christian, 52. Whence he derived a complete knowledge of Christian teaching, 54. On Tertullian’s books against the Jews, 58. On his *Apology*, etc., 59. On other books written in good faith, 64. On books redolent of Montanism, 72. On the time and cause of his defection, 75. On Tertullian’s final Montanist books, 77. At what time he flourished, 82. How he ended, 83. What the editors of the *Patrologia* (Migne) think of these Tertullianic annals written by Pamelius, 69, preface.

The same Pamelius published Tertullian’s *Paradoxes* with an *Antidote*, I, 179. On the apostate angels who took the daughters of men, ibid. On angelic appearances in true human flesh, ibid. On the soul from God’s substance, 180. On the souls of Adam’s descendants as propagated by transmission, 181. On the sex of the soul, 182. On the corporeality of the soul, ibid. That the soul cannot suffer without a body, 185. On the condition of the souls of the saints after death, ibid. That every incorporeal manifestation of the souls of the dead is an illusion, 187. That the most wicked human souls become demons after death, 189. On baptizing heretics, ibid. On Christ as God’s Spirit, 191. On God as corporeal, because nothing is incorporeal, 102. God’s wrath, 195. That the Church exists in three persons, even laypersons, 194. On prophetic ecstasy or loss of reason, 195. On flight during persecution as unlawful, 197. On the Virgin Mary: that she gave birth to Christ through the ordinary law of an opened body, 198. On the Virgin Mary, who was to marry once after giving birth, 199. On the thousand years after the resurrection of bodies, 200. On second marriages as adulterous, 202. On penance to be denied to adulterers, 203. On Montanus the Paraclete, ibid. On the “Psychics,” by which name he slandered Catholics, 205. On the two Lents, ibid. Concerning the Trinity, 206.

Moreover, Pamelius elucidated Tertullian’s works with certain annotations and notes, which may be seen throughout the course of the commentary under his signature.—Preface to Rabanus Maurus’s Commentary on Judith, CIX, 593. On the authority and canonicity of this book, ibid. At what time, under what king, and by what author the history of Judith was written, 595.—Preface to the exposition of the Epistle to Philemon, CXII, 834.—Notice on the book *On the Sacraments* by Grimald, abbot of St. Gall, CXXI, 795.—Preface to the *Micrologus on Ecclesiastical Observances*, CLI, 974.—On the author of the *Micrologus*, 975.

PANCIROLI (Guido), born at Reggio in 1523; died at Padua in 1599. He taught jurisprudence and inserted annotations into certain works of Tertullian, I, 1153 and following pages throughout.

PAPEBROCHIUS (Daniel), of the Society of Jesus, learned jurist, historian, and chronologist; born at Antwerp in 1628 and died in 1753.—Preliminary commentary on the Life of St. Norbert, founder of the Premonstratensian Order and archbishop of Magdeburg, CLXX, 1235. Chronological synopsis of his Life and of his cult, sanctioned by Gregory XIII, ibid. On his Life written by Hugh, 1241. Testimonies of certain authors, 1248.—Critical and explanatory notes on the Life of St. Norbert, 1257 ff.

PAULIUS (Sebastian), a most distinguished man of the Congregation of the Mother of God of Lucca. In 1750 he published at Venice the works of St. Peter Chrysologus.—Preface to the works of St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 9 and 89. On the excellence of St. Chrysologus’s sermons, ibid. His frequent use of Scripture, ibid. His method, ibid. Yet his works have very often been badly edited, 11. What has been accomplished in this edition.—Life of Blessed Peter Chrysologus: his appearance, lineage, birthplace, and year, LII, 13 ff. His ordination, 16. Various deeds, 17. He foretells his own death, 18.

PEARSONIUS (John), born at Snoring in Norfolk in 1612; made an Anglican minister in 1639 and eventually bishop of Chester. He added many notes to the Life and Works of St. Cyprian published by John Fell, bishop of Oxford, in 1672, III, 853.

PEREGRINUS (Camillus). Notice on the Chronicle of Falco of Benevento, CLXXIII, 1445 ff.—Critical notes on the same Chronicle, 1151 ff.

PEREZIUS (Juan Bautista), a Spaniard, published notes around 1599 on St. Isidore of Seville’s *On Illustrious Men*, in Grial’s edition. Labbe calls them most learned, LXXXI, 562, and LXXXIII, 1084 ff.—His studies on the collection of canons, LXXXI, 731 ff.

PERRONETTUS (Denis), of Melun and ecclesiastic of Auxerre, published at Auxerre in 1609 Abbot Ernald’s treatise on the works of the six days, CLXXXIX, 1513.

PERTZIUS (Georg Heinrich), a learned philologist, published the works of Charlemagne at Hanover in 1835.

Prolegomena and notes on the Life of the Blessed Emperor Charlemagne by Einhard, XCVII, 9 ff.—Variant readings of the same Life, 26 ff.—Preface to Charlemagne’s capitularies, XCVII, 107. On the scholarly labours of earlier writers in this field, ibid. What was accomplished in the sixteenth century, 109. Plan of this edition, 110. Survey of ancient manuscripts, 111 ff. Notices on the chapters of each capitulary, with the year’s indiction, 122 ff.—Pertzius’s notice on the capitularies collected by Ansegisus, abbot of Fontenelle, XCVII, 489. Review of the chapters, ibid. ff. How favourably this collection was received, 491. Who corrected the errors that had been introduced, 494. Translation into German, ibid. Parallel presentation of the German editions of Brower and Jacob Grimm, with an interlinear Latin translation, 494. Who published this collection, 497. Various manuscripts, 499.—Notices on the Aachen capitularies, 590 ff. Notices on spurious capitularies, 671, 673 ff.—Notice on the collection of capitularies by Benedict the deacon, 697.—Preliminary notice on the books of Annals describing the Deeds of Charlemagne in verse by a certain Saxon poet, XCIX, 683.—Notes on the same books, 687 ff.

Preface to the Bertinian Annals of St. Prudentius of Troyes, CXV, 1375.—Notes, 1377 ff.—Notes on the chapters of Gunthar, bishop of Cologne, CXXI, 377.—Notes on Annals attributed by Pertz to Hincmar of Rheims, CXXV, 1203 ff.—Notice and notes on Ratpert, monk of St. Gall, CXXVI, 1055.—Notice on Erchembert, CXXIX, 743. Notes on his writings, 746 ff.—Preface to Regino’s Chronicle, CXXXII, 9. On his life and writings, ibid. Testimonies concerning Regino, 183.—Notice on the inquiry to be conducted by bishops, 186.—Notes and variant readings on Bertharius’s book *On the Deeds of the Bishops of Verdun*, CXXXII, 503.—Preliminary notice on Abbo’s *On the Parisian War*, 721.—Notice on Sigehard’s book *On the Miracles of Maximinus*, CXXXIII, 966.—Notes on Flodoard’s Annals, CXXXV, 417 ff.—Preliminary observations on the Life of St. Matilda, 885.—Preliminary observations on the Life of Wenceslas, duke of Bohemia, by Gumpold, 919.—Notice on Heraclius, bishop of Liège, 943.

Historical notice on Liutprand, bishop of Cremona, CXXXVI, 769.—Notes on Liutprand and his writings, 769 ff.—Preliminary notice on the Life of John, abbot of Gorze, CXXXVII, 239.—Notice on the book *On the Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, by Folcuin, 542.—Notice on the Life of St. Adalbert, 859.—Notes and variant readings on the book *On the Passion of St. Adalbert*, 843 ff.—Notice on Richer, monk of Rheims, CXXXVIII, 9. His birth, father, homeland, and age, ibid. The design and plan of his work, 11. What sort of author that work proves him to have been, 14.—Notes and variant readings, 17 ff.—Chronological observations, notes, and variants on the capitularies of Frankish kings, A.D. 840–921, CXXXVIII, 526 ff.—Notice on Benedict, monk of St. Andrew, and on his Chronicle, CXXXIX, 9.—Notes and variants on the Synod of Rheims, CXXXIX, 290 ff.—Historical and literary notice on John the Deacon of Venice, 871.

Inquiry into the life and writings of Heriger and Anselm, CXXXIX, 957.—Explanatory notes, 959 ff.—Notices on Thietmar, bishop of Merseburg: his age, homeland, deeds, and writings, CXXXIX, 1169.—Notes and variant readings, 1183.—Notice on the Life of Adalbero II, bishop of Metz, by Abbot Constantine, 1552.—Annotations on the laws of Emperor St. Henry, CXL, 225.—Notice on Thangmar, priest of Hildesheim, 386.—Notice on the Life of Burchard, bishop of Worms, with notes, 505.—Notice on St. Ademar, monk of Angoulême, CXLI, 9.—Preliminary notice on the Hildesheim Annals, 443.—Notice on Arnold, monk of St. Emmeram, 983.—Notice on the Regensburg Annals, 1103.—Notice on the Hildesheim Chronicle, 1233.—Notice on the Short Annals by Berno, CXLII, 1215.

Notice on the life and writings of Othloh, with notes, CXLVI, 25.—Notice and notes on the Life of St. Wolfgang, bishop of Regensburg, by Othloh, CXLVI, 389. Historical and bibliographical notice on Adam, canon of Bremen, 433. Variant readings and notes on the *Deeds of the Bishops of the Church of Hamburg*, 458.—Historical notice on Gundekar, bishop of Eichstätt, 979. Variant readings and notes on the Pontifical Book, 985 ff.—Variants and notes on the Annals of Lambert of Hersfeld, 1027.—Notice on Pope Alexander II, 1271.—Notes on Letter 108 of Pope Alexander II, 1395 ff.—Notice on Arnulf, cleric of Milan, CXLVII, 279. Notes and variant readings, 285 ff.—Historical notice on Berthold, priest of Constance, 339. Notes and variant readings on Berthold’s Annals, CLXVII, 343.—Historical notice on Bruno, cleric of Magdeburg, 483. Notes and variant readings, 489 ff. Notice on Landulf: his age, birth, homeland, deeds, and writings, CXLVII, 803. Notes and variant readings, 817. Notice on the Catalogue of the Archbishops of Milan, 954.—Notes on the Constitutions of Conrad II, 1039, and Henry III, 1081 ff.—Notice and notes on Andrew’s Chronicle, 1266.—Notice on Peter the Librarian’s abridged history of the Franks, 1279.—Preliminary notice on the panegyric of Berengar by an anonymous author, 1283.—Preface to the ancient Life of St. Matilda, 1311.—Notes on the same Life, ibid. ff. Preliminary observations on the Deeds of the Bishops of Cambrai, CXLIX, 9. Author and sources of the *Deeds*, ibid. Whether the author was Balderic, 12. Deeds of Lietbert, 14. Deeds of Gerard, 15. Manuscripts, 17.

Proem to the Chronicle of Hugh, abbot of Flavigny: Hugh’s age, homeland, birth, and deeds, CLIV, 9. Hugh’s autograph manuscripts, 18.—Variant readings and notes, throughout.—Preface to the Chronicles of Ekkehard of Aura, 434.—Prolegomena to the Chronicle of St. Hubert of Andage, 1338. Notes and variants, 1341 ff. Notice on the Chronicle of Lupus the protospatharius, CLV, 122. Notes and variant readings, throughout. Notes, observations, and variants on the Genealogy of the Counts of Boulogne, 462.—Prolegomena on Sigebert of Gembloux, CLX, 9. His age, homeland, birth, deeds, and writings, ibid.—Notes, 9 ff.—Sigebert’s writings, 15. Manuscripts, 39.—Variant readings and notes on Sigebert’s Chronicle, 62 ff. Various additions and continuations of Sigebert’s Chronicle; see throughout.—Notes and variant readings on the Chronicles of the Poles, 834 ff.—Notice on Francis Camenus, CLXII, 720.

Prolegomena to the Chronicles of the Bohemians by Cosmas of Prague, CLXVI, 9.—Cosmas’s age, birth, and deeds, ibid.—On his writings, 26. Manuscripts, 40.—Variant readings and notes, 55 ff.—Notice on the Chronicle of Affligem, appendix to Franco, 874.—Notice on the Life of Conrad, bishop of Constance, by Udalric, CLXX, 863.—Prolegomena to the *Deeds of the Abbots of Saint-Trond*, by Abbot Rudolph, with explanatory notes, CLXXIII, 11. On Rudolph’s life, 13. On his writings, 16. He composed the book *On the Deeds* in 1114, 18. On his other writings, 21. Manuscripts, 30. (R. Koepke).—Variant readings and notes, 33 ff.—Prolegomena to the Chronicles of Leo of Marsi, a Benedictine later cardinal-bishop of Ostia, and Peter the Deacon, monk of Monte Cassino: Leo’s deeds, birth, and writings.—Materials for the edition, CLXXIII, 440 ff. Facsimile of the autograph Munich manuscript, 447. Likewise a facsimile of the royal Munich manuscript, 451.—Peter’s birth, life, and writings, 462. Explanatory notes, ibid. ff.—Variant readings and annotation, 479 ff.—Notice on the Bamberg and Emmeram Annals, CLXXIII, 1363.—Notes and variant readings on the Genealogies of the Counts of Flanders, appendix to Baldwin, CCIX, 927.

PETAVIUS (Paulus), a most learned chronologist and antiquarian; born at Orléans in 1568, died in 1614.—Short account of Nithard, Charlemagne’s grandson, CXVI, 35 ff. Notes, 35 ff.

PETIT (Jacques). He published the works of Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury, with notes and dissertations.

Dedication, XCIX, 901.—Preface to Theodore’s Penitential, 903. It is the most ancient and celebrated of all, ibid. Ancient practices of dispensation, 905. Chapters gathered from various places, 906.—Annotation on Theodore’s Penitential, 927 ff.—Observations and notes on Theodore’s Penitential, 1107. On the church and matters conducted within it, ibid. On the three ranks of the Church, 1116. On the ordination of various persons, 1127. On confirmation after baptism, 1130. On abbots, monks, and monasteries, 1136. On women’s ministry in the Church, 1139. On communion with Scots and Britons, 1142. On questions of marriage, 1144. On male and female slaves, 1160. On reconciliation, 1162.—Theodore’s teaching on penance is cleared of every suspicion, 1163. The Fathers deny that there was an ecclesiastically decreed custom of doing public penance for hidden sins, ibid. The Fathers affirm that secret penance is sufficient for hidden sins, 1170. The Fathers testify that public penance was canonically instituted by the Church only for public crimes, 1182. Morin’s arguments are refuted, 1187. Certain words of the *Penitential* are explained, 1209. It is demonstrated that Morin did not set forth the definite grounds and true causes of Theodore’s *Penitential*.

PETREIUS (Theodore), of the Carthusian Order; born at Kamp in 1567, died in 1640. He issued a new, more accurate and corrected edition of the works of St. Bruno at Cologne in 1611.—Notice to the reader, CLII, 635.—Approval of the censor, 638.

PETRIUS (Suffridus), of Leeuwarden, philologist; in 1580 he published Gennadius’s writings at Cologne.—Preface, LVIII, 1055. Whether Gennadius was bishop or only a priest of Marseilles, ibid. Discussion of Gennadius’s teaching, ibid.

PEZIUS (Dom Bernard), Benedictine and scholar; born at Ippesheim in Austria in 1683, died in 1735. In the *Bibliotheca Anecdotorum* he published the Treatise on the Passion of Blessed Emmeram, Martyr, written by the priest Constans, XCVI, 1367.—Notes on the writings of Heiric the monk, CXXIV, 1131 ff.—Notice on Anamod’s book of Traditions, CXXIX, 897.—Notice on Purchard the monk, CXXXIX, 350.—Notice on Gospert, abbot of Tegernsee, 365.—Notice on Adelbold’s booklet *On the Method of Finding the Thickness of the Earth*, CXL, 1102.—Notice on Berno, abbot of Reichenau, from Eggo’s book *On Illustrious Men*, CXLII, 1047. Literary notice on the same by Pez himself, 1051.—Notice on Hermann the Lame, monk of Reichenau, from Eggo’s book *On Illustrious Men*, CXLIII, 9.—Appendix to the notice, 17.—Notice on Hermann the Lame’s book *On the Measurement of the Astrolabe*, 379.—Inquiry into the life and writings of Othloh, CXLVI, 9. What he teaches about himself, 10. Survey and occasion of his works, 13 ff.—Notice on Theodoric, canon of Paderborn, CXLVII, 3[lacuna]1.—Notice on the book *On the Good of Peace* by Bishop Rufinus, CL, 1591. Notice on the Life of St. Hugh by Alexander, CLIII, 937.—Dissertation on the year in which St. Hugh was consecrated bishop of Lincoln, 939.—Notes on St. Hugh’s Life, 945 and throughout.—Notice on the description of the Holy Land by John, priest of Würzburg, CLV, 1054.—Notice on the book *On the Honour of the Church*, by Placidus, Benedictine prior of Nonantola, CXLIII, 614.—Notice on Honorius of Autun, 26. Survey of his works, CCXXII, 27.

Dissertation on the life and writings of the Venerable Godfrey, abbot of Admont, CLXXIV: on the foundation of Admont monastery, 9. Godfrey’s name, origin, virtue, and learning, ibid. He gives distinction to monastic life, ibid. He becomes abbot and extends his care to monasteries of women as well as men, 12. His monastery is consumed by flames in 1152, 14. His reputation had reached all people, 15. His death is recorded in the year 1165, 17. His writings, ibid. His opinion against the Immaculate Conception of the Blessed Virgin is noted, 19.

Notice on Peter Abelard’s book entitled *Know Thyself*, CLXXXIII, 631.—Notice on John, monk of St. Lawrence at Liège, CLXXX, 177.—Notice on the book *On Free Will* by Alger, 967.—Notice on the Venerable Hervé, monk of Bordeaux, CLXXXI, 9.—Notice on a sermon on St. George by Zacharias, bishop of an unknown see, CLXXXVI, 619.—Preliminary dissertation on the Life and Writings of the Venerable Gerhoh, provost of Reichersberg, CXCIII, 462. Some material on the Life of Venerable Gerhoh, 465. His deeds, 467. On his writings, 469. Survey of his works, 472.—Notice on Eckbert, abbot of Schönau, CXCV, 9.—Notice on the history of the calamities of the Church of Salzburg, by Archdeacon Henry, CXCVI, 1539.—Notice on Adam the Scot’s soliloquies concerning the instruction of the soul, CXCVIII, 841.—Historical-literary notice on Reiner, monk of St. Lawrence at Liège, CCIV, 9.—Notice on an anonymous Dialogue on the Conflict between the Love of God and the Deceitful Tongue, CCXIII, 851.—Likewise on a treatise on penance, 863.—Likewise on the book *On the Stability of the Soul*, 911.—On the dialogue *On Eating Birds*, 930. Likewise on the Paschal play concerning the coming and destruction of Antichrist, 947. Likewise, notice on an anonymous writer of Melk, prominent in the twelfth century, concerning ecclesiastical writers, CCXIII, 959.

PHEREPONIUS (John). Observations on the letters of St. Augustine, XLVII, 211.—Notice to the reader, XLVII, 535. Preface to Augustine’s book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, first published at Augsburg in 1611, 556. Introductory letter, 537.—Observations on the book *On Rebuke and Grace*, 561.

PHILIPS (Dr. George), an English doctor.—Inquiry into the Pseudo-Isidorian collection, CXXX, xvi. The collection is described, ibid. The Pseudo-Isidorian collection in relation to the sources of ecclesiastical law, xix. Summary judgment, xxii.—Authors to be consulted on this collection, xxiv.

PICARDUS (John), canon of the Church of St. Victor at Paris, about 1607. He first published the letters of St. Anselm of Canterbury and illustrated them with notes.

Notes, CLIX, 13 and throughout.—See also CLVIII, 1059 ff.—At Paris in 1608 he published the Gregorian work of Reverend Father Garnerius, regular canon and superior of St. Victor at Paris, CXCIII, 9. Dedicatory letter, ibid.—Notice to the reader, 12. The excellence and usefulness of this work, 14. Editor’s preface, ibid.—Notice on Nicholas, monk of Clairvaux, CXCVI, 1589.—Preface to Nicholas’s letters, ibid.

PINIUS (John), of the Society of Jesus, priest and theologian, distinguished among the Bollandist associates.

Commentary on St. Bernard the Confessor, first abbot of Clairvaux and Doctor of the Church. Bernard’s year and place of birth; his distinguished lineage, CLXXXV, 643. Parents, brothers, sister, reasoning, upbringing, and studies, 649. His resolution to embrace monastic life, 654. His novitiate and the virtues he practised, 660. His departure for the monastery of Clairvaux from Cîteaux, 664. He is consecrated abbot, 669. Growth of the monastery, 674. On the beginnings of the monastery of Trois-Fontaines, 679. On the place of Prémontré, 684. Miracles performed by St. Bernard, 690. Sudden conversion of certain soldiers, 695. The dead appear and provide assistance, 699. Grain multiplied, 704. Bernard’s actions on behalf of Stephen, bishop of Paris, 709. He writes the book *On Grace and Free Will*, 714. He settles the complaints of the Roman Curia, 719. Pope Innocent II’s journey to Liège with St. Bernard, 726. Very many converted, 732. He refuses the see of Milan, 746. Conversion of Duke William of Aquitaine, 756. He expounds the Song of Songs, 760. He establishes a new order in England and sets out for Rome against the schismatics, 765. His deeds among the Cassinese, 770. He returns to Rome, 782. Actions for the Church of Langres, 787. He attacks Peter Abelard, 794. He wins a cleric by dice, 801.

Bernard’s new labours, 806. He comes to the aid of France amid tragic dissensions, 809. On Arnold of Brescia and Bernard’s letters to him, 819. Eugenius withdraws to Viterbo; Bernard writes against the bishop of York; the ambition of Nicholas of Arras, 625. Bernard’s deeds for the holy war, 832. He travels through Germany for the sacred expedition, 843. Council of Étampes, 849. The holy doctor’s contest with Gilbert of Poitiers, 853. The Henricians are restrained by Bernard, 858. The hardened are punished by God, 865. He labours to reform morals, 870. Apparitions to Bernard, 880. Conversion of Arnulf, 886. The archbishop of Lund attacks him, 899. Bernard’s illness and death, 905. Apparitions, tomb, epitaphs, 909. On editions of his works, etc., 917. He is enrolled in the canon of saints, 921. His office, 928. Books concerning his life, 942.—Posthumous glory, or supplement to the commentary on the Life of St. Bernard, 943. Public veneration; spread of monasteries; Bernard’s shade, 943. Apparitions and predictions of St. Bernard, 951. Certain prophecies, 961. Supplement to the miracles, 963.

PITRA (Dom), of the Order of St. Benedict, 1848. He supplied a preface to Tertullian’s works, I, 9. He published documents on St. Bernard’s journey in Flanders and on the cult of the Most Blessed Virgin Mary at Affligem, CLXXXV, 1798.—Documents and proofs, 1817. See EDITORS OF THE NEW SERIES OF PATROLOGY.

PONTACUS (Arnald), bishop of Bazas, philologist and archaeologist; he published and annotated the works of St. Jerome, year uncertain.—He prefixed to the book of Chronicles an apparatus full of inquiries of great importance, XXVII, 725. On the various titles of this book, ibid. Jerome distinguishes three things therein: numerical lines, little strokes, and the history to which they are applied, 727. The character of the foundation of the history, 728. Whether what Jerome transmitted to us is Eusebius’s Chronicle itself or only its epitome, ibid., 729. That both exist, 729. So far is it from having come down to us mutilated, as some maintain, 731. On the method of Eusebius or Jerome, 733. How the Greek era is determined, 734. On Prosper’s Chronicle, hitherto incorporated with Jerome’s Chronicle, 735. On its title, ibid. The author of this Chronicle truly bears the name Prosper, 737. He is called, and was, an Aquitanian and bishop of Riez, whatever Gennadius may say, 738. Whether the city of Riez is in Gaul or Italy, 739. On manuscript copies, 740.—Corrections and notes on the Chronicle of Eusebius Pamphilus, 746.—Corrections and notes on the Chronicle of St. Prosper, 1181.

PONTIFICAL BOOK. The lineage, homeland, deeds, and writings of Pope St. Hilary, LVIII, 9 ff.—Likewise the lineage, homeland, and acts of Pope Simplicius, 31 ff. Notice on Pope Gelasius I, LIX, 9. Notice on Pope Symmachus, LXII, 39.—Notice on Pope Hormisdas, LXIII, 363.—Notice on Pope Felix IV: his lineage, homeland, and year, LXIV, 9. His deeds and writings, ibid.—Notice on Pope Boniface, 30.—Likewise on Pope John II, LXVI, 9.—Likewise on Pope Agapetus I, 31.—Notice on Pope Silverius, 79. On Pope Vigilius, LXIX, 9.—On Pope Pelagius, 391.—Life of Pope John III, LXXII, 9. Life of Pope Benedict I, 681.—Notice on Pope Pelagius II, 701.—On Pope St. Boniface IV, LXXX, 97.—On Pope St. Deusdedit, Roman pontiff, 355.—Notice on Pope Boniface V, 329.—On Pope St. Adeodatus, 1139.—Likewise on Pope Donus, 1146.—Likewise on Pope St. Agatho, 1153.—On Pope Sergius I, LXXXIX, 9. On Pope John VI, 35.—On Pope John VII, 53.—On Pope Constantine, 315.—On Pope St. Gregory II, 453.—On Pope Gregory III, 557.—On Pope Zachary, 981.—On Pope Stephen II, 959.—On Pope St. Paul I, 1125.—On Pope Stephen III, 1235.

POSSEVINUS (Antonio), of the Society of Jesus, diplomat and learned bibliographer. Born at Mantua in 1534 and died in 1611. Notice on Samuel the Moroccan, a Jew converted to Christianity and author of the book *On the Advent of the Messiah as Already Past*, CXLIX, 334.

PREVOTIUS (John), canon of Rouen, published in 1679 the book *On Ecclesiastical Offices* by Bishop John, with notes and observations, CXLVII, 63 ff.

PRIEUR (Philippe Le), most learned; born at Saint-Vaast in Flanders, died in 1680. He worked on Tertullian’s writings already annotated by Pamelius and Rigault, adding new annotations, I, 59; preface, 310; note, 346; and throughout.

QUADRATUS (Francis), monk of Bec. His letter of 1540 to the distinguished Ratus, professor of theology, concerning Blessed Lanfranc’s book *On the Body and Blood of Christ*, appears at CL, 407.

QUERCETANUS (André du Chesne), royal historiographer; born at Tours in 1584 and died in 1640. He published the works of Blessed Alcuin. Preface: nearly the same subject as in Froben’s dissertation on Alcuin’s Life, C, 107 (see FROBENIUS).—Notice on Louis I, surnamed the Pious, and his diplomas, CIV, 927 ff.—Variant readings on the Bertinian Annals of St. Prudentius, CXV, 1377 ff.—Notice on the book *On the Customs and Deeds of the First Dukes of Normandy*, by Dudo, CXLI, 607.—Notes on the histories of the saints written by Blessed Peter, CXLIV, 925 ff.—Arguments and notes on Peter Abelard’s letters, CLXXVIII, 114 ff.—Notes and commentary on the letters of Peter the Venerable, CLXXXIX, 61.

QUESNELLUS (Paschasius), Oratorian theologian and defender of the Jansenists, born at Paris in 1634 and died at Amsterdam in 1719. He published an edition of the Works of St. Leo the Great at Paris in 1675.

General Preface, LIV, 31. The purpose and method of this edition, ibid. Certain earlier editions are mentioned, 33, 34. Arrangement of the work, 36 ff. On the altered order of the letters, 39. On the Grimanus manuscript, 41. On the composition of the volumes, 43. The calumnies of the Magdeburg Centuriators against the holy popes Zosimus, Boniface, and Celestine are refuted, 45. The aids he employed, 47. Quesnel’s dedication to St. Leo, ibid. Quesnel’s notes, variant readings [Col. 0386], and observations on the writings of St. Leo, LIV, 1263 ff.

Dissertation I. On the life, deeds, and writings of St. Leo the Great, LV, 183.---Dissertation II. In which the books *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, commonly attributed to Prosper of Aquitaine, are assigned to Leo the Great, LV, 339. Some attributed them to St. Ambrose, 340. Erasmus judged the work to be by Eucherius of Lyons, ibid. Others, however, attribute it to Hilary, 341. On Hilary of Syracuse and of Arles, 341. Yet they are commonly ascribed to Prosper of Aquitaine, 314. But the divergence of style is everywhere evident, 345, and the method of writing differs greatly from Prosper’s manner of proceeding, 345. The work was written before the time of Gelasius, ibid.---Dissertation III. In which the chapters on the grace of God and the freedom of the will, commonly attributed to Pope Celestine, are vindicated for St. Leo the Great; and the celebrated exception, “Concerning the deeper and more difficult aspects of questions that arise,” is re-examined, LV, 387. Part I. The several chapters, furnished with various titles by their author himself, are not by Celestine, 389. Part II. By this clause, “Concerning the deeper matters,” etc., not all the chapters concerning Christ’s grace are included, 399.---Dissertation IV. In which the letter to Demetrias, hitherto ascribed to St. Prosper, is shown truly to be a work of St. Leo the Great, LV, 413.---Dissertation V, or an Apology for St. Hilary of Arles and the ancient rights of his church, LV, 425.---Dissertation VI. On the Saturday fast observed in the Roman Church in the time of Pope Leo I; on the ancient and differing customs of the Churches, LV, 62.---Dissertation VII. On the case of Eutyches, archimandrite of Constantinople, condemned by Flavian in the council, 645.---Dissertation VIII. On the case of Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, condemned and deposed in the pseudo-synod, 669.---Dissertation IX. On the case of the bishop of Antioch and his condemnation; on the letters of Leo, LX, LXXVIII, etc., 701.---Dissertation X. On the case of Theodoret of Cyrrhus, deposed by the sentence of the pseudo-synod of Ephesus and restored by St. Leo, 739.---Dissertation XI. On the spuriousness of the letter to the bishops of Germany and Gaul concerning the privilege of chorepiscopi and presbyters, fabricated under Leo’s name in earlier editions, LXXXVIII, LV, 757.---Dissertation XII. On the most ancient of all the codes of canons of the Roman Church hitherto published, LVI, 899.---Dissertation XIII. On the African councils held in the Pelagian controversy from the death of Innocent to Zosimus, LVI, 859.---Dissertation XIV. On the various statements of faith contained in the ancient code of the Roman Church, LVI, 1041.---Dissertation XV. On the spurious Council of Telles and the pseudo-letter of Pope Siricius called the *tractoria* to the African bishops, LVI, 1075.---Dissertation XVI. On the first use of the code of canons of Dionysius Exiguus in Gaul, 1105.

RAM (P. F. X. de), doctor of Sacred Theology and of both canon laws, member of the Royal Historical College of Belgium, at Louvain in 1845. He published the *Chronicle* of Idatius, illustrated with notes by Juan Matías Garzón, LXXIV, 675.---Notice to this new edition, ibid.

RAMIREZIUS (D. Laurentius), Franciscan; year lacking. He supplied notes to the *Chronicle* of Liutprand, CXXXVI, 961 ff.

RAVAISSON, imperial librarian at Paris. He published, in 1841, a report to the Minister of Public Instruction concerning the libraries in the western part of France.

Notice on the catalogue of books of the Abbey of Bec, about the twelfth century, CL, 770.

RAVERDY (Jean). A letter of 14 February 1737 to Cardinal Quirini shows that he collected variant readings for the book *On Heresies* by St. Philastrius, XII, 1099, 1112.

RAYNAUDUS (Fr. Theophilus), of the Society of Jesus, controversial theologian, born at Sospel in 1583 and died in 1663.---Apology for St. Valerian, bishop of Cimiez, against Nicolas Chichon. Preface: the grounds and manner of conducting Valerian’s defense, LII, 757. On Valerian’s age, nation, family, private station, and associated conjectures, 759. Things alleged, or capable of being alleged, against Valerian, 764. First defense of Valerian against Semi-Pelagianism, 771. Introduction to Valerian’s proper vindication from such a stain, 774. It is shown that Valerian abhorred Semi-Pelagianism, 789. That Valerian’s statement, “it is ours to will and God’s to accomplish,” is altogether Catholic, 801. Valerian imitated the manner of speech of the Scriptures, 811. The most weighty Fathers would equally fall under condemnation together with Valerian, 816. Whether Valerian ought to be deprived of the title of saint which he has long possessed in manuscripts, 832.

REUSS (F. A.), professor at Würzburg in 1854. Notice of the life and writings of St. Hildegard, CXCVII, 139. Works printed in type, 142. Works not yet published from manuscript codices, 143.

RHEINWALDUS (Frederick Henry), doctor of philosophy, licentiate in theology, etc. In his collection entitled *Anecdota Pertaining to Ecclesiastical History* [Col. 0387], he published Peter Abelard’s dialogue between a philosopher, a Jew, and a Christian, Berlin, 1831.---Preface, CLXXVIII, 1610.---He also published by the same author an *Epitome of Christian Theology*.---Preface, 1686.

RHENANUS (Beatus), of Sélestat, in 1521, in the first Basel edition, supplied *Proverbial Expressions Extracted from the Whole Work of Tertullian*, illustrated with brief scholia, I, 209 ff.---The extent of Rhenanus’s efforts to draw Tertullian’s works out of obscurity, 56, 57, Preface. He annotated the works of Tertullian, as may be seen in the commentary.

RICHARDUS (F.), of Le Mans, of the Franciscan Order, doctor of theology, at Paris in 1541.

He edited and corrected the works of Peter Lombard.---Dedication, CXCI, 31. Prologue to the Master, or comparison of the different translations of the Psalter, CXCI, 35. Discussion concerning the authors of the Psalms, 37. On St. Jerome’s commentaries on the Psalter, 40. Whether the present commentaries are the Master’s, 51.---Notice to the reader, 54.

RICHTERUS (Aemilius-Louis), doctor of both laws at the University of Marburg, Leipzig, 1833.

He published the works of Gratian, illustrated with notes and variant readings, following the edition of Henning Boehmer.---Preface to the reader, CLXXXVII, 21 ff. Notes of the Correctors, 29 ff.

RIGALTIUS (Nicolas), an accomplished philologist, from the Jesuit congregation.

He published at Paris in 1634 the works of Tertullian corrected in very many places and illustrated with observations and notes, shortly after La Cerda had published his Tertullian, I, 50, Preface. What Rigaltius accomplished in this edition, ibid. He compiled an index-glossary of African style, ibid. What is said about Rigaltius and his care for the works of Tertullian, 51, Preface. What our editors say of him, 52, note. Rigaltius’s annotations and observations, inserted throughout the commentaries, may be seen under his own signature.---Rigaltius corrects and annotates the writings of Commodianus, V, 99.

ROBERTUS (Jean), priest of the Society of Jesus and doctor of theology, at Luxembourg in 1619. He published the works of Thiotfrid, abbot of Echternach, illustrated with notes.---Preface, CLVII, 298. Life of Thiotfrid, 303. His name, ibid. His deeds, 304. He acquires allods, 305. He restores peace on the island of Walcheren, 306. His virtues and holiness, 310. His associates and contemporaries, 311. His writings and date, 312. Annotation, 313 ff.

ROCCA (Angelo), antiquarian and philologist. Born at Rocca Contrata in 1545 and died in 1620.---He supplied observations on images of St. Gregory the Great, LXXV, 461.---On the marble votive tablets at Rome dedicated by St. Gregory the Great to the holy apostles Peter and Paul, 483.---Scholia on the *Book of Sacraments* of St. Gregory the Great, LXXVIII, 383.

ROSWEYDUS (Heribert), of the Society of Jesus, hagiographer, born at Utrecht in 1569 and died in 1629.---Notes and observations on the letters of St. Paulinus, LXI, 835 ff.---The *Lives of the Fathers*, edited by Rosweyde, crown the series of Fathers from Tertullian to Gregory the Great, LXXIII, Preface, 9. The care which he devoted to them, ibid.---New address, 11.---Prolegomena. What the title of these books is, 13. Who their authors are, 20 ff. Who is the author of the first book, 21; of the second, 22; of the third, 38; of the fourth, 39; of the fifth, 40; of the sixth, 42; of the seventh and eighth, 43; of the ninth and tenth, 44. In what language they were written, 47. Who translated these books, 48. Their authority, 53. Their usefulness, 61. On editions of these books, 63. What each edition accomplished, 73. On translations, 77. On manuscripts, 79. On the appendix to this edition, 85. Various notices, 86. Rosweyde’s notes, 101 ff., and LXXIV, 115. Notice to the reader, 243, 394. Onomasticon of more difficult matters and words, 399 ff.---Dedicatory letter to the *Martyrology* of St. Ado, bishop of Vienne, CXXIII, 139.---Notice to the reader, 142.---Testimonies concerning this martyrology, 143.---Commentarial notes on Ado’s martyrology, 145.---Notice on the Appendix to St. Ado’s martyrology, 419.

ROTA (Julius Martianus). Dedicatory letter in the works of Severinus Boethius, addressed to George, pope-elect of Treviso, LXIII, 541. What was accomplished for this edition, ibid. On the life and deeds of Boethius, 543. On his writings, 545. The death and eulogy of Boethius, 547.

ROUTH (Martin Joseph).

Commentary on the book *On the Canon of Scripture*, III, 173. He corrected this fragment and marked many of its variant readings, 173 and throughout. The notes of the commentary are treated at length and learnedly, 173 and throughout. His notes on the letter of Blessed Cornelius, pope, 745 ff. A note by the same writer, 851 ff.---Also on the writings of St. Victorinus, V, 301 ff.

[Col. 0388] ROZERIUS (Eugenius) [Eugène de Rozière], chief secretary to the Minister of Public Instruction, at Paris in 1851, published previously unedited ancient formulae of Angers from a manuscript codex in the Strasbourg Library.

Notice, CLI, 1410.---Explanatory notes, 1411 ff.---He also published others extracted from a manuscript in the Library of St. Gall, 1429.---Introduction to the account of the ancient cartulary of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre at Jerusalem, CLV, 1106. Notes, ibid. Corrections, 1111 ff.

RUBEIS (Fr. Maria Bernardus de), of the Order of Preachers, born in 1686 and died in 1775. Investigation concerning St. Chromatius. Valerian dies and Chromatius is elected, XX, 407. He receives from Ambrose an interpretation of Balaam’s prophecy, and from St. Jerome a Latin translation and commentaries on several books of Holy Scripture, 407. On the condemnation of Origen; Rufinus accused, 413. Chromatius urges Jerome to silence, 421. Chromatius dies, 426.---Dissertations on St. Chromatius, XX, 429. On the death of St. Valerian and the election of St. Chromatius, 429 ff. At what time he wrote, 431. Who first published the works of Chromatius, 433.

RUBEUS (Antonius), a most learned printer, at Rome in 1740. He edited the works of Rufinus the presbyter. He prefixed a preface, XXI, 45, in which he dedicates the edition to Daniel Delfino, Patriarch of Aquileia, ibid. He reports the corrections and elucidations, 42. On Rufinus’s life composed by D. Fontanini, 49. Critical observations concerning certain insufficiently considered deeds of Rufinus, 51. On the two books *On the Blessings of the Patriarchs*, 55. On the commentary on the Apostles’ Creed, 57. Order of the works, 58. The edition of Cacciari is examined and shown to be erroneous in many places, 59. What is added concerning spurious works, 63. Some matters concerning Rufinus, 66. On the time at which he wrote, 67. Critical notes on the text, 295 ff.---Observation concerning Peter the Cleric, or the prior of Porto, CLXIII, 702.

RUGGERIUS, canon of the Eusebian cathedral church of Novara, in 1738.

He wrote a letter to Blanchini of Verona concerning the description of the Vercelli codex of the Gospels, XII, 69. On the precious preservation of that codex, ibid. At what time and in what place it was begun, ibid. On its present condition, 70. Memorial of Ferrerius, bishop of Vercelli, concerning the relics of St. Eusebius, 71. Another document of Atto, bishop of Vercelli, 72.

RUINARTIUS (Dom Thierry), a most learned Benedictine; born at Reims in 1657 and died in 1709. He worked for a long time with Fr. Mabillon. In 1689 he published the authentic *Acts of the First Martyrs*. In the preface to that work he refutes Dodwell’s paradoxes; introductory matter extracted from it, III, 9. Its following synopsis: first, on the printed and manuscript witnesses of these Acts, ibid. Second, were Perpetua and Felicity women of Tuburbo? ibid. Third, they are known to have suffered not at Tuburbo but at Carthage, 11. Fourth, the date of the passion is investigated, ibid. Fifth, on the author or collector of these Acts: was it Tertullian? ibid. Sixth, he was not a Montanist, whatever Valesius may say, 12. Seventh, the fiction of the author’s Montanism is again rejected, ibid. Eighth, on the cult and commemoration of these martyrs, 13.---Thierry Ruinart’s notes on the Acts of St. Saturninus and his companions, with a preliminary notice, VIII, 705 ff.---Notice on the passion of St. Maurice and his companions, L, 821.---Ruinart’s historical commentary on the Vandal persecution, LVIII, 359. The Vandals’ invasion of Gaul, ibid. Spain occupied by the Vandals, 361. The Vandals’ entry into Africa, 366. Beginnings of Genseric’s persecution, 371. Letter of Honoratus Antoninus, bishop of Constantine, to Arcadius, exiled for the faith, 372. Genseric rages in captured Carthage, 374. Passion of St. Julia, virgin and martyr, 378. Genseric invades Rome, 381. Huneric succeeds Genseric, 390. St. Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, 396. His passion, 404. On the holy confessors of Africa under Genseric and Huneric, 405. On the Vandal persecution under Guntamund, 414. On the persecution under Thrasamund, 420. Letter of Pope Symmachus to the bishops deported to Sardinia, 426. Peace restored to the African Church, 430.

A new edition of the works of St. Gregory of Tours, illustrated with notes and observations, LXXI, 9.---Dedicatory letter, ibid.---Preface to this new edition: On the renown of St. Gregory, 13. On the method of this edition, ibid. On the recension of manuscript codices, 14. What Valesius thought, ibid. On the authority of St. Gregory of Tours, 15. On the first incursions of the Franks into Gaul, 16. On the decline of Roman power and the increasing fortune of the Franks, 17. What the ancient form of government among the Gauls was, 18. On the authority of bishops in those times, 23; and reverence for the supreme Roman pontiff, 25. Gregory describes Gaul under Clovis the Great, 25, 26. On ecclesiastical discipline concerning bishops, 27. On the reverence of the Gallican Church for the sacred canons, 31. On parishes, 32. On clergy, 33. On monastic orders, 34. How abbots and abbesses were elected, [Col. 0389] 35. On the offices performed, 38. On the celebration of masses, 41. On the relics of saints, 45. The consecrated right of asylum in churches, 47. On the administration of the sacraments, 49. On ecclesiastical censures, 50. On the use of St. Gregory’s works for the history of the Franks, 53. What is to be said of his credulity concerning miracles, 55. That Cyprian and Augustine thought the same as Gregory, 60. On the catalogue of St. Gregory’s works, 61. Which works are attributed to him, 62 ff. On the time at which Gregory wrote each book, 69. On the various codices, 72. On Fredegar’s authority, 80. Cointius’s objections, 86 ff. What was accomplished in this edition, 96. Which codices were consulted, 97. To which editions they were added, 102. Account of the principal editions, 103. On Fredegar and his works, 105. What Valesius and Cointius judge concerning his country, 106. On Fredegar’s codices and editions, 107, 108. On the authenticity of Fredegar’s *Chronicle*, 110. On the Appendix, 114.---Annotations on the life of St. Gregory composed by Blessed Odo, LXXI, 115 ff. Testimonies concerning St. Gregory, bishop of Tours, 129 ff.---Frankish annals from the year 255 to Charlemagne, 137. The Frankish people, ibid. Evidence from Gregory, 152; from Fredegar, 156.---Notes and elucidations on the ten books of the ecclesiastical history of St. Gregory of Tours, 101 ff.---Notice on Fredegar’s *Chronicle*, 605.---Notes and elucidations on the same *Chronicle*, ibid. ff.---Also on the books *On the Glory of the Blessed Martyrs*, 705.---Notice on the time when the aforementioned books were written, 911.---Elucidations and notes on the books *On the Miracles of St. Martin*, 913 ff.---Also on the book *On the Lives of the Fathers*, 1010.

Life of Pope Urban II. Notice, CLI, 9. Urban’s name, country, and parents, ibid. Whether Urban was a canon of Reims, 15. He becomes a monk, 17. He is elected bishop, 20. Counselor to the pope, 21. On Wibert the antipope, 22. Peace is negotiated; Odo is released, 23. Odo takes part in a conference in Saxony, 25. Gregory VII dies, 26. Odo goes to Cluny, 27. Odo’s defense against Hugh of Lyons, 29. Death of Victor III; Odo is elected, 30. Urban’s rescripts, 31. Urban is loved by all, 32. He dedicates the monastery of Bantin, 35. He journeys to Sicily, 37. He sends the pallium to Anselm, 38. Artaldus of Helenes is consecrated by Urban, 42. Cluniac privilege, 43. The state of affairs in Germany, 45. Urban remains in Rome, 47. On German affairs, 48. The fury of the schismatics, 50. Peace is made with the Greeks, 54. The Council of Melfi and its canons, 56. Urban transfers the bones of St. Nicholas to Bari, 59. Whether a council was then held at Troyes, 60. He visits Reggio, 61. St. Bruno accompanies Urban, 62. Council of Saintes, 63. He entrusts the province of Tarragona to the archbishop of Narbonne, 65. Decree concerning freedom of marriage, 67. Council at Toulouse, 70. Henry’s expedition into Italy, 73. The Charterhouse is restored to Bruno’s disciples, 74. Death of Adalbero, bishop of Würzburg, 78. Henry’s party prevails at Rome, 79. Council of Benevento, 81. Disturbances in Germany, 86. Urban’s letters for St. Cyprian of Poitiers, 88. Urban celebrates Christmas outside the City, 93. His party prevails, 94. Falco, abbot of Leves, flees to Urban, 96. Urban’s judgment concerning the Church of Créon, 102. Council of Troyes, 107. Council of Reims, 110. Urban resides in Rome, 119. He ordains Godfrey priest, 125. Synod of Constance, 126. Council of Ostia, 132. Urban deals moderately with King Philip, 135. He comes to Bologna, 138. Heresies proscribed, 142. Urban is received at Cremona by King Conrad, 146. He dedicates the church at Como, 150. He crosses into Gaul, 154. He travels through various regions, 156. Urban arrives at Clermont, 163. Very many bishops assemble there, 164. The council begins, 168. What was decreed, 170. The holy expedition is decreed there, 180. Urban’s magnanimity, 183. Urban passes through Aurillac, 187. At Angers he preaches the crusade, 192. Council of Rouen, 197. Council of Tours, 199. He goes from Toulouse to Carcassonne, 208. Departure of the crusaders, 218. Urban returns to Italy, 218. Lateran Council, 221. The pontiff’s affection for monks, 222. Council of Saintes, 224. Crusaders from every quarter make for the East, 126. Urban writes to Emperor Alexius on their behalf, 227. Council of Girona, 230. Urban resides in Rome; Guibert flees, 232. The pontiff visits Roger and withdraws to Benevento, 236. The crusaders capture Antioch, 239. Acts of the synod of Bari, 242. King Philip is again placed under interdict, 246. Urban convenes a synod at Rome, 249. Anselm leaves Rome, 255. Urban dies at Rome, 258.

SACEDO (Franciscus), of the Order of St. Benedict, published the works of Peter Comestor at Madrid in 1699.---Dedicatory letter, CXCVIII, 1030. Censure by R. Fr. Juan de Arguelles, 1051. Preface to the reader, ibid.

SAINT-GENOIS (Julius de), professor and bibliographer, published in French at the University of Ghent a notice on the *Florid Book* of Lambert the Canon, [Col. 0390] CLXIII, 1004 ff.

SALMASIUS, Saumaise (Claude de), born at Saumur in 1588; he withdrew to Heidelberg, then went to Leiden, where he became professor of theology. He devoted effort to purging and correcting the works of Tertullian. He died in 1653, I, 10. Salmasius supplied a codex for the polishing of the book *On the Pallium*, 35, Preface.---Notes on the writings of Arnobius, V, 718.

SANTANDER (Christopher Anthony de la Serna), Spaniard and learned bibliographer, born in 1752 and died in 1813.

At Brussels he published the Spanish Collection of Canons with a historical-critical preface, LXXXIV, 849. Dedication, ibid. Preliminary discourse, ibid. Survey of the codices, 852. Their description and account, 856. On the origin and composition of this collection, 866. On the ancient code of canons before the time of Isidore of Seville, 877. It is maintained that he compiled this collection, 881. It is proved that the Spanish Church always recognized the authority of the Apostolic See, 902. His explanatory notes.

SAVILIUS (Henry), learned patron of letters, born at Bradley in 1549 and died in 1622, published the books of Henry of Huntingdon, CXCV, 799.---Prologue, ibid.

SAXIUS (Joseph Anthony), prefect of the Ambrosian College and Library. Notice on the *History of Milan* by Landulf, CLXXIII, 1431.---Chronological series of events pertaining to this history, 1433.---Notes on the same history, 1437 ff.

SCALIGERUS (Joseph Justus), born at Agen in 1540 and died in 1609. A most accomplished philologist. Among his numerous works, he annotated and corrected the works of Tertullian, I, 10. Laurence Barraeus, editor of Tertullian in 1580, found much in him, I, 42.

SCHELESTRATUS or SCHELSHATTIUS (Emmanuel), theologian and ardent controversialist for the Roman cause, born at Antwerp in 1649 and died in 1692.---Dissertation on the ancient catalogues of Roman pontiffs, CXXVII, 157. On writers who described the succession of the Roman pontiffs, 157. On the catalogue ending with Pope Liberius, 164. Whether an older catalogue was written by Pope Damasus, 174. On the second catalogue ending with the acts of Felix IV, 180. On the *Liber Pontificalis*, 188. Whether it was composed by Damasus, 193. Whether it should be attributed to Anastasius the Librarian, 198. By whom and when it was written, 204. From what monuments it was compiled, 213.---Appendix to the preceding dissertation, 219.

SCHLUETERUS (C. B.). He corrected and published John Scotus Eriugena’s book *On the Division of Nature* at Osthendorf in 1838.---Preface, CXXII, 101. Notice concerning Scotus, ibid. On his deeds and writings, ibid. ff. Notes, ibid. ff.

SCHILLINCKIUS (D. Daniel), abbot of the monastery of Springiersbach. At Cologne in 1534 he published the writings of Absalon, abbot, as appears from the dedicatory letter of Gymnich, the printer, CCXI, 11.

SCHOENEMANNUS (C. Traugott Gottlob), historiographer, born at Eisleben in 1766 and died in 1802.

On the writings of Pope Julius, VIII, 870.---Literary notice on St. Hilary, IX, 207. Hilary’s life, ibid. His writings, 209. Editions, 210.---Literary notice on Zeno, XI, 213. Zeno’s life, ibid.; writings, 214. Editions of his works, ibid. ff. Various codices, 251, 252.---Literary notice on the life, writings, and editions of St. Optatus, XI, 875.---Notice concerning Faustinus, XIII, 34. His life, ibid., and writings, ibid. Editions of these books, 33.---On the writings of Pope St. Anastasius, XX, 57. On their editions, ibid.---Notice on St. Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia, XX, 791. His life and deeds, ibid. Writings of the holy Doctor, 793. Various editions, ibid.---Notice on Rufinus, presbyter of Aquileia, XXI, 9. On his life, ibid. On genuine, doubtful, and lost writings, 15. On the various editions of these writings, 16 ff. Editions of Eusebius’s history translated and enlarged by Rufinus, 21. The book *On the Lives of the Fathers*, 25. Four books of Origen and homilies, 37. Translated works of Gregory Nazianzen, 39. Sayings of Sextus, 40. Works of Evagrius, 42. Clement’s *Recognitions*, 43. Notice concerning the works of Julian, Pelagian bishop of Eclanum, XXI, 1167. On genuine writings, ibid. On doubtful works, 1169. Various editions of his works, 1170.---Historical-literary notice on Marius Mercator, XLVIII. His life, 47. On his writings, 49. Editions of Marius Mercator’s works, 59. Codices, 60.---Literary notice on John Cassian, XLIX. Life of John Cassian, 9. His writings, 10. Editions of John Cassian’s works, 11. Translations, 22. Codices, ibid.

Literary notice concerning the life, writings, and editions of the works of St. Augustine, XLVII, 9.---Life of St. Augustine, ibid. His family, education, and youth, ibid. He goes to Milan [Col. 0391] and is drawn from vice by Ambrose, 12. He loses his mother Monica, 13. He returns to Tagaste, 14. He is made priest by Valerius, bishop of Hippo, ibid. At Valerius’s request he is made bishop and colleague, 15. Erasmus’s passage on St. Augustine’s genius, 18. Possidius’s words on Augustine’s wonderful eloquence, 19. He compels pagans, Manichaeans, and Donatists in turn to emerge from darkness, ibid. He fights the Pelagians for ten years, 21. Terrible to the enemies of the faith, he showed himself in all respects holy, simple, and gentle, 23.---One hundred and twenty-two genuine writings of St. Augustine are enumerated, 24 ff. Twelve lost works, 34. Doubtful, falsely attributed, and spurious writings, 83.---Various editions of the works of St. Augustine: preface, 40. How important it is for literary history to inquire how such precious monuments were preserved, ibid. and 41. On the earliest editions after the invention of printing: the first book of Augustine printed was the book on the art of preaching, namely the last of the four books *On Christian Doctrine*, Strasbourg, 1465, by Johann Mentelin, 41. Then in 1467 the work *On the City of God* appeared from the renowned monastery of Subiaco, ibid. Johann Amerbach was the first to conceive the collecting of all the works of St. Aurelius Augustine into one body; he completed this at Basel in 1506, and again at Paris in 1515. Erasmus and Froben compiled a new and most ample recension with the greatest labour, 44. Afterwards the theologians of Louvain, joining their studies, purged, elucidated, and enlarged it by examining and comparing ancient codices, 45. But they were surpassed by the Benedictine monks, who restored the order and submitted these works of the holy Doctor to the press in an excellent typeface, 46. Typographical annals of St. Augustine’s minor works and collections, 37. Editions of doubtful works, 191. Principal excerptors and commentators on the works of St. Augustine, 192.

Historical-literary notice on Possidius, L, 401. His life, ibid. Writings and editions, 404. Translations and codices, 406. Likewise, notice on Pope St. Celestine, 409. Life, ibid. Writings of Celestine, 412. Editions of his works, 413. Notice on Antoninus Honoratus, bishop of Constantine, L, 565.---Notice on the life and writings of Xystus, 577. Notice on Vincent of Lérins, 629. His life, writings, and editions, ibid.---Notice on St. Eucherius, bishop of Lyons. His life, L, 685. Writings, 686. Editions, 687. Notice on St. Hilary of Arles, L, 1213. His life, ibid. Writings, 1216. Editions of his writings, 1217.---Notice on the life, writings, and editions of Paschasinus, L, 1291.---On Aeneas Sylvius, 1293. On Turibius, bishop of Astorga, ibid.---Notice on St. Prosper: his life, LI, 43. Writings, 45. Editions, 49 ff.---Notice indicating the place, date, and form of every edition of the works of St. Peter Chrysologus, LII, 79.---Notice on the writings and editions of St. Valerian, LII, 685 ff.---On St. Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia: his life, LII, 839. Writings, 841. Editions, 842.---On the life, writings, and editions of Salvian, LII, 11 ff.---On St. Patrick: on his life, 795; writings, 797; and editions, 798. Codices of his writings, 800.

Notice on St. Maximus, bishop of Turin, LVII. His life, 177. Writings, 178. Editions of his works, 184. Various codices, 197.---Explanation of the age of manuscript codices, 211. Specimen of writing, 213, 217.---Notice on Pope Leo IV, CXV, 629. Leo’s virtues; he lives in a monastery and is summoned by the pope, ibid. He is ordained priest, ibid. He is elected pope, 630. Churches endowed by him, 631. Leo’s miracles, 633, 634. Various deeds, 635 ff. He sings Mass at Ostia, 641. At Leo’s prayers the Saracens are dispersed, ibid. Emperor Lothair assists the pope in building the Leonine City, 645. Corsican exiles flee to the pope, 647. He repairs cities and churches, 649. He convenes a synod at Rome, 651. He is falsely accused before the emperor, 655. The accuser is handed over to Gratian, 656. Leo dies, ibid.---Notice on Pope Benedict III: Benedict’s virtues; he is ordained priest, CXV, 683. He is unwillingly elected pope, 685. Many conspire against him, ibid. A pseudo-pope deposes Benedict; the people mourn, 687. Anastasius is expelled and Benedict restored, 688. The king of the Saxons comes to Rome for religious reasons, 689. The pope customarily attends the burial of clerics, 690.

SCHOTTUS (Andreas), learned philologist of the Society of Jesus, born at Antwerp in 1552 and died in 1629. He corrected and enlarged Fabricius’s edition of the works of Paulus Orosius, as appears from his letter to the printer D. Cholinus at Cologne, XXXI, 653.---Preface to the works of St. Eucherius, L, 697.

SCHRAMMUS (Christian Godfrey), in 1781.---He published arguments and summaries for various works of Tertullian, I, 65, Preface, 1198, 1288.

SCHURTZFLEISCHIUS (Conrad Samuel), learned philologist, born at Korbach in 1641 and died in 1708. He published the works [Col. 0392] of the virgin Hrotsvitha.---Dedicatory letter, CXXXVII, 942. Preface to the reader, 943. Hrotsvitha learned Latin and also Greek letters, 944. That she was Saxon by birth, 945. But not English, as Laurence Humfrey maintains, 946. On Hilda the Englishwoman, 948. In what year Hilda died, 951. Succession of the abbesses of Gandersheim, 955. Some observations on the works of Hrotsvitha, 959 ff.

SCHUTZIUS (Christian Gottfried), philologist and learned man, born at Duderstadt in Prussia in 1747 and died in 1832. At the University of Jena he taught humane letters and eloquence. He was the author of the *Index of Tertullianic Latin*, II, 1251; concerning his view, II, 1250. He also published other writings on Tertullian, I, 65 and 66, about the year 1780, Preface.

SCULTETUS or SCHULTZIUS (Bartholomew), born at Głogów in 1540 and died in 1610. He authored an analysis of Lactantius’s book *On the Anger of God*, VII, 77.

SELDENUS (John), learned archaeologist, born in England in 1584 and died in 1634.---Notice on the laws of William the Conqueror, CXLIX, 291.---Notes on the *History of Recent Events*, by the monk Eadmer, CLIX, 523.

SEMLERUS (Johann Salomo), theologian most learned among the Calvinists, born at Saalfeld, a town of Saxony, in 1725, and died at Halle in 1791. He added corrections and critical notes to the works of Tertullian, I, 10.---Notes on the *Etymologies* of St. Isidore, LXXXII, 849 ff.
