SERRARIUS. Preface to his recension of the letters of St. Boniface, LXXXIX, 671. On the usefulness of these letters, ibid. On the manuscripts and the principal exemplar of this work, 672. On the style of those letters, 673.

SIRMONDUS (Jacques), most distinguished scholar, of the Society of Jesus, born at Riom in Auvergne in 1559 and died in 1651. He first published the writings of Commodianus, V, 198.---Posthumous notes on certain letters of Pope St. Innocent I, XX, 635 ff.---Preface to St. Augustine’s new sermons collected from ancient exemplars, 1631, XLVII, 382. Observations on each sermon, ibid. ff.---Sirmond published the works of St. Prosper of Aquitaine with notes at Paris in 1619.---Preface to the works of St. Prosper, ibid., 9. On the various editions, ibid. What was accomplished in this edition, 13. On the order of the works, ibid. On certain doubtful matters, 15.---Notice on St. Prosper’s letter to St. Augustine, LI, 53. Also on his letter to Rufinus, 73; on the poem *Against the Ungrateful*, 89; also on two epigrams, 147; on the epitaph of the Nestorian and Pelagian heresies, 151; on the responses to pious Augustine, 155; on the responses to the chapters, 173; on the responses to the extracts of the Genoese, 185; on the book *On Grace and Free Will*, 201; on the book *Against the Collator*, 211; on the exposition of the Psalms, 275; on the book of Sentences, 425; on the book of Epigrams, 495; on the *Chronicle*, 531; on the *Confession*, 607; on the poem to his wife, 609; on the poem *On Providence*, 615; on the book *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, 639; on the canons of the Council of Orange concerning grace and free will, 721; on the book *On the Promises and Predictions of God*, 729; on the new chronicle, 837.

Dedicatory letter in the works of Valerian, bishop of Cimiez. Whether Valerian ought to be called a saint, and whether he is found blameworthy in his doctrine: these two questions are answered, LII, 581.---Sirmond published the book *Predestined* at Paris in 1644. Preface to the anonymous author’s *Predestined*, LIII, 583. On errors concerning predestination, ibid. A certain book formerly and wrongly attributed to St. Augustine taught these errors; but the anonymous author refuted it in three books, 584, 585.

Notes on the letters of Saint Pope Hilary, LVIII, 13 ff. Likewise on the letters of Saints Lupus and Euphronius, 65 ff.—Preface to Victor of Vita’s *History of the Vandal Persecution*, LVIII, 141.—Observation on a fragment of Saint Veranus, LXXII, 599. Explanatory notes on the Council of Auxerre, 761. The savagery of the Vandal people, 141. They persecute Christians, 142. Victor of Vita’s work, ibid. On the author of this work, 143. By whom the title of the work was corrupted, 144. Chifflet’s opinion concerning Victor’s primacy, 145. Whether he is to be numbered among the saints, ibid. At what time he composed this history, 146. Another opinion of Chifflet, 147. What Victor’s history contains, 148. On ancient copies, 149. Its editions, ibid.—Notes on Victor’s writings, 179 ff.—Notice on the first appendix to Victor’s writings, 239. Notice on the second appendix, 265. Notice on the *Register of the African Church*, 257. Notes and observations on the same register, 275 ff.

Dedicatory letter in the works of Sidonius Apollinaris, addressed to Cardinal de Rochefoucauld, LVIII, 435.—Life of Sidonius Apollinaris prepared by Sirmond, 441. His family and native country, ibid. He unwillingly accepts the episcopate, ibid. His deeds, 442, and writings, ibid.—Notes and observations on Sidonius’s writings, [Col. 0393] 443 ff.—The Sidonian coronis, concerning certain philological questions, 747. Explanation concerning proper names of the Middle Ages, 749.—On the various editions of the code of ecclesiastical canons, LXVII, 135. A word to the reader, 137. Notice on the collection of canons by Dionysius Exiguus, 229.—Notice on Pope Vigilius’s letter to the envoys of the Franks, LXIX, 113. Notes on the life of Pope Pelagius, 391. Critical observation, 397. On the order of the letters, 399.—Notes on the letter of Pope John IV, LXXX, 601.—Sirmond published certain formularies according to Roman law, LXXXVII, 779.—Notes on the letters and canons of Saint Pope Gregory II, LXXIX, 49.—Likewise on the letters of Gregory III, 575. Note on the capitula of Pope Adrian, XCVI, 1068.—Prefaces to the sayings of Saint Augustine collected by Amulo of Lyons, CXVI, 105.—Sirmond’s preface to Hincmar’s works, CXXV, 46. Chronological synopsis of the works, ibid.—New edition of the works of Geoffrey, Abbot of Vendôme. Dedication, 1610, CLVII, 27. A word to the reader, 30.—Life of Geoffrey, ibid.—Notes on Geoffrey’s letters, 33 ff.

SMITH (John), learned Oxford doctor, edited the works of the Venerable Bede at Cambridge in 1722. His notes on Bede’s *On the Reckoning of Time*, XC, 321 ff. Editor’s notice on the book *On Speech* and on the revised book *On the Reckoning of Time*, 685.—Notes on the lives of the holy abbots, XCIV, 713 and throughout.—Preface to the martyrology, XCIV, 799.—Notes on Bede’s Martyrology, 799 ff.—Notice on Bede’s *Ecclesiastical History*, XCV, 18.—Notes on the same *History*, 21 ff.—Appendix, or observations on all Bede’s works, and especially on the *Ecclesiastical History*, 204. On the boundaries of the provinces of the Heptarchy, ibid. On the twenty-eight cities of Britain, 313. At what time Saint Alban flourished, 297. On Roman monuments in Britain, 301. On the Gregorian books, 313. On the donation of vestments, 314. On relics conveyed by Saint Augustine, 315. On the celebration of Easter, 317. On the clerical tonsure, 327. On ecclesiastical chant, 332. On the school founded by Sigeberht, king of the East Angles, 335. Catalogue of the relics of Durham Church, 356. On the dwelling Saint Chad had made for himself, 362. On the teachers of the Church, ibid. Various charters, 364 ff.—Indulgence granted by William, Bishop of Dunblane, to those visiting the incorrupt body of Saint Cuthbert, 390.

SOLLER (Jean-Baptiste), of the Society of Jesus, hagiographer, born at Herselt in 1669 and died in 1740. He annotated, corrected, and published Usuard’s Martyrology.—Dedication, CXXIII, 453 ff.—Preface. Brief survey of the whole work, 459. The affinity and connection of ancient martyrologies with one another and with Usuard’s, 665. New conjectures concerning the martyrologies of Bede and Florus, 482. On three other martyrologies related to Usuard’s, 489. On the martyrology which Rosweyde called and published as the ancient Roman Martyrology, 495. That it should be called Roman, against Valesius and Florentinius, 501. Refutation of opponents maintaining that this little Roman martyrology is not the very martyrology in question, 507. On the descent of Ado and Usuard, 531. On the manuscript codices of Usuard, 554. On codices of which we possess only extracts or variant readings, 573. The reliability, method, etc. of this edition, 580. Matters to be noted for the indexes, 582.—Notes and variant readings, 601 ff. Observations, 603 ff.

SOMMER (J.-C.), theologian and official of the Archbishop of Caesarea, born at Vallisvillers in Burgundy in 1661 and died in 1737.—Annotations on the life of Saint Pope Boniface IV, LXXX, 102.—Likewise on Saint Pope Deusdedit, 350.—On John VI, LXXXIX, 38. On John VII, 59. On Pope Constantine, 318. On Saint Pope Gregory, 458.—On Pope Stephen II, 974.—Analytical treatise on the authority and preeminence of the Holy See, CXXVII, 937. Arguments drawn from Holy Scripture, 937. From tradition, 939. Second- and third-century tradition concerning authority, 942. Fourth-century tradition, 946. Fifth-century tradition, 952. On Leo the Great, 959. Testimonies from Saint Augustine, 965.—Notes on the life of each Roman pontiff written by Anastasius, CXXVII, 1044 ff.

SOUCHET (J.-B.), Doctor of the Sorbonne, theologian, and canon of Chartres, died at Chartres in 1654. He enriched the works of Ivo of Chartres with observations, CLXII, 429 ff.

SPARAVERIUS (Francis), a Veronese nobleman and learned philologist, of uncertain date, exceptionally versed in Latin and Greek authors; by collating various codices of Zeno, he corrected, restored, and illustrated with notes the writings of that Doctor, XI, 215, 252. His annotations, 535 ff.

SPARK (Thomas). He edited Lactantius with notes at Oxford in 1684, VI, 107; VII, 10 and throughout.

STEWECHIUS (Godescalc). He corrected and enriched Arnobius’s works with notes in two editions, one published at Antwerp in [Col. 0394] 1587 and the other likewise at Antwerp in 1604, V, 359, 364. He is frequently cited in the commentaries on Arnobius.

SUHM (Peter Frederik), historian and man of letters, born at Copenhagen in 1728 and died in 1798.—Preliminary observations on the Life of Saint William, Abbot of Saint Thomas of Paraclete in Denmark, by an anonymous author, his disciple, and now collected and prepared by Dom Jacob Langebek, CCIX, 590.—Notice to the reader concerning Saint William’s letter, 635.—Likewise, notice concerning the testament of Absalon, Archbishop of Lund, 755. Appendix to William’s works.—Notes on the same testament, 761 ff.

SURIUS (Laurentius), Carthusian and ascetical writer, born at Lübeck in 1522 and died in 1578.

Life of Saint Anno, Bishop of Cologne, CXLIII, 1517. Prologue, ibid. Book I. The parents and education of Saint Anno, ibid. He is ordained bishop, 1520. He preaches frequently, 1523. Some plot his death, 1525. He reforms monasteries, 1529. Now beloved, now disliked by the emperor, 1535. A memorable saying, 1539. Book II. What Anno thought concerning sacred relics, 1543. He is displeased at being praised, 1545. Various miracles, 1546 ff. His devotion to Saint Severinus, 1551. A distinguished encomium of Saint Anno, 1563. Book III. Anno predicts his death, 1567. He urgently requests burial among the Siegburg community, 1571. He distributes everything to the poor, 1572. He happily departs to God, 1573. His funeral, 1574. He performs miracles after death, 1579 ff.

TEMPESTINI (F.), author of a translation of the Gothic Grammar and Glossaries from German into Latin.

Preface, XVIII, 879. Introduction, 881. On writing and orthography, 897. On the inflection of words, 945. On word-formation, 1001. On syntax, 1031. On the simple sentence, 1116. The compound sentence, 1183. Appendix: Pleonasm, 1223.—Translation of the Glossary of the Gothic language, 1237. Preface, ibid. Gothic-Latin Glossary, 1243.—Greek-Gothic Glossary, 1511.

THEINER (August), author of *Critical Investigations into the Principal Collections of Canons*. Rome, 1836.—Dissertation on the *Decree* attributed to Ivo, Bishop of Chartres, and on other collections of canons preceding Gratian, Rome, 1836. CLXI, L: How the tripartite collection relates to other collections of canons, LI. What distinction exists between the tripartite collection and Ivo’s works, LXVI.—Notice on Gregory, Roman presbyter, CLXIII, 751.—Encyclical letters from the cardinals who supported the cause of Alexander III, Rome, 1836. CC, 61.—Critical investigation into the compilation of decrees prepared by Laborans, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church.—Division of the work, CCIV, 870. On the sources used by Laborans, 873. On the order of the chapters, 880. On the sources he employed for Gratian’s *Decree*, 895. On the merit of the collection, 897. Appendix to the preceding investigation, 901.

THIBOUT (Louis), Parisian printer, born in 1667 and died in 1737, edited the works of Paulus Orosius.—His dedicatory letter, XXXI, 643.

THOMASIUS (Joseph Maria), priest of the Congregation of Regular Clerics at Rome, 1680. He published the Gelasian Sacramentary annotated by Muratori.

Preface, LXXIV, 1049. On the Petavian Codex, 1050. That codex is held by Morin, as also by Cardinal Bona, to be Gelasius’s, 1051. What John the Deacon declares, 1052. In what respects that codex differs from the Gregorian, 1053. Who have already illustrated it with annotations, 1056.

THOMASSIN (Louis), of the Congregation of the Oratory, distinguished ecclesiastical writer, born at Aix-en-Provence in 1619 and died in 1695.

Dissertation on the synods assembled under Pope Stephen regarding the baptism of heretics, III, 1217. Synopsis of it.—The calumny of the Innovators is refuted, 1217. What the calumny is; the controversy is twofold, 1219. Stephen is shown not to have erred from Firmilian, ibid.; from Cyprian, 1221; from the Council of Carthage, 1222; from Tertullian, ibid.; from Eusebius, 1223. Stephen is defended against Cyprian from Jerome, 1224; from Basil, 1227; from Innocent and Augustine, 1228; from Vincent of Lérins, 1230; from Hincmar, 1231. The second controversy is discussed, 1232. That Cyprian cannot be excused, 1233; from Jerome, Vincent of Lérins, and Augustine, 1234. That Stephen proceeded no further than threats, 1235. That Cyprian ought to have yielded to weightier authority, 1236. Another method of resolving the controversy, 1238. That this question concerns customs, not faith, is proved from Firmilian, 1238; from Cyprian himself, 1239; and from others, ibid. ff. Augustine frequently invokes plenary councils for regulating customs, 1245; by no means for questions of faith, 1247.

Dissertation on Stephen’s true judgment concerning the baptism of heretics.—It is shown that his judgment was not without reason, III, 1249. Whether Stephen accepted every baptism conferred by heretics, 1251. Whether he understood baptism in the name of Jesus, or in the name of the Trinity, [Col. 0395] 1253. Whether Stephen attributed excessive efficacy to baptism by heretics, 1255. Whether Stephen wished hands to be laid upon heretics who converted, 1258. Stephen, defender of apostolic tradition, 1265. Whether Stephen excommunicated those who rebaptized, 1268.

TILLIUS (John), Bishop of Meaux, dedicated a new edition of Lucifer’s works to Pius V in 1568, XIII, 759. Textual and critical notes.—Edition with notes of the writings of Saint Pacian, Bishop of Barcelona, XIII, 1031.—He edited the Capitularies of Charlemagne.—Preface to Charlemagne’s capitulary concerning images, XCVIII, 989. Annotation, 999 ff.

TIRENAEUS HAUTENAEUS (John), advocate of the treasury in the province of Rouen.

Dedicatory preface to William of Apulia’s poem on the deeds of the Normans in Sicily, Apulia, and Calabria, CXLIX, 1021.

TISSIER (Dom Bertrand), reformer of the Abbey of Bonnefont, died in 1670, author of the *Cistercian Library*.

Preface setting forth the life and catalogue of books of Blessed William, Abbot, CLXXX, 202.—Notice on Blessed Guerric, disciple of Saint Bernard and Abbot of Igny, CLXXXV, 9.—Notice on Aelred, Abbot of Rievaulx, CXCV, 205.—Notice on the book *On Spiritual Friendship*, 659.—Notice on Henry of Château-Marsiac, CCIV, 213.—Notice on Baldwin, Archbishop of Canterbury, 401.

TOINARD (Nicolas), antiquarian and philologist, born at Orléans in 1629 and died in 1706. He issued notes on Lactantius’s book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* at Utrecht in 1692, VI, 108. Notes on the aforementioned book, VII, 433 ff.

TRITHEMIUS (John), abbot, theologian, and critical scholar, born at Trittenheim in 1462 and died in 1546.

Notice on Eugippius, priest and abbot, LXII, 547.—Observation on Saint Adomnán, LXXXVIII, 725.—Notice on Paul Winfrid, deacon, author of the *History of the Lombards*, XCV, 431.—Notice on Smaragdus, Abbot of Spanheim, CII, 13.—Life of Rabanus Maurus with Bollandist notes, CVII, 67.—Life of Haymo, Bishop of Halberstadt, and review of his writings, CXVI, 189.—Life of Dom Rupert, Abbot of Deutz, CLXVII, 11.

TORINUS (Godfrey) of Bourges, edited the writings of Marcus Valerius Probus at Paris in 1510.

Historical notice on Marcus Valerius Probus, CXXX, 1117. Notice to the reader, ibid. Dedicatory letter, 1178.

TROMBELLI (John Chrysostom), celebrated philologist, born at Nonantola in 1697 and died in 1784.

Preface at the head of the book *On Penance* attributed to Saint Cyprian, IV, 1149; likewise observations on the title, purpose, and subject of the same book, 1157. Chapter 1. The title itself, *Exhortation concerning Penance*, is foreign to Latin idiom, ibid. What difficulty arises, 1159. On Cyprian’s apparently excessive severity and the incredible laxity of some. Chapter 2. On the interpretation and sense of certain passages of Scripture.

Preface to Hilary’s letter, or short treatise, X, 727. In which codex it was found, and to whom it should be attributed, ibid. To whom the same letter was sent, what its subject is, and when it was written, 741.—Very extensive annotations on the aforementioned letter, 751–825.—Dissertation 1 on the same letter attributed to Hilary, 825. Whether all sensible things described by Moses were created for humanity’s sake, ibid. Dissertation 2 on certain passages of the same letter in which the relations of Father and Son are expressed, X, 839. Dissertation 3 on the human being created in God’s image, 848.—Preface to the sermon on the dedication of a church attributed to Saint Hilary, X, 877.—Notice to the reader on the book of *Soliloquies* attributed to Augustine, brought to light from obscurity, XLVII, 1157.—Notice on the Florilegium of Saint Prudentius of Troyes, CXV, 1421.

TURCIUS (Octavius), canon.

He illustrated an ancient Sacramentary with notes.—Preliminary observations on it, CLI, 826. Notes, 829 ff.

UGHELLI (Ferdinand), ecclesiastical writer, born at Florence in 1595 and died in 1670. Author of *Italia Sacra*.

Historical notice on Saint Alphanus, Bishop of Benevento, LXXX, 325.—Observation on the notice concerning Damian, Bishop of Pavia, LXXXVII, 1261.—Historical notice on Felix, Bishop of Ravenna, LXXXIX, 357.—Likewise on Saint Benedict Crispus, Bishop of Milan, 361.—Notice on Maxentius, Patriarch of Aquileia, CVI, 50. Notice on the poem of Cosmas of Iapygia in honor of Saints Theopompus and his companions, CXXXIII, 879.—Notice on John, Bishop of Sabina, CXLIII, 907.—Notice on Leo, Bishop of Atina, 1415.—Notice on Alphanus, Archbishop of Salerno, CXLVII, 1214.—Notice on the Life of Saint Secundinus, Bishop of Troja, 1293.—Notice on Angilbert, Archbishop of Milan, CLI, 1259.—Notice on Anselm, Archbishop of Milan, CLV, 1653.—Notice on John of Marsica, [Col. 0396] Bishop of Tusculum, CLX, 1035.—Notice on Conon, Cardinal Bishop of Palestrina, CLXIII, 1431.—Historical notice on Matthew, Cardinal Bishop of Albano, CLXXIII, 1261.—Historical notice on Henry of Château-Marsiac, Abbot of Clairvaux, CCIV, 211. And innumerable diplomas of Roman pontiffs.

ULIMMERIUS (John), Regular Canon of the Monastery of Saint Martin at Louvain, published sermons and other minor works of Saint Augustine at Louvain in 1564.

Preface, XLVII, 377.—Preface on Possidius’s short catalogue, addressed to Jacobus Pamele, 568. Observations on the Life of Saint Augustine written by Possidius, 569.

USSERMANN (Aemilian), learned Benedictine of the Abbey of the Black Forest, born at Saint Ulrich in 1737 and died in 1798.—An eulogy of Herman the Lame, illustrated with notes, CXLIII, 26.—Preliminary dissertation on Herman the Lame’s Chronicle, 31. On his reputation and learning, ibid. Editions of Herman’s Chronicle, 33. Manuscript codices, 34. Plan and sources of the new edition, 42. Method of the new edition, 51. On Berthold, continuator of Herman, 52. Annotation, 55 ff.—Preface to the Chronicle of Peterhausen Monastery, CXLIII, 271.—Inquiry into the lineage of the Counts of Bregenz, 275. The authentic genealogy of the counts from charters and contemporary writers, 278. The genealogical system of Saint Gebhard, 287. Genealogical table of the Counts of Bregenz by the same Father Saint Gebhard, 299.—Notes, 301 ff.—Notes on Herman the Lame’s sequence concerning the Blessed Virgin Mary, 443.—Life of Saint Otto, Bishop of Bamberg, CLXXIII, 1267. Writers of his life, his native country and studies, 1269. Otto at the imperial court, 1271. He is elected bishop, 1273. His various deeds, 1276 ff. Synod of Bamberg, 1310. His death, 1313.

URSTISIUS (Christoph), in 1587 at Frankfurt, edited Herman the Lame’s Chronicle with notes and corrections, CXLIII, 33. Notes on the continuator of Herman’s Chronicle, 363.

VALERIUS (Augustine), Cardinal Bishop of Verona, wrote in 1586 a dedicatory letter to Sixtus V, prefixed to the edition of Saint Zeno of Verona, XI, 237. He greatly values Zeno and his writings, ibid. What Schoenemann thinks of this edition, 247.

VALESIUS (Henri), learned philologist and critic, born at Paris in 1603 and died in 1676. He edited the works of Constantine the Great with critical notes and corrections, VIII, 253 ff. through 283. Likewise, from 402 through 554, he treated the Greek portion in particular.—His notes, 751 ff.

VALLARSI (Domenico), priest of outstanding learning, born at Verona in 1702 and died in 1771. He edited the works of Saint Jerome at Verona from 1734 to 1756, assisted by the labors of Maffei and other scholars.

Dedication to Pope Clement XII, XXII, VI. General preface. The excellence of Saint Jerome’s works, VII. The need for a new edition, ibid. Why he undertakes it, IX. This preface has three parts, ibid. Part I, concerning manuscript collections, ibid. Part II, on the character of Saint Jerome’s works and those that have been lost, XVIII. Part III, concerning what has been accomplished in this edition, XXXVIII.

Preface to Volume I. The merits of Saint Jerome’s letters, XLIII. The confusion of older editions in their recension, ibid. Treatises and minor works are placed elsewhere, XLV. Five letters not yet published, ibid. Likewise another six, XLVII. Five classes of letters, their subjects, etc., ibid. First class: those written by Jerome from 370 to 380, L. Second class, 382–385, LIV. Third class, 386–410, LIX. Fourth class, 400–420, namely to the end of his life, LXXVIII.—Notes on the anciently written Life of Jerome, XXII, 175. What should be thought of this Life, whether it is by Gennadius, ibid., note.—Notice concerning the work *On the Death of Jerome*, 239. Likewise on a fragment of Saint Augustine, *On the Glories of Blessed Jerome*, 281; and another, by Cyril of Jerusalem, *On the Wonders of the Holy Father Jerome*, 289. Critical and textual notes throughout Volume XXII.

Preface to Volume II of Saint Jerome, on the various arrangement of the minor works, XXIII, 9. Notes placed below the text, 17 ff. Notice on the three lives of Saints Paul, Hilarion, and Malchus, XXIII, 14. Likewise notice on Didymus’s book *On the Holy Spirit*, 102. Critical notes, 103. On the *Dialogue against the Luciferians*, 154. Notes, ibid. and throughout. Notice on the book *On Perpetual Virginity*, 181. Likewise on the two books *Against Jovinian*, 205. On the book *Against Vigilantius*, 338. Notes, 339 and throughout. *Against John of Jerusalem*, 351. Notice on the book *Against Rufinus*, 395. Likewise on the *Dialogue against the Pelagians*, 495. On the book *On Illustrious Men*, 598.

Preface to Volume III, XXIII, 765. What order it follows, ibid. Preface to the book *On Hebrew Names*, 771.

Preface to the book *On the Sites and Names of Hebrew Places*, 859. Notice on Jerome’s geographical table, 927. Preface to the book *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, XXIII, [Col. 0397] 935. Critical notes on the text, ibid. and throughout. Preface to the commentary on Ecclesiastes, 1009. Notes, ibid. ff. Notes on Origen’s homilies translated by Jerome, 1118. Notice on Greek fragments of Hebrew names, 1143.—Notice on the book of the names of Hebrew places, 1295. Likewise on the minor work *On the Blessings of Jacob*, 1307. On the short book *On the Ten Temptations of God by the People of Israel in the Wilderness*, 1317. Notice on the Hebrew questions in the Books of Kings and Chronicles, 1327 ff. Likewise on the exposition of Job, 1401.

Preface to Volume IV, XXIV, 9. In what year he wrote these commentaries, ibid. Against whom, XI. Why translations of Origen’s homilies are added, 13. It is shown, against some critics, not to be from Jerome’s pen, ibid. ff. Critical notes attached to the text, throughout Volume XXIV. Notice on Origen’s homilies, 900.

Preface to Volume V of Jerome. On its arrangement and order, XXV, 9. Which Paris editions are not admitted, and why, ibid. Observations on Huet and Genebrard, ibid.; and on Origen’s homilies translated into Latin by Jerome, XI. When and how long Jerome wrote on Daniel and Ezekiel, 12–13. Critical notes attached to the text throughout Volume XXV.

Preface to Volume VI. On the commentaries on the twelve minor prophets, XXV, 809. On the Holy Father’s ability in expounding them, ibid. On the time at which Jerome wrote them, 811.

Preface to Volume VII. On the eminent genius of Saint Jerome, XXVI, 9. What parts of the New Testament the holy Doctor expounded, ibid. On what occasion he wrote the individual works, 10–11. How he translated Origen’s homilies on Luke, ibid. At what time he translated these homilies, 13. How the individual works are arranged, ibid. Critical notes attached to the text, 15 ff.—Notice on the Breviary on the Psalms, XXVI, 801. On the excellence of this book, although spurious, ibid. How its style differs from Jerome’s, ibid. It defends not merely views alien to, but views wholly contrary to, Jerome’s, 803. This is proved from the testimonies of the author himself, ibid. Other arguments, 805. Objections are answered, 807. Not even Florus, Deacon of Lyons, is its author, ibid. and 809. What Dom Martianay thinks, ibid. What Erasmus and Marianus report, 811. On the codices of this Breviary, ibid. On a certain exposition of the Psalms under Jerome’s name in the Milan Library, Codex C. N. 301, 813. Its description, ibid. It should be attributed to Saint Columbanus, ibid.

Preface to Volume VIII. It contains the Chronicles, XXVII, 9. They are precious monuments of antiquity, ibid. On the editors of this little work, ibid. Eusebius, the first author of chronicles: what sort of writer he was, 11. Julius Africanus composed a similar work, ibid. How Eusebius is supported in many cases, 13. Controversy concerning the integrity of Eusebius, ibid. Nothing has reached us except what Jerome transmitted to us, 17. According to Scaliger’s testimony, ecclesiastical learning owes more to no one than to Jerome, 19. How Scaliger was led into error regarding Jerome’s translation, 22. To what year this translation should be assigned, 23. On Scaliger’s edition, 27.—Critical notes attached to the text, 33 ff.

Preface to Volume IX. On the translation of the Holy Books from Hebrew, and why it is included here, XXVIII, 9. What place it occupies in the Benedictine edition, ibid. It is included for understanding the notes, 11. On the different wording of the title, 14. The efforts of Charlemagne and Alcuin to correct the Bible, ibid. Thus the Alcuinian codex came to be commended, 18. Comparison of ancient codices, 20. Saint Augustine’s judgment on correcting sacred codices, 23. What authority Jerome’s version possesses, 26. On the year in which he completed it, ibid. He seems to have translated the whole Old Testament, 27.—Critical notes on these works of Jerome, 147 and throughout.

Preface to Volume X. On those works Jerome translated from the Greek text when the Hebrew was lacking, XXIX, 9. What kind of labor this was, ibid. On those that have been lost, ibid. Arguments proving that he translated other books besides those listed, XI. The method of his work, 14. Some remarks on the individual books, 15. On the Verona Codex, 19.—Notice on the Psalter, revised once and then again, 114.—Preface to Volume XI. On spurious works, XXX, 9. Erasmus’s classification, ibid. That of Martianay, XI. How Jerome’s style and genius should be investigated, ibid.—Notice on Pelagius’s letter to Demetrias, XXX, 13. Likewise on the letter to the daughters of Gerontius, 45; on the letter to Marcella, 50; on the letter to a sick friend, 61; again to a friend, 105; on the letter to Paula and Eustochium, 112; on another letter, 145; on the letter concerning the seven orders of the Church, 147. Notice on the letter in praise of virginity, 162. On the letter to Praesidius concerning the Paschal candle, 181. On the letter concerning true circumcision, 188. Likewise on the treatise concerning the observance of vigils, 232. On the letter to Damasus, 292, 293, 294.—Notice on the homilies to monks, 311. Likewise on the Rule of Monks, 319. Likewise on the penitential canons, 425. Notice [Col. 0398] on the martyrology attributed to him, 433. Likewise on the book of the count, 485.—Notice on the exposition of the Gospel of Matthew, 531. Likewise on the exposition of Mark’s Gospel: preface, 589. Notice on the commentaries on the letters of Saint Paul, 643.

VALLINIUS (Renatus). He published the works of Severinus Boethius at Nantes with notes, corrections, and variant readings.—Variant readings of the books *On the Consolation of Philosophy*, LXIII, 863 ff.

VAN DE PUTTE (D.-F.), rector of the Episcopal College at Bruges, Ghent, 1843.—French-language introduction to the *Greater Chronicle* of Aldenburg Abbey, appended to Hariulf, CLXXIV, 1506.

VENDEMOERUS (Joseph) and VANHECKIUS (Joseph), Jesuit priests and continuators of the Bollandists, provided at Brussels in 1845 a notice on Saint Ambrose, Bishop of Cahors, LXXXIX, 1197. The saint’s remembrance in sacred calendars and his cult, ibid. Saint Ambrose’s episcopate and the deeds performed during it, 1203. Whether he is the author of the books *On the Mysteries* and *On the Sacraments*, commonly attributed to Saint Ambrose of Milan, 1213. Saint Ambrose travels to Rome, 1225.

VERGERIUS (Pier Paolo), Bishop of Capodistria; finally, while opposing the Lutherans, he passed over to their side, and died in 1565. He produced an oration in praise of Saint Jerome, XXII, 231.

VIT (Dom Vincent). Date and place are lacking. He edited, with notes and observations, Hildebert, Bishop of Le Mans’s book *On Moral Philosophy*. Preface to the reader, CLXXI, 1004. Notes, 1007 ff.

VIVES (Juan Luis), highly learned Spanish man of letters, born at Valencia in 1492 and died in 1540; he became a doctor at Oxford in England, prepared an edition of certain works of Saint Augustine, and illustrated them with notes.

Preface, XLVII, 435.—Preface to the book *The City of God*, 439. On earlier interpreters of this work, 445. Who the Goths were and how they captured Rome, 452. Observations on each book of this work, 458.

WADDING (Dom Luke), of the Order of Saint Francis, theologian and historian. Born at Waterford in 1588 and died in 1657.—Preliminary notice to certain minor works, CXLIX, 567.

WAITZ (Georg), Doctor of Philosophy, edited the writings of Bertharius, priest of Verdun, illustrated with notes.—Preface to Bertharius’s book *On the Deeds of the Bishops of Verdun*, CXXXII, 502. He edited Widukind’s book *On the Deeds of the Saxons* with notes and variant readings.—Preface, CXXXVII, 115. On the author and his age, ibid. His purpose in the work, 117. What aids the editor used, 119. On the author’s corrections and elucidations, 122.—Notes and variant readings, 125 ff.—Notice on the Annals of Saint Benignus’s Monastery at Dijon, by Abbot William, CXLI, 873.—Notes and variant readings on the aforesaid Annals, 875.—Notice on Marianus and his Chronicle, with notes and variant readings, CXLVII, 602.—Preface to the Chronicles of Ekkehard of Aura, CLIV, 435. Explanatory notes, 435 ff.—Prolegomena to the *Deeds of Trier*, with notes and observations, CLIV, 1063. On those who wrote about the affairs of Trier, ibid. ff. On Trithemius’s errors, 1069. That the *Deeds of Trier* were not written before the twelfth century, 1070. It is probable that they originated in the Monastery of Saint Eucharius, 1074. Preliminary observations on the *Deeds of the Bishops of Metz*, by an anonymous author, CLXIII, 575.—Notes and variant readings on the same deeds, 579 ff.—Preface to the *Deeds of the Bishops of Verdun* and of the Abbots of Saint Vito, CCIV, 915. Notes and variant readings, 919 ff.

WALCH (Johann Georg), theologian and learned philologist, born at Meiningen in 1693 and died in 1775, edited Lactantius’s writings at Leipzig in 1715. He added notes that bear the stamp of a youthful author, VI, 107; VIII, 89 and throughout.

WARTON (Henry), born in England, died in 1694; author of *Anglia Sacra*, London, 1691.—Notice on Eadmer, monk of Canterbury of the Order of Saint Benedict, CIX, 342. Review of his works, 343.—On the death of Blessed Lanfranc, Archbishop of Canterbury, CI, 99.—Notice on Ernulf, Bishop of Rochester, CLXIII, 1441.—Notes on Ernulf’s collections, 1443.

Dissertation on Ælfric or Elfric, Archbishop of Canterbury, CXXXIX, 1459. On the time when he held the see, ibid. What order he belonged to, 1461. What is established concerning Elfric, 1462. What William of Malmesbury relates concerning Ælfric the Grammarian, 1163. His opinion is rejected, 1465. Ælfric writes to Bishop Vultinus in 908. He is sent to the Cernelian monastery to restore discipline, 1488. Ælfric succeeded Wulfstan the Younger, 1470.

WELCHMAN (Edward), born at Corsham in Wiltshire in 1664 and died in 1727. This philologist issued a second English edition of Novatian’s writings around 1724, with notes and many corrections, reprinted by Galland, III, Preface LII and 893 throughout.

WELSER (Mark), learned historian and philologist, born at Augsburg in 1568 and died in 1614.—Conjecture concerning the author of the synodal sermon, CXXXV, 1069.

WILKINS (David). He provided an observation on Dinoth, Abbot, LXXX, 22 ff.—Observations on the decree that property belonging to God and the Church is not to be alienated, 345 ff.—Notes on Pope Formosus’s letter, CXXIX, 848.

WILMANS (Roger). Cited by Pertz (no date or place is given). In the introduction to fragments of Honorius’s *Summa of All Things* and *Image of the World*: notice on Honorius of Autun, CLXXII, 9. Explanatory notes on the notice, ibid.

WISCH (Dom Charles de), learned bibliographer, prior of the Abbey of the Dunes, died in 1666.

Notice on Elias of Coxyde, seventh abbot of the Cistercian Abbey of the Dunes, CCIX, 992.—He published at Antwerp in 1654 the works of Alan of Lille.—Dedicatory letter, CCX, 27.—Historical account of the life and death of Alan of Lille, 35. His country and birth, ibid. He assumes the monastic habit among the Cistercians, 37. He remains long unknown among the lay brothers, 38. How he became known at Rome and among his own people, 39. His death and burial, 40.—Preface to the reader, CCX, 51. Notice on Alan’s *Summa on the Art of Preaching*, 110.—Notice to the reader on the minor work *On the Six Wings of the Cherubim*, 266.—Likewise on the book *On the Catholic Faith*, 306.—Notice on the book *On the Complaint of Nature*, 430.—On the *Anticlaudianus*, 482. On the book of Parables, 379.—Preface to the *Theological Rules* of Blessed Alan of Lille, 618.

WOWERS, WOWERIUS (Jan), born at Antwerp in 1576, friend of Justus Lipsius, died in 1635. He added notes and observations to Tertullian’s works.

WURDTWEIN (Stephan Alexander), learned antiquarian, born in the Bishopric of Worms in 1719 and died in 1796.—Preface with notes to Saint Boniface’s letters, LXXXIX, 675.—Another preface to the same letters, 678.—Notes, 689 and throughout.

ZACCHARIAS (Francesco Antonio), learned Jesuit and librarian to the Duke of Modena, Venice, 1758. He edited the corrected works of Saint Isidore, illustrated with annotations, LXXXI, 256. Annotations on the book of *Etymologies*, LXXXII, 854 ff.

ZIEGELBAUER (Magnoald), learned Benedictine, born at Eningen in 1696 and died in 1750.—Historical notice on Robert, King of the Franks, CXLI, 897.

[Col. 0399]

## XII. BIOGRAPHICAL INDEX, ARRANGED ALPHABETICALLY, OF ALL THE DOCTORS, FATHERS, WRITERS, AND OTHERS OF THE WESTERN CHURCH WHOSE WORKS AND WRITINGS, EVEN THE SMALLEST, ARE PRINTED IN THE NEW SERIES OF THE *LATIN PATROLOGY*, FROM TERTULLIAN IN A.D. 245 TO POPE INNOCENT III IN A.D. 1216.

## NOTICE.

After the general index of authors, arranged in a twofold order—chronological and alphabetical—we have not thought it burdensome, for the reader’s greater benefit, to compile that other index which we call biographical, since it presents a concise account of every writer, donor, or founder whose writings, donations, and foundations are published or merely mentioned in the course of the *Patrologia Latina*.

[**BIOGRAPHICAL INDEX.**]

## A

[Col. 0399]

**ABAELARDUS (Peter),** abbot of the monastery of Rhuys. A man renowned for intellect among the more distinguished men of the Middle Ages, perhaps more renowned for his misfortunes and repentance, if Peter the Venerable is to be believed. He was born in Brittany in 1079. He was at once theologian, philosopher, orator, and poet. He died in 1142. There are letters, sermons, and various works by him, both philosophical and theological. (See Heloise), CLXXVIII.

**ABBAUDUS,** abbot of an unknown monastery. He was a contemporary of Abelard, against whom he wrote a brief treatise on the breaking of Christ’s body in 1130, CLXVI, 1340.

**ABBO (St.),** bishop of Metz. Raised to the episcopate in 690, he wisely governed the Church of Metz until 700, when he died. He made the old abbey of St. Felix, later called St. Clement’s, into a parish. Of his writings only a letter to St. Desiderius, bishop of Cahors, survives, LXXXVII, 217, 262.

**ABBO,** son of Felix and Rustica, and grandson of Symphorianus, bishop of Gap, who had founded the monastery of St. Peter of Novalesa in the Valley of Susa, executed a testament by which he endowed that monastery and at the same time bequeathed innumerable goods situated near the Alps to various churches and persons, in 739, LXXXVIII, 1290.

**ABBO,** son of one Gerhard, sold to the brethren of St. Saviour of Werden two hides situated in the village of Lopanheldi, and in addition five slaves, for twenty-four pounds. The transaction was carried out in the monastery of Werden in 835, XCIX, 805.

**ABBO,** monk of Saint-Germain. A Neustrian by birth, he flourished under Kings Charles and Odo. He wrote sermons and poems, and three books *On the Parisian War*, in 923, CXXXII, 721.

**ABBO (St.),** abbot of Fleury. Born in the territory of Orléans, he was first entrusted to the monastery of Fleury to be educated, and was afterward made abbot of the same monastery. He died in 1004. Several writings of various kinds by him survive, CXXXIX, 375.

**ABEDOC,** Irish abbot. Nothing has been handed down about him except that he arranged an ancient collection of canons into sixty-five books (eighth century), XCVI, 1279.

**ABSALO,** bishop of Roskilde and successor of Peter, flourished about 1214. A letter and several charters by him survive, CCIX, 678, 745 and passim.

**ABSALO,** bishop of Lund, confirmed for the brethren of the Church of St. Thomas of Paraclete in Denmark all privileges formerly granted to them by himself or by others. Bartholinius assigns this charter to 1178, CCIX, 751, 757.

**ABSALO,** abbot of Springiersbach, of the Order of Canons Regular of St. Augustine, near Trier. Called from the abbey of St. Victor at Paris to govern the aforesaid abbey, he introduced the pious observances which he had learned in his own monastery. He left fifty festival sermons and flourished about 1203, CCXI, 9.

[Col. 0401]

**ARCHADEUS,** a count, offered his own son, named Hilduin, to God, to remain permanently in the monastery of St. Remigius at Rheims—a practice then not uncommon—about 880, CL, 601, note.

**ACHARDUS,** first abbot of St. Victor at Paris and later bishop of Avranches. A Norman by origin, born in the county of Domfront, he wrote many learned little works. He died in 1172, CXCVI, 1371.

**ADALAIS,** lady of Évreux, formerly wife of Hugh, promised to pay an annual rent of twelve Byzantines to the chapter of the Holy Sepulchre in 1135, CLV, 1196.

**ADALARDUS,** abbot of Sithiu. He was first made a canon under Fridugisus, then succeeded Abbot Hugh in 861. There survives a charter of his by which he granted a precarial tenure of a certain piece of land to Odwin in 863. He died in 864, CXXXVI, 1229.

**ADALBERO,** archbishop of Rheims, son of Godfrey, count of Ardennes, studied in the abbey of Gorze and advanced so greatly that by unanimous consent he was judged worthy of promotion to this dignity in 969. He founded the monastery of Mouzon, into which he introduced monks of the Order of St. Benedict. He died in 988. Letters by him survive, CXXXVII, 503.

**ADALBERO,** surnamed Ascelin, bishop of Laon. Born in Lorraine into a most noble family, he had Gerbert as his teacher. Though young, he was promoted to the episcopate under King Lothair; he died in 1030. Some metrical writings by him survive, among them a poem addressed to Robert, king of the Franks, CXLI, 567.

**ADALBERO or ALBERO,** bishop of Liège. Several charters of his survive in favour of the monasteries of Cluny and Stavelot, from 1124 to 1139, CLXXXIX, 1055, 1477.

**ADALBERTUS,** scholastic of Metz, born of noble family; first a deacon and monk, he was raised to the priesthood. According to Trithemius, he was a man endowed with every kind of learning. Among his writings are especially listed the *Compendium of the Moral Works of St. Gregory* and a *Chronicle of the Bishops of Metz* down to Adalbero. He died in 979, CXXXVI, 1309.

**ADALBERTUS (St.),** bishop of Prague and martyr. He was born in Sclavonia of noble stock in 939. He studied under the distinguished Adalbert, to whom his father sent him, and from whom he afterward took his name. On returning to his native country, he began to preach the Gospel and was soon made bishop; finally he was crowned with martyrdom in 997. A homily for the feast of St. Alexis the Confessor is attributed to him, CXXXVII, 859.

**ADALBERTUS,** priest and monk, afterward provost of Nemetum. He is the man whom Berthold, or Bernaldus, thus honours in his *Chronicle*: “Doctor Adalbertus, eloquent in deed and word, having for thirty years been crucified to the world and at last brought to evangelical perfection, departed to the Lord on 3 December 1079.” There survive letters by him to the aforesaid Bernaldus concerning those who dared reject the pope, CXLVIII, 1141, 1166, 1217.

**ADALBERTUS,** archbishop of Mainz. Previously a monk of the monastery of St. Maximin, he wrote to Pope Calixtus II to inform him of the afflictions inflicted by Emperor Henry upon Cono, bishop of Strasbourg, after Cono had been reconciled with the Roman Church. He flourished about 1136, CLXIII, 1356. See also CLXXII, 1335 and CLXXIX, 657.

**ADALEGIDA, countess.** See **AMEDAEUS, count.**

**ADALGERUS,** bishop of an uncertain see. We have discovered nothing concerning him. There remains to us only an exhortation to Nonsuinda the recluse, or a book, *On the Cultivation of Virtues*, about 964, CXXXIV, 915.

**ADALGISELUS GRIMO,** an illustrious and wealthy man, when near death bequeathed by testament all the goods which he possessed to the monastery, hospice, and poor people of the castle of Longiacum, where he had lived. He dictated the testament himself to the deacon Erchnulf in 634, LXXXVII, 1343.

**ADALHARDUS (St.),** abbot of Corbie. Said to have been born in a village of Belgium, he piously and successfully held various offices after professing the monastic life. The year of his death is not entirely certain, but it was about 826, CV, 533; CXX, 1507.

**ADALHUNUS,** mayor of the community, or of the Church, of St. Emmeram, with episcopal permission completed a certain exchange of lands with Meginhard, ninth century, CXXIX, 957.

**ADALSINDA,** abbess of the monastery of St. Martin at Dornatiacum, founded by her parents Amalgarius and Aquilina. Since she was subjected there to various vexations, she gave her monastery to the monks of Bèze in 657, in order that she might retire to the monastery of St. Peter, LXXXVIII, 1166.

**ADALUNGUS,** archpriest, donated to the monastery of St. Emmeram the property he possessed in the place called Sullactata, though it was to be held only after the death of his nephews Amalungus and Adalungus (ninth century), CXXIX, 958.

[Col. 0402]

**ADAMNANUS (St.),** abbot of a monastery on the Scottish island of Hy. He was distinguished by innocence and simplicity of life. According to Vossius, he flourished about 690. He wrote the *Life of St. Columba*, LXXXVIII, 721.

**ADAMUS,** canon of Bremen. He was skilled in history and geography and laboured in spreading the Christian faith. He composed a history of the churches of Hamburg and Bremen from 788 to 1072. The years of his birth and death are uncertain, CXLVI, 433.

**ADAMUS,** regular canon of St. Victor at Paris. A Breton by birth, distinguished for learning and scholarship, he flourished around the time of the celebrated Master Hugh. He expounded St. Jerome’s prologues to both the Old and New Testaments. He also produced a compendium on biblical words. He died in 1177, CXCVI, 1422.

**ADAMUS SCOTUS,** Premonstratensian canon. He long held a chair of theology. The church of Whithorn, which had become regular and was vacant, chose him as abbot and bishop. He died in 1180. He left ascetical works, CXCVIII, 9.

**ADAMUS,** abbot of Perseigne, of the Cistercian Order, flourished from 1190, distinguished for eloquence and piety. He produced writings chiefly on the Blessed Virgin Mary, whom he always venerated with the greatest reverence. He died in 1203, CCXI, 579.

**ADAMUS,** abbot of Ebra, lived at the end of the twelfth century. He wrote to St. Hildegard, commending himself to her prayers and seeking her advice as to whether he ought to retain or resign the office of abbot, CXCVII, 190.

**ADELA,** daughter of Dagobert II. On behalf of the monastery of Palatiolum near Trier, of which she was abbess, she wrote a testament in 732, specifying what she had left to her son Alberic and her sister Regentrudis. She entrusted it to the judgment and protection of the bishops of Trier, LXXXVIII, 1286.

**ADELA,** formerly wife of Hubert, lord of the castle of Medanta, now advanced in age, declares that she held certain lands from her parents without lawful title, and therefore restored them to their owners, namely the monks of St. Peter of Chartres, in 1066, CLV, 318.

**ADELA** (perhaps read *Isabella*), queen of the Franks and wife of Philip Augustus, at the request of Maurice, bishop of Paris, decreed that the canons of St. Exuperius should pay him fifty solidi whenever he celebrated Mass in their church on the feast-day of its patron, but nothing if his archdeacon celebrated, or on any other day of the year, in 1190, CCV, 912.

**ADELAIDIS,** surnamed Riveria, daughter of Guido Osmundus, with the consent of her mother Arenburgis, granted to Lord Robert of Arbrissel and his pious congregation the valley of Fontevraud, so that he might build there a church in honour of the Blessed Virgin Mary. There are two texts of this charter (twelfth century), CLXII, 1104.

**ADELBERTUS,** bishop of Verdun. He flourished after the middle of the twelfth century. He wrote to St. Hildegard, abbess of the monastery of St. Rupert at Bingen, CXCVII, 174.

**ADELBOLDUS.** See **GUNDWINUS.**

**ADELBOLDUS,** bishop of Utrecht. Born of noble family, he was first counsellor to Emperor Henry II, then became a monk at Sobiensis, of the Benedictine Order; in 1008 he was chosen bishop of Utrecht. He died in 1027. He wrote lives of St. Henry and St. Walburga, CXL, 1036.

**ADELGORIUS or ADELGOTUS,** archbishop of Magdeburg, flourished at the beginning of the twelfth century. A letter of his to Erchambert, abbot of Corbie, survives, about 1140, CLVII, 483.

**ADELHEIDIS,** abbess of Gandersheim, flourished in the twelfth century. She had been educated by St. Hildegard, to whom she sent a letter requesting the intercession of Hildegard and her sisters, and that mutual fellowship might remain between the two convents, CXCVII, 317.

**ADELINA COQUILLA,** with the consent of her husband Bartholomew and her son Guidard, bequeathed to Clairvaux Abbey whatever she possessed at Petrecinium and within its boundaries, through the hands of Godfrey, bishop of Langres, in 1147, CLXXXV, 989.

**ADELMANNUS,** bishop of Brescia. Under Fulbert, the very famous master of the school of Chartres, he devoted himself to the study of letters. He was placed over the Church of Brescia in 1048 and governed it until his death in 1061. There survive a letter by him and some alphabetic verses concerning illustrious men of his age, CXLIII, 1279.

**ADELWOLDUS.** See **ETHELWOLDUS.**

**ADEMARUS,** monk of St. Cybard at Angoulême. Born about 988 into a noble Aquitanian family, he was educated in the monastery of St. Eparchius at Angoulême; afterward he went to Limoges to his uncle Adalbert and studied under Rotger. Returning thence to Angoulême, he entered the monastery of St. Cybard and was ordained priest. He died in 1029. He wrote three books of histories and a letter concerning St. Martial, CXLI, 9.

**ADEMARUS,** viscount of Limoges, and his wife Humberga gave the abbey of St. Martial to Hugh, abbot of Cluny, to govern in 1062, CLIX, 957.

**ADEMARUS,** viscount of Scales and afterward abbot of Tulle. Before taking the monastic habit, he gave to the monastery of St. Martin everything which he possessed by hereditary right. Tenth century, CXXXII, 469.

**ADEMARUS,** the viscount who, together with Viscount Arthmannus, founded the monastery of Brunechilde in the district of Cahors, entrusting its government to Hunaldo of Moissac and Hugh, abbot of Cluny, in 1082, CLIX, 971.

**ADEODATUS (St.),** pope, formerly a monk distinguished for piety and gentleness. He died in 676. A letter of his to all the bishops of Gaul, and a privilege granted to the monks of Canterbury, survive, LXXXVII, 1139.

**ADHELMUS (St.),** bishop of Sherborne, was of the most illustrious English lineage. At the monastery of Malmesbury he first became a monk, then priest and abbot, and was finally raised to the see of Sherborne in 705. After four or five years as bishop he died. Fourteen letters, a *Treatise in Praise of Virginity*, and charters by him survive, LXXXIX, 63.

**ADINULFUS and LANDULFUS,** sons of one Gregory, renounced their right in the castle of Falbateria in Italy in favour of Pope Alexander III, from whom they afterward received it as a fief in 1178, CC, 1372.

**ADO,** abbot. He bestowed many gifts upon the basilica of St. Remigius at Rheims in 715. Mabillon conjectures that he was abbot of St. Remigius at Rheims; but Flodoard, speaking of him, says only “a certain abbot,” which he would not have said of the abbot of St. Remigius, LXXXVIII, 1261.

**ADO (St.),** bishop of Vienne. Born of noble stock in the diocese of Sens, he first embraced monastic life and devoted himself to letters and history. He died in 875. He left not a few writings, among which the *Martyrology* should be noted, CXXIII, 9.

**ADOLPHUS,** archbishop of Cologne. He flourished at the beginning of the twelfth century; he wrote to Pope Innocent III asking that Otto of Saxony be crowned king of Italy in 1209, CCXVI, 1003.

**ADOLPHUS of Nassau,** king of the Romans. He lived in the time of Pope Boniface VIII and Philip the Fair, king of the Franks. A letter of his to Guy of Dampierre, count of Flanders, survives, 1297, CLXXXV, 1856.

**ADREWALDUS,** monk of Fleury. According to Renart, he flourished in the time of Louis the Pious. He wrote several Lives and a book on the body and blood of Christ against John Scotus. He died about 878, CXXIV, 900.

**ADRIAN I, pope.** Still a deacon, he was raised to the Apostolic See after Stephen III. Born at Rome of a noble family, he was distinguished in learning and virtue; he died in 797. Several letters by him survive, XCVI, 1168.

**ADRIAN II, pope.** A Roman by birth, son of Talarus, who afterward became a bishop; he died in 872. He left letters and decrees, CXXII, 1245.

**ADRIAN III, pope.** A Roman by birth, he was made supreme pontiff in the time of Emperor Basil and Charles III. He died in 885. A privilege for the monastery of Piacenza and a letter to Sigibodus, archbishop of Narbonne, survive, CXXVI, 972.

**ADRIAN IV, pope.** Born in England, he rose from the humblest circumstances to the supreme pontificate in 1154 and died in 1159. Besides letters, he wrote an account of his legation, a treatise on the conception of the Blessed Virgin, and homilies, CLXXXVIII, 1349.

**ADROALDUS,** lord of Troarn, gave part of his inheritance to the holy monks Bertinus, Mommelinus, and Ebertram for the founding of a monastery; a charter concerning this survives from 648, LXXXVIII, 1155.

**ADSO,** monk and afterward abbot of the monastery of Montier-en-Der, of the Benedictine Order, distinguished in learning; he died in 992. He wrote several Lives and a treatise on Antichrist, CXXXVIII, 598.

**ADVENTINUS,** bishop of Metz. Born of noble family, he was educated among the clergy of the Church of Metz and was made bishop in 857; he died in 875. He wrote a short book concerning Waldrada, concubine of Lothair, CXXI, 1142.

**AEGIDIUS,** bishop of Évreux, lived in the twelfth century; he wrote to Pope Alexander III, humbly asking him to deal more gently with King Henry of England, CC, 1408, 1411.

**AEGIDIUS,** deacon of Paris. Having taught the liberal arts, especially grammar, he was distinguished among the poets of his time. He wrote a poem on the punishments of hell and a history, in four books, of the first expedition to Jerusalem after Fulk, about 1200, CCXII, 15.

**AELFRICUS (St.),** archbishop of Canterbury. Born of noble family, he first lived the monastic life in the monastery of Abingdon, of which he became abbot. He was raised to the see of Winchester in 909 and afterward to Canterbury. He laboured greatly to promote ecclesiastical affairs, as is evident from his canons. He died in 1006, CXXXIX, 1455.

**AELREDUS,** abbot of Rievaulx, of the Cistercian Order. A most eloquent man, remarkable alike for his life and eloquence, he flourished from 1160 to 1166. He produced sermons, the treatise entitled *Mirror of Charity*, and another, *On Friendship*, CXCV, 195.

**AELIDIS,** queen of Cyprus, relinquished to Theobald, count of Champagne, whatever rights belonged to her in the counties of Champagne and Brie, in 1234, CCXVI, 988.

**AEMILIANUS (St.),** priest and abbot. He first withdrew to the monastery of Bilibium in Spain. Leaving it to govern a new monastery which he had built in the diocese of Tarazona, he lived there forty years. Bishop Didymus entrusted the care of souls to him. But because of the accusations brought against him by wicked clergy, he returned again to the monastery, where he soon died and became renowned for innumerable miracles. He was a contemporary of St. Braulio and St. Isidore. Some letters of his to St. Braulio survive, LXXX, 674.

**AENEAS,** bishop of Paris. An outstanding preacher of the divine word and a most renowned professor in the palace schools, he afterward became chancellor of the sacred palace. On the death of Erchanradus, he was chosen bishop; he died in 870. He wrote a book against the Greeks, CXXI, 762.

**AENGELBERTUS,** son of Gaobert, donated at Tilburg in 709 to St. Willibrord, bishop of Utrecht and abbot of Echternach, certain lands situated in the district of Toxandria and called Alfhesin, LXXXIX, 542.

**AENGILBALDUS,** son of Hildibold; an illustrious man of Thuringia, he gave to St. Willibrord, bishop of Utrecht, whatever he possessed in the village of Vaterlo on the river Dutmala, in 704, LXXXIX, 538.

**AETHELBERTUS,** king of Kent, became king in 725. A letter of his to St. Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, survives, in which the pious nun Rugga is mentioned and by which he requests falcons from Germany in 749, LXXXIX, 774.

**AETHELREDUS.** See **ETHELREDUS.**

**AETHELSTANUS.** See **ETHELSTANUS.**

**AGANO or HAGANO,** bishop of Autun. Previously abbot of a monastery in the same city, he died in 1098. We have a charter of his concerning the foundation of the church of St. Germanus and several letters, CL, 1539.

**AGAPETUS I (St.), pope.** A Roman by birth, his father was Gordianus, who afterward became a priest. He was first a cleric attached to Saints John and Paul; he died and was buried in St. Peter’s basilica in the same year in which he was elected, namely 536. He wrote one letter to Emperor Justinian and another to the bishops of Africa, LXVI, 34.

**AGAPETUS II, pope.** Historians are silent about his origin. He occupied the chair of St. Peter in 946 and died ten years later, leaving several letters, CXXXIII, 889.

**AGATHO (St.), pope.** A Sicilian by birth, he was raised from monkhood to the supreme pontificate because of his exceptional kindness and gentleness. He defended the faith against the Monothelites. He died in 679. Letters by him survive, LXXXVII, 1154.

**AGERADUS,** bishop of Chartres and successor of Deodatus. Under King Childebert III, he granted a privilege in 696 to the monastery of St. Mary situated on the Loire. The charter survives mutilated, LXXXVII, 1228.

**AGILES RAIMUNDUS.** See **RAIMUNDUS de Agiles.**

**AGIO,** archbishop of Narbonne. After the murder of Arnulf, he was raised to Arnulf’s see. He died in 927. He composed a history of the Church of Vabres, CXXXIII, 782.

**AGIUS,** priest and monk. He flourished in Germany at the end of the tenth century and was a contemporary of St. Hathumoda, whose life he described, CXXXVII, 1169.

**AGNELLUS,** bishop of Ravenna. Born of noble family, he was first married and followed the profession of arms. After his wife’s death, he devoted himself wholly to God and was finally raised to the episcopate in 558. He died in 566, LXVIII, 379.

**AGNELLUS or ANDREAS,** abbot of St. Mary at Blachernae and of St. Bartholomew at Ravenna. He flourished about 842. He wrote the *Liber Pontificalis*, or Lives of the Bishops of Ravenna, from St. Apollinaris to Petroniacus, CVI, 430.

**AGNES,** empress of Germany and wife of Henry III. After his death, she commended his soul through a messenger to the prayers of St. Hugh, abbot of Cluny, in 1056, CLIX, 932.

**AGOBARDUS (St.),** bishop of Lyons. He was a Gaul by birth. When Leidrad had grown old, he chose Agobard as his coadjutor and withdrew to a monastery near Soissons. In the following year Agobard succeeded the deceased Leidrad and occupied this see until 840. Distinguished in virtue and learning, he composed many little works, CIV, 9.

**AHYTO or HETTO,** bishop of Basel. Born of illustrious family about 763, he was first a monk and then abbot of the monastery of Reichenau; finally he was made bishop. Having resigned that office, he returned to his monastery and died in 836. Of innumerable works, very few survive, including a capitulary and a little book on the vision and death of Wetti, monk of Reichenau, CV, 762.

**AIGLIBERTUS,** bishop of Le Mans and successor of Berarius, flourished under King Theuderic III. He granted certain immunities in 700 to the monastery of St. Mary on the Sarthe; two charters survive, but with different subscriptions, LXXXVIII, 1228, 1240.

**AILERANNUS (St.),** an Irish abbot, surnamed “the Wise.” He appears to have flourished at the beginning of the seventh century. He wrote *Deeds* and, the sole work to survive the passage of time, a mystical interpretation of Christ’s ancestors. It is deeply regrettable that this curious monument has not come down to us complete, LXXX, 327.

**AIMERICUS,** count of Auch, and his brother Bernard entrusted the monastery of St. Orientius to Hugh, abbot of Cluny, for reform in 1068, CLIX, 961.

**AIMERICUS de Haya and his brother Effredus** confirm the grant of the mill of Ponzay, made by Gautherius of Clichon to Lord Robert of Arbrissel, in the same year, twelfth century, CLXII, 1108.

**AIMERICUS, viscount of Château-Gontier,** gave to Lord Robert of Arbrissel, for the support of the monks of Fontevraud, what he possessed near the mill of Le Bois, and in addition the land called Jarumda, to be cultivated by four oxen, at the beginning of the twelfth century under King Louis the Fat, CLXII, 1108.

**AIMERICUS, king of Jerusalem,** promises on oath to assist the preaching of the Gospel and to defend various possessions of the Church for the patriarch, without a stated year, CLV, 1238.

**AIMERICUS DE MARILLEIO** consecrated his daughter to the monastery of Fontevraud, to which he gave five yokes of land in Champvert and another holding near the mill of Combrigneium. His wife Oda subscribed this donation, twelfth century, CLXII, 1114.

**AIMERICUS, patriarch of Antioch.** Born at Limoges, he successfully brought the Maronites of Lebanon to the practice of the Roman Church. He died about 1187. Certain acts and fragments concerning him survive, CCI, 1403.

**AIMERICUS, ninth king of the Latins and of Cyprus.** He was of the house of Lusignan. The Saracens occupied his kingdom, and he died at Acre in 1205. He granted Casale Panduki to the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in 1201, CLV, 1254.

**AIMO,** bishop of Valence in Gaul. With the consent of his fellow bishops—namely St. Theutbald, archbishop of Vienne; Guido of Le Puy; Amblard of Lyons; Faron of Grenoble; and Gerald of Geneva—he prohibited divine services to a certain Aicardus who unjustly held goods of his Church, about 999, CLI, 751.

**AIMO,** abbot of St. Peter of Dive in England. He flourished in the middle of the twelfth century. He wrote a letter to his brethren at Tewkesbury, CLXXXI, 1703.

**AIMO ROSELLUS, count.** During the rule of Blessed Robert of Arbrissel, he granted to the monastery of Fontevraud the freehold of Bociacum outside Trincheiae, and entrusted this donation to the hands of Philippa, countess of Poitou, at the beginning of the twelfth century, CLXII, 1108.

**AIMOINUS, or Aymoinus,** monk and notary of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, flourished in the ninth century. Little works concerning the translation of St. Vincent the martyr and the miracles of St. Germanus, together with a letter to Theotger, survive, CXXVI, 1010.

**AIMOINUS,** monk of Fleury, of the Benedictine Order. A native of Périgueux, born about the middle of the ninth century, he wrote several Lives and arranged a history of the Franks in four books, CXXXIX, 586, 617.

**AISTULFUS,** king of the Lombards. He granted to Lopecinus, bishop of Modena, the estate called Zena in 752. He also subscribed a petition against the bishop of Siena on behalf of a certain man of Arezzo, in which the authority of the *Digest* is operative; furthermore, he issued a privilege in favour of the monastery of Nonantola, LXXXVII, 1384, 1411.

**ALANUS,** first monk and then abbot of Farfa. A native of Aquitaine, he flourished in the eighth century. He produced a collection of homilies to confirm everything chiefly attested on this subject by Holy Scripture, the Fathers, and various ecclesiastical writers. He died in 770, LXXXIX, 1198.

**ALANUS,** abbot of Tewkesbury. Previously he had been prior of Canterbury. Very many letters concerning him survive, as well as a Life of St. Thomas the Archbishop (year uncertain), CXC, 1475.

**ALANUS,** bishop of Rennes, wrote to Suger, abbot of St. Denis, that he would come to him after completing his journey to Nantes, about 1150, CLXXXVI, 1409.

**ALANUS,** bishop of Auxerre. First a monk of Clairvaux and later abbot of Reigny under Lord Bernard, he was raised to the see of Auxerre under Pope Eugenius III. But in the fourteenth year after attaining the pontificate, he resigned that dignity and again withdrew to the monastery of Reigny. He died in 1185. His testament and several letters survive, CCI, 1383.

**ALANUS of Lille,** called the Universal Doctor, was born about the middle of the twelfth century and composed very many works. He died in 1203. Some confuse him with Alanus of Auxerre, CCX, 9.

**ALBERICUS,** bishop of Langres. He flourished about the middle of the ninth century. Nothing is known to us about his life. He wrote a double letter to Frotharius, bishop of Toul, CVI, 880.

**ALBERICUS,** deacon. Nothing is found concerning him except a sermon for St. Benedict, LXVI, 941.

**ALBERICUS,** bishop of Ostia. We have nothing certain concerning his life. He wrote in 1100 to the brethren of the monastery of St. Orientius at Auch concerning the preservation of concord with the archbishop of Auch, CLV, 1831.

**ALBERICUS of Aix, or ALBERTUS,** canon and custos of the Church of Aix. Born about the middle of the eleventh century, he wrote, from hearsay and the reports of others, a twelve-book history of the expedition to Jerusalem under Godfrey of Bouillon, from 1095 to the second year of the reign of Baldwin II. He died in 1120, CLXVI, 390.

**ALBERO,** bishop of Verdun. After often warning the abbot and monks of St. Paul’s, in vain, about their declining discipline, he expelled them from the monastery and gave it to Premonstratensian canons in 1142, CLXXIX, 672.

**ALBERO,** archbishop of Trier. He flourished in the middle of the twelfth century and was perhaps identical with the bishop of Verdun (see above). He wrote to Suger in 1147, asking what the king’s messengers had told him concerning the expedition to Jerusalem, CLXXXVI, 1361.

**ALBERTUS,** abbot of Micy, flourished about the end of the tenth century. First married, he afterward took the monastic habit. There survive a letter of his to Pope John XVII and a charter by which he confirms certain estates to the monastery of Saint-Mesmin, CXXXIX, 586.

**ALBERTUS,** son of Hugh, vidame of the Church of Chartres, granted to the brethren of the monastery of St. Peter of Chartres the junior prebend of the church of St. Sabinus, founded by his father William in the castle of Brezolles on the river Avre, retaining the tithe for himself, in 1080, CLV, 337.

**ALBERTUS, cardinal.** He flourished under Alexander III in the twelfth century. A letter of his to the convent of Canterbury concerning the killing of St. Thomas the Archbishop survives, CXC, 682.

**ALBINUS.** See below, **ALCUINUS.**

**ALBOINUS,** a certain priest forgetful of the sacramental order, who, asserting that priests’ marriage was lawful, wrote several letters to Berthold, or Bernaldus, priest of Constance. The latter refutes them in his responses, about 1080, CXLVIII, 1059, 1079.

**ALBUINUS,** hermit of Clairvaux. Sanderus mentions a certain Albinus who dedicated a book to Heribert, archbishop of Cologne, in 999. Only the dedicatory letter prefixed to the work survives, CXXXVIII, 186.

**ALCHERUS,** abbot, or rather monk. Under the rule of St. Bernard and his successors, he cultivated letters and piety in the abbey of Clairvaux and distinguished himself in both sacred and secular learning. He died about 1169. His treatise *On Loving God* survives, CXCIV, 1687, 1693.

**ALCUINUS,** surnamed **ALBINUS FLACCUS,** monk of Canterbury, afterward abbot of Tours and the distinguished teacher of Charlemagne. He was born at York in Northumbria in 736, of noble lineage. He studied under Ecgbert and became so eminent in the sciences and letters that he was appointed teacher to Charlemagne. He died in 804. He wrote many eloquent works, C–CI.

**ALDEGUNDIS (St.),** daughter of Alpertus and Bertilia, and of most illustrious origin, preserved her virginity and, after the death of her parents, embraced religious discipline in the monastery of Maubeuge, to which she assigned many gifts on the day of her consecration in 661. Another charter records that in the same year she established twelve canons in the church of St. Quentin and gave them a sufficient endowment. These charters, however, are considered doubtful by some, LXXXVIII, 1160, 1162.

**ALDRICUS (St.),** archbishop of Sens, formerly abbot of Ferrières. He was ordained at the Council of Paris in 829. He was most devoted to Emperor Louis, who had appointed him palace tutor so that the greater affairs of the imperial court might be settled at his discretion. Stricken with a fatal illness, he ordered himself carried to the monastery of Ferrières, where he died in 836. He left letters, CV, 796.

**ALDRICUS,** bishop of Le Mans, born of royal lineage, flourished in the ninth century. Received as a youth into Charlemagne’s court, he was later consecrated bishop on account of his learning and knowledge. He died in 856. Three testaments and rules of canonical discipline concerning him survive, CXV, 30.

[Col. 0407]

**ALEXANDER THE GREAT.** King and emperor of the Macedonians, known to all, he flourished before Christ in 324. Letters of his to Didymus, king of the Brahmans, are found in Alcuin; but these appear to be apocryphal, CI, 1366.

**ALEXANDER I (St.), pope and martyr,** succeeded St. Evaristus. Nothing is known concerning this pope’s life. Certain letters attributed to him survive, but are generally regarded as spurious. He died in 119, CXXXIII [lacuna].

**ALEXANDER II, pope.** A native of Milan, he obtained the chair of Peter in 1061. He held a Lateran council at which he struck Simoniacs and concubinary clerics with an anathema. He died in 1073. Letters and charters by him survive, CLXVI, 1275.

**ALEXANDER,** canon of Liège, continued the deeds of the bishops of Liège described by Anselm. Some information concerning him occurs in the *Life of Wazo, Bishop of Liège*. He flourished in the twelfth century, CXLII, 725.

**ALEXANDER and THEODERICUS,** cardinals of the Roman Church, congratulate Guarinus, prior of St. Victor, on his promotion and dissuade him from spending his time erecting buildings, in 1173, CXCVI, 1387, 1395.

**ALEXANDER III, pope.** A native of Siena, he was elected in 1159 and died in 1181. Very many letters and charters by him survive, CC, 9.

**ALEXANDER,** monk and afterward abbot of St. Augustine’s, Canterbury, of the Benedictine Order. According to Pitseus, he flourished in 1217; he wrote the *Life of St. Hugh, Bishop of Lincoln*, in five books, CLIII, 937.

**ALEXANDER de Monte Aculo,** lord of Maelein, granted certain rights to the brethren of Buxeria of the Cistercian Order and attests that Albert of Savigny gave the same monks five day-measures of land in 1265. The language of his charter was written in French according to the custom of the period, CLXXXV, 1429, 1431.

**ALEXIUS COMNENUS,** emperor of Constantinople. He was nephew of Isaac Comnenus; he often waged war against the Turks and Scythians, dealt cunningly with the crusaders, and led them to destruction. He died in 1118. Letters by him to Robert, count of Flanders, and to Bohemund survive from 1095, CLV, 465, 499.

**ALFRICUS.** See **AELFRICUS.**

**ALFRED THE GREAT,** king of the English. A Saxon by origin, he overcame the Danes, made laws for his own subjects, restored learning and the arts, and was deservedly surnamed “the Great.” He died in 900. Constitutions and charters by him survive, CXXXVIII, 447.

**ALGERUS (St.),** canon of the Church of Liège. Born at Liège at the end of the eleventh century, he devoted himself from childhood to the study of letters. He first served God in the Church of St. Bartholomew, as a deacon by rank and scholasticus by office. He died in 1132. He published various writings through which he acquired renown, CLXXX, 728.

**ALGRINUS.** See **JOANNES.**

**ALIENOR or ELEANOR,** daughter of William IX, duke of Aquitaine, first married Louis, king of the Franks, who repudiated her. Having likewise married Henry II, king of England, she was again repudiated and shut up in a monastery until her son Richard obtained the kingdom. She died in 1203. Several letters concerning her survive, CC, 1362, 1380. See also CCVI, 1262, 1265; CCVII, 432 and following.

ALYPIUS, bishop of Tagaste. A disciple and intimate friend of St. Augustine, the Doctor, he journeyed through Palestine chiefly to see Jerome. He was a great support to St. Augustine, both in actions and writings, against the Donatists and Pelagians. He died in old age in 429. See his letters in Augustine, XXXIII, 180 and elsewhere.

ALMODIS, countess of Narbonne, widow of Count Pons, and her son Raymond, count of Rouergue and Nîmes, granted the abbey of Saint-Gilles to Lord Hugh, abbot of Cluny, in 1066, CLIX, 959.

A certain ALOINUS, a layman, granted certain estates to the monastery of St. Gall, not far from which he lived, about 680, under Theuderic III, king of the Franks, LXXXVIII, 1204.

ALOIS and her husband Girard sold to the Church of the Holy Sepulchre two shops with their upper room for 170 bezants in 1155, CLV, 1207.

ALPERTUS, monk of St. Symphorian at Metz. He flourished at the beginning of the eleventh century. He composed two little books, *On the Bishops of Metz* and *On the Diversity of Times*, CXI, 443.

ALPHANUS (St.), bishop of Benevento. He seems to belong to the seventh century. Of his writings only a charter renouncing the rights of the church of St. Martin survives, LXXX, 325.

ALPHANUS, archbishop of Salerno. An Italian by birth, first abbot of Monte Cassino and finally raised to the see of Salerno in 1057, he attended the council of Benevento, held in 1050 under Nicholas II [Col. 0408]. He died in 1086. He completed various writings, CLXVII, 1219.

ALPHONSUS BONUSHOMO, a man skilled in the interpretation of languages, translated from Arabic into Latin the books of Rabbi Samuel, a Jew converted to Christianity, as appears from the letter which he sent to Hugh, master of the Order of Preachers, in the thirteenth century, CXLIX, 335.

ALPHONSUS VIII, king of the Spains, succeeded his mother Terraqua, frequently defeated the Moors, and died in 1157. A letter from him to Hugh, abbot of Cluny, survives, CLIX, 938.

ALPHONSUS I, first king of Portugal. He was the son of Henry, duke of Burgundy; after a notable victory over the Moors he was proclaimed king, and died in 1185. Several letters concerning him survive in various volumes of the *Patrology*, CLXXIX, 935. See also CLXXXII, 675; CLXXXV, 981; CLXXXVIII, 1675.

PETER ALPHONSI. See PETER.

ALREDUS, king of England, successor of Ethelred, and Queen Ogiva flourished in the eighth century. They sent a letter to St. Lull, archbishop of Mainz, commending themselves to his prayers, XCVI, 823.

ALULFUS, first a cleric and then a monk in the monastery of St. Martin at Tournai, where he performed the office of cantor for forty-seven years, flourished in the twelfth century. Like Paterius, he collected the testimonies of the Old and New Testaments found in St. Gregory the Great, and from them composed a book entitled the *Gregorian*, LXXIX, 682, 1137.

ALVARUS (Paulus), a layman and distinguished man of Córdoba, contemporary of St. Eulogius, bishop of Toledo, whose Life he wrote. Other small works and letters by him survive, from which he appears to have been a Jew. He flourished in the ninth century, CXV, 706, 734, 959. See also CXXI, 387.

A certain ALWALO, married and having children, after being excommunicated by a bishop, wrote him a letter seeking absolution. But it is not known who he was or when he lived, CLI, 641.

AMALARDUS and Wido, monks of St. Peter of Horbach, wrote to St. Lull, archbishop of Mainz, on behalf of a certain priest, that he might be able to celebrate Mass in a church within their jurisdiction, in 774, XCVI, 847.

AMALARIUS, archbishop of Trier. Previously a Benedictine monk, he was promoted in 810; he consecrated the church of Hamburg in honor of the Blessed Virgin. He died in 815. There is a letter from him to Charlemagne. He also wrote a treatise *On Baptism*, XCIX, 854, 855. See CI, 1287.

AMALARIUS (Symphosius). See SYMPHOSIUS.

AMALASWINTHA, queen of the Goths, daughter of Theodoric and mother of Athalaric, whose virtues and greatness of spirit are commemorated by Procopius. She died in 352. Several letters from her survive, LXIX, 795, 797, 803, 804.

AMALFRIDUS, a distinguished man, built a monastery in the district of Cambrai, at a place called Hunulfocurtis, of which his daughter Auriana was abbess. He later gave it to be governed by the monastery of Sithiu, without prejudice to the aforesaid abbess, in 605, LXXXVIII, 1209.

AMALRICUS, count of Ascalon, brother of Baldwin III, king of Jerusalem, made and confirmed certain donations to the monastery of the Holy Sepulchre at Jerusalem in 1160, CLV, 1153 and following.

AMALRICUS V, king of Jerusalem, granted immunity to the Church of the Holy Sepulchre and confirmed a grant previously made in 1164, CLV, 1232.

AMALRICUS, patriarch of Jerusalem, flourished in the twelfth century. Letters from him to Louis the Younger survive, CLV, 1266.

AMANDUS (St.), bishop of Maastricht, was born in the district of Herbales, of illustrious and most devout parents. Before becoming bishop, he had embraced the religious life. He died about 679. We possess charters and hymns from him, LXXXVII, 1268.

AMATUS, archbishop of Bordeaux, was made from a monk in 1088. He attended the Council of Clermont under Urban II, at which war was decreed for recovering the holy places. He died in 1101. Letters and diplomas from him survive, CLV, 1638, 1641.

AMBLARDUS, abbot of Solignac, whose year and indeed century are unknown. We have from him a letter to Hervaeus, canon of Tours, CXXXVIII, 187.

AMBRICHO, bishop of Regensburg and at the same time abbot of St. Emmeram, successor of St. Adelwin, a notable exchanger of his possessions, lived in the ninth century. Countless charters survive concerning the exchanges and transfers which he carried out daily, CXXIX, 904 and elsewhere.

AMBROSE (St.), archbishop of Milan and Doctor of the Church. Born of noble stock, after his father’s death he went with his mother to Rome, where he devoted himself to the liberal arts and sciences. Still a catechumen, and unwilling, he was chosen bishop by the people and clergy of Milan [Col. 0409]. He governed that church until 397, when he died. He left many writings distinguished by eloquence and learning. XIV–XVII.

AMBROSIUS, steward of King Liutprand in the Tuscan city of Arezzo. When two bishops disputed before him over the boundaries of their jurisdictions, he adjudged the case to the possessor on grounds of prescription. The act was performed at the royal court at Siena in 713, LXXXVII, 1399.

AMBROSE (St.), bishop of Cahors. He was born in the territory of Bourges. His biographers are silent concerning his parents and upbringing. He is conjectured to have died in 770. Two books *On the Sacraments and Mysteries* survive from him; these were formerly ascribed to St. Ambrose of Milan, LXXXIX, 1197.

AMBROSE AUTPERT (St.), abbot of Benevento in the monastery of St. Vincent at the Volturno, an orator and poet distinguished in his time. He died about 778. Sermons, homilies, and certain Lives survive from him, LXXXIX, 1266.

AMBROSIUS, priest of Milan and legate of Atto, bishop of Vercelli. When he had been questioned by him concerning a certain issue about marriage, he set out his view in a reply, about 955, CXXXIV, 112.

AMEDEUS, count, son of Humbert, and his wife Adelaide gave the church of St. Maurice to the monastery of SS. Peter and Paul of Cluny in 1025, CXLII, 1042.

AMEDEUS (St.), bishop of Lausanne. Born of noble stock in 1110, St. Bernard made him abbot of the monastery of Hautecombe; later raised to the episcopate, he became renowned for knowledge and learning, as well as zeal and piety. He died about 1159. There survive from him a letter to his sons of the church of Lausanne and homilies on the Blessed Virgin Mary, CLXXXVIII, 1277.

AMELIUS, bishop of Toulouse, entrusted to Pons, abbot of Cluny, the church of St. Columba, situated in the territory of Toulouse called Cherchorbense, in 1110, CLXVI, 848.

AMELIUS, abbot of Aurillac, being unable to reform the corrupt customs of his monastery, begged St. Hugh, abbot of Cluny, to undertake the reform of the monastery of Cariacum (eleventh century), CLIX, 942.
