AMMONIUS, Alexandrian philosopher, surnamed Saccas because he once carried sacks as his trade. Having become skilled in Plato’s philosophy, he established a school attended by Plotinus and Origen. He was the author of a *Harmony of the Four Gospels*, later translated by Victor of Capua. He died about 243, LXVIII, 255.

AMOENUS, an author of the fifth century. Biographers are wholly silent about his life. There survives from him a *Handbook of the Old and New Testament* and an acrostic poem addressed to Bishop Leontius, LXI, 1075.

AMPHILOCHIUS (St.), born in Cappadocia, was made bishop of Iconium in 344; he obtained laws from Emperor Theodosius against the Arians. He attended the ecumenical Council of Constantinople in 381 and died in 394. He wrote the Life of St. Basil of Caesarea, LXXIII, 293.

AMULO, bishop of Lyons. A Gaul by nation, he succeeded Agobard and held that see from 841 until his death in 852. Letters and two small works by him survive, *On God’s Foreknowledge and Human Free Will*, CXVI, 78.

AMULRICUS gave St. Ludger, abbot of Werden, certain lands situated in a place called Ad Crucem, beside the river Arnapa, in 799, XCIX, 802, 811.

ANACHARSIS, philosopher. A Scythian by nation, born of royal stock, he travelled through Greece for a long time, learning the laws of every city; but scarcely had he returned home when he was killed, in 548 before Christ. A letter from him to St. Ambrose, translated from Greek, survives, XVII, 1150.

ANACLETUS (St.), pope and martyr, who is also sometimes called CLETUS. He succeeded St. Linus or St. Clement. He died in 83. Certain letters are ascribed to him, but without justification, by Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 59.

ANACLETUS, antipope called Peter Leo. Since he belonged to a most powerful Roman family, he persuaded certain cardinals by promises to elect him, while others, far more numerous, named Innocent II. Peter Leo exercised his usurped authority for eight years, partly by favors and partly by terror, through every lawful and unlawful means. At last, after his brother and protector had been defeated, he was expelled from Rome. He died in 1138. Several letters concerning him survive, CLXXIX, 687.

ANAMODUS, subdeacon of the church of Regensburg, flourished at the end of the ninth century; a collection of traditions is attributed to him, CXXIX, 1034.

ANASTASIA Augusta commended the emperor’s safety to Pope Hormisdas in 519; from the letter she appears to have been the mother of Emperor Justin, LXIII, 1151.

ANASTASIUS I (St.), pope. He succeeded Siricius and sat about three years, dying in 401. Of his writings only two letters have come down to us: the first to John, bishop of Jerusalem [Col. 0410], the second to Simplicianus of Milan, warning them against Origen’s errors, XX, 51.

ANASTASIUS I, emperor of the East, surnamed Silentiarius. He was born at Dyrrachium. He married Ariadne, widow of Zeno, and thus attained the throne; while favoring the Eutychians, he inflicted many persecutions upon Catholics. He died in 518, LXIII, 369 and elsewhere.

ANASTASIUS, priest and apocrisiarius of Rome, defended the cause of St. Maximus, abbot of Constantinople. He wrote to Theodosius, bishop of Gangra, recounting what he had suffered with St. Maximus in exile, in which he died in 666, CXXIX, 659.

ANASTASIUS, monk of Constantinople and disciple of St. Maximus, not to be confused with the others, left two letters: one to John the deacon, and another to the monks of Cagliari. He flourished in the seventh century, CXXIX, 356, 623.

ANASTASIUS, abbot, priest of the Roman Church, and librarian. Learned and distinguished among writers of the ninth century, he was present at the Eighth Ecumenical Council of Constantinople, at which Photius was condemned. He translated the acts of this council from Greek into Latin. He wrote Lives of holy popes and Lives of certain saints, CXXVII–CXXIX.

ANASTASIUS III, pope. He succeeded Sergius in the times of the emperors Lambert and Leo, commendable especially for gentleness and mildness. He sat only two years and died in 913. Two privileges from him survive, CXXXI, 1182.

ANASTASIUS, monk and hermit. Born in Venice, distinguished in ability and eloquence, he preached the Gospel to the Saracens in Spain, then came into Gaul and lived for a long time with the brethren of Cluny. He died in 1086. There is a letter from him to Abbot Gerald, CXLIX, 1134.

ANASTASIUS IV, pope, whose name was Conrad. Already burdened with many years, he succeeded Eugenius III. A Roman by birth, he first distinguished himself as bishop of Sabina by virtue and experience. He died in 1154. We have nine letters of this pontiff, CLXXXVIII, 986 and following.

ANATOLIUS (St.) was elected successor to Flavian in the see of Constantinople by the impious Dioscorus and other bishops of the Ephesian pseudo-council, rightly called the Robber Council of Ephesus. Although the ordination was illegitimate, the holy pontiff recognized it as valid because Anatolius renounced heresy, and so that peace and concord might more readily be restored among the Easterners. He died in 458, LIV, 970, 1082.

ANAXIMENES, Ionian philosopher and disciple of Anaximander, flourished before Christ in 580. A double letter from him to Pythagoras, translated from Greek into Latin by St. Ambrose, survives, XVII, 1151.

ANDGERUS, a man distinguished for piety, distributed all that he possessed, partly to the poor and partly to the brethren and church of St. Saviour, reserving the usufruct for himself and his wife by a charter of donation, in 848, XCIX, 820.

ANDREAS, monk of Fontevraud. He was both disciple and confessor of Blessed Robert of Arbrissel, founder of that congregation, and wrote his Life. He flourished about 1120, CLXII, 1057.

ANDREAS, bishop of Praevalitana, informed Pope Hormisdas of the unhappy outcome of the synod held in New Epirus, and of the return to the faith of the bishops of Scampa and Lignidum upon the legates’ arrival, in 519, LXIII, 443.

ANDREAS, abbot. See AGNELLUS.

ANDREAS, priest and canon of Bergamo, flourished at the end of the ninth century. He composed a chronicle from the entry of the Lombards into Italy to the end of the reign of Emperor Louis II, CLI, 1265.

ANDREAS I, king of Hungary, son of Ladislaus the Bald, attacked and defeated Peter, king of the Russians; but was himself afterwards defeated and killed by Béla in 1062. Certain enactments by him survive, CLI, 1257.

ANDREAS, a native of Parma, monk of the Vallumbrosan order and disciple of St. John Gualbert, later became abbot of Struma. He compiled the Life of St. Gualbert, founder of the Vallumbrosan order, and the Life of St. Ariald, martyr. He flourished about 1080, CXLXI, 714, 766.

ANDREAS, son of Bernard of Montbard, acknowledged and confirmed all donations formerly made by himself or his predecessors for the benefit of Fontenay Abbey, twelfth century, CLXXXV, 1466, 1468.

ANDREAS, chancellor of Canute, king of the Danes. There is a letter from him to Master Melior, cardinal, concerning the divorce of the king and queen of the French; for she was Canute’s full sister, in 1145, CCIX, 716.

ANDREAS of Calvignac, lord of the castle of Raoul, rendered an oath of fidelity and homage to the Roman Church; he had been entrusted with the custody of the tower of Bordeaux in 1202, CCXVII, 286.

ANFREDUS, castellan of Saint-Abraham, sold a certain Martin one small enclosure, for two bezants to be paid annually, in 1149, CLV, 1209.

ANGELOMUS, monk of Luxeuil of the Order of St. Benedict in Burgundy, wrote commentaries on Genesis and expositions both on the Books of Kings and on the Song of Songs. He died in 854 [printed “8547”], CXV, 106.

ANGELRAMNUS, bishop of Metz. He had previously been a monk. He governed the church of Metz for twenty-three years. He died in 791, while accompanying King Charles on an expedition against the Huns. Charters and a compilation of canons survive from him, XCVI, 1032.

ANGELRANNUS, abbot of the monastery of St. Richarius in England, flourished in the eleventh century. He wrote in verse the Life of St. Richarius, first abbot of Canterbury, CXLI, 1422.

ANGILBERT (St.), abbot of Centula. He had formerly held offices at court, which he renounced in order to serve God in the monastery of Centula under Abbot Symphorian; later he was elected abbot. He died in 814. Of his writings only verses and a charter concerning the restoration of the monastery of Centula survive, XCIX, 826.

ANGILBERT PUSTERLA, archbishop of Milan. Not content with such dignity, he did not fear to aspire to and force his way into the Roman see, leading his people into schism during the reign of Charlemagne, in 827. A written response of consultation concerning him to Lord Emperor Louis survives, CLI, 1259.

ANGILBERT, abbot of Corbie. He flourished at the end of the ninth century. He prefixed certain elegiac verses to St. Augustine’s book *On Christian Doctrine* and composed other hexameters, CXXIX, 784.

ANIANUS, deacon of Celeda. He was a most vigorous defender of Pelagius’s heresy; nothing certain is known concerning the year of his birth or death. In 413. For his writings, see XXI, 1173 and XLVIII, 626.

ANICETUS, or ANICUS (St.), pope and martyr, succeeded St. Pius. St. Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, visited him, and they discussed the observance of Easter; they agreed that each should retain his own custom. He protected the flock from the errors of Valentinus and Cerdon. He died in 168. Certain decrees are falsely attributed to him, CXXX, 118.

ANNAEUS POLEMAEUS SYLVIUS, bishop of Octodurum. He flourished in 603, when he compiled his *Laterculus*, or Calendar, according to the custom both of Christians and of the gentiles, XIII, 671; I, 1292.

ANNEMUNDUS (St.), bishop of Lyons. He succeeded St. Viventiolus; he confirmed gifts to St. Peter’s Parthenon and himself made new ones to it, in 653, LXXXVIII, 1164.

ANNIANUS, quaestor under Constantine the Great. We possess nothing else concerning him except a letter sent by him and his colleagues to Celsus, vicar of Africa, informing him that the bishops who, by the emperor’s command, had come into Gaul regarding the case of Caecilian, were to return to their own places at the expense of the imperial treasury, VIII, 749.

ANNO (St.), archbishop of Cologne. He was first devoted to military service, but soon, by his uncle’s advice, embraced the clerical life and obtained the see of Cologne in 1055. After many illustrious and miraculous deeds, he died in 1072, CXLIII, 1583.

ANNO, abbot of the monastery of Inde, two leagues from Aachen, flourished about 1147. He wrote to Wibald, while Wibald was still abbot of Stavelot, about a certain Ebroin, to whom, at Wibald’s urging, he had done good, CLXXXIX, 1143.

ANSA, queen of the Lombards and wife of Desiderius, was distinguished by piety and generosity toward the poor. She affixed her name to numerous charters about 758, LXXXVII, 1388, 1393.

ANSALDUS, chaplain of the sacred palace. A Sicilian by nation, he gave to the Church of the Holy Sepulchre a house which he himself had built at Messina in Sicily, describing its appearance and location, in 1171, CLV, 1243.

ANSBALDUS, son of Wigibald, who seems to have been brother of Bertilendis, the donor and abbess of Kellen, embraced the monastic life and gave certain goods to St. Willibrord, bishop and likewise abbot of the monastery of Echternach, in 711 and 712, LXXXIX, 544.

ANSCHARIUS (St.), bishop of Hamburg. He flourished from about 811 to 865; some think him Frisian by birth. He was first a monk. He wrote the Life of St. Willehad, bishop of Bremen, CXVIII, 960.

ANSEBERTUS, bishop of Autun, called Autbertus and Amalbertus by different persons, had a brother Autarius and a sister Segolina, a nun in the monastery of St. Mary at Autun, now St. John’s. By a charter he distributed his goods among certain churches in 695, LXXXVIII, 1131.

ANSEGISUS, abbot of Fontenelle. Born of a noble French family, after Charlemagne had placed him over the government of many monasteries and frequently sent him on embassies, he became abbot of Fontenelle [Col. 0412]. He collected the laws of Charlemagne and died in 834, CV, 734.

ANSEGISUS, bishop, whose see is not indicated. With other bishops he went to Compiègne to Louis the Pious for the blessing of his son Charles, for whose commendation he gave a written declaration, in 877, CXXXV, 1285.

ANSELLUS, schoolmaster and monk of St. Remigius at Rheims, said to have been a disciple of St. Abbo of Fleury, wrote in verse, by order of Abbot Addo, a certain vision which he had experienced, at the beginning of the eleventh century, CLI, 643.

ANSELLUS, cantor of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. He seems formerly to have belonged to the clergy of Blessed Mary at Paris; he followed the Jerusalem expedition and, after the Christians entered Jerusalem, attached himself to the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. From there he wrote to Galon, bishop of Paris, and the clergy, sending a portion of the wood of the Holy Cross, in 1100, CLXII, 729.

ANSELMUS, monk of St. Remigius at Rheims. The celebrated basilica of this monastery was dedicated and consecrated by Pope Leo IX himself, whom Abbot Herimar had invited. Anselm, an eyewitness, composed the history of this dedication in 1049, CXLII, 1[lacuna]11.

ANSELMUS, canon of Liège. Born of noble stock, he was still more distinguished for piety and character, but all are silent as to the day of his death. He continued the Chronicle of Lobbes, CXXXIX, 957; CLII, 725; CXLIII, 861.

ANSELMUS, bishop of Lucca. A native of Mantua and of illustrious lineage, he was elected to the bishopric of Lucca by Alexander II. Sent to King Henry, he received investiture from him by ring and pastoral staff; moved to repentance for this, he withdrew to Cluny, but Gregory VII recalled him to his diocese. He wrote against Guibert, the antipope. He died in 1086, CXLIX, 436.

ANSELMUS of Ribemont, born of noble stock, was distinguished among the crusaders both in the battle of Nicaea and in that of Antioch, at the walls of Ptolemais or Acre. Struck by a stone, he died in 1099. A letter from him to Pope Urban II survives, CLV, 471.

ANSELMUS, archbishop of Milan. Confirmed by Urban II in 1196, he preached the holy war and led fifty thousand Lombards with him into Syria; but, routed by the Saracens, he died at Constantinople in 1100. Certain privileges from him survive, CLV, 1655.

ANSELM (St.), archbishop of Canterbury. Born of an illustrious family, moved by Lanfranc’s reputation, he fled to the monastery of Bec, where he held the office first of prior and later of abbot. Upon Lanfranc’s death he was raised to the see of Canterbury in 1093. He left dogmatic, ascetic, and hortatory writings, and letters; he died in 1109. CLVIII, CLIX.

ANSELMUS, schoolmaster and canon of Laon. Born of very humble stock, he made such progress in learning and the liberal arts that, after teaching them first at Paris and later at Laon with the greatest distinction, he had Abelard himself as a pupil. Expositions on various books of Scripture and a letter to the abbot of St. Lawrence at Liège survive from him. He died about 1117, CLXII, 1170.

ANSELMUS, monk of Gembloux and later abbot, first continued Sigebert’s Chronicle. He appears inferior to him in ability, wavering in judgment, and excessively intent on miracles and portents. He carried the chronicle from 1112 to 1135. He died in 1126, CLX, 239.

ANSELMUS, bishop of Havelberg in the margraviate of Brandenburg, was distinguished for learning and achievements. He wrote one book on the order of the Canons Regular of St. Augustine, another against the Greek schism, and Lives of certain saints. He flourished in the twelfth century, CLXXXVIII, 1088.

ANSERINUS, archbishop of Besançon, and Joceramnus of Lyons informed Gerard, bishop of Angoulême, of the decision of the Roman see concerning the controversy of Gurhandus, abbot of Holy Cross at Kemperlé, with Hervaeus, abbot of Redon, in 1120, CLXXII, 1326.

A certain ANSOLDUS, knight, and his wife Hildegard granted the vicariate of Domna Maria for the benefit of St. Peter’s at Chartres in 1088, CLV, 358.

ANTERUS (St.), pope. A Greek by birth, he succeeded St. Pontian in 235, but sat only forty days. Bede and Ado call him a martyr. The decrees attributed to him by Isidore Mercator are spurious.

ANTHELMUS. See NANTHELMUS.

ANTIGONUS, king of Asia, one of Alexander’s generals, perished in battle near the river Ipsus, defeated by Cassander, Seleucus, and Symmachus, in 241 before Christ. A letter is attributed to him in St. Ambrose, XVII, 1151.

ANTO for ZANETO. See ERFO.

ANTONINUS HONORATUS, bishop of Constantina in Africa, flourished in the fifth century during the persecution stirred up against Christians by Genseric, king of the Vandals. In a letter he consoles a certain Arcadius, a Spaniard exiled for the faith, and exhorts him to endure graver things, L, 565.

ANTONINUS of Piacenza seems to belong to the sixth century. Nothing certain is known concerning him. A certain account of a journey to the holy places is ascribed to him, LXXII, 898 and following.

ANTONINUS (St.), born at Florence, entered the Order of St. Dominic. He then became so distinguished in piety and learning that by common consent he was made archbishop of Florence. Pope Eugenius summoned him when near death, and Adrian IV enrolled him among the saints. He died in 1450. There survives from him testimony both concerning St. Peter Damian and concerning Pope St. Gregory VII, CXLIV, 184; CXLVIII, 215.

ANTHONY (St.), father of monks. Barely grown, after his parents’ death he distributed all his property to the poor and withdrew into the desert of the Thebaid. There he had countless disciples, overcame most grievous temptations, and died at a very advanced age in 356. He wrote several letters in Egyptian, LXXIII, 115; CIII, 423.

ANTONIUS, entirely uncertain, to whom is attributed a poem against the gentiles, which some conjecture, by comparison of style, to be the work of St. Paulinus, V, 262.

ANTONIUS, a young man, came to St. Simeon the Stylite; having marvelled at such great virtues, he committed them to writing. Some think him the same as Evagrius, who translated into Latin the Greek Life of St. Antony written by St. Athanasius, in 384, LXXIII, 325.

ANULINUS, sent by Diocletian into Africa as proconsul, was at first a persecutor of Christians. But when Constantine attained the empire, he acted more moderately and took up the case of Caecilian, bishop of Carthage, against the Donatists, whose petition he sent to Constantine himself with a letter in 312, VIII, 479, 705.

APOLLINARIS (St.), bishop of Valence in Gaul, brother of St. Avitus, bishop of Vienne, flourished at the end of the fifth century; his memory is still celebrated throughout the diocese as its principal patron. Two familiar letters from him to his brother and colleague Avitus survive, LIX, 231, 273.

AQUILINUS JUVENCUS. See JUVENCUS.

ARATOR, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church. A celebrated poet, he flourished in the sixth century under the emperors Justin and Justinian. He wrote the Acts of the Apostles in verse and dedicated them to Pope Vigilius; he died in 555, LXVIII, 44.

ARCADIUS Augustus, son of Theodosius the Great, had St. Arsenius as his instructor from childhood. Raised to the empire, he surrendered himself too much to the flatteries of Rufinus and of his wife Eudoxia. He died in 408. A letter from him to Pope Innocent survives, XX, 633.

ARCESILAUS, Peripatetic philosopher, was a disciple of Polemon. He lived at Athens and, at the end of his life, sent his will to a certain Thaumasia through Diogenes, in 241 before Christ. A letter from him, translated from Greek, survives in St. Ambrose, XVII, 1151.

ARCHYTAS, Pythagorean philosopher. A native of Tarentum, he died by shipwreck near the coast of Apulia. He is believed to have invented certain machines. Letters from him to Dionysius and Plato survive in St. Ambrose. He flourished in 361 before Christ, XVII, 1151, 1152.

ARCULFUS (St.), bishop of a certain city in Gaul, flourished in 690. For religious reasons he journeyed to the East and left a description of the places which he visited, through the hand of Adamnan, abbot of Hy, LXXXVIII, 722.

ARDO. See SMARAGDUS.

ARDUICUS, archbishop of Besançon, imprudently accepted Gunthar’s complaints against Hincmar of Rheims and rashly subscribed a letter composed with Theutgaud and Gunthar himself, on account of which he narrowly escaped being excommunicated with him in 868. See GUNTHARIUS, CXXI, 381.

ARDUINUS, knight of Chartres and adherent of Count Odo, at the request of Gisbert, abbot of St. Peter’s at Chartres, granted certain meadows and water-rights for the modest rent of two solidi in 996, CLV, 249.

AREDIUS, or PETRUINUS, bishop of Vaison, granted many gifts and privileges to the monastery of Grasse, which he had built; moreover, he confirmed gifts made by others in 683. This charter mentions Lady Gregoria, an *episcopia*; *episcopiae* were the wives of men who had been married before ordination, and such women commonly lived in monasteries, LXXXVIII, 1204.

AREFASTUS, first a knight under Richard, duke of Normandy, then became a monk and gave his inheritance to the monastery of St. Peter at Chartres, to which he had retired, in 1028, CLV, 262.

AREGIUS (St.), abbot of Altanum. At the beginning of the sixth century he was born at Limoges, in Aquitaine, in Transalpine Gaul, of parents less distinguished by patrician blood than by outstanding piety. He became abbot of the monastery of Altanum which he himself had founded and, after many miracles, fell asleep in the Lord in 591. A testament by him survives, LXXI, 1119.

ARIALDUS and HERLEMBALDUS (Saints), monks and martyrs, whose acts and life were given by Andrew the Vallumbrosan; see him, CLXIII, 1433.

ARIBO, archbishop of Mainz, born of illustrious stock, flourished from 1021 to 1031. He presided over the councils of Mainz in 1023 and of Seligenstadt in 1024 and 1026, and drew up their acts, together with an instruction concerning the manner in which a synod ought to be celebrated. He left certain other writings, CXLI, 1109.

ARIBO, schoolmaster of Freising, concerning whom we have nothing certain. Some think that he was a monk of Hirsau. He wrote a treatise *On Music* about the end of the eleventh century, CL, 1307.

ARIDIUS is the same as AREGIUS.

ARICHIS, duke of the Lombards and prince of Benevento, issued a capitulary for the church of St. Mary at Benevento in 769, and granted a privilege to the church and monastery of St. Sophia in the same city in 774, LXXXVII, 1417.

ARISTOTLE, the celebrated Greek philosopher. Born at Stagira in 384 before Christ, he was Plato’s disciple and Alexander the Great’s teacher. He wrote much on rhetoric, logic, politics, and other liberal arts, and long enjoyed great authority among the schoolmen. Certain books by him, translated and explained by Boethius, survive, LXIV, 159, 639, 711, 1007.

ARIUS, priest of Alexandria and notorious heresiarch. About 312 he began to preach a new doctrine, denying the consubstantiality of the Word. He was condemned by the general Council of Nicaea in 325 and driven into exile. But afterward, with Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, favoring him, he so deceived Emperor Constantine by promises that he returned to Constantinople almost in triumph; there, however, suddenly seized with internal pain, he died miserably in 336. Sts. Athanasius and Alexander, patriarchs of Alexandria, wrote especially against him. There survive the memorandum presented to Constantine by Arius and Euzoius, and Constantine’s letter to Arius, VIII, 561, 583.

ARMENIUS and HONORIUS, commonly called monks; a profession of faith according to the canon of the sacred books is attributed to them. It is not known when they flourished, nor who was that Theophilus to whom the book is addressed, LXXIV, 1243.

ARNALDUS, abbot of Sens, otherwise Ernaldus. In 1096 he became abbot of St. Peter-le-Vif at Sens. In 1103 he went to Rome and obtained from Pope Paschal a broad privilege for his monastery. He died in 1124. Letters by him survive, CLXIII, 1474.

ARNALDUS, abbot of Cîteaux, accompanied Milo, the pope’s legate, in the war against the Albigensians, during which he became archbishop of Narbonne. He informed Pope Innocent III of the progress of this war in 1209, CCXVI, 137, 842.

ARNALDUS, prior of the Holy Sepulchre. With the counsel and consent of the chapter, he made certain exchanges with some burgesses of the place called Mahumeria, without a year being specified, CLV, 1219.

ARNO, first dean and then provost of Reichersberg, a man commendable alike for learning and piety. He wrote a book against Fulmar of Triefenstein, refuting his errors concerning the Eucharist. He also produced another book entitled *The Shield of Canons*. He died about 1180, CXCIV, 1490.

ARNOBIUS, African rhetorician and Christian apologist. At Sicca, a city of Africa, he taught rhetoric under Diocletian while still a pagan; soon, divinely admonished, he embraced the worship of the true God. He died about 320. He wrote seven books *Against the Gentiles*, demonstrating the absurdities of their superstition, V, 349.

ARNOBIUS, commonly called the YOUNGER, to distinguish him from Arnobius of Africa, seems to have been a Gaul by nation and to have flourished about 460. Under his name survive a commentary on the Psalms of David, a *Conflict with Serapion concerning the Triune and One God*, etc., LIII, 238.

ARNOLDUS, monk of St. Emmeram at Regensburg. Born of noble stock, he departed for Saxony because of the envy of his brethren and at Magdeburg became a friend of Meginfrid, master of the school. He then returned to his monastery and died about 1040. He wrote two books *On the Miracles of St. Emmeram* and a homily on the eight beatitudes, CXLI, 986.

ARNOLDUS, bishop of Halberstadt. Very little concerning him has been transmitted to us. He died in 1012. He wrote a letter to Henry of Würzburg concerning the establishment of the bishopric of Bamberg, CXXXIX, 1494.

ARNOLDUS II, bishop of Cologne. He informed Lord Wibald that, by the counsel of the whole clergy and honorable men, his journey to the pope ought to be delayed until peace should be secured and every storm calmed, in 1151 [Col. 0415], CXXXXIX [probably CLXXXIX], 1377, 1379 and following.

ARNOLDUS, or ARNALDUS, of Solnhofen, was made archbishop of Mainz from chancellor. In 1160 he was killed by citizens in a sedition. In 1158 he had written to Wibald, abbot of Corvey, complaining of the deeds of the count palatine of the Rhine and requesting the emperor’s aid against him, CLXXXIX, 1455.

ARNOLD, bishop of Trier. He flourished at the end of the twelfth century. In a letter he attested his affection for Saint Hildegard, abbess. CXCVII, 181.

ARNULF, hermit, addressed a letter to Peter, monk of Poitiers, in which he discusses certain practices established among monks (without mention of the year), twelfth century. CLXXXIX, 560.

ARNULF, duke of the Burgundians, son of Drogo, flourished under King Childeric III. Around the year 706 he gave an estate called Floriacum and certain other properties to the monastery of the Holy Apostles near Metz. But the charter on which this donation rests is marred by many faults, through which it is shown to be false. By another charter he granted gifts to the monastery of Echternach and to Saint Willibrord. LXXXVIII, 1249; LXXXIX, 549.

ARNULF, king, illegitimate son of Carloman of Bavaria, succeeded Charles the Fat. He was crowned emperor by Pope Formosus, but reigned only two years and was carried off by poison in 899. On his coronation and the decision of the Council of Tribur, see CXXXVIII, 805.

ARNULF, archbishop of Rheims, formerly bishop of Laon. He was the natural son of Lothair and nephew of Charles, duke of Lorraine. According to Alberic, he died in the year 102[...]. His letters and privileges survive. CXXXIX, 1539.

ARNULF, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter at Chartres. Mindful of a benefit bestowed upon him by Robert, archbishop of Rouen, who had freed the church of Fontenay from the violence of an archdeacon, he established that an annual alms should be given in perpetuity for the soul of this bishop, in 1033. Another charter by him survives. CLV, 269, 311.

ARNULF, cleric of Milan, wrote a history, as an eyewitness, of events that occurred at Milan from 1060 to 1077, prefacing it with a brief account of events after 926. CXLVII, 279.

ARNULF, chaplain of the duke of Normandy, afterwards patriarch of Jerusalem, established secular canons as regulars with the consent of King Baldwin and provided for their maintenance, about 1124. CLV, 469, 1115.

ARNULF, priest and celebrated Christian preacher, a native of Flanders, urged peoples both in France and Germany to undertake the Jerusalem expedition, and joined an expedition against the Moors in Spain. He flourished about 1147. Of him there survives only a letter to Milo, bishop of Thérouanne. CLXXIX, 1811.

ARNULF, monk of Boeries of the Cistercian order in the diocese of Laon, flourished about the middle of the twelfth century. There survives a little book by him entitled *Mirror of Monks*, published among the writings of Saint Bernard. CLXXX, 1657; CLXXXIV, 1175.

ARNULF, bishop of Lisieux. A Norman by birth, trained from childhood in discipline and every kind of virtue, he became canon and prior of Saint-Victor at Paris, and afterwards bishop of Lisieux. He left letters, sermons, and a treatise on the schism which arose under Honorius II. He died in 1182. CCI, 7.

ARTHALD, archbishop of Rheims, formerly a monk of Saint-Remi, was elected through the favor of King Ralph in 921 and consecrated before eighteen bishops. He died in 961 and was buried at Saint Remi’s feet. A letter from him to the Synod of Ingelheim survives. CXXXIII, 954.

ARTAMANNUS and ADEMAR, viscounts, entrusted the governance of the monastery of Brunechilde in the district of Cahors, founded by them in 1082, to Blessed Hugh, abbot of Cluny, and Hunald of Moissac. CLIX, 971.

ARVEUS of Gion granted his protection to the monastery of Saint Mary of Fontevraud. Philip then being king, twelfth century. CLXII, 1109.

ARVERIUS, or Herveus, lord of Sombernon, granted a certain fief called Socé to Herveus, lord of Safres, for one hundred Dijon pounds, in 1233. CLXXXV, 1433.

ASCARICUS, bishop of Braga. He seems to have adhered to the party of Elipandus and Felix of Urgel, that man’s master. A letter of his survives, mentioned by Elipandus himself. XCIX, 739 and following.

ASCHOLF, abbot of Fulda, succeeded Wibald. But because of his harsh government of the monks, he was deprived of office by Pope Eugenius III about 1149. A letter by him survives in which he complains of his own subjects. CLXXXIX, 1149.

ASPERIUS, bishop of Regensburg, made certain agreements and exchanges [Col. 0416] concerning various matters belonging to the monastery of Saint Emmeram, ninth century. CXXIX, 959.

ASTERIUS (TURCIUS RUFUS), illustrious man, former ordinary consul, and patrician by origin, collected and published Sedulius’s poems. He seems to have been Sedulius’s contemporary. An epigram survives in which he taught us these facts. XIX, 486, 779.

ATALARIC, king of the Goths, son of Amalasuntha, was the great-grandson and successor of Theodoric. He died in 534. We have several letters concerning him in Cassiodorus. LXIX, 733; LXXII, 1118.

ATHANASIUS (Saint), patriarch of Alexandria. He flourished from 296 to 376. An eminent opponent of the Arians, who obtained from the imperial power that he should be deposed and driven into exile. Only after twenty years, having endured countless horrors, was he able to return to his see. He issued many writings in Greek. Letters concerning him survive in Liberius. VIII, 1397—See further XIII, 1037; LXXIII, 125; CIII, 665.

ATTO, bishop of Vercelli, distinguished for learning, conduct, and zeal. He flourished from 934 to 960. We have his *Letters*, *Sermons*, and *Exposition of the Epistles of Saint Paul*. CXXXIX, 9.

ATTO, or HATO, bishop of Troyes, was a contemporary of Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, to whom he wrote several letters and issued privileges in 1160. CLXXXIX, 271, 303, 1066.

ATTO, bishop of Pistoia, formerly a Vallombrosan abbot. He flourished in the twelfth century. He compiled the *Life of Saint John Gualbert*, founder of his order. CLXXXVIII, 986.

AUDAX, a most devout man, lived in Africa not far from Saint Augustine. One day he asked him to write a longer letter to him. The holy Doctor excuses himself on account of his occupations and advises him to consult Augustine’s books, or to hear him preaching in person. XXXIII, 1075.

AUDEBURGIS of Montreuil gave Blessed Robert of Arbrissel and the nuns of Fontevraud land and an estate at the Valley of Suchart, under Louis VI, twelfth century. CLXII, 1112.

AUDOENUS (Saint), bishop of Rouen. This prelate, whose earlier name was Dado, was born at Sancy among the Suessiones of pious parents, and had as his elder brother the venerable Odo. He wrote the *Life of Saint Eligius*, bishop of Noyon, in 662. LXXXVII, 478.

AUDOMAR, bishop of Thérouanne, built, by charter in 662, a basilica beside the monastery on the island of Sithiu, in which he reserved a place for his burial. By the same charter he exempted the monks of Saint-Bertin from all episcopal subjection. LXXXVIII, 1174.

AUDRAD, chorepiscopus of Sens, was appointed in 849. He bore the surname Modicus. He was related to Burchard, bishop of Chartres, attended the Council of Sens in 853, and died in 864. He wrote a book *On Revelations*. CXV, 16.

AUGUSTINE (Saint), bishop of Hippo Regius and illustrious doctor of the Church, was born at Tagaste in Africa about 354, of a pagan father and a Christian mother, the most devout Monica. At first he followed the errors of the philosophers and was ensnared by the attractions of pleasure. At Milan he was at last recalled to better fruit by Saint Ambrose and baptized. Returning to his homeland, he devoted himself to meditation, prayer, and study. Ordained priest by the bishop of Carthage, he was soon made his coadjutor and afterwards advanced to the see of Hippo. He produced countless books against the heretics of his time; he delivered four hundred sermons from the pulpit to his people; he founded a monastery in his own house; and he deserved to hold first place among all doctors of the Latin Church. He died in 430. The writings of Saint Augustine are published in sixteen volumes of the new course of the *Patrology*, XXXII–XLVII.

AUGUSTINE (Saint), first archbishop of Canterbury and apostle of the English. He was first a monk at Rome of the Order of Saint Benedict. Sent to England with several companions by Saint Gregory the Great himself, to evangelize these peoples, he first won King Æthelberht to Christ. Distinguished by virtues and miracles, he rested in the Lord in 610. LXXX, 94.

AUGUSTINE GRADONICUS, patriarch of Aquileia, lived at the beginning of the seventeenth century. In the archive of the chapter of Udine there survives a charter by which that patriarch granted a *pedum* concerning the *cano* of the aforesaid chapter (both readings uncertain) on Christmas Day in 1629. XCIX, 682.

AUIULFUS, bishop, known to us only through a letter which he wrote to Desiderius, bishop of Cahors, in 645. LXXXVII, 258.

AUMARIUS (Saint), bishop of Auxerre. He spent his youth at the court of King Guntram; when the see became vacant, he was elected by unanimous voice. When he died is uncertain. [Col. 0417] Two letters by him survive, as well as the canons of a synod which he held. LXXI, 760.

AURELIANUS (Saint), bishop of Arles, was born at the beginning of the sixth century, became bishop in 545, and departed this life in 553. Besides several letters and certain fragments, we have from him a Rule for the monks and virgins of the monasteries that he himself founded. LXVIII, 386.

AURELIANUS, monk and afterwards bishop of Rheims, if Sigebert of Gembloux is to be believed. This alone is certain concerning him: he lived about 900. He wrote a book on ecclesiastical chant and a letter to Bernard, archcantor. CVI, 1521.

AURELIUS (Saint), bishop of Carthage, was made bishop in 392. He was the first to strike with anathema the impious Celestius, who refused to confess original sin. For nearly forty years he governed his Church. An encyclical letter by him to the bishops of the province of Byzacena survives. XX, 1010.

AURELIUS SYMMACHUS. See SYMMACHUS.

AURINANDUS and GODEFRIDUS, citizens of Lucca, founded the monastery of Saint Peter in the place called Castellione for their sons in 723. LXXXVII, 1368.

AUSONIUS, grammarian of Bordeaux, eloquent poet and persuasive rhetorician, flourished at the end of the fourth century. He was Saint Paulinus’s teacher. Although his writings breathe pagan manners, he was a Christian. XIX, 817.

AUSPICIUS (Saint), bishop of Toul. A most distinguished man among the bishops of Gaul, he flourished in the fifth century. Of his writings only a letter to Arbogast, count of Trier, survives. LXI, 1006.

AUTBERT, bishop of Cambrai, was made bishop in 633 and died in 640 at the court of King Dagobert. A charter by him survives for the monastery of Wallaves. LXXX, 594.

AUTCONDA and NATALIA, sisters, expended the very ample inheritance which they held from their parents in founding a convent for women in the city of Verona, in 744, and placed it under the governance of the abbot of Saint Mary at Organo. LXXXVII, 1374.

AUXENTIUS, born in Cappadocia, professed Arius’s doctrine. He held the see of Milan under Emperor Constantius, but was anathematized at Rome by ninety-three bishops in 372. His impious confession of faith survives; Saint Hilary called it an “Example of Blasphemy.” X, 617.

AUXILIUS, priest. It is not known who he was. About 894 he was ordained by Pope Formosus. He wrote two books *On the Ordinations Performed by Pope Formosus*. CXXIX, 1040.

AVESGOT, or AVESGOD, abbot of Saint Peter of La Couture at Le Mans, must not be confused with another of the same name, who was abbot of Saint Vincent in the same city of Le Mans. A letter by the former survives to Saint Anselm, afterwards archbishop of Canterbury, in 1072. CXLIII, 1434.

AVITUS (Saint), bishop of Vienne, was equally distinguished by piety and learning. His father was Isicius, or Hesychius. First a senator and afterwards archbishop of Vienne, he most vigorously refuted the errors of Arians, Eutychians, and Nestorians, and died in 518. Letters and small metrical works by him survive. LIX, 192.

AYMARD (Saint), abbot of Cluny, son of the count of Angoulême, succeeded Odo in 944. Weak in body and deprived of sight, he chose Saint Maiolus as his successor. He died in 994. His cartulary survives. CXXXVIII, 699.

AYMERICUS and other names in *ay*: see under *at*.

AZO of Asmurgen and his wife Mactilda complete a donation of certain goods to the canons of the Church of Aquileia, reserving usufruct for themselves and for the survivor of them, in 1129. XCIX, 643.

B

BACHIARIUS, monk, a Spaniard by nation and a man thoroughly versed in Christian philosophy, flourished in the fifth century. We have from him a little work, or letter, *On Receiving the Fallen*. XX, 1015.

BADO, son of Widucus, gave to the monastery of Werden a village called Porribec, situated in the district of Borotra. This was done in 821, during the reign of Louis the Pious. XCIX, 816.

BALDERIC, born in the diocese of Liège, attached himself to the court of Pope Eugenius III. He was made master of the schools by Archbishop Albero himself, whose life he wrote shortly after Albero’s death, because he had been familiar with him, in 1157. CLIV, 1297.

BALDRIC, archbishop of Dol, a native of Orléans, was first a monk and then abbot of Bourgueil in Anjou. He was a man trained in the liberal arts and adorned with virtues. He died in 1131. He wrote a history of the Jerusalem war in four books, an account of the translation of Saint Valentine’s head, certain lives, poems, and a diploma. CLXVI, 1057.

[Col. 0418] BALDRIC, bishop of Noyon, lived in the twelfth century. A letter by him survives to Lambert of Arras, commending to him a certain Peter who had departed from his household. CLXII, 676.

BALDWIN, a certain man, became a monk in the monastery of Saint Peter at Chartres, to which, with the consent of his wife and son, he had given certain estates divided into gardens, in 1080. CLV, 342.

BALDWIN I, king of Jerusalem, brother and successor of Godfrey of Bouillon, formerly prince of Edessa, occupied Tripoli and certain other places. He died in 1118. Many diplomas concerning him survive throughout CLV, 1121.

BALDWIN II, king of Jerusalem, succeeded Baldwin I, his kinsman, both in the principality of Edessa and on the throne of Jerusalem; but he was held captive among the Turks for a long time and died in 1131. Several diplomas concerning him survive. CLV, 1122.

BALDWIN, dean of the Church of Noyon. While the see was vacant and Baldwin of Châtillon had been elected bishop, he wrote to the king asking him to ratify this election by his authority, in 1148. CLXXXVI, 1371.

BALDWIN of Châtillon, bishop of Noyon, flourished in the middle of the twelfth century. A letter by him survives to Pope Eugenius, whom he informs how, amid troubles and reproaches, he had introduced religious monks into the Church of Compiègne in place of canons of corrupt morals. CLXXX, 1628; CC, 1418.

BALDWIN III, sixth king of the Latins. A charter by him survives, by which he granted to the Church of the Holy Sepulchre two quintals of grapes to be gathered in his vineyards, in 1177. CLV, 1248.

BALDWIN RUFUS and his wife Artemisia donated their house to the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, to be possessed after the death of both of them, in 1178. CLV, 1251.

BALDWIN, archbishop of Canterbury, surnamed the Devonian, an Englishman by nation, was born at Oxford in humble circumstances. First a monk and then abbot of the Cistercian monastery of Ford, he was finally elected to the see of Canterbury in 1184. He had taken the cross and gone to Syria; he fought against the Saracens and crushed them with a great slaughter. See his writings, CCIV, 402.

BALDWIN, count of Flanders, afterwards emperor of Constantinople, flourished at the beginning of the thirteenth century. There are many letters, diplomas, and statutes concerning him. He died about 1204. CCIX, 914 and following.

BALDWIN of Valence, canon of the church of Braine, joined Walter in composing a treatise against the Jews in dialogue form. He seems to have flourished at the beginning of the thirteenth century. CCIX, 423.

BATHILDIS (Saint), queen of the Franks. Anglo-Saxon by origin, endowed with intelligence and beauty, she fell captive into the hands of raiders, was taken to France, and, through Erchinoald, by God’s providential action, became the wife of Clovis II. She built a monastery on the Marne in a place called Chelles, to which countless young women gathered, and there she herself died in 680. LXXXVII, 661.

BANDINUS, master, distinguished theologian. Nothing concerning his life survives; he flourished in the twelfth century. He wrote four books of *Sentences*, in which the whole sum of theology is treated simply and clearly. CXCII, 966.

BAPTISTA of Mantua, from whom there survives an encomiastic poem on the life and death of Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux. CLXXXV, 267.

BARBA. See FROGERUS.

BARBEDAURUS, dean of the Church of Paris, concluded an agreement with Henry the Great and Arnulf of Corberon concerning a certain tithe of the territory of Boneis (otherwise Bonollo), lying between Créteil and Sucy, in 1173. CCV, 910.

BARBOTINUS. See RADULFUS.

BARNARD (Saint), bishop of Vienne, and LAOF, or FAOVA, of Chalon, together with Agobard write to Emperor Louis the Pious against the impieties and perfidies of the Jews, about 830. CIV, 77.

BARTHOLOMEW, abbot of Marmoutier, succeeded Albert in 1063. He wrote a letter to Ernald, bishop of Le Mans, and died in 1084. CXLIX, 367.

BARTHOLOMEW, bishop of Laon, granted to Blessed Norbert an allod free from every customary due, located in the place commonly called Huberts Bridge, for the construction of a church in honor of Saint Mary, in 1121. CLXX, 1359.

BARTHOLOMEW, bishop of Châlons, was made bishop in 1147. He attended the Council of Rheims against Gilbert de la Porrée, bishop of Poitiers. We have from him a letter to Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis. He died in 1151 while on pilgrimage to Jerusalem. CLXXXI, 1722.

BARTHOLOMEW of Sombernon, lord of Fontaines, presented himself to the chapter of Saint Stephen at Dijon and, in the presence of Lord [Col. 0419] Herbert the abbot, Warner the provost, and the other canons, gave a day’s measure of uncultivated land. Other charters are attributed to him. About 1154. CLXXXV, 1417, 1420.

BARTHOLOMEW, bishop of Laon, held the see for thirty-eight years and afterwards humbly became a monk of Clairvaux. When he was accused of having dissipated the good works of the Church of Laon, which he had accomplished with great praise, he complains to the archbishop of Rheims about this matter and clears himself of the charge in a letter, in 1154. CLXXXII, 696.

BARTHOLOMEW, bishop of Exeter in England, flourished in the twelfth century. A letter by him survives to Pope Alexander III in 1171, which also bears the name of Roger, bishop of Worcester. CXCIX, 363; CC, 1461.

BASIL (Saint), bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, son of Basil, an illustrious and noble man, and Emmelia; brother of Gregory of Nyssa and Peter, bishop of Sebaste, and friend of Gregory Nazianzen. He boldly withstood Modestus, the emperor’s prefect, when he tried to draw him over to the Arians. In many writings he defended the faith, gave monks a Rule, and died in 379. Monastic constitutions by him survive. CIII, 483.

BASIL, prior of the Grande Chartreuse. He flourished in the time of Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, and replied to his letter, offering a eulogy of the Cluniac order. CLXXXIX, 458.

BASIL, archbishop of Zagora, otherwise Trnovo among the Bulgarians, informed Innocent III of the joy which all had received from the happy arrival of the priest from Brindisi and from the letters which he had brought with him, in 1202. CCXIV, 1115; CCXV, 288.

BASVINUS and PAPINUS of Montibus donated to Blessed Robert of Arbrissel and the monastery of Fontevraud the fief of Varens, which they held from Aimeric Floccel, at the beginning of the twelfth century. CLXII, 1109.

BATURICUS, bishop of Regensburg, in the ninth century, made certain exchanges with Erchampert and Veciandus, as is evident from the charters surviving in the traditions of Saint Emmeram. CXXIX, 935, 938.

BAUDONIVIA, a nun in the convent at Poitiers and contemporary of Saint Radegund, wrote the second book of that saint’s *Life*, which, as appears in the prologue, she dedicated to her sister Deduinia, an abbess. XXII, 663.

BEATUS (Saint), Spanish priest. Born of a noble and ancient Asturian family, he was instructed in the sacred Scriptures and conspicuous for zeal for the faith. With the assistance of Etherius, his disciple, he composed two books against Felix of Urgel and Elipandus. Distinguished by miracles, he died in 778. XCVI, 248.

BEDE THE VENERABLE, priest and abbot. Born in Northumbria beyond the borders of Scotland about 673, he displayed tireless zeal for safeguarding the truth of the faith and restoring moral integrity. He left very many dogmatic, exegetical, philosophical, and historical writings, and died in 735. XC–XCV.

BELISARIUS, scholar, is known to us only through an acrostic in which he praises Sedulius. Yet many conjecture that he was Sedulius’s contemporary; indeed, some suspect that he was the same as the celebrated general who flourished shortly after 540. XIX, 303, 782.

BELLOTA, prince of the Bulgarians, having received Dominic, envoy of Pope Innocent III, wrote back to him seeking communion with the Roman Church in 1202. CCLIV, 1116.

BENEDICT (Saint), leader and restorer of Western monks. Born in the province of Norcia among the Sabines in 480, he withdrew, when his first solitude was disturbed, to Monte Cassino, where he founded a most celebrated monastery consisting of twelve houses. He died in 543. He wrote his remarkable Rule, which many have elucidated with commentaries. LXVI, 126.

BENEDICT I, pope, surnamed Nonosus. A Roman by nation, he was consecrated in 573 and died in 577. Two letters survive from his writings. LXXII, 682.

BENEDICT II (Saint), pope. A Roman by nation, he was elected in 684 and held office for only one year. A lover of the poor, humble, gentle, and eminent in every merit, he died in 685. Two letters by him survive. XCVI, 422.

BENEDICT CRISPUS (Saint), archbishop of Milan. He defended his see even in the Roman court and founded a Benedictine monastery. He died in 725. See his writings, LXXXIX, 362.

BENEDICT, bishop and *vicedominus* of the holy apostolic see. Having received Boniface’s letters, in which he recounted various tribulations, especially those inflicted by wicked clerics, Benedict urged him not to lose heart, since with God’s help he would obtain victory, in 750. LXXXIX, 776.

BENEDICT (Saint), abbot of Aniane. A man noble by birth and [Col. 0420] distinguished by piety and learning, he was educated at the court of King Pippin, became abbot of the monastery of Aniane which he had founded, and died in 821. He compiled a code of monastic rules and issued letters and several charters. CIII, 352.

BENEDICT III, pope. A Roman by nation, he succeeded Pope Leo IV in 855. He held the Holy See for three years and died in 858. Several letters by him survive, as well as a diploma by which he received the monastery of Fulda under the protection of the apostolic see and confirmed its immunities. CXV, 684.

BENEDICT, called Levite and deacon, began by order of Autgar, archbishop of Mainz, a new collection, after Ansegisus, of the constitutions and capitularies of Charlemagne, Louis the Pious, and Lothair himself, during whose reign he seems to have flourished. XCVII, 697.

BENEDICT IV, pope. Born at Rome, he was appointed after an interregnum of one year to succeed John IX, in the time of Emperor Lambert, in 901, and died two years later. We have several letters by him and a diploma granted to Huog, abbot of Fulda. CXXXI, 40.

BENEDICT VI, pope. A Roman by birth, he succeeded Donus in 972. He was seized by Cardinal-Deacon Boniface, a most wicked man, thrown into prison, and shortly afterwards strangled in 974. See his letters and privileges. CXXXV, 1079.

BENEDICT VII, pope. Roman by race and descended from the counts of Tusculum, after Boniface VII had been slain he was elected in 975 through the support of his relatives and by lawful assemblies. He died in 983. Letters and diplomas concerning him survive. CXXXVII, 315.

BENEDICT, monk of Saint Andrew. Nothing certain is known of his life. He wrote a chronicle. CXXXIX, 9.

BENEDICT VIII, pope, was created in 1012 under King Henry. Driven from Rome by the antipope Gregory, he was restored to his see through King Henry’s aid and remained there until 1024, when he died. Several letters and decrees by him survive. CXXXIX, 1578.

BENEDICT IX, pope, of Tusculum, succeeded his uncle John XIX. Twice expelled from the see, he was twice restored to it. Four years later he voluntarily resigned this dignity and died in 1054. See his letters and privileges. CXLI, 1342.

BENEDICT, first a monk at Canterbury under Saint Thomas the archbishop, later became abbot of the monastery at Peterborough. He wrote a life of Saint Thomas recounting what he himself had seen, in 1175. CXC, 267.

BENEDICT, canon and cantor of the Church of Saint Peter at Rome, flourished in the twelfth century. He wrote a book on ecclesiastical order, which he dedicated to Cardinal Guido of Castello, afterwards Pope Celestine II. CXLXXIX [probably CLXXIX], 731.

BENEDICT XIV, pope, highly celebrated for talent and learning, granted indulgences in 1745 to those who celebrated Masses at the altar of Blessed Mary of Affligem, whose sacred image, according to report, spoke to Saint Bernard himself. CLXXXV, 1831.

BERENGAR, emperor of Germany, son of Eberhard and Gisela, was overthrown by Rudolf II and slain at Verona in 924. A diploma by him survives for the castle of Puzzuolo, in 921. XCIX, 638, 639.

BERENGAR, viscount of Narbonne, is known only from a complaint against Geoffrey, bishop of Narbonne, at the Council of Toulouse held under Raimbald, bishop of Arles, and Pons, bishop of Aix, in 1056. CXLIII, 843.

BERENGAUD, monk of the fourth century, is presumed to be the author of an exposition on the seven visions of the Book of Revelation, formerly ascribed to Saint Ambrose. XVII, 764.

BERENGER, heresiarch of the eleventh century, a native of Angers, taught many errors concerning the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood. He was condemned six times in councils and finally issued a retraction, which survives. CXLVIII, 1455.

BERENGOSUS, abbot of Saint Maximin at Trier, of the Order of Saint Benedict. He became renowned at the beginning of the twelfth century. He wrote three books on the praise and discovery of the Holy Cross, another little book on the mystery of the Lord’s wood, and several sermons. CLX, 935.

BERLAIUS of Montreuil and Hugh, son of Gregory, gave land called Bornio to the church of Fontevraud in the twelfth century. CLXII, 1102.

BERMUND (PETER), lord of Anduze and of Salve, having married the lawful and only daughter of the count of Toulouse, whose vacant goods had been declared forfeit because of his excommunication, sent a letter to Pope Innocent III asking that he should not be deprived of the inheritance and that it should not be handed over to a mere bastard son, in 1212. CCXVI, 754.

BERMUND, bishop of Aix. He flourished at the beginning of the thirteenth century. He seeks to persuade Pope Innocent III that the impious Raymond, count of Toulouse, or his son, [Col. 0421] should especially not be restored either to power or to possessions; otherwise evils far worse than the former ones would threaten from this. CCVI, 844.

BERNALD and BERNOLD. See BERTHOLD.

BERNARD (PETER), canon of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, lived in the twelfth century. He granted certain properties to a certain Andrew for an annual rent of two Byzantine coins, in 1136. CLV, 1206.

BERNARD, monk of Gallic origin, lived in the ninth century. An *Itinerary to the Holy Places* by him survives. CXI, 570.

BERNARD, second abbot of Saint Gall. He became renowned in the ninth century and composed several verses and brief maxims. LXXXVII, 30, 62.

BERNARD, abbot of Tulle, was bound to the brethren of Aurillac by an annual rent of three pounds of pepper and paid it with difficulty; he obtained from the abbot of Aurillac that it be remitted to him, ninth century. CXXXII, 472.

BERNARD, scholar of Angers, was Fulbert’s disciple about 1010. He wrote a book on the miracles of Saint Faith the Virgin. CXLI, 123.

BERNARD, count of Bigorre, lived in the eleventh century. He granted to the monastery of Cluny, with the consent of the bishop of that place, the governance of the monastery of Saint Felix situated in his territory. CXLIX, 958, 963.

BERNARD, knight and lord of the castle of Évreux, donated to the monastery of Saint Peter at Chartres in 1070 the village of Nantilly, which he held from his grandfather Rodheto. CLV, 288.

BERNARD, count of Auch, son of William, gave to Cluny the church of Saint Mary of Arombodio in 1070. CLIX, 962.

BERNARD, count of Besalú, gave Blessed Hugh of Cluny, for reform and restoration to the vigor of discipline, in their entirety certain monasteries which he held by succession, in 1078. CLIX, 968.

BERNARD, bishop of Lodève, called de Provenquiers, endured immense labors in defending ecclesiastical rights. He attended the Council of Clermont under Urban II, enlisted in the holy warfare, and died in 1098, three years after Jerusalem had been captured. A charter by him of donation for the Church of Saint Gregory at Rodez survives. CL, 1549.

BERNARD, archbishop of Toledo, attended the councils of León, Nîmes, and Girona held from 1091 to 1097. He produced four sermons on the antiphon *Salve Regina*, formerly published among the works of Saint Bernard. CLV, 146.

BERNARD, monk of Saint Saviour in Italy and afterwards abbot of Saint Anastasius at Aquae Salviae near Rome, was finally pope under the name Eugenius III. Several letters by him survive, published among the works of Saint Bernard of Clairvaux, in 1140. (See EUGENIUS III.) CLXXXII, 547.

BERNARD, bishop of Hildesheim and count of Rottenburg on the Tuber, secured the enrollment of Saint Godehard among the saints. We have from him a letter to Pope Eugenius III in 1148 and another to Wibald, abbot of Corvey, in 1149. CLXXXIX, 1165, 1220.

BERNARD, bishop of Paderborn. Wibald entrusted a certain case to him; he endeavored to settle it and reported to Wibald what he had decided in 1149. CLXXXIX, 1242 and following.

BERNARD, first prior of the Charterhouse of Portes. He flourished in the twelfth century. Several spiritual letters by him survive. CLIII, 386.

BERNARD, count of Bourges, and his wife Aloys donated to the Church of the Holy Sepulchre a house which they possessed near the gate of that Church, twelfth century. CLV, 1203.

BERNARD, lord of the castle of Radulf, and his wife Havidis bought from George Roricus and Bursard a house for eighty Byzantine coins, in the time of Patriarch Garmond and during the reign of Baldwin II, twelfth century. CLV, 1203.

BERNARD (Saint), first abbot of the monastery of Clairvaux. He was born about 1090 of the noble stock of the lords of Fontaines in the duchy of Burgundy. With his brothers and several companions he sought the wilderness of Clairvaux, where, with the favor of Theobald, count of Champagne, he founded a celebrated monastery, from which came Pope Eugenius III and a great many bishops. Bernard refuted Peter Abelard, preached the holy war, aided the wavering apostolic see, and everywhere was a burning lamp in the Church through the power of his speech and the learning of his writings; he deserved to be numbered among the Fathers and Doctors. He died in 1155. He produced sermons, letters, and various treatises. CLXXXII–CLXXXV.

BERNARD, bishop of Lydda, and Peter, prior of the Holy Sepulchre, subscribed certain agreements between themselves in 1171. CLV, 1256.

BERNARD, bishop of Nevers, flourished in the twelfth century. He wrote to Pope Alexander III, asking him [Col. 0422] to act with indulgence toward the king of England in the case of Thomas of Canterbury. CC, 1417.

BERNARD, bishop of Porto and cardinal, flourished in the twelfth century. He wrote a consolatory letter to Saint Thomas of Canterbury. CXC, 985; CXCVI, 1393.

BERNARD, knight of Épinac, bought a meadow called Brolium for the monks of Fontenay through the hand of Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux. CLXXXV, 1463.

BERNARD, abbot of Fontis Calidi, of the Premonstratensian order, flourished in the twelfth century. He wrote a book against the heresy of the Waldensians, condemned by Pope Lucius III. CCIV, 793.

BERNARD of Montebarro, lord of Époisses, declares that his mother Helwida, at her death, directed that the Church and brethren of Fontenay should receive every year ten sextaries, partly of oats and partly of wheat, from the lands of Corseinz, and in addition twenty solidi from land at Vassé, in 1210. CLXXXV, 1468.

BERNARD, count of Comminges, together with his son submitted himself into the hands of Peter, king of Aragon, when he saw that the cause of the count of Toulouse, whom he had followed, was utterly ruined. He promised obedience to the Roman Church under oath in 1213. CCXVI, 848.

BERNARD, treasurer of the Holy See and called master, was sent to Lausanne. When Rudolf, emperor of Germany, arrived there, Bernard did not visit him, but merely wrote him a letter. Writing in reply, the emperor asked the reason for this. Bernard’s answer survives, from 1276. XCVIII, 746.

BERNARD GUI, a native of Limoges, was from the village of Roeria. He entered the Order of Preachers of Saint Dominic in 1305; he became inquisitor against the Albigensian heresy, bishop of Tuy in 1323, and finally bishop of Lodève in the following year, in Narbonnese Gaul. He died in 1331. A life of Pope Innocent III by him survives. CLXXIX, 27.

BERNARD of Marey, of the lords of Fontaines in the district of Dijon, born of Saint Bernard’s family and dwelling in the same castle from which the saintly abbot had come, in 1462 gave to Humbert of Cîteaux a fourth part of his house and revenues, so that prayers might be offered for his then deceased mother. An old charter survives in French. CLXXXV, 1454.

BERNELINUS, while still young and a monk, composed a treatise on music at Paris, which he dedicated to a certain Amelius, priest and monk. He wrote another little work on the division of the monochord. CLI, 653.

BERNERUS, abbot of Homblières, of the Order of Saint Benedict. About 964 he wrote the *Life of Saint Hunegundis*, and died near the end of the tenth century. CXXXVII, 50.

BERNO was made the first abbot of the monastery of Cluny by William the Pious, count of Auvergne, founder of that monastery. Berno’s nephew was the venerable Guy, whom he made abbot of the monastery of Baume; his disciples were Odo and Adhegrin. A testament by Berno survives, by which he bestowed many things on that monastery, in 926. CXXXIII, 853.

BERNO, abbot of Reichenau. He was first a monk of Saint Gall, of Saint Benedict’s order, in Germany. But after he had distinguished himself for many years under regular discipline, he moved to Reichenau near Constance on the Rhine, having become abbot. He died in 1048. Many works by him survive. CXLII, 1047.

BERNOWINUS, bishop of Clermont, aided by the generosity of Charlemagne, built in the episcopal city a church in honour of St. Allyre, in the year 824. Certain poems by him survive, CV, 446.

BERTARIUS (St.), abbot of Monte Cassino and martyr, descended from the stock of the kings of the Franks, flourished in the ninth century. Slain by the Saracens, he received the crown of martyrdom in 884. From him we have a poem in praise of St. Benedict, CXXVI, 976.

BERTARIUS, priest of Verdun and monk of St. Vito, lived at the beginning of the tenth century. He wrote the Deeds of the Bishops of Verdun, CXXXII, 502.

BERTHA, countess and sister of Count Theobald, bought vineyards from a certain Ralph called “the Calculus,” with the consent of Abbot Landric, to whom they belonged, in 1069, CLV, 336.

BERTHEFREDUS, bishop of Amiens, flourished under King Clotaire and Queen St. Balthild, founders of the monastery of Corbie, to which he too granted privileges, in 662, LXXXVIII, 1178.

BERTHOLDUS, priest of Constance and monk of the monastery of St. Blaise, also called Bernaldus and Bernoldus. He wrote many small works concerning the authority of the Apostolic See, against the corrupt morals of clerics, and against the schismatics of his time. He flourished in the tenth century, CXLVII, 330; CXLVIII, 103, 209, 1057, and elsewhere.

BERTHOLDUS, monk of Reichenau. He flourished in the eleventh century under Hermann the Lame, whose disciple he was and whose Life he wrote, CXLIII, 25, 263.

BERTHOLDUS, a man freeborn and of noble status, gave as a gift all that he possessed in Swabia [Col. 0423] to Lord William, patriarch of Jerusalem, and to Peter, prior of the Holy Sepulchre, in return for an annual payment of ten solidi for as long as he should live, in 1142, CLV, 1179.

BERTHOLDUS, abbot of Zwiefalten, lived in the twelfth century. Being in distress and suffering persecutions, he sought words of consolation from St. Hildegard, abbess, CXCVII, 284.

BERTHWALDUS of Somerford, who in his subscription assumes the title of sub-king, bestowed many splendid gifts upon St. Aldhelm, abbot in England, in 686; King Æthelred of Mercia also subscribed this charter, LXXXIX, 313.

BERTICHRAMNUS, bishop of Le Mans. From childhood he devoted himself wholly to God’s service. Having completed the course of his studies, he fulfilled the office of archdeacon in the Church of Paris, whence he was raised to the see of Le Mans. He wrote several poems. He founded the monastery of St. Peter, in which he was buried, and by his testament gave it many possessions in 623, LXXX, 385.

BERTIGISILUS, on account of a lawsuit which he had brought against a certain Philip, a patrician, had recourse to St. Desiderius while the latter was still residing in King Dagobert’s palace, so that he might set forth and commend his cause to the king, in 640. But where he flourished is uncertain, LXXXVI, 257.

BERTILINDIS, born of noble lineage and possessing many goods, was soon divinely inspired to renounce the world; having assumed the monastic habit, she gave to St. Willibrord, archbishop of Utrecht and likewise abbot of Echternach, all that she possessed from her maternal inheritance. This was done at Calais, where perhaps she was abbess, in 710, LXXXIX, 543.

BERTOENDUS, bishop of Châlons, granted various privileges to the monastery of Der, over which St. Bercharius presided, and also to another neighbouring monastery of nuns. These monasteries had been founded by Watmer and his wife Watild, together with St. Bercharius, about 692, LXXXVIII, 1225.

BERTRADA, or BERTA, wife of King Pippin, founded and richly endowed the monastery of Prüm. She had a son named Caribert, and must be distinguished from another, elder Bertrada, who was her grandmother. This charter dates from 721, LXXXVIII, 1274.

BERTRANDUS, count of Tripoli, son of Raymond of St. Gilles, granted to the Church of the Holy Sepulchre situated in the castle of Mount Pilgrim three villages which he had promised, in 1112, CLV, 1198.

BERTRANDUS de Blancesfort, master of the Templars, flourished in the twelfth century. Several letters from him to Louis the Younger, king of France, survive, CLV, 1269, 1272.

BERTRANDUS, bishop of Bordeaux, flourished in the time of Pope Alexander III. He wrote to him concerning the rebellion of the monks of St. Macarius against the Church of Holy Cross at Bordeaux, in 1170, CC, 1368.

BERTRANDUS, bishop of Agen, flourished in the twelfth century. When Henry, son of Henry king of England, had died, and the condition of his testament by which he had chosen his burial-place in the church of Blessed Mary at Rouen could very difficultly be fulfilled, Bertrand consulted Pope Lucius III as to what should be done, CC, 1377.

BERTRANDUS, bishop of Béziers and suffragan of Narbonne. In 1213 he warned Pope Innocent III not to be swayed by the entreaties of Peter, king of Aragon, who had secretly made a most wicked alliance with heretics and coveted the possessions of Count Raymond of Toulouse, CCXVI, 843.

BERTRANDUS, patriarch of Aquileia. By decree of Pope Innocent IV, having first requested it, he transferred the provostship of St. Odalric to the church of St. Mary of Udine, and by a special statute united it to that church in 1334, XCIX, 635.

BERYNTHUS, a spurious Greek bishop, to whom, together with persons like him, is attributed a forged letter fabricated by heretical hands, year uncertain, VIII, 977.

A certain BETTO sold several lands to Blessed Ludger, abbot, in 806, XCIX, 819.

BILEHILT, niece of Sigebert, bishop of Mainz, founded and endowed a convent of nuns near Mainz in 734, LXXXVIII, 1289.

BLANCA, lady of Sombernon and widow of Hervey, testifies that William Fromunt and his brother Peter gave to the church of St. Mary of Bussière one half of a meadow in the territory of Varoilles and the entire tithe of the territory of Poissins, in 1242, CLXXXV, 1427, 1475.

BLANDUS, priest. See GERMANUS.

BLIDEGISILLUS, a deacon, founded the monastery of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés out of all that he had received from King Clovis and from Queen Nantechild, mother of Clovis; by a charter he granted it all his possessions in 640, LXXXVIII, 1157.

BLOMENVENNA, PETER. See FRANCIS a Puteo.

BOCARDUS AIMO and his wife ASCELINA gave to the monastery of Clairvaux all that they possessed at Petrocinium, in the twelfth century, CLXXXV, 990.

BODALUS, also read as BODOLUS, son of a certain Hugh, granted to the monastery of St. Gregory in Alsace all that he possessed in the village of Hodulsesheim in 747, and by another charter all that he possessed on the island of Hohenhaugen in 748, LXXXVIII, 1311, 1318.

BOETHIUS (Anicius Manlius Severinus), born at Rome about 470, studied letters first there and then at Athens. He became skilled in the sciences and disciplines, and therefore produced very many works, both philosophical and mathematical. His principal work was the book *The Consolation of Philosophy*. He steadfastly professed the faith when handed over to torturers, in 524, LXIII–LXIV.

BOHEMUND, also called BOHAMUND, son of Robert Guiscard, prince of Taranto and later of Antioch, one of the most celebrated leaders of the crusaders, performed many distinguished deeds in the holy war. He flourished from 1096 to 1111. Letters by him survive, CLV, 389 and elsewhere.

BOMA, and according to Pez IMMA, wife of Einhard and of royal blood, wrote to the wife of a certain Albin, her friend, asking her to deal more gently with a slave who had secretly married a free woman, about 820, CIV, 514.

BONACURSUS, formerly a heretic and then a Catholic. How and when he embraced the faith is uncertain. Near the end of the twelfth century he wrote a book against the Cathars, who denied marriage, CCIV, 776.

BONAVENTURE (St.), of the Order of Friars Minor and Doctor of the Church. His family name was John Fidanza; he was born in Italy. He was especially renowned for preaching, and, while present at the Council of Lyons, died of illness in 1274. In the new *Course of Patrology* there is an encomium of him by Dom Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, CLXXXV, 629.

BONIFACE I (St), pope. His country and lineage are uncertain. He succeeded Pope Zosimus in 418 and held the Apostolic See until 422, when he died. See the surviving letters and decrees, XX, 746.

BONIFACE, count, originally a soldier from Thrace, was sent to Africa as a tribune and became involved in many anxieties and affairs. On Augustine’s advice he was made count; but, without Augustine’s knowledge, he married after having previously vowed continence, a course Augustine disapproved. Later, wounded in battle, he paid the debt of death in 432. Several letters to Augustine from him survive, XXXIII, 1095.

BONIFACE II, pope. A Roman by nation, he succeeded Felix IV. He lived in the time of the heretical King Athalaric and of Emperor Justinian; at the beginning he had Dioscorus as a rival claimant, whose death soon ended the dissension. He died in 531. Several decrees by him and a letter to St. Caesarius of Arles survive, LXV, 30.

BONIFACE IV (St), pope. A Roman by nation, born in the city of Valeria, he succeeded Boniface III and held the see for six years. He dedicated to the martyrs and the Blessed Virgin, under the name of St. Mary Rotunda, the ancient temple which Agrippa had built in honour of all the gods. Distinguished for piety, he converted his palace into a monastery. He received letters from St. Columban, requesting permission to follow ancient traditions concerning the celebration of Easter, but this holy pope’s replies have not reached us. He died in 614, LXXX, 102.

BONIFACE V, pope. A Campanian by nation, from the city of Naples, he sat for seven years. Among other enactments, he decreed that a testament should be valid according to the ruler’s command; three letters by him to various persons in England survive. He died in 625, LXXX, 430.

BONIFACE, author of the Life of St. Livinus, is, according to Mabillon, not the same as Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, who is later. Who this man was, therefore, is wholly uncertain, LXXXVII, 327.

BONIFACE (St), archbishop of Mainz, martyr, and apostle of Germany. Born of noble English stock in 680, he was formerly named Winfrid and was most distinguished for learning, holiness, and untiring zeal for propagating the Catholic faith. Pope Gregory III invested him with archiepiscopal dignity and the pallium in 732. But he chose a successor for himself, that he might devote himself more freely to the salvation of unbelievers; as an old man he was slain in Frisia in 755. We possess no few letters, sermons, and other small works by him, LXXXIX, 598.

BONIZO, or BONITIUS, appears to have been Italian by birth and was first bishop of Sutri. Expelled from his see by Emperor Henry because he supported Pope Gregory’s party, he was promoted to the see of Piacenza, where he was seized by criminals, had his eyes gouged out, and was slain in 1089. He produced nine books on the persecution of the Church and fragments of papal history, CL, 782.

BONUSHOMO. See ALPHONSUS.

BONUSHOMO, canon of the cathedral church of Troyes, gave a description in French of the coats of arms of the counts of Champagne, in 1586, CLXXXV, 1480.

[Col. 0425] BORONUS, an illustrious man of Alsace, gave certain estates to the monastery of Honau, over which Abbot Benedict Tubanus presided, in 746. Two charters of this donation survive, LXXXVIII, 1280, 1312.

BOVO, abbot of St. Bertin. Reared and educated from childhood in the abbey of St. Bertin, he became its abbot after the death of Roderic, which occurred in 1045. From him we have an account of the discovery and translation of the body of St. Bertin, which had been concealed for fear of the Northmen, in 1052. He died in 1065, CXLIII, 1367.

BOVO, provost of the monastery of Stavelot, informed Wibald, abbot of Corvey, of the injuries which the count of Namur had inflicted upon him and the monastery in 1148, CLXXXIX, 1155.

BOWINUS, an Anglo-Saxon abbot, wrote to Blessed Lullus, archbishop of Mainz, and sent him certain small gifts at the same time, in 756, XCVI, 836.

BOZO, count of the Ardennes, afterwards made duke of Lombardy by Charles the Bald, and finally elected king of Arles by twenty-three bishops, waged war against Louis and Carloman, by whom he was defeated near Vienne. He died in 887. We have his election and his reply to the bishops, CXXXVIII, 787.

BRACILAUS, or BRACILIO, duke of Bohemia, having taken by arms Gniezno, the metropolitan city of Poland, regarded nothing as more important than recovering the relics of St. Adalbert the martyr. But when the Bohemians attempted to open the tomb, they were suddenly struck with stupefaction. Understanding this, Severus, bishop of Prague, warned the prince and soldiers that, if they wished to have Adalbert as a fellow citizen, they must first promise reform of morals. Therefore in 1039 Bracilio issued the decree which survives, CLI, 1257.

BRAULIO (St), bishop of Saragossa. He succeeded his brother John in the episcopate in 627. A learned man and illustrious among the bishops of the Spanish Church, he restored ecclesiastical discipline, protected letters, and attended many councils. He died about 633. From him survive letters, the Life of St. Aemilianus, and the Acts of the Martyrs of Saragossa, LXXX.

BREGWINUS, an Anglo-Saxon abbot. He wrote a letter to St. Lullus, archbishop of Mainz, in which he mentions the affection which all the brethren have for him and informs him on what day the venerable Abbess Bugga died, XCVI, 843.

BRIDFERTUS, monk of Ramsey and disciple of Abbo, flourished at the close of the tenth century. He composed a commentary on Bede’s book *On the Nature of Things* and, in addition, compiled the Life of St. Dunstan, CXXXIX, 1423.

BROCARDUS. See BURTRADUS.

BROCARDUS, or BURCHARDUS, abbot of the monastery of Balerna, wrote to Nicholas of Clairvaux about his own conversion, in the twelfth century, CXCVI, 1605.

BRUNO, or BRUNHILD, queen, wife of Sigibert and the famous enemy of Fredegund, performed many good deeds as well as evil ones. St. Gregory the Great wrote to her more than once. For what she herself did, see Gregory of Tours, LXXI, 594, 1171, 1174.

BRUNO (St), archbishop of Cologne, brother of Emperor Otto the Great, whose chief chaplain he was at first, succeeded Wifrid in the see of Cologne. A diploma by him survives, and according to some he is the author of a commentary on the books of Moses. He died in 965, CXXXIV, 987.

BRUNO, bishop of Langres. Born of noble lineage, he had as father Ragenhald, who assumed for himself the title of count of Rheims. He became bishop in 981 and sat for thirty-five years. Only a charter and a letter to the clerics of Langres survive from him, CXXXIX, 1534.

BRUNO (St), bishop of Würzburg, born of illustrious stock, was elected after the death of Meginhard through the care and effort of Emperor Conrad II. He governed this Church piously for eleven years and died in 1045. He expounded the Psalms and commented on the Lord’s Prayer, CXLII, 9.

BRUNO, cleric of Magdeburg and intimate of Werner, bishop of Merseburg, flourished in the eleventh century. He wrote a book on the Saxon war, full of historical documents, CXLVII, 486.

BRUNO (Eusebius), appointed bishop of Angers in 1047, attended the Council of Rheims in 1049; the monastery at Angers, in 1062 [sentence fragment in the source]. A letter by him survives to Master Berengar, a most distinguished man of approved life, who held the offices of archdeacon and treasurer at Angers. He died in 1081, CXLVIII, 1199.

BRUNO, whose birthplace and life we nowhere discover, undertook to restore Paterius’s collection entitled the *Gregoriale*, because through the passage of time it had suffered very great loss, CLV, 145.

BRUNO (St), founder of the Carthusians. A German by nation, born of distinguished parents, he was first a canon of Rheims and master of the schools. Thence he withdrew to the wilderness of Chartreuse near Grenoble, and presided for about six years over the monastery he had founded. Then, at the command of Urban [Col. 0426] II, whose counsellor he was, he went to Rome; soon, with the holy pontiff’s consent, he withdrew to the wilderness of Calabria, established the rule of the order, and died there in 1101. He expounded the Book of Psalms and the Epistles of St. Paul, and composed a discourse on contempt for the world, CLII, CLIII.

BRUNO, archbishop of Trier, informed Rodolph, archbishop of Rheims, of the vexations inflicted by certain nobles upon the nuns of Blessed Mary at Trier, in 1115, CLXII, 1419.

BRUNO (St), abbot of Asti and afterwards bishop of Segni. Born of illustrious family, he completed his first training in piety and learning in a monastery; afterwards, going into Etruria, he was enrolled among the canons of Segni. At length, made bishop of Segni by the authority of his superiors, he governed that church until his last day, namely 1125. He wrote commentaries on various books of Scripture, homilies, sermons, and treatises, CLIV, CLV.

BRUNO, bishop of Strasbourg. First provost of Honau, then canon of Bamberg, he finally became bishop of Strasbourg in 1123. He died in 1130. A letter by him to Gerhoh, provost of Reichersberg, survives, CLXVI, 1347.

BRUNO, bishop of Hildesheim, succeeded Bernard in 1153 and died in 1160. In 1156 he entreated Wichmann, archbishop of Magdeburg, to excuse the bishop of Osnabrück, who, being detained by illness, could not come to him. (See Wichmann.) CLXXXIX, 1445.

BUGGA, abbess, lived about 720. Under St. Boniface of Mainz, to whom she wrote a letter after the death of the impious King Radbod, she mentions the venerable Willibald, whom she greatly revered. Some maintain that she is identical with Eadburg, who wrote to Boniface and was no little skilled in the liberal arts. Several letters by her survive, LXXXIX, 690, 726.

BULGARANNUS, count and prefect of Narbonne under King Guntram, addressed several letters to various persons in 632; see them, LXXX, 108.
