BURCHARDUS, bishop of Worms. A German by nation and a native of Hesse, he was first a monk at Lobbes in Belgium, afterwards abbot, and finally made bishop in 996; he died in 1125. He compiled a valuable collection of canons; we also have letters concerning him, CXL, 491.

BURGUNDOFARA, sister of St. Faro, bishop of Meaux, lived a long time in the monastery of Faremoutiers. When near death she dictated a testament in favour of the same monastery in 632, LXXXVII, 1137.

## C

CADURCUS, royal cleric and chancellor, superintendent of the guard of the tower of Bourges, heard from Suger that soldiers had been sent to occupy the tower and that he himself had received an order to surrender it. He wrote to Rotrou, count of Perche, asking him to inform Ralph of Vermandois of this and obtain from him letters commanding that the surrender be refused, about 1148, CLXXXVI, 1396, 1404.

CAECILIA, countess of Tripoli. After the death of her husband Count Pons, she granted permission to the canons of the Holy Sepulchre, then governed by Wlgrin, to bake whatever they wished, free from all payment, in the oven which they had on Mount Pilgrim, in 1139, CLV, 1182.

CAECILIA and her co-heirs, daughter of Humbert de Fontaines, sold a garden to William de Fontaines in 1282, CLXXXV, 1452.

CAECILIANUS, bishop of Carthage. Ordained by Felix, he was calumniated by the Donatists but was cleared of blame and error against Novatus at the Roman council held under Pope Miltiades in 313, and was again acquitted by Constantine the Great at a trial held at Milan. He died about 347. A brief letter by him to Felix, bishop of Aptunga, survives, VIII, 749.

CAESARIUS (St), bishop of Arles. A Gaul by nation and native of Chalon, he embraced monastic life in his youth at the monastery of Lérins; later, though reluctant, he was made bishop and governed this province with zeal and piety for forty years. He died in 542. His letters, sermons or homilies, and several small works survive, LXVII, 1165.

CAESARIUS, Roman patrician, under whose rule were then the regions which still rendered obedience to the Roman emperors. He flourished under King Sisebut, to whom he sent several letters, about 621, LXXX, 366.

CAESARIUS, monk of Heisterbach of the Cistercian Order, long served as master of novices in the monastery of the Valley of St. Peter and published several writings. He died in 1210; he spoke finely of St. Bernard, CLXXXV, 636.

CAIUS (St), pope. A man of the highest prudence and remarkable virtue, born of noble family, he succeeded St. Eutychian in 283 and held the Holy See until 295, when he died. He is customarily numbered among the martyrs in various martyrologies; only one decree of his, concerning ordinations, survives, V, 179.

CALDONIUS, priest of Carthage and confessor, skilled in the understanding of the Scriptures, whose faith and integrity St. Cyprian extols. We have a letter from him to St. Cyprian, whom he consults about granting peace to certain lapsed persons, in 250, IV, 271.

CALIXTUS (St), pope and martyr, succeeded St. Zephyrinus and founded the cemetery on the Appian Way. He suffered under Alexander Severus in 222. The decrees attributed to him in Pseudo-Isidore are spurious, CXXX, 129.

CALIXTUS II, pope. Previously called Guy, a Burgundian by birth, son of Count William and kinsman of Emperor Henry, he was first archbishop of Rheims and legate of the Apostolic See. After Pope Gelasius died, the cardinals fled into Gaul and elected him at Cluny. At a council in Rheims he excluded Emperor Henry from communion with the Church. He died in 1124. His letters and decrees survive, CLXIII, 1024.

CALO de Sauz, lord of Fontaines, and his wife Dannez gave to the monks of Bussière all that they possessed in the territories and villages of Dez and Hauteville, to establish an anniversary service for the repose of their souls, in 1267. According to his epitaph, he died in 1272, CLXXXV, 1430, 1431.

CALOJOANNES, king of the Bulgarians. About the beginning of the thirteenth century he wrote to Pope Innocent III, giving thanks for the letter which the pope had sent to him through S., priest of Brindisi, in 1202. His letter, written in Bulgarian, was first translated into Greek and afterwards into Latin, CCXIV, 1112; CCXV, 155.

CALVIN (John), ironically called “the Pope of Geneva,” completed his studies at Paris and was then soon expelled because of his novel opinions. He went to Geneva in Switzerland, where he taught theology; he openly introduced the poison of heresy and fought against the faith in writings and words. He died in 1564. Yet he made certain statements about St. Bernard which we judged not useless to report, CLXXXV, 639.

CAMBIUS (Peter). See PETER.

CAMENUS (Francis) appears to belong to the twelfth century. A native of Perugia, he composed a Sapphic hymn on St. Nicholas, the pilgrim of Apulia, who died in 1194, CXLII, 719.

CANAPARUS (John). See JOHN.

CANCELLINUS, count, gave an allodial estate to Frederick, patriarch of Aquileia, in 1085, in order that the monastery of Moggio might be founded; this instrument was carried into effect under Ulrich, Frederick’s successor, XCIX, 641.

CANDIDUS, an Arian, apparently educated in letters but ignorant of the Scriptures, flourished in the fourth century. He wrote a book on the divine generation to Marius Victorinus, the Christian rhetorician, VIII, 1013.

CANDIDUS, monk of Fulda, whom Mabillon distinguishes from that Candidus, disciple of Alcuin, of whom this man makes mention in more than one place, flourished in the ninth century. He is the author of the Life of St. Eigil and of a small work on the Passion of the Lord, CV, 381; CVI, 57.

CANDIDUS, of whom there survives a fragment on the image of God in the appendix to Alcuin, is of uncertain identity. Perhaps he is that Candidus to whom Alcuin wrote a letter (vol. C, 408), perhaps the monk of Fulda who wrote the Life of St. Eigil, CI, 1359.

CANGITHA, also called Cangith and Eangith, a relative of Ethelbert, king of Kent, was the mother of Bugga and sister of St. Boniface of Mainz; first a nun and afterwards an abbess. She wrote to St. Boniface of the many tribulations she suffered, especially from the king, who held her people in great hatred, in 733, LXXXIX, 726.

CANISIUS (Peter), born at Nijmegen in 1521. Having entered the Society of Jesus, he became famous for preaching in Germany. He was made provincial of the Society and soon became legate of the Holy See. He published the works of St. Cyril of Alexandria and of certain other Fathers with annotations. He died at Fribourg in 1597. An encomium of St. Bernard survives, CLXXXV, 637.

CANUTE II of Denmark, but the first English king of that name, called the Great, gained England by arms and went to Rome for religious reasons. He died in 1056. He enacted ecclesiastical laws and granted various diplomas, CLI, 1171.

CANUTE VI, king of England and Denmark. At the end of the twelfth century he wrote to the cardinals, before whom he complained that Philip, king of France, had repudiated his sister in order to marry another woman, CCIX, 668, 754.

CAPPIDUS of Staveren, a Frisian priest who flourished in the tenth century. He is the author of the Life of St. Odulphus, priest. The Lives of Saints Lebuin, Otger, and Plechelm are also attributed to him, CXXXIII, 858.

CAPREOLUS, bishop of Carthage, succeeded St. Aurelius. [Col. 0428] He wrote a book on the one person of Christ against Nestorius, in which, according to Baronius, he showed himself a truly eminent theologian. The year of his death is uncertain; three letters survive from his writings, LIII, 844.

CARILEPHUS (St), first abbot of Anisole. He flourished under King Clotaire, whose brother he was. At first he lived in the territory of Auvergne with a certain Avitus as his companion; soon, when many gathered there, he was elected abbot, and later Childebert of Le Mans built a monastery for them. A letter of St. Carilephus to Innocent, bishop of Le Mans, survives, dated 540, LXXIV, 1263.

CARLOMAN, son of Charles Martel, reigned for a time with his brother Pippin over the Franks, but, having abdicated power, became a monk at Monte Cassino. He died at Vienne in 753. He subscribed certain diplomas, XCVI, 1501.

CHARLES, mayor of the sacred palace, called Martel, was the son of Pippin and later obtained royal power. In 741 he gave the estate of Clichy, situated in the district of Paris, to the monastery of St. Denis, in which his father had been buried, after King Theuderic IV had already been dead for five years without a successor. He also granted many things to the monastery of Echternach, over which St. Willibrord presided, LXXXVIII, 1302; LXXXIX, 550 ff.

CHARLEMAGNE, son of Pippin, king of the Franks and later emperor of the West, proclaimed such by Pope Leo III because he had delivered him from the tyrannical power of the Lombards. He waged a severe war against the Saxons. He enacted very many laws, restored the arts and letters in Gaul, and vigorously protected religion. He died in 814. He left capitularies, constitutions, letters, and diplomas, XCVII–XCVIII.

CHARLES THE BALD, king of the Franks and emperor, reigned from 840 to 877; he was crowned emperor by John VIII in 875. During his reign the Normans invaded Gaul. He issued certain capitularies, letters, and diplomas, CXXIV, 861.

CHARLES III, king of the Franks, son of Louis the Stammerer, granted Neustria to the Normans. Later, when attacked by Hugh, he surrendered himself to the count of Vermandois; held captive by him, he died in 929. An appeal by him to the bishops at the Council of Tongeren survives, CXXXVIII, 813.

CHARLES II, king of Sicily and Jerusalem, received a letter in which Peter, king of Aragon, complained that Charles was persecuting his subjects. Charles replied that he was ready for war in 1282, CLXXIV, 1560.

CHARLES III, king of Sicily and afterwards of Hungary; after committing many crimes, he died by poison in 1386. A letter from him to the people of Udine, in favour of the cardinal of Alençon, survives, dated 1382, XCIX, 669.

CHARLES, called the Bold, duke of Burgundy. An illustrious man in war, born at Dijon in 1433, he was killed in battle in 1477. A foundation in French by him of an annual Mass for the repose of his own soul and those of his parents in the abbey of Clairvaux, dated 1472, survives, CLXXXV, 1754.

CARREUS (Francis), monk of the abbey of Bec. He flourished in the sixteenth century and wrote the chronicle of that abbey, CL, 691.

CASSIAN, priest of Marseilles. According to some he was born in Thrace about 380. Educated among the monks of Palestine, he himself became a monk, attached himself at Constantinople to St. John Chrysostom, and was ordained deacon by him. Made a priest at Marseilles, he founded two monasteries there. He opposed the errors of Nestorius, but St. Prosper also opposed him and accused him of Semi-Pelagianism. He wrote twelve books *On the Institutes of the Coenobia*, twenty-four *Conferences*, and seven books *On the Incarnation of the Lord against Nestorius*. He died about 433, XLIX–L.

CASSIODORUS was born at Squillace, in the territory of Bruttium, of most distinguished parents. Under Theodoric, king of the Goths, he held the consulship, in discharging which office he showed himself highly praiseworthy. Already seventy years old, he founded the monastery of Vivarium, where he took care that the monks should be perfectly educated. He produced many historical, exegetical, and grammatical writings. He died in 562, LXIX–LXX.

CASTELLIONE. See GUIDO de and GODEFRIDUS.

CATHWALONNUS, abbot of Redon and successor of Mainard from 1026 until his death in 1049. He wrote one letter to Hildegard, wife of Fulk of Anjou, and another to Letgarde, abbess of St. Mary of Charity, CXLI, 1282.

CATULFUS. We know nothing else of him except that he sent a letter or instruction to Blessed King Charles, in the seventh century, XCVI, 1363.

CEADWALLA, king of the Saxons, bestowed certain gifts upon the monastery of Malmesbury, over which St. Aldhelm presided, in 682, LXXXIX, 312.

[Col. 0429] CELER, an illustrious man, informed Hormisdas in 519 that, through the efforts of the envoys, all were living peacefully at Constantinople, and that the same would soon be the case in other cities; for at that time the Eastern Church was being divided by the heresies of Nestorius and Eutyches, LXIII, 487.

CELERINUS, an African confessor whom St. Cyprian, in Epistle 22, calls “a good and strong confessor,” appears to have been a priest, or at least a deacon. He wrote a letter to Lucianus, his colleague and fellow confessor, in 230, rebuking him concerning certain matters and asking the confessors at Carthage to grant peace on behalf of sisters who had fallen away and been taken to Rome, IV, 274.

CELLANUS, a certain man. An exile from his native England, he wrote from the furthest regions of Gaul to St. Aldhelm in 705 and greatly celebrated his praises; otherwise we know nothing about him worth reporting, LXXXIX, 99.

CELSUS, that writer whose time and homeland we do not know, was a Christian and very learned. He translated from Greek into Latin the disputation between Jason and Papiscus concerning Jewish unbelief and dedicated the work to a certain Bishop Vigilius; only his preface survives, VI, 49.

CENA, an Anglo-Saxon priest, flourished in the eighth century. He wrote to St. Lullus, archbishop of Mainz, excusing himself for not yet having sent the books Lullus had requested, because he had found no copyists, XCVI, 841.

CENE, apparently a nun, wrote to St. Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, commending herself to his prayers in 733, LXXXIX, 735.

CENTIUS, chamberlain and later Honorius III. See HONORIUS.

CEOLFRIDUS, an Anglo-Saxon priest and afterwards abbot, for thirty-five years, of the monasteries of Sts. Peter and Paul of the Order of St. Benedict at Wearmouth and Jarrow in England. He died at Langres in Gaul in 716. Bede celebrated his praises. His homilies and letters survive, among which especially noteworthy is the letter to Naiton, king of the Picts, LXXXIX, 347.

CEREALIS, bishop of Castellum. He flourished in Mauretania in 485 and vigorously attacked the opinions of Maximinus, an Arian bishop, against whom he wrote a dogmatic treatise, LVIII, 755.

CERETIUS, a Gallic bishop, flourished in the fifth century. With his colleagues Salonius and Veranus he wrote a letter to Pope St. Leo, which survives among the letters of that pontiff, LIII, 1011.

CHENULFUS, who notified St. Desiderius of Cahors of his arrival, appears to be the same as Chodulphus to whom the holy bishop wrote. Other matters concerning him are uncertain, LXXXVII, 262.

CHEZIACO (S. de), was superintendent of the guard of a certain tower and of lands which paid a rent to Geoffrey of Rasconia, debtor to the king of the Franks himself. When the latter urgently demanded not merely the rent but the tower itself, S. de Cheziaco refused and prepared to resist; he informed Suger of these matters, asking him to command what should be done, in 1148, CLXXXVI, 1387.

CHILDEBERT II, king of Austrasia, son of Sigibert and Brunhild, issued a constitution in 595 for abolishing the remnants of idolatry and for celebrating feast days chastely, LXXII, 1121.

CHILDEBERT III, king of the Franks, brother and successor of Clovis III, reigned under Pippin’s guardianship until 711. Several diplomas concerning him survive, LXXXVII, 1089.

CHILDERIC II, king of Austrasia, second son of Clovis the Great, perished by the hand of Bodillo in 673. Several diplomas concerning him survive, LXXXVII, 1283.

CHILDERIC III, king of the Franks in name but not in fact, succeeded Theuderic IV in 743. He lived until 760. See his diplomas, LXXXVIII, 1147.

CHILO, Lacedaemonian philosopher, one of the seven sages of Greece and ephor of the city, flourished in 556 before Christ. Moral and political maxims by him survive. St. Ambrose attributes to him a letter to Periander, XVII, 1149.

CHILPERIC II, king of the Franks and son of Childeric II, king of Austrasia, was set upon the throne by Raginfrid. He wished to resist Charles Martel, son of Pippin, but, defeated, retained only the title of royal dignity. Diplomas by him survive, dated 720, LXXXVIII, 1116.

CHINDASWINTH, king of Gothic Spain, reigned about 646. He raised St. Eugenius III, formerly archdeacon of St. Braulio, to the see of Toledo, and was succeeded by Recceswinth. A letter by him to St. Braulio survives, LXXX, 678.

CHONRADUS, bishop of Constance. Born of noble Alemannic stock, he devoted himself to study among the brethren of the monastery of Constance and was ordained by the pious Bishop Noting, whom he later succeeded because of his outstanding virtues. He died in 976, CLXX, 865.

CHOZIL, count, gave to the monastery of St. Emmeram all that he possessed at Stromag; the donation survives without a date, CXXIX, 924.

CHRISTIANUS succeeded Arnold, who had been killed, in the see of Mainz in 1160. He wrote to Blessed Hildegard, abbess, commending himself to her prayers, CXCVII, 158, 160.

CHRISTOPHER, antipope. This usurper of the Apostolic See drove the legitimately elected Leo V from his seat, and was himself likewise deposed by another usurper, namely Sergius, and cast into prison; in 903 he embraced the religious life. There survives of him a diploma confirming the privileges of the abbey of Corbie, CXXXI, 46.

CHRODEGANG (Saint), bishop of Metz. Born of noble stock in Austrasia, he was raised to the see of Metz in 742, which he administered piously for twenty-three years. He is regarded as the founder of the regular canons; he founded three monasteries, to which he gave the Rule of Saint Benedict. He died in 766. He wrote a Rule for the clergy of Metz, LXXXIX, 1053.

CHRODOBERT, bishop of Tours. He flourished about 670. He is the author of a short work entitled: *Judgment concerning an adulterous woman who, after being consecrated and having professed before God to preserve chastity, committed adultery*, LIV, 1424; LXXXVII, 1131.

CHROMATIUS (Saint), bishop of Aquileia in his native country, distinguished for holiness and learning, succeeded Valerian; he defended the Nicene faith most vigorously and died about 407. Of his writings there remain a sermon on the eight beatitudes and seventeen treatises on the Gospel of Saint Matthew, XX, 309.

CHRYSOLANUS, see PETER.

CHRYSOLOGUS, see PETER.

CHUONRAD, or CONRAD, king of Burgundy, son of Rudolf II, who drove off the Saracens and Hungarians, reigned until 994. There remains of him a diploma by which, in 943, he granted to the monastery of Cluny the estate called Thosiacum, situated in the district of Lyons, CXXXIII, 842.

CICERO (Marcus Tullius), the celebrated Roman orator and philosopher, was born at Arpinum; first quaestor in Sicily, he was afterwards made consul at Rome in 56 BC. He eloquently crushed the schemes of Catiline and Verres. He wrote much, in a flourishing style, on politics and oratory. He died in 43 BC. Bede and Boethius himself collected certain materials concerning him, LXIV, 1039; XC, 1053.

CIRITTA, see JOHN.

CLAREMBAUD of Capis and his wife Alix granted to the monastery of Clairvaux whatever the brothers might wish to acquire from his fief, in 1147, CLXXXV, 988.

CLAUDIUS, bishop of Turin: in the eighth century, a most obstinate iconoclast and disciple of Felix of Urgel, he came from Spain to Italy by order of Louis the Pious, to teach sacred doctrine, in which he was most highly proficient, and was at the same time made bishop. He composed exegetical works, a brief chronicle, and a eulogy of Saint Augustine, CIV, 610.

CLEMENT (Saint) I, pope and martyr, succeeded Anacletus. He died in 100; he belongs to the apostolic age. The *Apostolic Constitutions* and certain letters found in Pseudo-Isidore are attributed to him, but are regarded as largely apocryphal, CXXX, 15.

CLEMENT II, pope. German by nation, after Gregory VI’s abdication he was made pontiff through the efforts and zeal of King Henry in 1046; but he occupied the see for only one year. His letters and privileges survive, CXLII, 578.

CLEMENT III, antipope, formerly Guibert or Wibert of Corrigia, whom Alexander II had made archbishop of Ravenna, was intruded into the Roman See by Emperor Henry IV against Gregory VII. He died at Rome, in the Castle of Saint Angelo, in 1101, CXLVIII, 825.

CLEMENT III, pope. A Roman by birth, formerly Cardinal Paulinus and bishop of Palestrina, he was elected in 1188. He stirred up kings for the holy war. He built the monastery of Saint Lawrence and died in 1191. He left letters and privileges, CCIV, 1273.

CLEMENTIA, countess of Flanders. After her husband’s death, knowing that the monks of Saint-Bertin had departed from their original fervour, she invited Saint Hugh, abbot of Cluny, to reform them, and therefore promised that the monastery should be made subject to Cluny. She flourished in the eleventh century, CLIX, 939.

CLEMENTIA, countess of Flanders and former wife of Robert. Believing that she had been wronged by clerics of the Church of Thérouanne, she brought the matter before Lambert, bishop of Arras, and asked him to exact punishment from them; otherwise, she herself would punish the guilty. She lived at the beginning of the twelfth century, CLXII, 664.

CLEOBULUS, son of Evagoras, king of the Rhodians, succeeded his father. He was counted among the seven sages of Greece and died in 560 BC. There survives an epistle concerning him, translated from Greek, in Saint Ambrose, XVII, 1149. [Col. 0431]

CLICHTOVEUS (Jodocus), the distinguished theologian of Nieuwpoort and canon of Chartres, was among the first to undertake a refutation of Luther; he died in 1543. There survives of him a celebrated testimony concerning Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, CLXXXV, 634.

CLOVIS I, king of the Franks. Having defeated Syagrius, he gained possession of Gaul; soon afterwards, repeatedly urged by his wife Saint Clotild, he triumphed over the Alemanni at Tolbiac by divine aid and received baptism from Saint Remigius. Yet, in the manner of barbarians, he slaughtered many people; at his death he divided the kingdom among his four sons, in 511. There survive of him a letter to the bishops and a diploma for the monastery of Micy, LXXI, 1158.

CLOVIS II, king of the Franks, son of Dagobert I, possessed the kingdoms of Neustria and Burgundy. He died in 656, scarcely twenty-three years old. Certain diplomas concerning him survive, LXXXVII, 678.

CLOVIS III, king of Neustria and Burgundy, son of Theuderic III, reigned under the guardianship of Pippin the Short until 695; Childebert III succeeded him. His diplomas survive, LXXXVIII, 1079.

CLOTHAR I, king of the Franks, born of Clovis and Clotild, shared in the killing of the sons of his brother Clodomir and put his own rebellious son to death. He died in 558. Some ecclesiastical ordinances of his survive, LXXII, 1119.

CLOTHAR II, king of the Franks. Born of Chilperic and Fredegund, he reigned in Neustria. He died in 628. See his ordinances, LXXII, 82; LXXX, 447.

CLOTHAR III, king of the Franks, reigned in Neustria under Ebroin’s guardianship; he died in 670. His diplomas survive, LXXXVII, 1277.

CLOTILD (Saint), queen of the Franks, niece of Gundobad, king of Burgundy. Married to Clovis I, by her prayers and outstanding holiness of life she brought her husband from idolatry to the faith. As a widow she withdrew to a monastery at Tours and died in 543. There survives concerning her, in Aimoin, an address to her sons, the kings, CXXXIX, 662.

CLOTILD, a noble matron, lived under Clothar III. By a charter of 670 she bestowed many gifts upon the convent of women at Brocarium, in the district of Étampes, LXXXVII, 1341.

CAECILIA, CAECILIANUS. See under A.

CELESTINE (Saint), pope. A native of Campania, he was elected in 423 and held the see for nine years. His letters survive, including a decretal letter to bishops, L, 407.

CELESTINE II, pope. A Tuscan by nation, formerly named Guido and cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Mark, he was created pope, in accordance with the constitution of his predecessor Innocent, without the votes of the people. He remained in the see for only one year. He died in 1144. He left letters and privileges, CLXXIX, 761.

CELESTINE II, pope. A Roman by birth, formerly Cardinal-Deacon Hyacinth, he succeeded Clement II. He died in 1198. He left many privileges as well as letters, CCVI, 864.

CELESTIUS, a Pelagian. A disciple of Pelagius, he began to spread the poison of heresy with greater boldness. Of noble birth and keen intelligence, he was nevertheless deceitful and factious, in 415. Some fragments of his writings remain among the works of Saint Augustine and in Marius Mercator, XLVIII, 61, 615.

COELIUS SYMPHOSIUS, whom Heumann indiscriminately identifies with Caecilius Lactantius. Jerome mentions him, but his birth and death are wholly uncertain. He is the author of many riddles, which he dedicated to a certain Sextus, a friend, VII, 289.

COGITOSUS, a historical writer, whom we believe to belong to a much later age, though he was once assigned to the seventh century without any information concerning him. He wrote the Life of Saint Brigid the Virgin, LXXII, 775.

COLUMBANUS (Saint), abbot and confessor. He founded many monasteries: first he was abbot of Luxeuil in Gaul, then of Bobbio in Italy. He was born in Ireland in 540 and died in 615. We have from him a monastic Rule, a book on determining the measure of penances, sermons, letters, and poems, LXXX, 201.

COLUMBANUS, abbot of Saint-Trond. Nothing concerning him has been handed down by the ancients. He is regarded as the author of a poem entitled *On the Origin and Beginnings of the Franks*, and of a funeral poem on the death of King Charlemagne, CVI, 1258.

COLUMBUS, bishop of Numidia, together with Stephen of Byzacena and Reparatus, bishop of Mauretania, after holding councils concerning the case of Pyrrhus, who had been deposed from the see of Constantinople and withdrawn to Africa, wrote to Pope Theodore in 641 asking him to determine what they ought to do, LXXXVII, 81.

COMMODIANUS of Gaza, a poet of the fourth century. He appears to have flourished in Africa under the pontificate of Saint Sylvester. Some, however, consider him Italian, indeed Roman. In verse, and in a style insufficiently polished, he wrote a book against the pagans, more suited to refuting errors than to confirming doctrines, V, 190. [Col. 0432]

CONAN II, duke of the Bretons, son and successor of Duke Alan. He flourished from 1112 to 1148. He made an alliance with Louis the Fat against the English. There survive of him a letter to Gilbert, archbishop of Tours, in which he promises to repair certain damages, and a charter of surrender and confirmation of Belle-Île, CLXXII, 1325.

CONDRAMMUS, a certain man, transferred three slaves to Avo, advocate of the monastery of Saint Emmeram, in exchange for three others received from him, ninth century, CXXIX, 957.

CONO, cardinal and bishop of Palestrina, formerly a regular canon of Saint Nicholas of Arrouaise, was a man commended for holiness of life. He was made cardinal by Paschal II, who sent him as legate to the East in 1124. His letters survive, CLXIV, 1431.

CONRAD II, called the Salian, emperor of Germany, son of Henry, duke of Franconia, received the crown in 1027. He died at Utrecht in 1039. He issued constitutions and diplomas, CLI, 1039, 1043.

CONRAD, author of the Life of Blessed Wolphelm, abbot of Brauweiler. Trithemius wrote thus of him: “He was a monk and disciple of Blessed Wolphelm, whose Life he committed to writing for Everard, abbot of Brauweiler, and Hermann, abbot of Saint Pantaleon. Not inadequately learned in letters, he was trained in every branch of learning by such a teacher.” He flourished in 1092, CLIV, 403.

CONRAD, bishop of Salzburg. In 1128, when the patriarchal see of Aquileia was vacant and certain persons, moved by ambition, were disturbing the election, he supported the election of Gilbert, dean of Bamberg and a man of proven life. For this reason he wrote to Otto, bishop of Bamberg, and to the canons of that place, CLXXIII, 1344.

CONRAD III, emperor of Germany, first duke of Franconia, succeeded Lothair II in 1157. He made the journey to Jerusalem with Louis the Younger. He died in 1152. His letters and diplomas survive, CLXXX, 1613, 1616.

See also CLXXXIX, 1132 and elsewhere.

CONRAD, after obtaining the administration of the monastery of Saint Peter at Paderborn in 1154, complained to Wibald, abbot of Corvey, that he had not been willing to receive him while travelling through his territory, and congratulated him on his happy return in 1155. He died in 1180, CCXXXIX, 1439.

CONRAD, abbot of Keixem, lived at the end of the twelfth century. He wrote to Saint Hildegard, abbess of the monastery of Saint Rupert at Bingen, and consulted her concerning several doubtful matters, CXCVII, 197.

CONRAD, bishop of Worms. He flourished after the middle of the twelfth century. He wrote to Saint Hildegard, abbess, whom he adorns with praises and to whose prayers he commends himself, CXCVII, 173.

CONSENTIUS wrote books against the Priscillianists; and, having asked Saint Augustine whether it was permissible to use a lie in order to expose heretics, he received from the holy Doctor the book *On Lying*. Whether he was a bishop or merely a priest is uncertain, as is the place where he flourished. In 410 he sent his books and a letter to Augustine, XXXIII, 449.

CONSTANS, a priest, wrote a treatise on the Passion of Blessed Emmeram, martyr. Otherwise, historians have handed down to us nothing about this priest’s country, birth, or death, XCVI, 1365.

CONSTANTIA, formerly wife of Andreota, and Sebyllia, wife of Hyacinth Peter Deusvossalvet, full sisters, together with their brothers Nicholas and Octavian, renounced their inheritance in favour of Lord Peter the advocate, in 1195, CCVI, 1275.

CONSTANTINE THE GREAT, emperor, whose life and deeds are known to all. He left decrees, constitutions, addresses to the assembly, and many letters. He died in 336, VIII, 93.

CONSTANTINE IV Flavius, called Pogonatus, or “the Bearded,” ordered his brothers Tiberius and Heraclius, who reigned with him, to be blinded so that he alone might possess the empire; he fought against the Monothelites and Saracens; he died in 681, LXXXVII, 1147; XCVI, 387, 31.

CONSTANTINE, pope. A Syrian by nation, he sat for seven years during the reign of Justinian and died in 715. Under Constantine a great famine occurred at Rome. His letters and diplomas survive, LXXXIX, 315.

CONSTANTINE, antipope. Although a layman, with the aid of his brother Toto, duke of Nepi, he invaded the Holy See after the death of Pope Paul and promptly committed murders and crimes. But Christopher the *primicerius*, having fled to King Desiderius, obtained soldiers from him and marched against Toto. After Toto was killed and the usurper deposed, Stephen III was elected in 768. There survive letters of Constantine to Pippin, king of the Franks, XCVIII, 227, 233. [Col. 0433]

CONSTANTINE COPRONYMUS, emperor of Constantinople, succeeded Leo the Isaurian; he inflicted many evils upon the orthodox and died in battle against the Bulgars in 775. Of him and his wife Irene there survives an imperial letter addressed to Pope Adrian, CXXIX, 199.

CONSTANTINE, abbot of Saint Symphorian at Metz. Amid the disturbances by which all Lorraine was being devastated, Abbot Constantine undertook to write the Life of Adalbero, bishop of Metz. The year of his death is uncertain, CXXXIX, 1539.

CONSTANTINE, monk of Monte Cassino. A native of Carthage and a most distinguished physician and philosopher, he flourished about 1057. He travelled through various regions of the East, studying the learning of each people. He left many writings, CL, 1559.

CONSTANTIUS, bishop of Albi. He attended the Council of Reims in 256. During his lifetime the monastery of Castres was begun, with Robert as its first abbot. There survives of him a letter to Saint Desiderius, LXXXVII, 258.

CONSTANTIUS, servant of Saint Quarantena, and William together obtained from Eustace Granier the land which the inhabitants of Saint Quarantena had formerly possessed; a little later they obtained the water they needed, in 1124, CLV, 1213.

CORNELIUS (Saint), pope and martyr. A Roman by birth, he succeeded Fabian and anathematized Novatian. He died in exile in 252. Some letters of his survive, III, 676.

CORONATUS THE NOTARY (Venerable). It is wholly uncertain where and when that author flourished. The Ballerini, editors of the works of Saint Zeno, assign him to the seventh or eighth century; but he was not a contemporary of Saint Zeno, whose Life he wrote. Tillemont places this author’s composition at the translation of Saint Zeno’s relics, which occurred in 805. There survives of him a sermon on the Life of Saint Zeno, XI, 76, 199, 623.

COSMAS JAPIGUS, a poet of Matera, published a poem about 950 in honour of the holy martyrs Theopompus, Theonas, and Synesius, who suffered under Diocletian at Nicomedia. Nothing is known of this author’s life, CXXXIII, 879.

COSMAS, dean of Prague, was born about 1045, of a family originating in Poland. He learned letters in the schools of Prague; afterwards he went to Liège, where he diligently devoted himself to grammar and dialectic. He died in 1125. His *Chronicle of the Bohemians* survives, CLXVI, 9.

COTTO. See JOHN.

COXIDA. See ELIAS (of).

CRESCONIUS, an African bishop whose see is unknown, flourished at the end of the seventh century. He compiled a canonical breviary and sent it to Bishop Liberius, arranged in 300 titles. The work is compiled from the Apostolic Canons, LXXXVIII, 815.

CRISPINUS MILO. See MILO.

CRISPINUS GISLEBERTUS. See GISLEBERTUS.

CUMIAN (Saint), surnamed Fota, that is, “the Tall.” He was born in 592 of a royal lineage exercising dominion in the western part of Scotland. At first a monk, later an abbot, and according to some made bishop in 640, he died in 661. He left a letter on the Paschal controversy and a book on the measure of penances.

CUNO, abbot of Mount Saint Disibod, flourished in the twelfth century. In a letter he asked Saint Hildegard, abbess, to deign to reveal to him whatever God might have disclosed to her concerning Saint Disibod, CXCVII, 203.

CUTHBERT, Bede’s disciple and afterwards abbot of Jarrow in Britain after Huethert, about 740; not to be confused with Saint Cuthbert, whose Life Bede composed. There survives of him a Life—or rather a eulogy—of his teacher, the Venerable Bede, and several letters, XC, 35; XCVI, 828, 838.

CYNEARD, bishop of Winchester in England, wrote to Blessed Lull, archbishop of Mainz. He relates all that he himself and Hunfrith, successor of Bishop Daniel, had done for Lull’s sake, and urges him to ask for anything that he himself might grant, in 756, XCVI, 831.

CYNEWULF, king of the Anglo-Saxons, sent a letter in the name of the bishops to Blessed Lull, archbishop of Mainz, declaring that he would comply with all that Lull might request, in 772, XCVI, 846.

CYPRIAN, bishop of Carthage, martyr and Doctor of the Church. Born at Carthage, initially a pagan, he was overcome by the advice and prayers of Bishop Caecilius and received baptism; afterwards he was ordained priest and finally made bishop. For several years he lived in exile for Christ’s faith and ended his life by martyrdom in 258. We have his letters and writings, both dogmatic and moral, III, IV, and V. [Col. 0434]

CYPRIAN of Toulon, Firminus of Uzès, and Viventius, bishop of an uncertain see, were contemporaries of Saint Caesarius, archbishop of Arles, and wrote about his life around 545, LXVII, 997, 1253.

CYPRIAN (Saint) of Antioch, first a magician and the lover of a certain Justina, had involved himself in various impious acts; yet he soon converted to the faith and, led by repentance, became a priest and finally a bishop. Justina, however, was consecrated to God and suffered death for the faith. Certain fragments concerning him survive, including a prayer for the martyrs and another for the day of his own passion, IV, 177, 905.

CYPRIAN, monk of Monte Cassino. First a priest, then a monk in the Cassinese monastery, he flourished around 760. Learned and a poet celebrated for his age, he wrote a hymn on the miracles of Blessed Benedict, to be sung on his feast day, LXXXIX, 1050.

CYPRIAN, archpriest of Córdoba, a poet of no mean rank, flourished at the beginning of the tenth century. He left various poems, namely epigrams, epitaphs, and hymns, CXXXII, 787.

CYRIL (Saint), patriarch of Alexandria and successor of Theophilus, was first expelled by the Nestorians and afterwards restored to his see. He wrote very many works against these heretics and died in 444, XLVIII, 851; l. 447 *passim*.

CYRIL, general master of the Order of the Holy Spirit of Saxia, established by Pope Innocent III and Count Guy of Montpellier to visit and protect hospitals. There survives under Saint Cyril’s name an exhortation to the knights of this order, CCXVII, 1155.

CYRICIUS, bishop of Barcelona in Spain. He flourished around 662. There survive two letters: one to Saint Ildefonsus, *On the Virginity of Blessed Mary against Jovinian and Helvidius*, and another to Bishop Taio, XCVI, 9.

## D

DADO, bishop of Rouen. Together with Constantius of Albi, he wrote to Saint Desiderius, bishop of Cahors, about 645. His name and see are indicated in a certain charter of Clovis II, LXXXVII, 258, 692.

DADO, bishop of Verdun. Nephew and disciple of Berhard, a man of the highest intelligence and outstanding holiness, he was first abbot of Saint-Vanne and afterwards, with the favour of Louis, king of Germany, was honoured with episcopal rank in 881. He died in 923. He wrote the Lives of Hatto and Berhard, his predecessors, and a historical fragment, CXXXII, 779.

DAGOBERT I, king of the Franks. Son of Clothar II and Bertrude, he first reigned with justice, prudence, and equity, but afterwards gave himself over to pleasures. He died in 638. Ecclesiastical ordinances from him survive.

DAGOBERT II, king of the Franks. Son of Sigebert II and successor of Childeric II, he reigned at the end of the seventh century. Diplomas are attributed to him, though not all are genuine, as are several ecclesiastical ordinances, LXXXVII, 1302.

DAGOBERT III, king of the Franks. He succeeded his father Childebert III, but was wholly under the authority of Theudoald, mayor of the royal palace. He paid nature’s debt in 715. His diplomas survive, LXXXVIII, 1111.

DAGULF, abbot of Saint-Denis. He flourished at the beginning of the ninth century. Nothing certain is known about his life. He wrote a psalter in golden letters, which Charlemagne offered as a gift to Pope Adrian I, XCIX, 826.

DAIMBERT, patriarch of Jerusalem. Godfrey of Bouillon, the first king of Jerusalem, granted him many goods and even the Tower of David by will at his death; Daimbert complains to the prince of Antioch about 1100 that this was not carried out. In William of Tyre, CCI, 457.

DAIMBERT, archbishop of Pisa. He flourished at the beginning of the twelfth century. He sent letters to Pope Paschal II, in which he set out the letters of the leaders of the crusaders and their victories, CLXIII, 448, 453.

DAMASUS (Saint), pope. A Spaniard by birth, born about 304, he attained the supreme pontificate in 367. He held many councils against the Arians and anathematized Ursacius, Valens, Auxentius, and others. He died in 385. His letters, anathemas, and certain poems survive, XIII, 109.

DAMIAN (Saint) Peter, cardinal. Born at Ravenna to poor but honourable parents, he embraced the monastic life in the monastery of Fonte Avellana, of which he later became abbot in 1041. He was then made bishop of Ostia and cardinal; he left many writings—sermons, letters, and various shorter works. He died in 1072, CXLIV, CXLV.

DAMIAN, bishop of Pavia. He succeeded Anastasius in 680. He was distinguished for piety and learning under the name Mansuetus. He wrote several letters and died in 710, LXXXVII, 1259. [Col. 0435]

DANIEL, bishop of the West Saxons. He flourished in the time of King Sigebald. He sent Saint Boniface to Rome with letters of recommendation to Pope Gregory II in 718. Several letters from him to that same Boniface, who had become archbishop of Mainz, survive, LXXXIX, 687, 703, 707.

DARIUS, son of Hystaspes and king of the Persians. He was defeated by the Greeks at Marathon in 490 BC. He died while planning a new expedition against the Greeks. There is a letter from him to Heraclitus of Ephesus in Saint Ambrose, XVII, 1153.

DARIUS, a count sent to Carthage to restore peace, was converted from paganism to Christ’s faith by reading Saint Augustine’s books. If he did not settle the conflicts, he at least postponed them in 429. He procured certain medicines for the holy Doctor when he was ill. There survives of him a letter to Saint Augustine, XXXIII, 1020.

DARMUNDUS is known to us only through a sale which he concluded with Erlifrid, abbot of Saint-Bertin, of certain estates in the districts of Vermandois and Noyon in 708, LXXXVIII, 1251.

DATIVUS and his companions, African confessors condemned to the mines, received aid from Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, together with a letter, and wrote back to him a letter of thanks in 258, IV, 420.

DEFENSOR, grammarian and monk of Ligugé among the Pictavians, flourished in the eighth century. He collected sayings of the Holy Fathers under the title *Sparks*, LXXXVIII, 595.

DEODATUS, a cleric, gave a substantial part of the property he possessed in the district of Thérouanne and certain other places to the monastery of Saint-Bertin in 800, CXXXVI, 1215.

DEODUIN, bishop of Liège, also called Theuduin, Dietwin, and Tuthwin. A Norican from Bavaria, he was appointed by Emperor Henry III in place of Wazo, provost of Saint Donatian at Bruges. He died in 1075. He left letters and a diploma, CXLVI, 1438.

DERMATIUS, an Irish monk who calls himself a Scot, went to Jerusalem with Raimbald of Liège; from there, around 1095, he wrote to his brothers an exhortatory letter, CLV, 485.

DESIDERIUS (Saint), bishop of Cahors. Born in the city of Albi to a noble family, he had as distinguished brothers Syagrius, a magistrate, and Rusticus, bishop, whom he succeeded. He died in 651. His letters survive (see HERCHENEFREDA), LXXXVII, 218.

DESIDERIUS, king of the Lombards, and Queen Ansa bestowed many gifts upon the monastery of Saint Michael and Saint Peter in the city of Brescia, in 758. Anselberga, Desiderius’ daughter, had been abbess of these monasteries. The same king gave much to the brothers of Monte Cassino in 768, LXXXVII, 1388, 1393.

DEUSDEDIT (Saint), pope. A Roman by nation, he was elected after the death of Boniface IV in 614. He died in 617. A decretal letter to Gordian, bishop of Seville, is falsely attributed to him, LXXX, 362.

DEUSDEDIT, cardinal-priest, vigorously defended the party of Pope Gregory VII. He wrote four books *On Ecclesiastical Expressions*, a book *On the Privileges and Authority of the Roman Church*, and a work *Against Simoniacs*. He died in 1099, CL, 1566.

DEXTER (Saint) Flavius Lucius, a man plainly learned and distinguished for prudence and piety, was born in 368. He made great progress in humane letters. Devoted to military service from youth, he was a poet of no small ability, as the epitaph of King Ataulf indicates. He died in old age in 444. He is the author of a *Chronicle*, XXXI, 12.

DIDYMUS, born at Alexandria, though blind from his earliest years, advanced so far in knowledge of Scripture that all who heard him were astonished when he discoursed. Saint Jerome himself, admiring his learning, wished to translate one of his books from Greek into Latin, namely the book *On the Holy Spirit*. About 385, XXIII, 101.

DINDYMUS, an Indian king, to whom letters and replies addressed to Alexander the Great are attributed. But he plainly seems to be a fictitious author, since this Dindymus is mentioned nowhere except in Alcuin, CI, 1366.

DINOTHUS, abbot of Bangor. He flourished in the time of Saint Augustine, apostle of the English. There survives of him a reply to that same Augustine in which he acknowledges the authority of the Roman Church, LXXX, 22.

DIONYSIUS (Saint), the Areopagite, won to Christ’s faith by Saint Paul and afterwards crowned with martyrdom in 95. Greek writings translated by John Scotus are published under his name, CXXII, 1023. [Col. 0436]

DIONYSIUS of Alexandria, patriarch, fought against the heretics of his time, especially the Novatians, in 265. His letters, or fragments of them, survive, III, 1001.

DIONYSIUS (Saint), pope. He is believed to have been Greek by origin and a native of Calabria. After Sixtus II had been killed in the persecution of Valerian, he succeeded him and departed to God in 269. There survives a fragment of his letter against the Sabellians and a letter to Bishop Severus, V, 99.

DIONYSIUS, bishop of Lydda, known through a letter to Theophilus of Alexandria, translated by Saint Jerome and extant, XXII, 771.

DIONYSIUS EXIGUUS, a Scythian by nation, was a monk by profession and an abbot at Rome; he enjoyed the friendship of Cassiodorus. He corrected the calendar and compiled a collection of canons. He died about 540, LXVII, 9.

DIONYSIUS THE CARTHUSIAN lived for a long time in the monastery at Roermond; he died in 1471. He wrote many ascetical works. He spoke beautifully concerning Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, CLXXXV, 636.

DIOSCORUS, deacon and papal legate. See GERMANUS.

DODANA, or DUODENA, a pious matron who married Bernard, duke of Septimania and count of Barcelona, in AD 824. She wrote a handbook, which she addressed to her son William, CVI, 110.

DODECHINUS, abbot, whose life is unknown to us. He continued the Chronicle of Marianus Scotus; a fragment by him survives, CXLVIII, 1441.

DOMINIC, patriarch of Grado and Aquileia in the Venetian dominion, flourished about the middle of the eleventh century under Pope Leo IX. There survives of him a letter to Peter, patriarch of Antioch, CXLI, 1455.

DOMNIZO, priest and monk of Canossa, of the Order of Saint Benedict. He wrote the Life of the celebrated Countess Matilda of Italy in two books adorned in verse. In 1130, CXLVI, 1339.

DOMNOLEUS, Bodoardus, Rigobertus, and other debtors from Villa Arduno each gave Herlemund, then bishop of Le Mans, a charter acknowledging their respective share, in 721, when Theuderic IV began his reign, LXXXVIII, 1276.

DOMNOLUS (Saint), bishop of Le Mans. He flourished in the sixth century. He succeeded Blessed Innocent in the see of Le Mans in 560. He was especially distinguished for charity toward the poor and pastoral care. He died in 576, LXXII, 630.

DONATUS (Saint), bishop of Besançon. Born of noble parents, he was given to God from earliest infancy to be educated in the monastery of Luxeuil under Saint Columbanus. He died in 651. He wrote a Rule for virgins, LXXXVII, 267.

DONIZO, see DOMNIZO.

DONUS, pope. A Roman by nation, he was elected in 676 and held the see for two years. Nothing survives of his writings that we can report, LXXXVII, 1146.

DOROTHEUS, bishop of Thessalonica. During Anastasius’ reign he sent a letter through a certain patrician to Pope Hormisdas, in which he professes orthodox faith, longs for unity, and seeks the Church’s peace. Yet he appears to have held a different view from the letter of Dioscorus, the papal legate. He was therefore soon exiled to Heraclea. In 514, LXIII, 371, 446.

DOTO, monk and apparently abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter in England, sent a letter to Saint Lull, archbishop of Mainz, together with a list of the names of brothers and fellow countrymen which Lull had requested from him, in 756, XCVI, 837.

DRACONTIUS, a poet of whose birth and life we have nothing certain, flourished in the fifth century. There remain of him a poem on God and an apology to King Gunthar, LX, 595.

DRAUSICUS, bishop of Soissons, at the request of Ebroin, mayor of the palace, and his wife Leutridis, granted several privileges to the convent of women of Saint Mary at Soissons, which they themselves had founded, in 666, LXXXVIII, 1183.

DREPANIUS FLORUS, a poet, Gallic by nation, flourished at the end of the fifth century. There remains of him a hymn to Wulfinus the grammarian, LXI, 1081.

DROCO, count of Amiens, in 1036 remitted the *cons* or customary due which he received at the fairs of Saint Peter of Ghislenghien, as well as the *brenagium* which he levied at Calderinck and Saint-Cyr, CLV, 310.

DROCO of the castle of Cuflante above the Seine gave the land of Loconis to the monks of Saint Peter of Chartres, whose abbot at that time was Landricus, in 1060, CLV, 329.

DROGO, duke of Burgundy and Aquitaine, son of Pippin, gave to the church of Saint Arnulf at Metz all that he possessed in the estate of Marialis in 691, LXXXIII, 1221.

DROGO, bishop of Beauvais, in 1033 founded the monastery of Saint Symphorian and in the following year restored two other monasteries. Summoned by Pope Leo IX to the Council of Reims, which he did not attend, he was excommunicated; but soon released from the censure, he did not cease to govern his diocese. He died in 1058. There survives of him a letter to W., his fellow bishop, CXLIII, 862. [Col. 0437]

DROGO, cardinal-bishop of Ostia, formerly a Benedictine monk in the monastery of Saint Nicaise near Reims. He died in 1138. He wrote a sermon—or rather a book—on the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion, and a book on the creation and redemption of man, etc., CLVI, 1514.

DROGO, called the Fat, and his wife Hodierna granted to the abbey of Clairvaux all that they possessed in the district of Gundria in Spain in 1147, CLXXXV, 987.

DROGO, abbot of Clairvaux, records that Garnerius of Fontaines gave the monastery a third part of the property which he possessed at the place called Changesium, and granted that gift in perpetuity to the nuns of Saint Mary of Praslon at Admodiasse, for one modius to be paid every year, in 1234, CLXXXV, 1243.

DRUTMARUS CHRISTIANUS, monk of Corbie, distinct from Druthmar the grammarian. He is the author of an exposition of the Gospel of Saint Matthew, which he addressed to the monks of Stavelot, and also of an exposition of the Gospel according to Luke, in 850, CVI, 1260.

DUCHESNIUS (André), royal historiographer. He flourished in the eighteenth century and wrote much concerning the history of the dukes and counts of Burgundy. He died in 1640. Certain fragments by him, written in French, concerning the counts of Champagne survive, CLXXXV, 1480 ff.

DUDO, dean of Saint-Quentin. Historians have transmitted nothing concerning his birth. He wrote three books on the deeds of the Norman dukes, CXLI, 606.

DULCIDIUS, bishop of Salamanca, attended the consecration of the church of Compostela in 878. He published the Chronicle of Albelda in 883, which was continued by Vigila, monk of Albelda, CXXIX, 1223.

DUNGAL, recluse. Born in Ireland in the eighth century, he was brought to Gaul in childhood, where he cultivated the liberal arts and astronomy. While living a solitary life, he wrote to Charlemagne on the double solar eclipse said to have occurred in 810. He also refuted a treatise on the veneration of images by Claudius of Turin. A very extensive collection of verses is attributed to him, CV, 447.

DUNSTAN (Saint), archbishop of Canterbury. Born in 925, of distinguished parents near Glastonbury in Ireland. He was first bishop of Worcester, but in 978 was raised to the see of Canterbury. He died in 988. His letters and a decree for establishing concord among the monks of England survive, CXXXVII, 407.

DURAND, abbot of Troarn. He vigorously attacked the heresy of Berengar. First a monk of Fécamp, he later became abbot of the monastery of Troarn, newly founded in the diocese of Bayeux by Count Roger of Montgomery; he was a contemporary of Fulbert of Chartres. He wrote a book *On the Body and Blood of Christ against Berengar*. He died in 1088, CXLIX, 1374.

DURANDUS, bishop of Clermont. Born of humble stock, which he ennobled by his own merits and distinction; in 1076 he succeeded William, bishop of Clermont, who had been deposed from the see for simony. He died in 1075. Of his writings there survives only a letter to Anselm, prior of Bec, CL, 1487.

DYNAMIUS, a patrician among the Gauls, born of a noble family. Venantius Fortunatus calls him “of Marseilles,” because he had been governor of that province, an office in which he conducted himself very badly; but, moved by repentance, he withdrew to a monastery in 601. There survive only two letters by him and the Lives of Saints Marius and Maximus, LXXX, 24.

E

EADMER, monk of Canterbury. An Englishman by nationality, he was Saint Anselm’s disciple and inseparable companion. He was elected to the bishopric of St Andrews in 1220, but resigned that office and returned to the monastery, where he died an old man in 1137. His biographical works survive, along with the book *On the Excellence of the Blessed Virgin Mary*, the book *On the Blessedness of the Heavenly Country*, letters, and the *History of Recent Events*, CLIX, 342.

EANVULT, an English monk, sent a familiar letter to Saint Lull, archbishop of Mainz, in which he commends himself to Lull’s prayers, in 758, XCVI, 839.

EAOF. See BARNARDUS.

EARDULF, bishop of Rochester, sent a letter to Blessed Lull, archbishop of Mainz, begging him to remember him in his prayers, in 756, XCVI, 833.

EBALUS, archbishop of Reims, formerly count of Roucy, had married Beatrice, daughter of Count Rainerius and Harvidis, sister of Robert of the Franks. [Col. 0438] After Arnulf’s death he was elevated to the see of Reims in 1021. A charter of his survives, CXLI, 1110.

EBBO, or EBO, archbishop of Reims, succeeded Wulfarius in 816. He attended the council at which Louis the Pious was deposed in 833; but he too was later accused of disloyalty to the emperor and, after Louis had been restored, was deposed from his see. At last, having regained his liberty, he became provost of the church of Hildesheim. He died in 850. His confession, an *Apology*, and several verses survive, CXVI, 9.

EBERHARD, abbot of Tegernsee. He flourished in the eleventh century. His letters survive, CXLI, 1307.

EBERHARD, bishop of Bamberg, having incurred the hostility of the archbishop of Mainz, who threatened both him and his church, complained to Pope Eugenius III about these actions in 1147, CLXXX, 1615; CXCVII, 167.

EBERHARD, bishop of Salzburg, flourished in the twelfth century. He wrote to the archbishop of Reims, asking him plainly to state which pope ought to be recognized, Octavian or Alexander. He notes, however, that the whole Church hopes in Pope Alexander, in 1159, CXCVI, 1569.

EBERHARD, archbishop of Juvavum, flourished after the middle of the twelfth century. He wrote to Saint Hildegard, abbess, commending himself to her prayers, CXCVII, 164.

EBERWIN, abbot of Saint Martin’s, Trier. He flourished at the beginning of the eleventh century. He wrote the Life of Saint Magnericus, archbishop of Trier and founder of the monastery over which Eberwin presided, and an account of the miracles of Saint Simeon, CLIV, 1245.

EBLO and GARNER gave Blessed Robert of Arbrissel and the monastery of Fontevraud as much arable land as twenty oxen could plough in one day, together with meadows and woodland for the building of a convent of nuns, at Fontaine-Archier, in the twelfth century, CXLIX, 1118.

EBRARD, monk of the monastery of Watten, regular canon of that place, and disciple of its founder Olfrid, apparently belongs to the twelfth century. He wrote the Chronicle of Watten, CXLIX, 1514.

EBROIN, count, son of Oda or Odo, and distinguished from Ebroin the mayor of the palace, bestowed many gifts for the soul of his deceased wife upon the basilica of Saint Peter at the place called Rinharim, in the diocese of Utrecht, in 721 under Saint Willibrord, bishop, LXXXVIII, 1277.

EBROIN, bishop of Bourges, issued letters of recommendation for Magnon, archbishop of Sens, to the priest Dodobert, so that Magnon might remain in his parish with Hercambald, in 810, CXXIX, 1389.

EBWALD, king of the East Angles, whose remarkable piety is shown in the letter which he wrote to Saint Boniface, apostle of Germany, in 733, LXXXIX, 725.

ECKBERT, also called Egbert, priest and canon of Brunnen, afterwards monk and abbot of the monastery of Schönau in the diocese of Trier, flourished about 1160. He wrote the Life of Saint Elizabeth, sermons, and various minor works not unworthy of reading, CXCV, 9 and following.

ECKERHARD, monk of St Gall, flourished in the ninth or tenth century. He composed several verses for his brother Immo, abbot, LXXXVII, 29, 66.

EDGAR, king of the English, son of Edmund and successor of King Edwin, whose unjust decrees he abolished and whose injuries he redressed. He recalled Saint Dunstan from exile and died in 975. His ecclesiastical constitutions, canons, and diplomas survive, CXXXVIII, 485.

EDMUND I, king of the English, son of Edward and successor of his brother Æthelstan. He reigned from 941 to 946, when he was slain. Certain ecclesiastical laws of his survive, CXXXVIII, 479.

EDWARD, called the Elder, king of the English, son and successor of Alfred the Great. He defeated Æthelwold, king of the Danes, and subdued the Scots. He died in 925. His ecclesiastical laws survive, CXXXVIII, 459.

EDWARD (Saint), king and confessor of the English; son and successor of Edward II. He recovered Scotland by arms, besieged John, king of the French, more than once, enacted laws, and restored the arts; he died in 1066, CLI, 1189.

EDWARD GRIM, monk of Canterbury, was himself the first to meet Thomas on his return from exile and an eyewitness of Thomas’s slaughter. He wrote the Life of this holy prelate, CXC, 1.

EGBERT (Saint), archbishop of York. He flourished from 732 to 767, and shortly before his death received from Bede a letter concerning the office of a Christian bishop. Excerpts from the sayings and canons of the Holy Fathers, a *Dialogue on Catholic Instruction*, and canons on remedies for sins survive from him, LXXXIX, 378.

EGILMAR, bishop of Osnabrück. He sent complaints to Pope Stephen V against certain disturbers of the peace [Col. 0439] who were attempting to usurp authority, CXXIX, 808.

EGINHARD and EINHARD, surnamed “the Wise.” After Charlemagne’s death in 814—whose son-in-law he was, if a certain tradition is to be believed—he educated for many years Lothair, son of Louis the Pious, and governed several abbeys. He died in 840. His *Life of Charlemagne*, annals, letters, history of the translation of Saints Marcellinus and Peter, and charters survive, CIV, 532.

EGINO, abbot of the monastery of Saint Ulrich from 1109. He endured much from Bishop Herman, whom Popes Paschal, Gelasius, and Calixtus had condemned because he had been promoted schismatically by Emperor Henry IV. Egino died amid these disputes in 1119. Several letters concerning him, preserved by Udalric, survive, CLXX, 855.

EGWIN, bishop of Worcester. In a diploma in which he lists the various foundations he had made, he himself recounts how visions induced him to carry them out under Kings Cenred and Offa, in 714, LXXXIX, 310.

EIGIL (Saint), abbot of Fulda. Born of free parents in the province of Noricum, moved by God’s grace he withdrew to the monastery of Fulda, where he became a monk and then abbot in 818. He died in 822. He wrote the Life of Saint Sturmi, the first abbot of Fulda, CV, 382.

EINHARD, priest, together with one Erhard, donated to the monastery of Bishop Adalwin the property they possessed in the village of Wolfmuntingas, in the ninth century, CXXIX, 922.

EKKEARD, first abbot of the monastery of Saint Lawrence called Aurange, of the Order of Saint Benedict. A German by nationality, he was a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and inferior to no contemporary writer. He published minor works under Emperor Conrad III and died in 1130. A chronicle by him survives, CLIV, 434.

EKKIBERT, count, through his vassal Theotpert bestowed many gifts upon the monastery of Saint Saviour, in which Blessed Bishop Adalwin was fulfilling the office of abbot, about 810, CXXIX, 901.

ELDEFONSUS, bishop of Seville. He lived in the middle of the ninth century, during the ravages of the Moors, about two hundred years after the great Ildefonsus, bishop of Toledo. He wrote down a certain revelation which he himself had seen, CVI, 882.

ELDEGARDIS, countess, with the consent of her son Walter and for the soul of her father Waleran, granted the village of Ganherium to the monastery of Saint Peter at Chartres in 987. Perhaps the same countess made another donation in 1020 to the same monastery, of the allod of Chaudfontaine, CIV, 247, 269.

ELEAZAR, an apostate who became a Jew from being a Christian. He dared to dispute about the faith with Paul Alvarus in his letters and replies, about 860, CXXI, 482, 513.

ELEUTHERIUS (Saint), pope and martyr, a native of Nicopolis. At first he was deacon to Saint Anicetus, and afterwards a priest ordained by Saint Soter, whose place he succeeded by the unanimous wish of all. He died in 192. The decrees attributed to him are spurious, CXXX, 119.

ELEUTHERIUS (Saint), bishop and confessor of Tournai. Born at Tournai in 456, he succeeded Theodore in the bishopric. Having most vigorously attacked heretics, he suffered death at their hands for the faith in 532. Two letters by him survive, LXV, 59.

ELEUTHERIUS, or LEUTHERIUS, bishop of Winchester, granted Saint Aldhelm, priest and abbot, certain land on which they might dwell, in 675. He confirmed this grant by a new charter in 680. The reason for the gift was that Blessed Aldhelm had been educated there from earliest childhood, LXXXIX, 309.

ELFLEDA, abbess, from whom survives a letter to Adolana, abbess, of uncertain year and place, included among the letters of Saint Boniface of Mainz (seventh century), LXXXIX, 803.

ELFRIC. See ÆLFRIC.

ELIAS, abbot of Saint Columba at Sens, and JOHN, master of the schools at Orléans, were appointed commissioners by the Apostolic See to settle and confirm peace between Odo, bishop of Paris, and the abbot of Saint Geneviève concerning the parish of Mont, about 1202, CCIV, 1188, 1190.

ELIAS OF KOKSIJDE, seventh abbot of the Cistercian monastery of the Dunes. He took his name from his native Koksijde, in the territory of Veurne in Flanders, and possessed complete authority with Leopold, duke of Austria. Two sermons by him survive (1203), CCIX, 991.

ELIAS OF EVESHAM, a monk who appears to have flourished at the beginning of the thirteenth century. He wrote the Life of Blessed Thomas of Canterbury and the history of his translation, CXC, 253.

ELIGIUS (Saint), bishop of Noyon. He was born at Limoges to distinguished parents. At first, as a highly skilled goldsmith, he won the favour of the king and his nobles; but soon, because of his outstanding learning and holiness, he was elevated to the episcopal mitre of Noyon in 640. He held that see from 640 until 659, when he died on the day before the Kalends of December [30 November]. His homilies survive, LXXXVII, 594.

ELIPANDUS, bishop of Toledo, disciple and follower of Felix of Urgell, whose various errors he embraced; thus he was condemned together with him. He is said to have died in 790, XCVI, 847.

ELIZABETH, mistress at Schönau, requested prayers and consoling words from Hildegard at the end of the twelfth century, CXCVII, 213.

ELIZABETH, queen of Hungary, daughter of King Stephen and wife of Louis the Great. After his death she ruled the kingdom because of her son’s minority. She suffered much after being thrown into prison with her son and later perished when cast into the waters in 1386. A letter from her survives to the citizens of Udine, asking them to receive and treat well her brother Andrew as he passed through their city, in 1383, XCIX, 670.

ELLINGER, abbot of Tegernsee, flourished about the middle of the eleventh century. From Mabillon we learn that he was highly commendable for learning and holiness. Seven letters by him survive, CXLI, 1317.

EUPIDIUS RUSTICUS lived in the times of Symmachus and Boethius, under Emperor Anastasius, and was a man of noble lineage. His poem on Christ’s benefits survives, LXII, 543.

ELPIS, daughter of Festus, leader of the senate, and wife of Boethius, greatly surpassed others in gifts of mind, body, and fortune. She wrote highly polished verses, among them a hymn in honour of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul (525), LXIII, 538.

EMMA, queen of the English, daughter of Richard I, duke of the Normans, and wife of Cnut the Great. A letter from her survives to her sons Edward and Alfred, about 1040, CXLI, 1392.

EMMANUEL PORPHYROGENNETUS, emperor of Constantinople. Having received Wibald’s letter informing him of Emperor Frederick’s marriage, he replied with a congratulatory letter in 1154, CLXXXII, 1438.

EMMO, bishop of Sens. Agon, abbot of the monastery of Saint Columba, had consulted him about his own authority; Emmo wrote to him that he and the monks depended on God alone. He demonstrated this with various testimonies and arranged for innumerable bishops to subscribe to it, in 659. Another charter of his survives, granting privileges to the monastery of Saint Peter at Sens in the same year, LXXXVIII, 1168.

ENCHERIADES, who set forth the rules of the monochord. Who he was and where he came from is uncertain, but he appears to have been an eleventh-century monk. Only a fragment by him survives, CLI, 693.

ENGELBERT, prior of the valley of Saint Peter, together with Simon, prior of Mont-Dieu, was sent by Pope Alexander III to restore concord between Henry, king of the English, and Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury. He gives an account of his mission (see SIMON, prior), CC, 1436.

ENGELMOD, bishop of Soissons. He dedicated several verses to Saint Paschasius Radbertus, abbot of Corbie, a native of the district of Soissons and his contemporary, CXX, 25.

ENGILBERT and GUNDPERT, deacons, gave their property to the monastery of Saint Michael, reserving its usufruct to themselves for as long as they lived, in 852, CXXIX, 920.

ENGILMAR, a certain priest, transferred seven slaves to the church of Saint Peter. Solomon, vassal of Bishop Ambricho, received this transfer after 860, CXXIX, 921.

ENODIUS (Magnus Felix), bishop of Ticinum (Pavia). He was born at Arles of noble family and was raised to the episcopal see of Ticinum in 510. He died in 521. There survive nine books of letters, ten minor works, and two books of poems by him.

EODEBERT, a certain man, sold to Rigobert, abbot of Nuntiacum, a part of the inheritance which he owned at Rumliacum in the district of Tervanna, in 700, CXXXVI, 1198.

EODEBERT, who seems to be the same as the person mentioned above, sold to Rigobert, abbot of Sithiu, all the property he possessed at Rumeliacum in 704, LXXXVIII, 1248.

EPHIBIUS, abbot of a wholly unknown monastery, granted many gifts by testament to the church of Vienne while Ceoldus was bishop. He also inserted into his charter the testament of his sister Rufina, in 696. Very many persons subscribed to this charter with the title of senator, but the charter is wholly spurious, LXXXVIII, 1234.

EPHRAEM (Saint), first a hermit and later deacon of Edessa. Although he did not cultivate secular learning, he was nevertheless so taught from heaven that he was able vigorously to attack the Arians, Apollinarians, and Sabellians. He wrote many ascetical works, among which should be noted the Life of Saint Abraham the Hermit, translated from the Syriac language. He died in 379, LXXIII, 281, 651.

EPIMENIDES, Cretan poet and philosopher. He flourished in the time of Solon, 598 years before Christ. A letter from him to Solon survives in Saint Ambrose, XVII, 1150.

EPIPHANIUS (Saint), bishop of Salamis in Cyprus. Like Theophilus, patriarch of Alexandria, he persecuted the Origenists and even John Chrysostom, and at Jerusalem performed certain ordinations improperly; but these faults are outweighed by his many virtues and excellent writings. Letters by him survive in Saint Jerome. He died in 403, XXII, 517, 757.

EPIPHANIUS, priest of Thessalonica. He denounces the infamy of those who preserve both heresy and office by means of abundant money, and everywhere preach persecution as imminent. These men were stirring the people to sedition, which Bishop Dorotheus, a witness, tolerated, in 520, LXIII, 481.

EPIPHANIUS, patriarch of Constantinople. He succeeded John and firmly adhered to the Council of Chalcedon against the Eutychians. Pope Hormisdas himself appointed him to reconcile dissident bishops if they renounced their heresy, LXIII, 494. He died in 535.

EPIPHANIUS, deacon of the church of Catania in Sicily. In 787 the office of *cubuclesius*, that is, spokesman, was entrusted to him at the Eighth General Council, the Second Council of Nicaea, whose conclusions he drafted, CXXIX, 379 and passim.

ERACLIUS, bishop of Liège. Born of noble family, distinguished for wisdom and learning. Formerly dean at Bonn, he had studied at Cologne and became bishop in 960. More than once he administered affairs of the realm. He died in 971. A letter from him to Bishop Ratherius and an account of a miracle of Saint Martin survive, CLIX, 958.

ERACLIUS, bishop of Bigorre, and Bernard, count of the same region, granted the monastery of Blessed Felix and another of Saint Licerius to Cluny in 1064.

ERARD OF BRESCIA, after a long dispute and by the arbitration of highly eminent men, relinquished to Theobald, count of Champagne, and his heirs in the direct line whatever he claimed by right of his wife Philippa in the counties of Champagne and Brie, in 1213, CCXVI, 986 and following.

ERBERT OF BAR-SUR-SEINE, Stephen Raerius, Aimo Bocardus, Marco of Vignac, Roland of Patrocinio, and very many others gave to the monastery of Clairvaux everything they possessed at Petrocinium and within the bounds of that place, about 1147, CLXXXV, 989 and following.

ERCHAMBERT, bishop of Freising, flourished in the ninth century. Nothing is transmitted concerning his life. A fragment from the *Short History of the Kings of the Franks* survives from him, CXVI, 32.

ERCHAMPERT, with the consent of the canons and monks of Saint Emmeram, upon whom he depended, carried out certain exchanges with Bishop Baturic in the ninth century (from the cartulary of Saint Emmeram), CXXIX, 935.

ERCHANFRID, bishop—perhaps of Regensburg—acting through his advocate Wicram, concluded with the nobleman Eparho a transaction concerning a certain exchange, and below, with Bishop Hartwig. Ninth century (from the cartulary of Saint Emmeram), CXXIX, 934.

ERCHANFRID, deacon, effected an exchange with Apollonius, abbot of Saint Emmeram, under Louis, called the Pious, king, CXXIX, 936.

ERCHEMBERT, monk of Monte Cassino. A Lombard by nationality, after losing all his possessions and becoming an exile, he was brought to Capua. On entering Monte Cassino, he was again removed from the monastery with his brethren by Atenulf, duke of Capua; he complained of this to Pope Stephen V. He lost the very cell which he governed at Capua. He composed a history of the Lombards from the time of Prince Adelchis to 889, CXXIX, 743.

ERFO and ZANETO, brothers and laymen from the city of Forum Julii, founded two monasteries in honour of the Blessed Virgin Mary and Saint Peter on the bank called Salto, and by charter bestowed many gifts upon them in 760, XCIX, 629.

ERFOIN, together with his two sons Theotarius and Rotarius, donated certain property to the monastery of Saint Gall in 720, LXXXVIII, 1268.

ERFURWIN, HILDIRAD, and IRMINEVIN, brothers and co-heirs, gave a part of their inheritance to Blessed Liudger, abbot of Werden: namely, the wood called Hoissi. This was done at Diapanbeci in 805, during Charlemagne’s reign, XCIX, 802.

ERIC and ERMENFRID sold a wood near the river Arno to Bishop Hildigrim. This was done in 817 before the doors of the church of Saint Saviour at Werden, for thirty solidi, XCIX, 812.

ERINGIUS, or rather ERWIG, cleverly obtained the kingdom of the Goths after Wamba. He enacted new laws and convened councils at Toledo, but was burdensome to his subjects. He died at Toledo in 687. Addresses to bishops by him survive (in Pseudo-Isidore), CXXX, 549, 563.

ERKEMBALD, bishop of Strasbourg. From boyhood he was educated in humane letters; he was promoted to the episcopate in 965 and later consecrated seventeen bishops, among them Hatto and Rupert. He received a eulogy from Pope John XIII and died in 391. There survive his *Sigh of Erkembald*, epigrams, [Col. 0442] and the municipal laws of the city of Strasbourg, CXXXVII, 581.

ERLEFRID, abbot of Saint-Bertin. He purchased certain lands called Saroadslusta in the districts of Noyon and Vermandois from one Darmund in 709, CXXXVI, 1199.

ERMANRIC, monk of Reichenau, also called Ermenric, disciple of Walafrid Strabo. After Walafrid’s death he wrote a book on grammar and a short work on the foundation of the monastery of Reichenau, in 850, CXVI, 23.

ERMENFRID. See above, ERIC.

ERMENGAUD, or ERMENGARD, a German monk. At the end of the twelfth century he wrote a treatise against the Albigensians and Waldensians; this small work survives in mutilated form, CCIV, 1236.

ERMENOARA, a nun, bestowed many gifts on the monastery of Saint Benignus at Dijon, then governed by Bobolinus under Astericus, bishop of Langres, in 715. Mabillon dates this to 737, when Theuderic IV died and Charles succeeded him, LXXXVIII, 1259.

ERMENTRUDIS, first the wife of Erchembard and afterwards of Bernard, gave a double estate to the monastery of Saint Peter at Chartres in 1024, CLV, 255.

ERMINETRUDIS, a most noble matron of Paris, made many gifts by testament to various churches and persons. She gave to the basilica of Saint Symphorianus the cart in which she was drawn by yoked oxen. The document is subscribed by Count Monmolo, Sculpilion the sword-bearer, and others, in 700; this charter is torn and mutilated, LXXXVIII, 1245.

ERMOLD, or ERMENOLD NIGELLUS, flourished in the ninth century. In verse he sang the deeds of Louis the Pious from 781 to 826. All biographers are silent concerning this writer’s life, CV, 552.

ERNALD, abbot of Bonneval in the territory of Chartres. He was a man of considerable repute, although born of very low origin; contemporary of Saint Bernard of Clairvaux, he died in 1156. He wrote treatises on the works of the six days, on Christ’s cardinal virtues, on the praise of the Blessed Virgin Mary, on the gifts of the Holy Spirit, on Christ’s seven words on the cross, besides a commentary on Psalm 132 and meditations, CLXXXIX, 1507.

ERNULF, bishop of Rochester. He held this see from 1114 to 1124. He compiled a book *On the Foundation, Endowment, Charters, Pleas, and Other Matters Pertaining to the Church of Rochester*; he also wrote a letter on incestuous marriages, CLXIII, 1442.

ERP, son of Aldric, gave part of his inheritance to the church of Saint Saviour at Werden in 838, during the reign of Louis the Pious, XCIX, 812.

ERPA, a certain man, sold land lying near the monastery of Werden to Bishop Hildigrim (ninth century), XCIX, 810.

ERPO, a certain man, transferred part of his inheritance to the church of Saint Stephen at Werden: namely, two *journals* of land lying in the village called Meinthinne, in 847, during Lothair’s reign, XCIX, 806.

ERPO, dean of Halberstadt, flourished about 1136. He informed Pope Innocent II of the election of Gerard, provost of Saint John’s, to the bishopric of Halberstadt, CLXXIX, 666.

ERWISIUS, or ERVEUS, also called Ernest, an Englishman by nationality, became abbot of Saint Victor’s, Paris, but resigned that dignity because of the relaxation of discipline. A letter concerning him to the papal legate survives (1177), CXC, 687; CXCVI, 1374.

ETHELBERT, king of the English, the first Christian king in England, married Bertha. He enacted new laws in the Anglo-Saxon language and died in 816. His diplomas survive, by which he made gifts to various churches, together with a decree forbidding the removal of church property, LXXX, 342.

ETHELRED, king of the Mercians, reigned at the end of the seventh century and is distinct from Æthelred, king of the English, who flourished in the ninth century. He gave certain lands to Saint Aldhelm, then abbot of Malmesbury, in 681, LXXXIX, 311, 312.

ETHELRED, or Æthelred II, king of the English, brother and successor of Saint Edward, ordered all Danes dwelling in the kingdom to be killed; in 1013 he left the sceptre to his son Edward. His laws and diplomas survive, CLI, 1165.

ETHELWALD, of whom nothing is found except a letter which he wrote to Saint Aldhelm, bishop of Sherborne, calling him his teacher, about 705. Aldhelm replied to this young man and disciple, urging him to abstain from the vices of his age, LXXXIX, 97.

ETHELWOLD (Saint), bishop of Winchester, his native city. He was educated under Saint Dunstan at Glastonbury and became a monk; later he was abbot of Abingdon, from which he was raised to the episcopate. He published a book *On the Manner of Life among Monks of the Order of Saint Benedict*. He died in 984, CXXXVII, 78.

[Col. 0443] EUCHERIUS (Saint), bishop of Lyons. Born of noble family, after receiving a careful education he first married a Gallic wife; with his children and wife he withdrew to the island of Lérins, near Lirinum, where he lived as an anchorite, teaching his sons and maintaining a pleasant literary correspondence with friends. Renowned for holiness, he was elevated to the bishopric of Lyons. He died in 454. He left letters and minor works, L, 686.

EUCLID, the illustrious mathematician whom writers long confused indiscriminately with another, a Megarian philosopher. He taught arithmetic and geometry at Alexandria under Ptolemy, son of Lagus, in 320 before Christ. He wrote the *Elements* in two books, which are available translated from Greek into Latin in Boethius, LXIII, 1307.

EUDOXIA LICINIA, first wife of Valentinian III and then of Maximus himself, who had killed Valentinian. Afterwards she placed herself in the hands of Genseric, king of the Vandals, who kept her captive with him. She lived in the fifth century. A Greek-Latin letter by her to Emperor Theodosius survives in Saint Leo, LIV, 861.

EUGENIUS (Saint), bishop of Carthage. An African by race, he was elected by his church with the consent of Huneric, king of the Vandals; for twenty-four years the see had stood vacant through the malice of the Arians. He offered the king an eloquent profession of faith, which reduced these heretics to silence; nevertheless he was afterwards exiled by that same king to Tripolitania and entrusted to a heretical bishop to be tortured. Carried to the Gallic city of Albi, he died in 485. A letter by him survives to his citizens concerning the preservation of the Catholic faith, LVIII, 767.

EUGENIUS (Saint), bishop of Toledo, flourished in the seventh century. He was first enrolled among the clergy of Toledo, then, from love of solitude, withdrew to a monastery at Saragossa, from which he was taken to assume the episcopal mitre. He wrote a book on the Trinity and produced certain poems, LXXXVII, 358.

EUGENIUS II, Roman pontiff. A Roman by birth, in the year of the Lord 824 he succeeded Pope Paschal I and occupied the see for three years. His diplomas, letters, and decrees survive, CV, 642.

EUGENIUS III, pope, called Bernard before he was raised to the supreme pontificate, flourished in the twelfth century. At first he was a canon and *vicedominus* of the church of Pisa; then, moved by Saint Bernard’s preaching and miracles, he renounced the world and withdrew to Clairvaux. As a monk, he zealously desired to fulfil the duties of monastic life; afterwards he was chosen abbot of the monastery of Saint Anastasius at Acquas Salvias.
