He governed it so vigorously that, after Pope Lucius’s death, he was elected pope. He died in 1154, CLXXX, 1009.

EUGYPPIUS, abbot of an uncertain monastery, apparently African by race, very learned in Scripture and letters and distinguished for holiness of life. He flourished under Emperor Anastasius. He successfully compiled an epitome of the works of Saint Augustine, LXII, 549.

EULOGIUS (Saint), archbishop and martyr of Toledo. He was born at Córdoba from a noble and patrician family and, devoted to the service of the Church, shone in many virtues and crowned his life with glorious martyrdom in 859. His *Memorial of the Saints* and letters survive, CXV, 704.

EUMENIUS, Greek by origin, withdrew to Autun in Gaul, and thence became master of the sacred memory in the court of Caesar Constantius Chlorus. He fulfilled that office with such distinction that he was appointed director of the schools of the city of the Aedui, with a generous annual sum of money which he spent on restoring the schools. He nevertheless appears to have been a pagan. He flourished in the third century. Four panegyrics by him survive, VIII, 619.

EUPHEMIA, empress and wife of Emperor Justin, replied to Pope Hormisdas’s letter, praising his authority and diligence and commending both herself and her husband to his prayers, in 519, LXIII, 487.

EUPHRONIUS (Saint), bishop of Autun. We have learned nothing concerning him. He and Lupus, bishop of Troyes, wrote a letter to Talasius, bishop of Angers, concerning vigils for Christmas, Epiphany, and Easter; concerning bigamists; and concerning married men admitted to orders, in 479, LVIII, 64.

EUREMARUS, patriarch of Jerusalem. He flourished at the beginning of the twelfth century. He wrote to Lambert of Arras, with whom he had been instructed and educated; therefore he publicly declares his affection and every service for him, CLXII, 677.

EUSEBIUS (Saint), pope. According to Tillemont, he died in the same year, 310, in which he was created supreme pontiff. Three letters and decrees by him survive, VII, 1101.

EUSEBIUS PAMPHILUS, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine. One of the most celebrated bishops of the Church, but the cause of many disturbances. His *Life of the Emperor Constantine* survives. He died in 338, VIII, 9.

EUSEBIUS, THEOGNIUS, THEODORE, BERYNTHUS, and other eastern bishops who had condemned Marcellus of Ancyra at the Council of Antioch wrote to Pope Julius, accusing him of having received into communion the same Marcellus, whom they had deposed. But Julius refutes and rebukes them in his reply and urges them to return to Athanasius’s side, about 341, VIII, 977.

EUSEBIUS (Saint), bishop of Vercelli. A Sardinian by nationality, he was first lector of the Roman Church and afterwards became bishop. He was the first in the West to unite monastic life with the clerical vocation. For some time he lived in exile from his church and attended the Synod of Alexandria under Saint Athanasius. Finally, having returned to his own people, he died about 370. He carefully collected manuscripts of the Gospels and had them copied. Three letters by him survive, XII, 9.

EUSEBIUS, bishop of Milan. When Pope Leo’s legates returned from the East, he held a council at Milan with the bishops of the province about 452, at which the heresies against the Lord’s Incarnation then troubling the eastern Church were condemned. By a synodal letter he informed Saint Leo of the acts of this council, LIV, 945.

EUSEBIUS, a certain man, transmitted much material concerning the Life of Saint Jerome to Damasus, bishop of Porto and later pope, under the name of Formosus; but nothing is known of his country or date. He lived in the ninth century, XXII, 239.

EUSEBIUS OF CREMONA published a Life of Saint Jerome from an ancient manuscript preserved at Milan, in which certain excerpts from John Beleth are found. When he published it is uncertain, but it cannot be dated later than the fifteenth or sixteenth century, XXII, 235.

EUSEBIUS BRUNO, bishop of Angers. Elected in 1041, he attended the Council of Reims in 1049. He is wrongly said to have held erroneous views on the sacrament of the altar and to have followed the opinions of the heresiarch Berengar. He died in 1281. A letter by him to Berengar survives, CXLVII, 1282.

EUSTACHIUS, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter at Chartres. In a charter he records a certain matron who had had two sons by her first husband; one of these she offered to the aforesaid monastery, and for his sake gave it certain estates. Besides this, several other diplomas concerning him survive (1088), CLV, 348.

EUSTACHIUS II, count of Boulogne, and his wife Ida (Saint) had three sons, among them the illustrious Godfrey, who was the first proclaimed king at Jerusalem. A charter of donation by them for the church of Lens survives, in 1170, CLV, 453.

EUSTACHIUS, count of Boulogne, brother of the illustrious Godfrey, whom he followed to the holy war. His name is appended to certain letters, CLV, 390.

EUSTACHIUS, abbot of Saint Peter at Chartres, in the name of the whole convent purchased from the sons of Hugh Gauscelin of Vernou the half of an old, partly ruined church situated at the village of Crucey, for fifteen solidi of coin, in 1102, CLV, 286.

EUSTACHIUS OF MESNILLO, professor and dean of the faculty of studies at Paris, by the common vote of the bishop and other members of that faculty drew up a report against an inveterate and shameful abuse called the Feast of Fools, demanding its abolition in 1444, CCVII, 1169.

EUSTATHIUS OF SEBASTE, Theophilus of Cabala, and Silvanus of Tarsus, bishops, were sent as envoys to Pope Liberius in 366 by those who upheld the cause of the heretic Macedonius against the Arians. Pretending to profess the Nicene faith, they deceived him. Eustathius—now an Arian, now a supporter of Macedonius, and, when circumstances required, orthodox—played only the base part of an actor. A profession of faith by him and his companions survives, VIII, 1377.

EUSTATHIUS, whom Cassiodorus calls a most eloquent man, flourished about 440. He translated from Greek into Latin nine homilies of Saint Basil on the *Hexaemeron*, dedicating this translation to his own sister, LIII, 866.

EUSTOCHIUM (Saint), a virgin consecrated to God, withdrew with her mother Paula to Bethlehem near Saint Jerome. Under his guidance she pursued the way of perfection. A letter from her and her mother Paula to Marcella survives, concerning the praises and delights of the desert. She died in 419, XXII, 483.

EUSTOCHIUS, bishop of Tours, flourished in the fifth century and attended many councils. Together with Leo, bishop of Bourges, and Victorius, bishop of Le Mans, he wrote to the bishops of the Third Lyonnaise, declaring excommunicated those clerics who, bypassing ecclesiastical judgment, had appealed to secular authority, LIII, 1013.

EUSTOCHIUS, priest of the Roman Church. He translated the Life of Saint Pelagia, written by James, deacon of the Church of Edessa, after the sixth century, LXXIII, 665.

EUTHERIUS, bishop of Tyana and suffragan of Nestorius’s diocese, [Col. 0445] followed him into heresy. He subscribed to the deposition of Cyril and Memnon and attended the Council of Ephesus—or rather the “Robber Council”—with Nestorius’s supporters. Fragments of his sermons against Saint Cyril survive, XLVIII, 1085; L, 593.

EUTRANDUS, a subdeacon of Toledo and, apparently, later a deacon of Pavia, an exile from his native land and harassed by the Moors. He copied the Chronicle of Dexter which he had found in the monastery of Fulda, carried it down to the year 630, and then continued it as far as Regismund of Eliberis and his own bishop, about the year 960, LXXX, 633.

EUTROPIUS (St.), bishop, previously abbot of a monastery whose name the historians do not mention, was born in Spain in the fifth century. Two letters of his survive, praised by St. Isidore of Seville: one to Licinianus, the other to Peter, bishop of Hurbica, LXXX, 9.

EUTROPIUS, Lombard priest. He flourished at the end of the ninth century. Nothing is recorded of him except that he was the author of a little book on the rights and privileges of the Roman emperors in the Roman Empire, CXXIX, 961.

EUTYCHES, monk and abbot of Constantinople. At first distinguished by virtue and learning, he left his monastery in order to crush Nestorius’s impious teaching; but he fell into the opposite error and—sad to say—stubbornly adhered to his own opinion. He was condemned at the ecumenical Council of Constantinople in 448 under Patriarch Flavian, and afterwards at the general Council of Chalcedon in 451, at which Dioscorus of Alexandria, his adherent, was deposed. This sect of heretics survived for a long time among the Easterners, LIV, 713.

EUTYCHIANUS (St.), pope. An Etruscan by birth, he succeeded Pope Felix in 275. He opposed the sect of the Manichaeans, which arose during his pontificate. Several letters and decrees of his survive, V, 157.

EUTYCHIUS, bishop of Constantinople. Under the Emperor Justinian, he attended the council held there in 553 against the Eutychians. Deposed and driven into exile, he was restored to his see after Justinian’s death, having retracted a certain error concerning the resurrection of the dead, in 582. His letter to Pope Vigilius survives, LXIX, 64.

EVAGRIUS, priest and perhaps bishop of Antioch, mentioned by St. Jerome. He translated from Greek into Latin the Life of St. Antony written by St. Athanasius of Alexandria; historians do not agree as to the year in which he flourished, LXXIII, 124.

EVAGRIUS, monk, flourished about 420. He wrote a dialogue between a Jew and Theophilus the Christian, and maxims for the monks and virgins of his time. Nothing has been found by which he may be distinguished from the preceding Evagrius, nor anything proving that they are the same person, XX, 1062, 1165.

EVANTIUS, abbot. Basnage and Fabricius observe that he must be distinguished from another Evantius of Vienne who died in 586. He wrote a letter against those who consider animal blood unclean; the letter itself suggests that this man was a Spaniard and archdeacon of Toledo (eighth century), LXXXVIII, 719.

EVARISTUS (St.), pope and martyr. He succeeded Anacletus. He was the first to divide the City into several parishes. He died in 112 during Trajan’s persecution. Isidore Mercator attributes several decrees and letters to him, but the whole is sheer forgery, CXXX, 81.

EVERVINUS, or ERVINUS, provost and later abbot of the monastery of Steinfeld, wrote to St. Bernard of Clairvaux concerning the heretics of his time, CLXXXII, 676; CLXXXV, 390.

EVILO, count of Salz, and his wife Regina gave to the abbot of Alba Ripa everything that they possessed in that territory, in 1135, during the episcopate of Wilencus of Langres, CLXXXV, 1433, 1434.

EVODIUS, bishop of Upsala in Africa, flourished in the fifth century. He wrote a book on the miracles of St. Stephen, brought by Orosius into the West and praised by St. Augustine in Book XII of *The City of God*. Some also attribute to him a book on faith, XXXI, 1233.

EVREMARUS, archbishop of Caesarea, bestowed certain goods upon the canonical brethren of the Holy Sepulchre so that they might relieve the need of the poor, in 1129, CLV, 1168.

EWRWINUS granted by donation to the church of St. Saviour in the district of Ruriegoa two *jornales* of land beside the River Rura, in the place called With. This was done in the monastery of Werth in 847, under the reign of Lothair, XCIX, 806.

EZELO, monk of Cluny, wrote the Life of this holy man shortly after the death of Abbot Hugh; extracts from it survive. He flourished in the twelfth century, CLIX, 909.

F

[Col. 0446]

FABIANUS (St.), pope and martyr, a Roman by birth, was appointed in the place of St. Anterus. He built many churches and oratories in various Roman cemeteries, and ordained bishops whom he sent into Gaul. He died a martyr in Decius’s persecution in 250. Decrees falsely attributed to him survive, CXXX, 151.

FACUNDUS, bishop of Hermiane in the province of Byzacena in Africa, flourished after the consulship of Basil, under Emperor Justinian. Cassiodorus mentions him and calls him a destroyer of heretics. He wrote twelve books in defence of the Three Chapters, one against Marcion, and a letter on the Catholic faith. (547.) LXXVII, 520.

FALCO, cleric, gave a portion of his inheritance to Abbot Dominic of St. Bartholomew for the church of St. George. (Without mention of a year, among Lombard diplomas.) LXXXVII, 1441.

FALCO of Benevento, at first notary and scribe of the palace, was protected by Innocent II because of his steadfast fidelity in those troubled times. At the request of Abbot Peter he wrote a chronicle dealing with the events of his own time, CLXXIII, 1145.

FALTONIA (Valeria Proba), poet and wife of the proconsul Adelphius. From Virgil she composed a cento on the creation of the world and on the Gospels. She flourished about 400, XIX, 801.

FARDULFUS, abbot of Saint-Denis, was Lombard by birth. When Pavia was captured, Charlemagne brought him into France; he became dear to the king, who soon set him over the monastery of St. Dionysius. He is believed to have died in 806. Metrical works of his survive, XCIX, 822.

FARICIUS, apparently an eighth-century monk of British origin, whose life is disclosed by no one. He himself handed down to us the Life of St. Aldhelm, LXXXIX, 63.

FARO (St.), bishop of Meaux, born of Burgundian parents, spent the first part of his life at the court of King Theudebert III. Afterwards, at his sister’s urging, he renounced the world and entered the clergy; he became bishop in 626 and died in 672. Charters concerning him survive, LXXXVII, 1132.

FAROALDUS, duke of Spoleto, a most devout man, made many gifts to the monastery of Farfa in the Sabine territory, apparently by a letter which he wrote to Pope John VI in the eighth century, CL, 1306.

FARSITUS Hugh. See HUGH.

FASTIDIOSUS, Arian priest. A sermon containing the poison of error survives among the letters of St. Fulgentius of Ruspe; nothing has been discovered about Fastidiosus himself, LXV, 375.

FASTIDIUS, British bishop, flourished in the time of Cyril of Alexandria and Theodore of Ancyra. He followed the heresy of his compatriot Pelagius. His book on the Christian life survives, L, 379.

FASTREDUS, abbot of Clairvaux. Born of noble stock, he flourished in the twelfth century. From childhood he was entrusted to skilled teachers; he became a monk and afterwards abbot of the monastery of Clairvaux. We have only two letters from him. He died in 1163, CLXXXVIII, 1657.

FAUSTINUS (St.), priest or bishop, lived in the fifth century. But no monument concerning him survives, for he differs from the Faustinus mentioned by Gennadius, who, far from being a saint, openly adhered to the Luciferians. A homily on the Passion of the Lord survives from the present Faustinus, LIX, 407.

FAUSTINUS, priest. According to Gennadius, he supported the Luciferians and wrote seven books against the Arians, addressed to Queen Flaccilla (384), XIII, 29.

FAUSTUS the Manichaean flourished at the end of the fourth century. Nothing concerning his life has been handed down to us. He wrote a book against the Catholic faith, which St. Augustine refuted, XX, 79.

FAUSTUS (St.), bishop of Riez in Gaul, first became a monk in the monastery of Lérins. He opposed the heresy of the Pelagians, but for a while deviated from the faith; soon converted, he died holily and piously in the communion of the Church, in 485, LVIII, 775.

FELICITAS (St), an African woman, while still a catechumen was arrested at the command of the proconsul Hilarianus together with Perpetua, Saturus, and others, and attained the crown of martyrdom in 203. She is thought to have contributed to the compilation of the Acts, III, 17, 46.

FELIX, JADER, and POLIANUS, African bishops, condemned with many priests and Christians to the mines in the province of Sigua, replied to the letters of St. Cyprian, warmly thanking him for the assistance sent to them by him. (258.) IV, 423.

FELIX I (St), pope and martyr. A Roman by birth, he succeeded St. Dionysius in 269. During his pontificate the heresy of Paul of Samosata arose, and he procured its condemnation; but while persecution raged under Aurelian, he died a martyr in 274. Four letters of his survive, C, 135.

FELIX of Aptunga, bishop in Africa, ordained Caecilian bishop of Carthage. He was afterwards accused of having surrendered the sacred Scriptures while persecution was raging. How he cleared himself may be seen in his Acts. (305.) VIII, 715.

FELIX II (St), pope. A Roman by birth, he was appointed by the Arians in place of Liberius, who had been exiled and banished. But he soon acted vigorously against the Arians, excommunicating Constantius, Ursacius, Valens, and their adherents; thus, from being a schismatic, he began to be regarded as the legitimate pontiff of the universal Church and, because of his eminent virtues, was enrolled among the saints. He died in 365. Letters and decrees of his survive, XIII, 9.

FELIX III (St), pope. A Roman by birth and son of Felix, formerly a priest, he became supreme pontiff in 483; he anathematized the impious Zeno and his errors. He died in 492. Letters and decrees of his survive, LVIII, 890.

FELIX IV, pope. A Samnite by birth, he attained the see of the Roman Church through the favour of Theodoric, king of the Goths, in 526, and succeeded Pope John I. He died in 530. Three letters are attributed to him, but the first two appear to be apocryphal, LXV, 9.

FELIX, deacon and papal legate. See GERMANUS.

FELIX, bishop of the church of Messina in Sicily, succeeded Eucarpus. He died about 590. His letter to Gregory concerning marriage between blood relatives survives, LXXVII, 4320.

FELIX, bishop of Limoges, successor of Simplicius, sent Abbot Paternus to the Council of Chalon about 644. His letter to St. Desiderius, bishop of Cahors, survives, LXXXVIII, 266.

FELIX, bishop of Narbonne, sent complaints to St. Desiderius concerning a certain layman or cleric of the church of Cahors. Desiderius, to redress this wrong, sent the accused back so that Felix himself might do with him what he wished; but, through the poison of slanders, discord prevailed between them for two years. At last Felix repented of the matter and sought forgiveness from Desiderius. (648.) LXXXVII, 266.

FELIX, bishop of Lucca, confirmed to the monastery of St. Frigidian what had been given by Faulo and added new gifts himself in 685. Cumbert, king of the Lombards, confirmed this charter in 700, LXXXVII, 1347.

FELIX, bishop of Ravenna, was elected in 707. He collected the sermons of St. Peter Chrysologus into a single volume. Distinguished alike for eloquence and piety, he died in 717, LXXXIX, 358.

FELIX, bishop of Toledo, contemporary of and successor to St. Julian in the episcopate. He governed the church of Toledo for seven years and died about 700. He composed the Life—or rather the eulogy—of his predecessor St. Julian, XCVI, 413.

A certain FELIX, priest, gave a cell situated in the place called Rocasham, in the district of Flanders, to the monastery of Sithiu, then governed by Abbot Nantharius, about 745. Another charter of purchase concerning the same man survives, CXXXVI, 1207, 1211. See a charter probably concerning the same person, LXXXVIII, 1304.

FELIX, bishop of Urgell in Spain. A heretical man, destroying Christ’s divinity, he was condemned in several councils, deposed, and banished to Lyons; there, repentant at last, he issued a retraction. According to some, he died unrepentant about 818, XCVI, 848.

FERENTIANUS, bishop in Italy, consulted Pope Innocent III concerning the marriage case of a certain man who had pledged faith to a woman not yet marriageable and was afterwards betrothed to another, in 1200, CCXIV, 23.

FERNANDUS II, king of the Spains, son and successor of Alfonso VIII, died in 1187. In 1172 he wrote a letter to Pope Alexander III acknowledging the lordship of the Supreme Pontiff, CC, 1369.

FERRANDUS FULGENTIUS, deacon of the church of Carthage and kinsman of St. Fulgentius the bishop, flourished about 530. He was eminent in prudence and counsel. Letters and short works of his survive, LXVII, 878.

FERREOLUS (St), bishop of Uzès. He founded the monastery bearing his name in 558 and gave its monks a rule which he dedicated to Lucretius, bishop of Die, LXVI, 959.

FESTUS (Sextus Pompeius), fourth-century grammarian, epitomized the books of Verrius Flaccus, the distinguished grammarian; Paul the Deacon subsequently reduced them to a compendium. Thus Paul the Deacon was almost the cause of this work’s being lost altogether, so that only fragments survive, XCV, 1605.

FIDIS, viscountess of Narbonne, gave to the monastery of Moissac, dependent on Cluny, the church of St. Peter of Sermur in the diocese of Rodez and the whole mountain called Poieth, in 1077, CLIX, 967.

FIRMATUS, canon of St. Leobinus, gave a house and vineyards to the monastery of St. Peter at Chartres in 1049, CLV, 322.

FIRMILIANUS, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia. He flourished in the third century. A contemporary of St. Cyprian, he upheld Cyprian’s view concerning the rebaptism of heretics against Pope St. Stephen. Yet, like Cyprian, amid vehemence of expression he did not renounce charity. His letter to Cyprian survives, III, 1153.

[Col. 0448] FIRMINUS. See CYPRIAN.

FLAVIANUS (St), archbishop and patriarch of Constantinople. He anathematized Eutyches at the sham council of Ephesus, where the impious Dioscorus of Alexandria so battered him with blows and beatings that he died three days later, in 449, LIV, 723, 743.

FLODOARDUS, or FRODOARDUS, canon of Rheims, was born in 894 at Sparnacum on the Marne, commonly called Épernay. He flourished under Kings Louis the Foreigner and Lothair. He compiled a history of Rheims, left a considerable number of poems, annals, and other short works. He died in 966, CXXXV, 9.

FLODOINUS gave certain estates at the stream Hesepesita to Bishop Hildigrim in Germany (ninth century), XCIX, 813.

FLORENTIUS, master of offices at the court of the Emperor Constantius, was sent into exile in Dalmatia by Emperor Julian. In 359 he wrote to Lucifer of Cagliari, asking whether he was the author of a book against Constantius, in which he had bestowed upon that impious prince the title “Eternity”; Lucifer answered him fearlessly, XIII, 935.

FLORENTIUS of Worcester, historical writer of the twelfth century. A fragment of his Chronicle from 1081 to 1117 is given, CXLVII, 795.

FLORIANUS, abbot of a Roman monastery, concerning whom historians are silent. Yet from a surviving letter by him to Bishop Nicetius, we learn that he was a pupil of Ennodius, bishop of Pavia. Elsewhere it appears that “abbot of Remani” should be read instead of “Roman,” meaning that he was abbot of St. Remigius at Rheims, LXXII, 918.

FLORUS, deacon of Lyons, whom some make much earlier, attained such a reputation for learning and skill that he was entrusted with refuting John Scotus’s book *On Predestination*. He wrote several commentaries, poems, and a letter to Empress Judith. He died in 860, CXIX, 9.

A certain FOLBERTUS, an illustrious man, gave his possessions in Champagne to the monastery of Sithiu in 811, during Charlemagne’s reign, CXXXVI, 1219.

FOLCBERTUS, or rather FOLEBRAT, as the instrument states, concluded an exchange with Ludger, abbot of Werth, in 805, XCIX, 818.

FOLCHARDUS, first a monk of the monastery of Sithiu, flourished about 1080. A learned man for his age, he was placed by William the Conqueror over the abbey of Tournai; he wrote many Lives, CXLVII, 1083.

FOLCHARDUS, abbot of Lobbes in the diocese of Cambrai, succeeded Arnald in 1094; he restored the former discipline in this monastery. He died in 1107. His letter to Emperor Henry survives, CLVII, 482.

FOLCRADA, full sister of Hemming, formerly an official, sold to Blessed Abbot Ludger, for a suitable price, a certain field situated at the Cross beside the River Arnapa. (Without mention of a year), ninth century, XCIX, 806.

FOLCUINUS, abbot of Lobbes. Born of noble family in Lotharingia, he led the monastic life from childhood in the monastery of St. Bertin. While still young he became abbot and, after a wise administration, died in 990. He wrote the Chronicle of Lobbes and several homilies, CXXXVII, 320.

FOLLIETO (Hugh of). See HUGH.

FOLMARUS, provost of Trieffenstein, or “Dripping Rock,” in Franconia, lived in the time of Pope Alexander III. Through letters, treatises, and books he did not hesitate to disseminate various errors against the sacrament of the blessed body and blood of the Lord, especially in Bavaria. Many promptly refuted him, CXCIV, 1481.

FOLQUINUS, bishop of Thérouanne, successor of Fridegisus, who through negligence of duty had allowed everything to fall into ruin. Folquinus therefore took care to restore all things; under him the monastery of Sithiu flourished, as is evident from his charter of 817, CXXXVI, 1223.

FOLQUINUS, monk of St. Bertin. Born of a noble Lotharingian family, he became a monk and was afterwards ordained deacon by his abbot; he died before old age, in the tenth century. We have from him the Cartulary of St. Bertin, the Epitaph of Folquinus his kinsman, and another cartulary relating to various monasteries, CXXXVI, 1182.

FORMOSUS, pope. Originally of Ostia, a man conspicuous for religious devotion and integrity of character, he was made pope by a tumultuous election, while Deacon Sergius himself rivalled him for the pontificate. He died in 896. His letters and privileges survive, CXXIX, 822.

FORTUNATUS (Venantius Honorius), bishop of Poitiers, was born at Treviso in Italy and educated at Ravenna. Having become skilled in the sciences and liberal arts, he came into Gaul to visit the tomb of St. Martin. He soon went to Poitiers, where, after entering the clergy, he was later elected bishop in 599. He died in 609. Many Lives of saints, miscellanies, and verses not to be despised survive from him, LXXXVIII, 19.

FORTUNATUS, priest of Lucca, and his son, likewise a priest, gave their estates to the monastery of St. Peter at Lucca, into which both had retired, with the consent both of their bishop Telesperianus and of Duke Walpert, in 713, LXXXVIII, 1351.

FRANCISCUS A PUTEO, prior general of the Carthusian order. He flourished about 1514 and composed the Life of St. Benedict, the holy Father; not much later Peter Blomenvenna, a member of the Charterhouse of Cologne, made it much fuller, CLII, 18, 491.

FRANCISCUS CAMENUS. See CAMENUS.

FRANCISCUS CARREUS. See CARREUS.

FRANCO, schoolmaster, a man renowned for devotion and literary learning, flourished in the eleventh century. He first demonstrated his ability by a book on squaring the circle, and by treatises on computation, mensural music, and other subjects. He died in 1083, CXLIII, 1374.

FRANCO, first a monk and then abbot of Afflighem, flourished at the beginning of the twelfth century. While a monk, he wrote twelve books on grace, or God’s beneficence, to his predecessor, Abbot Fulgentius, CLXVI, 718.

FRECULFUS, bishop of Lisieux, formerly monk and abbot of Fulda, of the Order of St. Benedict. He died in 850. He wrote two books of Chronicles, CVI, 915.

FREDEGARIUS, called the schoolmaster, born in Burgundy, flourished in the seventh century. He produced an epitome of the history of Gregory of Tours together with its continuation. He preserved historical documents of the greatest importance. But no traces whatever of his life survive, LXXI, 695, 697.

FREDEGISUS, abbot of the monastery of St. Martin at Tours. He flourished in the age of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious and had Alcuin as his teacher. He collected the laws of Charlemagne and of Charlemagne’s successor. His letter on nothing and darkness survives. He died in 834, CIV, 159; CV, 751.

FREDEGUNDIS, first mistress and afterwards wife of King Chilperic. She waged much enmity against Brunhild, queen of Austrasia, and committed abominable crimes. After Chilperic’s death, as guardian of her son, she administered the kingdom. Certain sayings of hers to Chilperic are recorded, in 597, CXXXIX, 695, 696.

FREDERICUS, called Salvator, an illustrious man, and his wife Hersendis gave the monastery of Clairvaux all that they possessed in the territory of Gundria in Spain, not far from that abbey, in 1147, CLXXXV, 987.

FREDERICUS, abbot of the monastery of St. Godehard, wrote to Wibald, abbot of Corvey, that he had seen his own predecessor Henry, who had been deposed, and that he was not wholly averse to reconciliation; he therefore urged Wibald toward concord, in 1148, CLXXXIX, 1210.

FREDERICUS, king of Sicily, granted the houses of the canons of the Holy Sepulchre existing throughout his kingdom a privilege of freedom for their mills, in 1210. The same man ceded the county of Fondi to Pope Innocent III in 1212, CLV, 1251.

FREDERICUS, provost of Val-Dieu, flourished in the twelfth century. By letter he commended himself to the prayers of St. Hildegard, abbess of St. Rupert’s, CXCVI, 305.

FRETELLUS, archdeacon, flourished at the end of the eleventh century. He wrote a book on the holy places and dedicated it to Raymond, count of Toulouse. We do not know of which church he was archdeacon, CLV, 1038.

FRIDEGODUS, monk of the Order of St. Benedict and deacon, attained great learning. He wrote the Life of St. Audoenus, bishop of Rouen, and that of St. Wilfrid, archbishop of York. He died in 963, CXXXIII, 978.

FRIDERICUS, count of Toul, and his wife Hawidis confirmed a gift of a certain measure of salt to be bestowed annually upon the monastery of Tart, established by Matthew, duke of Lotharingia, in 1142, CLXXXV, 1412.

FRIDERICUS, archbishop of Cologne. Nothing concerning him is related by biographers. His letter and several diplomas survive, from 1131, CLXVI, 1350.

FRIDERICUS, called Barbarossa, accompanied his uncle Conrad III to Palestine. Having returned, he became emperor in 1152. Setting out again for Jerusalem, he perished in a river of Cilicia in 1190. Many of his letters and diplomas survive, scattered through various volumes, CLXXX, 1636, 1638. See further CLXXXV, 1457, 1753; CLXXXVIII, 1641; CLXXXIX, 1070, 1409, 1425; CXC, 1058; CXCVII, 186; CC, 55; CCXII, 327.

FRIDERICUS, archbishop of Salzburg, sent many letters to Rudolph, emperor of Germany, and suffered much from a certain most wicked duke, Ottocar, XCVIII, 742, passim.

[Col. 0450] FRIDRICUS, Hildibertus, and Alperctus gave by donation to the churches of St. Saviour, St. Mary, and St. Peter, in the district of the Ripuarian Franks, at the place called Verithina on the River Rura, certain lands in 819, during the reign of Louis the Pious, XCIX, 804.

FRIGULUS, whose writings or words Smaragdus often uses, is wholly uncertain, so much so that some call into question whether he existed at all. Yet, such being the case, from the context of his words he must be assigned to times that were obscure and uncultivated, CII, 1119.

FROGERIUS BARBA gave much to the monastery of Fontevraud for the support of his two daughters, who had embraced the monastic life there at the beginning of the twelfth century, CLXII, 1115.

FROLLANDUS, bishop of Senlis, was elected in 1043. He attended the Council of Rheims held by Pope Leo IX. He died in 1065. His letter to Berengar survives, CXLIII, 1370.

FROMUNDUS of Nouâtre, for the soul of his son who had been killed, gave to Lord Robert of Arbrissel, for his monastery of Fontevraud, half of what he possessed in Bremio, at the beginning of the twelfth century, CLXII, 1107.

FROTHARIUS, bishop of Toul, formerly abbot of St. Aper, in 813. He departed this life about 837. Twenty-five letters of his survive, addressed both to Emperor Louis the Pious, to Empress Judith, and to various others, CVI, 864.

FROUMUNDUS, monk of Tegernsee, flourished in the eleventh century. We know nothing of him except certain poems and letters, CXLI, 1283.

FROWINUS, abbot. Nothing certain is known concerning him except that he was first a monk, then abbot of the monastery of Einsiedeln, and afterwards of the abbey of Mount of the Angels. He wrote eight books on free will to the monk Adelbert, in 1131, CLXXIX, 1801.

FRUCTUOSUS (St), bishop of Braga. Born of royal Gothic blood, he despised worldly splendour and embraced the monastic life. He was then taken up for pastoral office in the place of Potamius, who had voluntarily resigned the episcopate. Distinguished by virtues and miracles, he was famous throughout Spain; he died in 670. His monastic rule, another rule called the Common Rule, and several poems survive, LXXXVII, 1088.

FULBERTUS (St), bishop of Chartres. Born of humble station in the tenth century, he was distinguished alike by learning and singular virtue. First master of the school at Chartres, he had many pupils, among them Berengar; he was elected bishop in 1007. Full of merits and good works, he passed to God in 1029. His letters, various treatises, sermons, hymns, a praise of monastic life, and diplomas survive, CXLI, 163.

FULCANDUS granted certain gifts to the monastery of St. Peter at Chartres in 1080, CLV, 331.

FULCHERIUS, holder of the abbey of St. Leobinus in the suburb of Chartres, declared that he held it through the generosity of Count Odo. He granted to the priest Sigemund a small portion of this abbey’s lands for an annual rent, in 981, CLV, 232.

FULCHERIUS, priest of Chartres, followed Duke Robert of Normandy into Palestine and became chaplain to King Baldwin. He wrote a history of the Jerusalem expedition from 1095 to 1124. He died in 1127, CLV, 823.

FULCHERIUS, patriarch of Jerusalem, and Amalric, prior of the church of the Resurrection, warn all the brethren not to neglect any alms and not to cause any loss to the possessions of the community (without heading), CLV, 1259.

FULCHREDUS of St. Léger, in the twelfth century, granted a gift to Lord Robert of Arbrissel and the nuns of Fontevraud for building a hospice, CLXII, 1109.

FULCO, archbishop of Rheims. A noble man accustomed to offices at court, he was first a monk in the monastery of St. Bertin, of which he was later elected abbot; but after Hincmar’s death he was raised to the see of Rheims. After sitting for seventeen years, he perished, pierced with lances, in 900. You have two letters from him, CXXXI, 9.

FULCO III, called the Black, count of Anjou, made two journeys to Jerusalem and twice defeated Odo of Blois. He died in 1039. His letter to Robert, king of the Franks, survives, CXLI, 938.

See also what he did for the monastery of St. Nicholas of Anjou in 1032 and for the monastery of Fontevraud, CLV, 481; CLXII, 1097.

FULCO, abbot of Corbie, surnamed the Great, perhaps because of the firmness of spirit which he displayed in defending the rights of his abbey, then harassed by another Fulco, bishop of Amiens. In 1048 he attended the Council of Rheims presided over by Pope Leo IX. He died in 1095. He wrote a Chronicle of Corbie and a letter to Pope Alexander II, CL, 1431.

[Col. 0451] FULCO IV, count of Anjou, fought against William of Aquitaine and his own brother Geoffrey, whom he held captive as long as he lived. His wife Bertrada was carried off by Philip, king of the Franks. His diploma for the church of St. Maurice at Anjou survives from 1096. He died in 1109, CLV, 479.

FULCO, third king of Jerusalem, formerly count of Anjou, defeated the king of England. Having set out for Palestine, he succeeded Baldwin II. He died in 1142. Several of his diplomas survive, CLV, 1123.

FULCOIUS, a very celebrated subdeacon and poet of the eleventh century, was born at Beauvais of noble stock. At the school of Rheims he studied under the distinguished Herman and cultivated poetry especially. Once made a subdeacon, he refused to be raised to higher orders lest he lose his freedom. He died in 1083, leaving countless poems which display the fertility of his mind but reveal ignorance and contempt for the rules of poetry, CL, 1551.

FULCOIUS FESSARDUS, having dedicated one of his daughters to God, granted by donation to the monastery of Fontevraud land situated at Borno, sufficient for four oxen to plough, at the beginning of the twelfth century, CLXIII, 1115.

FULGENTIUS (Fabius Claudius), bishop of Ruspe in Africa. He was born in Byzacena in 468 to devout parents. Though he had strayed from the faith, he was enlightened by reading the works of St. Augustine, dedicated himself to God, and became a monk. He went to Rome and, on returning, was raised to the see of Ruspe; but King Thrasamund of the Vandals exiled him, and Hilderic recalled him. He died in 533. His polemical and dogmatic works survive, together with sermons and letters, LXV, 105.

FULGENTIUS, abbot of Afflighem, flourished about 1125. By letter he asked his brother Franco and commanded him, under the bond of most holy obedience, to write a treatise on God’s grace, CLXVI, 717.

G

GAIDOALDUS, physician of Desiderius, king of the Lombards, founded outside the walls of the city of Pistoia the church and monastery of St. Bartholomew, and endowed them by a new charter, in the eighth century, LXXXVII, 1432.

GALBERTUS, bishop of Bruges, flourished in the twelfth century. He was first a public notary of his city. He wrote the Life and Martyrdom of Blessed Charles, count of Flanders, and was an eyewitness of the events he reported, CLXVI, 874.

GALCRANNUS, count of Mellent and lord of Gournay Castle, granted the monks of Clairvaux free exit and passage for their goods from place to place, and immunity from every toll, 1143–1157, CLXXXV, 1753.

GALERIUS MAXIMIANUS, Roman emperor, was called the Evil Beast by Lactantius because of his mental madness and ferocity. After the bloodiest persecutions of Christians, he himself, struck down from heaven, was consumed by horrible putrefaction; at the end he repented of his deed and by an edict in 311 commanded that they should pray to God for him, VII, 249.

GALLA PLACIDIA. See PLACIDIA.

GALLUS (St), abbot and confessor, was a disciple of St. Columbanus. Struck with a severe fever among the Alemanni, where he recovered his health, he devoted himself to building a cell which later became the highly celebrated monastery bearing his name. A sermon delivered at Constance concerning him survives. 646, LXXXVII, 9.

GALLUS (St), bishop of Clermont, formerly archdeacon to Bishop Aratius, built a chapel in honour of St. Amabilis and translated his sacred body to it. His letter to St. Desiderius, bishop of Cahors, survives. He died in 554, LXXXVII, 265.

The death of St. Gallus, bishop of Clermont, must rightly be placed in 554, as the biographer rightly maintains (Michaud, editor), and not in 650, as nearly all other biographers after the Bollandists have mistakenly copied. The latter falsely gave St. Quintian a certain Desiderius as successor instead of St. Gallus, and therefore moved the latter’s death to 650, contrary to the explicit statements of Gregory of Tours, bishop and nephew of St. Gallus himself (LXXI, 1031). Nor did they observe that St. Gallus’s death cannot be assigned to the aforementioned year 630, since the same Gregory of Tours—whom his uncle Gallus had received as a boy to educate—certainly departed this life in 595. St. Gallus’s death is therefore rightly fixed in 554; and to approximately the same period should be assigned those whose letters show that they were contemporaries of St. Gallus, such as St. Desiderius of Cahors, Palladius of Auxerre, Constantius of Albi, Abbo of Metz, and others.

GALO, bishop of Paris, was born at Beauvais of a noble family. He was first the disciple and successor of Ivo of Chartres in the abbey of St. Quentin. Pope Paschal II sent him as legate to Poland to reform certain abuses; on his return he was made successor to Fulco in the bishopric of Paris. He died in 1116. His letter to Lambert of Arras and a diploma survive, CLXII, 722.

GALTERIUS SAVEYR, bishop of Meaux, succeeded Bomerus in 1052; he attended the consecration of King Philip and died in 1082. His letter to Bartholomew, bishop of Tours, is given, CXLVII, 1214.

GALTERIUS, who calls himself chancellor, is commonly confused with another Galterius, canon of Thérouanne, though he is demonstrably different from him by diversity of style. Certain words show that he was a Gaul; he recounted the wars of Antioch, of which he was an eyewitness. 1119, CLV, 993.

GALTERIUS, lord of Caesarea and son of Eustace Granier, gave to the canons of the Holy Sepulchre a certain village estate and adjoining lands, then bounded both by crosses and by stones fixed in the ground, in 1145, CLV, 1169.

GALTERIUS CHESNELLUS gave to the Cluniac monks remaining at St. Dionysius in the castle of Nogent-le-Rotrou the church of St. Peter of Ceton, to which he added certain other things. (Without date), twelfth century, CLIX, 983.

GALTERUS of Lille, bishop of Maguelonne and kinsman of Provost Robert, was elected bishop and apostolic legate in 1103. Very well practised in Sacred Scripture, he acquired a great reputation for learning. He died in 1119. Only his letter to Robert, provost of Versulanum, and a diploma survive, CLVII, 707.

GALTERUS, bishop of Langres, flourished in the twelfth century. He founded the Charterhouse of Lugny and bestowed many gifts upon, or confirmed gifts made to, the monks of Alba Ripa of the Cistercian order about 1179, the year in which he died according to his epitaph, CLXXXV, 1436.

GALTERUS, knight of Montbard, and his wife Ermengard gave to the monastery of Fontenay all that they possessed in the forest adjoining that abbey as far as the main road leading to St. James, in 1215, CLXXXV, 1473.

GALUANUS of Chamillac granted to the nuns of Fontevraud the tithe from the milling of six mills, in the twelfth century during the reign of Louis VI, CLXII, 1117.

GAMMO, an illustrious man, and his wife Adalgudis bestowed many gifts upon the monastery of Le Mans which they had founded, and arranged for their confirmation in an assembly of nobles in 697, LXXXVIII, 1235.

GARCIAS, monk of St. Michael of Cuxa, flourished in the eleventh century. From his writings survives a letter to Oliva, bishop of Ausona, concerning the beginnings of the monastery of Cuxa and the relics deposited there, CXLI, 1443.

GARLANDIA (John of). See JOHN.

GARNERIUS, abbot, whose life and country are wholly uncertain; he is believed to have flourished in the eighth century, since Pippin, king, sent him as legate to Astolf, king of the Lombards, who was threatening plots against Stephen III, XCVI, 1370.

GARNERIUS and his brother EBLO gave to the church of St. Mary of Fontevraud and to Lord Robert of Arbrissel as much arable land as twenty oxen can plough, and, besides, meadows, woodland, etc., for the use and maintenance of the nuns (twelfth century), CLXII, 1118.

GARNERIUS, bishop of Langres, brother of Simon de Rochefort, was first a monk of Longuay, then of La Rivour and Clairvaux, and ninth abbot of Clairvaux. He succeeded Manasses about 1195. Forty sermons of his survive, for feasts of the Lord and of the saints. He died in 1198, CCV, 555.

GARNERIUS de Fontanis made many gifts to the nuns of St. Mary of Praslon in 1230, CLXXXV, 1424.

GARNERUS, regular canon of St. Victor at Paris, flourished in the eleventh century. He wrote a book entitled *Gregorianum*, in which he collected explanations of Holy Scripture drawn from the works of St. Gregory, CXCVI, 9.

GARSIRIUS de Macheco granted certain customary dues to the monastery of Fontevraud and to Lord Robert of Arbrissel; he made his gift upon the altar of St. Benedict in the chapel of the infirmary, under King Louis VI, CLXII, 1114.

GASTO, count of Bigorre and viscount of Béarn, like others who had followed Raymond, count of Toulouse, into heresy, abjured it and placed himself in the hands of Peter, king of Aragon, at the same time confessing that he would obey the Holy Roman Church, in 1213, CCXVI, 848.

GAUCHERIUS, monk of Clairvaux, wrote in the twelfth century to a certain Templar knight dwelling in the Holy Places a letter redolent of most beautiful charity, CXCVI, 1616.

GAUDENTIUS (St.), bishop of Brescia, succeeded Philastrius, declaring himself unworthy of that burden. In 405 he undertook an embassy to the emperor Arcadius on behalf of St. John Chrysostom. His sermons and a poem in praise of St. Philastrius survive, XX, 791.

GAUFREDUS FULCHREDUS. See FULCHREDUS.

[Col. 0453] GAUFREDUS MALATERRA, a Benedictine monk of Norman origin, went to Apulia. He wrote a Sicilian history, in 1099, CXLIX, 1087.

GAUFREDUS, duke of Normandy and count of Anjou, called Plantagenet, died in 1151. Several letters of his to Suger survive, CLXXXVI, 1351.

GAUFREDUS, archbishop of Bordeaux; a letter of his to Suger survives, CLXXXVI, 1359, 1369.

GAUFRIDUS, knight and brother of Hugh, abbot of Cluny, gave to him and to his monastery the church of Marcigny in the district of Autun, in 1080, CLIX, 969.

GAUFRIDUS, bishop of the church of Chartres, granted to Eustace, abbot of St. Peter’s, the altar of Brueroles in 1084; and in 1086 granted to that same monastery freedom concerning five churches in Perche, CLV, 362.

GAUFRIDUS, surnamed Niger, monk and procurator of the monastery of St. Peter at Chartres under Abbot Eustace, reports that William suppressed certain evil customs in 1088, CLV, 350.

GAUFRIDUS, bishop of Châlons. He was first abbot of St. Medard at Soissons; he was elected bishop in 1131 in place of St. Bernard, who had been elected before him but declined. He confirmed to Lawrence, abbot of St. Viton, the foundation of the monastery of Fontaine-Chaude, and attended the council of Sens against Peter Abelard. He died in 1142. His letters and charters survive, CLXXIII, 1394.

GAUFRIDUS de Rancon wrote to Suger that the king had entrusted the land of Poitou to him, with instructions to distribute its revenues according to the king’s pleasure, in 1147, CLXXXVI, 1384.

GAUFRIDUS Felenia gave the brothers of Clairvaux, in the territory of the village, a meadow called Berold’s meadow, about 1147, CLXXXV, 992.

GAUFRIDUS, called Grossus, monk of Tiron, had as his teacher the venerable Bernard, founder of the abbey of Tiron. He wrote Bernard’s life and dedicated it to Gaufridus, bishop of Chartres, in 1148, CLXXII, 1361.

GAUFRIDUS, mayor of the community of St. Riquier, asks Suger not to delay in sending to him Peter, monk of Bourges, the abbot-elect, in 1149, CLXXXVI, 1363.

GAUFRIDUS, disciple and notary of Bernard, became abbot of Igny after Guerric, and later succeeded Fastrad as abbot of Clairvaux. About 1166 he composed two books on Bernard’s life and a sermon concerning him, CLXXXIV, 435.

See also CLXXXV, 321, 395, 573.

GAUFRIDUS, treasurer of the Temple, received from Pope Innocent III letters concerning the affair of Lord Erard of Brienne and Philippa, daughter of Henry, count of Troyes; he forwarded them to the patriarch of Jerusalem and the bishop of Tyre in 1213, CCXVI, 975.

GAUSFRIDUS, monk and steward of the monastery of St. Peter at Chartres, attests that Girard and Pagan granted certain lands to that monastery in 1077, CLV, 291.

GAUSLINUS, bishop of Bourges, illegitimate son of Hugh Capet, king of the Franks, made great progress under Abbo, abbot of Fleury, both in letters and in the pursuit of virtues. He became abbot of Fleury and was afterward elected bishop, not without difficulty because he was illegitimate. Two letters and a sermon on St. Martial survive from him. He died in 1029, CLXI, 759.

GAUTERIUS de Clichon and his wife Seria agree that their daughter Roberga be received into the monastery of Fontevraud, and give to Lord Robert, the prior, their mill of Ponzay, at the beginning of the twelfth century, CLXII, 1106.

GAUTERIUS de Montsoreau granted to Lord Robert of Arbrissel and the monastery of Fontevraud his *vigeria* [jurisdiction or office of a *vigerius*] and the customary dues of all the land possessed by the nuns, at the beginning of the twelfth century. By another charter he gave them fishing rights, CLXII, 1109.

GAUTHERIUS, lord of Sobernon, and his brother Garnerius confirm a gift made by Haimo, son of Humbert de Moelen, to the monks of Bussière, in 1188. Gauthier himself added other gifts to this donation, CLXXXV, 1421, 1422.

GAUTHERIUS, bishop of Autun, makes known that Oliverius de Grignon approved and confirmed to the brothers of the church of Fontenay all the gifts his father had formerly granted them, and moreover added the land called Montarlant, in 1191, CLXXXV, 1472.

GEBHARDUS, archbishop of Salzburg, flourished in the eleventh century. Once made bishop, he devoted himself wholly to defending the cause of the Holy See and refuting schismatics. Only his letter to Hermann, bishop of Metz, survives. The date of his death is uncertain, CXLVIII, 847.

GEBUINUS, archbishop of Lyons, son of Hugh III, count of Dijon, formerly archdeacon of Langres. He died in [Col. 0454] 1082. His letter to Rodulfus of Tours survives, CXLVII, 1210.

GELASIUS I (St.), pope. An African by birth, son of Valerius, he succeeded Felix II in 492. Under his pontificate followers of Mani first appeared at Rome; he promptly ordered them deported and their books burned before the doors of the basilica of St. Mary. Letters and decrees survive from this pope. He died in 495, LIX, 9.

GELASIUS II, pope, formerly called John. A Campanian, of noble birth, he was educated in good letters and morals in the monastery of Monte Cassino under Abbot Oderisius. Paschal II made him cardinal-deacon of the title of St. Mary. Driven from Rome by the emperor Henry, he withdrew into Gaul and died in 1119 in the monastery of Cluny. His letters and privileges survive, CXLIII, 474.

GEMMULUS, deacon of the Apostolic See under Pope Zachary, wrote to St. Boniface, bishop of Mainz, explaining all that he had done on Boniface’s behalf and how the impious Aldbert had been condemned, LXXXIX, 753.

GENNADIUS, priest of Marseilles. A Gaul by race, he flourished in 495, as he himself declares at the end of the catalogue which he compiled and sent to Pope Gelasius. Some formerly accused him of Semi-Pelagianism, but more recent writers generally exempt him from that accusation, because no trace of error is found in his writings. He wrote a book on ecclesiastical doctrines and another on ecclesiastical writers, LVIII, 980.

GERALDUS, bishop of Ostia, cardinal and legate of the Holy See. Passing through Gascony on his way to Spain under Pope Alexander II, he visited the monastery of Saint-Mont, founded by Count Bernard and his wife Ermengarde and entrusted to Cluny, where the aforesaid count and his wife had taken the habit in the perfect service of God. In 1073 Gerald, at their request, enriched it with privileges, CLIX, 963.

GERALDUS (St.), abbot of Corbie. Born of honorable parents, he was given over as a boy to the monastery of Corbie for education, and later became abbot of that monastery. In 1080 he founded the abbey of La Sauve-Majeure. Renowned for deeds and miracles, he fell asleep in the Lord in 1095. He wrote the life of St. Adalard, abbot of Corbie, two books on that saint’s miracles, and a charter, CXLVII, 1003.

GERALDUS, bishop of Cahors, flourished at the end of the twelfth century. He wrote to Emperor Frederick, asking him to order his release from harsh imprisonment, CCV, 923.

GERARDUS, dean of St. Medard at Soissons, flourished in the tenth century. Most of what is read about him is uncertain. His prose prologue to the Life of St. Romanus, bishop, survives, CXXXVIII, 171.

GERARDUS I, bishop of Cambrai, son of Arnold or Arnulf, lord of Florennes, born at Liège, flourished in the eleventh century. He studied letters at Rheims under Gerbert and was at last raised to the episcopal mitre in 1013. He wrote the acts of the council of Arras against the Manichaeans and several letters, CXLII, 1267.

GERARDUS II, bishop of Cambrai. Previously a monk and provost at the monastery of St. Vedast under Abbot Adolphus, he then became abbot at St. Liébert. He died in 1092. His charters survive, CL, 1380.

GERARDUS, to whom the Life of St. Ulrich, who lived in the tenth century, is attributed. He is wholly unknown: nowhere do we read either his homeland or his date, CXXXV, 1001.

GERARDUS, or GIRARDUS, priest, a Gaul by birth and canon of the church of Compostela, one of the writers who compiled the history of Compostela, CLXX, 875.

GERARDUS, bishop of Angoulême, native of Blaye, a man famous for his age, whom some pursued with praise and others with criticism. Although of humble birth, through industry, talent, and uprightness of life he was elected bishop in 1117; he attended the Roman council presided over by Paschal II and died in 1136, CLXXII, 1311.

GERARDUS, monk of Clairvaux, wrote with Gaufridus and other brothers of the same order, contemporaries of St. Bernard, concerning Bernard’s miracles, as an eyewitness, CLXXXV, 385.

GERARDUS Itherii, seventh prior of Grandmont. He died in 1198. He is the author of the Life of St. Stephen of Muret, CCIV, 1177.

GERBERTUS, advocate of the monastery of St. Emmeram. By order of Bishop Aspert, he gives the girl Otnia in exchange for a small wood situated at Reinna, which that Otnia gave to the monastery of St. Emmeram, ninth century, CXXIX, 958.

GERBERTUS. See Pope SYLVESTER II.

GERFRIDUS, bishop, and a certain Frithuard arrange an exchange between themselves in 835, under Emperor Louis the Pious, XCIX, 807.

[Col. 0455] GEROHUS (Venerable), provost of Reichersberg, of the order of regular canons of St. Augustine, formerly master of the schools at Augsburg; he flourished in the time of Conrad, bishop of Salzburg, and died in 1169. He wrote *On the Glory and Honor of the Son of Man*, a book of letters to Innocent II, treatises against simoniacs, an exposition of the Book of Psalms, etc., CXCIII, 480.

GERMANUS and JOHN, bishops; BLANDUS, priest; FELIX and DIOSCORUS, deacons: Pope Hormisdas sent them as legates to the East because of disturbances stirred up by schismatics and Eutychians. In a letter they reported what they had done: the names of the impious Acacius, Anastasius, and Zeno had been erased from the diptychs and were no longer recited in the sacred rites; many bishops were also returning to the orthodox faith, etc., in 519, LXIII, 445 and elsewhere.

GERMANUS (St.), bishop of Paris, was born at Autun to distinguished parents. St. Agrippinus made him deacon and priest. He shone so brightly in holiness of life and power of miracles that, upon the death of Eusebius, he was chosen by unanimous vote as successor in the episcopal see of Paris. He died in 576. His letter to Queen Brunhild, a privilege, and a brief exposition of the ancient Gallican Church survive, LXXII, 54.

GERMINIUS was elected bishop of Sirmium in place of Photinus, who had been condemned for heresy and later deposed at the council of Milan, 347–349. He, however, inclined toward the Arians with Valens and Ursacius, from whom he appears to have withdrawn only in appearance, as is evident from the letters in which he makes a profession of faith about 365, X, 717, 719; XIII, 575.

GERSONIUS (John), distinguished doctor of the Faculty of Theology and chancellor of the University of Paris, attended the Council of Pisa and afterward that of Constance in 1409, where he defended the supreme authority of general councils. He died in 1429, CLXXXV, 634.

GERTRUDIS, formerly wife of Hilduin, gave to the monastery of St. Peter at Gésy the cell which she possessed at the court of Aiga in the territory of Chartres, in 1062, CLV, 317.

GERTRUDIS (St.), abbess of the monastery of Helfta in the county of Mansfeld, died in 1333. Her book of revelations survives, in which she gives remarkable testimony concerning St. Bernard, CLXXXV, 638.

GERVASIUS, archdeacon of Rheims, son of Count Hugh and Melesinda. When he attempted to seize the see of Rheims, Pope Paschal II struck him with excommunication. His letter to Pope Paschal survives. Do not confuse him with the following Gervasius, who flourished in 1067, CLXIII, 461.

GERVASIUS, archbishop of Rheims, was born near the castle of Ledi to Hamelin and Hildirade de Bellême, sister of Avesgaud, bishop of Le Mans, whom he first succeeded in 1036. He was elevated to the see of Rheims in 1055 and died in 1067. His charters and letters survive, CXLIII, 1403.

GERWINUS, bishop of Amiens, having procured a golden shrine for enclosing the relics of St. Fuscian the martyr, invited Lambert, bishop of Arras, by letter to the ceremony about 1118, CLXII, 647.

GEZO, abbot of Tortona, who flourished in the tenth century, attended the Council of Augsburg in 950. He founded at Tortona a notable monastery under the title of St. Martian the martyr. He wrote a book on the Body and Blood of Christ, CXXXVIII, 371.

GILBERTUS, monk of Elnone, flourished late in the eleventh century. He became dean of the church of St. Andrew, one of the three churches comprising the monastery of Elnone, or St. Amand. A man of exceptional learning, he has left only a history of the miracles of St. Amand, CL, 1436.

GILBERTUS, master of the Hospitaller congregation at Jerusalem, wrote to Louis the Younger, king of the Franks, requesting leave to punish certain wrongdoers who had burned down the house of a worthy man. The year is not stated (twelfth century), CLV, 1264, 1270.

GILBERTUS, bishop of Limerick in Ireland, where he held a synod in 1110 to define the boundaries of bishoprics. He was made the first legate of all Ireland; worn out by illness, he died in 1139. His booklet on the condition of the Church in Ireland and two letters survive: one addressed to the bishops and priests of Ireland, the other to St. Anselm of Canterbury, CLIX, 995.

GILBERT FOLIOT, bishop of London. This distinguished man was first made abbot of the monastery of Gloucester; from there he was elected bishop of Hereford and finally promoted to the see of London. He left numerous letters. He is charged with having abandoned the cause of St. Thomas of Canterbury. He died in 1168, CXC, 740.

GILDAS, called the Wise, a Briton by race, had Hildulf as his teacher. Having received orders, he entered the monastery of Bangor. He wrote the book entitled [Col. 0456] *The Complaint*, in which he unfolds the causes of Britain’s ruin and especially rebukes the clergy. He died about 570, CLXIX, 328.

GILDUINUS, viscount of Chartres, and his wife Emmelina grant to the monastery of St. Peter at Chartres certain customary dues, a kind of tax, in 1046, CIV, 301.

GILDUINUS, abbot of St. Victor at Paris, joined himself as companion to William of Champeaux, whom he afterward succeeded; he was called the first abbot. We possess two of his letters. He died in 1155, CXCVI, 1366.

GILDUINUS, abbot of the monastery of Anchin. Having voluntarily resigned that office, he sought quiet in solitude; when the monks and Bishop Lambert himself again asked for him, he wrote that they should excuse him because of his various bodily infirmities, at the beginning of the twelfth century, CLXII, 688.

GILLAS, widow of Hervé, lord of Saffres, reports that her husband died as he was returning from overseas; she therefore assigns her son Guy to the count of Champagne, in order that he may render him the homage once owed by her husband, in 1249, CLXXXV, 1433.

GILLEBERTUS of Hoiland, abbot of the Cistercian Order. English by origin, he so excelled in learning and piety that he was surnamed “the Great” and “the Theologian.” He died at Cîteaux in 1168. He left various theological and moral writings, CLXXXIV, 11.

GILO of Paris. Nothing certain is known of him except that he flourished in the time of the First Crusade, whose history he wrote in verse, CLV, 941.

GILO, monk of Cluny, added certain things to the Life of St. Hugh the abbot, whose author was Ezelo. He flourished in the twelfth century, shortly after St. Hugh, CLIX, 909.

GILO, cardinal, formerly a monk of the Benedictine Order. He was born near Auxerre; having completed his course of studies, he consecrated himself to God in the monastery of Cluny, from which Pope Calixtus II raised him to the bishopric of Tusculum. He died in 1142. He wrote the Life of St. Hugh of Cluny and a poem on the road to Jerusalem, CLXXIII, 1385.

GILO, son of Rainald de Ville, gave to Clairvaux a meadow called Coiprat beside the river Aube, and confirmed whatever his father had given that abbey in the territory of Gundrée in Spain, in 1147, CLXXXV, 992.

GIRALDUS of Compostela, a close associate of Diego II, bishop of the see of Compostela, compiled a history of his own time, of which a fragment survives. He flourished under King Alfonso VI, in the eleventh century, CLI, 267.

GIRALDUS de Terrazo, abbot of St. Peter of Solignac, wrote to Wibald, abbot of Corvey, exhorting him to give thanks to St. Remaclus for the people of Solignac, because he had delivered them from tribulations, in 1149, CLXXXIX, 1267.

GIRARDUS PUCELLE, master, at the Council of Tours held in 1163 under Alexander III, abjured the heresy and schism of Octavian and Guy of Cremona and promised fidelity to the pope, CXC, 391.

GIRARDUS de Péronne and GAUCHERIUS, or Calcherius, cellarer, monks of Clairvaux, wrote to Abbot Nicholas, consulting him concerning a vow, twelfth century, CXCVI, 1648; CCI, 474.

GIRARDUS de Châtillon, lord of Échallot, and his son Milo gave the brothers of St. Mary of Fontenay everything they possessed within the bounds of Puteaux-Francs, in accordance with the grant of Theobald de Saliva (without a stated year), twelfth century, CLXXXV, 1465.

GIRARDUS de Puy-Brunel and his wife Aldeardis granted Lord Robert of Arbrissel and the nuns of Fontevraud the meadow called Long Meadow and the land beside that meadow. Another grant of the mill of Mortonne also survives, CLXII, 1110, 1111.

GIRBERTUS de Montbard and his son Tecelin gave to the church of St. Mary of Fontenay the meadow called God-given Meadow (without a stated year), twelfth century, CLXXXV, 1462.

GISLEBERTUS PORRETANUS, bishop of Poitiers, born in the eleventh century, a Gaul by race, devoted himself to philosophical study from youth. He was first made canon of St. Hilary the Great; in 1142 he was raised to the episcopate. He taught many things which very many judged ought to be refuted, CLXXXVIII, 1247.

GISLEBERTUS CRISPINUS, abbot of Westminster, appears to have been Norman by birth. He lived with St. Anselm in the monastery of Bec and heard his lectures; thereafter he went to Rome and composed a book on a disputation with a Jew. He died in 1117, CLIX, 1006.

GISLEBERTUS, monk of the Order of Hermits, flourished in the twelfth century; he wrote to Peter, monk of St. John of Poitiers, of the same order, CLXXXIX, 362.

[Col. 0457] A certain GISLUINUS gave a portion of his inheritance to the church of St. Saviour built in the district of the Riparii; this gift was received in the monastery of Werth, without a stated year, ninth century, XCIX, 816.

GISULFUS II, duke of the Lombards, son of Grimoald II, gained possession of the duchy of which his uncle had deprived him in 742, and made many gifts to the monastery of Monte Cassino in 768, LXXXVII, 1392.

GLABER RODULFUS. See RODULFUS.

GLIRIGEOTI, duchess, when Guy de Bonnaval wished to convict one of her men, John de Alluyes, of homicide, fled to Theobald, count of Blois, and his brother, asking him to intervene, in 1200, CCVII, 476.

GLYCERIUS, Roman emperor, was invested with the purple by Gundobad, king of the Burgundians. But Leo, emperor of the East, captured him and banished him to Salona, where he died in 480. His edict against simoniacal ordinations survives, LXXII, 111.

GODEFRIDUS, monk of Stavelot of the Benedictine Order, a man learned in the sacred Scriptures, wrote the triumph of St. Remaclus of the monastery of Malmedy as an eyewitness, about 1080, CXLIX, 287.

GODEFRIDUS, son of Drogo and duke of Burgundy, granted to the church of St. Arnulf at Metz everything he possessed in the village of Flavigny in 691. This charter is regarded as spurious, LXXXVIII, 1222.

GODEFRIDUS, duke of Alemannia, subscribed a donation in 708 for the benefit of Magulf, priest and monk of St. Gall. The act was done at Cannstatt on the Neckar, in the city of Württemberg, LXXXVIII, 1253.

GODEFRIDUS (St.), bishop of Amiens, formerly abbot of Nogent in the district of Laon. After his election he was consecrated at Rheims by Manasses, the metropolitan; he then returned to Amiens barefoot and thus entered the church of St. Firmin. He died in 1115. He left letters and charters, CLXII, 735.

GODEFRIDUS of Bouillon, first king of Jerusalem, born of Eustace, count of Lorraine, and holy Ida, was among the first to take the cross. He assembled a great army and set out for Palestine with his brothers; he performed many illustrious deeds and, after the capture of Jerusalem, was elected king by the other leaders of the crusaders. He died in 1100. He compiled a code of the usages and customs by which that new kingdom was to be governed, and wrote various letters and charters, CLV, 309.

GODEFRIDUS, bishop of Langres, confirmed in 1158 the gift of Warnerius de Sobernon to the monastery of Clairvaux. Other charters and gifts concerning him also survive, CLXXXV, 1409, 1418, 1466, 1476.

GODEFRIDUS, founder of Lucca. See AURINANDUS.

GODEFRIDUS, abbot of St. Victor at Paris. A Gaul by birth, he was first master of sacred letters in the Parisian academy under Abbot Ervisius; he chose a holier life among the canons of St. Victor. He died in 1194. Nineteen sermons and several poems survive from him, CXCVI, 1418.

GODEFRIDUS de Saigny gave to St. Mary of Fontenay all the lands he possessed within the bounds of Aringy, without a stated year, twelfth century, CLXXXV, 1462, 1463.

GODEFRIDUS de Châtillon, his wife Gertrude, and their sons Hugh and Nivard gave all their wealth in lands and woods to the monastery of Fontenay, with St. Bernard of Clairvaux as witness, twelfth century, CLXXXV, 1465.

GODEFRIDUS, bishop of Utrecht, flourished late in the eleventh century. He writes to Blessed Hildegard and expresses his affection for her, CXCVII, 176.

GODEFRIDUS, surnamed Viterbiensis from his birthplace, was chaplain and secretary to the emperors Conrad III, Frederick I, and Henry IV. He wrote a universal chronicle from Adam to 1186, a work divided into twenty books and dedicated to Urban III, and another little work entitled *Mirror of Kings*, CXCVIII, 871.

GODEFRIDUS, monk and biographer of St. Hildegard, wrote only the first book of her life, in 1200, CXCVII, 91.

GODEFRIDUS, abbot of the monastery of St. Eucharius in the suburbs of Trier, which he governed from 1181 to 1210. He wrote to Guibert of Gembloux, promising him his prayers and support, CCXI, 1305.

GODEFRIDUS, monk of Clairvaux, about 1256. His abbot Stephen sent him to Italy to visit monasteries and record what he saw; this report survives, CLXXXV, 1769.

GODEHARDUS (St.), bishop of Hildesheim, was born to Christian parents in the village of Bittenbach in the diocese of Passau. In his thirtieth year he became a monk and thereafter was elected bishop. He died in 1038. He wrote [Col. 0458] letters and a Chronicle of Hildesheim, CXLI, 1159.

GODESCALKUS, concerning whose life and origin historians are wholly silent, flourished in the eleventh century. He wrote various sequences, CXLI, 1324.

GODESCHALKUS, author of a chronicle both of the bishops and of the abbots of Liège. He seems to have been a monk of Gembloux, like Anselm and Sigebert himself, and to have flourished at the beginning of the thirteenth century, CLX, 627.

GOFFRIDUS MARTELLUS, count of Anjou, founded and kept under his protection the monastery of Holy Trinity at Vendôme in 1150, CLVII, 35.

GOFFRIDUS, abbot of Vendôme and cardinal of St. Prisca. An Angevin by birth and of noble family, he was educated from childhood in the monastery of Vendôme. Still a novice and scarcely a deacon, he was elected abbot of that monastery. A vigorous defender of the Roman Church, he went to Rome three times, but at last, detained by the pope’s adversaries, died in 1132. He left letters, various shorter works, and many sermons, CLVII, 9.

GONDEMARUS, king of the Goths, ascended the throne in 610 and died at Toledo in 612. His decree concerning the Church of Toledo survives, LXXX, 180.

GONTHERUS, bishop of Speyer, flourished in the twelfth century. He wrote to St. Hildegard, abbess of St. Robert’s Mount at Bingen, commending himself to her prayers, CXCVII, 171.

GORGA (Peter) made many gifts to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, twelfth century, CLXVI, 1574.

GOSBERTUS of Curamonte and his son Gunbert gave to the monastery of Saint-Bertin everything they possessed in the district of Boulogne along the river Edivinia, in 831. By another charter they had already given the basilica of St. Saviour in 828, CXXXVI, 1270, 1272.

GOSBERTUS, concerning whom nothing certain is known. His acrostic poem to William, count of Blois, survives, CXXIX, 1147.

GOSCELINUS, or GOTSELINUS, monk of Canterbury, a native of the Morini. He was first a monk of St. Bertin and afterward, because of his outstanding gifts of mind, became abbot. He wrote several lives of English saints. He died in 1100, CLV, 9 ff.

GOSCELINUS, dean of Beauvais, flourished in the twelfth century; he wrote to Radulf, archbishop of Rheims, concerning the prohibition against secular persons possessing the houses of canons, CLXIII, 1421.

GOSLENUS, bishop of Chartres, flourished in the time of Suger, abbot of St. Denis. He excuses himself to Suger for being unable to attend, although invited, the feast of the saintly patron, because of the unexpected arrival of the lord bishop of Auxerre, in 1145, CLXXXVI, 1399.

GOSLENUS of Soissons. See JOSLINUS.

GOTHERUS, dean of the chapter of Tournai, writes to Lambert, bishop of Arras, that the dispute of his chapter with the monks of St. Martin should be settled in writing, twelfth century, CLXII, 697.

GOTHMANNUS, resident and landholder in Syria, sells certain lands to the canons of the Holy Sepulchre in 1161, CLV, 1200.

GOTTESCHALCUS, monk of Orbais of the Benedictine Order in the diocese of Soissons, professed certain errors concerning predestination and stirred up disturbances in Gaul. Summoned before many councils, condemned, excommunicated, and thrown into prison, he finally declared for the orthodox profession in 860, CXXI, 346.

GOYLA, or GOYLANA, wife of a certain Bonuasius, made many gifts to the church of St. Benignus at Dijon, to be possessed after her and her husband’s death, in 734 under King Theuderic, LXXXVIII, 1287.

GOZECHINUS, a schoolmaster and German by birth, taught letters for some time at Liège, where among his pupils he had a certain Walcher, very dear to him, to whom he wrote a long letter in 1059, CXLIII, 907.

GOZPERTUS, abbot of Tegernsee, flourished at the beginning of the eleventh century. He left several letters full of piety, CXXXIX, 350.

GRADONICUS (Augustine), patriarch of Aquileia. His charter granting the pastoral staff to the chapter of Udine survives, in 1629, XCIX, 682.

GRATIANUS (Flavius), emperor of the West. Born at Sirmium in Pannonia, he was made Caesar in 367 and succeeded his father Valentinian in 378. He was killed in 383. Certain decrees and letters of his survive, XI, 1181; XIII, 583; XVI, 875.

GRATIANUS of Chiusi, monk of St. Felix at Bologna, of the Benedictine Order. A man outstanding in learning, he produced the very famous work entitled *Decretum*, or *Concordance of Discordant Canons*, on which he labored for twenty-four years. He died in 1152, CLXXXVII, 9.

GRATIANUS, Roman subdeacon and notary of Pope [Col. 0459] Alexander III, flourished in the twelfth century. Two letters of his concerning the death of Blessed Thomas of Canterbury survive, CXC, 985.

GRATUS, bishop of Carthage, restrained the spirit of the schismatics and induced very many to obey the authority of the Church, relying on Constantine’s laws. In 349 he presided over the Council of Carthage and issued canons against the Donatists, VIII, 774.

GREGORIUS (St.), bishop of Tours. Born of illustrious parents in Auvergne, in the Celtic region of Gaul, he was educated by St. Gallus, bishop of Clermont and his paternal uncle; thereafter he came into the care of the most pious Avitus. The fame of his learning and holiness grew so greatly that he was elevated to the see of Tours. He composed an ecclesiastical history of the Franks and lives of the early apostles of Gaul. He died in 595, LXXI, 9.

GREGORIUS I (St.), pope, deservedly called the Great, Doctor of the Church. Roman by birth, son of Gordianus and Silvia, of an eminent senatorial family, he first became a monk and was finally made pope in 590. He brought the Britons to the faith and recalled the Goths from Arianism. From him we have the *Morals on Job*, the *Pastoral Rule*, and countless letters, which seem like so many different treatises. He died in 604, LXXV–LXXIX.

GREGORIUS II (St.), pope. Roman by birth, he was first elected as a monk of the Benedictine Order in 715 and died in 731. His letters and decrees survive, LXXXIX, 454.

GREGORIUS III (St.), pope. Syrian by birth, formerly a cardinal-priest, he became pope under Emperor Leo III in 731 and died in 741. His letters and extracts concerning various crimes and the remedies to be applied survive, LXXXIX, 538.

GREGORIUS IV, pope. Roman by birth, he reigned from 828 to 844, succeeding Valentine. His letters are found at CVI, 842.

GREGORIUS V, pope. Born in Alemannia and formerly called Bruno, he professed the monastic life in the Benedictine Order and was made pope by the Roman people and clergy in 996, on account of the abundant alms he bestowed. He was called Gregory the Younger, to distinguish him from Gregory the Great. He died in 999. His letters and privileges survive, CXXXVII, 899.

GREGORIUS VI, pope. A Roman by race, formerly called John Gratian, a Benedictine monk and man distinguished for holiness, he was substituted for Benedict in 1045. But in the following year, accused of simony by certain factions, he voluntarily resigned his office. His letters and privileges survive, CXLII, 569.

GREGORIUS VII (St.), pope. First a monk of Cluny under the name Hildebrand, a Tuscan by birth and son of an ironworker, he had been taken into Gregory VI’s household. He was made pope in 1073. He restored firm discipline to the Church and endured many tribulations throughout his pontificate. He died in 1085. He wrote innumerable letters and privileges, CXLVIII, 9.

GREGORIUS, Roman priest and cardinal. He flourished under the pontificate of Gregory VII and died under Pope Urban II, in 1119. His collection of canons survives, CLXIII, 731.

GREGORIUS, legate of the Roman Church, flourished in the twelfth century. He wrote several letters to the abbot of Anchin and to Angelramnus, bishop of Amiens, CLXVI, 851.

GREGORIUS, uncle of Peter, deacon of Monte Cassino, on hearing that his nephew had been expelled from the monastery by envious monks, and also that the nephew and his father were living in poverty, wrote to them asking them to come to him and not hesitate to sit at his table, in 1128, CLXXIII, 465.

GREGORIUS VIII, pope, succeeded Urban III in 1187. Formerly named Albert, born at Benevento, he was chancellor of the Roman Church, a man as learned as he was devout. He died in 1187. Three letters of his survive, CCII, 1535.

GREGORIUS de Montelongo, patriarch of Aquileia. Before the notables of his province, he established provisions concerning the power and right of the archdeaconry of Aquileia, and made certain determinations concerning the church of St. Vorlicus at Udine, in 1263, XCIX, 647.

GREGORIUS, called Sabinensis from his native place, monk of Farfa. He flourished in an uncertain year. He added prefaces to the cartulary of that monastery, CL, 1299.

GREGORIUS IX, pope (Hugolinus), succeeded Honorius III in 1227. He had many difficult disputes with Emperor Frederick and issued the five books of decretals; but in the *Patrologia* only his letter concerning the canonization of St. Bruno, bishop of Würzburg, has thus far appeared, CXLII, 34.

GRIM (Edward), monk of Canterbury. He was the first to meet Thomas as he returned from exile, and was his faithful companion even while Thomas spoke with the criminals who were about to kill him. He wrote the Life of St. Thomas, in 1175, CXC, 1.

GRIMALDUS, abbot of St. Gall. Historians report little concerning him. He lived in the ninth century, wrote a book of sacraments, and a letter to Regimbert, master of the school in the monastery of St. Gall, CXXI, 796.

GRIMAUDUS de Montibus and his brothers Pippinus, Rainaldus, Berengarius, and Goffridus possessed a lock situated at Gaine. Since Hersendis, abbess of Fontevraud, objected, having granted it to her house at the request of Peter of Poitiers, they renounced this land for the benefit of that monastery, during the reign of Louis VI over the Franks, CLXII, 1103.

GRIMLAICUS, a priest and, apparently, a monk of the ninth century. He established a Rule for recluses—that is, for holy men who, out of love for a more perfect life, freely shut themselves within an underground cell walled on every side. CIII, 573.

GRIMOALD, son and successor of the elder Pippin in the office of mayor of the palace under Sigebert II. Upon the latter’s death, he attempted to establish his son Childebert in the kingship, but was compelled to yield to Clovis II. He died in 656. There survives a charter concerning him by which, in 650, he gave the estate of Germiniacum to the monasteries of Stavelot and Malmedy. LXXXVII, 325.

GUAIFERIUS, monk of Monte Cassino. A native of Salerno, he published many poems; in prose he wrote the Life of Saint Secundinus, bishop of Troia, as well as the Life of Saint Lucius, pope and martyr, in 1084. CXLVII, 1282.

GUALFREDUS, son of a citizen of Pisa named Ratehaus, founded, in a place called Palatiolum in the territory of Lucca, a monastery under the invocation of Saint Peter in 754, under King Aistulf. LXXXVII, 1384.

GUALTERUS, bishop of Chalon. He flourished in 1118. He wrote to Pope Paschal II concerning the departure of the monks of Molesme. CCXIII, 448.

GUALTERUS, regular canon and archdeacon of Thérouanne. He flourished about 1120 and must not be confused with another chancellor of the same name. He wrote the Life of Saint Charles the Good, count of Flanders. CLXVI, 875.

GUALTERUS, archbishop of Ravenna. In 1130 he received a letter from Norbert, archbishop of Magdeburg, seeking certain information concerning the election of the new pope appointed in place of Honorius II. Walter informed him that Innocent II was the true successor of Saint Peter, whereas Peter Leonis had attempted to seize the Holy See under the name Anacletus. CCXXIX, 38.

GUALTERUS, prince of all Galilee, confirmed in 1165 the gifts of his predecessor William of Bures to the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. CLV, 1217.

GUALTERUS, monk of Cluny. The biographers are silent concerning him; and GUALTERUS, abbot of the abbey of Saint Martin, or the Greater Monastery, a native of Compiègne, at the end of the eleventh century. The latter rather than the former was the author of the little book on the miracles of Blessed Mary. CLXXIII, 1379.

GUALTERUS, prior of Saint Victor at Paris. He was the author of the book concerning the four Labyrinths, who, according to Mabillon, were Abelard, Peter Lombard, Peter of Poitiers, and Gilbert of Poitiers, 1180. CXIX, 1127.

GUALTERUS of Châtillon, called Master, native of Lille and provost of the canons of Tournai. He flourished at the end of the twelfth century. He was the author of the epic poem *Alexandreis*, in ten books, and of the treatise or *Dialogue of Master Walter of Tournai and Baldwin of Valenciennes against the Jews*. CCIX, 419.
