GUARINUS of the castle of Dorcas, son of Aldric and a knight, gave to the monastery of Saint Peter at Chartres, ruled by Abbot Arnulf, the estate called Pinus in 1034. CLV, 271.

GUARINUS, count of the territory of Rosnay, became a monk and gave the church of Saint Margaret at Cluny; he also bestowed certain other gifts upon the brothers of the monastery of Dervent, to which he himself had withdrawn, in 1082. CLIX, 970.

GUARINUS, bishop of Amiens, makes known that Bernard de Balliol, a valiant knight, having realized that he was unjustly withholding certain altars, restored them, with his wife’s consent, to the monastery of Cluny in 1138. CLXXXIX, 1065.

GUARINUS, abbot of the monastery of Mount Tabor, with the consent of Letard, bishop of Nazareth, and of Lancelin the prior, renounced possession of certain *casalia* because of their excessive distance; and in 1175 he granted these to Peter, prior of the Holy Sepulchre. CLV, 1230.

GUARINUS, abbot of Saint Victor. Following the resignation of Ervisius, and in the presence of Prior Richard, he was consecrated abbot by Maurice, bishop of Paris. He flourished in the twelfth century and devoted great care to repairing losses. He died in 1192. CXCVI, 1175.

GUDELINA, queen and wife of Theodatus after the death of Amalasuntha. About 536 she wrote several letters in pursuit of peace, both to the Empress Theodora and to Justinian. LXIX, 812 and following.

GUDINUS, apparently a monk of Luxeuil, concerning whose life and date nothing is known. He was the author of a poem entitled [Col. 0461] *Gudinus’s Lament over the Death of Constantius the Monk*. CLI, 636.

GUENILO, bishop of Sens. Nothing has been transmitted to us concerning him except that he wrote two letters: one to the faithful of his diocese, commending to them a certain pilgrim; the other to Pope Nicholas, in 860. CXIX, 581, 608.

GUENRICUS, scholastic of Trier, who flourished in the eleventh century. Under the name of Saint Ulrich, he wrote to Pope Nicholas II concerning priests’ marriages. CXLIII, 1361.

GUERRICUS, Blessed, abbot of Igny. First a canon of Tournai and master of its school, then a Cistercian monk and disciple of Saint Bernard, he was finally made abbot of Igny in the diocese of Reims. He left many sermons and some spiritual letters. He died in 1157. CLXXXVIII, 983.

GUIARDUS of Juvencourt and his brothers Philip and Arlebald gave the monastery of Clairvaux part of the allod which they possessed in 1147. CLXXXV, 987.

GUIBERT, abbot of Saint Mary of Nogent. A Frenchman by birth and native of the district of Beauvais, he set aside the distinction of his lineage and became a monk at Fleury, or Saint-Germain monastery; afterward, the monks of Saint Mary of Nogent, in the territory of Laon, elected him abbot. He died in 1124. He left both moral and dogmatic writings. CLVI, 9.

GUIBERT of Gembloux, later abbot of Florennes, surnamed Martin. About 1194 he was made abbot of Gembloux, whence he moved to the monastery of Villers; later he went to Tours, and eventually returned as prior to Gembloux, where he died in old age in 1208. Several letters of his survive. CCXI, 1280.

GUICHARD, archbishop of Lyons, also called Wicardus and Vicardus. First a monk of the Cistercian Order, then abbot of Pontigny, he was elected bishop in 1164 against Drogo, as appears from the letter of Drogo and the canons of Lyons. He wrote ancient records of the Church of Lyons. CXCIX, 1086.

GUIDO, bishop of Le Puy, son of Fulk the Good, count of Anjou, and formerly abbot of the monastery of Cormery. He died in 996. His statutes and three charters survive. CXXXVII, 855.

GUIDO of Arezzo, monk and later abbot of Holy Cross of Avellana, of the Order of Saint Benedict, was summoned to Rome by Pope Benedict VIII because of his remarkable study of chant. He died in 1034. His musical works survive. CXLI, 375.

GUIDO of Châtillon, archbishop of Reims, was elected in 1033; he died and was buried at Saint-Remi in 1053. Some of his diplomas survive. CXLII, 1400.

GUIDO of Amiens attended the anointing of Philip, king of the Franks, in 1059. He cultivated learning under Enguerrand in the abbey of Saint-Riquier. He died in 1074. His brief chronicle of the monastery of Saint-Riquier survives. CXVI, 1503.

GUIDO of La Roche and his brother Richard remitted, in 1080, the toll which they levied upon ships passing to and returning from Rouen by the Seine. CLV, 316.

GUIDO, abbot of Farfa, was elected at Saint Benedict’s in the duchy of Spoleto in 1039. He wrote a book on the customs and regulations established in his monastery. He died in 1098. CL, 1191.

GUIDO, archbishop of Vienne in Germany. He convened a council and excommunicated Emperor Henry V because he had usurped investitures; in a letter of 1112, he informed Pope Paschal II of this. CLXIII, 465.

GUIDO, abbot of Molesme, of the Order of Saint Benedict. With the consent of the entire convent, he granted to the monks of Clairvaux everything he possessed in the place called Hais, for an annual rent of twelve denarii, in 1131. CLXXXV, 979.

GUIDO, supreme chancellor of the Holy See and cardinal. The monks of Stavelot wrote to him concerning the election of their abbot Wibald to the abbey of Corbie. He himself wrote to Wibald and issued confirmation of his election in 1147. Another letter from him to the same person survives. CLXXXIX, 1147, 1162.

GUIDO, count of Sombernon, his wife Ermengard, and his nephew Odo of Mirabeau ceded certain lands to the monastery of nuns of Saint Mary in 1149. CLXXXV, 1419.

GUIDO, abbot of Châtillon. Almost nothing certain is known of him; he flourished in the twelfth century. He was abbot of the Benedictine—not Cistercian—abbey of Châtillon in Burgundy, situated on the Seine. Guido, to whom Saint Bernard wrote two letters, was the author of a treatise on correcting the chant of the Cistercian Order, which some have attributed to Bernard himself. CLXXXI, 1720.

GUIDO, abbot of Pontigny, flourished in the twelfth century. In letters he commends to Suger the cause of the treasurer of Auxerre. CLXXXVI, 1413.

GUIDO, archbishop of Sens. He writes to Pope Gregory VII that the bishop of Laon may be cleared of the crimes alleged against him, in 1080. CCII, 1565.

[Col. 0462] GUIDO of Sauz and his wife Elizabeth founded the collegiate church of Sauz in 1197. CLXXXV, 1437, 1438.

GUIDO, count of Auvergne, interceded with Innocent III for his brother, who, although bishop of Clermont, had joined the bands of Coterelli and Bascoli, with whom he carried out burnings and devastations everywhere, including in his brother’s lands, in 1198. CCXIV, 460.

GUIDO, count of Ponthieu, hoping to see at Abbeville Prince Louis, the king’s son, urgently asks Lambert, bishop of Arras, to come with him and not refuse him leave. He lived in the twelfth century. CLXII, 664.

GUIDO, abbot of Clairvaux, afterward bishop of Palestrina and cardinal, and finally made archbishop of Reims. He flourished from 1190 to 1210. Several charters concerning him survive. CLXXXV, 1415; CLXXXIX, 1447.

GUIDO, bishop of Chalon, attests that Lady Beatrice, wife of Lord William of Sauz, acknowledged before him that she had received and held from Duke Hugh of Burgundy, for twenty Viennese pounds, everything she possessed at Andenay, in 1265. CLXXXV, 1454.

GUIDO of Dampierre, count of Flanders. He came into conflict with King Philip the Fair, against whom he made an alliance with the king of England; but he was captured and confined in the castle of Compiègne, where he died in 1305. Letters of his to the king of England and to Robert, that king’s son, survive. CLXXXV, 1853, 1861.

GUIGO I, prior of the Carthusians, surnamed of Château. A Frenchman by nation and a native of Dauphiné, born in the territory of Valence, he was the fifth prior of the Grande Chartreuse after Saint Bruno and very dear to Saint Bernard. He wrote several works worthy of immortality: letters, meditations, customs, and especially the Life of Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble. He died in 1137. CLIII, 591.

GUIGO II, prior general of the Grande Chartreuse. Nothing has been transmitted concerning his native country. He resigned his office in 1176 and died in 1188. Various treatises of his survive: *The Ladder of Paradise*, the book *On the Fourfold Exercise of the Cell*. CLIII, 785.

GUILENCUS, or WILENCUS, was made bishop of Langres in 1125 and successor of Joseran. He recounts how the abbey of Morimond was founded in 1114 by Lord Odalric of Acrimont, then lists the abbeys built thereafter by monks of Morimond down to 1126. CLXXXV, 1441.

GUILLELMUS, monk of Chalon. Nothing is known of him except that he left an account of the church of his monastery struck by lightning in 865. CXXXIV, 1017.

WILLIAM V, duke of Aquitaine, son of William IV, count of Poitiers, excelled in innocence of conduct and in virtues; he founded many monasteries and died in 1030. We possess letters and a charter of his. CXLI, 823.

WILLIAM, Saint, abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. Noble by birth, but nobler in holiness: first a monk of Luciacum in Italy and of Cluny in Gaul, then prior of Saint-Saturnin-des-Portes on the Rhône, in the diocese of Uzès—commonly called Le Pont-Saint-Esprit—afterward abbot of Saint-Bénigne at Dijon, and finally, by order of King Robert, abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés at Paris. A letter or charter of his to the brothers of Saint-Germain-des-Prés survives. CXLI, 834.

WILLIAM of Apulia. Nothing is reported concerning his profession. He is considered the author of a poem praising the deeds of the Normans in Sicily, Apulia, and Calabria. CXLIX, 1019.

WILLIAM, abbot of Saint-Arnulf at Metz, was a confidant of Pope Gregory VII, Hildebrand, who wished to raise him to the much more distinguished abbey of Saint-Remi; but the man, plainly modest, declined. In 1090. Letters of his survive, as well as an oration to be delivered on the feast of Saint Augustine. CL, 871.

WILLIAM, archbishop of Rouen. He lived at the beginning of the twelfth century, in the time of Lambert, bishop of Arras, to whom he wrote two letters commending certain persons to him. CLXII, 650, 683.

WILLIAM, bishop of Périgueux and abbot of the canons of Saint-Front, granted a place to live to Blessed Robert of Arbrissel for the nuns of Fontevraud in 1120. CLXII, 1195; CLXVI, 851.

WILLIAM, archbishop of Besançon, gave the church of Haute-Pierre, formerly deprived of religious life, to Pons, abbot of Cluny, so that he might hand it over to be inhabited by monks, in 1120. CLXVI, 847.

WILLIAM of Champeaux, bishop of Châlons. Born at Champeaux in the diocese of Paris, in Brie, he pursued studies under Anselm, then became archdeacon of Paris and was finally raised to the episcopate of Châlons. He died in 1121. He wrote a charter and several small works. CLXIII, 1037.

WILLIAM of Biront and his wife Alpaidis gave many gifts to Robert of Arbrissel and his monastery of Fontevraud at the beginning of the twelfth century. CLXII, 1110.

[Col. 0463] WILLIAM of Maucé, the king’s seneschal, about to depart for Jerusalem, wrote to Suger, whom he calls his friend, around 1147. CLXXXVI, 1357.

WILLIAM Guarescous of Cowleng gave to the monastery of Clairvaux, without any reservation, everything he possessed in the territory of Petrecini in 1147. CLXXXV, 989.

WILLIAM, abbot of Saint-Thierry near Reims, was made abbot in 1120; but, for the sake of his friend Saint Bernard, he entered the monastery of Igny. He died in 1153. He left many outstanding writings. CLXXX, 185.

See also CLXXXIV, 365; CLXXXV, 221, 225.

WILLIAM, monk of Saint-Denis at Paris. He lived in the time of Suger, his teacher and abbot, whose life he described in three books; he also produced a poem with an encyclical letter on Suger’s death. CLXXXVI, 1193.

WILLIAM DANDINA, monk of Grandmont, flourished after the middle of the twelfth century. He supplied the Life of Blessed Hugh of Lacerta, disciple of Saint Stephen, founder of this order, and left an *Itinerary of the Relics of Saint Ursula*. CCIV, 1181.

WILLIAM, fourth bishop of Troyes, for the sake of William, prior of the canons of the Holy Sepulchre, and of his brother, granted freedom to the church founded at Troyes and belonging to that chapter in 1172. CLVI, 1252.

WILLIAM of Trahinac, sixth prior of Grandmont, was born in the diocese of Limoges. Devoted to fasts, vigils, and prayers, he successfully administered the priorship. He wrote letters. In 1174. CCIV, 1176.

WILLIAM, archbishop of Tyre in Syria. Born of noble stock, he was first archdeacon of the Church of Tyre and afterward raised to the archiepiscopate. In 1183 he wrote the outstanding work entitled *History of Deeds Done Beyond the Sea*. CCI, 201.

WILLIAM II, king of Sicily, called the Good, son and successor of William the Bad, flourished from 1166 to 1189. A letter of his to Henry II, king of England, survives, in which he says that he grieves over the troubles Henry suffered because of the rebellion of his sons. CXC, 1062.

WILLIAM, marquis and son of Marquis Pelavicini, after rebelling against the Roman Church, returned and swore to obey the commands of the Church and pope. This was done at Reggio, under the portico of the church of Saint James “of the Care of God,” in 1205. He made another gift to the bishop of Modena. CCXV, 695, 696.

WILLIAM, abbot of Flavigny, sent the testament of Lady Blanche of Sombernon to Stephen, prior of the Valley of Saint Mary of Talant, and to Simon, Major of the House of Saint Anthony of Cîteaux, in 1271, in the old French language. CLXXXV, 1475.

WILLIAM, lord of Salins and Domicellus, and his wife Margaret gave to the canons of Saint Mary of Salins seven cartloads of salt, payable annually on the feast of All Saints in 1284. This charter was written in the French language of the twelfth century. CLXXXV, 1439.

WILLIAM FLAMMENG, first a canon of Langres, then priest of Montlier, and finally entrant into the Order of Clairvaux. He cultivated poetry and wrote saints’ lives. There survives from him, in the French language, a Life of Saint Bernard and an epitaph for Bernard’s mother. He flourished at the beginning of the sixteenth century. CLXXXV, 1403.

GUILLERMUS of Montaigu, lord of Moalein, and his wife Jacquetta promise to pay annually six sextaries of grain, according to the measure of the district of Sombernon, from their grange of Moalein, in accordance with the intention of Hervé, formerly lord of Sombernon, in 1255. CLXXXV, 1428.

GUILMUNDUS, archbishop of Aversa and cardinal. Formerly a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict in the monastery of Saint Leufroy in Normandy, in 1090. There survive three books, *On the Truth of the Lord’s Body and Blood in the Eucharist*; a *Confession concerning the Most Holy Trinity and the Humanity of Christ*; a letter to Erfastus; and an oration to King William. CXLIX, 1426.

GUNDECHARUS, bishop of Eichstätt, also called Gunzo. Born in 1019 of Ragiuhar and Irmingard, he was reared and educated at Eichstätt from infancy; afterward he was a canon, chaplain to Empress Agnes, and finally elected bishop in 1047. He died in 1073. His *Pontifical Book* survives. CXLVI, 979.

GUNDULF, bishop of Rochester. Born in the diocese of Rouen, in the Vexin territory, he studied at Rouen and became a cleric of the church of Saint Mary; afterward he took the monastic habit in the monastery of Bec; finally he was elected bishop in 1076. He died in 1108. Two letters concerning him survive. CLIX, 835.

GUNDWINUS and ADELBOLDUS sold certain estates to Bishop Hildigrim in 784, in the reign of Charlemagne. XCIX, 809.

GUNTHARDUS and ALTIWINUS sold to Bishop Altfrid everything they possessed in the forest of Witerowald for [Col. 0464] three pounds. This was done at the monastery of Werden in 848. XCIX, 813.

GUNTHARIUS, bishop of Cologne. Carried away by ambition in the affair of King Lothair of Lotharingia and his lawful wife Theutberga, he attacked the judgment of Pope Nicholas; consequently, this faithless bishop, a transgressor against the Church, was deposed and excommunicated. Later penitent, he died in Italy in 873. His diabolical chapters against Pope Nicholas survive, as does a retraction submitted to Adrian II. CXXI, 378.

GUNTHERUS, Cistercian monk and poet, first a scholastic and afterward a monk in the monastery of Basel around 1200. His book or treatise *On Prayer, Fasting, and Almsgiving* survives, as does a poem on the affairs and deeds of Emperor Frederick. CCXII, 95.

GUNZO, deacon of Novara and grammarian. Nothing certain is known of his life. Several letters concerning him survive. CXXXVI, 1279.

GURHEDENUS, monk of Quimperlé, recounts the dispute which formerly existed between the monks of Holy Cross at Quimperlé and Hervé, abbot of Redon, and which was entrusted to the judgment of Paschal II for settlement, in the twelfth century. CLXXII, 1327.

GUTHURNUS, king of the Anglo-Danes, who, after his conversion to the faith, was given by Alfred the name Athelstan (see Athelstanus). CXXXVIII, 455.

GWNIL BOOSDOTHER, canon of Saint William of the Paraclete, gave not a few goods with the consent of his brother Boossoni, without indication of date. CCIX, 869.

## H

HADOINDUS, Saint, bishop of Le Mans. A Frank or Gaul by nation and born of noble lineage, he succeeded Bertrand. He died in 638. His testament survives. CLXXX, 566.

HAIMINIUS, monk and abbot of Saint-Vaast at Arras. Formerly a disciple of Alcuin, he in turn had disciples, among them Chilon, whom he taught the liberal arts. He died in 834. Two letters and a sermon on the Nativity of Saint Vedast survive. CV, 756.

HAIMO, cleric of Laon, was brought in by Guy, dean of Laon and bishop of Châlons, and shortly afterward made archdeacon. After Bartholomew, Guy’s successor, he himself was consecrated about 1152. A letter of his to Saint Bernard survives. CLXXXII, 691.

HAITO, see AHITO.

HALDOINUS, formerly abbot of Hautvillers in the district of Reims. He composed several verses in praise of Saint Remigius, to be placed upon his tomb after the translation carried out, for fear of the Normans, to the aforesaid monastery in 849. CXXIX, 1033.

HALINARDUS, archbishop of Lyons. Born of a noble Burgundian house and highly learned, he first became a monk in the monastery of Saint-Bénigne at Dijon. He died in 1052. Several letters of his survive. CXLII, 1334.

HALITGARIUS, bishop of Cambrai, was elected in 817; he attended the assembly at Paris concerning the veneration of sacred images. He died in 831. Five books of his *On Vices and Virtues* and *On the Order of Penitents* survive. CV, 650.

HARDRADUS, abbot of the monastery of Loningheim, bought from a certain Waldebert, for 200 solidi, everything he possessed at Loningheim in 776. CXXXVI, 1212.

HARIULFUS, abbot of Aldenburg. As a boy he entered the monastery of Saint-Riquier, where he made monastic vows under Abbot Gervin II in 1075. Later, owing to the fame of his merits, the brothers of Aldenburg elected him abbot in 1105; he held that office until 1142, when he died. He wrote a chronicle of the monastery of Saint-Riquier and, in addition, Lives of Saint Maldegisilus and of Blessed Gervin, whose successor he had been. CLXXIV, 1211.

HARMOTUS, abbot of Saint Gall. Born from the distinguished bloodline of the dukes of Burgundy, he assumed the monastic habit in the monastery of Saint Gall from youth; afterward he went to the monastery of Fulda to hear the renowned Rabanus Maurus. Having then returned to his own monastery, he remained there as a recluse for thirty years, until 884. He wrote many works which have not reached us. CXXVI, 990.

HARTMANNUS, monk of Saint Gall, flourished in 850 in the time of Abbot Grimald. He was one of the biographers of Saint Widerad; he also wrote certain verses. CXVI, 23.

HATO, bishop of Troyes. At the request of Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, he granted to Abbot Guido and the monks of Arremar the old courtyard at Clarey and the chapel situated there, on condition that the priest of Clarey receive nothing, in 1145. CLXXXV, 985, 1919.

HAWARDUS, through the hand of his kinsman Armimar, gave to the monastery of Saint Emmeram part of the property which he possessed at Tegarendorf, in the ninth century. CXXIX, 940.

[Col. 0465] HAYMO, bishop of Halberstadt. A German by nation, first a disciple of Alcuin and then of Rabanus Maurus, who counted him a friend. From being a monk of Fulda he became the third abbot of Hersfeld and finally bishop of Halberstadt; he died in 853. We have from him biblical commentaries, homilies, and *Miscellanea*. CXVI–CXVIII.

HAYMO of Marmania, before entering the monastery of Fontenay, whose abbot was William, gave it a certain piece of land situated near Saigniac, without indication of year. He gave the same estate for the foundation of the Cistercian abbey of Sept-Fontaines in 1156. CLXXXV, 1462, 1479.

HAYMO of Asnières, mayor of the commune of Dijon, attests that Lord Milo of Fontaines, burgess of Dijon, and his son John sold and delivered to Alais, duchess of Burgundy, a house and holding which they had at Dijon, above the bank of the Suzon, in 1237. CLXXXV, 1456.

HEBERNUS, archbishop of Tours. He flourished in the middle of the ninth century and had first been abbot of Marmoutier. He wrote a history of the miracles of Saint Martin after the translation of Martin’s body. CXXIX, 1035.

HEDDO, bishop of Strasbourg, confirmed the gifts bestowed upon the monastery of Saint Arnulf on Reichenau by Rottard, its founder, and granted it privileges in 748. LXXXVIII, 1314, 1318.

HEDENUS, also HETANUS, son of Gosbert, duke of Thuringia, together with his wife Theodrada granted certain gifts to Saint Willibrord, archbishop of Utrecht, in 704 and 716. LXXXIX, 535, 548.

HEDILO, bishop of Noyon. He wrote to Dido, bishop of Laon, on behalf of the priest Arnegisus, seeking permission for him to transfer to Dido’s parish and be subject to him, in 892. There also survives a letter of his to Rodulf, bishop of Laon, on behalf of the deacon Rotger, in 902. CXXIX, 1394.

HELDERICUS, provost of the monastery of Saint Simeon at Trier, flourished in the twelfth century. He wrote to Saint Hildegard, to whose prayers he commended himself. CXCVII, 312.

HELENA Augusta, mother of Constantine the Great, distinguished for piety, founded many churches, made a pilgrimage to the Holy Places, found the Savior’s cross, distributed generous alms to the poor, and died at about eighty years of age around 325. A letter from her to her son Constantine survives. VIII, 60, 527.

HELGAUDUS, monk. A Gaul by nation, he died in 1048 at the abbey of Saint Benedict on the Loire, or, according to others, at the monastery of Fleury, at the time when Goscelin was appointed abbot in place of the learned Abbo. He wrote the Life of Blessed Robert, king of the Franks. CXLII, 1263.

HELINANDUS, monk of Froidmont. Born of noble family in Flanders, he distinguished himself in Gaul, to which his father had fled, and embraced monastic life at the Cistercian monastery of Froidmont. He elegantly wrote sermons, a book *On the Good Government of a Prince*, a letter to Walter, and a chronicle. He died about 1219. CCXII, 477.

HELINGERUS, abbot of Saint Disibod. He lived at the end of the twelfth century. He accuses himself before Saint Hildegard, abbess of Mount Saint Robert, and complains of the declining discipline in his monastery. CXCVII, 204.

HELLADIUS, bishop of Tarsus, followed Nestorius in his heresy. He and Eutherius sent a letter to Saint Xystus, pope, hoping that he would be favorable to them, railing against Cyril of Alexandria and corrupting the truth concerning the Council of Ephesus, in 450. L, 593.

HELMBRATTUS, son of Regimbert. Having lost his own son Ledbrat, he gave a notable part of his inheritance to the Church of Saint Saviour at Werden, in the reign of Louis the Pious, in the ninth century. XCIX, 808, 812.

HELOISSA, niece of Fulbert, canon of Paris, was first the beloved and afterward the wife of her teacher Abelard; Fulbert exacted savage vengeance upon him. Thereafter Heloise took the veil and became the first abbess of the Paraclete nunnery founded by Abelard. She was skilled in languages and cultivated the liberal arts. She died in 1164. Her letters to Abelard survive. CLXXVIII, 181, 191.

HELPERICUS became a monk of Saint Gall in 980. He was the author of a book on ecclesiastical computation. CXXXVII, 17.

HEMMINGUS, monk and priest of Worcester. An Englishman by nation, he flourished at the end of the eleventh century. He wrote five books on the Church of Worcester—its endowment, privileges, and possessions. CL, 1490.

HENRICHEZIUS, Chrysostom, monk of the Cistercian Order. He died in 1632. He was the author of many writings pertaining to the history of his order. There survives from him a fragment concerning the mother of Saint Bernard. CLXXXV, 1102.

HENRY, son of Bernger, conveyed certain goods to the Church of Saint Saviour situated in the district of the Ripuarians, in 835. XCIX, 810.

[Col. 0466] HENRY I, son of Otto, succeeded Emperor Conrad I; he defeated the Danes, Slavs, Hungarians, and others, and issued various diplomas and constitutions. He died in 936. XCVIII, 609, 625.

HENRY, bishop of Parma, flourished in the eleventh century. Nothing is known to us concerning his life. He wrote a sermon on the Lord’s Easter. CXXXIX, 1530.

HENRY II, Saint, Augustus and emperor of Germany, born to Duke Henry in 972, proclaimed emperor in 1002, and died in 1024. His laws, constitutions, and ecclesiastical diplomas survive. CXL, 9.

HENRY III, emperor of Germany, brother and successor of Conrad II, opposed Pope Gregory VI and waged war against the Bohemians and Hungarians. He died in 1056. Some diplomas concerning him survive. CXLII, 33; CLIX, 931; CL.

HENRY I, son and successor of Robert in France. During his reign famine and wars decimated the common people; he died in 1060. Some diplomas of his survive. CLI, 1025.

HENRY and his brother MORINUS, men devoted to warfare, were at first carried away by ambition and derived profit from corrupt customs which they imposed upon the place of Saint George; but afterward, overcome by the admonitions and prayers of Abbot Eustace, they abolished those customs in 1086. CLV, 362.

HENRY, cleric of Pomposa. Nothing concerning him is related by the biographers. He flourished in the eleventh century; a letter to Stephen, master of philosophy, survives. CL, 1346.

HENRY, duke of Burgundy, son of Robert and successor to Hugh I. In 1098 he acquired the kingdom of Portugal; in 1093 he granted certain things to Gregory, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Seine, so that the anniversary of his father’s death might be celebrated every year. CLXXXV, 1402.

HENRY IV, emperor of Germany, son of Agnes and Henry III, whom he succeeded, gained the crown amid many difficulties; finally, defeated by his son Henry, he was compelled to surrender the scepter to him and died miserably at Liège in 1106. In rebellion against the pope, he had established the antipope Clement, whom he imposed upon all his subjects. Several letters of his to Saint Hugh of Cluny survive. CLIX, 932, passim.

HENRY, bishop of Bayeux, granted to the canons of his church the houses of Conan, formerly his treasurer, to possess in perpetuity for an annual rent of six Angevin pounds, in 1108. By another charter he gave the same chapter the tithe of the forest of Nuille and Racinet. CCVII, 1157, 1159.

HENRY V, emperor of Germany, who had been excommunicated by Guido, archbishop of Vienne, and reproved by Pope Paschal, wrote to the aforesaid Guido that all ecclesiastics of his province should surrender their royal rights and fiefs to Caesar and should live content with tithes in the Church, about 1112. CLXIII, 467.

HENRY, bishop of Lucca. Norbert, archbishop of Magdeburg, had written to him concerning the election of Pope Honorius’s successor. Henry informed him that Peter Leonis had attempted to usurp the supreme pontificate under the name Anacletus and had provoked disorders and killings; but that all orthodox faithful and bishops from Tuscany, Lombardy, and regions beyond the mountains professed and proclaimed Innocent II alone to have been legitimately elected, in 1130. CLXXIX, 40.

HENRY, archbishop of Sens. He wrote to Stephen, bishop of Paris, inviting him to come to Provins in order to explain the matter of the interdict concerning his archdeacon and, if possible, to bring it to an end, in 1132. CLXXIII, 1411.

HENRY I, king of England, third son of William the Conqueror, succeeded his brother William Rufus in 1100. He waged war with the king of the Franks and the counts of Anjou; he died in 1137. Several letters concerning him survive. CLIX, 235 and passim.

HENRY, archdeacon of Huntingdon, formerly a canon of Lincoln. We have from him a history of the English in eight books, of the twelfth century. CXCV, 797.

HENRY of Saltrey, an Irishman by nation, was a monk of the Cistercian Order. He wrote a little book, *On Saint Patrick’s Purgatory*, which he dedicated to Henry of Sartis in 1140. CLXXX, 971.

HENRY, bishop of Winchester. A refugee from England to France, he asks Suger to send a messenger to Sibylla, countess of Flanders, to seek a safe-conduct for him. A letter to the same person survives in which he commends the affairs of the king of England, in 1147. CLXXXVI, 1432, 1434.

HENRY, monk of Stavelot, was sent to Rome to obtain from the Supreme Pontiff confirmation of Wibald’s election as abbot of Corbie. He reports on what he did before the pope, in 1147. CLXXXIX, 1145, 1365 and following.

[Col. 0467] HENRY, count of Namur. Having a certain case with the archdeacon of Verdun, he wrote to Pope Eugenius that he was prepared to observe what had been ordered at Trier in the papal court, fearing that both he and his possessions might be subjected to interdict, in 1148. CLXXX, 1622.

HENRY, brother of King Louis and a monk of Clairvaux. When he was being sought as bishop of Beauvais, he wrote to Suger, urging him that another be elected, about 1148. See below, Henry under 1175. CLXXXVI, 1374.

HENRY, archbishop of Mainz, reports to Wibald, abbot of Corbie, what he had done at the Council of Erfurt in 1149. CLXXXIX, 1214; CXCVII, 156.

HENRY, bishop of Minden, formerly abbot of Saint Maurice, wrote to Wibald, abbot of Corbie, in 1149. He consulted him about the dispute dividing the bishops of Paderborn and Münster. CLXXXIX, 1219 and passim.

HENRY, king of the Romans and son of Conrad III. With his father’s consent, he assumed the reins of empire while the latter undertook his journey to Jerusalem in 1148. Several letters of his to Pope Eugenius III survive. CLXXX, 1618.

HENRY, son of Theobald, count of Blois, wrote to Suger and, as though to a friend, asks him to come to Meaux on account of Anseric of Mont-Royal, his man, whom Rainald of Pomponne had taken prisoner in war, in 1150. CLXXXVI, 1385.

HENRY, notary of the royal court, informs Wibald, abbot of Corbie, that he had laid the letters before the king and added certain remarks. The king replied that he greatly regretted the injury done to Wibald and was prepared to confirm all that he had granted to the monastery of Corbie, in 1150. CLXXXIX, 1296.

HENRY, bishop of Liège, wrote to Eugenius III asking him to confirm the election of Arnold, bishop of Cologne, whom he had supported, in 1151. CLXXX, 1631.

See another letter of his to Wibald, in which he complains concerning certain matters. CLXXXIX, 1353.

HENRY, bishop of Troyes, flourished in the twelfth century. He wrote to Saint Bernard concerning the abbey of Boulancourt, where discipline had perished through lapse of time; with the consent of the abbot and canons, he gave this monastery itself to the Cistercian Order, for Bernard to reform. A charter of donation is appended to this letter, in 1152. CLXXXII, 693.

HENRY, count of Salm, pursued the venerable Wibald, abbot of Corbie, with such confidence that he entrusted all his controversies to Wibald’s arbitration for settlement in 1153. CLXXXIX, 1434.

HENRY, abbot of Clairvaux, wrote in 1163 to Stephen, king of the English, concerning the elevation of the body of Blessed Bernard, sending him one of the holy abbot’s fingers. He appears to be the same person as Henry of Châtel-Marsiac, mentioned below. CLXXXV, 627.

HENRY, bishop of Autun. Charters of his survive from 1165, CLXXXV, 1467, 1469.

HENRY, count of Troyes, in 1168 confirmed all the gifts made by his predecessors to the brothers of the abbey of Clairvaux, and himself made certain new donations, CLXXXV, 1750.

HENRY, abbot of the monastery of St. Saviour at Villeloup, with the consent of the whole chapter, granted the monks of the Charterhouse a certain place commonly called Liget, about 1173, CCVII, 1162.

HENRY, archdeacon of Salzburg. After the expulsion of Adalbert, archbishop of Salzburg, he undertook the administration of that office. He wrote a history of the calamities of the Church of Salzburg, in 1174, CXCVI, 1539.

HENRY I, archbishop of Rheims. Born of noble stock, he was brother of King Louis VII himself; he died in 1175. His letters and diplomas survive (see above, Henry, under the year 1148), CXCVI, 1559.

HENRY of Châtel-Marsiac, cardinal and bishop of Albano, was made so by Alexander III from being abbot of Clairvaux. He attended the Lateran Council. Born of noble family, he entered the monastery of Clairvaux as a boy and was educated under Abbot Robert; he died in 1186. Numerous letters by him survive, together with a treatise On the Pilgrim City of God, CCIV, 211.

HENRY II, king of the English, son of Geoffrey Plantagenet, succeeded Stephen in 1154. He ordered St. Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, to be slain by assassins; he died in 1189. Various letters and diplomas concerning him survive, CLXXXVI, 1063.

See also CXC, 395 and passim; CC, 1383; CCVII, 1160.

HENRY of Septimello, poet. Native of Etruria and of a Florentine village, he flourished at the end of the twelfth century. He himself admits that his family was rustic and humble; he studied at Bologna; he is said to have been so poor that, lacking paper, he was compelled to write his verses on an old sheepskin. He was a poet celebrated in his age. There survives from him [Col. 0468] a remarkable elegiac poem, *On the Diversity of Fortune*, CCIV, 841.

HENRY of Crowland, abbot in England. He flourished at the beginning of the thirteenth century. He sent a letter to Stephen, archbishop of Canterbury, concerning the life of St. Thomas of Canterbury, CXC, 257.

HENRY, bishop of Winchester and legate of the Apostolic See, lived in the twelfth century. He complains to the prior and convent of St. Mary’s, Worcester, that they have not yet sent St. Peter’s penny, although all the others have already paid it; and he threatens exclusion from the offices unless they pay it within fifteen days, CXC, 1041.

HENRY of Bevez, bishop of an uncertain see, flourished at the end of the twelfth century; he requests the prayers and letters of St. Hildegard, abbess of Mount St. Robert, CXCVII, 180.

HENRY, dean of the chapter of St. Paul’s, London, commends Bishop Gilbert, who was journeying to Rome, in the twelfth century, CC, 1412.

HENRY, abbot of the monastery of Stratford, was a contemporary of Lord Thomas of Canterbury. Two letters by him survive, CXC, 686; CC, 1441.

HENRY, king of Hungary, lived at the beginning of the thirteenth century. In 1204 he wrote to Pope Innocent III against certain persons who had not accepted the constitutions promulgated by the legate of the Apostolic See, CCXVII, 289.

HENRY, son of Baldwin, emperor of Constantinople, tells Pope Innocent III how his father was defeated and captured in 1205, CCXVII, 292.

HENRY, the emperor’s brother, in 1205 informed Pope Innocent III through messengers that Baldwin, emperor of Constantinople, had been captured by the Bulgarians, CCXV, 706.

HENRY, abbot of St. Denis, and Odo, bishop of Paris, when they were disputing with one another over the church of Argenteuil, reached an amicable settlement in 1207, CCXII, 88.

HENRY of Hesse, born in Germany, taught theology and philosophy at Paris, following the Nominalists; but afterwards he entered the Carthusian Order. In a treatise addressed to James, abbot of Eberbach, he vigorously attacks the calumniators of St. Bernard. He died about 1397, CLXXXV, 633.

HENRY, count of Portugal. See RAYMOND of Galicia.

HERACLIDES, who appears to have flourished in the time and places of Palladius, visited various monasteries in Syria, Egypt, and Italy, everywhere collecting what seemed worthy of note. He composed an account of this journey under the title *The Paradise of Heraclides*, which he dedicated to Lausus, prefect of Cappadocia, LXXIV, 243.

HERACLITUS, philosopher born at Ephesus, flourished about 500 before Christ. Thinking himself unjustly injured by certain persons, he lived in perpetual mourning, cursing humankind. A letter to Darius, king of the Persians, is attributed to him, XVII, 1154.

HERACLIUS, a distinguished man and close friend of St. Avitus, was ill with gout in bed when he received a letter from Avitus; he immediately replied to him, about 494, LIX, 288.

HERARD, archbishop of Tours, was endowed with outstanding gifts from childhood. Raised to the episcopate in 855, he governed his see piously until 871, when he died. There survive from him chapters collected from the capitularies of the Frankish kings, and an admonitory memorandum addressed to Wenilo, archbishop of Sens, CXXI, 762.

HERBERT, a knight of the castle of Gallardon, was converted to a better life under Hubert, abbot of St. Peter’s at Chartres, and made many gifts to that monastery in 1080, CLV, 345.

HERBERT, abbot of the monastery of Saints Joseph and Habakkuk, negotiated a certain exchange with Hugh of Ibelin, lord of Ramla, in 1160, CLV, 1162.

HERBERT, abbot of the monastery of Mores, afterwards became archbishop of Torres in Sardinia about 1180. He wrote three books on the miracles of Bernard, CLXXXV, 369, 453.

HERBERT of Bosham, confidential secretary of St. Thomas of Canterbury, to whom he was attached from the depths of his heart, wrote his life and the *Book of Apples*, in 1180, CXC, 1069.

HERCHEMFREDA, a most noble Gallic matron, married to the distinguished Salvius, had three sons, whom King Dagobert took with him. The eldest, Rusticus, bishop of Cahors, was slain; his brother Desiderius succeeded him in the same see. Letters from her to her son Desiderius survive from 640, LXXXVII, 224.

HERECA, a name borrowed from an old friend of St. Lullus, archbishop of Mainz, wrote to him concerning her election as abbess, recalling their former intimacy when he was still living in England, in 756, XCVI, 838.

HERIBERT of Champagne and his wife Megesinda, together with their sons, jointly conveyed part of their property to Lord Hilduin, abbot of Pithiviers, in 867, CXXXVII, 1240.

[Col. 0469] HERIBERT, bishop of Eichstätt, of whom little is known, was consecrated bishop in 1021 and governed his Church for twenty-one years; he died in 1042. His hymns survive, CXLI, 1370.

HERIBERT, apparently a monk of Périgueux, wrote a letter addressed also to all Christians, warning them of certain heretics who were ravaging this part of Gaul in 1150, CLXXXI, 1721.

HERIC, monk of Auxerre, of the Order of St. Benedict, flourished in the ninth century. He wrote, in verse, a Life of St. Germanus of Auxerre, dedicated to King Charles the Fat, CXXIX, 1130.

HERIGER, or HARIGER, abbot of Lobbes, of the Order of St. Benedict. He wrote the *Deeds of the Bishops of Tongeren, Maastricht, and Liège*, as well as the Lives of St. Berlinda and of the holy abbots Landuald and Ursmar (in 1007), CXXXV, 955.

HERIMANN, bishop of Metz. Born in Saxony of distinguished parents, a pupil of Anno, archbishop of Cologne, he became bishop in 1073 and died in 1090. Two charters by him survive, one of them for the monastery of Cluny, CL, 1178.

HERIMANN, count of Würzburg, bears witness to Wibald’s election as abbot of Corbie in 1146, CLXXXIX, 1141, 1166.

HERLEMBALD (St.), martyr. Born of distinguished family, he became a man prudent in counsel and valiant in arms, but more illustrious for the faith and constancy with which he endured death for Christ’s religion. Accounts of him survive. (In 1066.) CXLIII, 1434.

HERMANNUS CONTRACTUS, so called because of the weakness of his limbs, had as his father Wolfandus, count of Peringen, and Hiltrude as his mother. He was an eminent poet for his age, a learned historian, an outstanding musician, and a master of philosophy, theology, and mathematics; he died in 1054. There survive from him a *Chronicle*, a book *On the Measurement of the Astrolabe*, two others *On the Usefulness of the Astrolabe*, musical works, a sequence concerning the Blessed Virgin Mary, and a poem *On the Conflict of the Sheep and Flax*, CXLIII, 9.

HERMANN, a Jew who became a Christian, a native of Cologne from the tribe of Levi, was converted by Egbert, bishop of Münster; he suffered much at the hands of the other Jews. He wrote a book concerning his conversion (in 1134), CLXX, 803.

HERMANN of Arbon, bishop of Constance on the Rhine. A letter by him survives to Wilbald, abbot of Corbie, asking him to procure, by the emperor’s authority, the liberation of his kinsman Henry, held captive by Welf, in 1150, CLXXXIX, 1281.

HERMANN, bishop of Augsburg, wrote to Otto, bishop of Bamberg, informing him that his episcopal city had been plundered and that clerics had been cruelly killed by King Lothair, at the beginning of the twelfth century, CLXXIII, 1354.

HERMANN, abbot of St. Martin’s at Tournai, of the Order of St. Benedict. After nine years in office he resigned his charge into the bishop’s hands and undertook a journey to Jerusalem. He wrote a book on the Incarnation of the Lord, three books on the miracles of St. Mary of Paris, and an account of the restoration of the abbey of St. Martin at Tournai (in 1137), CLXXX, 9.

HERRAD, abbess of Hohenburg, an eminent and most learned nun. In Latin she wrote a book entitled *The Garden of Delights*, which she dedicated to the virgins of Mount St. Odile, besides several poems. She died in 1195, CXCIV, 1537.

HERTAWIG, archbishop of Bremen. He wrote to Blessed Hildegard, abbess, informing her of the death of his sister Richardis, whose soul he commends to her; after the middle of the twelfth century, CXCVII, 161.

HERVAEUS, archbishop of Rheims. He was nephew of Count Hucbald and passed from the royal court to the episcopate. He died in 922. A letter by him to the archbishop of Rouen survives, CXXXII, 659.

HERVAEUS, monk of Bourg-Dieu, a man venerable alike in life and teaching: after fifty years spent in the monastery, he died in 1149. His commentaries on Isaiah and the Epistles of St. Paul survive, CLXXXI, 10.

HERVARD, archdeacon of Liège, flourished at the beginning of the thirteenth century. He wrote to a certain canon of Laon concerning Guibert of Gembloux and the writing of the Life of St. Martin, CCXI, 1283.

HERVEUS, dean of St. Mary’s of Paris, attests that Robert, son of William of Gausanville, granted to the chapter of Paris whatever he had received from his father in 1189, CCV, 911.

HERVEUS, a cleric of the church of Canterbury, lived in the twelfth century. He wrote to St. Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury and exile in Gaul, informing him of the condition of his diocese, CXC, 694, 697.

HERVEUS, lord of Sombernon, and his brother GAUTIER made many gifts to the monastery of Bussière in Burgundy in 1217 and 1220, CLXXXV, 1424.

HERVIN, abbot of the monastery of Steinwald, described [Col. 0470] various miracles of St. Bernard which he had witnessed with his own eyes, or at least as a contemporary, in the twelfth century, CLXXXV, 870.

HESSO, a scholar who wrote a short commentary concerning the peace concluded between Pope Calixtus II and Emperor Henry V, of which he himself was an eyewitness. (In 1122.) CLXIII, 1081.

HESYCHIUS, bishop of Salona in Dalmatia, put certain questions to St. Augustine concerning the end of the world; the holy Doctor answered them in 419, XXXIII, 901.

HETERIUS, bishop of Osma. Formerly a monk in a monastery of Asturias together with Beatus, a Spanish priest, he stoutly taught Catholic truth in writings and sermons against Felix and Elipandus. (In 790.) We have letters and sermons by him which breathe zeal and piety, XCVI, 848.

HEYMO, priest and monk of St. Michael’s at Bamberg, or, according to others, canon of St. James outside the walls of the same city, appears to have flourished in 1595. He wrote the Annals of Bamberg, carrying them down to his own time, CLXXIII, 1363.

HIDDO, son of Heriwin, and his wife Madalgarda gave the greater part of their inheritance to Blessed Ludger, abbot of Werden and bishop of Mimigernaford, at the beginning of the ninth century, in the reign of Charlemagne, XCIX, 803.

JEROME (St.), Roman priest and Doctor of the Holy Church, a man endowed with tireless zeal and extraordinary intellect, was born at Stridon in Dalmatia. As a young man he at times indulged in pleasure; but overcome by God’s grace, he sought the wilderness of Bethlehem, intending to pursue an austere life. To immense learning he added the study of Hebrew, and devoted the greatest care and arduous labour to correcting and explaining the Scriptures. He left an immense body of works, among which are his letters, books against Jovinian, the Lives of Paul and Hilarion, commentaries, and the Divine Library. He died in 420, XXII–XXX.

JEROME of Riola, flourished about 1480. He translated into Italian the Life of St. John Gualbert by Andrew of Genoa, CXLVI, 715, 811.

HILARIANUS (Quintus Julius), flourished at the end of the fourth century. He wrote two short works in which he indicated the time when he composed them: the first treats of the duration of the world, the second of the day and month of Easter, XIII, 1094.

HILARY (St.), bishop of Poitiers and Doctor of the Church. Born in Poitiers itself of distinguished but still pagan parents, he excelled in the study of letters and, having already embraced piety, received baptism. Afterwards he became so highly esteemed that he was raised to the episcopate of his native city, though bound by marriage. Against the Semi-Arians and Anomoeans he asserted the consubstantiality of the Word. He wrote most learned books on the Trinity, expounded certain books of Scripture, and produced other polemical works. He died in 368, IX–X.

HILARY, deacon of the Roman Church, was a native of Sardinia. Contrary to the Church’s precept, he taught that baptism should be repeated for every heretic or person defiled by sins who converted to the faith. A commentary on the Epistles of St. Paul and Questions on the Old and New Testament are attributed to him. He died about 398, XVIII, 65.

HILARY, a layman of Syracuse, wrote to St. Augustine to consult him on certain questions; the holy Doctor replied to him in 414, XXXIII, 673.

ANOTHER HILARY, Gallic by origin and from Narbonne, is known from a letter he wrote to St. Augustine, in which, like Prosper, he consulted him about predestination, in 428, XXXIII, 1007.

HILARY (St.), bishop of Arles, a Gaul by nation, born into and liberally educated by a distinguished family. At the exhortation of Honoratus, he renounced the world; in 429 he was appointed to govern the Church of Arles. He died in 449. There survive from him a Life of St. Honoratus, a letter to St. Eucherius, a sermon on the miracles of St. Genesius, and several poems, L, 1213.

HILARY (St.), pope. A Sardinian by nationality, while still a deacon he served as legate at the Council of Ephesus; afterwards he succeeded St. Leo the Great in the Roman See. He confirmed decrees formerly issued against the Arians, Nestorians, and Eutychians. He died in 467. Eleven letters and two decrees by him survive, LVIII, 9.

HILARY, an Englishman by nationality and a disciple of Abelard, flourished together with Berengar. He composed an elegiac poem, CCXXVIII, 1851.

HILDEBERT (the Venerable), archbishop of Tours, was born in 1057 at the castle of Lavardin, in the territory of Vendôme, of pious but moderately endowed parents. From childhood he was instructed in learning and the liberal arts under Berengar as master; then he became a monk of Cluny and afterwards bishop of Le Mans. Finally transferred to the see of Tours in 1107, he died in 1135. His letters, poems, [Col. 0471] sermons, biographical, moral, and exegetical works survive, CLXXI, 9.

HILDEBRAND. See GREGORY VII.

HILDEBRAND THE YOUNGER flourished in the twelfth century. The biographers transmit nothing about his life. He is the genuine author of the little work entitled *Booklet on Contemplation* and of the commentaries on Matthew attributed to Gregory VII because he originally bore the name Hildebrand, in 1150, CLXXXI, 1691.

ILDEFONSUS (St.), bishop of Toledo. He was born at Toledo of noble family, nephew of his predecessor Eugenius, and studied under Isidore of Seville. Thereupon he embraced monastic life and received orders; at length he was appointed in the place of his deceased uncle. He died in 669. He wrote very much, especially on the virginity and veneration of the Blessed Virgin Mary, XCVI, 329.

HILDEGARD, formerly the wife of a knight named Geoffrey, gave certain property to the monastery of St. Peter at Chartres on behalf of an abandoned boy whom she had placed there in 1080, CLV, 344.

HILDEGARD (St.), abbess of the monastery of Mount St. Rupert or Robert at Bingen, became so renowned that she was regarded as an oracle of the Church. She produced three books of temptations and visions, then a book of divine works, answers to thirty-eight questions, an explanation of the Rule of St. Benedict, and the *Physica*. In 1179, CXCVII, 9.

HILDEGARIUS, canon of Chartres. He flourished in the time of St. Fulbert, whose pupil he himself acknowledges that he was. Several letters from him survive to various persons, and especially to Blessed Fulbert, in 1020, CXLI, 211, 266.

HILDEGRIM, according to an old cartulary of the monastery of St. Remigius at Rheims, offered his nephew, still in tender years, to this monastery, to remain there permanently, in 869, CL, 601.

HILDEMAR, a monk born in Romania, was summoned with Leutgar to Milan in the ninth century and wrote an exposition of the Rule of St. Benedict. According to Dupin, he died in 840. A letter by him to Ursus, bishop of Benevento, survives, *On the Correct Method of Speaking*, CVI, 394.

HILDEPRAND (Flavius), king of the Lombards, founded at Piacenza a church in honour of Saints Antony and Victor, entrusting its governance to Thomas, bishop of that place, in 768, LXXXVII, 1397.

HILDIGARD gave to Ambricho, bishop of Paderborn and at the same time abbot of St. Emmeram, the property which she possessed at Menzinpach, without mention of a year, in the ninth century, CXXIX, 920.

HILDIRAD granted part of his inheritance to the Church of St. Saviour at Werden, over which Blessed Ludger presided, in 807, XCIX, 807.

HILDO and his wife Maldalgarda conveyed to St. Ludger, bishop of Mimigernaford, part of their inheritance in 812, in the reign of Charlemagne, XCIX, 803.

HILDUIN, abbot. In succession he governed the abbeys of St. Denis, St. Medard at Soissons, and St. Germain-des-Prés, in which he restored monastic discipline. He was distinguished in character and intellect. He wrote the Life of St. Denis. He died in 840, CVI, 9.

HILDUIN, viscount, renounced the wrongful custom which he had formerly claimed, to the detriment of the monastery of St. Peter at Chartres, in 1080, CLV, 309.

HILTIN, archbishop of Trier. He flourished in the twelfth century. He wrote to St. Hildegard, asking her to permit a few drops to trickle down to him from the wine-cellar, CXCVII, 166.

HINCMAR, archbishop of Rheims. Born of noble Gallic stock, he was brought up from childhood in the monastery of St. Denis under Abbot Hilduin. He enjoyed no slight favour with Emperor Louis, and was finally raised to the archbishopric of Rheims in 845. When the Northmen invaded Gaul, he took the relics of St. Remigius and fled beyond the Marne into wooded places, to the estate called Épernay. He died in 882. His letters, theological treatises, chapters, and an exposition of Solomon’s banquet survive.

HINCMAR, bishop of Laon, called the Younger in order to distinguish him from his uncle of Rheims, by whom he had been received and educated from childhood. He had scarcely reached the age prescribed by the canons when he was elevated to the see of Laon. But he soon incurred the displeasure of Charles the Bald and of his uncle himself, by whom he was deposed and later restored. Treatises and letters by him survive, especially concerning these disputes, in 878, CXXIV, 968.

HIPPOLYTUS (St.), bishop of Portus near Rome, was sent into exile with St. Maximus the abbot; after suffering much, he finally died a martyr. Certain testimonies concerning him, written in Greek and Latin, survive from 666, CXXX, 561.

HIRPING, having received payment from Blessed Ludger, sold a vineyard situated on the bank of the river Melembach [Col. 0472] in 803, during the reign of Charlemagne, XCIX, 801.

HISIMO, abbot of Ambronay, when disputing with Lord Peter, abbot of Cluny, concerning the place of Prins, referred the matter to the judgment of Lord Hilary, abbot of St. Just, in 1132.

HLUDWIN gave part of his inheritance to the monastery of Werden and to Blessed Ludger, its abbot, in 793, XCIX, 797.

HOWEL DDA, prince of all Wales, ruled in the tenth century. Certain laws and ecclesiastical constitutions of his survive; he died about 940, CXXXVIII, 471.

HONESTIS (Peter de). See PETER.

HONORATUS (Antoninus). See ANTONINUS.

HONORIUS AUGUSTUS (Flavius) ruled the West from 395 to 423. He was driven from Rome by Alaric, king of the Goths. Many writings concerning him survive, both letters and decrees, XI, 1192 and passim.

See also XVIII, 398, 401, 402, 405; XX, 767.

HONORIUS I, pope. A Campanian by nationality, son of the consul Petronius, he succeeded Boniface V in 626 and held the see until 638, when he died. His letters survive, LXXX, 466.

HONORIUS II, pope, previously called Lambert, a native of Bologna, whom Pope Paschal II had made bishop of Velletri and later cardinal, attained the see in 1124. He died in 1130. We have letters and privileges from him, CLXVI, 1214.

HONORIUS III, pope, successor of Innocent III, died in 1227. He confirms certain settlements in the churches of Greece, necessary in those times because of changing circumstances, CCXVI, 968, 982.

HONORIUS of Autun in Burgundy, priest and scholar, flourished in the twelfth century and was also surnamed the Solitary. He wrote many works—didactic, historical, exegetical, dogmatic, and moral; he died about 1145, CLXXII, 9.

HORMISDAS, pope. Born at Frutiniana in Campania, he succeeded Pope Symmachus in 514 and showed himself vigorous in all that he did. Quite a number of his letters and decrees survive. He died in 523, LXIII, 363.

HORSTIUS (Jacob Merlo), priest of the Church of St. Mary at Cologne, was born in the village of Horst, whence he was called Horstius; he died in 1644. He wrote many ascetical works, and in a certain exhortation addressed to sectarians he clearly set forth an encomium of St. Bernard, CLXXXV, 639.

HRODULF, son of a certain Wibald, conveyed to Blessed Ludger, abbot of the monastery of Werden, part of the inheritance which he had sold to him for the foundation of the Church of St. Saviour, in 806, during the reign of Charlemagne, XCIX, 801.

HROSTEIN, count, gave as a donation part of his inheritance to the Church of St. Saviour situated in the district of the Ripuarian Franks. This was done in the monastery of Werden under Louis the Pious, in 815, XCIX, 805.

HROTSWITHA, or ROSWITHA, virgin and nun of Gandersheim in Germany, flourished at the end of the tenth century (in 999). She cultivated poetry and the liberal arts, wrote dramatic and religious works and numerous poems, CXXXVII, 739.

HUBERT, abbot of St. Peter’s at Chartres and successor of Landric, flourished at the end of the eleventh century (in 1080). He left certain charters proving his monastery’s lawful possession of particular lands, CLV, 280.

HUBERT (St.), monk of Andage or of Angers. Everything concerning him is rather obscure. A monastery bearing his name stood in the Forest of the Ardennes, where discipline had perished; Hubert, or Hubertinus, through his care and labour repaired everything and restored its former fervour, in the seventh century, CLIV, 1338.

HUBERT held the see of Canterbury about 1200. A letter by him survives to the dean of Salisbury, exempting a certain canon from the law of residence and teaching that clerics may be exempted from it for many reasons, CCVII, 473.

HUCBALD, monk of St. Amand, was born about 860. After the death of his uncle Milo, he took charge of the school founded in the aforesaid monastery. He was indeed a man of great learning. He died in 930. We have many writings by him, and especially verses, CXXXII, 815.

HUGH, priest of Metz, son of Drogo, duke of Burgundy, and brother of Arnulf, Pippin, and Godfrey, made certain gifts to the Church of the Holy Apostles in 715, during the reign of Dagobert III, LXXXVIII, 1262.

HUGH gave certain property to the monastery of Hohenau, which he held from his father Bleon on that same island, in 748, LXXXVIII, 1313.

HUGH CAPET, king of the Franks, first of his dynasty and son of Hugh the Great, was proclaimed king after the death of Louis V [Col. 0473] in 987; in the following year he ordered his son Robert to be crowned. He died in 996. A diploma from him, subscribed by Robert in 994, survives, CXLI, 945.

HUGH, bishop of Langres. Born at Breteuil in the territory of Beauvais, and formerly bishop of Chartres, he was elevated to the episcopate by the pious King Robert in 1031. He was deposed in 1049 because of crimes of a disgraceful life. Moved by penitence, he died in a monastery in 1051. His treatise on the Body and Blood of Christ against Berengar survives, CXLII, 1322.

HUGH, archbishop of Besançon, wrote a charter by which he gave much toward restoring the chapter of St. Stephen; Pope Leo IX confirmed it in 1049. He transferred the bones of the holy martyrs Ferreolus and Ferrucius from a certain monastery to the metropolitan church of St. John, as another charter of his reports. He died in 1055, LXXX, 421, 426.

HUGH, viscount of Nevers, manumitted the serf Letald, his wife Amalberga, and his brother Ranulf, in favour of the monastery of St. Peter at Chartres, in 1061, CLV, 315.

HUGH II, bishop of Nevers, son of the viscount of Nevers and Elizabeth, formerly a canon of Auxerre, was elected bishop in 1013. He died in 1065 while returning from Rome, where he had attended a council. A letter by him to Bartholomew, archbishop of Tours, survives, CXLIII, 1365.

HUGH, called “Brustans Salix,” who had had a wife and children, was born at the castle of Médan. Having given away all his goods, he cut his hair and beard and entered the monastery of St. Peter at Chartres under Abbot Landric, in 1069, CLV, 320.

HUGH I, bishop of Troyes, flourished in the eleventh century. He attended many councils. Nothing else certain is known of him except that he wrote a letter to Bartholomew, archbishop of Tours. He died about 1074, CXLVI, 1435.

HUGH (Stephen), priest of the diocese of Rodez, possessed a certain right in the church of Semur, which Viscountess Faith had given to Blessed Hugh of Cluny and the monastery of Moissac. He confirms this gift in 1077, CLIX, 968.

HUGH, surnamed Pirarius, and his wife Ledgard acknowledge that the estate which they had received in the court of Drogo did not lawfully belong to them, and declare that they renounce it, in 1080, CLX, 316.

HUGH, bishop of Senlis. At the request of Count Hugh of Crépy, he confirms, in 1095, the gift to the monastery of St. Arnulf at Crépy which Count Simon, Hugh’s father, had formerly made for the benefit of the monastery of Cluny in 1076, CLIX, 974.

HUGH, count of Troyes, first founder of the abbey of Clairvaux, married Constance; Simon, count of Bar-sur-Seine, was his son, in 1097, CLXXXV, 1419, 1460, 1477, 1535.

See below, HUGH, count of Champagne.

HUGH, archbishop of Edessa. Having obtained relics of St. Thaddaeus and of King Abgar, he sent them with a letter to the archbishop of Rheims and to the canons of the Holy Apostles and of the monastery of St. Symphorian, about 1096, CLV, 477.

HUGH, count of Vermandois, son of Henry I, king of the Franks, set out for the holy war, performed many distinguished deeds, and died of a wound in 1102. With other leaders he wrote a letter to all the faithful of the Christian commonwealth in 1098, CLV, 390.

HUGH, abbot of Flavigny. Born of imperial blood, he was born at Verdun in 1065 and, as a boy, was received into the monastery of St. Vitonus under Abbot Rodulf, where he was instructed in both sacred and secular learning. Afterwards he was elected abbot of Flavigny in Burgundy. He died in 1100. He is the author of the *Chronicle of Verdun*, CLIV, 9.

HUGH, archbishop of Lyons. Formerly a monk of St. Marcellus at Chalon, then made bishop of Die and legate of the Apostolic See, he was finally promoted to the see of Lyons in 1080. He died in 1106. Several letters and privileges from him survive, CLVII, 487.

HUGH (St.), abbot of Cluny. A Burgundian by birth, son of Dalmas of Semur and Countess Aremburga, he was born in 1023. From youth he professed monastic life at Cluny and had the Venerable Odilo as his teacher. Already prior when Odilo died, he became abbot; he died in 1108. His letters survive, CLIX, 845.

HUGH, count of Champagne and son of Count Theobald, made many gifts to the monastery of Molesme in 1104, confirming these donations by the fullest sanction. This Hugh founded the celebrated abbey of Clairvaux with St. Bernard in 1115, CLXXXV, 1444, 1447, 1449.

HUGH of St. Mary, monk of Fleury of the Order of St. Benedict, was eminent in learning and piety. His historical works survive: a *Treatise on Royal Power and Priestly [Col. 0474] Dignity*, a *Letter to Ivo*, and a *Life of the Holy Bishop Sacerdos of Limoges*. He died in 1119, CLXIII, 975.

HUGH, monk of Cluny, converted by the holy abbot of the same name, entered the monastery and was afterwards ordained priest. He wrote the Life of St. Hugh the Abbot at the beginning of the twelfth century (in 1120), CLIX, 917.

HUGH of Cléries, concerning whom we have learned very little, was an Angevin knight and was sent by Count Fulk V as envoy to King Louis. A short treatise by him survives concerning the mayoralty and seneschalship of France, in 1120, CLXIII, 1034.

HUGH of Ribemont. The biographers relate little concerning him. He wrote to a certain Grapho of Anjou concerning the nature and origin of the soul, showing himself in it to be truly both philosopher and theologian, in 1125, CLXXVI, 834.

HUGH, bishop of Portugal. Formerly a monk, he went to Spain with Bernard, bishop of Toledo, and his companions, where he soon became archdeacon of Compostela. In 1114, with the aid of Lady Theresa, queen of Portugal, he was made bishop of Portugal. He attended the Council of St. James of Compostela in 1125; he died in 1132. He wrote a History of Compostela, CLXX, 875.

HUGH (St.), bishop of Grenoble. He was a noble son of Odo of Valence; when he devoted himself to the clergy, he displayed such signs of holiness that he was made bishop of Grenoble. He died in 1132. His letters and diplomas survive, CLXVI, 1563.

HUGH II, duke of Burgundy, son of Odo I, defended the cause of Louis the Fat against the king of England; he died in 1142. He conducted certain business with Hugh, abbot of Auxerre, and the monks of Dijon, about 1103. He also assisted in the foundation of the nunnery of Tart in 1132, under Guilencus, bishop of Langres, CLXXXV, 1400, 1401, 1409.

HUGH of Dociac, archbishop of Sens. The biographers are silent about him, and he is known to us only through a consolatory letter which he wrote to the dean and canons of Paris concerning the death of the bishop, about 1142, CLXXIII, 1427.

HUGH of St. Victor, regular canon and prior. He was first educated among the canons of Hamersleben in Saxony, whence he came in 1118 to St. Victor’s at Paris, where he taught philosophy and theology. Free from all ambition, he refused every dignity; he died in his chair in 1142. He produced many writings, ascetical and dogmatic, as well as others of diverse kinds, CLXXV, 177.

HUGH FARSITUS. Several Hughs bear this surname Farsitus, and hence confusion has arisen. This one belongs to the twelfth century and seems to have been a regular canon in the abbey of St. John of the Vines before 1128. He is believed to have died in 1143. He wrote a little book on the miracles of the Blessed Virgin Mary in the city of Soissons, CLXXIX, 1774.

HUGH BOUEZ of Jouvencourt gave to the monastery of Clairvaux, without any reservation, whatever he possessed in the territory of Juvilla and Warencemont in 1147, CLXXXV, 991.

HUGH VII of Lusignan, count of Poitou, sent a certain Wiormand to Suger, to inform him fully concerning the affairs of Poitou. He departed for Palestine in 1147, where he is believed to have died in 1150, CLXXXVI, 1352.

HUGH, bishop of Auxerre, a contemporary of St. Bernard, with whom he had formed a friendship from early youth. Born from the noble stock of the counts of Mâcon, he was one of the thirty disciples who followed St. Bernard to Clairvaux. From there, because of his outstanding qualities, he was appointed abbot of Pontigny, and then bishop of Auxerre in 1136. He died in 1151. He wrote statutes for the abbey of St. Lupus, CLXXXI, 1739.

HUGH, bishop of Ostia. He was first a monk of Clairvaux under St. Bernard, to whom he wrote concerning the death of Pope Eugenius III in 1153, CLXXXII, 694.

HUGH of Helin, with the consent of his brother Baldwin and his sister Hermengard, sold to the chapter of the Holy Sepulchre the possessions which he had acquired in the territory of Huetdebes in Syria for three thousand Byzantine coins, in order to ransom himself from captivity, in 1158, CLV, 1158, 1160.

HUGH of Baux, knight, and his brothers write to Wibald, abbot of Corbie, concerning what they suffered at the hands of the count of Barcelona for the emperor’s cause, and entreat him to write to the emperor for them and bring relief to their misfortune, in 1153, CLXXXIX, 1430.

HUGH METELLUS, regular canon, was born at Toul in the land of the Leuci and had Tecelin as his teacher. He wrote many letters. He died about 1157, CLXXXVIII, 1270.

HUGH of Ville and his wife Heldiard had given to the abbey of Clairvaux all that they possessed in the territory of Gundree, Spain, in 1147, CLXXXV, 987.

HUGO of Amiens, archbishop of Rouen, was perhaps [Col. 0475] called “of Amiens” because he was descended from the counts of Amiens. He first professed the monastic life at Cluny in 1115. Having become prior of Saint Martial at Limoges, then abbot of Saint Pancras in England, he was thence elevated to the archbishopric of Rouen in 1129. He died in 1164. There survive letters by him and three books against the heretics of his time, CXCII, 1111. See also CLXXIX, 670; CLXXXVI, 1399, 1430.

HUGO, lord of Caesarea in Palestine, and his wife Isabel granted to the canons of the Holy Sepulchre the estate of Fessiculi, wholly free on every side and enclosed within defined boundaries, in 1166, CLV, 1238.

HUGO, a monk of Poitou and notary of William of Vézelay, flourished in the twelfth century, in 1167. By order of Abbot Pontius he wrote the history of the monastery of Vézelay, CXCIX, 1562.

HUGO ETHERIANUS, a native of Tuscany, although he lived at the court of Emperor Manuel, nevertheless took the side of the Latins in the disputes that divided them from the Greeks. He composed a work to demonstrate that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, and another book on the origin and nature of the soul. He died about 1170, CCII, 165.

HUGO of Folieto, so called from a suburb of ancient Corbie, was first a regular canon of Saint Lawrence of Helliac near Corbie, then became prior of Saint Lawrence at Amiens, and finally a cardinal, equally distinguished for learning and virtue. He wrote four books *On the Twelve Abuses of the Cloister* and two books *On Carnal and Spiritual Marriages*. He died in 1174, CXCVI, 1553.

HUGO of Campo Florido, bishop of Soissons, was one of the two men brought forward against Gilbert de la Porrée at the Synod of Paris in 1147. In succession he was chancellor of Louis VII, archdeacon of Arras, canon of Paris and of Orléans, and finally was consecrated bishop of Soissons in 1171. He died in 1175. Eight letters by him survive, CXCVI, 1583. See CLXII, 656 and following.

HUGO, cleric of Saint Thomas of Canterbury, to whom he sent a consolatory letter while living in exile in France. About 1175, CXC, 698.

HUGO, castellan of Saint Abraham in Syria, perhaps the brother of Ansbert, sold to a certain Martin one small plot of land for an annual rent of two Byzantine coins, with no year stated, twelfth century, CLV, 1210.

A certain HUGO, a Roman monk, wrote to Suger on behalf of a certain Master Peter, who had been bound by censures because of excesses, and who also had letters of recommendation from Cardinals Hugh and John, twelfth century, CLXXXVI, 1413.

HUGO RIGAUDUS gave certain lands and mills to Blessed Robert of Arbrissel and to his monastery of Fontevraud, twelfth century, CLXII, 1114.

HUGO, Cardinal Peter Leo, whom one must not confuse with the antipope Anacletus. He flourished in the time of Guarinus, prior of Saint Victor, to whom he wrote, expressing sympathy concerning certain actions of Ervisius, Guarinus’s predecessor, in 1192, CXCVI, 1392.

HUGO, prior of Saint Martin at Sées, wrote to Geoffrey, subprior of Saint Barbara, who had urged him to write the Life of Walter, in 1199, CCV, 874.

HUGO (Saint), bishop of Lincoln. Formerly a Carthusian monk, a man of the highest learning and holiness of life, he was elected bishop in 1185 and devoutly governed his church for fifteen years. He died in 1200. Letters, charters, and diplomas from him survive, CLIII, 937.

HUGO, duke of Burgundy, who ceded and gave the county of Langres to his uncle Walter, bishop of Langres; numerous charters are subscribed by him elsewhere. He flourished in the twelfth century, CLXXXV, 1435, 1453, 1465, 1475.

HUGO, cardinal of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, wrote to Suger, asking him kindly to receive Master Peter, who was bound by the bond of excommunication and repentant, twelfth century, CLXXXVI, 1414.

HUGO, abbot of Saint Mary of Adrianople and prior of Saint John at Constantinople. There survive letters by him to Louis the Younger, king of the Franks, from whom he requested letters of recommendation to the king of Sicily, whom he was going to visit, twelfth century, CLV, 1279; CC, 1373.

HUGO V, seventeenth abbot of Cluny, enjoyed great renown among all men. He issued very many statutes for the government of his abbey. He seems to have died at the beginning of the thirteenth century, in 1203, CCIX, 882.

HUGO, dean of the chapter of Saint Mary at Paris, established an endowment for the performance of the Mandatum on Maundy Thursday, for the benefit of all the clerics of the chapter, 1208, CCXII, 90.

HUGO, bishop of Riga, exercised an apostolic legation with Milo in the holy war against the Albigensians in 1209, CCXVI, 126.

HUGO, king of Cyprus, succeeded his father Aimery in 1205. [Col. 0476] He granted a privilege of immunity to the church of Lacridon in Cyprus, belonging to the canons of the Holy Sepulchre. He died in 1210, CLV, 1253.

HUGO, bishop of Langres, attests that Guy, canon of Langres and Auxerre, son of Bernard, lord of Spissia, granted to the church and brethren of Fontenay everything that he possessed in Marmunnia in 1220, CLXXXV, 1469.

HUGO, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Seine, and John of Saulz, dean of the diocese of Langres, attest that William of Montaigu, lord of Maclaein, a nobleman, granted to the brethren of Buxières of the order of Clairvaux half a measure of grain to be paid annually, in 1255, CLXXXV, 1428.

HUGO IV, duke of Burgundy, son and successor of Odo III. He set out for Palestine with Saint Louis, king of the Franks, and, having returned thence, died in 1272. He makes known an agreement made between Blanche, widow of Hervé of Sombernon, and the brethren of Buxières concerning the annual payment of half a measure of grain and the support of five households of serfs. He also confirmed certain gifts made by John of Montbarré to the monastery of Fontenay, CLXXXV, 1427, 1474.

HULDREUS of Lucenay, whose care in old age was undertaken by the monks of Fontenay, gave them one manor which he possessed at Fraviacum, with no year mentioned, twelfth century, CLXXXV, 1462.

HUMBALDUS, bishop of Ostia, lived in the twelfth century. There is a letter from him to Saint Thomas of Canterbury, in which he seeks to console him, CXC, 986.

HUMBALDUS, an illustrious man of Uriage, granted the church of Lenatia to the monastery of La Chapelle in the diocese of Bourges; but the charter lacks a year, CXXXII, 479.

HUMBERT, bishop of Silva Candida and cardinal. Born in Burgundy at the beginning of the eleventh century, he was first a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict in the monastery of Moyenmoutier of Saint Mansuetus in the diocese of Toul. He died about 1061. He wrote three books against the calumnies of the Greeks, against Nicetas, and against the Simoniacs, CXLIII, 911.

HUMBERT, archbishop of Besançon, teaches us in a letter how the dispute was ended between the mother church of Besançon and Odo of Champagne, nephew of Count William, concerning dependants whom Odo was claiming in the name of his authority over Quisgey, in 1155, LXXXV, 1456.

HUMBERT, abbot of the monastery of Charolles, makes known that he received from the canons of Blessed Mary at Paris, for an annually payable rent, a certain piece of land situated at Espiers, in 1164, CCV, 907.

HUNALDUS, an illustrious man, and his wife Deodata give to Berarius, bishop of Le Mans, while retaining the usufruct for themselves, everything that they possess in the village of Gaviriacum, which Berarius had granted them. A charter concerning this survives among the acts of the bishops of Le Mans, in 677, LXXXVIII, 1198.

HUNALDUS, monk of the monastery of Bonne-Espérance. There survives a letter by him to Provost John concerning Saint Hilary of Poitiers’ book *On the Trinity*. It is found at the end of the letters of Philip of Harvengt. He died in 1190, CCIII, 174.

HUNTBERT, also called HUMBERT and CHUNIBERT, abbot of the monastery of Mariscolensis, formerly built by Chronebert himself in honor of Saint Mary about 671. He bestowed many gifts upon it, as a charter shows, LXXXVIII, 1197.

HUNTIO, son of a certain Egilbern, gave certain property to the church of Saint Saviour at Werth in the reign of Emperor Louis II, in 821, XCIX, 813.

HYACINTH, cardinal of the Church of Rome, flourished under Alexander III; he sought to console the exiled Blessed Thomas, twelfth century, CXC, 987.

# I

IBBO was made bishop of Tours in 719. In the following year he granted extensive privileges to the monastery of Saint Martin of Tours. According to this charter, he was the successor of Bertho and Crotpert, LXXXVIII, 1264.

IDA (Saint), countess of Boulogne, daughter of Godfrey the Bearded and mother of the illustrious Godfrey, first king of Jerusalem. She died about 1113. Several diplomas concerning her, related in her Life, survive, CLV, 453 and following.

IDA, countess of Monts, attacked by accusations and fearing that a sentence of excommunication might be issued against herself or her possessions, wrote to Lambert, bishop of Arras, that she was ready to make satisfaction, at the beginning of the twelfth century, CLXII, 667.

IDATIUS, bishop of Aquae Flaviae, was born at Lemica, a city of the province of Gallaecia, in 388; he was raised to episcopal rank in 427. He was appointed envoy to Aetius, [Col. 0477] commander of the Romans, in 431. His *Chronicle* and a list of consuls survive. He died in 450, LI, 870.

IDATIUS, bishop of Barcelona. Biographers report very little about him. Two letters by him survive: one to Saint Julian of Toledo, the other to the bishop of Narbonne, to whom he also sent Saint Julian’s book of prognostics, in 690, XCVI, 845.

HYGINUS (Saint), pope and martyr, succeeded Saint Telesphorus. During his pontificate Valentinus and Cerdo came to Rome, teaching impious blasphemies; that holy pontiff vigorously opposed them. He died in 143. Certain spurious decretals are attributed to him in Isidore Mercator, CXXX, 107.

IMBERT, monk of Grandmont. We know nothing of him except that he was the companion of William Dandin in the translation of the relics of Saint Ursula from the diocese of Cologne to the church of Grandmont in 1174, CCIV, 1221.

A certain IMINA bestowed many gifts upon the monastery of Werth, in which Blessed Ulger had formerly flourished, during the reign of Emperor Louis the Pious, in 820, XCIX, 799.

INA, king of the Saxons and successor of Ceadwalla, reigned from 689 to 726. He granted liberty to the churches founded under Aldhelm and to all who lived in them, in 704, LXXXIX, 1113.

INGALLICE, priest and monk. He wrote to Saint Lull, still a deacon, and sent him several small gifts made in the monastery, about 753–819.

INGEBURGIS, queen of the Franks, complains to Pope Celestine III that her husband King Philip, having repudiated her, joined himself to the daughter of the duke of Merania, in 1196, CCVI, 1277.

INGOARA, a virgin consecrated to God and nun of the monastery of Saint Peter at Sens, under her brother Ebbo, bishop of Sens, bestowed many gifts upon her monastery in 711. She had a sister named Lotheria, who likewise made a gift to the same monastery, LXXXVIII, 1258.

INNOCENT I (Saint), pope. An Albanian by nationality, he was a man endowed with remarkable acuteness and prudence; he issued constitutions for the whole Church and concerning monastic rules; he condemned Pelagius and Celestius; he died in 418. His letters and decrees survive, XX, 458.

INNOCENT II, pope. A Roman by nationality, he was first a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict, then became cardinal-deacon; finally, after the death of Honorius, he was elected in 1130. He died in 1143. His letters and privileges survive, CLXXIX, 21.

INNOCENT III, pope. One of the Church’s most celebrated pontiffs, he was scarcely thirty-seven years old when he was elected to succeed Pope Celestine III in 1198. Born from the noble stock of the counts of Segni, he sat for eighteen years and died in 1216. Innumerable letters and privileges, sermons, and other writings by him survive, CCXIV, 21.

IOTSALD, monk and afterward abbot of Cluny, was a disciple of Saint Odilo, whose Life he wrote. According to an ancient charter, he was the son of Bernard and Ada. His epitaph may be read on the outer wall of the old church of Saint Peter. He flourished about 1060, CXLII, 831.

IRENE, empress of Constantinople. Born at Athens of an undistinguished family, she became the wife of Leo IV, son of Constantine Copronymus, because of her intelligence and beauty; she exercised great authority in imperial affairs. After Leo’s death, she held the reins of government and restored the veneration of images. But when her son came to the throne, he exiled her to the Propontis; restored to power, she ordered Constantine himself to have his eyes put out, and was again driven into exile by Nicephorus, where she died in 803. Several letters from her to Pope Adrian I survive, CXXIX, 199, 210.

IRMINA gave the village of Stanheim to the monastery of Echternach, of which she was abbess; this was done at Trier under King Childebert III in 704, LXXXIX, 537.
