IRMINTRUDIS, queen of the Franks and wife of Charles the Bald, lived in the middle of the ninth century, 860. A letter from her to Heribald survives, CXIX, 570.

ISAAC, abbot of l’Étoile. He chose the monastic life in a Cistercian monastery. He was then sent to a certain island, whose name and location are not indicated, in order to found a monastery. In 1147 he became abbot of l’Étoile in the diocese of Poitiers, where he died in 1169. Fifty sermons and a treatise *On Loving God* by him survive, CXCIV, 1683.

ISAAC, bishop of Langres, surnamed “the Good” on account of his kindness; formerly a monk of Saint-Germain-des-Prés under Abbot Hilduin, then a deacon in the church of Laon, and finally bishop in 856. He died in 880. His canons survive, CXXIV, 1071.

ISAIAH (Saint), a Syrian abbot of the fourth century, wrote certain works that survive among the sayings of the elders. In addition, twenty-eight highly useful homilies are attributed to him, CIII, 427.

ISARN, bishop of Toulouse, entrusted to Hugh V, abbot of Cluny, and Hunaldo of Moissac the church of Saint Saturninus in the city of Toulouse, with no year mentioned, CLIX, 982.

ISEMBERT, priest of Poitiers, wrote a letter to the bishop of Angers, offering an excuse for not attending the solemnity of a dedication to which he had been invited, year uncertain, CXLI, 270.

ISIDORE (Saint), bishop of Seville. Born of noble stock in 570 at Cartagena, the son of Severianus, prefect of that city, and brother of Saints Leander and Fulgentius, he restored ecclesiastical discipline in Spain and was the author and head of all the councils over which he presided; he died in 638. He left many works, dogmatic, moral, and miscellaneous, LXXXI–LXXXIV.

ISIDORE MERCATOR, or “the Sinner.” The author also called Pseudo-Isidore, because he was formerly confused with Saint Isidore. He produced many forged and spurious works; year uncertain, CXXX, 9.

ISIDORE of Pacensis, so called from the city of Pax in Lusitania, today Beja, then still subject to the Moors, of which he was bishop. His birth and death are wholly uncertain. A *Chronicle*, or *Epitome of the Emperors and Arabs in Spain*, is attributed to him. He lived in the eighth century, XCVI, 1246.

ISNARD, descended from his grandfather Teudon and his father Sulpicius, and himself devoted to military service among the Franks, granted in 1080 the church of Buxet, situated in Perche, to the monastery of Saint Peter at Chartres, CLV, 264.

ISO, monk of Saint Gall. From earliest childhood he was entrusted to the monastery of Saint Gall for education, and so advanced in letters that he was judged fit to teach others. Therefore he was placed over the schools of his monastery and had many outstanding pupils; but, seized by illness in the very flower of youth, he died in 871. Two books by him *On the Miracles of Saint Othmar* survive, CXXI, 780.

A certain IVO, an illustrious man, granted in perpetual gift the cell of Saint Gauzburgis, situated in the territory of Bellême, to the monastery of Saint Peter at Chartres, in 1061, CLV, 297.

IVO (Blessed), bishop of Chartres. Born in the Beauvaisis of distinguished parents, he devoted himself at Paris to humane letters and philosophy, and studied theology at the monastery of Bec under Blessed Lanfranc. He was first abbot of Saint-Quentin at Beauvais, then was made bishop of Chartres by Pope Urban II in 1092. He suffered no few injuries from King Philip because he rebuked the king’s manner of life. He died in 1115. His *Book of Decrees*, *Panormia*, sermons, letters, and chronicle survive, CLXI–CLXII.

# J

JACOB and TIMASIUS, born of a most honorable family, were at one time friends and disciples of Pelagius. They professed the monastic life and continence; finally, through the works of Saint Augustine, they were brought back from error to sound faith. Augustine addressed to them his book *On Nature and Grace*. Their letter to Augustine survives, in 415, XXXIII, 741.

JACOB, deacon of Edessa, lived with Saint Nonnus and wrote the Life of Saint Pelagia, whose conversion and burial at Jerusalem he witnessed. He mentions the Saracens, and therefore these matters must be referred to the sixth century, LXXIII, 663.

JACOB of Vitry, bishop of Ptolemais and cardinal, historian and hagiographer. Born at Argenteuil or Vitry on the Seine, he died in 1244. There survives from him a testimony concerning Saint Bernard, CLXXXV, 628.

JACOB, lord of Sauz, and his wife Mary founded the Chapel of Saint James of Sauz with a revenue sufficient for the food and clothing of one priest. He also granted to the canons of Blessed Mary of Sauz a fourth part of the tithe of Sauz in exchange for sixty Viennese pounds, in 1248, CLXXXV, 1436.

JACOB, custos of the principal church of Udine, knowing that he and his church depended only upon the patriarch himself, forbade the patriarch’s archdeacon to hold a synod in that church without the chapter’s consent. He did so not from perverse intention, but lest its immunity be injured in the future, in 1289, XCIX, 650.

JACOB of Boonen, archbishop of Mechelen, granted certain indulgences to those who visited and venerated the image of Blessed Mary in the church of Affligem in 1647. This image is said to have spoken to Saint Bernard, CLXXXV, 1829.

JADER, confessor. See FELIX, African confessor.

JEREMIAH, archbishop of Sens. First a monk of Saint-Riquier, then abbot of Saint Columba, he was finally elected bishop and successor of Magnon. Of his writings, only a letter to Frotharius, bishop of Toul, survives, in 828, CV, 729.

JESSE, bishop of Amiens. Nothing is transmitted concerning his birth, race, or family; he was elected in 798. He attended the Council of Paris in 829. Soon afterward he was deposed because he had supported Lothair’s rebellion against his father. Restored, [Col. 0479] he was again compelled to follow Lothair into Italy, where he died in 836. His treatise on baptism survives, CV, 780.

JOHN, bishop and patriarch of Jerusalem, once had a dispute with Saint Epiphanius because of the ordination of a certain priest. But after Epiphanius had written so that he might regard himself as excused, peace was made between them; John wrote back to Epiphanius, condemning the Origenists, about 410, XXII, 769.

JOHN CASSIAN. See CASSIAN.

JOHN, bishop of Antioch. He had joined the bishops who excommunicated Nestorius and adhered to the ordination of Maximinian, about 433, L, 591.

JOHN, deacon, concerning whose people and native land we find nothing, wrote a letter to a certain Senarius, an illustrious man, concerning various rites of baptism, at the end of the fifth century, in 496, LIX, 397.

JOHN, papal legate. See GERMANUS.

JOHN, bishop of Nicopolis, asked Pope Hormisdas by letter what he ought to do in a certain case; Hormisdas referred him to his own written memorandum, in 516, LXIII, 387.

JOHN, patriarch of Constantinople, became patriarch under Emperor Justin after first professing the Catholic faith. Having repudiated Acacius and all heretics, he agreed with Pope Hormisdas concerning the day on which Easter should be celebrated. His letters survive among those of Pope Hormisdas, in 520, LXIII, 429 and elsewhere.

JOHN II, pope, surnamed Mercurius on account of his eloquence. A Roman by nationality, he was elected in 532 and held the Holy See only three years. His letters survive, LXVI, 9.

JOHN, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, translated into Latin Book VI of the *Lives of the Fathers*, *The Sayings of the Elders*. He is mentioned by Sigebert. Some maintain that this John was the same man who occupied the Roman see after Pelagius and died in 572, LXXIII, 991.

JOHN III, pope, surnamed Catellinus. A Roman by nationality, born of Anastasius, he succeeded Pope Pelagius I in 560 and died in 573. We possess letters by him. (See JOHN the subdeacon in the preceding entry.) LXII, 9.

JOHN, archbishop of Ravenna, was rebuked by Saint Gregory the Great because he had extended the use of the pallium beyond the custom of his predecessors. He excuses himself to Gregory concerning this matter, in 604, LXXVII, 684.

JOHN MOSCHUS, surnamed Eucrates because of his piety, was a monk of Jerusalem; but he journeyed through the East and Egypt to visit monasteries with Sophronius, his disciple and companion. He dedicated to Sophronius the book *Spiritual Meadow*, written during the journey; thence he went to Rome and died about 619. His letters survive, LXXIV, 119.

JOHN, abbot of Biclar. Of Gothic origin, he embraced the monastic life, suffered much from the Arians, and was exiled to Barcelona. Nevertheless, he founded a monastery in a place called Biclar, of which he was abbot; afterward, under King Reccared, he became bishop in 592 and died in 620. His *Chronicle* survives, LXXII, 860.

JOHN IV, pope. A Dalmatian by nationality and son of Venantius, he was elected in 640 and succeeded Severinus. He crushed the errors of the Monothelites and held the Holy See until 642. His letters survive, LXXX, 598.

JOHN V, pope. A Syrian by nationality, successor of Benedict II, a most vigorous and learned man, but he sat only one year. His decree survives, in 686, XCVI, 425.

JOHN, bishop of Pistoia, elected in 700. By a written undertaking he bound himself toward Balthasar, bishop of Lucca, that thereafter no right of the church of Lucca would be diminished by him; this was not unusual in those times, LXXXVII, 1350.

JOHN VI, pope. A Greek by birth, he succeeded Sergius at the beginning of the eighth century, in 705. His letters survive, LXXXIX, 36.

JOHN VII, pope. A Greek by nationality, a most learned man endowed with eloquence, he succeeded John VI but sat only two years. Only his letter to Ethered, king of the Mercians, and to Alfred, king of the English, survives, in 707, LXXXIX, 53.

JOHN, patriarch of Constantinople, together with certain other bishops, at the instigation of Bardanes, who had usurped imperial power, pronounced an anathema against the Sixth General Council, at which the Monothelites had been condemned. His letter to Pope Constantine survives, in 713, LXXXIX, 341.

JOHN DAMASCENE (Saint), priest. Greek in speech but Syrian by nation, he was taught by a certain monk, Cosmas Damianus by name, who had been taken captive by the Saracens. He then served as minister to the caliph of that province; having left that office, he withdrew to the monastery of Saint Sabas near [Col. 0480] Jerusalem, where he died in 760. Several writings by him survive, among which the Life of the blessed Barlaam and Josaphat, king of the Indians, is noteworthy, LXXIII, 443.

JOHN, deacon and chancellor of Constantinople, attended the Second Ecumenical Council of Nicaea. He composed a refutation against the Monothelites, who were accustomed to accuse Christians, in 787, CXXIX, 375.

JOHN (Aurelius Flavius), an illustrious man and friend of Paul Alvarus of Córdoba, who sent him several letters. He flourished in Spain in the ninth century, in 860, CXXI, 420.

JOHN SCOTUS. See SCOTUS ERIGENA.

JOHN, bishop of Cambrai, gave to a certain priest Ursio a general letter addressed to all bishops, asking that Ursio be received in any parish of their dioceses, in 865, CXXIX, 1391.

JOHN VIII, pope. He was archdeacon of the Roman Church when he succeeded Adrian II in 872. He died in 882. He wrote more than three hundred letters or privileges, which are inserted in collections of councils, CXXVI, 648.

JOHN IX, pope. A native of Tivoli, he was first a monk and deacon. After Theodore’s death, he was elected in 898; he sat only two years and died in 900. His letters and a canon concerning the election of a pope survive, CXXXI, 28.

JOHN X, pope. A Roman by nationality, son of Sergius, he was first bishop of Bologna, then archbishop of Ravenna, and finally made pope in 912. He was a man born more for warfare than for the priesthood; for he dishonored the latter by various crimes. Letters of lesser importance by him survive; he died in 826, CXXXII, 778.

JOHN XI, pope, succeeded Stephen VII in 931, through the favor of Guy, count of Tuscany. But having fallen into the hands of his enemy Alberic, he was held in custody until his death in 936. You have several letters and privileges by him, CXXXII, 1055.

JOHN, monk of Monte Cassino. An Italian by nationality, he was brought by Odo, abbot of Cluny, on Odo’s return from Rome as far as Ticinum (Pavia), where Odo appointed him abbot. Because he had followed Saint Odo in many places, he wrote his Life. He flourished about 954, CXXXII, 883.

JOHN XII, pope. Son of the impious Alberic who was tyrant at Rome, he seized the Apostolic See in 955, in the time of Emperor Constantine Copronymus; afterward, however, with the consent of the people and the whole clergy, he was lawfully ordained, but was deposed in 963 and died in the following year. His letters and privileges survive, CXXXIII, 1011.

JOHN XIII, pope. Formerly bishop of Narni, he succeeded Leo VIII in 965. He died in 972. His letters and decrees survive, CXXXV, 950.

JOHN SMERA POLOVECIUS, a Russian by nationality, physician and rhetorician of King Wladimir, flourished about 990. Sent by the king among various peoples to learn all their religions, he travelled through Europe, Asia, and Africa in turn. When he reached Alexandria, he remained there for several days and, having been baptized in the sacred font, dissuaded the king from following the Greek religion and urged him instead to profess the Roman religion, as he himself had already done, CLI, 1405.

JOHN XIV, pope. Rector of the church of Pavia, he succeeded Benedict VII. Having held the see only eight months, he was deposed and cast into chains in the fortress of Monte Sant’Angelo, where he perished amid infamy and misery about 995, CXXXVII, 357.

JOHN XV, pope. A Roman by birth, whose father was a priest, he was elected by common suffrage after the tyrant’s destruction in 985; he died in 996. Three letters and privileges by him survive, CXXXVII, 826.

JOHN CANAPARIUS, monk of the monastery of Saint Boniface, built at Rome between the Aventine Hill and the Tiber, to which he had withdrawn with a few friends. He is said later to have been elected abbot after the death of his predecessor Leo. He is the author of the Life of Saint Adalbert, bishop of Prague. He died in 1004, CXXXVIII, 859.

JOHN, Venetian deacon and servant of Doge Peter Orseolo, was sent more than once as envoy to Emperor Otto III because of his great prudence and sagacity. He wrote a Venetian Chronicle, though he drew from obscure sources and fabulous narratives, in 1008, CXXXIX, 871.

JOHN XVIII, pope, formerly John Fasanus or Fassanus. A Roman by birth, he succeeded John XVII, who had sat only four months, under Emperor Henry the Younger; he died in 1009. His letters and privileges survive, CXXXIX, 1472.

JOHN XIX, pope. Born of the noble house of the counts of Tusculum and brother of his predecessor Benedict VIII, he held the Holy See from 1024 until 1033, when he departed this life. He issued letters and privileges, CXLI, 1114.

JOHN of Garland, grammarian and poet, an Englishman by nationality. His life is unknown to us. There survive his work *Synonyms*, [Col. 0481] and certain metrical fragments on equivocal terms, on the mysteries of the Church, and on orthography. He lived about 1040, CL, 1375.

JOHN, bishop of Sabina and cardinal, was appointed by Pope Leo IX. He attended the Roman council under Nicholas II. He died in 1059. His complaint against the monks of Farfa, from 1051, survives, CXLIII, 907.

JOHN GUALBERT (Saint). See GUALBERT.

JOHN LIPRANDUS, disciple of Blessed Peter Damian, appointed after him prior of Fonte Avellana and finally made bishop of Gubbio, wrote the Life of his holy master Damian about 1078, CXLIV, 89, 113.

JOHN, bishop of Avranches. Born about the beginning of the eleventh century, son of Ralph, count of Bayeux, and uterine brother of Richard, duke of Normandy, he was transferred from the see of Avranches to that of Rouen and died in 1079. His book *On Ecclesiastical Offices* survives, CXLVII, 9.

JOHN, abbot of Fécamp, called Joanelinus because of his small stature, was first a monk of Saint Benignus at Dijon, then prior and afterward abbot of Fécamp. He received the abbey of Erbrecten from Emperor Henry III. He died in 1079. His small book of prayers and several letters survive, CXLVII, 441.

JOHN COTTO, or Cottonius. We have learned absolutely nothing concerning him. Most excellent works on music are attributed to him. He flourished in the eleventh century, CL, 1391.

JOHN, bishop of Tusculum, also called bishop of Marsi, was made cardinal by Urban II. At the Council of Vasto he delivered his opinion with great gravity. He was of ready courage, and when the impious emperor cast Pope Paschal II into prison, he called the people to arms to bring assistance. He died under that same Paschal II about 1112. His address to the Roman people and letter to Richard, bishop of Albano, survive, CLX, 1035.

JOHN, monk of Bèze, of whom nothing certain is reported, flourished about the beginning of the twelfth century, in 1115. He is considered the author of the Chronicle of Bèze, CLXII, 733.

JOHN, monk and deacon of Saint-Ouen. He was distinguished among his contemporaries in learning and virtue; at the Council of Reims in 1119, when scarcely twenty years old, he served as secretary. He wrote the Life of Saint Nicholas in prose and verse. Four sermons by him survive, CLXII, 1154.

JOHN Michaelensis, whom we know only to have attended the Council of Troyes in 1128 and there performed the office of secretary. The Rule of the Templars survives from him, CLXVI, 854.

JOHN of Constance. Whether he was a bishop, priest, simple monk, or abbot is unknown to us. There survives from him a letter, or preface, to Abbot Geoffrey for a book on ecclesiastical computation. He lived in 1137, CLXIII, 1479.

JOHN, bishop of Acre. He granted the brethren of the Holy Sepulchre the right to build a church at Acre, and also gave them a church in the territory of the estate of Amienas, in 1138, CLV, 1170.

JOHN, abbot of the monastery of Casa Maria, founded in 1005 in the territory of Veroli in Italy, of the Order of Saint Benedict. He formed such a close friendship with Saint Bernard that he later joined himself to the Cistercians. His letter to Saint Bernard survives, in 1110, CLXXXII, 590.

JOHN, bishop of Alet. Formerly a Cistercian monk, he appealed to Saint Bernard of Clairvaux when certain persons slandered him, twelfth century, CLXXXII, 680.

JOHN, abbot of Ferrara, asked Suger to grant him a delay for paying the remaining money demanded from the monastery, in 1147, CLXXXVI, 1406.

JOHN, monk of Saint Lawrence at Liège, brother of Gislebert, wrote a vision of the state of souls after death, a miracle of Saint Lawrence the martyr, and certain poems, in 1147, LXXX, 177.

JOHN, cardinal of Saint Mary the New, commends to Abbot Suger the case of Master Peter, entrusted to his judgment by Pope Eugenius. There survives from him a letter to Wibald, abbot of Corbie, in 1146, CLXXXVI, 1414; CLXXXIX, 1163.

JOHN, abbot of Frithesell, informs the Venerable Wibald, abbot of Corbie, that he will shortly go to the king and asks whether Wibald has any message to send by him, in 1150, CLXXXIX, 1292.

JOHN, notary, warns his lords that Welf, traitor to King Conrad, having received money, is allied with the king of Sicily, that the pope himself adheres to the same king, and that they should therefore beware of plots, in 1151, CLXXXIX, 1323.

JOHN CIRITTA, abbot of Tarouca in Spain. A soldier under King Alfonso VI, he gained distinction in arms against the Moors; moved by God’s grace, he became a monk and abbot of the monastery of Saint John of Tarouca. He passed to God in 1164. He composed the Rule of the military Order of Avis, CLXXXVIII, 1661.

[Col. 0482] JOHN, Roman deacon, called “the Younger” to distinguish him from another celebrated writer who flourished under John VIII, was a canon of the Basilica of the Saviour at the Lateran. He wrote to Pope Alexander III concerning the Roman Church in 1149, CXCIV, 1541.

JOHN, Carthusian monk of Portes, calls himself the brother in flesh and spirit of Stephen, monk of the same monastery. Five spiritual letters by him survive, addressed both to his brother Stephen of Chalmet and to his nephew Bernard of the same order. He flourished in the twelfth century, CLIII, 899.

JOHN PATRICII and his wife Bruna exchanged two estates which they possessed in Syria with the canons of the Holy Sepulchre for two others in the same region under King Fulk, twelfth century, CLV, 1214.

JOHN GOTHMANNUS and his wife Amandala sold to the canons of the Holy Sepulchre a certain piece of land which they possessed at Jerusalem. This was done in 1161 under King Baldwin, CLV, 1200.

JOHN, the Saracen, flourished about 1170. There is a letter in John of Salisbury in which he informs him that he has translated Saint Dionysius’s book *On the Celestial Hierarchy of Angels*, and indeed not without great difficulty, in 1170, CXCIX, 143, 259.

JOHN, count of Augy, whose father had granted the church of Arrouaise to the canons of Saint Victor at Paris, in 1174, CXCVI, 1391.

JOHN of Salisbury, bishop of Chartres. An Englishman by nationality, he came to Paris, where Abelard was his master, and afterward Alberic and Gilbert de la Porrée. At first he was a cleric of Canterbury; then, with the approval of the king and clergy, he was elected bishop of Chartres about 1176. He died in 1180. Many letters by him survive, the book *Entheticus*, and the Life of Saint Anselm, bishop of Canterbury, CXCIX, 9 and following.

JOHN, called “the Hermit,” because he often visited Blessed Bernard in the solitude of Clairvaux, arranged the Life of that holy Doctor in two books. In 1180, CLXXXV, 531.

JOHN, provost of the monastery of Bonne-Espérance, who seems to have been the teacher of Philip of Harvengt, to whom he wrote two letters concerning Saint Hilary of Poitiers’ books *On the Trinity*. He flourished at the end of the twelfth century, in 1188, CCIII, 170.

JOANNES, abbot of the Cistercian monastery of Beaugé, flourished at the end of the twelfth century, in the year 1109. Several letters of his to Geoffrey, subprior of Saint Barbara in Neustria, survive, CCV, 827 and elsewhere.

JOANNES, bishop of Cambrai, lived at the end of the twelfth century, as appears from a letter which he wrote to Stephen, bishop of Tournai, CCXI, 504.

JOHN GUITARD, burgess of Mahumeria in Syria, takes an oath, as do all the other burgesses whose names are preserved, twelfth century, CLV, 1222.

JOHN GIRBALD granted as a gift to Blessed Mary of Fontevraud the harbour of Chalcio and all the land beside the bank; and he himself received from Hersendis, prioress of that place, a colt, twelfth century, CLXII, 1114.

JOHN F., abbot of Dol, with the consent of the entire community of brethren, gave to the nuns of Fontevraud level ground and the wood of Ursan; this was done at Dol, in the presence of Leodegar, archbishop, and Robert of Arbrissel, at the beginning of the twelfth century, CLXII, 1118.

JOHN OF CORNWALL, according to some, is the author of the *Apology concerning the Incarnate Word*, published at Paris among the works of Blessed Hugh of Saint Victor. Who he was and when he flourished is uncertain, twelfth century (?), CLXXVII, 295.

JOHN, master of the schools at Orléans. See ELIAS.

JOHN BELETH, Parisian theologian and rector of that faculty, very learned in sacred letters and equally skilled in philosophy, quick of intellect and scholastic in speech, was distinguished among the doctors. Sermons and a book *On the Divine Offices* survive by him. He died in 1190, CCII, 9.

JOHN DE BELMEIS, archbishop of Lyon, surnamed “Of the White Hands.” An Englishman by birth, formerly treasurer of the church of York, a generous and learned man, he was made bishop of Poitiers in 1162 and then raised by Pope Lucius to the see of Lyon in 1181. Finally, having resigned his office, he voluntarily withdrew to the monastery of Clairvaux. We have letters and charters concerning him, in 1201, CCIX, 873.

JOHN, bishop of Poitiers, lived in the twelfth century. He maintained a close friendship with Blessed Thomas of Canterbury and was initiated into the innermost secrets of his soul; he assisted him both in word and deed. Several letters to the blessed martyr survive by him, twelfth century, CXC, 1022 and following.

JOHN, prior of Saint Swithun’s, Winchester. He sent to Alan, prior of Canterbury, a letter dealing with spiritual matters. He flourished in the twelfth century, CXC, 1483.

JOHN OF NAPLES, cardinal-priest of the Roman Church, at the title of Saints John and Paul, consoles the illustrious exiled archbishop of Canterbury, twelfth century, CXC, 988.

JOHN DE CECCANO, master of the knights of Calatrava, takes an oath to the Roman Church to defend and preserve the temporal rights of Saint Peter, 1201, CCXVII, 286.

JOHN, abbot of Sainte-Geneviève in Paris, with the consent of the whole convent, reached an agreement with Odo, bishop of Paris, concerning certain churches of Sainte-Geneviève in Paris, in 1202, CCXIV, 1187.

JOHN DE CASEMATE, who had been sent as legate by Pope Innocent III into the kingdom of Bosnia, is informed by him of the donation of Sibyl, wife of the podestà of Constantinople. He then proposes that new bishoprics be created, 1203, CCXV, 153.

JOHN, an Armenian Catholic, wrote to Innocent III in 1205 and makes a profession of obedience toward the Holy Roman Church, CCXV, 692.

JOHN OF SAINT-LAURENT, archivist of the Roman Church and cardinal, received, in Innocent III’s name, liege homage from Count Hildebrand, in 1207, CCXVII, 298.

JOHN WILLIAM, a monk, wrote to Guibert of Florennes and declares to him that he deservedly suffers much from an unjust abbot, because he himself had formerly been the author of many evils to others. He flourished about 1208, CCXI, 1302.

JOHN, tenth king of Jerusalem, and Queen Maria granted exemption concerning a garden purchased by the canons of the Holy Sepulchre, Santio then being prior. This was done at Acre in 1211, CLV, 1236.

JOHN, king of England, having been excommunicated, sent four of his barons with letters to Pope Innocent III and accepted all the conditions, in 1213, CCXVI, 876, 878.

JOHN DE MONTEBARRO. See HUGH V, duke of Burgundy.

JOHN, lord of Fontaines, son of the lord of Saulz, gave the brethren of the Valley of Scholars three sextaries of walnut oil from 1220 onward, as Theobald, master of the purses of Bayeux, attests, CLXXX, 1478.

JOHN ALGRIN, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, surnamed of Abbeville from his birthplace, flourished in France in the thirteenth century. He was celebrated for learning and scholarship. First dean of Amiens, then bishop of Besançon in 1225, he was finally made cardinal. He died in 1237. Various sermons on the temporal cycle and the saints, on the Epistles and Gospels for the whole year, and annotations to the commentaries of Thomas the Cistercian survive by him, CCVI, 11.

JOHN DE THIELRODE, monk of Saint Bavo, compiled a work in 1294, of which certain excerpts survive concerning the genealogy of the counts of Flanders down to 1130, CCIX, 187.

JOHN DE SANCY, abbot of Clairvaux, sent to his fellow abbots a complaint concerning the taxes imposed upon him day after day by King Philip, about 1298, CLXXXV, 1851.

JOHN, priest of Würzburg, seems to have flourished in the thirteenth century. He is the author of a description of the Holy Land, CLV, 1053.

JOHN, abbot of Clairvaux, flourished about 1335. He established an annual rent of five Tours pounds, so that fish might be bought on the feast-day of Saint Bernard for distribution among the monks of his abbey, CLXXXV, 1754.

JOHN, lord of Fontaines, together with his brother Robert and his mother Simona, lady of Fontaines, came to an agreement among themselves concerning the lordship of Fontaines in 1350. This charter survives in French, CLXXXV, 1502.

JOHN OF CHÂLONS, abbot of the monastery of Clairvaux, flourished at the end of the fifteenth century. A charter concerning him survives from 1499, CLXXXV, 1767.

JOHN, abbot of Sponheim, delivered a panegyric on Blessed Rupert, abbot of Deutz, at the request of Gerlach of Breitbach, abbot of the same monastery, fourteenth or fifteenth century, CLXVII, 11.

JOBIANUS, subdeacon of Brescia, in 767 gave certain estates situated in the territory of Ferronia to Anselberga, abbess of the monastery of Saint Saviour and daughter of King Desiderius, LXXXVII, 1389.

JOCERANNUS, bishop of Langres, flourished at the beginning of the twelfth century. In 1121, in the presence of Humbald, archbishop and primate of Lyon, he confirmed to Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, immunity from tithes. There also survives a charter of his by which he restores to the canons of his church the church of Saint Martin of Fontaines-de-Pré in Champagne, in 1120, CLXXXV, 977, 1451.

JONAS, abbot of Elnone, was a disciple of Saints Columbanus, Attala, and Eustace. According to some he was Irish or Scottish; according to others, an Italian from Bobbio or Livine. [Col. 0484] He wrote the Lives of Saints Columbanus and Eustace, abbots, and a book on the miracles of Saint John of Réôme. He flourished in 670, LXXXVII, 1010.

JONAS, bishop of Orléans and successor of Theodulf, attended the Council of Paris in 827. Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, mentions him with praise; he died in 843. Three books *On the Instruction of Laymen* and a short work *On Royal Instruction* survive by him, CVI, 118.

JONAS, canon of Saint Victor in Paris, was sent to Caesaris Burgum; since that place was displeasing to him, he asks Ervisius, prior of that abbey, to recall him to Saint Victor, about 1170, CXCVI, 1388.

JORDAN DE LORON, bishop of Limoges. Born of noble stock and provost of Saint Leonard’s, he succeeded Gerard in the see of Limoges in 1024. He was elected provost in the assembly of Saint Leonard held at Saint Julian’s by the most prudent William, duke of Aquitaine. He died in 1052. Letters, charters, and acts of the Second Council of Limoges survive concerning him, CXLII, 1347.

JOSCELIN, bishop of Salisbury. A letter to Suger survives by him, 1148, CLXXXVI, 1364; CXC, 1038.

JOSCELIN, archbishop of Tours, who was called Josse and Jodocus. Originally from Brittany, he had formerly been bishop of Saint-Brieuc. A charter and six letters of his to King Louis the Younger survive, 1174, CXCVI, 1534.

JOSCERANNUS, archbishop of Lyon, and Anserinus, archbishop of Besançon, flourished about the beginning of the twelfth century. They inform Gerald, bishop of Angoulême, that the dispute between Gurhan, abbot of Sainte-Croix of Quimperlé, and Hervé, abbot of Redon, had been settled by Pope Paschal II, and that the case of the abbot of Sainte-Croix had been declared just and lawful, CLXXII, 1326.

JOSEPH, scholar and disciple of Alcuin. By his master’s command he abridged Saint Jerome’s commentaries on the prophet Isaiah. Yet only a poem in honour of Saint Ludger survives by him, in 804, XCIX, 777, 821.

JOSEPH, priest, chancellor of the king of Aquitaine and afterwards tutor of King Louis, flourished in the ninth century, in 846. He wrote the history of the translation of the bodies of Saints Ragnobert and Zeno, of which he was an eyewitness, CVI, 889, 92.

JOSEPH, master, excuses himself to Guibert of Florennes for not having visited him. He is, however, displeased that Guibert calls himself a master, and urges him, so far as lies in his power, to make his monastery of Florennes flourish. He wrote at the beginning of the thirteenth century, in 1201, CCXI, 1305, 1307.

JULIANIA ANICIA informs Pope Hormisdas of the peace restored to the Eastern Church through his legates and asks him not to allow them to depart until it is secured. But who this most noble woman was is not apparent, 519, LXIII, 451, 488.

JULIAN (Flavius Claudius), son of the emperor Julius Constantius. He attained the imperial office in 361. All know with what hatred he persecuted Christians and the faith of Christ. A fragment of a rescript in favour of the Donatists, taken from Saint Augustine, survives concerning him, XI, 1179.

JULIAN, bishop of Eclanum, a Pelagian. That boastful defender of the Pelagian heresy was born in Apulia and, according to Mercator, was ordained by Pope Innocent; but whether he was a bishop and where he held his see is uncertain. He died in 455. Fragments by him survive in Isidore Mercator, XXI, 1167; XLIV, 641; XLVIII, 109, 508, 622.

JULIAN POMERIUS. See POMERIUS.

JULIAN (Saint), bishop of Toledo. He was born at Toledo, where he was baptized and educated under the direction of Saint Eugenius, archbishop. Having passed through every grade of the clergy, he was finally appointed to Eugenius’s place after the latter’s death. He died in 690. He wrote a book *On Foreknowledge*, a treatise on the sixth age of the world, a history of the war of King Wamba, and verses, XCVI, 427.

JULIUS I (Saint), pope. A Roman by birth, he was consecrated in 337, during the reign of Constantius Augustus, son of Constantine the Great, and died in 352. Decrees and letters survive by him, VIII, 857.

JULIUS, abbot of the island monastery of Monte Cristo, sent a complaint to Roland, count of the island of Corsica, concerning rights usurped from his monastery, in 719, LXXXVIII, 1364.

JUNILIUS, African bishop, flourished about the middle of the fifth century. Instructed from childhood in the liberal arts, he was most skilled in sacred literature. He wrote two books *On the Parts of the Divine Law*, which he dedicated to Primasius, bishop of Hadrumetum, who in 553 subscribed to the Three Chapters of Pope Vigilius, LXVIII, 11.

JUSTINIAN, an illustrious man and envoy of Emperor Justin, recounts what was done for the sake of peace. He wrote concerning the deposition of Acacius and the excommunication of Dioscorus in 520, LXIII, 496, 508.

JUSTINIAN, nephew and successor of Emperor Justin, ordered certain rebels, especially Hypatius, to be killed. During his reign Narses and Belisarius distinguished themselves by victories. He revised laws and constitutions and arranged them in better order; hence various parts of Roman law bear his name, namely the *Code*, the *Digest*, the *Institutes*, and the *Novels*. He died in 565, LXIII, 430 and passim; LXVI, 14 passim; LXXX, 30 passim.

JUSTINIAN II, emperor of the East, succeeded his father Constantine Pogonatus. Because of excessive cruelty he was expelled and had his nose cut off; but after ten years, returning from exile, he was restored to the throne. When he ruled with still greater severity, he was killed in a rebellion at the command of Philippicus Bardanes, who succeeded him. Several letters survive concerning him. He died in 711, XCVI, 42.

JUSTIN, called the Elder, was first a shepherd of sheep in Thrace, his native country. Afterwards, in both the Isaurian and Persian wars, he distinguished himself with such valour that, when Emperor Anastasius died in 518, he was proclaimed emperor. He restored Catholic bishops to their sees but expelled Arians, against the will of Theodoric, king of the Goths. He died in 527. Letters concerning him survive, CXIII, 426 and passim.

JUSTUS (Saint), bishop of Urgell in Spain, flourished in the sixth century. He attended the Council of Toledo. A mystical exposition of Solomon’s *Song of Songs* survives by him, 540, LXVII, 962.

JUSTUS LIPSIUS, native of the Spanish Netherlands, converted from the Protestant sect to the Catholic faith and took orders in the Society of Jesus. He taught history at Louvain and Leiden with great renown. He flourished from 1547 to 1606. An encomium on Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, survives by him, CLXXXV, 637.

JUVENCUS (Aquilinus), Spanish priest and poet. Born of noble stock, he flourished under Constantius Augustus. Historians tell us very little concerning him. He translated the four Gospels into heroic metre. Some also attribute to him a book on Genesis and the *Triumph of Christ* in heroic verse. He flourished in 329, XIX, 9.

## K

KARLOMANNUS. See CARLOMANNUS.

KAROLUS. See CAROLUS.

KENRED, king of Mercia, in 709 bestowed many gifts upon the monastery of Evesham, especially lands in which Blessed Virgin Mary is said to have appeared to Saint Egwin, bishop; this donation was confirmed by Pope Constantine. Having abdicated the crown, Kenred went to Rome and embraced the monastic life. He died in 709, LXXXIX, 336.

KENULF, or COENULF, king of Mercia, successor of Ecgfrith, made his people, formerly most wretched, most flourishing. He was a great patron of religion and restored to his see Æthelhard, archbishop of Canterbury, formerly harassed by King Offa. William of Malmesbury calls this king a great man, devout at home and outstanding in war. He died in 821 and was succeeded by his son Kenelm. A letter to Pope Leo III, with its reply, survives concerning him, CII, 1023; CLXXIX, 1038.

KERVYN DE LETTENHOVE, of the Academy of Brussels, to which he dedicated, in 1853, a work entitled: *Researches into the Part Taken by the Order of Cîteaux and the Count of Flanders in the Struggle of Boniface VIII with Philip the Fair*, CLXXXV, 1833.

## L

LABORANS, cardinal-priest of the Holy Roman Church. That eminent philosopher and theologian flourished at the end of the twelfth century, in 1101. He published a highly elaborate collection of canons, a treatise *On Justice and the Just*, and a book *On True Freedom*, to which several letters must be added, CCIV, 867.

LACTANTIUS (Firmianus), Roman advocate, rhetorician, and Christian apologist, is thought to have been born in Africa to pagan parents. When he came to the faith is uncertain. He taught literature at Nicomedia and in old age came to Trier, where he died about 325. He wrote the *Apology*, the *Books of the Institutions*, *On the Workmanship of God*, *On the Wrath of God*, and *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*. He is one of the most eloquent writers of the Latin Church, VI–VII.

LAMBERT, bishop of Le Mans. When a certain Rayno was unwilling to pay either the ninth or the tenth, he declared him excommunicated, and informed Hildebrand, bishop of Séez, of this, ninth century, CXXXII, 467.

LAMBERT, son of Adalbert II, duke of Tuscany, became king of Italy and emperor. He ruled until 931, when, having had his eyes gouged out by his brother, he died miserably. An account of his council at Ravenna is given, CXXXVIII, 809.

LAMBERT, son of Ansbert, sold to a certain knight Girvard an allod in the village of Condal for twenty-three solidi in coin, in 954, CLV, 327.

LAMBERT OF LIÈGE, or LEODIUM, monk of the monastery of Saint Matthias at Trier, flourished from 1038 to 1047. He is the author of a short work *On the Discovery of the Body and the Miracles of Saint Matthias*, CLIV, 1279.

LAMBERT, abbot of Hersfeld, born at Schafnaburg, was ordained priest by Luitpold, archbishop of Mainz. When he died is uncertain (1077). Annals survive by him, CXLVI, 1027.

LAMBERT, abbot of the Cistercian monastery of Saint Nicholas of the Tower, informs his brethren of the passing of Blessed Father Bruno and requests that his death be entered in the brethren’s martyrology and commemorated in perpetual remembrance, in 1101, CLII, 590, 600.

LAMBERT, abbot of the Carthusian monastery of Pultaria on the Seine. He professes that Father Bruno had once been his teacher in literary learning and in the instruction of Catholic conduct. On the anniversary of the holy father’s death, he and the monks devoted themselves to spiritual hymns and almsgiving. A letter from him to Abbot Alberic survives; he flourished in 1110, CLII, 568; CVI, 398.

LAMBERT, bishop of Arras. Born of noble stock and endowed with great virtue, he was first archdeacon of Thérouanne, then canon and precentor of Saint Peter’s at Lille, and finally was elected bishop by the clergy of Arras and consecrated by Pope Urban II. He governed the Church wisely until 1115, when he departed to God. Letters and privileges survive concerning him, CXLII, 615.

LAMBERT, canon of Saint-Omer and later abbot of Saint Bertin, wrote the *Liber Floridus* and died in 1123, CLXIII, 1006.

LAMBERT, Carthusian prior of the house at Squillace, successor of Lanuin, first issued statutes both for the anchorites and for the cenobites living not far from Squillace in the monastery of Saint Stephen. He lived in the twelfth century, in 1125, CLIII, 1150.

LAMBERT OF BON ŒIL and STEPHEN DE LINERIES gave to the monastery of Fontevraud the land called La Plaine, at the beginning of the twelfth century, CLXII, 1111.

LANDERICUS (Saint), bishop of Paris, flourished in the middle of the seventh century during the reign of Clovis II, son of Dagobert. He governed the Church of Paris with great holiness and excelled in remarkable charity toward the poor, so that, when famine was raging in 651, he sold his household goods. Only a charter by which he grants immunities to the monastery of Saint-Denis survives by him, LXXXVII, 298.

LANDRICUS, abbot of Saint Peter’s at Chartres, testifies that land at the Royal Chapel had been granted to him by the noblewoman Bertha and Count Theobald in 1069. Several other charters of the same abbot survive, CLV, 273.

LANDRICUS, a knight, and his wife Ermelina make over a boy named Ernald and offer him to the monastery of Saint Peter at Chartres, that he may serve God there as a monk; in return for his maintenance, they grant to the same monastery land in the place called Baliolus, in 1080, CLV, 343.

LANDULF, called Sagax, historical author who flourished in the ninth century. He published a continuation of the history of Paul the Deacon, XCV, 1143.

LANDULF, a Milanese cleric, called the Elder, flourished in the eleventh century; biographers relate little concerning him. He wrote a history of Milan divided into four books. He died about 1085, CXLVII, 802.

LANDULF, called the Younger in order to distinguish him from the preceding, was born at Milan and was the nephew of Liutprand, the man who rose so fiercely against simoniacs. He visited many places for his education; on returning to Italy he became head of the church of Saint Paul at Milan. He wrote a history of his own times from 1095 to 1137, CLXXIII, 1429.

LANFRANC (Blessed), archbishop of Canterbury and primate of England, was Italian by birth. He was trained in the liberal arts from childhood; first a monk at the monastery of Bec, then called by Duke William to duties at court, he afterwards became prior and abbot of his monastery, and finally was raised to the see of Canterbury in 1070. There survive by him a commentary on Saint Paul’s Epistles; a book *On the Body and Blood of Christ against Berengar*; decrees for the Order of Saint Benedict; and letters. He died in 1089, CL, 9.

LAURENTIUS (Saint), bishop of Novara, whom they suppose to have been raised to the see of Milan in 507, was called “the Honey-Tongued” because of the sweetness of his eloquence. Only two homilies survive by him, on penitence and almsgiving. He flourished in 540, LXVI, 88.

LAURENTIUS, monk of Monte Cassino and subsequently bishop of an unknown see, than whom none of the predecessors after Saint Benedict was more learned, delivered an elegant discourse for the vigil of Blessed Benedict. He flourished in 950, CXXXIII, 886.

LAURENTIUS, Pisan deacon, a native of Verona, flourished in 1115 under Archbishop Peter II. In heroic verse he wrote the Balearic War, or the deeds of the Pisans in Majorca, in seven books, CLIII, 514.

[Col. 0487] LAURENTIUS, abbot of the monastery of Westin, sent to the venerable Ervisius, prior of Saint Victor at Paris, a letter recommending to him John, kinsman of his prior, who was seeking to direct schools, in 1170, CXCV, 1385; CC, 1452.

LAURENTIUS OF LIÈGE, of whom little is reported, flourished in the twelfth century. He embraced the monastic profession in the monastery of Saint Lawrence at Liège. Learned in letters, he wrote a history of the deeds of the bishops of Verdun, which he continued to 1114, CCIV, 915.

LEANDER (Saint), archbishop of Seville. A Spaniard by race and of a Carthaginian family, after a long monastic profession he was made archbishop; but in 584 he was sent into exile by Leovigild, king of the Goths. He died in 595. He wrote a Rule, or book *On the Instruction of Virgins and Contempt of the World*; and, secondly, a homily in praise of the Church, LXXII, 870.

LEBDRUDIS OF GUÎNES, a widow, gave to the monastery of Saint-Bertin the properties which she possessed in the district of Boulogne and at the place called Guînes, in 807, CXXXVI, 1218.

LEDUIN, abbot of Saint Vaast at Arras. A layman who became a monk under Balderic, he was placed over the monastery of Saint Vaast by Blessed Richard. Almost none among the abbots of Arras has a more honoured memory. Only his ordinance concerning the general assembly survives; he flourished in 1040, CXLI, 1334.

LEIDRAD, bishop of Lyon. A Norican by birth, very close to Charlemagne and, according to some, his librarian, he occupied the see of Lyon after Hilduin. He built many churches and monasteries, restored the chant of that church, and fulfilled other duties of a good shepherd despite ill health. He died in 813 in the monastery of Soissons, to which he had withdrawn shortly before after resigning his office. Letters on the sacrament of baptism survive by him, XCIX, 854.

LEO, bishop of Bourges in Gaul, 453: he attended the Council of Angers in 453 and that of Tours in 461. Together with Victorius and Eustathius he wrote a letter to the bishops of the province of Tours, declaring excommunicated those clerics who, passing over ecclesiastical judgment, had resorted to secular power. The aforesaid letter alone survives by him, LIV, 1239.

LEO THE GREAT (Saint), pope and doctor of the Church. A Roman by birth, descended from a noble family, he was first archdeacon of the Roman Church under Sixtus III; after Sixtus’s death he was raised to his place in 440. He opposed the heresies of his time most vigorously. Sermons, letters, and the book *On the Sacraments*, or *Pastoral*, survive by him. He died in 461, LIV–LVI.

LEO (Saint), bishop and confessor of Sens, ascended the episcopal see in 518, attended the Second and Third Councils of Orléans, and departed to God in 541. Nothing survives of his writings except a letter to Childebert, king of the Franks, LVIII, 9.

LEO II, pope, a Sicilian by birth and son of Paul, was elected in 683 and died in the following year, 684. Letters survive by him, XCVI, 384.

LEO III (Saint), pope. Born in Rome to a father named Azuppius, he first professed the monastic life according to the Rule of Saint Benedict. Letters survive by him, especially to Emperor Charles. He died in 816, XCVIII, 488; CII, 1023.

LEO IV, pope, son of a Roman named Bodoald, succeeded Pope Sergius II in 847. At the beginning of his pontificate he miraculously drove from the city a deadly basilisk, and extinguished a fire by the sign of the Cross. Devout and generous, he was especially zealous for reforming morals and instructing God’s ministers. He held the see about eight years and died in the year of the Lord 855. Letters and decrees survive by him, CXV, 630.

LEO VI, pope, son of Christopher the primicerius, succeeded Pope John X. But after seven months he was ejected from the see and thrust into prison, where he died miserably, in 928. A letter to the bishops of Dalmatia survives by him, CXXVII, 814.

LEO VII, pope, whose lineage is unknown but whose modesty, wisdom, and affability are praised. A Roman by birth, he succeeded John XI in 936 and died in 939. Privileges and constitutions survive by him, CXXXIV, 990.

LEO IX (Saint), Roman pontiff, was the son of Hugh. Of Alsatian origin, he studied under Berthold, bishop of Toul; afterwards he was raised to the see of Toul and, with the support of Emperor Henry III, elected pope in 1040. He died in 1054. A short work *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, an oration to Count Albert, charters, and numerous letters survive by him, CXLIII, 458.

LEO, bishop of Atina. A man distinguished by learning and knowledge of the Holy Scriptures, he was ordained by Adenulf, bishop of Capua, in 1044. There survives by him an account of his translation of the relics of Saint Mark to the church at Atina, in 1072, CXLIII, 415.

[Col. 0488] LEO VIII, antipope, formerly protoscriniarius, was deceitfully installed in place of the deposed John XII at a Roman synod in 963. But John XII returned in the following year, drove him out, and compelled him to surrender the usurped office. At last, after John’s death, he again held the see until his own death in 965. Certain privileges and constitutions survive by him, CXXXIV, 990.

LEO, abbot and legate of Pope Gerbert, or Sylvester II, was sent into Gaul to attend the Council of Mouzon. He addressed a letter to Kings Hugh and Robert, who had procured Arnulf’s deposition in a synod without the advice of the Roman see; but both the letter and the acts of the Council of Mouzon are spurious works, in 995, CXXXIX, 337.

LEO, called Marsican from his birthplace and also known by the surname of Ostia, entered Monte Cassino as a young man and was received, reared, and educated by Abbot Desiderius. He advanced so greatly in piety and learning that he became dean and librarian, and was afterwards made cardinal and bishop of Ostia by Pope Paschal II. His history or chronicle of Monte Cassino and several other writings survive, though some are still lacking today. He died in 1115, CLXXIII, 439.

LEO, king of the Armenians, obtained from Pope Celestine and Emperor Henry VI that he should be called king because of his victories over the Turks. He died in 1219. A letter of his to Innocent III survives, informing him of the peace reconciled between himself and the Templars, CCXV, 187.

LEOBAUD OF GUÎNES and HUMBAUD OF ROUGEMONT gave to the monastery of Fontenelle a meadow situated between the villages of Bonnes and Courcelles, without a stated year; twelfth century, CLXXXV, 1463.

LEOBGITHA, first called Trutgeba but afterwards Leobgitha, Lioba, and Lieba. Her father was Diemo, or Tinne, and her mother Ebba. Consecrated to God from childhood, she was placed under the discipline of Tetta, abbess of Wimborne. She devoted herself to study and the liberal arts. She cultivated calligraphy and poetry under Eadburga, who excelled in them. Letters of hers to Saint Boniface of Mainz survive. She flourished in 725, LXXXIX, 720.

LEODEBOD, abbot of Saint Aignan about 667 under King Clotaire III, made many gifts to the monasteries both of Saint Aignan and of Fleury. In his charter, *Clothario* must be read instead of *Clodovaeo* because of the chronology, LXXXVIII, 1186.

LEODEGAR (Saint), bishop of Autun. Born of noble Frankish lineage, from earliest childhood he was received into the royal palace; but the pious king entrusted him to the bishop of Poitiers, his uncle, for instruction in letters. He attained the see of Autun in 659. During the siege of his city, he confronted his enemies, who gouged out his eyes. He died in chains in 678, XCVI, 360.

LEODEGAR, archbishop of Vienne, of whom nothing certain is transmitted except that he flourished in the eleventh century, in 1067. Charters survive by him, CXLIII, 1398.

LEOGARTIUS, his wife Eremburgis, and their daughter Adelaide gave to Lord Robert of Arbrissel and the nuns of Fontevraud stones necessary for the building of the church, at the beginning of the twelfth century, CLXII, 1108.

LEONIUS OF LONGIAC gave to the monastery of Fontevraud, founded by Blessed Robert of Arbrissel, a piece of land called *Calidus Furnerius*. His wife Barbota first subscribed to this donation, and it was made in Robert’s presence, at the beginning of the twelfth century, CLXII, 1105.

LEONTIUS, bishop of Naples in Cyprus. Among the many other works enumerated by the Seventh General Council, he wrote the Life of Saint John, bishop of Alexandria, called the Almsgiver. He flourished toward the end of the sixth century, in 590, LXXIII, 337.

LEOTALD, count of Mâcon, and his wife Ermengard give the estate of Dardania, situated in the district of Lyon, to the monastery of Cluny, in the year 9[.....]5, while Rudolf was reigning in Gaul, CXXXIII, 842.

LEOVIGILD, priest of Córdoba. When he flourished is uncertain. A preface by him to the book *On the Dress of Clerics* survives, CXXI, 565.

LEPORIUS, monk and priest, flourished in the fifth century. A Gaul by birth, he was first a monk at Marseilles. For a time he inclined toward the Pelagian heresy; but, crossing to Africa, he approached Saint Augustine, who rescued him from error. Of his writings, a short book of correction, or satisfaction, survives, XXXI, 1215.

LETALD, Benedictine monk of Micy near Orléans, wrote a book *On the Miracles of Saint Maximin, Abbot of Micy*. Perhaps he is also the author who polished the Life of Saint Julian, bishop of Le Mans, CXXXVII, 781.

LETGARDIS, most noble countess, gave to the monastery of Saint Peter at Chartres the royal estate of Grescic, another at Fontenay, and likewise that of Limay, in 478, CLV, 230.

LEUTHERICUS, archbishop of Sens, flourished about 1026 in the time of Saint Fulbert of Chartres. A letter of his to the clergy of Paris survives, concerning the punishments inflicted by their bishop, CXLI, 246.

LIBERATUS, deacon of Carthage, one of the African defenders of the Three Chapters in 556. He wrote a short work on the Nestorian and Eutychian heresies, in which he teaches us who those heresiarchs and their followers were, LXVIII, 964.

LIBERIUS (Saint), pope. A Roman by birth, he undertook many labours in defence of the faith; forced into exile, he returned only after three years. He died in 366. Some have wished to maintain that this pope subscribed words suggestive of heresy, but it is proved that these are spurious and false. Letters and decrees survive by him, VIII, 1331.

LIBERIUS, whom some call Liberatus and Libertus, was a poet of the fifth century. But he is no less uncertain than the Belisarius concerning whom verses are supplied; some think that these were one and the same author, given different names. He was contemporary with Sedulius and with Asterius, of whom some verses survive, XIX, 502, 784.

LICINIA EUDOXIA. See EUDOXIA.

LICINIUS, or LICINIANUS (Gaius Flavius), was born in Dacia in 263. Emperor Galerius associated him with himself. After twice defeating Maximian, he alone, together with Constantine, gained possession of the empire; but discord arose between them over the Christians, and he lost the empire and soon afterwards his life, about 324. Certain letters and constitutions concerning him survive, VIII, 30, 479, 489 passim.

LICINIANUS, bishop of Carthago Spartaria in Spain, flourished in 384. Isidore tells us that Licinianus died at Constantinople, poisoned, as they report, by his rivals. Three letters survive by him: to Saint Gregory, pope; to Epiphanius, deacon; and to Vincent, bishop of the island of Ebusus, LXII, 687.

LIETBERT (Saint), bishop of Cambrai. A native of Brabant and nephew of Saint Gerard, bishop, he was entrusted to Gerard for education. In turn he became schoolmaster, archdeacon, provost, and finally bishop in 1049. He founded the monastery of the Holy Sepulchre at Cambrai and died in 1076. A charter of his concerning the establishment of regular canons in the church of Saint Autbert at Cambrai survives, CXLVI, 1483.

LIETBERT, abbot of Saint-Ruf, an Augustinian regular canon, became abbot of Saint-Ruf near Valence in Narbonese Gaul. He seems to have flourished at the beginning of the twelfth century. Two letters survive by him, CLVII, 715.

LIETHARD, bishop of Soissons, succeeded Hugh. He instructed and ordained a certain Odo, but afterwards sent him to Lambert, bishop of Arras, with a letter commending him, at the beginning of the twelfth century, CLXII, 692.

LIODRICUS OF MEKERIAS conveyed many possessions in the district of Thérouanne to the venerable Hilduin, abbot of Saint-Bertin, in 867, CXXXVI, 1243.

LISIARD, cleric of Tours. Although he is called a simple cleric, he was nevertheless dean of Laon. He wrote on the ceremonies of the divine office. According to Barthius, he was the author of the history of Jerusalem published by Bongars without an author’s name, CLXXIV, 1589.

LIUTAD, bishop of Vienne, issued testimonial letters to the deacon Wlfad on behalf of Wenilo, bishop of Rouen, in 868, CXXIX, 1392.

LIUTPRAND, king of the Lombards, son of Ansprand. Several charters of his survive, from 715 to 730, LXXXVII, 1353.

LIUTPRAND, bishop of Cremona. A Lombard by birth and of no low rank, he flourished in the tenth century. He first lived at the court of King Hugh, then entered the clergy and served as deacon of the church at Pavia, and finally became bishop. He died in 974. His *History of the Deeds of Kings and Emperors*, *Book on the Deeds of Emperor Otto*, and account of the embassy to Constantinople survive, CXXXVI, 770.

LIVINUS (St), bishop of Metz and martyr. Born in Scotland, he came to Flanders, where he preached the Catholic faith. Made bishop of Metz, he endured many persecutions and was finally beheaded in 659. There survives a letter concerning him to Abbot Florbert, LXXXVII, 327.

LONEGISILUS, founder and abbot of the monastery of Bussières, about 625, under Hadoind, bishop of Le Mans. In a charter he himself states that he was born in Germany of noble but pagan parents, who dedicated him to military service; but that he abandoned everything in order to become a Christian. He professed the monastic life and afterward bequeathed all his possessions to the monastery, LXXX, 455, 458.

LONGINIANUS, a pagan philosopher and a close acquaintance of St Augustine. Asked by Augustine by what path he believed one might attain the blessed life, he gives such an answer as he can in his letter to Augustine (427), XXXIII, 1030.

LOTHAIR I, emperor, son and successor of Louis the Pious. Rebellious against his father, he afterward waged war with his brothers for the kingdom; defeated by his brother Charles in the battle of Fontenoy [Col. 0490] in 841, he retained only the title of emperor. He died in 855. Diplomas concerning him survive: XCVII, 371; CXXXVIII, 523; CXXI, 371.

LOTHAIR II, son and successor of King Louis Overseas. He waged war in Germany and was himself, shortly afterward, attacked by enemies in the very city of Paris. He died in 986. Various diplomas concerning him survive, CXXXVII, 779; CXXXVIII, 544, etc.

LOTHAIR II, emperor of Germany, son of Count Gebhard. He succeeded Henry V and defended the cause of Pope Innocent II against Peter Leonis. He was crowned at Rome in 1133 and died in 1137. Diplomas concerning him are preserved, CLXXIX, 47, 668.

LUCAS, deacon of León and afterward bishop of Tuy. While a regular canon of St Augustine in the royal monastery of St Isidore at León, he wrote a book *On the Miracles of St Martin* at the beginning of the thirteenth century, in 1201, CCVIII, 9.

LUCIANUS, confessor of the Church of Carthage. He was thrown into prison with many others; daily expecting death and, apparently, crowned with martyrdom; a man distinguished by faith and charity, but not fully furnished with learning. For, obeying the imprudent statement of a certain martyr Paul, he indiscriminately granted certificates of peace to everyone—a practice especially condemned by Cyprian—in 258, IV, 274.

LUCIFER, bishop of Cagliari, whose origin is uncertain. He rejected the decrees of the Council of Alexandria and thus gave both a place and a name to a certain schism. He died in 371. Whether he renounced the schism before his death is uncertain. Many books by him survive: *On Not Associating with Heretics*; *On Apostate Kings*, two books; *For St Athanasius*; *On Not Sparing Those Who Sin against God*; and *That One Must Die for the Son of God*, XIII, 737.

LUCIUS, African bishop and martyr. Greatly encouraged by Cyprian’s letters, he answered them together with his fellow confessors. A letter survives, IV, 422.

LUCIUS (St), pope and martyr. A Roman by birth, he succeeded St Cornelius in 252; shortly after his consecration he was sent into exile and crowned with martyrdom. A few letters concerning him survive, III, 969.

LUCIUS DEXTER. See DEXTER.

LUCIUS II, pope. A native of Bologna, formerly called Gerard, he succeeded Celestine II in 1144 and died in the following year, 1145. His letters survive, along with a bull concerning the dispute between the bishop of Dol and the archbishop of Tours, CLXXIX, 823.

LUCIUS III, pope. A Tuscan by nationality, he was first bishop of Ostia, a man most learned in literary knowledge. He succeeded Pope Alexander III and died in 1185. Only three letters concerning him survive, CCI, 1067.

LUCRETIUS, bishop of the province of Gallaecia in Spain. He attended the Council of Braga held under Ariamir, king of the Goths, and uttered words there which survive. He flourished in 531, CXXX, 568.

LUCULENTIUS, who commented upon certain portions of the New Testament, is entirely unknown to us, for all biographers are silent about him, LXXII, 803.

LUDGERUS, son of Hrodger, granted certain estates situated at Berils and Sui-terbant to Ludger, priest and friend. This was done in 797, in the reign of Charlemagne, XCIX, 814.

LUDGERUS (St), bishop of Münster. As a boy he was entrusted to Abbot Gregory for education; afterward he went to England to Alcuin’s school. Returning thence to Utrecht because of Widukind’s persecutions, he came to Rome and, having obtained relics from Pope Adrian, went to Monte Cassino. Later, made bishop, he ruled his church piously and vigorously; he died in 809. He wrote the Life of Lord Gregory, abbot and rector of the Church of Utrecht, XCIX, 746.

LOUIS I, called the Pious, son of Charlemagne and Hildegard. He endured many great tribulations from his sons and died in 840. There survive concerning him a privilege confirming royal rights in favor of Pope Paschal, and diplomas, XCVIII, 580.

LOUIS II, called the Stammerer, king of the Franks. He was crowned in 877; while excessively intent upon currying favor with the nobles, feudal privileges soon spread throughout the kingdom. He died in 879. His Coronation and diplomas survive, CXXVI, 809, 1265.

LOUIS III, emperor of Germany. Previously king of Arles, he was the son of Boso, whom he succeeded in 887; he was crowned emperor in 900. Captured at Verona by Berengar, he was blinded. He died in 923. His election is preserved, CXXXVIII, 803.

LOUIS IV, king of the Franks, son of Charles the Simple. He succeeded Rudolf; he dealt with Richard, duke of the Normans; he died in 954. There survives a diploma by which he granted certain churches to the monastery of Cluny in 939, CXXXIII, 839.

LOUIS, Landgrave of Thuringia. Having received letters [Col. 0491] from Wulfram, bishop of Naumburg, exhorting him to abandon the cause of the Roman pontiff and follow that of Emperor Henry, he had them refuted by the Venerable Stephen Herand, bishop of Halberstadt, in 1110, CLIX, 985.

LOUIS VII, called the Younger, king of the Franks, son and successor of Louis VI. Several letters and diplomas concerning him survive. He died in 1180, CXC, 1055; CXCIX, 374.

LOUIS, firstborn son of Philip, king of the Franks. He informed the king of Jerusalem that Count Theobald ought not to be brought to judgment regarding his father’s land until he had completed his twenty-first year, about 1214, CCXVI, 975.

LOUIS IX (St), king of the Franks, son of Louis VIII and Blanche of Castile. He kept the vassals of the kingdom in check. He overthrew the Albigensian heretics by arms; having prepared all things, he set out for Palestine and achieved distinguished victories. But in a second expedition, ending unsuccessfully, he died in 1270. Certain writings by him survive, CLV, 1281.

LOUIS, a monk of Granada of the Order of Preachers of St Dominic, a Spanish ascetical author. He flourished from 1595 to 1588 [sic]. He composed a eulogy of St Bernard, CLXXXV, 634.

LUIDBERTUS, archbishop of Mainz. He is mentioned at the Council of Soissons in 866. He himself held another council in the city of Mainz, on account of King Arnulf and of ecclesiastical discipline, which had become much relaxed during the Norman incursions. He died in 889. A letter by him to King Louis survives, CXXIX, 1052.

LULLUS (St), bishop of Mainz. Born in England, he was reared and educated in the monastery of Malmesbury; he soon came to Germany to St Boniface, who ordained him priest. Finally, after Boniface’s death, he was appointed in his place in 754; he died in 787. Nine letters by him survive, XCVI, 819.

LUPUS (St), bishop of Troyes. He was ordained unwillingly; he was distinguished for piety and learning, spent nearly fifty years in the episcopate, and died in 479. Several letters by him survive, LVIII, 62.

LUPUS SERVATUS (St), priest and abbot of Ferrières. Born of a noble family of Sens, he was first a monk of the Order of St Benedict and was sent to Rabanus, abbot of Fulda, for study; afterward he became abbot. In 863 he attended the Council of Sens; he died in 862. His letters, canons, book *On Three Questions*, and *Life of St Maximinus* survive, CXIX, 424.

LUPUS PROTOSPATHARIUS. Born of a Greek family in Apulia, he wrote a short chronicle from 860 to 1102, CLV, 119.

LUTHER (Martin), the heresiarch, sufficiently well known. It may not be useless to know what he thought of St Bernard; he died in 1546, CLXXXV, 638.

## M

MABILIA, a woman, granted the canons of the Holy Sepulchre a garden and house for 170 bezants, one loaf, half a litre of diluted wine, and a dish of cooked food to be given to her daily. On Sundays a portion of the food eaten by the lords was to be added. This was done in 1133, CLV, 1204.

MACARIUS (St), a native of Alexandria, became a monk and disciple of St Antony. Upon Antony’s death he was made abbot of the celebrated monastery of Nitria, where more than 5,000 monks served God. He wrote for them a Rule and a letter; these are found in St Benedict of Aniane. He died in 390, CIII, 447.

See also XXIII, 65; LXXIII, 227.

MACCABAEUS (Macbeth), king of the Scots. He ordered his cousin Duncan to be killed in order to reign in his place; but, defeated by Malcolm, Duncan’s son, he fell in 1057. He enacted certain laws, CLI, 1189.

MACEDONIUS, vicar of Africa, cherished St Augustine with the greatest affection and aided him in combating the Donatists. He proved a protector of the commonwealth, more attentive to others’ interests than to his own. He obtained from the emperor an edict against the Donatists. Two letters by him to St Augustine survive, in 414, XXXIII, 652, 665.

MACHARIUS, confessor and cleric at Rome. He and certain others—namely Maximus, Urbanus, and Sidonius—had at first withdrawn from Pope St Cornelius, taking refuge in heresy and schism. But when persecution arose they returned to the faith, made peace with their bishop, and sent from the prison in which they were confined a letter to St Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, informing him of their return to the faith, about 252, III, 732; IV, 342.

MACROBIUS, Donatist bishop of Hippo. He is the person to whom St Augustine wrote, asking him not to rebaptize a certain subdeacon who had fled to him, and further exhorting him to return to sound doctrine. The Passion of Maximian and Isaac, of the Donatist party, about 409, is attributed to Macrobius, VIII, 767, 768; XXXIII, 404.

[Col. 0492] MADALGARDA, donor. See HIDDO.

MAGINGOZ, priest, who also appears to have been provost of a certain monastery of nuns. At one time St Lullus consults him regarding Christian marriage; at another, he consults St Lullus concerning the selection of a new abbess for his monastery, about 755, XCVI, 824, 825.

MAGISTER, an anonymous author known by this surname alone, because every work of his begins with the words: “The Rule of the Master for monks.” He appears to have been a monk, and indeed a Gaul, for he frequently uses expressions peculiar to that nation, seventh century, LXXXVIII, 943.

MAGNES, priest of Jerusalem, also called Macarius, flourished in the third century, in 280. He wrote five books of replies against the pagan Theosthenes, of which only a fragment on the Eucharist survives, V, 343.

MAGNUS, or MAGNO, archbishop of Sens, was consecrated by Leo III in 801, while he was staying in Rome in the retinue of Charlemagne, who sent him with Count Godfrey to Orléans, Troyes, Langres, Besançon, and Autun about 802. He died in 818. There survives a little book by him, *On the Mystery of Baptism*, and legal notes collected by him, CII, 980.

MAHILDIS, an illustrious matron, donated certain land to the monastery of St Germanus and, by another charter, granted a road to the monastery of St Peter at Chartres, in 1070, CLV, 324.

MAIOLUS (St), fourth abbot of Cluny. Born in Provence about 906, according to the common Cluniac tradition, he was first archdeacon of the church of Mâcon. Refusing episcopal mitres offered to him, he embraced the monastic life in the monastery of Cluny, of which he became abbot in 961; he died in 994. The Election of St Odilo and the Cartulary of Cluny concerning him are preserved, CXXXVII, 710.

MALATERRA, GAUFREDUS. See GAUFREDUS.

MALGERIUS, archbishop of Rouen. He remitted, in favor of the monks of St Peter at Chartres, who possessed much land there, the toll which he received at Andely, in 1056, CLV, 312.

MAMERTINUS, made consul by Emperor Julian, gave thanks to that prince in an Oration about 362. Otherwise nothing certain is known about him, XVIII, 407.

MAMERTUS CLAUDIANUS, priest of Vienne. He was first a monk, but was afterward ordained priest by his own brother, St Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, whose helper he was. He seems to have died in 474. He wrote *On the State of the Soul*, two letters, and a Hymn on the Passion of the Lord, LIII, 693.

MANASSES, bishop of Langres. He records that, when a dispute concerning a mill was being litigated between Otto of Sanz and Peter, abbot of St Benignus at Dijon, Otto, at his exhortation, granted the whole matter to the church of St Benignus in 1190, CLXXX, 1501.

MANASSES, archdeacon and afterward archbishop of Reims, wrote several letters to Lambert, bishop of Arras. He flourished in the twelfth century, CLXII, 650 ff.

MANASSES, bishop of Orléans. He wrote to Suger, informing him that the murderers of William de la Chambre had been forcibly dragged from the altar and church to which they had fled, and that therefore the church was subject to interdict and this could not be lifted unless they were restored; date uncertain, CLXXXVI, 1354.

MANEGOLDUS, priest and canon of Paderborn. Born in Alsace, he was a learned man and a vigorous defender of truth, becoming a master of schools. There survive a short work by him against Wolphelm of Cologne and a congratulatory letter to Wibald, abbot of Corvey, whose favor he seeks in a somewhat emphatic style, in 1149, CLV, 147; CLXXXIX, 1248.

MANIGUNDIS, a noble Lombard woman, having assumed the monastic habit, ordained by will that a monastery of nuns should be built at Cairate and that its necessities should be supplied from her property in 768, under King Hildeprand, LXXXVII, 1397.

MANSIO, bishop of Châlons. Almost nothing concerning him has been handed down to us. He flourished at the beginning of the tenth century, in 903, and wrote a letter to Fulk, archbishop of Reims, CXXXI, 24.

MANSUETUS (St), bishop of Milan. A Roman by nationality, he was appointed in the place of St Ampelius in 677. He held a synod against the Monothelites in 679 and attended the Lateran Council at Rome in 680. A letter by him to Emperor Constantine survives, LXXXVII, 1275.

MAPPINIUS, bishop of Reims. We know only a few things about him. He was elected bishop in 547 and held the see until his death in 572. Two letters by him survive, one to St Nicetas and another to Willicus, bishop of Metz, LXVIII, 43; LXXI, 1457.

MARBODUS, bishop of Rennes. Born at Angers about 1035, he shone in piety and learning. He first became provost and master of the schools of Angers; then Pope Urban II himself made him bishop of Rennes at the Council of Tours [Col. 0493]. He died in 1128. His letters, diplomas, Lives, and especially poems survive, CLXXI, 1457.

MARCELLINUS, tribune and notary in Africa. A most devoted student of the Scriptures, he was dear to St Augustine. Volusianus often visited him. Marcellinus attended the Conference of Carthage as commissioner and notary, and Augustine praises him in many places; but envious men slandered him to the emperor on a charge of treason. Arrested with his brother Apringius, he was shortly afterward put to death by Marinus, the successor, in 413, XXXIII, 514.

MARCELLINUS (St), pope. A Roman by birth, he succeeded St Caius. They relate that, terrified during the persecution of Diocletian, he sacrificed to idols; afterward, however, moved by profound repentance, he returned to the tyrant, courageously confessed the faith, and atoned for his fault by a glorious death in 304. Two letters by him survive, VI, 9; VII, 1085.

MARCELLINUS, priest, flourished in the fourth century, in 368. Historians have transmitted nothing concerning him. He offered a book *On Faith* to Emperors Valentinian and Arcadius, XIII, 29.

MARCELLINUS, count. A Roman by nationality, he was sent as count into Illyricum and, according to Cassiodorus, was chancellor of Justinian while the latter was still a patrician. He is the author of a Chronicle from 379 to 547, LI, 913.

MARCELLUS (St), pope, to be distinguished from Marcellinus, whom he succeeded. He held the Holy See for only one year and died in 308. Two letters by him survive, VI, 19; VII, 1091.

MARCELLUS, bishop of Ancyra, in 325. He was present at the Council of Nicaea and attacked the Arians vehemently; inflamed by anger, they deposed him as an adherent of Sabellianism. He hastened to Pope Julius, who at a Roman council declared him orthodox and restored him to his see. In his case bishops, especially those of Gaul, deceived by Arian denunciations, went astray. There survive a letter by him to Pope Julius, two professions of faith, and a fragment of the book which he wrote against Asterius, in 311, VIII, 913.

MARCELLUS MEMORIALIS, apparently exercising the office of bishop, attended the Conference of Carthage in Augustine’s time, about 411. He produced an abridgment of that conference, as is clear from his own preface addressed to Severianus and Julianus, his colleagues and friends. In the acts of this most celebrated conference are given together both the words and the names of those who uttered them, whether on the Catholic side or on the Donatist side, XI, 1234, 1227, 1231, 1257.

MARCIANUS, a Donatist bishop in Africa. He attended the Council of Carthage in 311, at which Caecilian was condemned and the Donatist Majorinus was appointed in his place, VIII, 746.

MARCIANUS, emperor. Born in Thrace, he distinguished himself in military service. Made a senator, he soon married Pulcheria, who had been raised to the eastern empire after the death of Theodosius the Younger. He waged war against Attila and had Leo as his successor in 457. Several letters and constitutions concerning him survive, LIV, 903, 970, 1017.

MARCUARDUS MALUS, a monk, donated four jugera of meadow to Blessed Robert of Arbrissel and the monastery of Fontevraud, in the reign of Louis VI, CLXII, 1113.

MARCULPHUS, monk. We know nothing about him except that he is the author of a collection of legal acts arranged in two books, in 660, LXXXVII, 691.

MARCUS (St), pope. A Roman by nationality, born to a father named Priscus, he began his pontificate in 336 and died in the same year. There survives a rescript by him to Athanasius and all the bishops of Egypt, VIII, 849.

MARCUS, monk of Monte Cassino and disciple of St Benedict. He wrote, or rather extracted from Gregory the Great, the Life of Benedict, and adorned it with heroic verse, about 612, LXXX, 183.

MARCUS, bishop of Otranto, known to us only through a hymn which he wrote for Holy Saturday, celebrating the creation of the world and Christ’s descent into hell; date uncertain, XCVI, 1345.

MARGARETA MUYANS, formerly a serf, having obtained freedom from her lord, James Marocla of Lucca, was led with her sons to the altar so that their manumission might be publicly announced, in accordance with the custom of the time. A charter concerning this, issued at Udine in 1352, survives, XCIX, 660.

MARGARITA, countess of Burgundy. She donated to the Church of Blessed Mary of Balerne and the brothers dwelling there a burgess at Arbois named Girard de Montaney, together with all his children and possessions, in 1200, CLXXXV, 1459.

MARIA, daughter of Humbert de Molenvilla, confirmed the gifts which her father had formerly granted to the monastery of Clairvaux in the pastures of Villa, in 1147, CLXXXV, 988.

MARIA DE MONT-SAINT-JEAN, lady of Salins, widow of James, lord of Salins, who had died overseas, [Col. 0494] promised to pay the Church of Blessed Mary twelve mines of grain—part rye, part mixed grain—by the measure of Salins, on condition that the canons should celebrate one Mass each day for her deceased husband, except on feast days and Sundays, in 1249, CLXXXV, 1439.

MARIANUS, priest and archimandrite, together with the other archimandrites of the Eastern Church, wrote a petition to Pope Agapetus against the impious Anthimus, who had left the see of Trebizond in order to seize that of Constantinople—an act which he actually accomplished with the help of the wicked woman Theodora, wife of Justinian. Agapetus himself deposed Anthimus and appointed Menas in his place in 536, LXVI, 49.

MARIANUS SCOTUS. See SCOTUS.

MABINUS I, pope. He succeeded Pope John II in 882, in the time of Charles III and Emperor Basil. He died in 884. Letters to the monks of St Giles and privileges by him survive, CXXVI, 966.

MARINUS II, pope. A Roman by nationality, he was appointed in place of Stephen VIII. He devoted much effort to restoring churches and assisting the poor. He died in 946. His letters and privileges survive, CXXX, 863.

MARIUS VICTORINUS. See VICTORINUS.

MARIUS MERCATOR, concerning whose country, place, and status we have no certain information, flourished at the beginning of the fifth century. He was a friend of St Augustine, as is evident from Augustine’s letter of 418, and, although a layman, defended the faith with great vigor, as appears from his writings. He died about 435, XLVIII, 9.

MARIUS, bishop of Avenches. Born at Autun of noble family about 532, he was ordained bishop among the Helvetians in 576 and died in 596. A brief chronicle by him, from 455 to 581, survives, LXXIII, 792.

MARQUARDUS, patriarch of Aquileia. On the day when he celebrated his first Mass in the metropolitan church of Aquileia, all the notable persons of the province, both clergy and magistrates, were present and made offerings for him, which are still recorded in a charter, in 1366, XCIX, 661.

MARTINIANUS, monk. We know little concerning him. He appears to have flourished in the tenth century, in 906; he wrote four books of exercises, two addressed to monks, one to clerics, and one to laypeople, CXXX, 24.

MARTIN (St), bishop of Tours. Born in Pannonia in 316, son of a tribune, he first entered military service. Martin was distinguished for charity; taught by St Hilary and initiated into the priesthood, he led an eremitical life. But his fame soon grew so great that he was elected bishop at Tours. He died an old man in 399. There survives his *Confession of the Threefold Unity and the One Trinity*, XVIII, 9.

MARTIN OF DUMIO (St), bishop of Braga. Although some believe him to have been born in Pannonia, it is more plausibly supposed that he was born in Galicia. He travelled through the holy places and, on his return, was raised to the see of Braga.
