He founded the famous monastery of Dumio, a town of Tarraconensis; he held a council in 582, the acts of which he compiled. Seven short works by him survive. He appears to have died in 584, LXXII, 17; CXXX, 571, 575.

MARTIN I (St), pope. A native of the city of Todi in Tuscany, he succeeded Theodore in 649. He defended the faith against the Monothelites, who, angered and supported by imperial authority, deposed him from his see and drove him into exile, where he suffered many hardships. He died in 655. Eighteen letters and three privileges by him survive, LXXXVII, 106.

MARTINUS CAROANA donated his inheritance to the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, reserving its usufruct for himself during his lifetime, in 1152, under Patriarch Fulcher and during the reign of Baldwin IV, CLV, 1210.

MARTIN (St), priest of León. Born of an illustrious family, he devoted himself to sacred literature from childhood. Having received holy orders, he applied himself to preaching and was distinguished for eloquence. He died in 1203. He left many sermons, CCVIII, 27.

MATERNUS (Firmicus). Historians report little concerning him. He flourished after the time of Constantine the Great, about 345. He wrote a work *On the Errors of Profane Religions*, from which it is understood that he was a devout and learned man. Some attribute to him the book *On Astronomy*, XII, 971.

MATHILDIS (St), queen of Germany. Born of the noble Ludolfing family and wife of King Henry, she was mother of Otto I, Duke Henry, Archbishop Bruno, Queen Gerberga, and Duchess Hatwida. She built many monasteries and died piously in 968. Her letter, published by Ph. Ant. Dethier, survives, CXXXV, 885; CLI, 1327.

MATHILDIS, countess, flourished from about 1046 to 1115. We have certain diplomas concerning her, XCVIII, 631; CXLVIII, 936.

MATHILDIS, countess of Grignon, confirmed in 1196 all her father Raymond’s gifts to the brothers of Fontenay [Col. 0495]. By another charter of the same year, she gave the same monastery a vineyard situated in the parish of Saigny, which she had bought from Erard, CLXXXV, 1470, 1471.

MATHILDIS, queen of the English, wife of Henry I, wrote letters to St Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, in the twelfth century, CLIX, 239, 240.

MATHILDIS, empress and mother of Henry II, king of the English. In an effort at reconciliation between her son Henry and St Thomas of Canterbury, she wrote to the pope a letter mentioning her son’s complaints against him and urging him to lay out his case fully before Archdeacon Laurence, whom she had sent to him, twelfth century, CXC, 1054.

MATTHEW, cardinal bishop of Albano. Of noble birth, he was first a monk in the province of Reims, then prior of Cluny; he was made bishop of Albano and cardinal by Honorius II in 1125. Distinguished for piety and learning, he assisted St Bernard in strengthening the chair of St Peter; he died in 1139. Several letters and diplomas concerning him survive, CLXXIII, 1261.

MATTHEW, duke of Lorraine, son and successor of Simon, was an associate of Frederick Barbarossa. He died in 1176. In consideration of his mother Atheleidis, who had become a nun in the monastery of Tart, he granted that monastery a fixed quantity of salt to be given annually, with the consent of Bertha his wife, Baldwin his brother, and his sister Agatha, in 1142, CLXXXV, 1411.

MATTHEW, treasurer of Sens, flourished in the twelfth century. In support of Thomas of Canterbury, he wrote to Pope Alexander III against King Henry, CC, 1434.

MATTHEW, bishop of Troyes. He flourished in the twelfth century. He wrote to Pope Alexander III for the cause of St Thomas, CC, 1422.

MATTHEW, called of Vendôme from his native place, born of the noble Bourbon family, flourished at the end of the twelfth century; he embraced the monastic life in 1159. He is to be distinguished from the abbot of Saint-Denis of the same name. His metrical paraphrase and several poems survive, CCV, 725.

MATTHIAS AGRICICIUS WITLICHIUS, whose date is wholly unknown, is the author of a declamation in praise of St Rupert, formerly abbot of Deutz, CLXVII, 15.

MAURICE DE SULLY, bishop of Paris. He was not of the illustrious family of the lords of Sully, but was born of humble mother Humberga at the town of Sully on the Loire, whence his surname de Sully. Endowed with outstanding gifts, he rose by his own merit to the episcopate in 1160 and ruled his church piously and energetically for thirty-six years. His letters and diplomas survive. He died in 1196, CCV, 887.

MAURILIUS (Blessed), archbishop of Rouen. Born of a noble house in the district of Reims, he was first a cleric of Reims, then a monk of Fécamp, became abbot of a monastery at Rouen, and finally archbishop in 1055. He died in 1067. There survive his letter to the bishop of Évreux, *Confession on the Sacrament of the Body and Blood of the Lord*, and epitaphs for Rollo and William, CXLIII, 1581.

MAURUS, bishop of Ravenna. He became patriarch in 648, rebelled against the pope out of pride, and died miserably. A letter by him to Pope Martin survives, LXXXVII, 103.

MAURUS, abbot-elect of the church of the Temple, swore an oath of fidelity to Lord Robert, patriarch, and his successors, twelfth century, CLV, 1113.

MAXENTIUS, patriarch of Aquileia. Supported by the favor of King Lothair, he began to trouble the suffragans of Istria and, though admonished by Pope Gregory, refused to desist. There survive his letter on the meaning of the rites of baptism and a collection concerning ancient baptismal rites, in 840, CVI, 50.

MAXIMUS, priest and confessor. See MOYSES.

MAXIMUS, priest, together with Urbanus, Sidonius, and Macharius, renounced their error in the hands of Pope St Cornelius and subsequently confessed the faith, as is clear from Cornelius’s own letters, in 351, III, 720, 736.

MAXIMUS (Magnus), tyrant of Gaul. By treachery he seized Gratian, assumed the purple, and transferred the imperial seat to Trier in 381. He himself was defeated in battle and killed by Theodosius in 388. Two letters concerning him survive, to Pope Siricius and Emperor Valentinian, XIII, 391.

MAXIMUS, grammarian. Born in the city of Madaura, he was well known to Augustine; but, devoted to pagan worship, he wrote to the holy Doctor in defense of the gods. He flourished in 399, XVIII, 405; XXXIII, 81.

MAXIMUS (St), bishop of Turin. His birthplace, year, and deeds are unknown to us; he flourished in the fifth century. He was raised to this dignity by Pope St Leo; he came to Rome in 465 and attended the council held under Pope Hilary, and died in the same year. His sermons, homilies, and letters survive, LVII, 137.

MAXIMUS (St), abbot and confessor of Constantinople, flourished in the seventh century. He endured much at the hands of the Monothelites, whom he had fought in his writings [Col. 0496]. John Scottus Eriugena translated his *Book of Ambiguities* into Latin, CXXII, 1193.

MAXIMUS, bishop of Zaragoza. He is mentioned by St Isidore; he flourished about the middle of the seventh century. He left many writings, among which especially notable is an abridgment of the history of the kings of the Goths. He attended many councils held in Spain and died in 644, LXXX, 610.

MECTHILDIS (Blessed), a nun of the monastery of Helfta, of the Order of St Benedict in Saxony, and companion of Abbess St Gertrude, wrote a book *On Spiritual Grace* and celebrated the praises of St Bernard of Clairvaux, in 1334, CLXXXV, 638.

MEFFRIDUS, prior of Eberbach monastery. He flourished at the end of the twelfth century; he wrote to St Hildegard, asking for her prayers and a letter, CXCVII, 259.

MEGASIUS. See MIGDONIUS.

MEGINFREDUS, monk of Fulda, flourished in the eleventh century, in 1010. His birth and death are equally uncertain. After discharging the office of scholastic at his monastery of Fulda, he held the same office in another monastery at Magdeburg. He was learned and among the more learned men of his age. There survives his book *On the Life and Virtues of St Emmeram*, CXLI, 970.

MEGINHARDUS and WOLF granted part of their inheritance to the Church of St Saviour at Werden in 845, under Emperor Lothair. Several charters concerning the same matter survive, XCIX, 809, 811.

MEGLINGER (Fr Joseph), religious priest of the monastery of Blessed Mary of Maris Stella, commonly called Wettingen; he is the author of a Cistercian Itinerary of 1667, which he sent in epistolary form to Jacob Mechler, parish priest in the March of Schwyz, CLXXXV, 1565.

MELCHIADES (St), pope. He succeeded St Eusebius in 311. African by nationality and highly commendable for his virtues and learning, he sat for three years and died in 314. Two decrees and two letters are attributed to this pontiff, VII, 1114.

MENSURIUS, bishop of Carthage, later succeeded by Caecilian. He was denounced by the Donatists, especially by Secundus, bishop of Tigisis, on the allegation that he had handed over the sacred books in the persecution. He cleared himself of this charge at a council and demonstrated the contradiction in Secundus’s own statements. Both their letters are mentioned, in 305, VIII, 426.

MEROBAUDUS, scholar, Spanish by nationality. Fleeing his homeland because of the barbarian invasions, he came to Italy, where, highly cultivated in humane letters, he won renown among the Romans. Of his writings only a poem on Christ survives. He died in 426, LXI, 971.

MESSIANUS, priest, and STEPHANUS, deacon, of Arles, lived under St Caesarius. After his death they wrote a book on his life and miracles, about 545, LXVII, 1025, 1253.

MICHAEL, dean of the Church of Blessed Mary at Paris, declares that he and the chapter of the same church consider valid the agreement between Adela, queen of France, and Maurice, bishop, concerning the church of St Exuperius, in 1191, CCV, 913.

MICHAEL, called Clokkett, received a mission from Guy, count of Flanders, to Pope Boniface VIII in 1297; an account of that mission survives, written in the French language of that age, CLXXXV, 1857.

MICHAEL NEANDER, follower of Luther. What he declared concerning St Bernard is usefully set forth, in 1595, CXXXXV, 638.

MIGDONIUS, MEGASIUS, VALENS, EPICTETUS, and other bishops from the Council of Rimini who professed Arius’s doctrine, unwilling to retract their opinion, wrote a letter full of flattery to Emperor Constantius and against accepting the *homoousion* (“of one substance”), in 359, in order that they might depart from there, X, 703.

MELISENDE, queen of Jerusalem and formerly wife of Fulk, granted certain diplomas in favor of certain stewards, in 1153, CLV, 1136, 1137.

MILETUS, abbot of the Church of St Sabas, sold to Nicholas, prior of the Holy Sepulchre, for 480 bezants a certain piece of land which he had received from Queen Melisende, nevertheless to fulfill the alms attached to that land (without mention of the year), CLV, 1229.

MILO, monk of St Amand on the river Elnon in Belgium, in the diocese of Tournai, of the Order of St Benedict. He was distinguished for literary learning and especially for cultivation of poetry from 840 to 871. There survive his Life of St Amand, bishop of Maastricht; sermon on the translation of that saint’s relics; poem on the conflict of spring and winter; epitaph of Pippin and Drogo, CXXI, 926.

MILO CRISPINUS, born of the noble Crispin family, became monk and cantor of the abbey of Bec. He committed to writing the Life of Blessed Lanfranc as well as those of certain abbots of the same monastery. He was Lanfranc’s contemporary and flourished about 1089, CL, 19, 713.

MILO, first a monk of St Albinus at Angers, afterward a cardinal under Pope Paschal II, whose eulogy he wrote in verse. He flourished in the twelfth century, in 1118, CLXIII, 27.

MILO, count of Bar, founded the monastery of nuns at Jully in 1145 and entrusted its government to Guy, abbot of Molesme, with the consent of Joserann, then bishop of Langres, CLXXXV, 1408.

MILO, archpriest of Milan, entered into a certain agreement with Osmund, canon of St Mary at Paris, and Aymeric, monk of Saint-Denis, in 1164, CC, 907.

MILO, bishop of the Morini, flourished in the twelfth century, in 1172. He wrote to Pope Alexander III against Gilbert, bishop of London. CC, 1416.

MILO (Master), notary of Pope Innocent and legate of the Apostolic See, reported all that was done in the war against the Albigensians and received the submission of those who returned to the faith and to the Lord Pope in 1209. CCXVI, 124 ff.

MILREDUS, bishop. He wrote an encomium of Saint Boniface, whom he had known in life, for Saint Lullus, in 756. XCVI, 834.

MINUCIUS FELIX. Of him we know only that he was born in Africa and went to Rome, where he practiced as an advocate. Lactantius and Jerome count him among the foremost orators of this age. There survives a book by him entitled *Octavius*, in which, in dialogue form, he establishes the faith and overthrows the worship of the gods. III, 193.

MIROSLAUS, one of the leading men of Bohemia, at the persuasion of Henry, bishop of Moravia, founded and endowed the monastery of Sedlec in 1143. Its government was entrusted to the Blessed Abbot Gerlac of the Cistercian Order. CLXXXV, 984.

MONTANUS, bishop of Toledo after Celsus, flourished in the time of Amalaric, king of the Goths, in 522. His name was celebrated throughout Spain. He attended the Council of Toledo. He died in 531. Two letters by him survive. LXV, 48.

The COUNT OF MONTFERRAT and other commanders of the holy army give an account to the bishops and faithful of all Christendom of the capture of Constantinople, in 1203. CCIX, 925.

MORAGE RAIZ, in order to discharge what he owed the king, sold a certain house in which he had a mill for 120 bezants and 12 measures of grain. (Without mention of the year.) At the end of the twelfth century. CLV, 1211.

MOSES and MAXIMUS, priests; NICOSTRATUS and RUFINUS, deacons; and other confessors held in prison at Rome, having received letters from Saint Cyprian expressing sympathy for their sufferings, send in return an answer and thanksgiving, in 252. IV, 290.

MUNIO, bishop of Mondoñedo, formerly treasurer of the church of Compostela and later chaplain and secretary of King Alfonso VII, who directed an expedition against the Saracens who had invaded Spain. There survives by him a history of the church of Compostela, in 1134. CLXX, 875.

## N

NALGODUS, monk of Cluny, flourished in the twelfth century; he wrote the *Life of Saint Odo*, monk of Cluny. CXXXIII, 85.

NANTHARIUS, abbot of the monastery of Sithiu; he bought from a certain Herlarius lands situated at Fletrin in 804. CXXXVI, 1217.

NANTHELMUS, bishop of Belley, commonly called Anthelmus, intervened between the monks of the monastery of Majeure and the house of Rougemont, who were disputing among themselves concerning certain rights, and happily brought them to agreement in 1164. CLIII, 935.

NARIODUS of Montbarro, with the consent of his sons Gualo and Bernard, gave to the Church of Fontenay the whole land of the grange of Flacey toward Saigny. (Without mention of the year.) Twelfth century. CLXXXV, 1465.

NAZARIUS, rhetorician, of whom biographers have handed down nothing, flourished before the middle of the fourth century and was distinguished for remarkable eloquence about 320. There survives by him a panegyric addressed to the Emperor Constantine. VIII, 581.

NEBRIDIUS, born not far from Carthage, was most dear to Augustine; through him his whole household received the faith of Christ. He followed Augustine to Milan and there taught grammar under Verecundus; he attacked astrologers and especially Manichaeans. Finally, he was an ardent seeker of the blessed life and died shortly after Augustine’s baptism. There survives a letter from him to Augustine, in 390. XXXIII, 67.

NECTARIUS, a pagan man distinguished among his own people, wrote twice to Augustine on behalf of his native town of Calama concerning the injuries which pagans had inflicted upon Christians. These letters survive among the letters of the Blessed Doctor, in 409. XXXIII, 313, 386.

NEMESIANUS, DATIVUS, FELIX, and VICTOR, African bishops and confessors, suffering various torments for the faith, reply by letter to Saint Cyprian and sympathize with his imprisonment, in 258. IV, 420.

NESTORIUS, originally a monk born in Syria, attained the see of Constantinople under Theodosius the Younger. But when he began to preach against the mystery of the Incarnation, he was denounced and condemned in several councils; he died miserably in the Thebaid, to which he had been banished, about 440. Some writings by him survive in Marius Mercator. XLVIII, 757, 898; L, 43, 432, 499.

NICEPHORUS (Saint), patriarch of Constantinople, upheld the veneration of holy images against Emperor Leo the Armenian. Harassed and expelled from his see by him, he withdrew to the monastery of Saint Theodore, which he himself had founded. He died in 828. He left many works in Greek. There survives by him, in Saint Pope Leo III, a letter written in Greek and Latin. CII, 1057.

NICETAS (Saint), bishop of Aquileia. Neither his family, nationality, nor year is certainly known. He wrote to Saint Leo concerning certain questions raised by Attila’s devastations. Of his writings, only this letter has survived. Sixth century. LII, 837.

NICETIUS (Saint), bishop of Trier. Born of most devout parents, he studied letters, then embraced monastic life, and finally was raised to the see of Trier in 527. He attended the Councils of Clermont held from 535 to 549, and the Second Council of Paris in 551; he died in 556. There survive by him shorter works and two letters. LXVIII, 36.

NICOLAS I, pope, born to Theodore the regionary, was first a deacon of the Roman Church. He succeeded Pope Benedict III and was consecrated in the presence of Louis II. He died in 867. During his pontificate the dispute with Photius, archbishop of Constantinople, began. His letters survive. CXIX, 769.

NICOLAS II, pope, formerly Gerard. A native of Burgundy, he came to Italy, where, because of his outstanding virtues and learning, he was soon made bishop of Florence. He was made Roman pontiff in 1058. He died in 1061. His letters and privileges survive. CXLIII, 1299.

NICOLAS, apparently an English priest, to whom Eadmer had revealed certain troubles, consoles his friend and then treats of the primacy of the see of York. He flourished in the eleventh century. CLIX, 809.

NICOLAS, legate and cardinal of the Apostolic See, together with Sixtus and Guido, wrote to Emperor Conrad against those plotting against the pope and clergy, in 1150. CLXXXIX, 1303.

NICOLAS, abbot of Corbie. There survives a letter to Suger, about 1153. CLXXXVI, 1416.

NICOLAS, prior of the Holy Sepulchre, granted to Richard Jaferinus, for an annual rent of fourteen bezants, in 1160. CLV, 1205.

NICOLAS, monk of Clairvaux, whose homeland is unknown to us, flourished under Saint Bernard, about 1175. He had first entered the monastery of Aremar in the Cluniac Order; afterwards, drawn by Bernard’s reputation and holiness, he came to Clairvaux and closely attached himself to the holy abbot, whose notary he became. Yet, when the sainted abbot found perversity in him, he removed him from office; leaving Clairvaux, he became an enemy. Bernard complains of him in writing to Pope Eugenius. When and in what manner he died is unknown. His letters and sermons survive. CXCVI, 1589.

NICOLAS, bishop of Liège. Historians report nothing concerning him except that he lived in the time of Master Alger, whose encomium he wrote. CLXXX, 737.

NICOLAS, monk of Mont-Rouen, flourished in the twelfth century and was a contemporary of Saint Thomas of Canterbury, to whom he wrote many letters. CXC, 679.

NICOLAS HACQUEVILLE, president of the sacred senate of Paris, composed several verses in praise of Saint Bernard and on the site of the monastery of Clairvaux. He belongs to a later age, the eighteenth century. CLXXXV, 566.

NICOLAS, monk of Saint Albans, was one of those pious men in England who attempted to spread the doctrine of the Immaculate Conception of the Blessed Virgin. Peter of Celle disputed against him, and both parties considered it necessary to have recourse to a definition of the Church, as indeed occurred under Pope Pius IX in our own time. He lived in the twelfth century. CCII, 622.

NICOLAS of Amiens flourished at the beginning of the thirteenth century. He wrote a short *Chronicle* in eight books, from the creation of the world to the year 1203 of Christ’s Incarnation, which he excerpted almost word for word from Eusebius, Jerome, and Sigebert of Gembloux. CLX, 409.

NICOLAS, patriarch of Aquileia. There survives a charter in which the ceremonies of his reception and installation in 1351 are described. XCIX, 658.

NICOLAS of Villalta, by his testament emancipated a certain slave, Leonard, and gave him and his sons full freedom: namely, the right to make wills, sell, pledge, give, buy, receive, contract, and so forth. This charter was drawn up at Aquileia in 1351. XCIX, 659.

NICOSTRATUS, deacon and confessor. See MOSES.

NITHARD, commonly described by biographers as abbot of Saint-Riquier, was born to Angilbert and Bertha, daughter of Charlemagne. The Benedictine authors of the *Literary History of France*, however, rightly judge that this man was not a monk at all but a soldier, and that he died at the time when the Normans invaded Gaul. Four books by him survive: *On the Dissensions of the Sons of the Emperor Louis the Pious*, in 859. CVI, 36.

NIVARDUS, bishop of Reims. He gave all that he possessed to the monastery of Hautvillers, on the condition that he and his successors should retain authority over that monastery’s monks, and that the monks should enjoy the power of electing a superior. Only a fragment of this charter survives, from 662. LXXXVIII, 1181.

NIVARDUS, brother of Saint Bernard, whom he had followed into the wilderness, was sent with companions as abbot to the monastery of La Spina in the diocese of Piacenza, about 1147. There survives a letter from him to Saint Bernard. CLXXXII, 578.

NIVELO, bishop of Soissons. He replied to Stephen, bishop of Tournai. From his words he appears to be suffering the same burden from the officials of the Roman Curia; he flourished at the end of the twelfth century, in 1199. CCXI, 473; CCXIV, 885.

NIZEZIUS, a man of the city of Cahors, equally pious and wealthy, and his wife Ermintrude gave many things, though under the form and title of a sale, to Leotadius, abbot of Moissac, in 680. LXXXVIII, 1202.

NORBERT (Saint), founder of the Premonstratensian Order and archbishop of Magdeburg. He was educated at the court of Frederick of Cologne. From there he withdrew to the monastery of Siegburg. He established his order in 1120 and attained the archiepiscopal office in 1127. He died in 1134. Two sermons to the people and charters by him are preserved. CLXX, 1355.

NORGAUDUS, bishop of Autun, entered into a settlement with Hugh, abbot of Cluny, concerning certain churches. This settlement was decided by Milo, bishop of Palestrina and cardinal, at the Council of Marseilles in 1103. CLIX, 977.

NOTGER, bishop of Liège. Born in Swabia of noble parents, he was first provost of the monastery of Saint Gall; from there Odilo summoned him to Stavelot to instruct the monks. Finally he was elected bishop of Liège and solemnly consecrated in 974. He died in 1008. He wrote the *Deeds of the Bishops of Liège* and several biographical works. CXXXIX, 1170.

NOTKER THE STAMMERER (Blessed), monk of Saint Gall. As a boy he was received at Saint Gall, where his teachers were Marcellus and Iso. He died at a very advanced age in 911. He wrote a book on the interpreters of Holy Scripture, sequences, a martyrology, letters, and poems. CXXXI, 985.

NOVATIAN, Roman priest. Born in Phrygia, he cultivated philosophy while not yet a Christian. Having become a priest, he attempted to seize the Roman See in 251. But he was expelled by the Roman council as a supporter of heresy and an enemy of the faith. There survive by him a book *On the Trinity*, a letter *On Jewish Foods*, and other writings composed in the name of the Roman clergy and addressed to Saint Cyprian. He died in 260. III, 862.

NOVATUS, a Catholic of the fourth century, who also appears to have been a monk, is known to us only through his exhortation to monks concerning humility and obedience. XVIII, 67.

NUMERIANUS, archbishop of Trier. Asked by Adeodatus, bishop of Toul, he granted certain privileges to the monastery of Val-Galilée, concerning which he informed the provincial bishops by letter in 667. But sound critics consider this charter spurious. LXXXVIII, 1191.

## O

OCEANUS, a Spanish priest, consulted Saint Jerome concerning the validity of the ordination as bishop of Carterius, who had married twice, first before and then after baptism. The holy doctor replied affirmatively, but the practice of the Church prevailed in the contrary direction, in 420. XXII, 653.

ODALRICUS, or Udelricus, and Ubricus, son of Count Hugh and Eva. A native of Lorraine, a learned man and conspicuous for virtue, he became archbishop of Reims with King Lothair’s favor; he died in 969. There survives by him a sentence against sacrilegious thieves. CXXXIII, 963.

ODALRICUS, provost of Reims. We have nothing certain about this man’s lineage, birth, or life. His testament survives, from 1100. CL, 1546.

ODDAG, son of a certain Othilric, sold part of his inheritance to the Church of Saint Saviour at Werden for twenty-two solidi, in 837, under Emperor Louis the Pious. XCIX, 809.

ODDO II, duke of Burgundy, son and successor of Hugh II, died in 1162. In 1149 he confirmed all the gifts made by Guy of Sobernon and his wife Ermengarde to the nuns of Saint Mary of Molesme; likewise, the gift of Girard, lord of Asnières, in 1162. CLXXXV, 1419, 1122.

[Col. 0500] ODILO, monk of Saint Medard at Soissons in Gaul, of the Order of Saint Benedict, about 930, wrote to Ingrandus, dean of his monastery and later bishop of Laon, concerning the translation of the relics of Saint Sebastian the martyr, performed in 926. CXXXII, 575.

ODILO, abbot of Cluny. Born in Auvergne of a noble and ancient family, from his earliest years he excelled in remarkable piety and love of study. He soon retired to the monastery of Cluny and received the habit from Blessed Abbot Maiolus, who shortly afterwards chose him as his successor, in 994. Out of humility he refused the see of Lyons together with the pallium. He died in 1049. There survive by him the Lives of Saints Maiolus and Adelaide, sermons, letters, and so forth. CXLII, 831.

ODO, king of the Franks (Eudes), son of Robert the Strong, first called count of Paris, succeeded Charles the Fat in 887 and died in 898. There survives by him the oath which he pronounced at his consecration before Walter, archbishop of Sens. CXXXVIII, 797.

ODO, bishop of Beauvais, formerly abbot of Corbie. He attended very many councils. He translated the relics of Saint Vedast to Beauvais with due veneration. He died in 881. His sermons on Saint Lucian, canons, an ordinance concerning property assigned to the congregation of Saint Peter, and other works survive. CLV, 287 ff.

ODO (Saint), abbot of Cluny, born of the royal stock of the Franks in 879; he was tonsured and educated in the monastery of Saint Martin at Tours. Afterwards he went to Burgundy and lived the monastic life at Cluny under Berno. He subsequently made many journeys through France, Aquitaine, Spain, and Italy. He died in 942. His exegetical works, hymns, conferences, sermons, and musical treatises survive. CXXXIII, 9.

ODO (Saint), archbishop of Canterbury. Born of a noble but still pagan family, he left his paternal home in early youth, soon received baptism, and took the monastic habit. About 937 he became abbot; finally he was raised to the archbishopric of Canterbury and died in 961. His constitutions and synodal letters to suffragans survive. CXXXIII, 931.

ODO, bishop of Chartres, granted a piece of land to Robert, canon of Saint Mary, for his lifetime, in return for an annual rent of ten solidi; he also bestowed certain gifts upon the monastery of Saint Peter at Chartres, in 974. CLV, 227 ff.

ODO, deacon of the metropolitan church of Auch. We know nothing of him except that he wrote a surviving letter to his archbishop Garcia. He lived in the tenth century. CXXXVII, 311.

ODO, apparently count of Blois, wrote a complaint to King Robert against Count Richard and complained to the king himself that he had spoken ill of him, in 1024. CLXI, 938.

ODO, son of Count Manasses. With the assent of his brother Hugh and his sister Eustachia, he gave to the monastery of Saint Peter at Chartres a serf named Rimbert and his sister Frodburga in 1061. CLV, 296, 310.

ODO, bishop of Bayeux, granted the monastery of Saint-Vigor to Jarenton, abbot of Saint-Bénigne at Dijon, in 1096. CLV, 475.

ODO, abbot of the monastery of Lézat, also governed the small monastery of Cours; but the monks of Cluny violently seized the latter. Odo, whose monastery as well as the little abbey of Cours depended upon the monastery of Moissac, and who did not dare resist those monks, together with Gerald, abbot of the little abbey of Cours, determined to restore it to the hands of the abbot of Moissac so that it might be freed from an evil and unlawful administration. He wrote to Pope Paschal II about these matters in 1104. CLXIII, 456.

ODO, monk of the abbey of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés near Paris, where he had been brought up from childhood. He endured persecutions, though he was commended for exceptional virtues; he died in 1112. There survives by him the *Life of the Venerable Count Burchard*, restorer of the aforesaid abbey. CXLIII, 845.

ODO (Blessed), bishop of Cambrai. Born at Orléans, he was first a teacher in his native country, then abbot of Saint Martin at Tournai, and finally was elected bishop of Cambrai in 1105. But because he refused to receive episcopal investiture from Emperor Henry, he was expelled from his see and withdrew to the monastery of Anchin near Douai, where he died in 1113. He wrote an exposition of the Canon of the Mass; a book *On Original Sin*; a disputation *On the Advent of Christ*; a double homily on the steward of iniquity; and charters. CLX, 1039.

ODO, monk of Asti of the Order of Saint Benedict. He flourished from 1106 to 1123 and wrote to Bruno, bishop of Segni, an exposition of the Psalms composed in contemplation. CLXV, 1142.

ODO and PETER, sons of Milo Debois, with the consent of their mother Dameron and their sister Agnes, gave to the monastery of Clairvaux all that they possessed in the land of Jurville and Warancemont, without any reservation, about 1147. [Col. 0501] CLXXXV, 991.

ODO, bishop of Beauvais, who had induced Peter of Miliac, a turbulent man excommunicated for an unlawful marriage, to take the cross and leave the kingdom, wrote to Suger that Peter, once absolved, should quickly depart from his country, about 1147. CLXXXVI, 1396, 1398.

ODO, abbot of Saint-Remi. First a monk in the abbey of Morigny, then abbot of Saint-Crépin at Soissons, he was summoned from there to succeed Azinarius as abbot of Saint-Remi in 1118. He governed that monastery until 1151. Two letters and a cartulary by him survive. CLXXII, 133.

ODO, abbot of Morimond. We know of him only his writings or sermons; he flourished in 1156. CLXXXVIII, 1643.

ODO, count of Issoudun, and his wife Matilda, daughter of Raymond, brother of Henry, bishop of Langres, granted the brothers of Fontenay the revenues of Casati from the lordship of Grignon, retaining the soil for themselves, in 1165. The charter is written in the name of Henry, bishop of Langres. CLXXXV, 1469.

ODO, prior of Saint-Victor at Paris, later abbot of the new Saint-Geneviève. He held the office of prior under Gilduin. He was a learned, eloquent, and exceedingly pious man. He died in 1166. Several letters by him survive. CXCVI, 1398.

ODO of Deuil (Deuil near Paris), abbot of Saint-Denis, flourished in the twelfth century. From childhood he had taken the monastic habit; he was distinguished by good character, prudence, and intellect. He was a close companion of Louis the Younger, whom he followed as secretary to Palestine. On his return, he was made head of the monastery of Saint Cornelius at Compiègne, dependent on the abbey of Saint-Denis; finally he succeeded Abbot Suger in 1151. He died in 1168. CXCV, 992. See also CLXXXV, 1199; CCV, 907.

ODO, bishop of Toul. Born to Hugh I, count of Vaudémont, and Agelina, and brother of Count Gerard II, he was educated in the church of Toul under Henry. He first discharged the offices of archdeacon and treasurer, was called to the episcopate in 1192, and died in 1198. His synodal statutes survive. CCV, 914.

ODO, cardinal of the Roman Church, wrote through a servant to Ervisius, abbot of Saint-Victor at Paris, and commended the servant as well. He flourished in the twelfth century. CXCVI, 1388.

ODO, count of Champagne, gave to the church of Saint Stephen at Besançon, for his brother Louis and his deceased predecessors, a manse at Paygne, in 1202. CLXXXV, 1459.

ODO of Sully, bishop of Paris. A man adorned both by illustrious birth and nobility of character, he succeeded the deceased Maurice by the unanimous consent of the chapter. His synodal constitutions, statutes, pious donations, and, in addition, an account of a miracle of Saint Geneviève survive, in 1208. CCXII, 47 ff.

ODO CAMBIERUS, who flourished about 1657, composed a prose hymn in praise of the Blessed Virgin Mary of Afflighem. CLXXXV, 1830.

ODOLRICUS, bishop of Chartres. He flourished at the beginning of the eleventh century, in 1027. CLV, 259.

ODORANNUS, monk of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif, was born in 985. From youth he embraced monastic life in the monastery of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif near Sens. Highly skilled in the goldsmith’s art, he wonderfully made for King Robert a golden shrine to receive the relics of Saint Savinian. Although he wrote much, only one *Chronicle* survives, which he composed when nearly sixty years old. He died in 1045. CXLII, 765.

OFFA, king of the East Saxons, reigned at the same time as Cenred, king of Mercia. Together with him, and in the same charter, he granted many possessions to the monastery of Evesham in 709. This was afterwards confirmed by Pope Constantine. Both kings, having laid down the sceptre, took the monastic habit at Rome. LXXXIX, 336.

OGERIUS, abbot of Lucedio in the diocese of Vercelli. Biographers relate little about him. He is the author of sermons inserted among the sermons of Saint Bernard, in 1149. CLXXX, 1657; CLXXXIV, 850.

OGERIUS and his wife gave to Blessed Robert and the monastery of Fontevraud a certain land at Vérone, at the beginning of the twelfth century. CLXII, 1113.

OGIVA, queen. See ALREDUS.

OLDEGARIUS (Saint), archbishop of Tarragona. Born about 1060 of an illustrious Barcelona family, he excelled alike in learning and in the virtues becoming to a prelate. He was first bishop of Barcelona, and shortly afterwards archbishop of Tarragona. Finally, distinguished for holiness and miracles, he died in 1136. Two letters and a charter by him survive. CLXXII, 1357.

OLIVA, bishop of Ausona or Vic. Son of Oliva Cebreta, count of Besalú, he was first a monk of Ripoll, then abbot of Cuxa, and was elected bishop in 1017. He died in 1047. His sermons and letters survive. CXLII, 589.

[Col. 0502] OLIVERIUS of Grignon. See GAUTHERIUS, bishop of Autun.

OODHELMUS, son of Oodwerc, gave a considerable part of his inheritance to the monastery of Werden, reserving for himself and his wife Theodelinda the usufruct for life, in 793. XCIX, 798, 815.

OPTATIANUS PORPHYRIUS, a Latin poet, to be distinguished from the philosopher of the same name, flourished in the fourth century. Although the Venerable Bede thought that Optatian lived as a pagan, his writings prove that he was nevertheless a Christian. There survive by him a letter to Constantine, and a metrical and acrostic panegyric addressed to the same Constantine. XIX, 387.

OPTATUS (Saint), bishop of Milevis and Doctor of the Church, known more through his writings than his deeds, attacked the Donatist heresy with tireless zeal. Under Pope Damasus he wrote six books against Parmenian. He seems to have died in 384. XI, 759.

ORDERIC VITALIS, an English-born monk and outstanding writer. He was born at Ettingesham above the river Severn, on the border of Mercia and Wales, in 1075. He was educated in the monastery of Saint Evroul under the eyes of his father, who had likewise retired there after his wife’s death; he was ordained priest. He died in 1142. He wrote an *Ecclesiastical History*. CLXXXVIII, 9.

ORIENTIUS (Saint), bishop of Auch in the fifth century. Endowed with divine eloquence, he rescued many unbelievers from the darkness of idolatry. Already an old man, he was sent as bishop by Theodoric, king of the Goths. He died happily about 450. CXI, 973.

ORIGEN, Alexandrian priest, one of the most celebrated Fathers of the Greek Church, was born at Alexandria in 185. He advanced so far in learning that, scarcely an adolescent and not yet ordained, he began to teach and write. He went to Caesarea in Palestine, where he received the priesthood from Bishop Theotistus. When persecution raged, he concealed himself, dictating and writing books day and night; captured by persecutors, he boldly confessed the faith and, after various torments, obtained freedom. He again undertook writing. Many bishops defended his cause, while others declared war upon him. He died in 254. He published many writings. His work *On First Principles* especially gave occasion for controversy. There survive homilies by him translated from Greek into Latin by Saint Jerome and by Rufinus of Aquileia. XXI, 176; XXIV, 901; XXV, 583; XXVI, 219.

PAULUS OROSIUS, a Spanish priest and citizen of Tarragona, flourished in the age of Emperor Honorius, in the fifth century. He came to Africa, where Catholics were being harassed by the perversity of heretics, in order, if possible, to bring some remedy and to visit Saint Augustine. When he died is uncertain. He is the author of an *Apology on the Freedom of the Will*. XXXI, 635.

ORSIESIUS (Saint), disciple of Saint Pachomius, was a monk and then abbot; he set forth his teaching in a certain treatise. He flourished in the fourth century. CIII, 453.

OSBERN, precentor and monk of the church of Canterbury. An Englishman by birth, he flourished about 1070. He was familiar with Archbishop Lanfranc and most skilled in chant. His *Lives* of Saints Dunstan and Ælfheah, archbishops of Canterbury, survive. CXLIX, 367.

OSIUS, a Spaniard and bishop of Cordoba. The Arians often attempted to draw this illustrious man to themselves; but Hosius stood firm in the faith. Therefore Constantius, inflamed with anger, kept him, though an old man, in exile from his country for a whole year at Sirmium, where he suffered insults, blows, and lashes, so that under violence he yielded for a moment to tortures; but when death was near he confessed the faith and pronounced an anathema upon the enemies of the faith. There survive statements of Hosius at the Council of Laodicea and a letter to Constantius. He died in 357. VIII, 1309.

OSMUNDUS, bishop of Astorga, wrote from Spain to Blessed Ida, who was seeking relics everywhere, about 1059. CLV, 459.

OSBERTUS CASTALDUS, of Lombardy, gave many things to the monastery of Saint Emmeram for the gaining of salvation; only mention is made of this donation. Ninth century. CXXIX, 922.

OTHELBOLDUS, thirty-sixth abbot of the monastery of Saint Bavo at Ghent, which he governed from 1019 to 1034. There survives a letter from him to Ogiva, countess of Flanders. CXLI, 1338.

OTHLONUS, priest and monk. Born in the diocese of Freising, endowed with a teachable and ready mind, he applied himself diligently to study from his earliest years. He embraced monastic life in 1032 in the monastery of Saint Emmeram. He wrote many books, among them a book on his own temptations. He died in 1083. CXLVI, 27.

OTHO I, emperor of Germany. He succeeded Henry I, subdued the Huns, Hungarians, and Bohemians, bore arms in Gaul against Louis, and performed many things for the benefit of his subjects. He died in 973. Various diplomas by him survive. XCVIII, 587, 603; CXXXVIII, 821.

OTHO II, emperor of Germany, son and successor of Otto I, deposed Henry of Bavaria and resisted Lothair in Gaul. He died in 983 and was succeeded by Otto III. His diplomas survive. XCVIII, 587; CXXXVIII, 851.

OTHO III, son and successor of Emperor Otto II, was proclaimed in 983. He waged war against the Slavs and throughout Italy; according to some, he died of poison in 1002. Two edicts by him survive. CXXXVIII, 853.

OTHO (Saint), bishop of Bamberg, called the apostle of Pomerania. He was born of noble stock in Savoy about 1060; from childhood wholly devoted to divine worship, he embraced the clerical life. Then, through Henry’s advancement, he became bishop of Bamberg in 1112. He died in 1139. His letters and diplomas survive. CLXXIII, 1267.

OTHO, bishop of Freising, flourished in the twelfth century, in 1152. He wrote a letter to the Venerable Wibald, abbot of Corbie, in which he comments on the words of the Psalm, “Lift up your gates, O princes,” etc. CLXXXIX, 1398.

OTHO and WILLIAM of Pavia, cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, who had been sent by Alexander III to Henry II, king of England, to settle the affair of the exile of Saint Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, give an account of their mission. Twelfth century. CXC, 993; CC, 1391.

OTHO II, emperor of Germany, son of Henry of Bavaria, succeeded Henry VI—or rather Philip—and was excommunicated by Innocent III. He died in 1218. Very many diplomas by him survive. CCXVI, 999 and passim.

OTKERUS, monk of Regensburg. We know nothing about him except that he was skilled in music, which he cultivated with distinction. CLI, 691.

OTTO. We have written OTHO everywhere; see that entry.

OWENUS, king of Wales, a God-fearing man who professed great affection for Saint Thomas of Canterbury, thereby incurring the anger and hatred of King Henry. There survives a familiar letter from him to Thomas in exile. Twelfth century. CXC, 1055.

## P

PACATUS LATINUS DREPANIUS, a Gaul by nationality and a native of Bordeaux, flourished in the fourth century, in 395, and was a friend of Ausonius. There survives by him a panegyric addressed to Emperor Theodosius before the senate. XIII, 471.

PACHOMIUS (Saint), monk in Upper Thebaid. Born about 292, he was first a soldier and afterwards a monk; he soon became abbot over more than 6,000 monks and devoted every care to governing them. He established a rule which Saint Jerome translated into Latin, as also several letters. He departed this life amid the tears of his followers in 348. XXII, 61, 87.

PACIANUS (Saint), bishop of Barcelona. He was distinguished in Spain by noble birth and remarkable talent; because of his eloquence he was raised to the see of Barcelona in 373. There survive by him three letters to Sempronianus, a short work or exhortation on penitence, a sermon on baptism, and so forth. He died about 391. XIII, 1051.

PAGANUS of Miribel gave to the Lord Robert of Arbrissel and the monastery of Fontevraud a wood called Ruret and an adjoining meadow beside the Andrus, while Philip was then reigning, in the twelfth century. CLXII, 1112.

PAGANUS, patriarch of Aquileia, ordered an ancient instrument, by which privileges had formerly been granted by Patriarch Berthold to the Church of Saint Nicholas of Sacello, to be renewed, copied, and carried into effect, in 1328. XCIX, 653.

PALLADIUS, born in Galatia, was first a monk in the desert of Nitria, then became bishop of Helenopolis, and finally bishop of Aspuna. On account of his friendship with Saint Chrysostom he endured persecutions. Expelled from his own see, he undertook various journeys; meanwhile he composed his *Lausiac History*, so called after a certain Lausus, prefect of Cappadocia, to whom he dedicated the book, about 420. LXXIII, 1065.

PALLADIUS (Saint), bishop of Auxerre. Formerly abbot of Saint Germanus, he devoted himself wholly to learning ecclesiastical disciplines. He attended the Council of Reims in 625 and that of Clichy in 633. He died in 653, having subscribed in that year to the diploma of Clovis II for the monastery of Saint-Denis at Paris. Only a letter from him to Saint Desiderius, bishop of Cahors, survives. LXXXVII, 264.

PAMMACHIUS, a learned man of noble birth, married Paulina, daughter of Saint Paula. At Rome he defended the cause of his close friend Blessed Jerome against malicious detractors; but after Paulina’s death, on Jerome’s counsel, he is said by some to have renounced the world. He maintained a pleasant exchange of letters with the holy doctor. There survives a letter from him [Col. 0504], also attributed to his companion Oceanus, in 420. XXII, 511, 568, 639, 743.

PAMPHILUS. See EUSEBIUS.

PANCRATIUS and HILARIUS, priests, together with Lucifer, bishop of Cagliari and legates of the Apostolic See at the Council of Milan in 355, wrote to Eusebius of Vercelli urging him not to delay in coming to drive away the Arian plague. XIII, 765.

PANDULFUS of Alatri, nephew of Hugh of Alatri, cardinal priest, was admitted to the palace of Pope Gelasius II and lived there in close familiarity with him; he died about 1119. He wrote the life of that pope and of certain others. CLXIII, 473, 1079.

PAPHNUTIUS (Saint), first a monk and disciple of Saint Antony, confessed the faith during the persecution of Maximian. Having become a bishop, he vigorously defended the cause of Saint Athanasius. The *Life of Saint Onuphrius* is attributed to him, in 350. LXXIII, 211.

PAPIAS, grammarian, flourished about 1053. A Lombard by nationality, under Emperor Henry he published an elementary work. CXLI, 1438.

PASCENTIUS, count of the royal household, was sent to Carthage and was a harsh collector of the revenue, as well as a zealous supporter of the Arian heresy. He dared to challenge Saint Augustine to a public disputation. The holy doctor came; but when the heretical man could neither resist nor answer him, he nevertheless boasted everywhere that he had won. Hearing this, the holy doctor sent him a letter justly complaining of this manner of proceeding; but Pascentius replied only with abuse. At the beginning of the fifth century. XXXIII, 1051.

PASCHAL I (Saint), pope. A Roman by birth, his holiness became known through miracles. He succeeded Stephen IV in 817. Previously he had professed the monastic life. He died in 824. His letters survive. CII, 1086.

PASCHAL II, pope. A Roman by birth, he was first called Rainerius or Ragengerius and was a monk of Cluny; afterwards he became abbot of the monastery of Saints Lawrence and Stephen outside the Walls at Rome. He was then clothed in the purple and finally elected pope in 1099. He died in 1118. His letters and privileges survive. CLXIII, 9.

PASCHASINUS, bishop of Lilybaeum, was especially distinguished by the legation undertaken at the command of Leo I to the Council of Chalcedon in 450. There survives by him a letter in which he complains of the oppression he suffered through the malice of Genseric. L, 1291.

PASCHASIUS, deacon of the Roman Church, flourished at the end of the fifth century, a man commendable for piety and uprightness of life. He died in 512. There survive by him two books *On the Holy Spirit* and a letter to Eugyppius, abbot and priest, LXII, 9.

PASCHASIUS RADBERTUS (Saint), abbot of Corbie. Born in 780 of unknown parents in the district of Soissons, he was educated in a monastery, which he left in order to live in the world; soon, however, wearied of it, he withdrew to the monastery of Corbie. He was later raised to the priesthood and finally elected to the office of abbot; he died in 860. Many of his writings survive, both exegetical and theological, as well as letters, the Passion of Saints Rufinus and Valerius, and the Life of Saint Adalhard, CXX, 9.

PATERIUS (Saint), priest, notary, and *secundicerius* under Saint Gregory the Great, whose counsellor and confidant he was. He later compiled into four books, from Saint Gregory’s writings, collected passages on both the Old and New Testaments. He is mentioned not only by Gregory the Great, but also by John the Deacon, Sigebert of Gembloux, and Trithemius. About 610, LXXIX, 677.

PATRICK (Saint), bishop and apostle of the Irish. He was a Briton by nationality, born in the town of Nemthur in 372, the son of Calpurnius. Saint Germanus of Auxerre sent him to Rome in 432 to disclose to Pope Celestine his intention concerning the conversion of the Irish to the faith; accordingly he received from him the episcopal office. After many distinguished deeds throughout all Ireland, he died in extreme old age in 493. There survive by him his *Confession*, a letter to Toratius, and synodal canons, LIII, 795.

PAULA (Saint). A noble Roman matron who, having become a widow, went with her daughter Eustochium to Bethlehem to be with Saint Jerome, so that, consecrated to God, she might devote herself to prayer and the study of Scripture. She learned Hebrew letters and distributed great wealth to the poor. She died in 407. There survives her letter to Marcella in Saint Jerome, XXII, 483.

PAULINUS, deacon of Milan, according to Saint Isidore, was raised to the priesthood. There survive by him a *Life of Saint Ambrose*, a short work against Caelestius, and another book, *On the Blessings of the Patriarchs*. He died about 418, XX, 703.

[Col. 0505] PAULINUS (Saint), bishop of Nola. He was born of a noble senatorial family about 367. At first bound by marriage, he was granted the consulship and the highest honours; but, after losing his only son, he bade farewell to the world and became a monk. Soon afterward he was ordained priest and then made bishop. He illumined the Church both by his virtues and by his learning. He died in 431. His letters and poems survive, LXI, 9.

PAULINUS of Périgueux, a Gaul by nationality, flourished from 461 to 490, when he died. He was the son of the rhetorician Paulinus whom Sidonius mentions in his letters. There survives by him a poem on the *Life of Saint Martin*, written at the request of Saint Perpetuus, and another work of lesser importance dedicated to the same bishop, LXI, 1008.

PAULINUS, patriarch of Aquileia. He was born in 730 and held in great veneration by Charlemagne; he was elected in 776. He attended many councils and preached the Gospel in Carinthia and Styria. He died in 804. There survive by him a book *Against Elipandus*, three books *Against Felix of Urgel*, hymns, and fragments of letters, XCIX, 9.

PAULINUS, to whom some verses on Duke Eric, transcribed in a semi-barbarous style, are attributed, seems to us wholly uncertain. He lived in the eighth or ninth century, XCIX, 683.

PAULULUS. See ROBERTUS.

PAUL and STEPHEN (Saints), abbots who handed down a monastic rule, are mentioned by Saint Benedict of Aniane and by Smaragdus. No other traces of them appear concerning the time and places in which they flourished. Fourth century, LXVI, 949.

PAUL, deacon of Mérida, concerning whom biographers transmit very little, composed a history of the Church of Mérida in 610, LXXX, 112.

PAUL, bishop of Constantinople, was installed in Pyrrhus’s place under Pope Theodore, while Monothelitism was disturbing the East. There survives by him a letter to Theodore himself. In 641, LXXXVII, 91.

PAUL (Saint), bishop of Verdun. A noble Belgian, he first lived as a hermit; with Dagobert’s support he was raised to the episcopate. There survive by him letters to Saint Desiderius, bishop. In 650, LXXXVII, 261.

PAUL I (Saint), pope, succeeded his brother Stephen II. He was Roman by nationality and held the Apostolic See from 757 to 767. His letters survive, LXXXIX, 1125.

PAUL, Greek by origin and military commander, was sent by Wamba, king of the Goths, against the authors of sedition who had arisen from the regions of Gaul and were ravaging the surrounding districts. But he plotted treachery, seized Narbonne, and made an alliance with the rebels, hoping through them to advance to the kingship. Wamba therefore sent an army, drove him from all the places he had occupied, and Paul, having fled to Nîmes, was captured after the terrible overthrow of the entire faction, in 710, XCVI, 761.

PAUL THE DEACON, son of Warnefrid, Italian by nationality, deacon of Aquileia and chancellor of Desiderius, the last king of the Lombards, whom he followed into Gaul after his capture by King Charles. A man most learned in the Scriptures, subtle in intellect, and eloquent in expression, he published historical, ascetical, and hortatory writings, letters, and poems. He died in 801, XCV, 1606.

PAUL ALVARUS. See ALVARUS.

PAUL, deacon of the Church of Naples, translated into Latin the Life of Saint Mary of Egypt, whose author was Sophronius the bishop. Sigebert mentions him in his catalogue of illustrious men, as does Hildebert in a certain poem; but when he flourished is unknown, LXXIII, 671.

PAUL, monk of Saint Peter at Chartres, flourished at the beginning of the eleventh century. There survives by him the ancient *Agano*, or cartulary of Aganon, CLV, 175.

PAUL, canon of the Church of Regensburg, having been exiled by Emperor Henry IV, took the habit of the order of regular canons in the newly founded monastery of Bernried about 1120; there he was ordained priest by the bishop of Passau. He died in 1131. He published a Life of Blessed Pope Gregory VII, CXLVIII, 39.

PELAGIUS, British monk. A crafty man of the most subtle intelligence, he taught errors concerning original sin and the grace of God, and was condemned in three councils. Saint Augustine fought most vigorously against him for the Catholic faith. For his writings and their fragments, see XXI, 1168; XLVIII, 83, 587.

PELAGIUS I, pope. A Roman by nationality, son of John, vicar of the praetorian prefect, he was raised to Peter’s chair in 555. He died in 559. His letters and decrees survive, LXIX, 392.

PELAGIUS II, pope. Gothic by origin, son of Vinigild, he was elected in 577, when the Lombards were ravaging Italy. He died in 590. His letters and decrees survive, LXXII, 702.

PELAGIUS, deacon of the Holy Roman Church, translated into Latin the fifth book of the *Lives of the Holy Fathers*. Some conjecture that he was the same man who later occupied the Roman see (see above). He lived in the sixth century, LXXIII, 851.

PELOQUINUS of the island of Buchard granted all his customary dues, by water and by land, to the nuns of Fontevraud, at the beginning of the twelfth century, CLXII, 1118.

PEREGRINUS, priest of the Church of Musti in Africa, one of the old Primianists, wrote against Donatus, convicted Maximinianus of heresy, and is called a venerable man by Augustine. There survives by him a supplicatory tract against the Maximianists; perhaps he is the Peregrinus mentioned in the Council of Carthage of 408, XI, 1191, 1201.

PEREGRINUS, patriarch of Aquileia. Having heard complaints from Hatturic, provost of the monastery of Saint Stephen, against a certain advocate, Meginhard, whose agents were inhumanely oppressing peasants and poor people, he summoned him, urged him to desist, and induced him to yield to the monastery the right of his advocacy. This was done for twenty marks of silver in 1134, XCIX, 644.

PEREGRINUS, abbot of Saint Mary of the Latins, swore an oath of fealty to Lord Robert, patriarch of Jerusalem, and to his successors, before Arnald, bishop of Lydda, his vicar, in 1240, CLV, 1111.

PERIANDER, tyrant of Corinth and one of the Seven Sages of Greece, flourished in 585 before Christ. There survive under his name, in Saint Ambrose, two letters, to the sages and to Proclus, XVII, 1149.

PERINGERUS, abbot of Tegernsee. Almost no documents concerning him survive, but twelve letters do. He lived about 1040, CXLI, 1313.

PERPETUA (Saint), noble Christian matron and martyr, was first cast into prison at Rome under the persecution of Valerian and Gallus, together with her companions; then, before the judge, she courageously confessed the faith of Christ. She herself wrote on tablets all that happened to her before the shedding of her blood, in 203, as also the sufferings of her companions, III, 9.

PERPETUUS (Saint), bishop of Tours. A man outstanding in piety and charity, and in tireless zeal for safeguarding and strengthening the doctrine of the Church. He succeeded Eustochius in 461 and died in 491. His testament and statutes survive, LVIII, 751.

PERTOLDUS, patriarch of Aquileia, granted exemption to the chapel of Saint Quirinus, where converted sinful women were kept, from the jurisdiction of the parish priest of Udine, in 1242, XCIX, 6478.

PERTUALDUS, a pious citizen of Lucca, founded and endowed the church and monastery of Saint Michael, with almsgiving for the poor prescribed in its foundation, in 721, LXXXVII, 1365.

PETILIANUS, made bishop of Cirta by the Donatists, was ingenious and eloquent. He wrote letters against the Catholic faith, to which Saint Augustine replied; Petilianus took this badly. He flourished in 398, XXXII, 640.

PETRARCH (Francesco), Italian and Latin poet of the fourteenth century, is regarded as a restorer of letters. Pursuing political life, he adhered to the Ghibelline party. While living at Avignon, he devoted many verses to his beloved Laura. Later he took orders and withdrew to Milan. He died in 1374. There survives by him a testimony concerning Saint Damian, CXLIV, 183.

PETRONILLA of Montaranto, Paganus of the Valleys, and certain others gave to the nuns of Fontevraud land at Podia; Elias of Tello and Geoffrey of Calvignac added certain things to this donation (without indication of year), twelfth century, CLXII, 1097.

PETRONIUS, ANNIANUS, and JULIANUS are known to us only from their letter to Domitius Celsus, vicar of Africa, from which it appears that they were regarded as officials under Emperor Constantine the Great, in 311, VIII, 749.

PETRUINUS. See AREDIUS.

PETER CHRYSOLOGUS (Saint), bishop of Ravenna, was so called because of his outstanding eloquence. He was born at Imola and from childhood devoted himself to piety and study. He was ordained priest by Saint Cornelius, gave himself especially to preaching, and discharged that office in such a manner that he was raised to the see of Ravenna by the unanimous consent of all. He died in 450, under Pope Leo the Great. His sermons survive, LII, 14.

PETER the Deacon, concerning whom biographical documents are lacking, nevertheless seems, from his short work addressed to Fulgentius, to have been adequately instructed in theological matters. He died about 513, LXII, 80.

PETER, abbot of Classe and of the Camaldolese Order, is known to us only from the oath that he rendered to Gerbert, archbishop of Ravenna, in 993, CXXXIX, 269.

PETER, archdeacon, appears to have flourished in the eighth century, a man of piety and learning. We have by him a commentary in dialogue form on the prophecy of Daniel, XCVI, 1347.

PETER, the Librarian. Nothing certain is known of him except that he wrote an abridged history of the Franks in 892, CLI, 1280.

PETER, monk of Maillezais, of the Order of Saint Benedict, a Gaul by nationality, flourished in the eleventh century, about 1070. He published for Abbot Godchramnus a short work *On the Antiquity and Growth of the Island of Maillezais*, and two books *On the Translation of Saint Rigomer*, CXLVI, 1247.

PETER DAMIAN (Saint), cardinal-bishop of Ostia. He was born near Ravenna in 988 to parents of honourable, though modest, means. Entrusted in childhood to the care of his elder brother, he tended pigs; but another brother, moved by pity for him, sent him to school. Having completed his studies, he embraced monastic life at the monastery of Fonte Avellana, of which he became abbot in 1041. He was later made cardinal by Pope Stephen in 1062. He died in 1072. His letters, sermons, lives of saints, hymn, poems, and collections on the Old Testament survive, CXLIV and CXLV.

PETER TUDEBODUS, priest of Cierac, flourished at the end of the eleventh century, about 1095. He is the author of an account of the *Journey to Jerusalem*, CLV, 758.

PETER ALPHONSI, a Jew converted to Christianity, formerly called Moses. A Spaniard by nationality, he was baptized by Stephen, bishop of Huesca, in 1106. The date of his death is unknown. He wrote a dialogue against the Jews, divided into twelve parts, CLVII, 527.

PETER THE SINNER, cleric of Ravenna. He compiled a monastic rule from other rules and sent it to Pope Paschal II for correction. Perhaps he is the same as Peter de Honestis, who flourished at the same time, was placed over the monastery at Porto, and to whom a rule for clerics is likewise attributed. In 1108, CLXIII, 461, 691.

PETER de HONESTIS. See the preceding PETER THE SINNER.

PETER GORGA remitted to Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, the tithe that he held at Cabanaria from Aimon the Elder, about 1128, CLXVI, 1574.

PETER BERNARDI, canon of the Holy Sepulchre. With the consent of the prior and other canons, he granted Andrew and his wife Hosanna permission to build a house on land of the Holy Sepulchre, on condition that they should have and possess it for as long as they lived, paying an annual rent of two bezants, in 1136, CLV, 1206.

PETER LEONIS, Roman by nationality, was factionally elected pope by a minority in 1130 and assumed the name Anacletus. He provoked great disturbances and even bloodshed in the city; by every lawful and unlawful means he occupied Saint Peter’s chair for seven years. He died in 1138 and was buried without ceremony. His letters and privileges survive, CLXXIX, 687.

PETER, prior of the Holy Sepulchre, granted to a certain Arnulf, son of Bernald, houses situated over the vaults of the hospital exchange, subject to an annual rent of nine bezants, in 1144. Another charter by him also survives, CLV, 1177, 1179.

PETER, archbishop of Bourges. When Abbot Suger informed him of King Louis’s return, he wrote two letters to the venerable abbot concerning this happy event, in 1149, CLXXXVI, 1400, 1402.

PETER, monk, appears to have lived about 1150 under Aimon of Saint-Pierre de Dives, in the diocese of Séez. Since he was accustomed to compose verses, Milo, monk of Bec, urged him to write in metre the life of the first seven abbots of that monastery, CLXXXI, 1703.

PETER THE VENERABLE, abbot of Cluny, formerly called Maurice of Montboissier, acquired exceptional knowledge of Scripture and was distinguished by uprightness of life: an accomplished grammarian, an elegant rhetorician, a sharp dialectician, an exact arithmetician, a regular geometer, and skilled in astronomy and music. He rested in a blessed end in 1158. We have by him six books of letters, various treatises, sermons, statutes, and poems, CLXXXIX, 9 ff.

PETER, monk of Poitiers, contemporary of Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, composed in verse a panegyric of him and an admonition to the calumniator of that panegyric, as well as letters to the same Peter. He died in 1160, CLXXXIX, 47, 57, 59, 661.

PETER LOMBARD, bishop of Paris, was from Lombardy and of humble birth and condition. With the assistance of the bishop of Lucca, he learned letters, in which he advanced so far that he later deserved to be called the Master of Sentences because he wrote a book of theological sentences. He learned Hebrew and Greek, as is evident from his commentary on the Book of Psalms. He died in 1160, CXCI–CXCII.

PETER, archbishop of Tyre. He granted to the chapter of the Holy Sepulchre and to Lord Nicholas, prior, the tithe of a certain village together with the Church of Blessed Mary, Amalric the patriarch being witness, in 1161. Another charter by the same man survives, CLV, 1167.

PETER OF PISA, dean of the Church of Saint Anianus at Orléans, flourished in the twelfth century. For some time he supported the antipope Anacletus (Peter Leonis) against Innocent, but his reconciliation took place under Paschal II, in 1162. Under Pope Alexander III, he wrote against contumacious bishops. He compiled a Life of Pope Paschal II, CLXIII, 13; CC, 1365.

PETER de ROYA, monk of Clairvaux. He flourished from 1155 to 1169. He was educated among the clerics of Noyon and later made a canon, but soon fell from fervour into a dissolute life. Finally, moved by repentance, he withdrew to the abbey of Clairvaux, where he embraced monastic discipline and ended his life in 1169. There survives by him a letter included among the letters of Saint Bernard, CLXXXII, Job; CLXXXV, 1683, 1687.

PETER COMESTOR, canon and dean of Blessed Mary of Troyes, called “Comestor” because of his eagerness for study and learning, was a Gaul by nationality. He flourished in the twelfth century, a theologian of great renown, and became chancellor of the University of Paris. He died about 1178. Of his writings, the *Scholastic History* and sermons survive, CXCVIII, 1043.

PETER, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church. First archdeacon, then abbot, afterward bishop of Meaux, and, through the favour of William of Champagne, made archbishop of Sens. On account of his singular learning he received the cardinal’s purple under Alexander III, who delegated him to suppress the Albigensian heresy in 1173. He appears to have died in 1182. Letters concerning him survive, CXCIX, 1119.

PETER MONOCULUS, eighth abbot of Clairvaux. A Gaul by nationality and born of noble stock, he was first a monk of Clairvaux, then made abbot of Igny, from which office he was brought to govern Clairvaux in 1179. He wrote elegant letters on various subjects. He died in 1186, CC, 1381; CCI, 1391.

PETER, abbot of La Celle, afterward of Saint-Remi at Rheims, and finally elected bishop of Chartres in 1180 to succeed John of Salisbury. There survive by him two books of letters, sermons, and a treatise on cloister discipline. In 1187, CCII, 397.

PETER LATRO and JOHN NICOLAI were appointed guardians of Odo, nephew of Peter Latro, whose grandmother and guardian was Lady Lucina. They refused this office into the hands of Cencius, cardinal-deacon of Saint Lucy in Silice, under Pope Celestine III, in 1193, CCVI, 1272.

PETER, bishop of Roskilde. He flourished about 1192. There survives by him a letter to Pope Celestine III, whom he advises concerning a statute issued by himself on the annual revenues of deceased priests, CCIX, 678.

PETER THE CHANTER, born at Paris or Rheims, devoted himself from childhood to literary study, and advanced so far in it that, while still a young man, he taught with great distinction at the University of Paris. He became precentor of the Church of that city. He refused first the bishopric of Tournai and then that of Paris in order to become a monk at Longpont of the Cistercian Order, whither he withdrew. He died in 1197. There remains by him an outstanding work entitled *The Abbreviated Word*, CCV, 21.

PETER, prior of the Hospital of Constantinople, by whom there survives a letter to Louis the Younger, king of the Franks. He undertook a mission from the emperor on behalf of the pope and King Louis. Twelfth century, CLV, 1275.

PETER OBLINCI bestowed upon the monastery of Fontevraud many lands situated at Beau Champ and elsewhere. During Philip’s reign over the Franks, he later took the monastic habit and gave himself wholly to the contemplative life. Twelfth century, CLXII, 1115.

PETER DE CHAMILIAC, through the hand of Lord Robert of Arbrissel, gave to the monastery of nuns at Fontevraud the customary due of Laine, situated in the castle of Chamiliac, during the reign of Louis the Fat. Twelfth century, CLXII, 1117.

PETER de GUSMACHIA, by testament, ordered that a church be founded in the place called Landa de Belloquercu, endowed, and handed over to the nuns of Fontevraud and to Blessed Robert of Arbrissel (without indication of year). Twelfth century, CLXII, 1104.

PETER, bishop of Bourges, granted and confirmed to Cluny the church of Carandigna under the administration of Abbot Pontius (without indication of year). Twelfth century, CLXVI, 845.

PETER OF PAVIA flourished in the twelfth century. Having received letters from Blessed Thomas of Canterbury, he declares that he shares in all his tribulations and exhorts him not to lose heart, CXC, 1021.

PETER OF POITIERS, faithful disciple of Peter Lombard, became a most celebrated master and chancellor of the theological faculty at Paris, distinguished for virtuous life and learning. He must be distinguished from another man of the same name who was a disciple of Peter, abbot of Cluny. There survive by him five books of *Sentences*. In 1205, CCXI, 779.

[Col. 0509] PETER CAMBIUS, bishop of Paris. In order to turn his clergy away from certain popular customs and games unworthy of their profession, he established a certain payment for the celebration of the offices of the Circumcision of the Lord and of the feast day of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, in 1208, CCVII, 1168.

PETER de NEMOURS, bishop of Paris, in 1208 confirmed the donations of his predecessor Odo, CCXII, 91.

PETER, monk of Vaux-de-Cernay in the diocese of Chartres, flourished at the beginning of the thirteenth century, in 1208. He wrote a history of the crusade against the Albigensian heretics initiated by Innocent III.

PETER de RIGA, a Gaul by nationality, native of Vendôme, flourished from 1191 to 1208. He was first a regular canon of Blessed Mary at Rheims; he then entered the abbey of Saint Denis in the same city. He published many poems on various passages of Holy Scripture. Of his writings only fragments of the book entitled *Aurora* survive, CCXII, 9.

PETER BERMUNDI, son of Bernard of Andissia and lord of Salve, remained faithful to the Roman Church. He had married the only daughter of Count Raymond of Toulouse. He wrote to Innocent III that his wife was the sole lawful heir, and that the man who claimed to have been born from the same count was illegitimate and not an heir, in 1212, CCXVI, 754.

PETER II, king of Aragon, son and successor of Alfonso II, drove out the Moors near Navia Tolosana. He had at one time taken the side of the Albigensians and the count of Toulouse, but later wrote to Innocent III that he was returning to the bosom of the Church. He died wounded in battle against the Albigensians in 1212. In the same year he had granted certain privileges to the houses of the Holy Sepulchre under Abbot Berengar’s administration, CLV, 1255; CCXVI, 839.

PETER, prior of Saint Peter at Langres; Paganus, official; and Humbert, provost of Bar, issued letters in 1215 resolving a controversy that had arisen between the monks of Clairvaux and Garnier of Chaleta, because the latter refused them the homage which his father had granted, CLXXXV, 1762.

PHERECYDES, an ancient Greek historical writer, flourished in 408 before Christ. A certain letter to Thales, found in Saint Ambrose, is attributed to him, XVII, 1150.

PHILASTRIUS (Saint), bishop of Brescia, whose lineage and native country are unknown to us, attended the Council of Aquileia in 381 together with Saint Ambrose. There survives by him a book *On Heresies*. He died in 387, XII, 1049.

PHILIP, priest and disciple of Saint Jerome, flourished especially about 440. Besides letters long since lost, he wrote a commentary on Job, which survives among the works of the Holy Doctor. He died during the reigns of Marcian and Avitus, LIII, 1012.

PHILIP I, king of the Franks, son and successor of Henry I. His letters and charters survive, CLIX, 838.

PHILIP, monk of Clairvaux, undertook to describe the miracles of his master, Saint Bernard, which he dedicated to Samson, archbishop of Rheims. He flourished about 1160, CLXXXV, 371.

PHILIP OF HARVENG, abbot of Bonne-Espérance of the Premonstratensian Order, an eloquent and learned man, pious and devoted, and a close friend of Saint Bernard. Born of modest stock, he first joined Odo, abbot of Bonne-Espérance, under whose instruction he advanced toward lofty perfection; after Odo’s death, he succeeded him. He died in 1182. His commentary on the *Song of Songs* and various other short works survive, CCIII, 1.

PHILIP, bishop of Beauvais, flourished at the end of the twelfth century. He wrote to Pope Celestine about the incursion of the king of England into the territory of Beauvais and about how he had been taken prisoner because he was hostile to the king of France, in 1196, CCVI, 1278.

PHILIP and BARTHOLOMEW, Lombard brothers, together with their sister Aldruda, grant to Pope Innocent III a third part of what they possess in the place called Castle of the Nymphs, in 1204, CCXVII, 290.

PHILIP, duke of Swabia and king of the Romans, shortly thereafter emperor, fought against Otto, whom the princes had chosen in opposition to him, and obtained power, which he held until 1208, when he was murdered, CCXVI, 1012.

See also CCXVII, 295 ff.

PHILIP II AUGUSTUS, king of the Franks, son of Louis VII and of Alix, daughter of Theobald. He married Ingeborg, sister of Canute, king of the Danes, but shortly afterward repudiated her in order to marry Agnes of Merania. Consequently he incurred excommunication, and an interdict was imposed upon all France. He died in 1223. His letters and charters survive, CCXI, 391, 395.

See further CCXII, 74; CCXVI, 976, 1007; CCXVII, 279.

PHILIP, bishop of Châlons. Since certain secular cares prevented him from carrying out ordinations, he referred to Lambert, bishop of Arras, the persons whom Poppo, bishop of Metz, had sent to him for ordination, and requested that he confer orders on them. This was done at the beginning of the twelfth century, CLXII, 665.

[Col. 0510] PHILIP, count of Flanders, lived in the twelfth century. He earnestly asks Saint Hildegard for prayers and seeks her advice whether, after the expedition, he ought rather to remain in the Holy Land or return from it, CXCVII, 187; CC, 1392.

PHILIP, dean of Cologne, flourished at the end of the twelfth century. He wrote to Saint Hildegard, commending himself to her prayers, and asks her to set down in writing the visions which she had revealed to him orally, CXCVII, 243.

PHILIP, abbot of Blessed Mary of Park, in the territory of Leuven, wrote to Saint Hildegard, abbess of Mount Saint Robert at Bingen, whom he praises and to whose prayers he commends himself. Twelfth century, CXCVII, 276.

PHILIP, archbishop of Cologne, flourished in the twelfth century. There survives by him a letter to Saint Hildegard, to whom he gives praise and from whom he seeks counsel, CXCVII, 183; CC, 10.

PHILIP DE ELEEMOSYNA, abbot, flourished in the twelfth century. He wrote to Saint Thomas of Canterbury, saying many things worthy of praise concerning Master Gerard, who seems to be managing his affairs and wishing to reconcile the king’s heart to him, CXC, 1045.

PHILIP, duke of Burgundy, called the Good, son and successor of John the Fearless, died in 1467. As lord of the castle, he confirmed in 1442 all donations that had been made to the canons of Saint Mary of Salz, CLXXXV, 1439.

PHILOCALUS, concerning whose life, profession, country, and death nothing certain is known. There survives by him an ancient calendar, fourth century, XIII, 671.

PHILOTHEUS, whose name appears to be assumed, was a monk of Brescia. An Italian by nationality, he wrote in verse a eulogy of the life and character of Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, at the end of the twelfth century, CLXXXV, 551.

PHOEBADIUS (Saint), bishop of Agen. A Gaul by nationality and Aquitanian by birth, he was raised to the episcopate shortly after 350 and attended the Council of Rimini concerning the Arians. He was a man distinguished by piety and learning, and a most vigorous opponent of Arian perfidy. Of his writings there survive a book *Against the Arians*, a *Treatise on the Divinity and Consubstantiality of the Son of God*, and a short work *On Faith*. In 392, XX, 10 ff.

PIBO, bishop of Toul. A Saxon by nationality and of noble lineage, he was first a canon in the Church of Halberstadt, then honoured with the offices of almoner and chancellor in the court of Emperor Henry IV. He was made bishop in 1107. His charters survive, CLVII, 415.

PICO, count of Mirandola, adhered to the Ghibelline party and attained the greatest reputation for learning from his youth. He died in 1494. A testimony concerning Saint Bernard of Clairvaux survives in his writings, CLXXXV, 632.

PIPPIN OF HERSTAL, duke of Austrasia and mayor of the palace, concentrated in himself all royal power, as did also his son Charles Martel. He and his wife Plectrude granted to the venerable Abbot Beregisus the castle of Amblève, in order that he might build a church and monastery, as the charter of 687 records. Besides this, certain other charters concerning them survive, LXXXVIII, 1215, 1219, etc.; LXXXIX, 539.

PIPPIN, son of Charles Martel and the first Carolingian king. At first he reigned with his brother Carloman. He waged war against the rebellious Gascons and died in 768. His charters survive, XCVI, 1504 ff.

PIRMINIUS (Saint), bishop and abbot, leaving behind country and parents, brought the light of the Gospel into Austrasia. He was made bishop, founded or restored very many monasteries, and governed many of them himself. He died in 758. There survives by him a short work *On Canonical Books*, LXXXIX, 1029.

PISISTRATUS, tyrant of Athens. Driven out and restored again to his power, he flourished in 560 before Christ. There survives under his name, in Ambrose, a letter to Solon translated from Greek, XVII, 1147.

PITHOU (Nicolas Pierre), distinguished jurist, philologist, and poet, born at Troyes, flourished in the sixteenth century. He offered an outstanding eulogy of Saint Bernard. There is also a fragment by him concerning the counts of Champagne, in 1596, CLXXXV, 637, 1479.

PITTACUS, called one of the sages, native of Mytilene, ruled Athens for some time in 579. There survives by him a letter to Croesus, king of Lydia, XXII, 1149.

PIUS I (Saint), pope and martyr, Italian by origin, condemned the heresy of Valentinus, endured many tribulations, and ended his life by the sword in 150, CXXX, 111.

GALLA PLACIDIA, empress, daughter of Theodosius, governed the Empire for thirty-five years in the name of her son Valentinian. She died in 450. Two letters by her survive, one to Theodosius and the other to the Empress Pulcheria, LIV, 859, 863.

PLACIDUS, prior of the Benedictine monastery of Nonantola and later bishop of an unknown see. Anonymous of Melk mentions only that monastery and its abbot. He wrote a book *On the Honour of the Church* against investitures and the unjust power of Henry IV, CLXIII, 614.

PLACIDUS (Dom), monk and deacon of Monte Cassino. Nothing is recorded of him except that he wrote a supplement to Peter the Deacon’s short work *On the Illustrious Men of the Monastery of Monte Cassino*. He flourished in the twelfth century, CLXXIII, 1049.

PLATO, son of Ariston, most celebrated among Greek philosophers and founder of the Academic school. He taught philosophy at Athens about 347 before Christ. There survives by him, in Saint Ambrose, a letter to the poet Archytas, translated from Greek into Latin, XVII, 1152.

POLEMEUS ANN. SILVIUS. See ANNAEUS.

POLIANUS, confessor. See FELIX.

POLYCARP (Saint), bishop and martyr of Smyrna, was a disciple of Saint John; under Marcus Aurelius he suffered about 166 in advanced age. Several fragments concerning him survive in Victor of Capua, LXVIII, 359.

POMERIUS JULIANUS, priest. A Moor by nationality, he went to Gaul, founded a school of rhetoric in the city of Arles, and was finally ordained priest. He flourished about 498. Of his writings, only the work *On the Contemplative Life* survives, LIX, 411.

POMPEIUS, prefect of Emperor Justin, wrote to Pope Hormisdas to inform him that peace had been restored in the Eastern Church. About 519, LXIII, 451.
