PONTIANUS (Saint), pope. After Urban’s death he was raised to Saint Peter’s chair; he suffered much for the faith under the tyrant Maximinus and died miserably in Sardinia, to which he had been exiled, in 235. Certain decrees and a letter are falsely attributed to him in Pseudo-Isidore, CXXX, 141.

PONTIANUS, African bishop. He flourished in the sixth century and is known to us only through a letter that he wrote to Justinian concerning the Three Chapters, LXVII, 996.

PONTIUS (Saint), deacon of Carthage, appears to have been African by nationality and deacon of Saint Cyprian, whom he followed into exile. He committed to writing the acts of the holy martyr, III, 1477.

PONTIUS, count of Toulouse, in 1060 subjected the abbey of Moissac to the monastery of Cluny. The charter bears the subscription of Bernard, bishop of Cahors, and of Countess Adalmodis, in 1060, CLIX, 955.

PONTIUS, abbot of Chaise-Dieu, entered into an agreement with Hugh, abbot of Cluny, in 1096, CLIX, 975.

PONTIUS, abbot of Cluny, son of Peter, count of Mâcon, previously monk of Saint-Pons, succeeded Blessed Hugh in 1109 and died in 1125. His statutes and instructions survive, CLXVI, 835.

PONTIUS, bishop of Clermont, formerly fifth abbot of Clairvaux, flourished about 1180. In a letter he asked Maurice of Paris and Stephen, bishop of Tournai, about the validity of a certain baptism in which the words appeared to have been truncated, CCXI, 312.

PONTIUS, abbot of Vézelay, wrote to Suger on behalf of the widow of Robert, a physician formerly his friend, and of her deceased son; the year is not given. Twelfth century, CLXXXVI, 1418.

POPPO, bishop of Trier. Born of distinguished parents and formerly provost of the Church of Bamberg, he was raised, through the favour of Emperor Henry II, to the see of Trier, which he held for thirty years. He died in 1047. There survives by him a letter to Pope Benedict IX, CXLI, 1402.

POPPO, bishop of Metz, brother of Count Palatine Henry, first archdeacon of Trier, succeeded Burchard in the episcopal see of Metz in 1091, which he governed piously and vigorously until his death in 1103. His letters and several charters survive, CLV, 1655.

PORPHYRY, Greek philosopher. He first followed Origen’s school, then soon passed to Apollonius and Photinus; he attacked Christian doctrine and died about 304. Certain fragments by him concerning dialectical art and Aristotle survive among Boethius’s commentaries, LXIV, 71.

POSSESSOR, bishop in Africa. He consulted Pope Hormisdas concerning a book by a certain Faustinus, bishop of Riez in Gaul, who was stirring up scandals and dissensions among his people over free will and the grace of God. The Supreme Pontiff gave him satisfaction about the year 520, LXIII, 489.

POSSIDIUS, bishop of Calama in Africa. At first a disciple and intimate associate of St Augustine, he was perhaps one of the clerics educated under the holy Doctor and living according to the rule. Subsequently, on account of his merits, he became bishop of Calama. There survives by him a *Life of Saint Augustine*, L, 401; XXII, at the beginning.

POTAMIUS, bishop of Lisbon. He flourished in the fourth century. At first he defended the faith; later, for the reward of an imperial estate which he coveted, he betrayed the faith in the year 366. Two treatises by him survive, one on Lazarus, [Col. 0512] the other on the martyrdom of the prophet Isaiah, as well as a letter to St Athanasius, VIII, 1409.

PRIMASIUS, bishop of Hadrumetum. An African by race, from Byzacena, he was one of those sent to Constantinople in 550 to conduct the affairs of the African Church. He subscribed Pope Vigilius’s constitution concerning the Three Chapters and was therefore thrown into prison; eventually restored to liberty, he died at Hadrumetum. His *Commentaries on the Epistles of St Paul* and on the *Apocalypse* survive, LXVIII, 408.

PRISCIAN, distinguished grammarian of the fifth century. He opened a very celebrated school at Constantinople and produced a grammatical treatise in eighteen books, of which only extracts survive in Rabanus Maurus, CXI, 613.

PROBUS (Valerius Marcus), grammarian. See VALERIUS.

PROSPER, who wrote to Augustine concerning the Pelagian heresy still surviving in Gaul, concerning predestination, prevenient grace, and the fixed number of the elect, seems to be altogether identical with St Prosper of Aquitaine. See what follows.

PROSPER (St), priest of Aquitaine, whose life is little known, cultivated theological subjects and the liberal arts with care, and proved especially useful in these fields, as his writings show. There survive dogmatic, exegetical, poetic, and historical works by him. He died about 450, LI, 10.

PROSPER, converted from Manichaeism to the Catholic faith. Nothing else has been handed down concerning him except that he abjured the heresy, as is shown by his anathemas and profession of faith, in 526, LXV, 23.

PROTADIUS (St), archbishop of Besançon. Born of noble stock, he was greatly revered and loved by Chlothar II, who frequently made use of his counsel. In 612 he succeeded Nicetius in the see of Besançon, which he held until 624. A liturgical work by him survives, LXXX, 410.

PROTERIUS (St), patriarch of Alexandria. In 454 he wrote Pope Leo I a letter concerning the day of Easter, of which a double translation survives and which shows that, in this question, the ancient Fathers paid particular attention to the fast, which was not permitted on Easter Day. He died in 460, LIV, 1084.

PRUDENTIUS, Aurelius Clemens (St), Christian poet. Born in the province of Tarragona, he was carefully instructed in the sciences and liberal arts and devoted himself especially to poetry. While still young, he sometimes departed from the right path toward pleasures; but later he expiated these by severe penitence. Not a few metrical writings by him survive; 348, LIX and LX.

PRUDENTIUS (St), bishop of Troyes. A Spaniard by birth, he came into Gaul under King Alfonso the Great, where he was soon raised to the bishopric of Troyes in 846. He attended the councils of Paris and Tours in 849, and that of Soissons in 855; he governed his church devoutly and vigorously. There survive letters by him to Hincmar and Pardulus concerning predestination, 861, CV, 977 and following.

PTOLEMY, a Roman consul of the Julian line and paternal uncle of Peter, monk and deacon of Cassino. Having heard that his nephew Peter had been expelled from the monastery by factional monks, he sent him a letter asking him to come to him; he would give him a monastery to govern, and he should bring with him his father, who was in need, so that he himself might lead a somewhat more fitting life, about 1128, CLXXIII, 465.

PUBLICOLA, the only son of Melania and Pinianus, of senatorial origin, was very dear to Augustine; but his unexpected death caused great mourning among his parents and friends. St Paulinus speaks of him in many honourable terms to the holy Doctor. There survives a letter of Publicola to Augustine, 408, XXXIII, 181, 347.

PUBLIUS VICTOR, concerning whom biographers are silent, was the author of a description of the city of Rome, fourth or fifth century, XVIII, 435.

PULCHERIA (Aelia), daughter of Arcadius and Eudoxia, held the sceptre under her brother Theodosius. Having at one time been banished, she was recalled after her brother’s death and became Marcian’s wife; she died in 453, LIV, 905.

PULLUS ROBERT. See ROBERT.

PURCHARDUS, monk of Reichenau. Under the flourishing instruction of Wilger he completed his studies; he himself became distinguished for talent and eloquence, a serious and outstanding poet. He celebrated in heroic verse the splendid achievements of his abbot Wittger, 1003, CXXXIX, 350.

PUSTELLA ANGILBERT. See ANGILBERT.

PYTHAGORAS, celebrated philosopher and mathematician. Born at Samos, he travelled through many places and visited very many regions in his eagerness to learn; he undertook every kind of science and art. He flourished in 590 before Christ. A certain letter to Anaximenes, translated from Greek into Latin, is attributed to him in St Ambrose, XVII, 1152.

## Q

[Col. 0513]

QUODVULTDEUS, deacon of Carthage. Twice he wrote to St Augustine asking him to complete a book on all the heresies that had sprung up in the Church down to his own times. He must not be confused either with another person of the same name who went over to the Donatists and against whom Petilianus had brought a most serious accusation, or with another Quodvultdeus, a bishop who attended the Council of Carthage about 416. He died in 428, XXXIII, 997, 1000.

## R

RABANUS MAURUS, abbot of Fulda and later archbishop of Mainz. Still a boy, he entered the monastery of Fulda; he became abbot in 825 and was elevated to the archbishopric of Mainz in 847; he died in 856. A man distinguished by virtue and learning, he devoted himself especially to commentaries on Scripture, in which he commonly transcribes the ancients. There also survive commentaries, sermons, and lives of certain saints by him, CVII–CXII.

RACHIO, bishop of Strasbourg. We have many documents by him; he flourished after the middle of the eleventh century. There survives an inscription in a codex containing canons and decrees of councils, a codex which Rachio ordered to be copied in 788, XCVI, 1030.

RACHIS, king of the Lombards in 747. In a decree concerning the monastery of Bobbio he defines certain boundaries. He also granted another privilege in favour of the church of Piacenza, LXXXVII, 1376, 1406.

RADALDUS, moved by piety, gave his entire inheritance to the church or monastery of Werden, ruled by St Liudger; this gift consisted both of land and woodland, ninth century, XCIX, 818.

RADBODO, bishop of Tournai. In a letter he asks Lambert of Arras either to excommunicate, or to permit the excommunication of, a certain Anselm and his steward, who had not feared to invade and plunder the monastery of St Amand and to lay impious hands upon the monks with atrocious injuries. These things occurred at the beginning of the twelfth century, CLXII, 656.

RADBODUS (St), bishop of Utrecht. He shone conspicuously in piety. Received from an early age at the court of King Louis, son of Charles, he learned the liberal disciplines. He became bishop in 899 and died in 918. Sermons, homilies, and poems by him survive, CXXXIII, 537.

RADBODUS, provost of Dol. He flourished in the tenth century, in 923. He is known to us only through a letter which he wrote to King Athelstan, CXXXII, 719.

RADBODUS, bishop of Tournai and Noyon. A man highly praised for learning and pious conduct, he was raised to the episcopal mitre of Noyon in the year of the Lord 1068. When accused of simony, he cleared himself of that charge; he died in 1098. Lives, sermons, letters, and charters concerning him survive, CL, 1494.

RADCHIS, abbot of St Michael in the territory of Lucca, issued a charter in 728 by which he appointed to the same office the cleric Waltprand, son of Duke Walpert, LXXXVII, 1371.

RADEGUND (St), queen of the Franks. Daughter of Bertharius, king of Tongeren, she was carried away captive and became the wife of Chlothar, king of the Franks. She became renowned for piety and good works; after Chlothar’s death she withdrew to the monastery of Holy Cross at Poitiers, where she died in 587. She sent bishops a testament in the form of a letter, to be executed, LXXII, 651.

RADULFUS ARDENS, priest. A native of Poitiers, he shone greatly in piety, zeal, and eloquence around the beginning of the twelfth century. He was preacher to William IV, duke of Aquitaine. Sermons by him for the seasons and for saints’ days survive, CLV, 1294.

RADULFUS, priest of Caen and associate of Tancred, was born about 1080. From childhood he was educated at Caen under the celebrated Arnulf, chaplain to the duke of Normandy; he died in Palestine in an uncertain year. He wrote a book, *On the Deeds of Tancred*, CLV, 494.

RADULFUS, lord of Silgery, and his wife Amicia gave a forest at Savigny to the hermit St Vitalis for building a monastery there; as its endowment, they granted that monastery an annual rent of one thousand pounds in their land of Silgery, in the year 112 [uncertain or incomplete date], CCVII, 1163.

RADULFUS, GAUFRIDUS, and other barons of the province of Bourges remitted to the nuns of Orsan certain customary dues called *pedagium* or *teloneum*—tolls—in the presence of St Robert of Arbrissel, under whose direction they were held, in 1113, CLXII, 1103.

RADULFUS TORTARIUS (de la Tourte), monk of Fleury. He was born at Orléans in the diocese of Auxerre about the middle of the eleventh century. From his youth he was trained in the liberal arts. Then, renouncing the world, he became a monk [Col. 0514] in the monastery of Fleury, where he shone in learning, teaching, and piety, in 1114. Among his writings survive an account in prose of the miracles of St Benedict and miracles of the same saint written in verse, CLX, 1171.

RADULFUS, archbishop of Canterbury. About 1122 he wrote Pope Calixtus II, complaining of the injury done to himself and to the church of Canterbury in the consecration of Stigand as archbishop of York, although Stigand had already been deposed from the see of Winchester, CLXIII, 1341.

RADULFUS, elected archbishop of Rheims in 1106. Endowed with learning and eloquence, devoted to worthy studies, he was father and instructor both of monks and clerics, and patron and defender of the poor. He died in 1124. Letters and charters by him survive, CLXIII, 1415.

RADULFUS, count of Vermandois, who also became chief seneschal under Louis the Fat, died in 1151. Certain letters from him to Suger survive; Suger had been associated with him in governing the kingdom while King Louis was making a pilgrimage to Palestine, CLXXXVI, 1351.

RADULFUS, count of Clermont, makes known that he brought a complaint against Maurice, bishop of Paris, concerning a prebend held by Peter of Monceaux; at the bishop’s request he surrendered whatever right belonged to him, in 1169, CCV, 909.

RADULFUS BARBOTINUS granted St Robert of Arbrissel and the monastery of Fontevraud a wood at Agudelle, at the beginning of the twelfth century, CLXII, 1117.

RADULFUS DE FONTANELLIS granted to Gaufridus Acu, who had long served him intimately, a certain vineyard beside the road leading to Bethlehem and not far from Jerusalem, without a date, CLV, 1215.

RADULPHUS. See RADULFUS.

RAGENFREDUS, bishop of Chartres. About 960, he restored many things which his predecessors had taken from the monastery of St Peter and in addition conferred new gifts, CLV, 219.

RAGINALDUS, chaplain of William III, bishop of Troyes, remitted to that bishop a rent of one ounce of gold which he had received from the church of the Holy Sepulchre, in 1171, CLV, 1243.

RAIMBALDUS, archbishop of Arles. Born of noble stock, he placed himself under the discipline of St Isarn and advanced so far that he was thought worthy to be raised to the see of Arles in 1031. He died in 1067. Certain charters by him survive, CXLIII, 1390.

RAIMUNDUS DE CURAMONTA, intending to journey to the Holy Land with Raymond, viscount of Turenne, mortgaged certain estates to the monks of Tulle in 1096, CLV, 483.

RAIMUNDUS, count of Galicia, and HENRY, count of Portugal, sent St Hugh, abbot of Cluny, a copy of the friendship entered into between them and of their agreement for dividing the succession of their father-in-law Alfonso, king of Castile, eleventh century, CLIX, 944.

RAIMUNDUS, viscount of Cahors. He became a monk in the abbey of Moissac, to which he also granted two churches through the hands of Abbot Ansquisitus in 1101, CLIX, 976.

RAIMUNDUS, archbishop of Tarragona. He sent Pope Innocent III the oath rendered by Raymond, count of Toulouse, upon returning to the Catholic Church, together with the oath of the counts of Foix and Comminges, in 1213, CCXVI, 845.

RAINALDUS, recluse of St Ragnebert. See GUIDO DE ARANDA.

RAINALDUS DE MONTEFALCONE, having been summoned to judgment because of a certain man who had refused him service, informed Suger that he was prepared, on the appointed day, to undergo judgment according to the customs of Bourges; this was accomplished through Suger’s management in 1148, CLXXXVI, 1405.

A certain RAINALDUS, priest and minister of the church of Mount Sion, granted his vineyard for the making of a reservoir for the common use of Christians, and received another small vineyard in exchange for it in 1176, CLV, 1249.

RAINALDUS DE SALMANCHE and his mother Juliana Essarta gave as alms to the monastery of Fontevraud what they possessed on this side of the ford of Rolay. This charter records another gift by Essarta, this distinguished lady of Le Mans: at the point of death she commanded that her son Rainaldus and his wife Corinda should enlarge the earlier gift and give everything they possessed from the head of Salis to the ditch of La Guarda, about the beginning of the twelfth century, CLXII, 1106.

RAINALDUS, bishop of Lyons, who flourished at the beginning of the thirteenth century, in 1213. He declares that he had seen ancient charters by which the Emperor Valentinian granted lands in the valley of Helnon to his chamberlain Majorevus, because, as the charter reports, Majorevus preferred to lose his right eye rather than hand over the key of the emperor’s chamber to Arbogast, the emperor’s enemy. Hence the place received the name of Majorevus, CLIII, 936.

[Col. 0515] A certain RAINALDUS emancipated his bondwoman Constantia and restored her to full freedom, so that she could now go or act freely; without mention of a year, from the cartulary of Uzerche in Gaul, CXXXII, 469.

RAINERIUS, lord of Acrimont, confirms gifts made by his father Ulric, or Odolric, to the monks of Morimond in 11[.....]8, CLXXXV, 1443.

RANGERIUS, first a disciple of St Bruno and later bishop of Lucca. He died in 1112. He inscribed his own name in his funerary epitaph, CLII, 556.

RANULFUS DE TURRI, bishop, sent to Gilbert Foliot, bishop of London, with letters the son of Adam, formerly in his service and that of his most beloved master; he earnestly commends to him this man, who was in need, twelfth century, CXC, 1063.

RATEFRIDUS, son of a certain Guilichisius, a Lombard under the reign of Rachis, founded a monastery of nuns and the hospice of St Peter at Pistoia, into which his mother, wife, and daughter might enter, if they wished, according to the terms of the charters, in 748.

RATHERIUS, bishop of Verona. Noted both for the varied calamities of his life and for his learning, he flourished in the tenth century. As a boy he was offered to the monastery of Lobbes, where he was educated and trained in study; thereafter he was made bishop of Verona in 916. Three times expelled from his see and three times restored, he died in 974. Six books of *Praeloquia*, shorter works, letters, a confession, and sermons survive by him, CXXXVI, 9.

RATPERTUS, monk of St Gall, born at Zurich. From boyhood he had as teachers Marcellus and Iso, men most renowned in that age; later, as head of the schools of that monastery, he applied himself tirelessly to letters. He died in 900. His book *On the Events of the Monastery of St Gall* and various poems survive, CXXVI, 1055.

RATPODUS, count, under the reign of Louis the Pious, made a donation to the monastery of St Emmeram of what he possessed at Tullina, in 837, CXXIX, 933.

RATRAMNUS, monk of Corbie of the Order of St Benedict, believed to have been provost of the monastery of Orbais in the diocese of Soissons. Dogmatic writings by him survive. He appears to have died about 868, CXXI, 9.

RAUBACUS, or RORACIUS, bishop of Nevers, attended the Council of Chalon in 647 under Chlodovech II, son of Dagobert. A letter from him to St Desiderius, bishop of Cahors, survives, LXXXVII, 259.

RAVENNIUS, bishop of Arles. After receiving letters from Pope Leo I, he summoned all the bishops of Gaul to a council in 452 to pronounce upon Eastern affairs; having done this, he sent a synodal letter to St Leo, LIV, 966.

RAYMUNDUS, count of Toulouse, granted much land and slaves for the foundation of Vabres Abbey in 846, CXXXII, 785.

RAYMUNDUS DE AGILES, canon of Le Puy and chaplain to his bishop. Previously—“count of Toulouse” in the supplied text [uncertain]—he set out for Palestine, where he also died. His history of the Jerusalem expedition survives, 1096, CLV, 591.

RAYMUNDUS ARNULLI, monk of St Victor at Marseilles. Nothing certain is known of his birth, homeland, or death. He wrote a letter to his abbot Bernard, eleventh century, CLI, 639.

RAYMUNDUS IV, count of St-Gilles and Toulouse, succeeded William, took up arms against the Turks in the holy war, and after victory refused the sceptre offered to him. He died in 1112. Letters and a charter by him for the monastery of St Victor at Marseilles survive, CLV, 390, 483, 1184.

RAYMUNDUS, count of Tripoli, son of Raymond of St-Gilles, and his wife Hodierna, daughter of the king of Jerusalem, granted many charters in favour of William, prior of the Holy Sepulchre, about 1144, CLV, 1191 and following.

RAYMUNDUS, guardian of the Hospital of Jerusalem, warns his subjects that nothing from property received by the congregation should be alienated, but that it should be spent to relieve the need of the poor in accordance with the pious intention of the benefactors; without heading, twelfth century, CLV, 1257.

RAYMUNDUS, count of Toulouse, duke of Narbonne and marquis of Provence, and his son Raymond had adhered to the most pernicious heresy of the Albigensians. Reduced to repentance by force of arms, they returned, and, having abjured their error, rendered an oath of fealty to the Lord Pope and to the Holy Roman Church in 1213, CCXVI, 845.

RAYMUNDUS, patriarch of Aquileia. He made a statute concerning the purchase of houses for the common life of the canons of Udine in 1278, defining certain matters concerning their provisions. Another charter by him survives concerning a special designation of a market in the middle of a field, XCIX, 649, 652.

RAYNALDUS, first abbot of Vézelay and later archbishop of Lyons. He wrote to Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, [Col. 0516] and to his brother, asking indulgence for a rebellious monk named Philip, in 1125, CLXXXIX, 471.

RAYNARDUS, lord of the castle of Montbard, uncle of St Bernard; Waldricus the monk and Milo the lay brother founded the abbey of Blessed Mary of Fontenay during the lifetime of St Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, twelfth century, CLXXXV, 1461.

RECCARED, king of the Visigoths, surnamed “the Catholic,” succeeded his father Leovigild; he embraced the Christian faith and endeavoured to bring his subjects to it. He belongs to the end of the sixth century. His edict confirming the Council of Toledo survives, LXXII, 1122.

RECESVINTH, king of the Goths and successor of Chindaswinth, died about 655. Two letters of his survive in St Braulio, LXXX, 685.

A certain RECHO, belonging to the schismatic party, brought objections against Berthold, who refuted each of them. This dispute was active in 1080, CXLVIII, 1281.

RIGINALDUS, FOLCHARDUS, and others grant land for the building of a church. This was done under Withmund in 805, under the rule of Charlemagne, XCIX, 800.

REGINALDUS, or REGINO, archbishop of Monreale in Sicily in 1198. He informs Innocent III of what was done in the mission for which he had been delegated together with the bishops of Palermo and Rossano, CCXIV, 369.

REGINALDUS DE PELLENTO granted to the monastery of Fontevraud, through the hands of Robert of Arbrissel, a piece of land sufficient for four oxen. The same charter states that both brothers, Calo and Hugh, while still living, gave the same amount of land to that monastery, together with meadows and a share of woodland, twelfth century, CLXII, 1116.

REGINO, abbot of Prüm. Born of noble parents at Altrip, he became abbot of the monastery of Prüm in the Ardennes in 892. But deprived of this office through the envy of certain persons, he withdrew to the monastery of St Maximin near Trier, where he died. He wrote a *Chronicle*, a book on ecclesiastical disciplines, and another on musical instruction, 915, CXXXII, 9.

REIMBOLDUS, provost of Liège. A native of Liège, he was received among the canons of that city in 1117 and attained the dignity of dean in 1144. According to some, he died in 1147. Letters by him survive, CLXII, 735.

REINALDUS I, archbishop of Rheims, treasurer of St Martin’s at Tours. Born of illustrious stock, but more illustrious through his own qualities, he attained the highest episcopal honour in Gaul in 1080. He died in 1095. Eleven letters by him survive, CL, 1382.

REINARDUS, abbot of Reinsdorf, formerly Wibald’s teacher, died in 1150, distinguished for holiness. A letter by him to Wibald, abbot of Corbie, survives from 1147, CLXXXIX, 1150.

REINARDUS, abbot of Cîteaux. He was the son of Milo, count of Bar-sur-Seine; first he was a monk of Clairvaux, in 1140. He reconciled Peter Abelard with St Bernard. In the same year he wrote Pope Innocent II against the monks of Vézelay on behalf of Humbert, bishop of Autun. He died in 1151. The statutes of the General Chapter and the aforesaid letter to Innocent II survive by him, CLXXXI, 1724.

REINERUS, monk of St Lawrence at Liège. Only obscure documents are handed down concerning him; he was a man of excellent and highly refined talent. He left many writings, both prose and verse, in 1182, CCIV, 9.

REINHARDUS, bishop of Halberstadt. He flourished at the beginning of the twelfth century. He wrote two letters to Pope Paschal II: in the first he requests confirmation of the tithes of his church; in the latter, having been suspended from office, he humbly asks absolution from the Supreme Pontiff, in 1107, CLXIII, 459.

REMBERTUS (St), bishop of Hamburg. Born in Flanders near Bruges in the ninth century, in 888, he was highly commendable both for learning and piety and was raised to the episcopal mitre to govern the church of Hamburg. He wrote the *Life of St Ansgar*, his predecessor, CXVIII, 959.

REMIGIUS (St), bishop of Rheims. Eminently learned and highly trained in rhetorical studies, he baptized Clovis I, king of the Franks. Gregory of Tours gives him high praise. Three letters and a testament by him survive. He died in 533, LXV, 961.

REMIGIUS, bishop of Strasbourg. His testament survives, by which on 15 March 778 he gave the monasteries of Eschau and Wörth to the church of Strasbourg; the formula of this charter is expressed in accordance with Roman laws, XCVI, 1582.

REMIGIUS, bishop of Chur in Raetia, appears to have flourished from 813 to 830. He decreed various canons for his diocese, CII, 1093.

REMIGIUS (St), bishop of Lyons. His birth is passed over in silence by biographers. He was the great almoner of Emperor [Col. 0517] Lothar and, after the death of Amolo, was promoted to the see of Lyons in 852. In every matter he showed himself highly learned in ecclesiastical affairs. There survive by him: a book *On Three Letters*, and two other treatises, *On the General Condemnation through Adam* and *On Maintaining the Truth of the Scriptures*, CXXI, 986.

REMIGIUS, monk of St Germanus of Auxerre, of the Order of St Benedict. He was born, as is believed, in Burgundy shortly before the middle of the ninth century; 908. At first he held the school at Rheims, entrusted to him by Archbishop Fulk, and he had as a pupil Odo, who became abbot of Cluny. Exegetical works, a treatise on the dedication of a church, homilies, and letters by him survive, CXXXI, 49.

RENALLUS, master of the school of Barcelona. We have discovered nothing concerning him in historical writers. He composed verses on the body of Christ in the sacrament of the Eucharist, a work which appears to have been written against the errors of Berengar of Tours in 1080, CXLVII, 599.

REOLUS, bishop of Rheims. He granted the estate of Gangiacum to Beracharius, who had requested it in order to build there a monastery of nuns, and at the same time gave him authority to reclaim the monastery of Hautvillers in the future if need arose, in 686, LXXXVIII, 1212.

REPARATUS, bishop of the first see of Mauretania in Africa, was one of three who wrote Pope Theodore concerning Pyrrhus, who, deposed from the see of Constantinople, had come to Africa, in 648, LXXXVII, 81.

RHETICIUS, bishop of Autun. Born of noble lineage and bound by marriage, he vowed continence with his wife’s consent and received holy orders; soon he was elevated to the see of Autun and gained great authority in settling affairs, especially in the Donatist matter, which he had to judge with Maternus, bishop of Cologne, and Marinus, bishop of Arles, by command of Constantine the Great. A commentary on the *Song of Songs* is attributed to him, fourth century, VI, 45.

RICHARDUS, abbot of Fleury. According to Mabillon, he was first provost of the cell of Patrinacum, then elected abbot of Fleury; under his administration, that monastery, twice burned within three years, was rebuilt from the foundations. He died in 979, CXXXVI, 1302.

RICHARDUS II, called the Good, duke of Normandy, son and successor of Richard I and faithful friend of King Robert II, died in 1027. There survives a charter by which he confirms to the monastery of Bec all gifts made by his father, CL, 579.

RICHARDUS, archbishop of Bourges. Two charters by him survive: one on the dedication of the church of Wipples, the other concerning the priestly estate of the church of Lanet, under Philip, king of the Franks, eleventh century, CXXXII, 475.

RICHARDUS DE DUMELLIS, abbot of the abbey of Préaux, founded in 1057, in the diocese of Lisieux. He wrote a commentary on Genesis, of which only fragments survive. He died in 1100, CLV, 1630.

RICHARDUS, cardinal and archbishop of Narbonne. Born of noble lineage, he embraced the monastic life in the abbey of St Victor at Marseilles, of which he became abbot after the death of his brother Bernard, when he had already been adorned with the purple of the cardinals. Later he was raised to the archbishopric of Narbonne in 1106, which he held until his death in 1121. His letters, charters, and an account of the persecutions he suffered from Americ survive, CLXII, 1594.

RICHARDUS DE FURNELLIS, abbot of Préaux. A Norman by birth, he was educated from boyhood at the monastery of St Vigor near Bayeux under Abbot Robert. After the death of Geoffrey, abbot of Préaux, he was elected to govern that abbey in 1101. He was a man of exceptional piety and, for his time, of no mean learning. There survives by him a prologue to Leviticus addressed to Anselm of Canterbury, 1131, CLXVI, 1358.

RICHARDUS and PAGANUS DE VILLA, brothers, gave the monastery of Clairvaux everything they possessed from Airablo to Alba, toward Clairvaux, with the consent of their mother Beatrice, in 1147, CLXXXV, 987.

RICHARDUS DE HAYA and his wife Matilda founded in 1154 a monastery at a place in their inheritance called Blanca Landa, in honour of the Blessed Virgin Mary and St Nicholas the Confessor, through the agency of Richard, bishop of Coutances. Henry II, king of England, confirmed this donation in 1157, CCVII, 1165.

RICHARDUS, bishop of Coutances, confirmed the agreement made between Peter, abbot of Cluny, and the monks of Montbourg concerning the church of Morsalines, about 1158, CLXXXIX, 1071, 1072.

RICHARDUS DE GRANDI SILVA, of the diocese of Toulouse, monk of the Cistercian Order, was a theologian and a poet of no mean distinction. About 1160 he wrote a poem in praise of Clairvaux Abbey, CLXXXV, 1563.

RICHARDUS, abbot of Bristol, who flourished in the twelfth century, in 1170, wrote to Ervisius, prior of St Victor’s, praising the holiness of that monastery and giving thanks for the benefits bestowed upon his brother, CXCVI, 1386.

RICHARDUS OF ST VICTOR. A Scot by nation, he was received and professed under Abbot Gilduin; under Master Hugh he applied himself to learning and made great progress. He became prior in 1159, after Nantherus. He died in 1175, leaving many writings, especially ascetical works, CXCVI, 9.

RICHARD I, king of England, son and successor of Henry II. At first he resisted his father; later he went to the East, where he distinguished himself in arms. But soon after his return, detained captive by the duke of Saxony, he regained freedom only by payment of money. He died in 1199. A letter by him to Pope Clement III concerning the peace made between himself and King Tancred survives, CCIV, 1505.

RICHARDUS, archdeacon of Poitiers, flourished in the twelfth century. He went to Rome concerning the controversy of St Thomas of Canterbury with King Henry, when many Englishmen were already bound by excommunication or interdict. He explains how the king’s envoys had been received by the pope, and what amazement there was when the report of St Thomas’s murder had already spread, CXC, 1036.

RICHARDUS, cardinal, legate of the Apostolic See, and bishop of Albano, wrote to Robert, count of Flanders, that he held Lambert, bishop of Arras, in the highest reverence. Accordingly, he urges him to treat as excommunicated a certain cleric named Robert, who lived with a widow and rebelled against his own bishop, at the beginning of the twelfth century, CLXII, 679, 687.

RICHARDUS, abbot of Springiersbach, flourished in the twelfth century. Wearied of pastoral care, he asks St Hildegard whether he ought to retain or cast it off, CXCVII, 296.

RICHARDUS, archbishop of Canterbury, flourished in the twelfth century. He accuses the abbot of Malmesbury of withdrawing himself from obedience to his bishop, CC, 1456.

RICHARDUS, lord of Fontaines, having become guardian of the daughters of his brother John, rendered homage to the duke of Burgundy on their behalf for all that they possessed, in 1366, CLXXXV, 1503.

RICHERUS, monk of St Remigius of Rheims outside the walls. His father was Rodulfus, soldier and counsellor of King Louis the Overseas; he was trained in letters under the outstanding master Gerbert. He died in 990. He wrote four books of histories, CXXXVIII, 19.

RICULFUS, bishop of Soissons. He attended the Synod of Rheims in 893; in the Synod of Rheims in 900 he consecrated Hervey, archbishop of Rheims, and excommunicated the men of Baldwin, count of Flanders, who had killed Archbishop Fulk. He is believed to have died in 902. Statutes by him survive, CXXXI, 14.

RICULFUS, bishop of Elne. His testament survives, 915, by which he bequeathed to the church of St Eulalia, metropolitan see of the churches of Roussillon, much of what he had acquired, CXXXII, 468.

RIGOBERTUS, perhaps abbot of the monastery of Saint-Bertin, sold certain estates situated in the districts of Thérouanne and Ponthieu to Erkembodo, bishop of Thérouanne, in 723. This was done at the monastery of Saint-Bertin under King Theuderic IV, LXXXVIII, 1279; CXXXVI, 1205.

RIHPALDUS, abbot of St Emmeram, and his paternal aunt bestowed many gifts upon that monastery; but his nephews later retained them, alleging a hereditary right. Therefore the bishop summoned them before the count, and, compelled by law, they restored everything to the monks. The bishop, however, acting mercifully, left these same possessions to them for as long as they lived, on payment of a small annual rent. Without mention of a year; ninth century, CXXIX, 929.

RILINDIS, abbess of Hohenburg, most highly endowed both with virtues and with learning, and exceptionally well taught in Latin, obtained such a reputation for piety that Emperor Frederick, called Barbarossa, entrusted to her the reform of the monastery of Hohenburg, which had departed from its former discipline. Certain poems by her survive, 1169, CXCIV, 1534.

RIQUINUS, administrator of Toul, gave the cell of Frondon to Pons, abbot of Cluny, in the general synod held in 1111 in the church of St Stephen, CLXVI, 849.

RISO, priest and formerly chaplain of Prince Bohemond, gave to the chapter of the Lord’s Sepulchre certain houses which he possessed at Antioch, together with an orchard, all specifically described, in 1138, CLV, 1183.

ROBERTUS, bishop of Metz. He was born of a noble Alemannic family. Notker taught him letters in the abbey of St Gall; and because of his exceptional gifts he was promoted to the episcopal mitre, consecrated by Ratbod, metropolitan, in 883. Letters and charters by him survive. He died in 916, CXXXII, 530.

ROBERTUS THE PIOUS, by surname, king of the Franks, son and successor of Hugh Capet, was a gentle king and quite learned and religious. He had as his teacher Gerbert, who was afterwards made bishop of Rheims. He died in 1031. Letters, hymns, and charters by him survive, CXLI, 935.

ROBERTUS DE TUMBALENA, abbot of St Vigor. A Frenchman by nation, he was first a monk of St Michael in Peril of the Sea; afterwards Odo, bishop of Bayeux, made him abbot of St Vigor in 1087. When his patron was thrown into prison, he resigned the government of his monastery and went to Rome, where Gregory VII received him kindly. He wrote commentaries on the *Song of Songs* and a letter to the monks of Mont-Saint-Michel. He died in 1093, CL, 1362.

ROBERTUS, monk of St Remigius in the diocese of Rheims, of the Order of St Benedict, a man very well versed in Holy Scripture and not ignorant of humane letters. He attended the Council of Clermont. He wrote a history of Jerusalem in 1095, CLV, 667.

ROBERT II, Count of Flanders, son of Robert I, took the cross and distinguished himself by his deeds in the holy war. He refused royal dignity in the East. On his return, he again undertook the care of his duchy. He died in 1108, CLV, 390.

ROBERT of Arbrissel, born about 1050 in the district of Rennes, in the village called Arbrissel. From his earliest years he applied himself to the liberal studies, but later withdrew into the wilderness and gave himself wholly to contemplation: he founded the women’s monastery of Fontevraud. He died in 1117. There remain from him the Rule of the nuns of Fontevraud, precepts for right living, and charters, CLXII, 1018.

ROBERT II, Count of Normandy, son of William the Conqueror, rebelled against his father, who denied him the duchy of Normandy. Among those who took the cross he distinguished himself in arms at Antioch and Jerusalem. Later, after returning, he contended unsuccessfully with his brother Henry for the realm; he died in prison in 1134. He wrote certain letters, CLV, 390.

ROBERT, bishop of Hereford. He replied to Suger that, although bound by an obligation of liberty, he could send only a modest sum, and was prepared to assist him by prayers rather than money. About 1148, CLXXXVI, 1359. See also CXC, 1019.

ROBERT, dean of the church of Blessed Mary of Chartres. He addressed a complaint to Suger, acting as the king’s deputy, against Hugh of Brétigny and Ebrard the viscount, about 1148, CLXXXVI, 1356, 1401.

ROBERT, dean of Stavelot. He congratulated Wibald, formerly abbot of this monastery and now abbot of Corvey, upon his return from a journey, in 1148, CLXXXIX, 1155.

ROBERT, bishop of Exeter. Indignant at the disorderly life of Hugh of Cotes, a canon, he wrote to Pope Eugenius III, requesting that he employ his authority to restrain Hugh’s scandals, in 1153, CLXXX, 1640.

ROBERT PULLUS, or PULLANUS, chancellor of the Apostolic See and cardinal, a man most thoroughly trained in every kind of wisdom and learning. Born in Britain, he devoted himself from youth to the study of philosophy, and refused the episcopal dignity offered him by King Henry. Having food and clothing, he was content with these. There remain from him eight books of *Sentences*, in 1153, CLXXXVI, 633.

ROBERT PORCARIUS, of Mahumeria in the district of Syria, gave himself and all his possessions to the canons of the Holy Sepulchre in 1155, CLV, 1225.

ROBERT, Count of Leicester, flourished about 1180. He wrote a letter to the pope and sought his protection for the monastery of Sirey, CC, 1390.

ROBERT DE TORIGNI, abbot of Mont-Saint-Michel. He first made profession at the abbey of Bec in 1149. He died in 1186. There remain from him a book on the deeds of Henry I, king of the Franks, and other smaller works, CCII, 1305.

ROBERT, abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. He subscribed an agreement with Maurice, bishop of Paris, by which the latter gave his female slave in marriage to Robert, a serf of Saint-Germain; and the same monastery gave Bishop Maurice the slave Emelina in marriage to Guarin, his own man, in 1194, CCV, 914.

ROBERT, lord of Péronne, and his wife wrote a letter to Bishop Lambert. At the beginning of the twelfth century, CLXII, 653.

ROBERT, Count of Flanders, informed Lambert of Arras by letter that, for the good of peace, he had done homage to the German emperor, while preserving his own dignity and obedience to the Roman pontiff. He flourished in the twelfth century, CLXII, 676.

ROBERT, bishop of Nantes. He wrote a letter to Lambert, bishop of Arras. Twelfth century, CLXII, 695.

ROBERT FENARD, son of Fulk, confirms his father’s donation to the monastery of Fontevraud. Twelfth century, CLXII, 1115.

[Col. 0520] ROBERT DE BLODO, through Lord Robert of Arbrissel, granted certain customary rights to the monastery of Fontevraud, twelfth century, CLXII, 1116.

ROBERT, perhaps a Cistercian or Clairvaux monk. There is by him a most beautiful letter to Peter of Poitiers, a monk of the Order of Hermits. Twelfth century, CLXXXIX, 361.

ROBERT PAULULUS, to whom is attributed the treatise *On Ceremonies, Sacraments, and the Various Offices of the Church*, published among the works of Blessed Hugh of Saint-Victor, is perhaps identical with Robert Pullus (see above), at an uncertain date, CLXXVII, 381.

ROBERT, of Reading in England, later archdeacon of Pamplona, translated the *Book of the Law of the Saracens*, or the Koran, to which he prefixed a preface, twelfth century, CLXXXIX, 657.

ROBERT, legate of the Apostolic See and cardinal priest, wrote to Pope Innocent III concerning the celebrated lawsuit brought by Erard and his wife against Philip Theobald, Count of Champagne, over an inheritance, about 1213, CCXVI, 379.

ROBERT, duke of La Chapelle, makes known that the knight Calo and his brother Othenin gave certain lands and immunities to the nuns of St Mary of Praslin in 1232, CLXXXV, 1425.

ROBERT DE BRUS, lord of Amand Valley, in 1273 granted to the monks of Clairvaux the whole land of Ostricost, to be possessed by them peacefully, so that a lamp might be kept burning forever at the altar of St Malachy the abbot, CLXXXV, 1759.

ROBERT, son of Guy of Dampierre, Count of Flanders, approached Pope Boniface VIII on behalf of his father, and later wrote to him, in the French language of that time, about all that he had done, in 1297, CLXXXV, 1867, 1876.

RODBERT, archbishop of Rouen. With the consent of certain other bishops, he freed the church of Fontenay in 1033 from every burden toward himself and his successors; that church belonged to the monastery of St Peter of Chartres. (See ARNULF, abbot of Chartres), CLV, 268.

RODBERT, son of William, and his wife Adelina, at the request of Guarin, abbot of St Peter of Chartres, granted to that monastery land situated in the Brogilus of Amarius, comprising one hundred arpents, for an annual rent of three solidi, in 1080, CLV, 289.

RODERICUS PETRI granted a village called Passerelle, with thirty-one *casalia*—small rural holdings—to the chapter of the Holy Sepulchre at Jerusalem in 1138, CLV, 1180.

RODHMUND, bishop of Autun, confirms the transfer of the chapel of Centissa by Udalmann the dean, Radulf the abbot, and Almar the archdeacon, to the two clerical brothers Gerard and Wichard, ninth century, CXXXII, 472.

RODINUS bestowed many gifts upon the monastery of Sithiu, on condition that the monks should offer prayers to God for himself, his wife Ava, and his sons, in 883, CXXXVI, 1251.

RODULF I, emperor of Germany and founder of the Austrian monarchy. Born of the House of Habsburg, he resisted the nobles and protected towns and villages. He died in 1290, and was succeeded by Adolphus of Nassau. Three books of letters by him survive, XCVIII, 661, 701.

RODULF, bishop of Bourges. Born of a noble and ancient family, he began to preside over the metropolitan see of Bourges about 840 and governed this church until 868, when he is believed to have died. Chapters by him survive, CXIX, 703.

RODULF assumed the abbacy of Sithiu in the same year in which Folco became archbishop, namely 883. He carried out certain exchanges with one Odgrin at the monastery of Sithiu in 887. He died in 892, CXXXVI, 1252.

RODULF III, king of Burgundy, called the Peaceful. Unable to restrain his subjects, he surrendered the crown to Emperor Henry II. He died at Lausanne in 1032. His charters survive, CXLII, 1039, 1041; CLI, 1021.

RODULF GLABER, monk of Cluny. Born in Burgundy, he was called Glaber, that is, “the Bald.” Still a boy, he was received in the monastery of St Leodegar called Capellae. He learned letters quickly; but because he was frivolous and turbulent in spirit, he was expelled by the brethren. In the last years of his life he withdrew to Cluny, where he died in 1049. Five books of histories and a Life of St William, abbot, survive from him, CXLII, 719.

RODULF, having possessed the village of Ermentières by an unjust seizure, restored it to the monastery of St Peter of Chartres. There is another similar charter in which Rodulf is called Roscellinus; but the reader should compare them personally, in 1070, CLV, 276, 288.

RODULF, monk of Cluny, disciple of Peter the Venerable and companion in his journeys, wrote his life, narrating matters of which he had in large part been a witness, about 1160, CLXXXIX, 15.

RODWALD bestowed all his goods on the monastery of Sithiu [Col. 0521], on condition that his son Meginfrid should receive food and clothing in that monastery as long as he lived, in 864, CXXXVI, 1240.

ROGER, jurist, according to some Frigerius. An Italian by birth and skilled in jurisprudence, he compiled a *Summa*, or compendium, of law, eleventh century, CXLVI, 1486.

ROGER, monk of Bec. A Norman by birth, from childhood he dedicated himself wholly to God in the abbey of Bec under the Rule of Benedict. He cultivated letters, and poetry especially. We possess from him a poem on contempt for the world among the writings of St Anselm, CL, 1431.

ROGER, Count of Foix, and his wife Amica, in the eleventh century granted to St Hugh, abbot of Cluny, a place dedicated to St Saturninus of Frodelais, to be established under monastic observance, CLIX, 940.

ROGER, bishop of Ramla, with the consent of the chapter of St George, granted several *casalia* to the brothers of the Holy Sepulchre in 1136, CLV, 1171.

ROGER OF ESCLANTIA and his sons Hildric and Hugh gave to the monastery of Clairvaux whatever the monks had brought under cultivation in the Wood and at Acunville, in 1147, CLXXXV, 991.

ROGER II, first king of Sicily. He wrote to Suger, asking him, in return, to keep him more frequently informed of his circumstances through travellers, about 1149, CLXXXVI, 1415.

ROGER OF PONTIGNY, monk, attached himself to St Thomas of Canterbury while the latter was in exile at the monastery of Pontigny, and later wrote his life, in 1175, CXC, 53.

ROGER, formerly prior of St Abraha, wrote to Geoffrey, subprior of St Barbara in Neustria, a letter concerning spiritual progress, at the end of the twelfth century, in 1199, CCV, 831.

ROGER, bishop of Worcester. He lived in the twelfth century and in the time of Blessed Thomas of Canterbury. After Thomas’s murder, he wrote to the chapter of Canterbury, uncertain whether the churches of his diocese lay under an interdict, CXC, 1040.

ROGER, or ROBERT, abbot of the monastery of St Evurtius at Orléans, wrote to Ervisius, prior of St Victor at Paris, excusing himself for not having come to him and commending to him the affairs of his monastery, twelfth century, CXCVI, 1386.

ROGER, Count of Foix, who had followed Count Raymond into heresy and had shared the same fate with him, made a profession of faith in which he renounced every error, in 1213, CCXVI, 847.

ROGER, Count of Saint-Pol, and his wife Haduis gave the abbey of St Bertha of Blangy to the monastery of Fécamp (without date), CXLVII, 475, note.

ROGER, monk of Crowland in England, is the author of a letter or prologue on the life of St Thomas of Canterbury, thirteenth century, CXC, 259.

ROGER, archbishop of Bourges. The translation of the body of St Odilo was performed by him in 1145, with the gathering of the entire Cluniac congregation in the church of Souvigny belonging to that monastery. He issued letters concerning this, together with certain privileges, CXLII, 1047.

ROGER, abbot of the monastery of Fossatus, manumitted the serf Garnerius of Domibus, son of Doda, together with all his family and possessions, in 1168, CCV, 908.

ROGER, abbot of St Evurtius at Orléans, perhaps the same as the Roger mentioned above. Biographical writers report little about him: he is believed to have been the first to discover the body of St Evurtius. There survives from him a revelation which he sent to the monks of St Audoenus, in 1182, CXCIX, 1125.

See above, ROGER, abbot of St Evurtius.

ROGER, archbishop of York. He flourished in the twelfth century under Alexander III, to whom he once wrote, as he did also to Hugh, bishop of Durham, CXC, 1006.

ROHINGUS, or RAUCHINGUS, and his wife Rebelina gave the church of Saints Peter and Paul, situated in the old town of Antwerp, to St Willibrord, bishop of Utrecht and abbot of the monastery of Echternach, in 726. This was done at the castle of Weimod, LXXXIX, 553.

ROLAND, first a Roman subdeacon, then bishop-elect of Dol, and Silvanus, abbot of Rievaulx, legates of the Apostolic See, rendered an account to Pope Lucius III regarding the affair of the bishopric of St Andrews in Scotland, in 1182, CCI, 1379.

POPE ROMANUS. A Welshman by birth, son of Constantine, he was elected in 900, but sat only a few months. He wholly disapproved the acts of Pope Stephen VI against his predecessor Formosus, and himself placed the crown upon Louis, son of Boso. Several letters by him survive, CXXIX, 860.

ROMARIC, first count of Habend in the Vosges, then a monk of Luxeuil, founded a monastery of nuns about 620, if credit is to be given to the charter attributed to him, LXXX, 461.

[Col. 0522] ROMUALD (St), founder of the Camaldolese Order, was born at Ravenna into a noble ducal family and was instructed in the liberal studies from childhood. He then sought solitude and endeavoured to reform the then more relaxed discipline of the Order of St Benedict. He flourished from 987 to 1007. There survives from him a fragment of an exposition of Psalm 68, CXL, 1119.

RORICO, bishop of Laon. He was elected in 949. Born of noble stock, he had as his brother King Louis, the illegitimate son of Charles the Simple. He died of paralysis in 976. There remains from him a decree concerning the restoration of monks in the monastery of St Vincent, CXXXIII, 951.

RORICO, monk of Moissac near Cahors. At the beginning of the eleventh century—he flourished in 1104—he wrote the *Deeds of the Franks*, from the origin of the people to the death of Clovis I, CXXXIX, 587.

ROSTANG, monk of Cluny. He flourished at the end of the fifteenth century, in 1481. He is the author of a brief treatise on the translation of the head of St Clement, pope and martyr, from Constantinople to Cluny in the time of Abbot Hugh, CCIX, 905.

ROTBERT, bishop of London and successor of Alwold from 1044. He had previously been abbot of Jumièges, but soon became primate of Canterbury. A charter by him survives, CXLI, 1442.

ROTBERT, prior of St Peter of Chartres. A charter by him survives. In 1080, CLV, 345.

ROTHAD II, bishop of Soissons. He was made priest in 822. Having become bishop, he was deposed at the Council of Senlis in 863 by Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims; nevertheless, he went to Rome and was there restored to his see by the pope in 855. He died in 868. There remains from him a booklet of appeal, CXIX, 746.

ROTROC OF NOGENT, a noble knight devoted to the allegiance of Count Odo, gave his land of Thevas to Gisbert, abbot of St Peter of Chartres, in 996, CLV, 247, 298.

ROTROD, bishop of Rouen, was a contemporary of Thomas of Canterbury. Several letters to different persons survive from him, chiefly relating to the cause of this saintly bishop. He died in 1180, CXC, 671; CC, 1400.

RUDOLF, or RODULF, monk of Fulda and disciple of Rabanus himself, the same man who composed the Life of Lioba, abbess. There survives from him the Life of Blessed Rabanus Maurus, formerly abbot of Fulda and later archbishop of Mainz, in 861, CVII, 39.

RUDOLF, bishop of Liège, flourished after the middle of the twelfth century. He wrote to Blessed Hildegard that he was in the greatest agitation of mind and body because of innumerable sins, and therefore commended himself to her prayers, CXCVII, 175.

RUFINUS, Roman deacon and confessor. See MOSES.

RUFINUS, priest of Aquileia. Born near Concordia about 340, he first lived a monastic life in the monastery of Aquileia and was baptized by St Chromatius. During his travels he visited Rome and Alexandria and various monasteries of Egypt and Syria. At Bethlehem he visited Blessed Jerome, whose friend he was. But afterward he was found at variance with him concerning Origen’s writings, which he translated in very large part from Greek into Latin. He was ordained priest in 388. There survive from him Lives of the Desert Fathers and many translations. He died in 420, XXI, 9.

RUFINUS, a Syrian by birth, a Palestinian priest, who seems to have been intimate with St Jerome. He came to Rome and frequented Pammachius, Jerome’s friend. But he soon began to err in faith and drew Caelestius with him into error. Two books *On Faith* survive from him: one shorter work consists of twelve anathemas; the other, larger in volume, manifestly errs in many respects. About 420, XXI, 1123; XLVIII, 261, 449.

RUFINUS, bishop of an uncertain see. From his dedicatory letter to Peter, abbot of Monte Cassino, he appears to have flourished in the eleventh century, in 1070. Two books *On the Good of Peace* survive from him, CL, 1591.

RUOTGER, cleric of Cologne. He was companion and chief intimate of Lord Bruno, archbishop; therefore Folcmar, or Poppo, Bruno’s successor in the see of Cologne, directed him to write the life of his predecessor, which survives, in 966, CXXXIV, 937.

RUSCA, JOHN, podestà of Milan, informed Innocent III that the princes of Cologne had chosen Otto, son of Henry, duke of Saxony, as king, and begged him to confirm Otto by coronation in 1209, CCXVI, 1002.

RUPERT, the Venerable, abbot of the monastery of St Heribert at Deutz. He was first a monk of St Lawrence near Liège under Abbot Berengar. Because of his renowned learning, Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, appointed him abbot of Deutz. He died in 1135. His dogmatic, exegetical, and historical works survive: a chronicle of St Lawrence at Liège [Col. 0523], and a dialogue between a Jew and a Christian, CLXVII–CLXX.

RURICIUS, bishop of Limoges, called the Elder, to distinguish him from his nephew, who also occupied the see of Limoges. He was born of the distinguished house of the Anicii; he was first devoted to secular life, then, returning to better conduct, received holy orders. He attended the Council of Agde in 506 and died shortly afterward, in 508. His letters survive, LVIII, 68.

RUSTICUS ELPIDIUS lived in the times of Symmachus and Boethius, under the emperor Anastasius, and was physician to Theodoric, king of the Goths. Born of noble stock, he fulfilled the office of quaestor. Of his writings, only poems on the history of the Old and New Testament and on the benefits of Jesus Christ survive, in 520, LXII, 543.

RUSTICUS, deacon of the Holy Roman Church, concerning whom we have no records. There is by him a disputation against the Acephali, in 549, LXVII, 1165.

## S

SALOMON, bishop of Constance, applied himself to study from youth in the monastery of St Gall. He became archchaplain to Louis the Pious and later abbot of St Gall; but he had governed the monastery scarcely a few months when he was elevated to the episcopal see of Constance in 893. He died in 919. He sent several verses to Dado, abbot of St Vitonus and later bishop of Verdun, CXXXII, 561.

SALONIUS, bishop of Vienne. A Gaul by race, he was the son of Eucherius, who became bishop of Lyons. From the beginning he was sent to the monastery of Lérins, where he was educated under the care and discipline of great men. It is not clear when he was elected bishop or when he died. There survives from him an exposition of the Proverbs of Solomon, in 453, LIII, 968.

SALVIAN, priest of Marseilles. A Gaul by birth, he was born at Cologne in 390. Having dissolved the bonds of marriage in which he had been bound, he embraced monastic life in the monastery of Lérins and was later ordained priest there. He died about 496. Eight books *On the Governance of God* and four others especially against the avarice of those who rule survive from him, LIII, 9.

SAMSON, archbishop of Rheims. Most devoted to St Bernard of Clairvaux, he took every care with Suger and the monks of St Denis to obtain from them the abbey of Morimond and establish there monks of the Order of Clairvaux. Once this had been done, he remitted the donation of this church to St Bernard, urging him that the desired foundation be promptly completed, about 1137. Letters from him to Suger survive, CLXXXII, 693, 1137; CLXXXVI, 1360, 1388.

SAMSON, priest of Worcester. The prudence and discernment of this man were so great that he was chosen to handle the by no means easy affair that once existed between Anselm of Canterbury and Thomas, archbishop of York, twelfth century, CLIX, 249.

SAMUEL THE MOROCCAN, a Christian convert from Judaism. His native place was Fez in Africa; in 1085 he received baptism and wrote a book *On the Coming of the Messiah*, whom the Jews await in vain. When he was born and when he died are wholly unknown to us, CXLIX, 333.

SANCIA, queen of Portugal and sister of King Alfonso, gave to Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, in 1134 the church of St Peter of Espin and the church of St Mary of Aborridos, so that he might build there a monastery to be inhabited by monks of his order, CLXXXV, 982.

SANDRATUS, archpriest, gave to the monastery of St Emmeram land which he possessed at Gliumin, and also ten serfs whose names the charter records (without date), ninth century, CXXIX, 954.

SATURUS, saint, confessor and martyr under the proconsul Hilarian, suffered at Carthage together with Saints Perpetua, Felicity, and others. They themselves, it is said, wrote the account of their passion, in 203, III, 42.

SAUL, a Spaniard by race and apparently bishop of Córdoba. He was a contemporary of Paul Alvarus; two letters by him survive, in 860, CXXI, 467, 474.

SEBASTIAN, bishop of Salamanca. We have learned nothing about him. He wrote a chronicle under the name of Alfonso III, CXXIX, 1111.

SCOTUS MARIANUS, born in Ireland in 1028, left the secular world at the age of twenty-four. He later came to Germany and entered the monastery of St Martin, then went to Fulda, where he was ordained priest by Sigefrid. He died in 1082. There remains from him a *Chronicle* from the Nativity of Christ to 1082, CLXVII, 601.

JOHN SCOTUS ERIUGENA, monk, master of theology and philosophy. Born in Ireland about 828, he came to France under Charles the Bald in 845, enjoyed that ruler’s friendship [Col. 0524] in the royal court itself, and moved in the highest circles of all. He is believed to have died in 884. He wrote exegetical, theological, and philosophical works, CXXII, 9.

SECUNDINUS, a Manichaean, formerly an intimate of St Augustine, wrote him a letter urging him to return to those whom he had abandoned, expounding and defending Manichaean doctrines. Against him the holy Doctor wrote a book, to which Secundinus’s letter is prefixed, in 405, XLII, 571.

SECUNDINUS, Irish bishop. Biographical writers are silent about him. There survives from him a hymn in praise of St Patrick, in 490, LI, 1081.

SECUNDUS, bishop of Tigisis and a most vehement defender of the Donatists in Africa, denounced Mensurius, bishop of Carthage, falsely accusing him of having surrendered the Scriptures during the raging persecution. Mensurius cleared himself of this accusation, in 305, VIII, 426, 742.

SEDATUS, bishop of Béziers. He flourished about the end of the sixth century and attended the councils of Toledo and Narbonne in 589. Homilies on the Epiphany of the Lord, two sermons, and three letters to Ruricius, bishop of Limoges, survive under his name. Those attributed to him seem rather to belong to Faustus of Riez, a contemporary of Ruricius, LXXII, 769.

SEDULIUS CAELIUS, priest and poet. Biographical writers disagree concerning his origin and nationality; many, following Trithemius, make him Irish by birth. It is established that, after residing for some time in Achaia, he came to Italy and wrote during the reigns of Valentinian and Theodosius. There survive from him a Paschal poem, an elegy, and a poem on the Incarnation, in 430, XIX, 433.

SEDULIUS SCOTUS, called THE YOUNGER to distinguish him from the preceding writer. He was Irish by race. It is uncertain whether he is the same person who subscribed the Roman council in 721; Epidamnus, a monk of St Gall, relates in his chronicle that he was distinguished. It is uncertain whether he was bishop or priest. We have from him collections on the Epistles of St Paul and on Matthew, and a book *On Christian Rulers*, in 800, CIII, 9.

SEGUINUS, archbishop of Sens. He was elected despite Count Ragenard, who had foolishly wished to usurp that dignity and also tried to prevent Seguinus from entering his episcopal city; for this reason he was excommunicated by Seguinus in 976, CXXXII, 473.

SEHERUS, abbot of the monastery of Chaumousey, whose history he wrote in two books. He died in 1120, CLXII, 1119.

SEIFRID, abbot concerning whom few records have been handed down. He governed the monastery of Tegernsee in the eleventh century, in 1048. He wrote six letters, CXLII, 719.

SERAPION, MACARIUS, PAPHNUTIUS, ancient monks who once flourished in the deserts of Egypt, handed down rules and precepts to monks living under them; these are partly extant in translation in St Benedict of Aniane, fourth century, CIII, 433.

SERGIUS I, pope. A Syrian by birth, he was born at Antioch to his father Tiberius; he became pope in 687 and died in 701. There survive from him a letter to Ceolfrid, abbot, and a privilege for Heron, bishop of Langres, LXXXIX, 9.

SERGIUS II, pope. A Roman by race, son of Sergius; after John, deacon of the Apostolic See and usurper, had been deposed, he peacefully held the see from 844, but only for three years, dying in 847. A letter by him survives, CXXIX, 997.

SERGIUS III, pope. A Roman by race, born to his father Benedict. At first, driven by ambition, he desired the pontificate; but defeated by the usurper Christopher, he went to the Franks, and with their aid overthrew his opponent. He himself seized the papacy and was only later canonically recognized. He died in 911. He issued letters and privileges, CXXXI, 970.

SERGIUS IV, pope. A Roman by birth, son of Peter Martin, he had previously been called “Pig’s-Mouth”; elected in 1009, he succeeded John XVIII. He was a man of remarkable virtue. He died in 1012. Letters and charters by him survive, CXXXIX, 1499.

SEULF, archbishop of Rheims, successor of Hervey, formerly archdeacon of the same city, a man highly versed in both ecclesiastical affairs and secular learning, who had studied under Remigius, master of Auxerre. He enacted canons at the Council of Rheims in 923. He died in 928, CXXXII, 1063.

SEVERINUS, saint, according to some bishop of Cologne, is the author of a small work *On the Doctrine of Wisdom*, although some think otherwise, LXXIV, 813.

SEVERUS, first a fellow citizen and friend of Augustine, later became bishop of Milevis. There survives a letter by him in which he praises Augustine in the highest terms and informs him of the miraculous manner in which his niece, a virgin consecrated to God, was freed from the hands of barbarians and restored joyfully to her parents, in 409, XXXIII, 418, 426.

SEVERUS, bishop of Majorca. Biographical writers furnish no records concerning him [Col. 0525]; he is known only through the letter or book which he wrote concerning the Jews, in 418, XX, 731.

SEVERUS, rhetorician. What is reported of him is very obscure and uncertain. He wrote a bucolic poem on the power of the sign of the cross, fourth or fifth century, XIX, 795.

SIBERT, abbot of the monastery of St Pantaleon in the diocese of Cologne. He flourished about 1134. He wrote to Rodulf, abbot of St Trond, concerning matters that had happened to him because of an avaricious father, who wished his son to be admitted to the monastery without payment, CLXXIII, 193.

SIBYLLA, abbess of the monastery of Holy Cross. At the request of the pious woman Hersendis, prioress of Fontevraud, she granted in 1104 one half of the revenues of land which she possessed in the parish of Cusey to the said monastery of Fontevraud and its pious founder Robert, and the other half to the monastery of Holy Cross, CLXII, 1095.

SICARD, bishop of Cremona, an illustrious man of the twelfth century. He was ordained subdeacon by Pope Lucius III himself at the age of twenty-three; scarcely two years later, he was consecrated bishop of Cremona in 1162. He died in 1215. There survive from him the *Mitrale*, or *Summa on Ecclesiastical Offices*, and a *Chronicle*, CCXIII, 9.

SICCA, a woman distinguished for piety, gave to the monastery of St Emmeram a portion of a church and of the estate dependent upon it near Ermingen (without mention of a year), ninth century, CXXIX, 927.

SICHELM, abbot of the monastery of Bèze, after certain evildoers had broken into his monastery and plundered it completely, sent letters to the mayors of the sacred palace, Reidebert, Chrodebert, and Emerulf, asking them to protect it so that his monks might live there in peace, in 663, LXXXVIII, 1167.

SICHIMUND, archpriest of Lucca, together with three *gazindii*, or royal household officers, of King Liutprand, founded a hospice in the very orchard of the city of Lucca, in 729, LXXXVII, 1372.

SIDONIUS, confessor. See MAXIMUS.

SIGEBALD, king of the West Saxons—or rather, according to some, a monk—wrote a letter to St Boniface declaring that he ardently desired the return of that bishop. He died in 732, LXXXIX, 723.

SIGEBERTA sold land at Fresingehem in the district of Harvan to the monastery of Sithiu for one hundred solidi, in 794, CXXXVI, 1213.

SIGEBERT I, king of the Franks, son of Chlothar, married Brunhild. By order of Fredegund he was murdered in 575. He is mentioned on account of a letter of the bishops at the Council of Paris in 573, urging him not rashly to defend the case of a certain promoted person, LXXII, 1123.

SIGEBERT II, saint, king of the Franks, son of Dagobert, was raised by his father to the kingdom of Austrasia. He was truly worthy of the name of king, because he governed both his subjects and himself excellently. He built twelve monasteries in different parts of his kingdom. After very many illustrious deeds, he died in 656. His charters survive, LXXXVII.

SIGEBERT, monk of Gembloux. By birth, apparently Gallo-Brabantine, he professed the Rule of St Benedict at the abbey of Gembloux at a very young age. Later he went for a time to the schools at Metz in the monastery of St Vincent; but he returned to his monastery and devoted himself wholly to composing books. He died in 1112. His *Chronicle* and many other writings survive, CLX, 9.

SIGEFRID, archbishop of Mainz. He took the side of Pope Alexander II against Henry, from whom he suffered much. He refused to consecrate as bishop a simoniacal priest offered to him, and saw to it that punishment was exacted for the wicked murder of Cuno, archbishop of Trier. He flourished about 1070, CXLVI, 1429; CXLVIII, 725.

SIGEHARD, monk of St Maximin at Trier. He was born in Aquitaine and made great progress in literary study. By command of his abbot, he wrote an account of the miracles of St Maximin. The time of his death is uncertain; in 963, CXXXIII, 865.

SIGIBAUD, bishop of Metz. He is known to us only through a charter in which he and Count Wolfand exchange certain estates with one another. He flourished at the beginning of the eighth century, in 708, LXXXVIII, 1252.

SIGIHARDUS gave certain lands to the church of St Saviour at Werden in 820, under Emperor Louis the Pious, XCIX, 807.

SIGIHARD gave certain lands to the church of St Saviour at Werden, in 820, under Emperor Louis the Pious, XCIX, 807.

SIGISMUND, son of Gundobad and king of Burgundy. Under St Avitus he displayed the greatest piety, having renounced the Arian heresy; but he was handed over by treacherous subjects to Clodomir, who ordered him killed, in 324. Three letters under his name survive in St Avitus, LIX, 243, 276, 284.

SIGIWIN, son of Gislebert, sold to Blessed Ludger, priest, a small estate with three fields at Hrotbertinga Hova, in 809, XCIX, 817.

[Col. 0526] SIGRANNUS, priest and monk, received the monastery of Anisole from Haldoind, bishop of Le Mans, about 637. But the charter from which we learned this appears spurious, LXXX, 571.

SIGLOARD, monk of St Remigius at Rheims, made an inscription to perpetuate the memory of the miracle performed during the translation of the body of St Remigius from the cathedral church to the abbey. There also survives his rhythmical poem on the death of Fulk, archbishop of Rheims, in 901, CXXIX, 1146.

SILVANUS, SOPHRONIUS, NEO, and others, bishops and delegates of the Synod of Seleucia, instructed those at Rimini—who were lending an ear to the Arians—what they ought to do in order to be considered orthodox, in 359, X, 705.

SILVANUS, bishop, already an old man of the church of Sumene in Africa, together with Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, before the conference with the Donatists wrote a double letter to the tribune Marcellinus concerning the conditions to be imposed upon the party that should be defeated, in 411, XXXIII, 487, 490.

SILVANUS, abbot of Rievaulx. See ROLAND.

SILVERIUS, pope. A Campanian by birth, son of Hormisdas, who had himself become pope. At first he was rejected by the Roman clergy, but later accepted to avoid schism. Two letters by him survive. He died in 537, LXVI, 80.

SIMON, count, gave the abbey of St Arnulf at Crépy to Blessed Hugh, abbot of Cluny. This was done in the church of Blessed Mary at Paris, in the presence of King Philip, on the feast day of All Saints, in 1076, CLIX, 966.

SIMON DE CHAMEON gave to the monastery of Clairvaux all that he possessed in the valley of the Dead Fountain as far as the spring of Amaury, and also the land called Middle Mount, in 1147, CLXXXV, 991.

SIMON, prior of Mont-Dieu, flourished in the twelfth century. He wrote to Pope Alexander III and to Cardinal Albert, commending to them the cause of Blessed Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, CXC, 678; CC, 1436.

SIMON, Count of Leicester, lord of Montfort, viscount of Béziers and Carcassonne, commander of the army sent against the Albigensians, wrote to Pope Innocent III that he was prepared to set out upon the expedition, in 1209, CCXVI, 141.

SIMON CAPRA AUREA. See SYMON.

SIMPERT, saint, abbot of Murbach and afterward bishop of Augsburg. From childhood he embraced monastic life in the abbey of Murbach. The fame of his holiness so grew that he was elected abbot and shortly afterward bishop of Augsburg. He died in 809. There survive from him statutes of the monastery of Murbach and an encyclical letter, XCIX, 746.

SIMPLICIUS, saint, pope. A native of Tivoli, son of Cassinus, he was made pontiff in 467. He was distinguished by holiness of life, integrity of faith, and firmness in government. He died in 483. Several letters by him survive, LVIII, 32.

SIRICIUS, saint, pope. A Roman by race, native of Tivoli, he was elected in 385 after the death of St Damasus, against the claims of Ursicinus. He sat for thirteen years and died in 398. His letters and decrees survive, XIII, 1115.

SISEBUTHUS, king of the Goths and successor of Gundemar. He reigned for eight years, until 621. He was distinguished not only by arms and deeds, but also by learning and writings. There survive from him letters and a life, or passion, of St. Desiderius, LXXX, 363.

SIVIARDUS, fifth abbot of the monastery of Anisole after St. Carilephus. He wrote the life of this holy founder and, as he himself acknowledges, did so by the counsel and command of his own bishop of Le Mans. He flourished in the seventh century, LXXIV, 1247.

SIXTUS I (St.), pope and martyr. He succeeded St. Alexander. He decreed that sacred vessels should be handled only by priests; he willingly shed his blood for the faith, in 129. Certain decrees and letters are falsely attributed to him, CXXX, 99.

SIXTUS II (St.), pope and martyr. An Athenian Greek by nationality, he succeeded St. Stephen and, having sat only one year, was crowned with martyrdom in 258. Letters by him survive, V, 99.

SIXTUS III, or XYSTUS (St.), pope. He confirmed the Council of Ephesus and crushed the Eutychians and Pelagians by anathema. He died in 440. Letters and decrees by him survive, L, 571.

SIXTUS, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church. See NICOLAUS, cardinal.

SIXTUS of Siena, a Jew who became a Christian, chose the Order of Friars Preacher. He is the author of the *Sacred Library*. He celebrates the praises of Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux. He died in 1569, CLXXXV, 636.

SMARAGDUS, or ARDO, abbot of St. Michael on the Meuse, in the diocese of Verdun, of the Order of St. Benedict. At first he taught grammar. In 810 Charlemagne sent him to Rome with certain other envoys to consult the pope concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit. Louis the Pious chose him as judge in the dispute which arose between Isnard, abbot of Milan, and the monks of that same house. We possess from him collections, commentaries, the *Diadem of Monks*, etc. He died in 824, CII, 9. [Col. 0527]

SMARAGDUS, monk of St. Maximin. He must be distinguished from the preceding person because he was somewhat later and made his profession in a different monastery. There survives from him a preface to the Book of Psalms, about 900, CXXIX, 1022.

SMUBURGA, daughter of a certain Bernard, conveyed part of her inheritance to the church of St. Saviour at Werden, in 839, XCIX, 814.

SOFFORDUS, prior of the Charterhouse of Les Écouges; Bernard, prior of Les Portes; Stephen, prior of Durbon; and John, prior of Alveria, assembled in chapter, send their decision to Falco, bishop of Lyons, that he may confirm it by his sanction, thirteenth century, CLIII, 1123.

SOLON, king and lawgiver of Athens, one of the Seven Wise Men of Greece, flourished about 600 before Christ. St. Ambrose attributes to him four letters translated from Greek, XVII, 1148.

SONNATIUS (St.), archbishop of Rheims. Previously archdeacon of the same diocese, he was elected in 594. He assembled at Rheims a council of more than forty bishops in 625. He is believed to have died in 631. Statutes by him survive, LXXX, 442.

SOPHIA, abbess of the convent at Kisingen. She flourished in the twelfth century. She consulted St. Hildegard as to whether she ought to relinquish the office she held, CXVII, 322.

SOPHIA RAIMFREDIS, daughter of Peter Achard, entered the monastery of Fontevraud, to which she granted her allod at Poligny, together with other lands and vineyards besides. This was done under King Louis VI the Fat and Peter, bishop of Poitiers, in the twelfth century, CLXII, 1105.

SOPHRONIUS (St.), patriarch of Jerusalem. Born at Damascus in Syria, he was distinguished by manifold learning, knowledge of the divine Scriptures, and piety. He took part in the Second General Council of Nicaea and died in 636. He wrote the life of Blessed Mary of Egypt, LXXIII, 671.

SOTER (St.), pope and martyr. He succeeded St. Anicetus and suffered martyrdom under Marcus Antoninus in 177. In those troubled times he became a model for the clergy and a consolation to the Church. Certain decrees attributed to him survive, but are regarded as spurious, CXXX, 117.

SOUCELINA, abbess of St. Cyricus, declares that she granted Maurice, bishop of Paris, two arpents of meadow in return for four pounds of Parisian currency received, in 1190, CCV, 912.

SPECIOSUS, bishop of Florence, in 724, during the reign of Liutprand, bestowed many gifts upon the canons of St. John the Baptist; a charter of that donation survives, LXXXVII, 1402.

SPERA IN DEO, abbot of a certain monastery in Spain in the time of St. Eulogius, archbishop of Toledo. He flourished about 859. He wrote several letters to Alvarus of Córdoba, CXV, 960.

STEPHEN (St.), pope and martyr. Born at Rome of Julius, he was installed in the Roman see in 253. He upheld the validity of baptism administered by heretics against St. Cyprian of Carthage. He died a martyr under the consul Valerian in 257. There survive from him two letters and decretal judgments concerning the baptism of heretics, dated 545 [an apparent chronological inconsistency in the source], III, 983.

STEPHEN, deacon of Arles. See MESSIANUS.

STEPHEN, abbot. See PAULUS, fourth century.

STEPHEN II, Roman pontiff. Born at Rome of Constantine, he was elected in 752; he sat until 757, when he died. Letters and decrees by him survive, LXXXIX, 960.

STEPHEN III, pope. A Sicilian by nationality, born of a father named Oliva, he was raised to the see in 768 and held it for three years. A vigorous man, learned in the divine Scriptures and ecclesiastical traditions, he died in 771. Five letters by him survive, LXXXIX, 1235; XCVIII, 239.

STEPHEN IV, pope. A Roman by birth, he succeeded Leo III with the consent of the Roman clergy. He was by no means unversed in sacred canons and ecclesiastical affairs. He died in 817, one year after his installation. The decree concerning the election of a pope, *Distinctio* 33, is wrongly attributed to him, CII, 1072.

STEPHEN V, pope. A Roman by nationality, born of his father Adrian, he succeeded Adrian III in 885, though elected unwillingly. He was distinguished by integrity of character and charity toward the needy. He died in 891. Letters and privileges by him survive, CXXIX, 786.

STEPHEN VI, pope. A Roman by birth, son of a father named John, and formerly a monk of the Order of St. Benedict, he succeeded Formosus. For the man who, under the name Boniface, seized the see after Formosus’s death sat only fifteen days and is not to be numbered among the pontiffs. Stephen, however, after the body of his predecessor Formosus had been violated, was thrown into prison by the latter’s relatives and shortly afterward strangled, in 897. Several letters and privileges by him survive, CXXIX, 854. [Col. 0528]

STEPHEN VII, pope. A German by people and country, he was elected through the agency of King Otto, after the votes of the cardinals had been obtained, in 929, and died in 931. Letters and privileges by him survive, CXXXII, 1050.

STEPHEN IX, pope, is said to have been German. He succeeded Leo VII in 939 and died in 942. Several letters and privileges concerning him are extant, CXXXII, 1087.

STEPHEN X, pope. A Gaul by nationality, of the noble house of the dukes of Lorraine, he was first a regular canon of St. Lambert in Lorraine, then cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the Apostolic See. In 1037 he was elevated to the supreme pontificate. He died in 1058. Letters and privileges by him are found at CXLIII, 866.
