STEPHEN, bishop of Liège. Born of a noble family, he was educated in the palace schools with Radbod of Utrecht; first he was a cleric at Metz, then a monk and abbot of Lobbes. He died in 920. There survives from him a Life of St. Lambert, bishop and martyr, CXXXII, 642.

STEPHEN (St.), king of the Hungarians, son and successor of Géza, received the crown in 997. He died in 1038, having devoted himself wholly to reforming the morals of the peoples. There survive from him admonitions to his son, laws, and a privilege granted for the abbey of St. Martin of Pannonia, CII, 1203.

STEPHEN, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church. A Gaul by nationality, a man exceptionally learned for his age, he was invested with the purple by St. Leo IX; at that time he was living the monastic life in the monastery of Cluny. Blessed Damian calls him the glory and defender of the Roman Church. He died in 1068. We possess from him the canons of the councils of Tours and Bordeaux, of 1060, and a letter to John, bishop of Dol, CXLIII, 1407.

STEPHEN, abbot of St. James at Liège. A man equally outstanding in learning and works, he was persuaded by the prayers of a certain monk to write the Life of St. Modoald; moreover, he corrected Thietmar’s account of the translation of that same saint. He flourished in 1106, CLIV, 1275.

STEPHEN HERRANDUS, bishop of Halberstadt. Having read the letters of Walram, bishop of Naumburg, to Louis, landgrave of Thuringia, by which he urged him to withdraw from the pope and adhere to Emperor Henry, he refutes and condemns them outright, in Louis’s name as well, in 1110, CLIX, 988.

STEPHEN of Muret (St.), so called from the place where he lived a solitary life for almost fifty years, was the first prior, organizer, and founder of the Grandmontine Order. Born of a noble house among the Auvergnats in 1044, he first studied under a man of outstanding holiness; afterward he came to Rome, where he remained four years. From Gregory VII, Hildebrand, he obtained permission to establish his order. He died in 1124, renowned alike for miracles and virtues. There survives from him a book of sayings and the Rule of Grandmont, CCIV, 999.

STEPHEN (St.), Cistercian abbot, surnamed Harding. Born of a noble family, he was English by nationality; at first he studied letters in Scotland. Then he completed his course of studies in France and at Paris, through the assistance of Stephen, abbot of Cîteaux, whom he afterward succeeded upon his death. He died in 1134. There survive from him a critical examination of certain passages of Scripture, a sermon at the death of his predecessor, letters and a charter of donation, the usages and customs of the Cistercians, and an account of the beginnings of the monastery and Order of Cîteaux, CLXVI, 1373.

STEPHEN of Baugé, son of Gunceram, lord of Baugé, had already held the see of Autun from 1112; but, from contempt for the world, he resigned the episcopate in 1129 and withdrew to Cluny. Later he rendered his soul to God in the hands of Peter the Venerable in 1136. There survive from him a treatise on the Eucharist and a charter for the monastery of Fontenay, CLXXII, 1271; CLXXXV, 1463.

STEPHEN, bishop of Paris. Born of the ancient and illustrious family of Senlis, he was cultivated in every kind of learning. He first became archdeacon of Paris, then was appointed successor to Gerbert in 1124. He died in 1142. Letters, diplomas, and donations by him survive, CLXXIII, 1399.

STEPHEN, monk and steward of Stavelot, reports to Abbot Wibald what he had done while inspecting the monastery’s lands, in 1148, CLXXXIX, 1201.

STEPHEN, bishop of Metz. He flourished in the middle of the twelfth century. In 1151 he wrote to Wibald, abbot of Corvey, that he should compel the monks of Hastière to obedience toward the church of Waulsort. In the same year he also wrote to Theoderic, abbot of Waulsort, summoning him, accused of wasteful dissipation, to the synod of Metz, CLXXXIX, 1367, 1431. [Col. 0529]

STEPHEN, king of the English. Formerly count of Blois, after the death of Henry I he usurped the crown to the prejudice of Matilda, Henry’s daughter; but, defeated by David, king of Scotland, he was compelled to lay it down in favor of Henry Plantagenet, Matilda’s son. He died in 1154. There survives from him a diploma of 1136 concerning gifts made by his father to Cluny, CLXXXIX, 1063.

STEPHEN of Liciac, fourth prior of Grandmont. A native of Limousin, a prudent, charitable, devout man, and austere in fasts, he greatly extended the order. He died in 1161. He arranged for the deeds of St. Stephen of Muret, the founder, to be written, CCIV, 1163.

STEPHEN, bishop of Meaux, flourished in the twelfth century, in 1172. He wrote to Pope Alexander III on behalf of St. Thomas of Canterbury in exile, CC, 1414, 1415.

STEPHEN, abbot of St. Geneviève at Paris and afterward bishop of Tournai. He was born at Orléans in France about 1135. From his earliest age he devoted himself ardently to piety, and succeeded Robert, the deceased abbot of St. Evroul. Later he became abbot of St. Geneviève and finally was elevated to the see of Tournai in 1192; he died in 1203. Letters and sermons by him survive, CCXI, 295.

STEPHEN Langton, archbishop of Canterbury. He wrote a history of the translation of the body of his predecessor St. Thomas, which took place in 1221, CXC, 407.

STEPHEN, Roman priest of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles, and Peter, cardinal of St. George at the Golden Veil, attest that Count Egino of Vrach and lord of Freiburg, for 200 marks sterling, pledged to his brother Conrad, bishop of Porto, various vestments and precious vessels for the celebration of sacred rites. In 1227 that pious bishop, with the lord pope’s permission, granted them to the monastery of Clairvaux, CLXXXV, 1771.

STEPHEN JORDANIS, canon of Padua, was commissioned by John, bishop of Padua, with letters of procuration to the patriarch of Aquileia, to swear an oath of fealty in his name, in 1296, XCIX, 651.

STEPHEN of Lusignan, bishop of Limassol, born of the Cypriot royal house, wrote many genealogies. He died in 1590. There survives from him an excerpt from a history of Cyprus, in the French language, CLXXXV, 1484.

STURMIUS (St.), abbot of Fulda. He was born in Noricum of parents distinguished both by rank and piety. Boniface, to whom he had been attached from childhood, entrusted him for education to Abbot Wigbert. Under such a master he made such progress that he was soon ordained priest and, by his preaching, drew many back from the mire of pleasures and the darkness of error. He then became abbot of Fulda. He died in 776. There survive from him the Order of the Office in monasteries of the Order of St. Benedict and their ancient monastic customs, LXXXIX, 1258.

SUAVIUS, abbot of St. Sever in the metropolitan district of Gascony, was elected in 1092. He was a conspicuous man, especially for his zeal in advancing the welfare of his monastery, which he in fact administered with happy success until 1107, when he died. Statutes for the monastery of St. Sever survive from him, CLVII, 478.

SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis. That celebrated man—whose very name was his praise and glory—flourished from 1080 to 1151. According to St. Bernard, no one was more faithful or prudent in temporal affairs, nor anyone humbler or more inflamed with zeal in spiritual matters. He was beloved by God and prince alike, wise at court, and a holy religious in the monastery. He died in 1151. He wrote many letters, a life of Louis the Fat, and certain diplomas, CLXXXII, 675; CLXXXVI, 1151.

SULCARD, monk of Westminster. A Norman by nationality, according to the more common opinion, he shone so greatly in virtue and knowledge that he became especially intimate with St. King Edward. We possess from him a small work on the foundation of Westminster Abbey, about 1100, CLV, 1634.

SULPICIUS SEVERUS, Aquitanian priest. A man distinguished by birth and learning, he first married a wife of consular lineage; after her death he renounced the world and devoted himself to monastic discipline. According to some, he became a priest. He died at Marseilles in 410. He left letters, dialogues, and historical works, XX, 79.

SULPICIUS (St.), surnamed the Pious, bishop of Bourges. Born of illustrious parents, he himself shone in virtues and became an outstanding shepherd of the city of Bourges. After many noble deeds and miracles, he died in 644. Three letters by him survive, LXXX, 594.

SUSO, Henry, monk of the Order of Friars Preacher. He was born at Constance and died at Ulm in 1366. He produced ascetical writings and sermons; but in the *Patrology* we have included only his distinguished testimony concerning St. Bernard, CLXXXV, 636.

SYLVESTER I (St.), pope. A Roman by nationality, born of his father Rufinus, he succeeded Pope Miltiades in 314. At first he became an exile during the persecution; afterward, having returned to his see, he is said in the *Pontifical of St. Damasus* to have baptized the Emperor Constantine. He died in 335. Chapters and decrees by him survive, VIII, 795. [Col. 0530]

SYLVESTER II, pope. Formerly named Gerbert, a Gaul by nationality and of humble birth, he was first a monk at Orléans and then abbot of Bobbio; in turn he was teacher of Emperor Otto III and of Robert, king of the Franks. Later he was raised to the archiepiscopal see of Ravenna and finally to the chair of St. Peter in 999. He held it until 1003, when he died. From this most learned man survive a small work *On the Division of Numbers*; another *On Geometry*; a book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*; letters, diplomas, and some poems, CXXXIX, 58.

SYMMACHUS the elder, father of Aurelius Symmachus. He devoted the greatest care to his sons’ education; nevertheless, he refused to embrace the Christian faith which he knew, and brought up his sons in the old pagan worship, in which they persevered until death. There survives from him a letter to his son Aurelius. He died about 360, XVIII, 147.

SYMMACHUS Aurelius, native of Rome, became senator and prefect of that city. He held the consulship in 391. He showed himself everywhere hostile to the Christian religion, especially in his memorial concerning the Altar of Victory, which he presented to Emperor Valentinian. He had St. Ambrose as his adversary, who refuted him vigorously and elegantly. Ten books of letters, distinguished for style and elegance, survive from him. He died in 398, XVIII, 141.

SYMMACHUS, pope. A Roman by nationality, born of his father Fortunatus, he succeeded Anastasius in 498, despite the opposition of the archpriest Laurentius, who seized the see and stirred up a schism among the clergy. But at a council the authority was adjudged to Symmachus, which he exercised until his death in 514. His letters survive, LXII, 77.

SYMON, master, surnamed the Golden Goat, canon of St. Victor at Paris. A supreme and very rapid versifier, at St. Bernard’s request he composed the epitaph of Count Henry in the twelfth century. Certain other epitaphs are also attributed to him, CLXXXV, 1251.

SYMPHOSIUS AMALARIUS, abbot of Hornbach. Formerly a priest of the church of Metz, he had Alcuin as his teacher and at one time was head of the palace schools under Louis the Pious, for he became most expert in learning and liturgy. He died in 836. There survive from him a rule for canons, four books *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, a book *On the Order of the Antiphonary*, and *Eclogues on the Office of the Mass*, CV, 815.

SYRUS, monk of Cluny. At the request of Abbot Warnerius, as he himself declares in the prologue, he undertook to write the life of St. Maiolus, abbot of the same order. When he flourished is uncertain, CXXXVII, 745.

## T

TAIO, bishop of Zaragoza. He was elected after the death of St. Braulio, about the middle of the seventh century, and flourished in 656. There survive from him a letter to Eugenius of Toledo and five books of *Sentences*, LXXX, 720.

TALESPERIANUS, bishop of Lucca, flourished under Liutprand, king of the Lombards. There survives from him an instrument by which he granted to a certain priest named Romuald a monastery with a hospice, in 725, LXXXVII, 1370.

TANCRED, prince of Sicily, set out with Bohemond of Taranto against the Turks and was renowned for many achievements. He was at times at odds with the other Christian leaders, and established a principality in Galilee. He died at Antioch in 1112. Ralph of Caen reports certain words concerning him, CLV, 505, 540.

TARASIUS, first imperial secretary under Emperor Constantine Copronymus, by whom he was elected patriarch of Constantinople. Under the same emperor the Second General Council was held in 785, at which the Monothelites prevailed. He resisted the emperor himself firmly. He died in 806. There survive from him an apology to the people, an address at the Seventh General Council, and letters to Pope Adrian, CXXIX, 201, 209, 497.

TARRA, monk. Almost no documents concerning him survive. Ambrosio Morales asserts that he found a letter written by this monk to King Reccared in 600, LXXX, 19.

TATTO, monk of St. Gall, contemporary of Grimald, presented to his teacher Reginbert the Rule of the holy Father Benedict, transcribed by himself and Grimald, as their joint letter to the same man reports, in 872, CXXI, 925.

TEDUINUS and ARDUINUS, devoted to secular military service, bestowed lands as a gift upon the monastery of St. Peter at Chartres in 984 and 996, CLV, 248, 249.

TELESPHORUS (St.), pope and martyr. A native of Greece, he succeeded St. Sixtus in the see of St. Peter and received the crown of martyrdom in 139. The decrees falsely attributed to him survive in Pseudo-Isidore, CXXX, 105. [Col. 0531]

TERALDUS, apparently a monk of Fleury, is known to us only through a letter which he wrote to a certain Guido, likewise a monk, CXXXVIII, 186.

TERRICUS, grand master of the Templars, flourished at the end of the twelfth century, in 1187. He wrote two letters: one to the Templar brethren concerning the defeat of the Christians, and another to Henry, king of England, *On Jerusalem Captured by the Saracens*, CCI, 1403.

TERTULLIAN, priest, born at Carthage in 160 of pagan parents. He was first raised in pagan worship, then became a Christian and a priest, and wrote much in defense of the faith. But, deceived by the austerity of the Montanists, he went over to them; hence the faith of this great writer is doubted. He died in 245, I, III.

TEUDERADUS, a Lombard priest, and his brother Teupertus resolved to found a church near Sesto, in a place called Croce, during the reign of Pippin in the eighth century, LXXXVII, 1439.

TESTALDUS, count, and EBRARDUS, viscount, gave certain serfs to the monastery of St. Peter at Chartres in 1070 and 1080, CLV, 299, 300.

TEUTGAUGUS, archbishop of Trier. There survives from him a general letter to Charles the Bald and all bishops on behalf of the priest Egino, who was making pilgrimage to the shrines of the holy Apostles, in 860, CXXIX, 1390.

TEUCHUS, monk of Morigny. From youth he was educated in Morigny Abbey, where he became cantor and prior. At last he was elected abbot, but because some opposed him, he willingly resigned his right. He afterward became abbot of St. Remigius at Rheims. He wrote the *Chronicle of Morigny* in 1147, CLXXX, 131.

TEUTPALDUS, DOMMULUS, and other pious citizens of Lucca built a sacred church dedicated to St. Sylvester, together with a hospice, in the city of Lucca in 718, under Bishop Talesperianus, LXXXVII, 1361.

THALASSIUS, bishop of Beirut, together with very many bishops of the East, sent a petition to Pope Agapetus against Anthimus of Antioch, usurper of the see of Constantinople, in 536, LXVI, 67.

THALES, celebrated philosopher, born in Phoenicia, founded a school at Miletus and was numbered by the Greeks among the true wise men. Two letters by him, translated from Greek, survive in St. Ambrose. He flourished in 587 before Christ, XVII, 1147.

THANGMARUS, priest of Hildesheim. A Saxon by nationality, he was first chief of the boys’ school, then was made priest and dean of the church of Hildesheim. He held St. Bernward, his pupil, in the greatest affection; Bernward was later elected bishop. There survives from him a Life of St. Bernward, written in 1025, CXL, 386.

THEGANBALDUS, son of a certain Hrodbald, granted Blessed Liudger a village called Fislac, beside the bank of the Ruhr River. This gift was confirmed by his grandson Bernger in 801, XCIX, 803.

THEGANUS, archbishop of Trier, flourished about the middle of the ninth century. He wrote a book on the Deeds of Louis the Pious down to 837. He died in 843, CVI, 402.

THEOBALD, count of Chalon, subscribed, for the benefit of St. Maiolus, abbot of Cluny, a gift which he had made to the monastery of St. Marcellus at Chalon in 960, CXXXVII, 780.

THEOBALD, count of Champagne, wrote to Blessed Hugh, abbot of Cluny, that he might receive his son for baptism in the eleventh century, CLIX, 943.

THEOBALD of Étampes, English by nationality and a secular priest, flourished from 1108. Letters by him survive, CLXIII, 759.

THEOBALD, archbishop of Canterbury. Almost no documents concerning him survive. He flourished in the twelfth century, about 1150. He wrote a letter, or rather a testament, found among the letters of John of Salisbury, CLXXXVIII, 1675. See also CXCIX, 30, 36.

THEOBALD, count of Blois. Having defeated Odo in 1125, he gained possession of Champagne and long resisted King Louis the Fat. He died in 1151. He confirmed the gift which Jobert of La Ferté, setting out for Jerusalem, had made to the monks of Clairvaux in 1145. Other charters concerning him also survive, CLXXXV, 986; CLXXXVI, 1352, 1365, 1403, 1405; CC, 1447.

THEOBALD IV, count palatine of Champagne and Brie and king of Navarre, set out for Palestine in 1239 through Blanche, his wife and daughter of Sancho VII; having returned thence, he died about 1253. Certain songs are attributed to him. There survives concerning him a diploma by which he grants wax to the monks of Clairvaux in 1232, CLXXXV, 1761. [Col. 0532]

THEOBAUD, count of Champagne. With the consent of Hugh, bishop of Auxerre; Hatto of Troyes; Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux; and William, abbot of St. Martin, he granted the church of St. Lupus to the canons of St. Martin, for restoring the divine worship neglected there, in 1135, CLXXXV, 980.

THEOBAUD of Saliva gave to the church of St. Mary of Fontenay everything he possessed within the boundaries of Puteolifranc, with Rainerius of Roche, Gerard of Châtillon, his brother-in-law, and others as witnesses; undated, twelfth century, CLXXXV, 1464.

THEODADRA, abbess of St. Mary at Argenteuil, exchanged certain slaves with Abbot Einhard in 834, CIV, 604.

THEODATUS, or THEODAHATUS, king of the Goths, was raised to the throne when he married Amalasuntha, widow of Athalaric, whom he afterward ordered killed. Defeated by Belisarius, he was deprived of the kingdom. He died in 536. Letters by him survive, LXIX, 797, 812; LXXII, 1118.

THODEBALD, king of the Austrasians, succeeded his father Theudebert in 548, kindly received Justinian’s envoys, and sent him through them a letter promising to maintain peace and form friendship. He died about 555, LXXI, 1165.

THEUDEBERT, king of Austrasia. He took up arms against Vitiges, king of the Ostrogoths, and Emperor Justinian, defeated both, and was already planning the siege of Constantinople itself when sudden death carried him off, about 548. There survives from him a letter to Justinian, LXXI, 1164.

THEODERIC IV, son of Dagobert III. After Childeric II he ascended the throne—or rather was put in place by Charles Martel—as king in name, not in fact. He died in 763, LXXXVIII, 1130.

THEODERIC, or DEODERIC, bishop of Metz and successor of Bruno of Cologne; formerly a canon of Halberstadt and provost of Worms. With Emperor Otto’s support, he was elevated to the episcopate in 964. He died in 984. There survive concerning him Count Evrard’s epitaph, an account by him of the discovery of certain saints, and a letter to Charles, brother of King Lothair, CXXXVII, 359.

THEODERIC entered the monastery of St. Matthias at Trier in 1006. At Abbot Richard’s request, he wrote a small work on the translation and miracles of St. Celsus—written indeed in an inflated style, but preserving much information about the affairs of Egbert and other matters worthy of notice. He also wrote the life and passion of Archbishop Conrad in 1020, CLIV, 1233, 1252.

THEODERIC, bishop of Chartres, attests that the monastery of the Holy Trinity at Vendôme was founded by Count Geoffrey and his wife Countess Agnes, and consecrated by himself together with several other bishops in 1050, CLVII, 289.

THEODERIC, abbot of the monastery of St. Peter at Chartres, attests that a priest called Walter the Child gave the priesthood of the church of St. Mary of Alogia to the monastery of St. Peter at Chartres in 1069, CLV, 336.

THEODERIC, count of Flanders, son of the duke of Lorraine and successor of William Clito, crossed over to Palestine once and again, and died in 1169. He granted Lord Bernard and his monks exemption from every payment of toll, going and returning through the lands of his whole county, in 1143, CLXXXV, 984.

THEODERIC, bishop of Amiens. Suger had written to him, as to other bishops, that he should grant certain subsidies to the king for the Jerusalem expedition. The latter replied that he should be regarded as excused, and that he remained, as it were, in a frying-pan between king and pope, about 1148, CLXXXVI, 1359, 1362.

THEODERIC, abbot of New Corvey, issued a statute that whatever noteworthy event occurred in the monastery should be committed accurately and faithfully to writing, year by year, in 1337, CLXXXIX, 1506.

THEODGAUDUS, primate of Belgic Gaul, Guntharius of Cologne, and Arduin, bishop of Besançon, jointly wrote to Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, because he had opposed Hilduin’s election. They complain bitterly of this and admonish him to attend the council soon to be held at Metz. The same persons wrote a letter to the bishops of the whole kingdom, with certain rather immodest chapters against Pope Nicholas, in 866, CXXI, 377 and following.

THEODGRIMUS, deacon and son of Aldgrin, conveyed by charter to the church of St. Saviour the whole inheritance which he had received from Ricfrid, in 821, during the reign of Emperor Louis the Pious, XCIX, 819.

A certain THEODO sold some property to the monastery of Murbach in the district of Hamaristod, near Neuf-Brisach, in 730, during the reign of Theoderic IV, LXXXVIII, 1285. [Col. 0533]

THEODOLDUS and his brother Thrudgerus, sons of Wigger, gave part of their inheritance to the church of St. Saviour at Werden, in the district of Rurrigo: namely, pasture-right for twenty pigs. This was done at Werden in 837, during the reign of Emperor Louis the Pious, XCIX, 810.

THEODORET, bishop of Cyrrhus. Born at Antioch, he first lived as a monk in a monastery near Apamea, devoted himself wholly to the cultivation of letters and learning, and attained vast erudition. For a time he inclined toward Nestorius’s party, but shortly afterward anathematized him. He opposed the Eutychians and the emperor himself, by whom he was deposed from his see, then restored; he wrote many works. He died in 458. Some fragments by him appear in our columns, XLVIII, 1063; LIV, 845; LXXIV, 9.

THEODERIC, king of the Goths. He was born in Pannonia about 455 and died in 526. Several enactments and letters by him survive, LXIX, 503; LXXII, 1111.

THEODERIC, canon of Paderborn, from whom almost no monuments survive. He wrote a book on the Lord’s Prayer in 1079, CXLVII, 331.

THEODERIC, monk of St. Ouen. We find little worthy of note concerning him. He flourished in the eleventh century and lived the monastic life in the monastery of St. Ouen at Rouen under Abbot Nicholas. Fragments of a Life of St. Ouen by him survive, CL, 1187.

THEODERIC, abbot of St. Hubert at Andage. This Theoderic flourished about the beginning of the twelfth century, in 1107. We know him only through a letter which he wrote to the people of Liège and the *Chronicle of St. Hubert at Andage*, CLIV, 1428.

THEODERIC, duke and margrave of Lorraine. There survives from him a letter to Pope Paschal, in 1115, CLXIII, 468.

THEODERIC, abbot of Campen, flourished in the time of St. Bernard, whose several miracles he wrote down as an eyewitness, in 1136, CLXXXV, 390, passim.

THEODERIC, author of the Life of St. Hildegard, or rather of its first two books. According to Trithemius, he was an abbot. Others, however, think that he was only a monk and a contemporary of St. Hildegard herself—namely, that he lived after 1200, CXCVII, 91.

THEODORITUS, bishop of Lignides, having returned from Eutychianism to the bosom of the Church, promised obedience to Pope Hormisdas about 519, LXIII, 452.

THEODORE, bishop of the Eastern Church. See EUSEBIUS.

THEODORE of Mopsuestia, born at Antioch, was led away from error by St. John, received orders, and afterward obtained the episcopal see of Mopsuestia; but he fell again into heresy. He died in 428. Certain fragments concerning him survive, XLVIII, 258, 416, 585, 1041.

THEODORE (St.), pope. A Greek by nationality, born of his father Theodore, a bishop, he was a gentle and most merciful man. He was raised to the see in 641 and died in 648. Two letters by him survive, LXXXVII, 75; CXXIX, 577.

THEODORE, bishop of Caesarea. Since he defended the heresy of the Eutychians, he was condemned and excommunicated by Pope Vigilius in 552. The propositions of this heretic, with Vigilius’s replies, survive, LXIX, 72.

THEODORE, bishop of Canterbury (St.). A native of Tarsus in Cilicia, he initially lived a monastic life. Pope Vitalian sent him to England and ordained him bishop in 668; he was the first to exercise authority over all England. He died in 690. His *Penitential* survives, XCIX, 902.

THEODORE, bishop of London. At the beginning of the eighth century he had caused St. Wilfrid, bishop of York, many troubles. When death was imminent, he strove to repair these harms. For this reason he sent letters to Æthelred, king of the Mercians, about 702, LXXXIX, 45.

THEODORE called the Studite because he was abbot of the monastery of Stoudios in the suburb of Constantinople. He defended sacred images against the Iconoclasts; for this reason he endured many persecutions and exile as long as Emperor Leo lived. At length he returned to his brethren and died in 826. There survives from him a sermon translated from Greek by Anastasius the Librarian, CXXIX, 729.

THEODOSIUS the Great, Flavius, emperor. He was born in Spain in 325. He was renowned for outstanding piety, especially in the public penance imposed upon him by St. Ambrose after the massacre at Thessalonica. After many illustrious achievements, he died in 395. His constitutions and letters survive, XI, 1192; XX, 769, 770.

THEODOSIUS II, son of Arcadius, ascended the throne in 408. He reigned until 450, when he died. Constitutions by him survive, LIV, 875.

THEODOSIUS, bishop of Caesarea in Bithynia, followed the party of the Monothelites. His words are reported in a Greek-Latin dialogue with St. Maximus, abbot of Constantinople, in 662, CXXIX, 625.

THEODULF, bishop of Orléans. An Italian by nationality and born from an illustrious Gothic house, he is regarded as a restorer of learning. Charlemagne brought him into Gaul. In 808 he was driven from his see and thrown into prison at Angers; but according to some he was reinstated in 821, the year in which he died. There survive from him *Chapters for Priests*, a book *On the Order of Baptism*, another *On the Holy Spirit*, and poems, CV, 187. [Col. 0534]

THEOGERUS, bishop of Metz. Born of noble stock and brother of Count Folcmar, he first professed the monastic life and was advanced to the priesthood. He discharged that office with such reverence that, when he placed the stole about his neck, he would almost faint. He was then made abbot of St. George’s in the Hercynian Forest, and shortly afterward raised to the episcopate. He died in 1120. He wrote on music, CLXIII, 778.

THEOGNIUS, a Greek bishop. See EUSEBIUS.

THEOPHYLACIAS, archdeacon of the Holy See, flourished in the eighth century, in 752. He wrote two letters to Blessed Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, whom he greatly revered and whom he encouraged against tribulations, LXXXIX, 782.

THEOPHILUS, bishop, one of the three legates of the synod of Lampsacus to Pope Liberius, in 366. See EUSTATHIUS.

THEOPHILUS, patriarch of Alexandria. With excessive zeal he persecuted the followers of Origen. For the same reason he denounced St. John Chrysostom and procured his expulsion from his see and exile; nevertheless, before his death, he was reconciled with him. Several of his letters to Jerome against the Origenists survive, 410, XXII, 755, 758, 773.

THEOPHILUS, SERGIUS, and HYGINUS, monks of whom we know nothing except that they are regarded as authors of the Life of St. Macarius, abbot of Rome; date uncertain, LXXIII, 415.

THEOTMARUS, archbishop of the Church of Juvavum, and other bishops of Bavaria wrote to John IX, complaining that an archbishop and three bishops had been created in Slavic lands previously subject to the bishop of Passau, in 904, CXXXI, 34.

THEOTWINUS, cardinal of the Holy Apostolic See. We find few records of his life. He flourished in the middle of the twelfth century, in 1149; several letters by him survive, CLXXXIX, 1140; CXC, 981.

THEUDOINUS, provost of Châlons, flourished in the seventh century, in 869, and is known to us only by the letter which he sent to Almannus, a monk of Hautvillers near Rheims, asking him to write the Life of St. Memmius, first bishop of Châlons, CXXI, 386.

THEUZO, hermit and monk of St. Mary’s at Florence, to be distinguished from the celebrated Theuzo, disciple of St. John Gualbert and contemporary of this man. He is the author of a commentary on the Rule of St. Benedict, dedicated to Bishop Odelric in 1057, CXLIII, 843.

A certain nobleman THEVIT and his wife Erhilt came to the monastery of St. Emmeram in order to renew and confirm the conveyance of certain properties. This was done under Bishop Ambricho, in 868, CXXIX, 923.

THIEBOLDUS, or THIEBALDUS, provost of Xanten. When the deposed abbess of Geseke came to him, he wished to defend her cause; accordingly, he wrote to Wibald, who dissuaded him from his undertaking in 1149, CLXXXIX, 1217, 1278.

THIETMARUS, bishop of Merseburg. A Saxon by birth, he was the son of Count Sigifrid and Cunigunda. First a monk, then abbot of Corvey, he died in 1008. His Chronicle survives, CXXXIX, 1169.

THIETPALDUS, monk of Tegernsee, known only from a letter that he wrote to St. Adalbert, bishop of Prussia. He flourished at the close of the tenth century, in 1003, CXXXIX, 374.

THIOFRIDUS, abbot of Echternach in the duchy of Luxembourg. He is believed to have died in 1110. There survive from him extracts from an epitaph of the saints, two sermons, and fragments of a Life of St. Willibrord, CLVII, 297.

THOMAS, second bishop of York by that name. A Norman by birth, he was called the Younger to distinguish him from his predecessor. Endowed with every kind of learning and virtue, he devoted himself wholly to God’s service and was raised to the episcopate in 1108. He died in 1114. There survives a letter by him to Lanfranc and another to the bishops established throughout England, CLV, 1626.

THOMAS, formerly abbot of Morigny. Having voluntarily laid down his office, he had withdrawn to St. Martin-des-Champs. Later, desiring to return and govern his abbey again, he was summoned by the legate Adhemar, who wished to oblige his nephews Macharius and Lancelin. Our abbot complains of him to St. Bernard. Shortly afterward he died in the monastery of Colombs, to which he had retired, in 1131, CLXXXII, 683.

THOMAS BECKET, Saint, archbishop of Canterbury. Born in London in 1117, he was initiated from early youth into humane letters; [Col. 0535] afterward he went to Paris, where he made great progress in knowledge of canon law. He took orders in 1138, and because of his outstanding merit gradually attained the see of Canterbury in 1161. But he had a most serious conflict with King Henry and was finally slain by wicked men; in 1174 he is venerated in the Church as a martyr. Many letters and various treatises by him survive, CXC, 9.

THOMAS, monk of Radolio, of whom few traces survive in the biographers, flourished at the end of the twelfth century. He wrote the Life of the Venerable Peter, abbot of Clairvaux, and dedicated it to Walcher, abbot of Longpont, about 1200, CCIX, 1007.

THOMAS, Cistercian monk, a man most learned, especially in the Scriptures, which he was accustomed constantly to turn over in his hands and meditate upon in mind. He labored long on a commentary on the Song of Songs, which he sent with a letter to Pons, bishop of Clermont. It survives here collated with the commentary of John Algrin, about 1200, CCVI, 9.

THOMAS AQUINAS, called the Angelic Doctor. A Neapolitan by birth, he entered the Order of St. Dominic. He had Albert the Great as his master and advanced in knowledge especially by meditating before the crucifix. With great labor he produced the outstanding work, the *Summa Theologica*. He died in 1274. His works are contained in the supplement to the 217 volumes of the *Patrologia Latina*; but an encomium of St. Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, is given concerning him, CLXXXV, 629.

THOMAS AGNI OF LENTINI, a Sicilian of the Order of Preachers: first bishop of Bethlehem and apostolic legate under Alexander IV; then archbishop of Cosenza under Clement IV; and finally made patriarch of Jerusalem in 1272. He died in 1285. A letter by him to Rudolf, emperor of Germany, survives, XCVIII, 820.

THOMELLUS. See TOMELLUS.

THRASYBULUS, Athenian general, twice restored his country to liberty. Victorious at Cyzicus and defeated at Ephesus, he waged war against the Lacedaemonians; he died in 390 before Christ. St. Ambrose attributes to him a letter translated from Greek into Latin, XVII, 1150.

THRUDGERUS, brother of Theodoldus and a donor. See THEODOLDUS.

TICHONIUS the African, whom St. Augustine calls a man endowed with keen intellect and abundant eloquence, but a Donatist, flourished in the fourth century, in 399. His book on the seven rules survives, XVIII, 13.

TIMASIUS, whose letter survives in St. Augustine. See JACOBUS.

TOMELLUS, monk of Hasnon, secretary to Count Baldwin surnamed of Mons. This weighty author wrote a history of the foundation of the monastery of Hasnon. He flourished in the eleventh century, in 1080, CLXVII, 586.

TORTHELMUS, bishop of an unknown see in Germany, flourished in the eighth century. A letter by him to Blessed Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, survives, 733, LXXXIX, 724.

TRACTEMUNDUS, otherwise called REGIMUNDUS, first subdeacon of Toledo, soon ordained priest, and finally consecrated bishop of Elvira by Bonitus, bishop of Toledo, in 946, CXXXVI, 967.

TRECCA, a British bishop, wrote to St. Lullus, archbishop of Mainz, requesting his prayers. There his deacon Aldbertus introduced certain words addressed to that holy bishop, in 756, XCVI, 835.

TRIFOLIUS, priest of the sixth century, whose life lacks records, wrote a letter to a certain Senator Faustus concerning the doctrine of the Scythian monks, about 514, LXIII, 534.

TROJANUS, bishop of Saintes, flourished around the middle of the sixth century, in 540. He is the same man of whom Gregory of Tours wrote in *The Glory of the Confessors*. He left us a letter to Eunarius, bishop of Nantes, LXVII, 995.

TROMUNDUS, monk of Clairvaux, went to Rome because of St. Bernard’s canonization, and afterward wrote from there what had been done by Pope Alexander III, about 1163, CLXXXV, 626.

TURGOTUS, prior of Durham, who also assumed the name Simeon, flourished in the eleventh century. He produced a Life of the Venerable Priest Bede and a history of the translation [of relics], XC, 53, 59.

TURRIBIUS, bishop of Astorga in the province of Tarragona. He was a most determined enemy of the Priscillianists; only a few records about him have been handed down. There survives a letter by him to Idacius, written in 447, concerning the refusal to receive apocryphal writings as authoritative for the faith, against the Priscillianists, L, 1294.

TURSTINUS, archbishop of York in England. His letter to William of Canterbury, about 1132, survives, CLXXXII, 697.

TUSAREDUS, about whom records are entirely lacking, received a letter from a certain Bishop Ascaricus and sent him a reply, XCIX, 1231.

[Col. 0536] TUTILO, Saint, monk of St. Gall, flourished near the end of the ninth century, in 898. He was called “the Traveller” because he often went out from the monastery for the benefit of the brethren; after his death he was numbered among the blessed. He was at once a poet, painter, and musician. The date of his death is uncertain. Several poems by him survive, CXXIX, 664.

## U

UDALRICUS, Saint, bishop of Augsburg, flourished in the tenth century, in 973. There survive from him a synodal sermon and a charter, CXXXV, 999, 1074.

UDALRICUS, abbot of Tegernsee. Very little concerning him has reached us; it is only clear that he wrote four letters, about 1048, CXLI, 1321.

UDALRICUS, monk of Cluny. This venerable man, born at Regensburg from a noble Bavarian family, introduced Cluniac customs into the monasteries of Alemannia at the request of William, abbot of the monastery of Hirsau, about 1086, CXLIX, 634.

UDASCALCUS, monk of the Augsburg monastery of St. Ulrich. Born of the noble family of Maissack, he embraced the monastic life under Egino, abbot of St. Ulrich, whose inseparable companion he was. He cultivated letters and the liberal arts, was then made abbot in 1126, and died in 1151, CLXX, 835.

ULFILAS, Arian bishop of the Moesogoths. Philostorgius relates that he was bishop of this people and descended from it. Most skilled in Gothic and Greek, he translated the Gospels and certain other books of both the Old and New Testaments from Greek into Gothic. Some think that he translated the entire Bible, but that very much has perished; at the end of the fourth century, XVIII, 462.

ULGERIUS, bishop of Angers, successively canon, scholasticus, and archdeacon; but because of his extensive learning and exceptional virtues he was raised to the episcopal see of Angers, which he held until 1147. Several letters survive from him, as do a report to Pope Innocent II on behalf of the monastery of Ronceay and his will, CLXXX, 1642.

ULRICUS, canon, and Gerard, called “Without Land,” lord of Acrimont, brothers of Rainerius, granted certain land to the monks of Morimond about 1148, CLXXXV, 1443.

ULTIANUS, notary of King Liutprand in Lombardy, was sent by him to settle a dispute that had arisen between Talesperianus, bishop of Lucca, and John, bishop of Pistoia, in 716, LXXXVII, 1360.

UNALDUS, abbot of Moissac, disposed by testament of the tithes which he had redeemed from various laymen, and delivered that instrument into the hands of Hugh, abbot of Cluny, in 1073, CLIX, 964.

UNIBERTUS, or HUMBERTUS, archbishop of Lyons, excuses himself to Suger for being unable to attend the conference at Chartres, convened to aid the wretched state of the Eastern Church, because the archbishop of Sens does not hesitate to derogate from his primacy, about 1149, CLXXXVI, 1411.

URANIUS, priest of the Church of Nola, was a disciple of St. Paulinus, to whom he brought the consolations of religion in his final illness, in 431. He wrote an account of St. Paulinus’s death for Pacatus, LIII, 859.

URBAN I, Saint, pope and martyr, succeeded St. Callixtus and suffered under Alexander Severus in 230. Certain decrees are attributed to him in Pseudo-Isidore, but they are forged and spurious, CXXX, 137.

URBANUS, confessor. See MAXIMUS.

URBAN II, pope. A Frenchman by birth, formerly named Otto and born at Châtillon in the territory of Rheims, he had already been made cardinal when he attained the Apostolic See in 1088. He died in 1099. He struck with anathema the antipope Guibert and certain clerics living with concubines. His letters, privileges, and sermons survive, CLI, 9.

URBANUS, bishop of Llandaff in British Wales, about 1119. While Callixtus II was at Rheims, he wrote him a letter mentioning the ancient renown of his Church and its weakening, especially since the coming of the Norman people; he beseeches him to assist in restoring that Church, 1119, CLXIII, 1338.

URBAN III, pope, formerly called Lambert. Born at Milan of the distinguished Ghibelline family, he succeeded Pope Lucius in 1185. During his pontificate Jerusalem was taken by the Sultan; this affected him with such grief that he died shortly afterward, in 1187. His letters and privileges survive, CCII, 1329.

URBAN V, pope. A Frenchman born of a noble family, formerly named Grimaldus, he was the sixth Avignon pope and successor of Innocent VI. He died in 1370. A rescript by him to Marquard, patriarch of Aquileia, survives concerning the correction of abuse in the rendering of judgments, 1367, XCIX, 664.

[Col. 0537] URSACIUS, bishop of Singidunum, an Arian. See VALENS.

A certain cleric URSUS founded a monastery of nuns in the city of Lucca in 722; his daughter Ursa was appointed its first abbess, LXXXVII, 1366.

URSUS, subdeacon of the Roman Church, translated into Latin from Greek the Life of St. Basil, written by St. Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium; Ursus added a preface. He flourished at the same time as Anastasius the Librarian, namely in 860, LXXIII, 293.

USUARDUS, monk of Saint-Germain and priest in the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés at Paris, flourished under Charles the Bald, to whom he dedicated his work, namely the *Martyrology*, in 875. He died about 877, CXXIII, 600.

UTHO, bishop of Strasbourg, son of Count Utho, a man renowned in military service. He devoted himself wholly to service of his Church and held office from 950 to 965, when he died. His Life of St. Arbogast, bishop of Strasbourg in First Germany, survives, CXXXIV, 1003.

## V

VALCANDUS, monk of the monastery of Moyen-Moutier in the diocese of Toul. Biographers are silent about the time when he flourished. He wrote a Life—or rather a commentary on the Life—of St. Hidulf, in the tenth or eleventh century, CLI, 583.

VALENS, bishop of Mursa, and Ursacius, bishop of Singidunum, supporters of the Arian heresy, condemned once and again, pretended to return to the faith. Supported by the influence of Emperor Constantius, they stirred up many persecutions against St. Athanasius. They deceived the fathers at Rimini and displayed bad faith everywhere. Several letters concerning them survive: 360, VIII, 911; X, 647, 649.

VALENS, Flavius, Roman emperor. Born in Pannonia, brother and successor of Valentinian, he supported the Arians and issued very many enactments against the orthodox. He died miserably in war against the Goths of Moesia, after a memorable defeat, in 378, XI, 1180 and following.

VALENTINIANUS, Roman emperor. A native of Pannonia, he was appointed in Jovian’s place in 364. He restrained the extravagance of the Arians and died in 375, leaving the empire to his brother Valens, whom he had made his colleague. He issued many enactments and letters, XI, 1180; XIII, 575, 583, 593.

VALENTINIANUS, Flavius Placidus III, emperor of the West. Born at Ravenna to Constantius, he succeeded Honorius through the agency of his mother Placidia. He ordered the general Aetius killed and lost Gaul and the greater part of Italy. He himself was slain by Petronius Maximus, whose wife he had violated, in 455. Several letters and enactments by him survive, LIV, 622, 636, 857, 899.

VALENTINUS, abbot of a certain monastery, wrote to St. Augustine concerning a disagreement among his monks about free will. He sets out the matter in order and explains how he referred the entire case, against their wishes, to Bishop Evodius. His letter survives, 426, XXXIII, 974.

VALENTINUS, pope. A Roman, born on the Via Lata to a father named Peter, he was elected to succeed Eugenius II but sat only forty days. He was a man of exceptional holiness, 827, CV, 649.

VALERIA FALTONIA PROBA. See FALTONIA.

VALERIANUS, Saint, bishop of Cimiez in Gaul, distinguished no less by learning than by piety. He attended the Council of Riez in 439 and that of Arles in 453. Twenty homilies by him survive, LII, 681, 755.

VALERIANUS and SIODOALDUS, sons of a certain Leo and citizens of Brescia, granted to the venerable Anselberga, abbess of the monastery of St. Saviour, the right to a channel for conducting water into the monastery, in 761, under Kings Desiderius and Adelchis, LXXXVII, 1390.

VALERIUS, Saint, abbot of St. Peter of the Mountains in Spain, under Wamba, king of the Goths. He left several little works or letters in which he recounts visions and revelations of various monks. Some attribute to him the Life of St. Fructuosus; seventh century, LXXXVII, 683.

VALERIUS, Marcus Probus, a grammarian whose country, family, and age are unknown to us. He wrote a small work on ancient signs and on abbreviations of words used by scribes, CXXX, 1177.

VALRAMUS, called by others Walcrannus, Gualerannus, or likewise Wal-Rabanus, bishop of Naumburg. He wrote to Louis, landgrave of Thuringia, urging him to abandon the Roman pontiff and follow the party of the schismatic Emperor Henry. Other letters by him survive concerning investitures made by kings. He was refuted by Stephen Herrand of Halberstadt, in 1110, CLIX, 986.

VANDEMIRIS, a nobleman, and his wife Erchamberta bestowed many gifts upon various churches of Paris [Col. 0538] about 690. This charter, written in Merovingian characters, is torn in many places. It was issued under the episcopate of Sigefrid and contains documents of the greatest importance, 690, LXXXVIII, 1216.

VASO, bishop of Liège, who was called Waso or Wazo. First a chaplain, then master of the schools at Liège, chaplain to Emperor Henry III, dean of Liège, provost, and archdeacon, he was finally made bishop in 1042; he died in 1048. His letters and charters survive, CXLII, 763.

VENANTIUS HONORIUS FORTUNATUS. See FORTUNATUS.

VERANUS, Saint, bishop of Cavaillon, whose country and family are unknown. He flourished at the end of the sixth century and attended the Council of Mâcon in 585. There survives from him the dictum concerning clerics: one should ask not how many they are, but what they are worth, LXXII, 701.

VERANUS, Saint, bishop of Vence, whose father was St. Eucherius, bishop of Lyons, and whose brother was Salonius, bishop of Geneva. He too was invested with episcopal dignity and presided over the Church of Vence. He is known from a letter that he wrote to Pope St. Leo the Great, fifth century, LIII, 1011.

VERUS, Saint, bishop of Rodez, of whom almost no records are given. He was present at the Council of Rheims in 625 and, with other bishops, subscribed the privilege granted by St. Faro to the monastery of Holy Cross. He died in 656. Only two letters survive from his writings, LXXX, 446.

VICTOR, Saint, pope and martyr. An African by birth, he succeeded St. Eleutherius in 187, excommunicated Theodore of Byzacena, and suffered for Christ’s faith in 197. According to Pseudo-Isidore, there survive from him a decree on Easter and a letter to the Africans, CXXX, 121.

VICTOR PUBLIUS. See PUBLIUS.

VICTOR OF VITA, African priest. During the persecution of King Huneric, he followed countless confessors into exile—not himself as an exile, but in order to serve and console the exiles. He wrote the history of this persecution in five books, entitled *On the Vandal Persecution*. He died in 481, LVIII, 126.

VICTOR MARIUS CLAUDIUS, of Marseilles, dedicated to his own son Aetherius his exposition of the beginning of Genesis, in which he appears as a man educated in secular literature and little exercised in the mystical sense of Scripture. He flourished in the reigns of Theodosius the Younger and Valentinian, in 426, LXI, 935.

VICTOR, African bishop, flourished in 533, when he wrote to Fulgentius of Ruspe. He differs from Victor, bishop of Carthage, since the latter is said to have flourished only in 646, LXV, 372.

VICTOR, bishop of Capua, of whom biographical writers are silent, is known to us by a little book on the Paschal Cycle, 550, LXVIII, 251, 1097.

VICTOR, bishop of Tunnuna or Tounouna. His Chronicle begins where Prosper ends, that is, from the year 444 to 566, LXVIII, 937.

VICTOR, bishop of Carthage, was appointed in place of Fortunatus, who had been deposed for heresy. His first concern was to profess himself Catholic, and according to ancient custom he sent his profession of faith to Pope Theodore in a letter which survives, 646, LXXX, 635.

VICTOR II, pope, formerly named Gebehard or Eberhard, bishop of Eichstätt. He was German by birth and descended from a noble family. A man of the greatest prudence and learning, he was raised to the chair of Peter in 1055 and died in 1057. His letters and diplomas survive, CXLIII, 799.

VICTOR III, pope. Born at Benevento in 1027 of the distinguished family of the princes of that city, he was first known by the name Dauferius and professed the monastic life as Desiderius in the monastery of Monte Cassino. He succeeded Gregory in 1086 and died in 1087. A letter and three books of *Dialogues* by him survive, CXLIX, 962.

VICTORINUS, Saint, bishop of Poetovio and martyr. Greek by birth, he flourished at the end of the third century and suffered under Diocletian. There survive from him a fragment *On the Making of the World* and scholia on the Apocalypse of St. John, 303, V, 301.

VICTORINUS MARIUS, an African by birth. According to Jerome, he taught rhetoric at Rome and became so famous that his students dedicated a statue to him. In old age he converted to the Christian faith. His book against Justinus the Manichaean survives, 372, VIII, 992.

VICTORIUS, bishop of Le Mans, attended the Council of Tours in 460. The bishop of Lyons, together with Leo of Bourges and Eustochius of Tours, sent to others a letter declaring excommunicated those clerics who, [Col. 0539] bypassing ecclesiastical judgment, had resorted to secular authority, 460, LIV, 1259.

VICTRICIUS, Saint, bishop of Rouen. He was first devoted to secular military service. Miraculously converted to the faith and made priest, he carried Christ’s Gospel into Flanders. He was elected bishop in 385, because his renown grew daily in the Church; he died in 410. He wrote the book *In Praise of the Saints*, XX, 438.

VIGILA, monk of Albelda in Spain, of whom nothing is handed down except that he continued the Chronicle of Albelda, begun by Dulcidius, in the ninth century, CXXIX, 1123.

VIGILIUS, Saint, bishop of Trent and martyr. A Roman by birth, he went to Athens to pursue liberal studies and was afterward made bishop by Valerianus, bishop of Aquileia. He was crowned with the twofold glory of martyrdom and virtues. Two letters by him survive, 381, XIII, 344.

VIGILIUS, deacon and monk, a man very learned in the Scriptures and guardian and director of monastic discipline. He wrote much for the edification of monks, of which only a monastic rule survives, commonly called the Eastern Rule. He died in 430, L, 374.

VIGILIUS, bishop of Tapsus. An African by birth, he flourished in Byzacena in 484 and was made bishop; but fleeing his country because of the cruelty of the Arian Vandals, he went to Constantinople, where he wrote his books against the Eutychians, Arians, and Sabellians. He produced a book *On the Unity of the Trinity* and twelve books *On the Trinity*, 518, LXII, 94.

VIGILIUS, pope. A Roman, born to a father named John, he reigned seventeen years. At first he was an usurper of the Apostolic See while Silverius was alive, but afterward his election became legitimate through Silverius’s death and the consent of the clergy. He died in 555. His letters and decrees survive, LXIX, 9.

VIGILIUS, bishop of Auxerre. He built a monastery in honor of Blessed Mary outside the walls of his city, then granted many possessions to the same monastery by a charter in 670, LXXXVIII, 1193.

VINCENTIUS, Saint, abbot or monk of Lérins, on which island he long practiced monastic life. Few records concerning him are available. This most learned theologian died in 450. His celebrated *Commonitorium*, on the authority of the Catholic faith against the profane novelties of heretics, survives, L, 629.

VINDICIANUS, bishop, known to us only through his letter to Pope John, in which the pope’s rescript is entered, confirming the privileges of the Church of St. Mary at Arras, 680, LXXXVIII, 1200.

VITALIANUS, pope, a native of Segni in Campania and son of Anastasius, was elected after the death of Eugenius I in 657. He died in 672. He took every care to preserve and strengthen ecclesiastical discipline. His letters survive, LXXXVII, 998.

VITIGES, king of the Goths, succeeded Theodahad and declared war on Belisarius; defeated, he was led captive to Constantinople, where he died in 563. Several letters concerning him survive, LXIX, 819.

VIVENTIOLUS, bishop of Lyons. He first lived the monastic life in the monastery of Condat, where he had been educated and initiated into the priesthood. In 557 he was raised to the episcopate of Lyons; the date of his death is uncertain. One letter by him to St. Avitus survives, LXVII, 994.

VIVENTIUS, bishop. See CYPRIANUS.

VIVIANUS, brother of Fulcherius, gave to the monastery of St. Peter at Chartres the estate called Pomeraria and the estate of Levoz, in 988, CLV, 244.

VIVIANUS, Premonstratensian canon, a man highly versed in theological matters, appears to have been one of St. Norbert’s disciples, since he flourished shortly after the foundation of that congregation. His *Harmony*, or treatise on free will and grace, survives, 1130, CLXVI, 1322.

VIVIANUS OF CAIPHA and his son PAGANUS granted certain lands situated in Syria between Caipha and Palmarea to the chapter of canons of the Holy Sepulchre, in 1165, CLV, 1218.

VIVIANUS, master, advocate of the Roman Church, who had gone to the king of England in the cause of Lord Thomas of Canterbury. He sent two letters to the holy archbishop; likewise he wrote to Alexander II and to the king of England concerning the same matter, twelfth century, CXC, 690, 691.

VOLDARIUS, patriarch of Aquileia, decreed that the feast of Blessed Mary Magdalene should be celebrated with an office of nine lessons, and granted to the canons of that church, by right of ownership, a certain station for meeting the expenses of this feast, in 1180, XCIX, 645.

VOLMARUS, otherwise Volkemarus. Several monks of Clairvaux, companions and disciples of St. Bernard, composed an account [Col. 0540] of the miracles of that holy Father, 1150, CLXXXV, 385.

VOLUSIANUS, to whom Augustine wrote, is believed to have been the uncle of Melania the Younger and brother of Albina. He held the consulship in Africa with the tribune Marcellinus, through the efforts of his niece Melania and Proclus, bishop of Constantinople. According to Photius and Metaphrastes, he was baptized at the end of his life. In a letter he put certain questions to St. Augustine, 412, XXXI, 1233.

VULFADUS, bishop of Bourges, was appointed in place of Radulph in 866 by Emperor Charles the Bald, whose son Carloman he educated. He received the archbishop’s pallium from Pope Adrian II in 869 and died in 876. His pastoral letter to his parish priests and parishioners survives, CXXI, 1136.

VULGRINUS, sixty-second archbishop of Bourges. He was a noble, learned, prudent counselor, adorned with every grace of virtue. He consecrated Lord Suger, abbot of St. Denis, in the presence of King Louis. When Girard, bishop of Angoulême, a factional man, began to defend the party of the antipope Peter Leo, Vulgrinus wrote vigorously for Innocent II and by his letters brought all the bishops of Gaul over with him, 1130, CLXXX, 41.

VULSTANUS, Saint, bishop of Worcester, flourished in the eleventh century. He performed many miracles; St. Anselm, bishop of Canterbury, consulted him very frequently. The year of his death is uncertain, but he does not seem to have died before 1095. His letter to St. Anselm survives, CLIX, 202.

## W

WALAFRIDUS STRABUS, or Strabo, so called because of a defect of the eyes. Scholars dispute his birthplace: according to Sigebert of Gembloux, he was a Swabian. He had Rabanus Maurus as teacher; first monk and dean of St. Gall, then abbot of Reichenau in the diocese of Constance. He died in 849 while travelling through Gaul, whither he had been sent to settle a certain affair. His *Ordinary Gloss*, or commentaries on Scripture, historical works, and poems survive, CXIII–CXIV.

WALBERTUS, count of Ponthieu and Ternois, a man of exceptional uprightness. In accordance with St. Bertin’s prediction, his leg was broken, but through the saint’s intercession he recovered his health. He therefore gave the estate of Arques and many other lands to the monastery of St. Bertin in 668, CXXXVI, 1192.

WALBERTUS, abbot of Esrum, flourished about 1180. He drew up certain agreements with the brethren of St. Thomas of the Paraclete in 1178, CCIX, 752.

WALDEBERTUS, seller. See HARDRADUS.

WALDRAMNUS, bishop of Strasbourg, was made bishop in 888 and died in 905. He must be distinguished from Waldram, monk of St. Gall, who flourished at the same time. He wrote an elegiac poem to Bishop Solomon, to console him over the death of his brother, 905, CXXXII, 574.

WALERANNUS, or Gualerannus, count of Meulan. When a certain man named Wallerius, without his knowledge, married one of his female servants, he seized both as slaves; but at the prayers of Landric, abbot of St. Peter at Chartres, he manumitted them for the benefit of that monastery in 1071, CLV, 309.

WALPRANDUS, son of Duke Walpert, was himself duke and bishop of Lucca. About 739, under King Astulf, by testament he granted all the property he possessed to the churches of St. Martin, St. Fridianus, and St. Reparata, and to the hospice of Lucca, LXXXVII, 1405.

WALTERIUS, bishop of Orléans. Almost nothing is found concerning his life. He promulgated certain chapters in a synod which he held at the estate of Bouzy in the second year of his ordination, 867, CXIX, 725.

WALTERIUS, bishop of Sens, nephew of the preceding Walterius of Orléans, formerly canon of the cathedral church, distinguished by learning and noble endowments. He succeeded Evrard in the see of Sens and was consecrated in 887. After he had threatened Duke Richard of Burgundy, he was captured and imprisoned by him in 896. Returning to his church some months later, he thereafter governed it peacefully. His statutes survive, 923, CXXXII, 717.

WALTERIUS, count of Dreux, and Theotfridus gave to the monastery of St. Peter at Chartres a church consecrated under the title of St. George, in 965, CLV, 222.

WALTERIUS, count, gave the cell of Lédon-Cour to the monks of St. Peter at Chartres in 1055, during the abbacy of Landric, CLV, 328.

WALTERIUS PAGANUS, son of Teduinus, remitted certain customary dues for the benefit of the monastery of St. Peter at Chartres in 1070. Likewise, by another charter he manumitted certain serfs in 1061, CLV, 319.

A certain WALTERIUS, cleric of Montmirail, restored to the monastery [Col. 0541] of St. Peter at Chartres the half-share of burial dues, bread, and candles belonging to the church of Alloges, which he had usurped, in 1080, CLV, 326.

WALTERIUS, son of Flodaldus, with his wife and sister gave to the monastery of St. Peter at Chartres the allod of Puy-Villars, which he held from his father-in-law Bernard, together with two other allods, in 1080. Another charter concerning him survives, CLV, 346, 356.

WALTERIUS, bishop of Chalon, also called Gualterius, was elected in 1080. He applied all his strength to the foundation and expansion of the Cistercian Order. He died in 1120. His diplomas survive, CLX, 1166.

WALTERIUS, son of Walterius Pinetus, and his brother Henry gave Clairvaux all that they possessed near Petrecinium and within its territory, without a stated year, 1147, CLXXXV, 988.

WALTERIUS, chamberlain of Corvey, rendering an account to Wibald concerning buildings to be constructed, expresses the wish that he may return to Corvey as soon as possible, 1148, CLXXXIX, 1181.

WALTERIUS, abbot of St. Lawrence at Liège, thanks Lord Wibald, abbot of Corvey, for having undertaken his defense at the Synod of Liège, 1152, CLXXXIX, 1416.

WALTERIUS, archbishop of Rouen, granted to the chapter of Rouen the tithe of Dieppe and Bouteilles in 1198, CCVII, 1166, 1179.

WALTERUS, bishop of Albano and vicar of the lord pope, flourished in the twelfth century. In a letter to Gilbert, bishop of London, he reports that a certain subdeacon had come to him and requested absolution from the excommunication incurred on account of homicide; because of your letters of recommendation, he dismissed him absolved, CXC, 1017.

WANDALBERTUS, monk of Prüm, flourished in the ninth century, in 870. A German by birth, he embraced monastic life from earliest age; later advanced to the diaconate, he became head of the school of the monastery of Prüm and a celebrated writer. The date of his death is uncertain. We possess from him a *Martyrology*, a book *On the Names of the Twelve Months*, a poem on the creation of the world, and a Life of St. Goar, CXXI, 574.

WARINUS, abbot of the monastery of Metz. At one time he had dealings with John, abbot of Fécamp, in 1078, CXLVII, 465.

WARNAHARIUS, Saint, priest of Langres, whose birth and death are unknown, flourished around the beginning of the seventh century, in 615. Asked by St. Ceraunius, bishop of Paris, as a learned man, he wrote the Acts of the holy martyrs, the Tergeminian brothers, LXXX, 186.

WARNEFRIDUS, “the Magnificent,” castaldus of the city of Siena, made certain gifts to the church of St. Eugenius at Siena, which he himself had founded. A charter of that donation survives, but is badly mutilated; it is dated 1403. He lived in 731, LXXXVII, 1403.

WENRICUS, and his brother Albert, in accordance with their father’s vow, granted the church of Blessed Mary at Treconis to the monks of St. Peter of Chartres, in 1080, CLV, 339.

WERNER, bishop of Minden, Henry’s successor, wrote to the venerable Wibald, abbot of Corvey, in 1156. He died about 1160, CLXXXIX, 1439, 1444.

WERNER, abbot of St. Blasius in the Black Forest, of whom Felix Faber speaks in his *History of the Swabians*. Born at Ellerbach of noble stock, he became abbot and governed his monks with great devotion and mercy; he built a hermitage for holy virgins beside his monastery. He died in 1126. He wrote books of selections from the Holy Fathers, CLVII, 719.

WERNER, abbot of Kirchheim, flourished in the twelfth century. Saint Hildegard urgently asks him for prayers and wishes to possess his words committed to writing, CXCVII, 268.

WETBERT, priest and monk, who had come from Britain to Boniface in order to preach the faith to the still-pagan Saxons and Hessians. He wrote to his brethren, the monks of Glastonbury, that he had happily reached the end of his journey, in 747, LXXXIX, 773.

WETZEL, an irreligious man and promoter of sedition, urged Emperor Frederick, in 1152, to cast off the yoke of the Supreme Pontiff and receive the Empire only from the senate and people of Rome, CLXXXIX, 1421.

WIBALD, abbot of Stavelot and afterwards of Corvey. He was born at Liège in the Forest of Ardennes, of a most noble family. While still a boy he was entrusted to the abbot of Stavelot for instruction; thence he came to Liège to complete his course of studies. Already intending to embrace monastic life, he entered the household of Master Wazo, and advanced so far that he was soon placed over the school. Among the monks of Stavelot he became monk and abbot, and afterwards assumed the government of the monastery of Corvey. This man was a friend of Pope Lucius II and possessed great influence at the imperial court, so that he was deservedly called the Suger of his people. [Col. 0542] He died in 1158. Not a few letters by him survive, CLXXXIX, 1075.

WIBERT, archdeacon of Toul, wrote the life of Saint Pope Leo IX, formerly bishop of Toul and his contemporary. He lived in 1055, CXLIII, 457.

WIBOLD, bishop of Cambrai, formerly archdeacon of Noyon. He was equally versed in secular and ecclesiastical learning. He was elected bishop in 965. To turn clerics away from dice-playing, he devised a game with rules of its own, through which they might learn to overcome vices by virtues. He died in the very year of his ordination, CXXXIV, 1007.

WICARD, abbot of a monastery not far from the town of Bonn, gave thanks by letter for a gift of relics, in 840, CVI, 872.

WICBERT, abbot in England, sent a letter to Saint Lull, archbishop of Mainz, in 756, XCVI, 836.

WICBOD, or Wigbald, flourished about the end of the eighth century, in 790. He wrote a commentary on the first eight books of the Old Testament, in the form of a Dialogue. A pupil raises difficulties, which the Master resolves by his answers, XCVI, 1102.

WIDBERT, abbot of St. Peter of Chartres in 967, concluded an exchange of certain lands with one Ingelerius, CLV, 225.

WICMANN, archbishop of Magdeburg, attempted to settle a dispute between Wibald, abbot of Corvey, and the bishop of Osnabrück, in 1156, CLXXXIX, 1441, 1446.

WIDEGERN, bishop of Strasbourg. Biographers are silent about him. He is known to us only from a charter by which he confirms the foundation of the monastery of Murbach by Count Eberhard and endows it with privileges, in 728, LXXXVIII, 1280.

WIDERAD, abbot of Flavigny, made a will by which he bequeathed much both to the basilicas of Saints Andochius, Ferreolus, and Regina, and to the monastery of St. Praejectus at Flavigny, in 721, LXXXVIII, 1268.

WIDERIC, son of Oacrius, duke of Lorraine, married Bertha, aunt of Sigebert, king of Metz, and gave her a most wealthy dowry. But when he saw that he was deprived of heirs, he spent the greater part of his possessions in founding the monastery of Hasterii; there, with the bishop’s consent, after certain ill-conducted clerics had been expelled, he introduced nuns, in 626, LXXXVIII, 1159.

WIDO, monk of Horbach, wrote with another brother to Saint Lull, archbishop of Mainz, asking him to allow Macharius, a priest of the same monastery, to perform the office in a certain church of his diocese, in 774, XCVI, 847.

WIDO was elected king of Italy and crowned at Pavia, but was soon compelled to yield to Arnulf. He died in 894. There survive an account of his election and laws, CXXXVIII, 797.

WIDO, a monk of an unknown monastery, wrote to Heribert, archbishop of Cologne, whom Rupert, abbot of Deutz, states had been attacked by various calumnies, about 1000, CLI, 637.

WIDO, abbot of Cîteaux, set down the constitutions of the knights of Calatrava, which he sent to Nonnus, master of that order, and to Innocent III for confirmation, in 1198, CCXVII, 284.

WIDO, lord of Sauz, and his wife Elizabeth granted to the brethren of Alba Ripa a portion of a certain *vaura* [uncertain term, perhaps a tract of land], in 1203. Several other charters concerning him also survive. He died in 1209, LXXXV, 1433, 1437.

WIDRAD sold to Bishop Hildigrim all that he possessed in the district of Nivensis for six solidi; this was done at the place called “At the Cross,” in 818, XCIX, 814.

WIDRIC, abbot of St. Ghislain in Hainaut, succeeded Abbot Heribrand in 1056. His letter to Emperor Henry III survives, against Count Baldwin, who was grievously harassing the monastery of St. Ghislain, in 1065, CXLIII, 1371.

WIDRIC, lord of Danobrium, and his wife Gepa offer the cell of St. Christopher of Magno Vicus to Hugh, abbot of Cluny, and promise to give many other things, eleventh century, CLIX, 941.

WIDUKIND, monk of Corvey. A Saxon by birth, from youth he embraced monastic life in the monastery of Corvey. But for the sake of learning he went to Hirsau, and afterwards returned to Corvey, where he presided over the schools. He died about 983 and wrote three books on the deeds of the Saxons, CXXXVII, 115.

WIFRED, or Guifred, archbishop of Narbonne. Invited by Oliva, bishop of Vic, he came with the bishops of his province and a great company of clerics to dedicate the church founded by Oliva, and in the same year held and presided over a synod at Narbonne. A synodical letter of Oliva, bishop of Vic or Ausona, survives, 1038, CXLII, 603, 607.

WIGAND, abbot of the monastery of Tharise, about 1127. [Col. 0543] He wrote to Otto, bishop of Bamberg, urging him to return quickly from Pomerania, where he had begun to preach the Gospel, because of the wars and fires then raging around his monastery, which only Otto’s presence could extinguish, CLXXIII, 1342.

WIGO, dean of Phyuthwang, flourished in 980. Almost nothing survives concerning his biography. Thirteen letters by him remain, CXXXVII, 9.

WIGO, count of Vizille near Grenoble, informed Hugh, abbot of Cluny, that the lordship of Vizille had been granted to him and his successors, although certain persons had opposed it; for these he requests pardon, eleventh century, CLIX, 941.

WILFRID (Saint), bishop of York. He suffered many disturbances because of certain persons’ ambition; for a long time he was exiled from his own see; he went to Rome to entrust his cause to the pope. But after King Alfred, who had deposed him, had already died, he convened a council and was restored to his see. He died in peace in 705. A letter by him to Pope John VII survives, LXXXIX, 47.

WILLIAM, son of Count Bernard and archbishop of Auch, together with his brothers granted the church of St. Michael of Montaut to Hugh, abbot of Cluny, in 1069, CLIX, 961.

WILLIAM (Saint), abbot of Hirsau. Born of a noble Bavarian family and religious parents, while still a boy he was offered to the monastery of St. Emmeram. In 1068 he became abbot of Hirsau, where he flourished until his death in 1091. He possessed outstanding intellectual gifts and skill in various arts, as his writings show. His Hirsau Constitutions, a treatise on music, and other works survive, CL, 890.

WILLIAM, prior of Ursicamp, a distinguished Cistercian monastery founded in 1129, asked Richard, prior of St. Victor, for something from his shorter works to copy, in 1172, CXCVI, 1226.

WILLEBURGA sold an estate or land to Bishop Hildigrim in the district of Ruraegavia. This was done at the monastery of Werth under the rule of Charlemagne.

WILLIAM, called the Pious, count of Auvergne and duke of Aquitaine. Although he is not celebrated as the actual founder of the abbey of Cluny, he is deservedly regarded at least as its chief restorer, as is evident from all that he gave to this monastery in 910, CXXXIII, 843.

WILLIAM, lord of the honor of Alogia, son of Mahildis and husband of Eustachia, granted the church of St. Leobinus of Châteaudun, with certain lands, to the monastery of St. Peter of Chartres in 1080, CLV, 338.

WILLIAM of Sumbernone, devoted to military service, declares by charter that one of his faithful servants, having vowed to give himself wholly to God’s service, and seeing that unforeseen death would soon carry him away, asked to be buried in the monastery in which he had vowed to live, and likewise that the gift he had formerly promised should be received, in 1081, CLV, 352.

WILLIAM CALCULUS, monk of Jumièges, concerning whom few documents survive, flourished at the end of the eleventh century, in 1087. He was a Norman by birth and professed the Rule of Saint Benedict. He wrote eight books of the *History of the Normans*, CXLIX, 778.

WILLIAM I, duke of the Normans, called the Conqueror because he acquired England by arms, was the illegitimate son of Duke Robert and Herleva, daughter of a citizen of Falaise. He was crowned in England in 1066 and died in 1087 after many outstanding deeds. His laws, letters, and diplomas survive, CXLIX, 1218.

WILLIAM, monk of the monastery of Chiusa, concerning whom we have learned almost nothing, flourished at the end of the eleventh century, in 1097, and professed monastic life under the venerable Abbot Benedict II. He wrote both a history of Chiusa and a life of Abbot Benedict, CL, 1447.

WILLIAM, archdeacon of Poitiers and afterwards of Lisieux, flourished in the eleventh century, in 1098. He wrote the deeds of William the Conqueror, king of England, CL, 1593.

WILLIAM, count of Burgundy and Mâcon, confirmed in 1107 all the donations made by his predecessors to the monastery of Cluny, CLIX, 979.

WILLIAM of Buris granted two hamlets to the monastery of the Holy Sepulchre under King Fulk and Patriarch William, in 1132, CLV, 1172.

WILLIAM, bishop of Périgueux, granted to Pons, abbot of Cluny, the church of St. Theodore of Rocaboucort, with the consent of all the clergy of the see of Périgueux, in 1121, CLXVI, 851.

WILLIAM, monk of Malmesbury. A Norman by birth, he spent the greater part of his life in monasteries, devoting to letters and learning the time not spent on duties. The dates of his birth and death are uncertain. Five books of the *Deeds of the English*, five books on the deeds of the bishops of England, one book *On the Antiquity of the Church of Glastonbury*, [Col. 0544] and a life of Saint Wulfstan survive from him, 1143, CLXXIX, 936.

WILLIAM, dean of the church of Autun, wrote to Suger, asking him to ratify the election of Henry, brother of the duke of Burgundy and archdeacon, as abbot of Cîteaux, in 1147, CLXXXVI, 1371.

WILLIAM, made prior of the church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, issued certain constitutions for all the houses of his congregation; afterwards he became patriarch. He flourished about 1148, CLV, 1111 and passim.

WILLIAM, count of Nevers, whose father withdrew to the Charterhouse in 1147 and was there devoured by a dog. Returning himself from Jerusalem in 1149, when shipwreck threatened on the journey, he bound himself by several vows; he wrote to Suger and begged that he might see him at St. Denis and speak with him, CLXXXVI, 1382.

WILLIAM, monk of Saint-Denis under Suger’s government, so won Suger’s affection that he became his secretary. He had disputes with Odo, Suger’s successor, and therefore left the monastery and transferred to the priory of Saint-Denis. Letters and a life of Saint Dionysius by him survive; he died in 1152, CLXXXVI, 1468.

WILLIAM, bishop of Auxerre, lived in the twelfth century. He wrote to Pope Alexander III against Gilbert, bishop of London, on behalf of Thomas of Canterbury, about 1174, CC, 1406.

WILLIAM, bishop of Chartres, flourished in the twelfth century, in 1174. He wrote to Pope Alexander III on behalf of Thomas of Canterbury, CC, 1407.

WILLIAM, son of a certain Stephen, fellow citizen of Saint Thomas, a cleric and subdeacon in his chapel, lived at his table and conversed with him daily. After Thomas’s murder, William wrote his life, beginning with a description of the city of London in those times, 1175, CXC, 103.

WILLIAM, king of Sicily, forbade anyone in any manner to harass persons belonging to the church of the Holy Sepulchre, or to injure their rights and possessions scattered throughout the kingdom, in 1178, CLV, 1250.

WILLIAM of Thierno in Auvergne, and his wife Adelaide, gave certain lands situated in the territory of Limagne to Blessed Hugh, abbot of Cluny, at the beginning of the twelfth century. Another donation made by him to the same person survives, CLIX, 980.

WILLIAM and AUDEBERT granted one half of a *mansus* to the monks of Font-Gombaud, and decreed that it should later be given to the nuns of Fontevraud. This was done in the church of Blessed Peter at Poitiers, twelfth century, CLXII, 1111.

WILLIAM, abbot of the monastery of the Holy Trinity, London, flourished in the twelfth century. His letter to Pope Alexander III survives, CXC, 687.

WILLIAM, abbot of Reading, flourished in the twelfth century under Alexander III. We find nothing else concerning him except several letters sent to that pope and to Thomas of Canterbury, CXC, 688, 692.

WILLIAM, bishop of Norwich, flourished in the twelfth century. He sent to Lord Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury, two priests who, having come from the land of Count Hugh, under interdict, had presumed to celebrate in his presence; he had already absolved them and asked Thomas likewise to absolve them after they had sworn to observe their bishop’s interdict, CXC, 1021.

WILLIAM of Ramsey commends Gilbert, going to Rome, to Pope Alexander III in the cause of Thomas of Canterbury, twelfth century, CC, 1439, 1440.

WILLIAM, bishop of Sens, who flourished in the twelfth century under the pontificate of Alexander III, requested him by letter to confirm the sentence of excommunication pronounced by Thomas of Canterbury against the bishops of London and Salisbury, CC, 1425.

WILLIAM, bishop of the church of Acre, chosen as judge in a case between the canons of the Holy Sepulchre and the monks of the Latin monastery concerning the tithes of a certain estate, after considering everything acquitted the canons (without a year), CLV, 1231.

WILLIAM, subprior of Canterbury, wrote the life of Blessed Thomas, of which only a few fragments survive in the form of the *Quadrilogus*; yet these do not preserve the character of the genuine work. No record of him survives, CXC, 233.

A CERTAIN WILLIAM added a dedicatory letter to the work of William, archbishop of Reims, entitled *Microcosmographia*, CCIX, 869.

WILLIAM, cardinal of Pavia. See OTTO.

WILLIAM (Saint), abbot of St. Thomas of Paraclete in Denmark. Born of noble lineage, he was entrusted in 1104 to Hugh, abbot of St. Germain-des-Prés, for education; he surpassed almost all his fellow pupils in liberal studies. When he became a regular canon, he faithfully carried out the duties belonging to him. Having come to Denmark in 1161, he became abbot of Roskilde, then of St. Thomas of Canterbury. [Col. 0545] He died in 1202. Two books of letters and diplomas by him survive, CCIX, 589.

WILLIAM of Champagne, called “White Hands,” archbishop of Reims, fourth son of Count Theobald IV and Matilda of Carinthia. From youth he was enrolled among the clergy; then he became bishop of Chartres in 1176, whence he passed to the archbishopric of Sens and finally to the church of Reims. He died in 1202. Letters and diplomas by him survive, CCIX, 825.

WILLIBALD, disciple and biographer of Saint Boniface. Born in England, he devoted himself to learning in the monastery of Waltham; thence he set out for Palestine to visit the holy places, and on his return withdrew to Monte Cassino. Then, in 738, Pope Gregory III sent him to Saint Boniface, by whom he was ordained priest, and finally he became bishop of Eichstätt. His *Life of Saint Boniface* survives, LXXXIX, 536.

WILLIBRORD (Saint), bishop of Utrecht. A Briton by birth, he crossed into Lower Germany and, at the request of Pippin, king of the Franks, was made archbishop of Utrecht by Pope Sergius of Rome. He governed that church for forty years. He died in 739. His diplomas survive, LXXXIX, 537.

WILLHELM, count, bestowed great gifts upon the monastery of St. Emmeram in a place called Bernicha in 833 and 834, CXXIX, 932.

WINFRID. See BONIFACE (Saint), archbishop of Mainz.

WIPPO, priest born in Burgundy. He was chaplain or almoner to Emperor Henry III. Of his writings there survive a *Life of Emperor Conrad the Salian*, a panegyric to Henry III, poems, and proverbs, CXLII, 1214.

WITGER, priest of Compiègne, compiled the genealogy of Arnulf, count of Flanders, about 959; an autograph manuscript of it survives at Saint-Omer, CCIX, 927.

WLFAJUS, also Wlfagus, fellow pupil of Master Milo under Haimin, abbot of Saint-Amand. A few verses by him survive in confirmation of the poem on Milo’s life, 872, CXXI, 966.
