## SECOND SERIES OF INDICES, COMPRISING TWELVE GENERAL TABLES

[Col. 0657]

### [PREFACE]

This second series will consist of twelve general indices concerning the works and shorter writings of the *Latin Patrology*. Here all works will be presented in turn in alphabetical and chronological order, as well as synoptically and by analogy. Next we shall furnish all writings of the regular and secular clergy, together with those of lay authors, as well as anonymous, doubtful, apocryphal, or falsely attributed writings. Moreover, we shall provide two bibliographical indices, through which modern works on ecclesiastical writers—namely commentaries, notices, prefaces, and various editions—will be made known.

Finally, towering as a giant, there will stand the analytical general Index of SUBJECTS. By consulting it, one will see at a glance whatever not merely this or that Father, but each and every one of the Fathers without any exception, has written on any subject whatsoever. Thereafter, as the crown of this series, there will follow an index of CONCORDANCES between the two courses, Theology and Patrology. In it, the various subjects treated by theology will be presented in logical order and supported by the writings or more notable passages of the Fathers, with the volume and page of each course indicated. Thus a student or teacher, in composing any thesis whatever, will have at hand not only theological but also patristic authors—that is, the universal tradition of the Catholic Church—without expending any labour of his own, while enjoying that of another.

Perhaps here too the reader will be astonished that we have not added specialized indices for every class of works or authors. Yet let him not take this ill, for they will not therefore be lacking. To prevent this preface to the indices from being drawn out too long, we have decided not to place them here, but to reserve them for their respective subjects. Thus, for example, specialized indices concerning dogmatic works and authors will later be found under DOGMA; those concerning historical works and authors, under HISTORY; and so with the others. Having said this, farewell, kindly Reader, and now enjoy our not inconsiderable labours.

[Col. 0659]

## XV. CHRONOLOGICAL INDEX OF ALL WORKS AND VARIOUS WRITINGS REPRINTED IN THE NEW COURSE OF PATROLOGY, WHETHER GENUINE, DOUBTFUL, SPURIOUS, OR ANONYMOUS; WITH THE NAME, PERIOD, AND STATUS OF EACH AUTHOR ADDED; INCLUDING ALSO RECENT WRITINGS WHICH RELATE TO THE SAME WORKS OR AUTHORS. ARRANGED ACCORDING TO THE CHRONOLOGICAL ORDER OF THE VOLUMES

### Notice

The following index makes it possible quickly to perceive the order followed in this edition. For everywhere three divisions are usually treated in one and the same sequence. The first, which concerns the person of the author and the labours of bibliographers, consists chiefly of dedications, prefaces, prolegomena, various notices, and testimonies of contemporaries. The second relates specifically to the writings; and it should here be noted that these are always listed in upright Roman type, whereas observations, annotations, dissertations, and every other kind of note are always printed in italic type, so that confusion is impossible. The third part comprises appendices or supplements, and writings that are doubtful, wrongly ascribed to the author, or merely related to him; there the same rule concerning the distinction of typefaces is maintained. If any writings have for some reason been transferred from their proper place to another, we inform the reader to which volume and column he should refer.

[Col. 0929]

XVI. SYNTHETIC INDEX, OR A UNIVERSAL BUT SYNOPTIC SURVEY OF THE SUBJECTS ELUCIDATED BY THE LATIN FATHERS ACCORDING TO THE SEQUENCE AND ORDER OF THE VARIOUS SCIENCES, AND CONTAINED IN THE COURSE OF PATROLOGY.

NOTICE.

Dear reader, while we have been composing this table—which could be produced only through the most difficult labor and the most minute attention—we wish you to know that, amid investigations so weighty and immense, three considerations guided and sustained us.

First, this synthesis will demonstrate most conclusively that, from its beginning and in every age, the Christian religion cultivated every branch of knowledge for the formation of peoples; and, like a mother, nourished them in its bosom, fostering and propagating each one and raising it to the summit of perfection.

By this indisputable proof, the pseudo-philosophers, the impious, and all the adversaries of the Catholic Church—who have often, with senile foolishness, disparaged and ridiculed it as hostile and baneful to light and to every science—are utterly refuted. Let them behold this golden chain of teachers of religion, without parallel, and acknowledge that the holy Church of Christ brings a full day before the eyes of the peoples and shines among the darkened minds of human beings like an everlasting torch.

The second reason moving us is this. The innumerable Fathers whom the Catholic religion venerates as masters and teachers brought glory to their people and their age. They surpassed other writers as well in loftiness of intellect as in holiness; and amid the most wretched storms of the nations, when entire regions, overgrown with the darkness of ignorance, seemed submerged as under night, did not the Fathers of the Church, by preserving with every effort the deposit of knowledge, rescue it from shipwreck? We owe them fitting and everlasting gratitude.

Through the supreme completeness of their learning and the wondrous, exalted wisdom of their intellect, they attained the praise of the whole world. Far from regarding them as men of lesser merit, we must unequivocally and loudly proclaim that the holy Fathers are prudent and excellent guides, whom it will be most glorious to follow in conduct and study.

Finally, as we hope with God’s help, this synopsis will firmly show that the doctors of the Church are to be considered not only guardians of the faith, but that their works are also most useful and excellent in every kind of learning; these works ought to be studied, together with the holy Scriptures, with hand turning them by night and day, as eminent and divine models of every good.

Therefore the religion which has such patrons, defenders, and teachers can display their writings as [Col. 0931] a manifest and unquestionable proof of its divinity. Hence there flow back to it immortal honor, the highest distinction, and that most sweet glory which, above all others, is to be desired during this brief course of life.

Let us also say with the poet: (*Hymn of the Holy Doctors*)

> Religion, now raise your starry head,  
> for you count so many defenders.  
> As many noble laurels you entwine for yourself  
> as battles have been stirred against you.

SYNTHESIS OF THE SCIENCES DRAWN FROM THE WORKS OF THE HOLY FATHERS.

[Col. 0931]

In this *Course of Patrology*, the works of all the Doctors of the Church may be reduced to the following headings:

I. Exegesis. II. Didactic writings. III. Canonical writings. IV. Liturgical writings. V. Synodal writings. VI. Pastoral writings. VII. Ascetical or mystical writings. VIII. Paraenetic writings. IX. Apologetic writings. X. Polemical writings. XI. Philosophical writings. XII. Critical writings. XIII. Historical writings. XIV. Literary writings. XV. Poetry. XVI. Pedagogy, or didascalia. XVII. Philology. XVIII. Grammar. XIX. Artistic writings. XX. Biography. XXI. Hagiography. XXII. Social writings. XXIII. Scientific writings.

These, moreover, are divided into various further sections, so that it may be evident that the holy Fathers treated every science insofar as the human mind can understand and express it.

FIRST SECTION.—EXEGESIS.

[Col. 0932]

(The Roman numerals indicate the volume of the *Patrology*; the Arabic numerals, the column.)

[Col. 0931] [Since the books of sacred Scripture make known to us both the Word and the adorable will of God, it is easy to understand that the teachers of the Faith devoted themselves steadily and with every effort to reading and explaining the holy Bible.

Throughout these twelve centuries, almost all the Fathers expounded something upon some part of the sacred text, or upon the whole of Scripture, as may be seen.]

Under the designation of exegesis are to be understood all works whatsoever composed by the Fathers upon the divine text: interpretations, polyglot editions, hermeneutics, history, controversy, criticism, philology, and moral expositions of every kind.

From this immense and most lucid fountain of learning have drawn all writers, preachers, and exegetes who lived in subsequent centuries, including our own age. Ought we not to express our admiration for labours so great, and at the same time repay these distinguished doctors with love and gratitude?

## SECTION II.—DIDACTIC WORKS

[Col. 0937]

### I.—DOGMATIC THEOLOGY

[Theology, as is evident to everyone, is discourse concerning God, or the knowledge of God and of divine things. In the order of the sciences it occupies first place, because all the loftiest and most salutary doctrines evidently flow from it, for the welfare and happiness of society and of every individual person. What it teaches has been drawn from the books of the Holy Fathers and confirmed by their authority.]

## II.—MORAL THEOLOGY

[If the matters proclaimed by dogmatic theology announce the loftiness of God’s mysteries and the true light of understanding, it follows that moral doctrine, which proceeds from them as from a most pure and divine fountain, must necessarily be most perfect, or most holy; and in fact there has been no moral teaching in the whole world like Christian morality, or even one that can be compared with it to the slightest degree.]

## SECTION III.—CANON LAW

[Col. 0947]

[Col. 0947] [From this synopsis of the doctors, let it be known how great was their knowledge of the divine Scriptures, as also their subtlety of intellect and their discipline of virtues for the correction of morals. Therefore their books are not to be treated with contempt, but rather to be consulted continually, since from them we may learn what we ought to do and what it is advantageous for us to avoid. We must now pass to the works of the Holy Fathers concerning canon law. For indeed, by their writings and decrees they have endeavoured to confirm and establish immovably all matters pertaining to sound doctrine and the form of justice.]

> [Note: [Col. 0955] NOTE. Canon law, as is clear from this series, is divided into two parts: the general, which establishes laws for the good of society, kings, peoples, and the whole world; and the particular, in which are found decrees, privileges, statutes, and rules issued by ecclesiastical authority for each individual church, monastery, or even person. With what vigilance the supreme pontiffs, bishops, and abbots preserved the rights of all, and, as need required, endeavoured that laws and statutes should be faithfully observed by everyone—especially in those most wretched times, when almost all peoples, recently recalled from barbarism and errors, were rushing headlong into every vice, and the will of kings or powerful persons was very often regarded as law! For this reason councils and synods were also celebrated more frequently by prelates and Roman pontiffs. See the following chapter.]

## SECTION V.—LITURGICAL WORKS

[Col. 0957]

[Certainly we must regard with equal admiration all the writings of all the doctors which discuss, so clearly and wisely, the rites and the meanings of the sacraments or offices of the Christian religion. Hence we may say with the prophet: “There is no other nation so great as to possess worship so holy and perfect.” Accordingly, Frederick the Great, king of Prussia, is said to have exclaimed that Catholics alone possess and worship God as God.]

## SECTION VII.—ASCETICAL WORKS

[Col. 0961]

[Col. 0961] [If, pious reader, you wish to peruse attentively the books of the Holy Doctors worthy of attention, you will find not only every refined and divine moral precept, but also all the means and exhortatory discussions capable of leading you to the highest and truly angelic perfection. The works of the Holy Fathers that form us for the heavenly life are almost innumerable, and nowhere has human philosophy been able to weave together such teaching.]

## SECTION VIII.—PARAENETIC WORKS

[Col. 0969]

[Col. 0969] [The doctors of the Catholic Church have striven to spread the Gospel of God not only by outstanding and manifold writings, but also through the frequency and authority of their sermons. Although the Latin Fathers have not attained, as have the Greek Fathers, the most glorious palm of eloquence, no one can doubt that they nevertheless handed down rules, precepts, and examples of true eloquence. They should therefore be consulted as faithful stewards of the word and mysteries of Christ.]

[Col. 0973] Although all the doctors of the Church have laid down unshaken foundations of belief in their preaching of the dogmas of faith, they nevertheless also produced arguments and books for the defence of the Gospel and the truth of Christian doctrine, in which the certainty of the doctrines of faith is made especially clear and established against every adversary of religion. And, to complete this parenetic synopsis, see the very useful special index of all the sermons of the holy Fathers of the Western Church.

## SECTION XI.—PHILOSOPHICAL WORKS

[Col. 0977]

[Col. 0977] [In the writings of the doctors of the Catholic Church there is to be found a sound and lofty philosophy, not only with respect to metaphysical and moral reflections, but also according to the principles and elements of this science. Their minds, freed from errors and prejudices and enlightened by the true light, could not but discuss the various branches of philosophy lucidly and wisely. If the philosophical books of the holy Fathers were more frequently handled by the hands of schoolmen or students, peoples would be delivered from many grievous sophistries, principles, and errors.]

## SECTION XIII.—HISTORICAL WORKS

[Col. 0979]

[Col. 0979] [Ecclesiastical writings relating to history exhibit every kind of narrative. Although they are not composed in a polished and more elegant style, nor can they attain Titus Livy, Sallust, or Tacitus in diction, they are nevertheless worthy to attract readers especially through the frankness and sincerity of their statements, as also through the supreme importance of their subjects.]

## SECTION XIV.—LITERARY WORKS

[Col. 0987]

[Col. 0987] [The holy Fathers showed themselves not only admirable preachers of the Gospel and defenders of religion, but were also the foremost ornaments of every age through every endowment of genius and variety of writings. They cultivated literature, just as they cultivated every branch of theology; consequently, those teachers excelled not only in prose but also in verse. They also transmitted to us the precepts and rules of metrical rhythm, as well as those of the most distinguished literature. It must therefore be said that, throughout this course of time, the Catholic Church was, as it was of truth and divine teaching, so also the best—and at times the only—teacher or source of the liberal arts, sciences, and poetic inspiration.]

## SECTION XIX.—BIOGRAPHICAL WORKS

[Col. 0995] [The doctors of the Church labored to set forth examples of great men, and especially of saints. This was their chief labor; this the goal of their preaching, whether in speech or in writing. Their every thought and sweetest hope lay in this: that Christian peoples might shape themselves by imitation of their most excellent forebears, embrace virtue, and thus, following in equal steps the footprints of the saints, attain heavenly blessedness after many good works. Therefore they wrote the lives of memorable persons, and above all the biographical and hagiographical lives of saints, which are treated here and in Section 20.]

## SECTION XXI.—SOCIAL WORKS

[Col. 1001] [Everything concerning the good of society and the happiness of peoples that has been promulgated and most wisely ordered by the holy doctors is found in dogmatic, moral, ascetic, and canon-law writings. ## SECTION XXII.—WORKS ON THE NATURAL SCIENCES

[Col. 1003]

[Col. 1003] [The following headings will furnish a new and irresistible argument for the universal learning of the holy doctors. In relation to the period in which they flourished, and to the extent of their capacities, they spoke of the natural sciences. It must therefore be concluded that the *Patrology* offers all Christians not only what appears necessary for a perfect knowledge of religion and for the conduct of life, but also whatever can enrich and instruct minds concerning human learning.]

From it, we hope, together with reverence for and admiration of the writings of the Latin Fathers, you will also derive the habit of repeatedly consulting the books of the *Patrology* and of ordering your life in accordance with their salutary and divine teachings. See the special index of the sciences treated throughout the whole *Patrology*.

[Col. 1009]

With regard to matters concerning biblical and exegetical writings, we have omitted them here, lest their being repeated twice prove tiresome. The reader should therefore consult the special indices on the Scriptures: there he will find whatever the Fathers have said about the inspiration, authority, excellence, and so forth of the divine Scriptures; all commentaries on the books, chapters, and even on every individual verse; and also the allegories, figures, and parables of the Old and New Testament.

[Col. 1125]

# XXI. GENERAL INDEX OF ALL ANONYMOUS, DOUBTFUL, APOCRYPHAL, OR SPURIOUS WORKS OR SHORTER TREATISES PRINTED IN THE COURSE OF THE PATROLOGY, ARRANGED CHRONOLOGICALLY BY VOLUMES

## NOTICE

Seeking at once the reader’s benefit and pleasure, we have listed in this index all anonymous or wrongly attributed works and shorter treatises, as the title indicates, following the order of the volumes, lest confusion should otherwise arise. Nor have we omitted any lost writings mentioned in the *Patrology*, so that, with the aid of this Index, the reader will be able at once and at a single glance to see and readily consult whatever doubtful or spurious material each volume contains; for we have assigned the column for each item.

[INDEX OF DOUBTFUL WORKS.]

### In Volume II

Five Books against Marcion, wrongly ascribed to Tertullian, 1051.—The First Book treats of the One God, 1053.—The Second, of the Harmony of the Old and New Testaments, 1062.—The Third, of the Harmony of the Fathers of the Old and New Testaments, 1070.—The Fourth, of Marcion’s Antitheses, 1078.—The Fifth, of Various Heresies of Marcion, 1083.

Book on the Judgment of the Lord, by an uncertain author, 1090.—Poem on Genesis, 1098.—On Sodom, 1102.—To a Senator Who Has Turned from the Christian Religion to the Service of Idols, 1106.—On Jonah and Nineveh, with notes by François Juret, 1107.—On the Tree of Life, 1114. All these poems falsely bear Tertullian’s name.

Fragment on the Gods of the Nations to Be Execrated, 1115.—Fragments of Greek Works, with notes by J. Pamelius, 1118.

Fragments, notices, and notes concerning Tertullian’s missing works, namely: I. Books on the Difficulties of Marriage, 1122.—II. Books on Fate, 1123.—III. Questions concerning Clean and Unclean Animals, ibid.—IV. Questions concerning Circumcision, ibid.—V. Books on Aaron’s Garments, ibid.—VI. Books on the Trinity, 1126.—VII. Books against Hermogenes, 1126.—VIII. Books against the Apelleians, 1127.—IX. Books on Paradise, ibid.—X. Books on the Hope of the Faithful, 1130.—XI. Six Books on Ecstasy, 1131.—XII. Books against Apollonius, 1134.—XIII. Several Other Works, ibid.—Fragment: In What Respect Tertullian the Montanist Differed from the Psychics, 1135.

Two books wholly lost: namely, the Book on Baptism, 1138, and the Book on Penance, 1210.—But there are here notes by the Reverend Father Dom Corbinian Thomas, Benedictine monk of the Congregation of the Holy Spirit in Bavaria, at 1138 and 1210.

### In Volume III

Headless fragment on the canon of the Holy Scriptures, by an uncertain writer, 174.—Chronicle composed under Alexander Severus, by an anonymous author, 651.—Notice of letters concerning Pope Cornelius which do not survive, or are now lost, 689.—Two letters ascribed to Pope St. Cornelius, 838.—Two decretal letters and a decree ascribed to the same Cornelius, 842.—Letters and decrees ascribed to Pope St. Lucius, 975.—Notice of letters concerning Pope St. Stephen I which do not survive, 985.—Decretal letters ascribed to the same St. Stephen, 998.

[Col. 1126] Book on Rebaptism, by an anonymous author, 1183.—Treatise against the heretic Novatian, maintaining that hope of pardon must not be denied to the lapsed, by an anonymous author, 1206.

### In Volume IV

Book on Discipline and the Good of Chastity, by an unknown author, perhaps St. Cyprian, though this is doubtful, 819.—Among the shorter works falsely attributed to the same Lord Cyprian are numbered: I. Book on Gamblers, wrongly ascribed to Cyprian, 827.—II. Treatise on the Singularity of Clerics, falsely ascribed, according to some, not only to St. Cyprian but also to Augustine and Origen, 835.—III. Treatise on the Twelve Abuses of the World, wrongly assigned both to Cyprian and to Augustine, 869.—IV. Book on the Twofold Martyrdom, addressed to Fortunatus, by an uncertain author, 882.—V. Prayer of Cyprian of Antioch for the Martyrs, 905.—VI. Prayer of Cyprian of Antioch, which he uttered on the day of his passion, 906.—VII. Treatise on Mounts Sinai and Zion, against the Jews, by an unknown author, 910.—VIII. Treatise against the Jews Who Persecuted Our Lord Jesus Christ, by an uncertain author, 919.—IX. *The Supper*, falsely inscribed to Cyprian, 926.—X. Treatise on the Discovery of the Head of Blessed John the Baptist, by an uncertain author, 931.—XI. Calculation of Easter, by Caecilius Cyprian, 939.—XII. Poem on the Resurrection of the Dead, 1026.—XIII. Exhortation of St. Cyprian on Penance, 1154.

Gunther, Cistercian monk (c. 1212), *Book on Prayer, Fasting, and Almsgiving*, ed. Basel, 1507, Gothic type.

“An exceedingly beautiful work on the three customary acts of Christians—namely prayer, fasting, and almsgiving—containing thirteen books by the venerable Father Gunther, of the order of the blessed Benedict, for the making of public sermons and conferences; not so much most elegant and most classical in Latin as most useful; long hidden, but recently discovered and printed.”

And at the end of the work:

“The little work on the three acts of Christians—namely prayer, fasting, and almsgiving—comes to an end. Printed at Basel by Michael Furter, in the year 1507, on the fifteenth day of March.”

The same volume contains Rabanus, *On the Instruction of Clerics*, etc. At the beginning of the work these verses are read:

> Cleric, would you serve the highest Thunderer in holy orders,  
> Yet do not know the duty and office of the clergy?  
>
> “I should like to learn it thoroughly, if only the means were granted me.  
> Tell me: by what source may I know it, or from where should I seek it?”  
>
> Receive the names which no cleric has ever neglected  
> Who desires to bear names corresponding to realities.  
>
> Farewell.

At the end:

“Thomas Anshelmi of Baden printed this at Pforzheim, in copperplate type and with most careful workmanship, in the month of August, on the fifth day before the Kalends of September [28 August], in the year 1505, under the illustrious prince Christopher the Elder, Margrave of Baden.”

## XXIV. GENERAL ANALYTICAL INDEX OF MATTERS FOUND IN THE COURSE OF LATIN PATROLOGY, ARRANGED ALPHABETICALLY.

This analytical index, which towers above the others like a giant, is mentioned here only because we do not yet have it completed and because, on account of the breadth of its subjects and the importance of its matters, we have decided to publish it separately; for it extends through a large part of the fifth volume. The reader should therefore not begrudge the delay, for it will soon see the light.

[Col. 1185]

## XXV. PATRISTIC-THEOLOGICAL INDEX, OR CONCORDANCE BETWEEN THE TWO COMPLETE COURSES OF THEOLOGY AND PATROLOGY PUBLISHED BY J. P. MIGNE, COMPILED IN THE LOGICAL ORDER OF SUBJECTS.

### NOTICE.

In this Index we have set forth, in logical order, the principal subjects of theology, supported by the more notable writings or passages of the Fathers, indicating the volume and page of each Course. Thus the student or teacher, for composing any thesis whatever, will immediately have at hand, with no effort, so to speak, not only theological but also patristic authorities—that is, the universal tradition of the Catholic Church. Moreover, providing at once for the usefulness and convenience of readers, we have prefixed a sequence of chapters and, in every article, have preserved the chronological order of the Fathers.

# THIRD SERIES

[Col. 1275]

## [PREFACE]

This third series comprises only three indexes, which we have decided to append here as a complement to the preface to the Tables; that preface, namely, will consist of this threefold series. By these three indexes will be made known both the pagan and the Christian poets whose writings the Fathers adduced in their works, and also writers alien to the faith, from whom they borrowed arguments in order to strengthen their own doctrine.

[Col. 1275]
